Summary
O
n March 30, 2026,
Act 126
was signed into law.
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10
,
8.15
,
8.20
,
8.40
, and
9.10
were amended to require a circulator of nomination papers, except Presidential nomination papers, and recall petitions to be a “qualified elector of this state.”
The key change was that in the past, circulators could be residents of other states who
would
have been eligible to vote in Wisconsin if they lived in the state.
Under the new law, circulators must be residents of Wisconsin for voting purposes
.
The new law requires that all petition circulators be a “qualified elector.” A qualified elector of Wisconsin is someone who:
Is a U.S. citizen
Is at least 18 years old
Has resided at their residential address in Wisconsin for at least 28 consecutive days with no present intent to move
Is not currently serving a felony conviction, including incarceration, parole, probation, or extended supervision
Has not been adjudicated incompetent with a finding that they do not understand the voting process
Has not made a bet or wager on the result of the election
Individuals who are not Wisconsin residents, or individuals who reside in Wisconsin but are disqualified from voting,
cannot
serve as a circulator.
On April 6, 2026, the Wisconsin Elections Commission held a public meeting to approve this memo and updated nomination paper templates.
These templates can be found at
https://elections.wi.gov/forms
.
Candidates and petitioners will need to follow the new law immediately.
Any person who is circulating nomination papers for the 2026 Fall Election cycle must reside in Wisconsin and must be qualified to vote in Wisconsin.
Background
On March 30, 2026, Wisconsin 2026 Act 126 required that all circulators must reside in Wisconsin and must be qualified to vote in Wisconsin. The law applies to circulators of nomination papers and recall petitions. While circulators are not required to be registered to vote, they must be
qualified
to vote. Therefore, if an individual is under 18, not a U.S. citizen, not a Wisconsin resident, serving any portion of a felony sentence, or is otherwise disqualified from voting in Wisconsin, they may
not
serve as a circulator.
Note: Circulators for presidential nomination papers and referenda petitions may still be adult U.S. citizens who are not Wisconsin residents but who would be qualified to vote under Wisconsin law.
For Clerks
The WEC encourages county clerks, municipal, or school district clerks who are filing officers for the Fall General Election, to contact candidates and parties in their area to inform them of the law change ahead of the April 15 circulation period.
Effective immediately, all circulators must follow the new law
. The first day potential candidates for the 2026 Fall General Election may start circulating nomination papers is April 15, 2026. Most candidates on the 2026 General Election ballot file their nomination papers with the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC). The WEC will be sending a communication to the major political parties and candidates to ensure that they know that the law has changed.
During the WEC staff’s facial review of nomination papers, we do not check that each circulator is qualified to vote in Wisconsin. Also, we will not strike signatures if a candidate uses the old nomination paper template, but the signatures must be valid, which means that the circulator must provide information showing that the circulator signature is facially valid by providing a Wisconsin residence address. If a circulator provides an address outside of Wisconsin, all signatures on the page will be struck.
Candidates and recall petitioners could face challenges to their signatures and petitions if they use the old template or use circulators who are not qualified electors. The Commission cannot pre-judge challenges and will make determinations on the outcome of any such challenges at its June 9, 2026 ballot access meeting.
The updated candidate nomination paper templates are now available at
https://elections.wi.gov/forms
.
Questions?
Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at
elections@wi.gov
or 608-261-2028.

__________________________________________________________________________________________ ___________ 
Wisconsin Elections Commissioners 
Ann S. Jacobs, chair | Marge Bostelmann | Don M. Millis | Carrie Riepl | Robert Spindell | Mark L. Thomsen 
Administrator 
Meagan Wolfe 
       Wisconsin Elections Commission 
212 East Washington Avenue | Third Floor | P.O. Box 7984 | Madison, WI  53707-7984 
(608) 266-8005 | elections@wi.gov | elections.wi.gov 
 
DATE: April 8, 2026 
 
TO: Wisconsin Candidates and Political Parties 
 
FROM: Wisconsin Elections Commission  
 
SUBJECT: 2025 Act 126- Qualifications of Nomination Paper and Petition Circulators 
 
Summary  
On March 30, 2026, Act 126 was signed into law. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10, 8.15,  8.20, 8.40, and 9.10 
were amended to require a circulator of nomination papers and recall petitions to be a “qualiﬁed 
elector of this state. ”  The key change was that in the past, circulators could be residents of other 
states who would have been eligible to vote in Wisconsin if they lived in the state.  Under the new 
law, circulators must be residents of Wisconsin for voting purposes.  Note: Circulators for 
presidential nomination papers and referenda petitions may still be adult U.S. citizens who are not 
Wisconsin residents but who would be otherwise qualiﬁed to vote under Wisconsin law. 
The new law requires that all petition circulators be a “qualiﬁed elector. ” A qualiﬁed elector of 
Wisconsin is someone who: 
• Is a U.S. citizen 
• Is at least 18 years old 
• Has resided at their residential address in Wisconsin for at least 28 consecutive days 
with no present intent to move 
• Is not currently serving a felony conviction, including incarceration, parole, probation, 
or extended supervision 
• Has not been adjudicated to be incompetent with a ﬁnding that they do not understand 
the voting process 
• Has not made a bet or wager on the result of the election 
 
This means individuals who are not Wisconsin residents, or individuals who reside in Wisconsin 
but are disqualiﬁed from voting, cannot serve as a circulator. Speciﬁcally, circulators must have 
lived at their Wisconsin residential address for at least 28 days.  
2025 Act 126- Qualiﬁcations of Nomination Paper and Petition Circulators 
4/8/2026 
Page 2 
 
 
On April 6, 2026, the Wisconsin Elections Commission held a public meeting to approve this 
memo and updated nomination paper templates to reﬂect this change in the law. The forms can 
be found on the WEC’s website at https://elections.wi.gov/forms.  
 
Candidates and petitioners must follow the new law immediately. Any person who is circulating 
nomination papers for the 2026 Fall Election cycle must reside in Wisconsin and must be 
qualiﬁed to vote in Wisconsin.    
Legal Analysis  
On March 30, 2026, Wisconsin 2026 Act 126 required that all circulators reside in Wisconsin 
and must be qualiﬁed to vote in Wisconsin. The law includes circulators of nomination papers, 
and recall petitions.  
Circulators for presidential nomination papers and referendum petitions do not need to be 
Wisconsin residents. However, they must be U.S. citizens, at least 18 years old, and otherwise 
eligible to vote under Wisconsin law. 
While circulators are not required to be registered to vote, they must be qualiﬁed to vote. 
Therefore, if an individual is under 18, not a U.S. citizen, serving any portion of a felony sentence, 
or is otherwise disqualiﬁed from voting in Wisconsin, they may not serve as a circulator.   
Qualiﬁed Wisconsin electors can serve as circulators. Wis. Stat. 6.02 deﬁnes a qualiﬁed 
Wisconsin Elector:  
(1) Every U.S. citizen age 18 or older who has resided in an election district or ward 
for 28 consecutive days before any election where the citizen offers to vote is an 
eligible elector. 
(2) Any U.S. citizen age 18 or older who moves within this state later than 28 days 
before an election shall vote at his or her previous ward or election district if the 
person is otherwise qualiﬁed. If the elector can comply with the 28-day residence 
requirement at the new address and is otherwise qualiﬁed, he or she may vote in the 
new ward or election district. 
Disqualiﬁed Wisconsin electors cannot serve as circulators. Wis. Stat. 6.03 deﬁnes a 
disqualiﬁed Wisconsin Elector:  
(1) The following persons shall not be allowed to vote in any election and any 
attempt to vote shall be rejected: 
(a) Any person who is incapable of understanding the objective of the elective 
process or who is under guardianship, unless the court has determined that the 
person is competent to exercise the right to vote. 
2025 Act 126- Qualiﬁcations of Nomination Paper and Petition Circulators 
4/8/2026 
Page 3 
 
 
(b) Any person convicted of treason, felony or bribery, unless the person’s right to 
vote is restored through a pardon or under s. 304.078 (3). 
 
(2) No person shall be allowed to vote in any election in which the person has made 
or become interested, directly or indirectly, in any bet or wager depending upon the 
result of the election. 
 
(3) No person may be denied the right to register to vote or the right to vote by 
reason that the person is alleged to be incapable of understanding the objective of 
the elective process unless the person has been adjudicated incompetent in this 
state. If a determination of incompetency of the person has already been made, or if 
a determination of limited incompetency has been made that does not include a 
speciﬁc ﬁnding that the subject is competent to exercise the right to vote, and a 
guardian has been appointed as a result of any such determination, then no 
determination of incapacity of understanding the objective of the elective process is 
required unless the guardianship is terminated or modiﬁed under s. 54.64. 
Action Items for Candidates and Circulators  
Effective immediately, all circulators must follow the new law.  
The ﬁrst day potential candidates for the 2026 Fall Primary and General Election may start 
circulating nomination papers is April 15, 2026.  Candidates are responsible for ensuring all their 
circulators comply with the new law.       
Use the new nomination paper template. 
The WEC has approved new nomination paper templates. The new templates include updated 
“Certiﬁcation of Circulator” language. The new language clearly states that the circulator is a 
qualiﬁed elector of the State of Wisconsin. Please use the new templates when preparing your 
nomination papers for the 2026 Fall Primary and General Election. If you have already submitted 
your nomination papers to the WEC or your local ﬁling officer for review, we encourage you to 
modify your templates to include the new “Certiﬁcation of Circulator” language.   
Challenges to the old template . 
During the WEC staff’s facial review of nomination papers, staff will not check that each circulator 
is a qualiﬁed elector. The WEC staff will also not strike signatures if a candidate uses the old 
nomination paper template. However, the signatures must be valid, which means that the 
circulator must provide information showing that the circulator has a Wisconsin residential 
address. If a circulator provides an address outside of Wisconsin, all signatures on the page will 
be struck.  
2025 Act 126- Qualiﬁcations of Nomination Paper and Petition Circulators 
4/8/2026 
Page 4 
 
 
Candidates and recall petitioners could face challenges to their signatures and petitions if they 
use the old template or use circulators who are not qualiﬁed electors. The Commission cannot 
pre-judge challenges and will make determinations on the outcome of any such challenges at its 
June 9, 2026 ballot access meeting.   
 
4. Communication with Candidates. 
 
This communication is being sent to political parties who have ballot access status. Most 
candidates on the 2026 Fall Primary and General Election ballot ﬁle their nomination papers with 
the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC).  However, WEC encourages county, municipal, and 
school district clerks, who are ﬁling officers for the 2026 Fall Primary and General Election, to 
contact candidates and parties in their area to inform them of the law change ahead of the April 15 
circulation period.   
 
5. Questions? 
Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at elections@wi.gov or 608-261-2028.

INSTRUCTIONS FOR PREPARING NOMINATION PAPERS FOR PARTISAN OFFICE 
This is a sample nomination paper form.  It conforms to the statutory requirements for nomination papers for partisan office. All information concerning the candidate must be completed in full before 
circulating this form to obtain signatures of electors. All information concerning the signing electors and the circulator must be completed in full before filing with the appropriate filing officer.  This form 
may be reproduced in any way. A candidate's picture and campaign information may also be added to this form.  The Wisconsin Elections Commission has determined that no disclaimer or other attribution 
statement is required on nomination papers.  Candidates are advised to send a sample of their completed form to the filing officer for review before circulation. Federal and state candidates file with the 
Wisconsin Elections Commission. County candidates file with the County Clerk. 
Page Numbers – Number each page consecutively, beginning with “1”, before submitting to the filing officer.  A space for page numbers has been provided in the lower right-hand corner of the form. 
Candidate's Name - Insert the candidate's name.  A candidate may use his or her full legal name, or any combination of first name, middle name, and initials or nickname with last name.  The 
Wisconsin Elections Commission has determined that, absent any evidence of an attempt to manipulate the electoral process, candidates are permitted to choose any form of their name, including 
nicknames, by which they want to appear on the ballot. 
No titles are permitted.  In addition, names such as “Red” or “Skip” are permitted, but names that have an apparent electoral purpose or benefit, such as “Lower taxes,” “None of the above” or “Lower 
Spending” are not permitted.  It is also not permissible to add nicknames in quotes or parentheses between first and last names. For example, J ohn “Jack” Jones or John (Jack) Jones are not acceptable, 
but John Jones, Jack Jones or John Jack Jones are acceptable. 
Candidate's Residence – Insert the candidate’s residential address (no P.O. Box addresses) and the municipality for voting purposes.  Indicate if the municipality of residence is a town, village or city. 
If a candidate’s mailing address is different from the residential address or voting municipality, a complete mailing address must also be given. 
Date of Election - Insert the date of the election.  If the nomination paper is being circulated for a general election, the date is the Tuesday after the first Monday in November of an even-numbered 
year.  If the election is a special partisan election, the date of the special election must be listed. 
Party or Statement of Principle – Insert the name of the party the candidate represents.  Independent candidates may provide a Statement of Principle, not to exceed 5 words. 
Title of Office - The name of the office must be listed along with the jurisdiction or district number that clearly identifies the office the candidate is seeking, for example, Representative to the 
Assembly – 1st district or Dane County District Attorney. 
Name of Jurisdiction - The nomination papers must also indicate the municipality or jurisdiction in which the signing electors are qualified to vote, as it relates to the office sought by the candidate 
named on the nomination paper.  For example, for a statewide office the jurisdiction is the State of Wisconsin.  Other examples are 1st Congressional District, 24th Assembly District or Brown County. 
Signatures and Printed Names of Electors - Only qualified electors of the jurisdiction or the district the candidate seeks to represent may sign the nomination papers. Each signer must also 
legibly print their name. Each elector must provide their residential address (no P.O. Box addresses), including any street, fire or rural route number, box number (if rural route) and street or road name 
and municipality of residence.  A post office box number alone does not show where the elector actually resides.  The name of the Municipality of Residence must be listed for each signing elector and 
must clearly identify the town, village or city where the elector's voting residence is located.  The date the elector signed the nomination paper, including month, day and year, must be indicated.  Ditto 
marks that follow correct and complete address or date information are acceptable.  The circulator may add any missing or illegible address or date information before the papers are filed with the filing 
officer. 
Signature of Circulator - The circulator should carefully read the language of the Certification of Circulator. THE CIRCULATOR MUST PERSONALLY PRESENT THE NOMINATION PAPER TO EACH SIGNER . THE CIRCULATOR 
MUST BE A QUALIFIED ELECTOR OF WISCONSIN. THE NOMINATION PAPER MAY NOT BE LEFT UNATTENDED ON COUNTERS OR POSTED ON BULLETIN BOARDS .  The circulator's complete residential address including municipality of 
residence must be listed in the certification. After obtaining signatures of electors, the circulator must sign and date the certification. 
Other Instructions - Candidates and circulators should review Ch. Wisconsin Elections Commission §§ 2.05, 2.07, Wis. Adm. Code. 
 Original nomination papers must be in the physical custody of the appropriate filing officer by the filing deadline. A postmark on the filing deadline is NOT sufficient. Nomination papers cannot 
be faxed/emailed to the filing officer.  Ch. Wisconsin Elections Commission § 6.04(2), Wis. Adm. Code. 
 Nomination papers with the required number of signatures must be filed with the appropriate filing officer no later than 5:00 p.m. on June 1st (or the next day if June 1st is a holiday or 
weekend) before the general election.  Nomination papers may not be circulated before April 15. Special elections may have d ifferent circulation time frames and filing deadlines.  Check with 
the filing officer. 
 In order for a candidate's name to be placed on the ballot, a candidate must file a Campaign Registration Statement (ETHCF-1), a Declaration of Candidacy (EL-162), and Nomination Papers (EL-
168) containing the appropriate number of signatures for the office sought no later than the filing deadline.  Wis. Stat. § 8.15(6).  Candidates for state office and municipal judge must also file a 
Statement of Economic Interests with the Wisconsin Ethics Commission by the third business day after the nomination paper filing deadline.  Wis. Stat. § 19.43.  If any one of these required 
forms is not filed by the deadline, the candidate's name will not be placed on the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 8.30. 
 If a candidate or circulator has any questions, he or she should contact the filing officer.

Monday, December 22, 2025
To
City of Milwaukee Election Commission
Milwaukee County Election Commission
Wisconsin County Clerks
Wisconsin Municipal Clerks
Priority
Timely Attention
The Wisconsin Elections Commission wanted to share a brief overview of changes to election administration that took effect this year to ensure they’re on your radar as we move into the 2026 election cycle.
These updates cover candidacy withdrawal requirements, privacy protections, town clerk appointments, election observers, along with other legislative and rulemaking matters.
New Laws
Privacy Protections for Elected Officials
-
Wisconsin Act 7
(date of enactment 6/9/25)
Summary: On July 1, 2025, a new provision of Wisconsin public records law will go into effect that requires records custodians to withhold the personally protected information of election officials upon a written request from those officials. This is a change in public records law, not election law, but it involves many records that are maintained by county and municipal clerks. Wis. Stat. § 19.36(14).
Candidacy Withdrawal–
Wisconsin Act 43
(date of enactment (10/31/25)
Summary: Allows candidates to withdrawal from certain offices and provides a penalty.
Wis. Stat. § 8.35(1m).
Town Appointments -
Wisconsin Act 71
(date of enactment 12/9/25)
Summary: Reforms how towns can fill vacant clerk positions.
Wis. Stat. §§ 60.10 (1) (b) 2m., 60.30 (1e) (f), 60.331, 60.341, 60.305 (4) (a) 2.
Voter ID Constitutional Amendment
In April, voters approved a constitutional amendment to enshrine the state’s photo identification requirement to the Wisconsin constitution. While the ID requirement has been in place since 2016, the move cements the requirement in the state constitution.
Wis. Const. Art. III, Sec. 1m.
Elections Bill Vetoed by the Governor:
SB 270
- The right of appeal for complainants aggrieved by decisions of the Elections Commission concerning the conduct of election officials.
Rulemaking/Admin Rules – Enacted in 2025
Observer rule
(enacted 8/1/25). Puts into law detailed procedures regarding the processes election observers and clerks must follow to ensure orderly observation of voting activity
Clerk training requirements
(enacted 9/1/25). Affirms Commission practice that training cycle runs from January 1 of an even-numbered year and continues through December 31 of an odd-numbered year. Requires clerks to provide to the Commission the mailing address and email address for the top elected official of their municipality so the Commission may notify the municipality if training requirements are not met.
Rulemaking / Admin Rules – Going into Effect in 2026
Certification of residence rule
(in effect 1/1/26) – Enacts the procedures for how the Commission will certify the residence of judicial officers and candidates so they can be exempt from listing their residential address on nomination papers and declarations of candidacy.
Mandatory use of uniform instructions rule
(in effect 2/1/26) – Requires all municipal clerks to use the Commission’s versions of the uniform instructions for absentee voting, and prohibits clerks from making any substantive edits or alterations to those instructions.
Ballot access challenge procedure rules (in effect 4/1/26) – Revises the current standards and procedures for nomination papers and challenges, and creates a new, similar process for challenges to declarations of candidacy.
If you have any questions, reach out to the WEC at
elections@wi.gov
.
Memo Type
Clerk Communication
Subject
Legislative Changes & Court Decisions

Welcome to a new elections training cycle! The current training term began January 1, 2026 and ends December 31, 2027. You are required to take 6 hours of training within that window to get/remain certified. For new clerks and clerks who did not certify by 12/31/2025, the requirement is MCT Core plus an additional 3 hours of election training. For all currently certified clerks, any 6 hours of election training that applies to your role.
To help you find trainings, see the attached the list of 2025-2026 webinars and training tidbits that are on the schedule. Recordings of past webinars and tidbits can be viewed in the Catalog on ElectEd and you register for upcoming ones in the Calendar.
To register for a training in the calendar, click on the event and click the red Register button. If you do not register in ElectEd, you will not receive credit for attending. WEC will no longer be manually adding attendees who do not register themselves.
To get a meeting invitation for your calendar, click the Zoom link on the event description and register there as well.
New this year! The newsletter will have a spot in each upcoming issue talking about any upcoming deadlines and relevant trainings so keep an eye out for that.

__________________________________________________________________________________________ _________________ 
 
Wisconsin Elections Commissioners 
Ann S. Jacobs, chair | Marge Bostelmann | Don M. Millis | Carrie Riepl | Robert Spindell | Mark L. Thomsen 
_________________________________________________________________________________________________________ 
Administrator 
Meagan Wolfe 
       Wisconsin Elections Commission 
 
201 West Washington Avenue | Second Floor | P.O. Box 7984 | Madison, WI  53707-7984 
(608) 266-8005 | elections@wi.gov | elections.wi.gov  
 
DATE:  January 15, 2026 
 
TO:  Wisconsin Municipal Clerks 
Wisconsin County Clerks 
City of Milwaukee Election Commission 
Milwaukee County Election Commission 
 
FROM: The Wisconsin Elections Commission 
 
SUBJECT:  2026-2027 Elections Training Cycle 
 
Welcome to a new elections training cycle! The current training term began January 1, 2026 and ends December 
31, 2027. You are required to take 6 hours of training within that window to get/remain certified. For new clerks 
and clerks who did not certify by 12/31/2025, the requirement is MCT Core plus an additional 3 hours of election 
training. For all currently certified clerks, any 6 hours of election training that applies to your role. 
  
To help you find trainings, see the attached the list of 2025-2026 webinars and training tidbits that are on the 
schedule. Recordings of past webinars and tidbits can be viewed in the Catalog on ElectEd and you register for 
upcoming ones in the Calendar. 
  
• To register for a training in the calendar, click on the event and click the red Register button. If you do not 
register in ElectEd, you will not receive credit for attending. WEC will no longer be manually adding 
attendees who do not register themselves. 
• To get a meeting invitation for your calendar, click the Zoom link on the event description and register 
there as well. 
  
New this year! The newsletter will have a spot in each upcoming issue talking about any upcoming deadlines and 
relevant trainings so keep an eye out for that. 
  
We look forward to another successful training term with you all. 
  
Best, 
The WEC Training Team

New Clerks Class  
September 18, 2025 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m. 
County and Municipal Clerks 
Recording Link: https://electiontraining.wi.gov/group/11021 
2026 will be a busy election year! As a new, “newer”, or an experienced clerk, this webinar will introduce you 
to our agency and staff and provide information on training requirements for local election officials and the 
wide variety of resources available to help you do a great job before, during, and after an election.   
 
 
WisVote Advanced  
                                                       October 21, 2025, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m. 
Clerks, Deputies 
Recording Link: https://electiontraining.wi.gov/group/11046 
For those clerks unable to attend the WEC Clerk Conference session, here’s your chance to see what you 
missed. This webinar will cover more advanced topics surrounding WisVote data including sorting vs filtering, 
system views, and a deep dive into Advanced Find in WisVote. 
 
 
Appointing Election Officials for the 2026-2027 Term  
November 6, 2025, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m. 
Clerks, Deputies 
Recording Link: https://electiontraining.wi.gov/group/11101 
This webinar will address the election official nomination procedure, including the submission of lists by the 
county’s primary political parties and the approval of election officials by the governing body. We will also 
review training requirements for election officials and available training resources (clean up accounts in EE).   
 
 
Training Election Officials  
December 11, 2025, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m. 
Clerks and Deputies 
Recording Link: https://electiontraining.wi.gov/group/11126 
This webinar will provide you with some best practices for adult education, the statutory requirements for 
training and tracking the training of your election officials, and an overview of ElectEd. 
 
 
Combining Wards, Establishing Polling Places, and Annexations  
December 16, 2025, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m. 
Clerks and Deputies 
Recording Link: https://electiontraining.wi.gov/group/11141 
This webinar will provide a comprehensive information to help municipal and county clerks navigate three key 
areas of preparing for your upcoming elections: combining wards, establishing polling places, and managing 
annexations. 
 
Absentee Part 1 – by-mail absentee voting  
                                                      January 13, 2026, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m 
Clerks, Deputies 
Recording Link: Not available yet 
Any Wisconsin voter may choose to vote absentee but what does that mean for election officials? In this 
webinar, we will go over the requirements for voters and clerks regarding absentee ballot requests, sending, and 
processing.   
 
   
 
 
Judicial Privacy Act (AS & KM) 
                                                      January 22, 2026, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m.  
                                          Clerks, Chief Inspectors and Poll Workers 
Event Link: https://electiontraining.wi.gov/events/wec-judicial-privacy-act-webinar 
As of April 1, 2025, judicial officers (judges) and certain immediate family members have the right to request 
that specific personally identifiable information be kept confidential. Join the WEC protected voter team as they 
discuss Act 235 and how it impacts the elections realm. 
 
Absentee Part 2 - IPAV and SVDs  
January 28, 2026, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m. 
Anyone working IPAV or as an SVD 
Event Link: https://electiontraining.wi.gov/events/wec-absentee-part-2-ipav-and-care-facility-voting-
svds-webinar 
In-Person and Care Facility absentee voting have specific rules and processes to follow. This webinar will go 
over all aspects of these types of absentee voting from issuing ballots and printing labels in WisVote, to 
scheduling times, posting notices, and the actual voting processes. 
 
Election Prep for BB users  
                                                     February 3, 2026, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m.  
Clerks, Chief Inspectors and Poll Workers at Badger Book Municipalities 
Event Link: https://electiontraining.wi.gov/events/wec-election-prep-badger-book-users-webinar 
This is a session for Badger Book municipal clerks, deputies, and chief inspectors ahead of the Spring 2026 
elections. Topics will include an overview of the new processes for protected and military voters, the new  
registration workflow, what’s new in the Admin area, and reminders to make election day a success. 
 
  
Contingency Planning  
March 5, 2026, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m. 
                                             Clerks, Chief Inspectors and Poll Workers 
Event Link: https://electiontraining.wi.gov/events/wec-contingency-planning-webinar 
While we may not want to think about it, situations arise that require a lot of communication and challenges. 
Without contingency plans in place, these situations could turn into catastrophes so let's work through how to 
do contingency planning. 
 
 
POR vs. POI (registration and check-in)  
March 19, 2026, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m. 
Clerks, Chief Inspectors and Poll Workers 
    Event Link: https://electiontraining.wi.gov/events/wec-proof-identification-vs-proof-residence-webinar 
Proof of Identification (photo ID) and Proof of Residence are different requirements in different processes but 
cause a lot of confusion. This webinar will walk you through when each is required, what the acceptable 
documents are, and how they must be presented and documented. 
 
 
WisVote Post-Election  
April 14, 2026, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m. 
Clerks, Deputies 
         Event Link: https://electiontraining.wi.gov/events/wec-wisvote-post-election-webinar 
   
 
Wrapping up the 2026 Spring Election in WisVote. WEC staff will be discussing the post-election in WisVote, 
with a special emphasis on WisVote Election Reconciliation. We will also discuss useful resources, checklists, 
and data quality.  
 
 
UOCAVA  
June 10, 2026, 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m. 
Clerks, Deputies

Federal and state laws specify what is required and the timeline for military and overseas voters to be issued 
their absentee ballots. This webinar will walk you through the process from initial request to reviewing a 
returned ballot for each of these types of voters. If you have any active requests from military and/or overseas 
voters, you NEED to attend this webinar.

### 2026 Election Security Subgrant Program for Municipalities

*Source: https://elections.wi.gov/memo/2026-election-security-subgrant-program-municipalities. Fetched: 2026-09-10 (first seen 2026-09-10). Publisher's currency statement: Index page (Wayback snapshot 2026-08-07) lists items through 'Update on Ballot Spoiling Litigation — Wednesday, July 29, 2026'; each item carries its own publication date. Source verified official on 2026-09-10. Capture note: Memo page captured through a headless browser session because the Commission's site blocks automated clients; the memo's attachment(s) were fetched from the Commission's static document path and are appended in full.*

Thursday, June 11, 2026
To
Milwaukee County Election Commission
Wisconsin County Clerks
Priority
Timely Attention
File Downloads
File
2026 Election Security Subgrant Program for Municipalities
1. Summary.
On May 7, 2026, the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) approved the renewal of the Election Security Subgrant for Municipalities program. Clerks are invited to attend the WEC June 17th, 2026, informational
webinar
and applications can be submitted from June 22nd to December 1st, 2026.
2.  Background.
The WEC previously awarded $1.3M in 1,305 subgrant awards via early iterations (2019, 2020, 2022) of the Election Security Municipality Subgrant programs. These federal funds were sub-awarded to municipalities for fundamental cybersecurity improvements including upgraded hardware and software, managed IT support, minimal physical security, and security training. Under the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2026, the WEC was offered additional funds to “improve the administration of elections for Federal office, including to enhance election technology and make election security improvements.”
The WEC will disburse up to $2.4 million of these and previously awarded federal funds through the approved 2026 Election Security Subgrant Program for Municipalities. All municipalities are eligible for the subgrant, even if they previously received funds from 2019, 2020, or 2022 Election Security Subgrants. Each municipality may receive up to $2,000 under this subgrant, until allocated funds are depleted.
More on the security subgrant program:
http://elections.wi.gov/2026-election-security-subgrant-program-municipalities
3. Authorized Uses
Per subgrant conditions, municipalities must use the funds for one or more of the following expenses:
Baseline complaint computer hardware and software (see Appendix B)
Baseline professional IT support (including for Badger Books, if baseline met) (See Appendix B)
Limited physical security improvements for election equipment
Security training (cyber or physical)
4. How do Jurisdictions Apply?
An authorized representative of each jurisdiction must complete and submit a 2026 Election Security Subgrant Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) form via AccessGov by December 1, 2026. The link to access that form is
here
and
will become available on June 22, 2026.
All subgrant information including a sample of the MOU and Appendices will be available on the WEC website
here
. This subgrant is only available to municipalities; counties are not eligible to apply. A webinar to review grant guidelines, compliance, applications, and common questions will be held June 17th, 2026 – sign up
here.
7. Questions?
Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at
elections@wi.gov
or 608-261-2028.

DATE: June 11, 2026 
TO: Wisconsin Municipal Clerks 
City of Milwaukee Election Commission  
Wisconsin County Clerks 
Milwaukee county Election Commission 
FROM: Wisconsin Elections Commission  
 SUBJECT: 2026 Election Security Subgrant Program for Municipalities 
1. Summary.  
On May 7, 2026, the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) approved the renewal of the Election 
Security Subgrant for Municipalities program. Clerks are invited to attend the WEC June 17th, 2026, 
informational webinar and applications can be submitted from June 22nd to December 1st, 2026.    
2.  Background.  
The WEC previously awarded $1.3M in 1,305 subgrant awards via early iterations (2019, 2020, 2022) of 
the Election Security Municipality Subgrant programs. These federal funds were sub-awarded to 
municipalities for fundamental cyber-security improvements including upgraded hardware and software, 
managed IT support, minimal physical security, and security training. Under the Consolidated 
Appropriations Act of 2026, the WEC was offered additional funds to “improve the administration of 
elections for Federal office, including to enhance election technology and make election security 
improvements.” The WEC will disburse up to $2.4 million of these and previously awarded federal 
funds through the approved 2026 Election Security Subgrant Program for Municipalities. All 
municipalities are eligible for the subgrant, even if they previously received funds from 2019, 2020, or 
2022 Election Security Subgrants. Each municipality may receive up to $2,000 under this subgrant, until 
allocated funds are depleted. 
3. Authorized Uses.  
Per subgrant conditions, municipalities must use the funds for one or more of the following expenses: 
1. Baseline compliant computer hardware and software (see Appendix B) 
2. Baseline professional IT support (including for Badger Books, if baseline met) (see Appendix B) 
3. Limited physical security improvements for election equipment  
4. Security training (cyber or physical) 
2026 Election Security Subgrant Program for Municipalities 
6/11/2026 
Page 2 
 
 
4. How do Jurisdictions Apply? 
An authorized representative of each jurisdiction must complete and submit a 2026 Election Security 
Subgrant Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) form via AccessGov by December 1, 2026. The link 
to access that form is here and will become available on June 22, 2026. All subgrant information 
including a sample of the MOU and Appendices will be available on the WEC website here. This 
subgrant is only available to municipalities; counties are not eligible to apply. A webinar to review grant 
guidelines, compliance, applications, and common questions will be held June 17
th, 2026 – sign up here. 
5. Questions? 
Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at elections@wi.gov or 608-261-2028.

Published 7/16/2026 
Absentee Ballot Return : Best Practices  
Introduction 
In Wisconsin, any voter can choose to cast their ballot one of three ways: 
a. At their polling location on Election Day 
b. Absentee ballot returned: (1) by mail, (2) by delivery to a clerk’s office, or 
(3) depositing in a drop box 
c. In-person absentee ballot (sometimes called early voting) at an officially 
designated site beginning two weeks before Election Day 
1. Voting Absentee  
Do I need a reason to vote absentee? 
No, you do not need a reason or excuse to vote by absentee ballot in Wisconsin. Any 
Wisconsin voter who wishes to vote absentee may do so by submitting a request as 
described below. 
How do I vote absentee? 
There are three ways to request an absentee ballot. 
1. Online. In just a few simple steps, you can officially request your absentee 
ballot online at MyVote.wi.gov, which will generate an email notification to 
your municipal clerk. 
2. By Mail. If you are a registered Wisconsin voter, you can download 
the Application For Absentee Ballot. Then, fill out the form and mail it to your 
municipal clerk’s office. With few exceptions (e.g., you are indefinitely 
confined, live permanently overseas), you must also include a copy of your 
acceptable photo ID with your absentee ballot request. Information on the 
Photo ID needed to vote in Wisconsin is available at BringIt.wi.gov. 
3. By Email or Fax. You can also request an absentee ballot by carefully 
composing and sending an email or fax to your municipal clerk that includes: 
• Your full name; 
• Voting address; 
 
Published 7/16/2026 
• Mailing address; 
• The election in which you are voting; 
• A copy of your photo ID (if you have not provided it with a previous 
absentee ballot request). 
Your clerk must receive your absentee ballot request no later than 5 p.m. on the 
Thursday before Election Day. However, we recommend making this request as soon 
as possible, so you have time to receive, complete, and return your ballot to be 
counted. 
Note: Before your clerk can send you an absentee ballot, you must be registered to 
vote. Find out if you’re registered at MyVote.WI.gov.  Select “Register to vote,” and enter 
your name and date of birth.  
2.   Returning an Absentee Ballot  
There are three ways to return your absentee ballot: 
• By Mail 
• Using a drop box 
• Directly to your clerk’s office 
When should I return my completed absentee ballot by mail? 
Mail transit times vary. Do not delay returning your completed absentee ballot.  If a 
mailed ballot arrives after 8 p.m. on Election Day, it will not be counted.1  
The Wisconsin Elections Commission recommends putting your ballot in the mail at 
least 10 days before Election Day to ensure it is received in time. Voters who are out-of-
state may need more time to ensure timely return. If you return your absentee ballot 
through the mail the week before Election Day, there is a significant risk that your ballot 
may not be received and counted.   
 Your returned ballot must be sent to your city, village, or town clerk. This means: 
• Do not mail or deliver the ballot to your county clerk. 
 
1 In Wisconsin, it does not matter when your ballot is postmarked.  Some other states use the postmark to 
determine if a ballot can be counted.  Wisconsin does not use the postmark.  In Wisconsin, absentee ballots 
must arrive before polls close on Election Day to be counted.   
 
Published 7/16/2026 
• Do not mail or deliver the ballot to the Wisconsin Elections Commission.  
• Do not mail or deliver the ballot to the Wisconsin Secretary of State. 
• Do not mail or deliver the ballot to the courthouse. The clerk of court is not your 
municipal clerk. 
Concerned your ballot will not arrive on-time through the mail? 
You can also hand-deliver your absentee ballot directly to your municipal 
clerk. On Election Day, you may hand-deliver your absentee ballot to your 
polling place or central counting facility (if applicable).2  Or, if your clerk has 
established drop boxes for absentee ballot return, you may return the ballot 
using a drop box.  
NOTE: You cannot return someone else’s ballot unless you are assisting a 
voter with a disability. 
When should I return my completed absentee ballot by drop box? 
When a drop box is available for use is determined by each municipality.  Some 
municipalities allow the drop boxes to be used on Election Day and some do not.  
Those available on Election Day usually have a time cut-off after which the drop box 
cannot be used. It is recommended that a voter only use a drop box prior to Election 
Day. If on Election Day, contact your clerk to determine if a drop box is available. 
When should I return my completed absentee ballot directly to my clerk? 
You may return your absentee ballot directly to your clerk prior to Election Day.  If you 
are concerned your absentee ballot will not arrive by Election Day, you must deliver 
your absentee ballot to your clerk.  On Election Day, you must return your ballot to your 
polling place or central counting facility (if applicable).
2 
 
2 Most Wisconsin cities, villages, and towns count absentee ballots at the polling place.  Some jurisdictions 
(mostly larger cities) count absentee ballots at a central counting facility.  Contact your municipal clerk  to 
determine where your ballot will be counted. 
 
Published 7/16/2026 
3.  Checking on Your Ballot 
Has my ballot arrived on time? 
First, check your absentee ballot status online at MyVote.wi.gov by selecting “Track My 
Ballot”. If the website does not show your ballot returned, you can also call your 
municipal clerk.   
If I received an absentee ballot, but did not return it, can I still vote at the 
polls on Election Day? 
Yes. As long as you do not return your absentee ballot, you can still vote at the polls.  
Once an absentee ballot has been returned to the municipal clerk, it cannot be spoiled 
and reissued for any reason. 
If I returned my completed ballot in the mail, can I change my mind and 
vote in person on Election Day? 
No.   
If you return your ballot in the mail, you cannot vote in person on Election 
Day, even if the absentee ballot has not arrived.  
What if I am a military or overseas voter? 
The Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP) provides detailed recommendations for 
absent military and overseas voters.  
• Military voters at sea or at overseas facilities without access to the military postal 
system should return their ballot at least 35 calendar days before the election. 
• Military voters with access to the military postal system and civilian voters 
overseas should return their ballot at least 30 calendar days before the election. 
• Stateside (CONUS) military voters and eligible family members should return 
their ballot at least 11 calendar days before the election. 
In all cases, FVAP recommends that military and overseas voters complete and return 
the ballot as soon as it is received.

Friday, June 5, 2026
To

Wisconsin County Clerks

Ballot Access Deadlines and Ballot Proofing Resources.pdf
1. Summary
As counties prepare, proof and print ballots for the August 11, 2026 Partisan Primary, please take note of the following dates and resources to assist clerks.
June 8 the WEC will draw for unofficial, preliminary ballot order.
June 9 at 10:00 a.m. the WEC will meet to consider challenges and ballots access for all candidates and contests that fall in the normal deadlines.
June 10 at 3:00 p.m. the WEC will meet for a second time to consider challenges and ballot access for all candidates and contests where the deadline was extended for failure to file a notice of non-candidacy. The WEC will also issue the Type B Notice (earliest possible date given deadlines).
June 24 is the deadline for county clerks to distribute ballots to all municipal clerks.
Because of the number of contests and candidates, clerks may need to plan for longer than usual ballot paper.
Please send county ballot proofs to the WEC as soon as they are ready for review.
Note additional resources at the end of this memo related to ballot access and challenges and ballot proofing.
2. Ballot Access Timeline
June 1 – Nomination Paper Filing deadline for Fall Candidates
June 2 – Filing deadline for Partisan Primary Referenda
June 4 – Statement of Economic Interest deadline for Fall Candidates
June 4 -- (5:00 p.m.) Deadline to file a challenge against a candidate’s nomination papers in contests without an extension
June 6 – (1:30 a.m.) Deadline to file a challenge against a candidate’s nomination papers in contests with an extension (Offices of Lieutenant Governor, Representative in Congress, District 7, Representative to Assembly District 56, and Representative to Assembly District 50)
June 7-10 -- Various deadlines related to challenge responses, replies, rebuttals, and correcting affidavits for all contests including extended contests.
June 8 – WEC draws unofficial, preliminary ballot order and emails preliminary order to counties. WEC is unable to draw for preliminary ballot order before this date given correcting affidavits can be filed (determining who may have enough signatures to qualify) until Sunday, June 7 at 5:00 p.m.
June 9 (10:00 a.m.) – WEC Ballot Access Meeting for contests that have not been extended. At the end of the day, WEC will send counties a list of candidates who have been approved for ballot access. However, the Type B notice cannot be issued until all candidates, including those in races with an extension, have been approved.
June 10 (3:00 p.m.) –WEC Ballot Access Meeting for contests that have been extended.
June 10 – The WEC sends county clerks Type B notice with candidates for Partisan Primary
June 11 – County clerks send ballot proofs to the WEC as soon as possible before printing
The WEC understands the urgency counties feel when trying to stay on top of deadlines for ballot design, proofing, printing and distribution. Because of the deadlines set in state statute for ballot access, some counties may have ballot proofs mostly prepared before the final Candidates on Ballot by Election Report – which includes candidate names and order – can be produced.
3. Expect Long Ballots
With five parties, dozens of contests, and a significant number of candidates, the 2026 August Partisan Primary ballot will be long. In some cases, counties may not be able to include all contests on the standard 14-inch ballot and must move to longer ballot stock instead. County Clerks should determine if that will be necessary for their ballots and prepare with relevant parties (vendors, printers, etc.) on the logistics. This may affect paper ballot stock as well as accessible equipment and counties should confirm with vendors.
Counties or municipalities planning to use hand count ballots for the 2026 Partisan Primary should note there is not a sample consolidated hand count ballot template due to ballot size limitations. Jurisdictions may need to either use separate party-specific ballots or work with their vendor/printer to determine if a consolidated ballot can reasonably fit on available paper stock. Counties with questions or concerns about accessing paper stock or preparing hand count ballots should reach out to WEC staff to discuss further.
4. WEC Ballot Proofing Process
Counties must provide a proof of their ballot to the WEC for review. The WEC reviews ballot proofs to verify that the ballot format substantially complies with the templates approved by the Commission. WEC staff will review county ballot proofs within one business day. If you have not received a response within one business day from submitting your proof, please reach out to us.
The WEC ballot review process covers:
Ballot Title
Ballot Template Language (Notice to Electors, instructions, etc.)
Office Title for federal and state-level contests
Candidate names and spelling for federal and state-level contests
Candidate ballot order for federal and state-level contests
Write-in lines for federal and state-level contests
The WEC
does not review:
Local contests and write-in lines (sheriff, mayor, school board, etc.)
Spelling of a local candidate’s name
Ballot order of local offices and candidates
Ballot district combination accuracy (also called ballot style)
County clerks are responsible for determining the correct ballot combination for municipalities and for ensuring each municipality receives the correct ballots.
This is a representative list. When WEC proofs ballots, a checklist is sent to the county following review.
5. Resources
Additional information regarding candidates, challenges, and general ballot proofing resources can be found at these links:
For a list of candidates who have filed nomination papers, as well as information regarding contests that were extended for failure to file a notice of noncandidacy, you can find WEC’s trackers here:
File
Candidates Tracking By Office as of June 4 2026 at 545pm.pdf
To view candidate nomination papers, correcting affidavits, supplemental nomination papers, challenges, and challenge replies visit
www.badgervoters.wi.gov
Memo outlining challenge deadlines and process for most contests and candidates:
https://elections.wi.gov/resources/quick-reference-topics/filing-challenges-nomination-papers
Memo outlining challenge deadlines and process for the extended contests of for Offices of Lieutenant Governor, Representative in Congress, District 7, Representative to Assembly District 56, and Representative to Assembly District 50:
File
Notice of Extension of Filing for Four Offices.pdf
On the morning of June 9 and on June 10 you will be able to access materials related to challenges posted to each Commission meeting:
https://elections.wi.gov/about-wec/commission-meetings-and-minutes
The Commission approved ballot templates for the 2026 Fall Election Cycle can be found here:
Ballot Templates | Wisconsin Elections Commission
To help clerks confirm the different contests that should appear on their various ballot styles, the X-Chart Report is available in WisVote. Counties can generate this report under the Elections Tile in Custom Excel Reports, the X-Chart is a chart that displays contests along one axis and ballot styles along another. When a particular ballot style will contain a particular contest, that is denoted with an “X”. This visualization of the various contests and ballot styles assists clerks in the ballot proofing process. Please visit X-Chart Report - ElectEd for information about the X-Chart Report and how it can be used in the proofing process. Please note, counties MUST verify that the Election Plans for your municipalities are correct prior to running the X-Chart Report. The data in the X-Chart is only as accurate as the data entered in WisVote.
6. Questions?
Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at
elections@wi.gov
or 608-261-2028.

logistics. This may affect paper ballot stock as well as accessible equipment and counties should confirm 
with vendors.  
Counties or municipalities planning to use hand count ballots for the 2026 Partisan Primary should note 
there is not a sample consolidated hand count ballot template due to ballot size limitations. Jurisdictions 
may need to either use separate party-specific ballots or work with their vendor/printer to determine if a 
consolidated ballot can reasonably fit on available paper stock. 
 
Counties with questions or concerns about accessing paper stock or preparing hand count ballots should 
reach out to WEC staff to discuss further.  
August Ballot Access and Proofing Dates and Reminders 
6/5/2026 
Page 3 
 
 
 
4. WEC Ballot Proofing Process  
Counties must provide a proof of their ballot to the WEC for review.  The WEC reviews ballot proofs to 
verify that the ballot format substantially complies with the templates approved by the Commission. 
WEC staff will review county ballot proofs within one business day.  If you have not received a response 
within one business day from submitting your proof, please reach out to us.  
 
The WEC ballot review process covers:  
• Ballot Title 
• Ballot Template Language (Notice to Electors, instructions, etc.) 
• Office Title for federal and state-level contests 
• Candidate names and spelling for federal and state-level contests 
• Candidate ballot order for federal and state-level contests 
• Write-in lines for federal and state-level contests 
The WEC does not review:  
• Local contests and write-in lines (sheriff, mayor, school board, etc.) 
• Spelling of a local candidate’s name 
• Ballot order of local offices and candidates 
• Ballot district combination accuracy (also called ballot style) 
o County clerks are responsible for determining the correct ballot combination for 
municipalities and for ensuring each municipality receives the correct ballots. 
This is a representative list.  When WEC proofs ballots, a checklist is sent to the county following 
review. 
5. Resources 
Additional information regarding candidates, challenges, and general ballot proofing resources can be 
found at these links: 
• For a list of candidates who have filed nomination papers, as well as information regarding 
contests that were extended for failure to file a notice of noncandidacy, you can find WEC’s 
trackers here: Candidates Tracking By Office as of June 4 2026 at 545pm.pdf 
• To view candidate nomination papers, correcting affidavits, supplemental nomination papers, 
challenges, and challenge replies visit www.badgervoters.wi.gov  
• Memo outlining challenge deadlines and process for most contests and candidates: 
• Memo outlining challenge deadlines and process for the extended contests of for Offices of 
Lieutenant Governor, Representative in Congress, District 7, Representative to Assembly 
District 56, and Representative to Assembly District 50 
August Ballot Access and Proofing Dates and Reminders 
6/5/2026 
Page 4 
 
 
 
• On the morning of June 9 and on June 10 you will be able to products related to challenges 
posted to each Commission meeting: Upcoming Events | Wisconsin Elections Commission 
• The Commission approved ballot templates for the 2026 Fall Election Cycle can be found 
here: Ballot Templates | Wisconsin Elections Commission 
• To help clerks confirm the different contests that should appear on their various ballot styles, 
the X-Chart Report is available in WisV ote.  Counties can generate this report under the 
Elections Tile in Custom Excel Reports, the X-Chart is a chart that displays contests along 
one axis and ballot styles along another. When a particular ballot style will contain a 
particular contest, that is denoted with an “X”. This visualization of the various contests and 
ballot styles assists clerks in the ballot proofing process. Please visit X-Chart Report - 
ElectEd for information about the X-Chart Report and how it can be used in the proofing 
process. Please note, counties MUST verify that the Election Plans for your municipalities 
are correct prior to running the X-Chart Report. The data in the X-Chart is only as accurate as 
the data entered in WisV ote.  
6. Questions? 
Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at elections@wi.gov or 608-261-2028.

Wisconsin Municipal Clerks

Clerk Communication Power Outages
Be Prepared: Continued Icy Weather May Impact Election Day
1.
Summary.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission is actively monitoring power outages caused by this week’s severe weather that may continue to affect some counties ahead of the April 7, 2026 election. Local officials are working closely with utility providers and emergency management teams to assess conditions to restore service as quickly as possible.
Severe weather and power outages are common contingency for which the WEC asks local election officials to prepare. This is a good reminder to ensure all staff scheduled to work on Tuesday are familiar with contingency plans.
Despite these disruptions, voters should be assured that Wisconsin’s election will carry on. Clerks have long-stablished backup procedures in place to ensure voting can continue safely and security, even in the event of a power loss.
If a polling place is impacted, clerks must provide timely updates to the WEC regarding any polling closures and relocations. Clerks are also advised to outline steps they’ve taken and communicate to the public of any impact.
2. Background.
This week, the WEC was made aware of widespread reports of power outages affecting various municipalities in central Wisconsin. Further, in some areas of the state, it’s reported that the ice will continue through tomorrow (April 4), meaning some power utilities may be unable to make the repairs until the icy conditions end. This means power outages may continue through the weekend and potentially into next week.
Clerks are coordinating directly with their power companies or county emergency management to obtain backup power supplies to prepare for today’s in-person absentee and registration activities, as well as Tuesday’s election.
3.
Action Items.
1.
If you are concerned that the power at your polling sites will not be restored by Tuesday’s election
, please contact your county clerk, your county emergency management, and your power utility to learn about the back-up power supplies, like generators, that may be available for your use.
Some counties and power utilities have generators available to municipal customers. Further, if you are concerned you will not have power for Tuesday and are having difficulty accessing resources, please contact the WEC at
elections@wi.gov
, and we will contact WEM and other state partners to escalate your concern.
2.
If you need to move polling places due to power outages, please report any moves
to your county clerk, notice the move for your voters, and contact the WEC at
elections@wi.gov
so we can ensure that your new polling place is appearing correctly on Myvote.wi.gov. For more information about polling place closures, see
Wis. statute
§
5.25(3)(a).
and
Wis. Stat.
§
7.37(1).
3.
Review your contingency plans.
Your municipality should have a contingency plan which outlines how you will adjust your procedures in the event of a power outage. Contingency plans include moving to a paper ballot and poll book process, having a backup power supply to continue using electronic equipment, and knowing how and where you would move your polling place.
Please review your contingency plan ahead of Election Day and know how you will contact your poll workers and voters in the event you need to change procedures due to a power outage or other unforeseen circumstances.
4. Questions?
Thank you for all you do to administer elections in your community even when challenges present themselves. Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at
elections@wi.gov
or 608-261-2028.

Social Media Calendar August 2026

Introduction
The Wisconsin Elections Commission has developed a social media calendar designed to help inform and educate voters on key election-related topics.
This version of the social media calendar is tailored for a statewide audience as the August 11, 2026 election approaches. While there is no requirement to use this resource, we are sharing it as an optional tool that may be helpful.
All graphics can be downloaded in a zip file above.
Each graphic is titled by topic, for example, absentee voting, in the zip file that corresponds with individual social media posts in this document.
Please feel free to reach out if you have any questions by contacting the Help Desk at
elections@wi.gov
or (608) 261-2028.
What’s New?
Clerks may notice some new graphics in this version. That’s in large part due to the
U.S. Election Assistance Commission (EAC) Social Media Toolkit
that provides editable social media graphics, sample text, and alternative text or alt text, to provide accessible descriptions for individual posts.
You will also notice suggestions for alt text below each graphic. Alt text is crucial for making web content accessible to visually impaired users. Social media sites have the option to add alt text to an image once it is added to a draft post.
The EAC graphics are editable in Canva, a free online graphic design tool, and are available in multiple versions to accommodate different social media platforms.
We encourage clerks to use this resource as they see fit in addition to the WEC’s social media graphics.

The Wisconsin Elections Commission needs your assistance in ensuring the clerk contact records we have in WisVote reflect our current municipal clerks and their contact information.
Background
: As you are aware, turnover is common amongst municipal clerks and therefore our records become outdated quickly.  It is important that our clerk contact records are current to make sure voters are being directed to the appropriate clerk.  In addition to the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC), many different agencies, such as the Federal Voting Assistance Project, rely on the clerk contact records provided to the WEC through WisVote. The MyVote Wisconsin website relies on the clerk information in WisVote.  MyVote displays the name and address of the clerk to voters who use the site to find out who their clerk is and where to mail or deliver a voter registration form.
Request: verify the contact records for the municipal clerks in your county.
You may use WisVote, MyVote or the “Directory of Wisconsin Clerks” posted at the following link:
https://elections.wi.gov/clerks/directory
to verify the contact information.
If the contact information is correct no action is required.
If any of the clerk contact information is incorrect, the municipal clerk needs to complete the WisVote Clerk Contact Information Update Form (EL-362).
The WisVote Clerk Contact Information Update (EL-362) form is attached to this communication and published on the agency website:
https://elections.wi.gov/forms/el-362
.
We ask that the municipal clerk mail, fax or email the EL-362 Clerk Contact Information Update Form to the attention of the Elections Help Desk by email to
elections@wi.gov
, by mail to 212 E. Washington Ave, Third Floor, P.O. Box 7984, Madison, WI 53707-7984, or by fax to (608) 267-0500. It is important that WEC updates the contact records directly into WisVote as this will then make the appropriate changes to the clerk training record maintained by the WEC. If the clerk contact records need to be updated, you will not be able to make any changes to the clerk training records as this can only be viewed by WEC staff with state level WisVote access. Therefore, these changes must be made by WEC staff.
The WEC will be providing friendly reminders, via our regular notifications, in order to maintain sufficient clerk contact information.
If you have questions, please contact the Elections Help Desk at (608) 261-2028, or
elections@wi.gov
. As always, thank you for your effort and time in getting this information to us.
