Election Law and Administration 
in Wisconsin 
Release Notes 
Part Two - Getting on the Ballot 
Changes to Existing Guidance 
Previous New 
Regarding nomination by caucus, the 
previous version of the manual appeared to 
suggest, incorrectly, that ballots could be 
dispensed with in favor of acclamation. 
The new manual makes clear that, if the 
chairperson or president is a candidate, 
another person can be elected to run the 
meeting by acclamation under Wis. Stat. § 
8.05(1)(c), but Wis. Stat. § 8.05(1)(f) 
unambiguously requires ballots unless there 
are fewer people placed in nomination than 
can be added to the ballot. 
The previous manual included references to 
“arrow” ballots. 
The new manual removes references to 
“arrow” ballots from the Ballot Format 
chapter since municipalities no longer use 
them. 
New Guidance 
• The manual mentions, as a Best Practice, that candidates nominated 
through the caucus procedure, if not present, can receive their 
nomination notification “hand-delivered, emailed, or, if necessary, 
mailed.” 
• Based on law changes since 2024: 
• As of December 1, 2027, local candidates will need to file their campaign 
finance registration statement with the Wisconsin Elections 
Commission. 
• Added detail about the new certification of residence process in the 
ballot access section so clerks know what to do when they see 
“Residence Certified with WEC” on declarations of candidacy and 
nomination papers. 
Expanded Information 
• Expanded Frequently Asked Questions in the Ballot Access Procedure 
section based on WEC staff experience with questions clerks have had 
over the past few years. 
• Added Frequently Asked Question section in the Notification of 
Noncandidacy section based on WEC staff experience with questions 
clerks have had over the past few years. 
• Updated Common Ballot Access Challenges that the Commission has 
decided since 2018. 
• The Qualifications for Office chapter has been expanded to include 
federal and state offices, and also addresses the important question of 
what it means to be a “qualified elector” as a potential candidate. The 
qualifications have also been better arranged visually in two charts so it 
is easy for clerks and candidates to find particular offices. 
 
 
 
Part Five – Ballots 
Changes to Existing Guidance 
Previous New 
The previous manual included references to 
“arrow” ballots. 
The new manual removes references to 
“arrow” ballots from the Ballot Format 
chapter since municipalities no longer use 
them. 
The previous manual included references to 
a “reduced size diagram,” an obsolete term. 
A “Best Practice” now recommends clerks 
should use a regular sample ballot, or 
optical scan ballot, rather than a “reduced 
size diagram.” 
 
New Guidance 
Expanded Information 
• The Commission’s existing guidance on ballot proofing best practices 
was added to the Ballot Procedures chapter. The Commission regularly 
sends this guidance out ahead of each election, but it has been 
incorporated in the manuals so clerks can more readily access the 
information. 
• The Commission’s existing guidance on ordering ballots was also 
added to the Ballot Procedures chapters. 
• The Commission’s existing guidance on A/B Ballots was added as a new 
chapter in the manual. 
 
 
Part Seven – Absentee Voting 
Changes to Existing Guidance 
Previous New 
The Commission’s previous Tips for 
Clerks info sheets on reviewing the FPCA 
and FWAB stated that those forms need 
not be signed by voters in certain 
circumstances. 
The manual now states that when a 
voter uses the FPCA or the FWAB, they 
should be required to sign those forms 
to attest that the information in them is 
true and correct. 
The previous manual stated that an 
absentee ballot request delivered in 
person by someone other than the voter 
could be considered a by-mail request. 
The update brings the manual in line 
with current information available on 
the Commission’s website, and states 
that absentee ballot requests can only 
be delivered by the voter in-person 
during IPAV, and that if a clerk 
encounters someone attempting to 
deliver their own absentee request or 
that of another voter, the clerk should 
inform them that it will need to be 
mailed or emailed to the clerk instead. 
The previous manual states that a 
Power of Attorney for a voter can 
request a ballot on behalf of a voter. 
 
The right to vote is not transferrable, and 
while any voter may receive assistance 
in making an absentee ballot request, 
the voter must on their own make the 
decision to complete and submit the 
request. 
The previous manual says that a clerk 
should change a voter’s registration to 
ineligible if a clerk receives an absentee 
ballot request from the voter and the 
voter is on the felon list from the 
Department of Corrections.  
 
This is a best practice in the new 
manual. Such requests should be 
considered incomplete until the voter 
clarifies that they believe they are able 
to vote. However, if the voter insists that 
they are eligible, the clerk must still send 
them an absentee ballot but ensure 
that the elections inspectors know that 
the ballot must be challenged on 
election day. In the statutes, such voters 
do have the ability to receive a ballot 
and vote, but the clerk and election 
inspectors have the responsibility to 
challenge the vote. Thus, the best 
practice still ensures that the clerk is 
performing these checks, but it does not 
prevent a voter from voting under the 
challenged ballot procedures if they 
believe they are qualified. 
The previous manual indicated that it 
is possible for permanent overseas 
voters to cast their ballots in person. 
The new manual offers clear guidance 
that voting in person on Election Day is 
not possible for permanent 
overseas voters. 
The previous manual stated that special 
voting deputies (SVDs) must initial 
ballots. 
Only municipal and deputy clerks need 
to initial ballots (instead of the clerk and 
the SVDs.) 
 
New Guidance 
• A “member of a uniformed service,” as grounds for military voter 
eligibility, is defined to be someone who is on active-duty orders. 
• Military voters who are at home retain some—but not all—of the benefits 
and procedures of military voting, including exemptions from 
registration (and proof of residence), as well as from photo ID to 
request an absentee ballot. Military voters who are away from home by 
reason of their service also receive those exemptions as well as some 
additional benefits, including the option to receive the ballot materials 
electronically. Additionally, military voters who are away from home can 
request their absentee ballots until 5 p.m. on Election Day, though they 
still must ensure it is returned with enough time to make it to the polling 
place by 8 p.m. 
• The Commission interprets Wis. Stat. § 6.250(1)(c) to mean that 
permanent overseas voters do not need to make a regular application 
for an absentee ballot before they use the Federal Write-in Absentee 
Ballot (FWAB.) 
• Voters who reside in a facility that has been served by special voting 
deputies and must receive a ballot by mail must provide photo ID. The 
Commission recommends that voters either request a ballot as 
indefinitely confined electors if they qualify and wish to receive ballots 
for all elections, or provide a photo ID if they have one. 
Expanded Information 
• SVD: Expanded the description of appointing and training special voting 
deputies to more clearly describe the process and relevant timelines, as 
well as adding a best practice of communication with political parties 
regarding nominees.   
• SVD: Added suggestions for identifying residential care facilities and 
qualified retirement homes, as well as suggestions for designating 
retirement homes as qualified retirement homes. 
• SVD: Clarified that the scheduling of SVD visits should be a role 
performed by the clerk rather than the SVDs and when communications 
with facility or home administrators should take place.  
• SVD: Expanded and clarified the processes used when a voter 
temporarily resides in a residential care facility or qualified retirement 
home, which involves communication between the voter’s municipal 
clerk and the clerk who will be sending the SVDs.  
• SVD: Added the information from the SVD portion of the Commission’s 
Observer Rule.   
• UOCAVA: Reorganized and clarified a new initial step to UOCAVA voting 
that focuses specifically on which voters qualify as military voters, 
including explaining the Commission’s new active-duty orders 
clarification for uniformed service.   
• UOCAVA: Added additional detail explaining the difference and purpose 
of when military voters are at home or away from their residence.  
• UOCAVA: Expanded information for temporary overseas voters to 
provide additional context for how they are similar to UOCAVA voters 
and how they are similar to regular absentee voters.  
• UOCAVA: Added much more detail on the federal forms used by military 
and overseas voters so that clerks know what to look for and what to do 
when they receive one.  
• UOCAVA: Greatly expanded the guidance and procedure for how 
municipal clerks should review and process military and overseas 
absentee ballot requests. The current manual does not cover this topic 
at all, and the revisions walk clerks through step by step of each 
application type.   
• UOCAVA: Added additional guidance for how clerks should format 
overseas addresses for military and diplomatic mail.   
• UOCAVA: Added additional guidance and tips for military and overseas 
voters to return their absentee ballots, including a new checklist to 
ensure they have completed all required steps. Also included a new 
section on Ballot Delivery Guidance and Best Practices.   
• Deadlines: This section introduces the absentee voting part of the new 
manual, and the legislative policy and interpretation statutes have 
been added to the first page, noting also relevant Wisconsin Supreme 
Court interpretations.   
• Types of Absentee Voters: Regarding reliable evidence that a voter is no 
longer indefinitely confined, staff added a best practice that clerks only 
remove a voter from the mailing list after consulting with the clerk’s 
local counsel, and that such things as voting in person does not mean 
that the voter no longer qualifies for the service.   
• Types of Absentee Voters: A section on calendar year requests was 
added to the manual.   
• Requests and Processing: The requirement to mail or transmit and 
absentee ballot within one business day was expanded to clarify that 
business days means Monday to Friday with the exception of legal 
holidays, and not based on when a specific clerk’s office is open.   
• Proof of Identification: paragraphs describing confidential voter and 
license surrender voter processes were added.   
• IPAV: Added a statement that the Commission believes that clerks must 
offer at least some hours for IPAV voting and specify them in the Type E 
notice.   
• IPAV: States that while the EL-122 certificate envelope functions as both 
a request and a certificate, that the Commission recommends having 
voters fill out the EL-121 request form so that the requests can be kept 
separately in the clerk’s office.   
• Absentee Replacement Ballots: A new section was added explaining 
under which narrow circumstances clerks can cancel an absentee 
ballot that was sent to the clerk but not received. Voters sometimes 
mail a ballot back but the ballot does not arrive in the clerk’s office 
during the anticipated time, and staff believe that in these 
circumstances the clerk can cancel the absentee ballot and send the 
voter a new one. If the ballot has been received by the clerk, the clerk 
cannot cancel the ballot under Kormanik v. WEC.   
• Correcting Defective Certificate Envelopes: Added a best practice for 
separating ballots that have defects and clearly labeling them as 
defective for the benefit of the election inspectors who will need to 
review them and who may also need to administer the process of 
voters correcting them at polling places and boards of absentee ballot 
canvasser sites. 
• Processing, Sorting, and Transfer of Ballots: This is a new section that 
draws on the Commission’s findings during the Madison investigation 
and explains the law and also recommends a series of best practices to 
better help municipal clerks and election inspectors to keep absentee 
ballots organized and ensure accurate ballot counts on election day. 
  
Part Twelve – Emergency Preparedness & 
Contingency Planning 
Changes to Existing Guidance 
Previous New 
  
 
New Guidance 
• Municipal clerks can relocate their office to a designated alternate 
location in the event of emergency as an exercise of their discretion. 
• If the governing body has only designated a single alternate site that 
becomes unusable due to an emergency, the Commission 
recommends that the emergency response plan include instructions for 
how the governing body may immediately convene to address the 
situation as consistently as possible with Wis. Stat. § 6.855. 
• Whenever it becomes impossible or convenient for an election to 
continue at a polling place after the polls have opened, election 
inspectors should utilize the same procedures to relocate outlined by 
Wis. Stat. § 7.37(1) as an exercise of their authority under § 7.37(2).  
• If an emergency impacts the canvassing of absentee ballots at the 
designated location, the best practice would be for the board of 
absentee ballot canvassers to pause their work, notice the change in 
plan to the public, and then move to an alternate location. 
Expanded Information 
• More detail on how clerks can establish a basic emergency response 
plan. 
• Expanded information for how clerks can plan to move operations to 
alternate locations, not just for polling places on Election Day, but also 
for any other location where voting activity occurs. 
 
 
 
 
Part Thirteen – Polling Place and Supplies 
Expanded Information 
• Added Commission guidance for considerations on choosing polling 
place locations. 
• Added sections to provide guidance on common clerk questions for 
when polling places can be combined. 
• Law update: 
o In 2023, a new law went into effect governing when polling places 
can be closed ahead of Election Day, now codified at Wis. Stat. § 
5.25(3). This part includes guidance the Commission approved at 
the time.

The Commission's Election Observer Rule, which can be read online at
Wis. Admin. Code Chapter EL 4
, took effect on August, 1, 2025. Accompanying this rule, the Commission has now updated several forms that will be needed at all observable locations for all elections.
The prior versions of these documents are now outdated and can no longer be used. Use the links below to print new forms
. Please ensure that your election officials know the new rules and have an adequate supply of these forms for each election.
The EL 109
Elections Observers Log
has been updated and the statement signed by each observer now
acknowledges that they must follow EL 4 while observing. Please ensure each observable location has
enough copies of this log to allow all observers to sign in.
The EL 109R
Election Observers: Rules-at-a-Glance brochure
has been thoroughly revised to reflect the
new rule and now contains individual sections explaining what observers must, may, and may not do
while observing. It also contains explanations of the new process for communications media and lists the
specific rules for each type of observable location. Enough copies should be printed so that each
observer can receive a brochure. When printing, select “actual size” to fold the document on the lines
provided.
The EL 110
Order to Leave Polling Place
is now a required form that must be completed and given to
any observer who is ordered to leave an observable location. A copy of the order must also be sent to the
Commission, ideally by email, within 60 days of issuance. Hopefully, you will not need any of these
forms, but a few should be available at any location if the need arises.

Election Observers 101
training on ElectEd, which may be useful for

Elections Communication
Toolkit & Templates

For Local Election Leaders
September 2026











How to Use This Toolkit

This toolkit can help municipalities of all sizes navigate various scenarios, major and minor, and adapt the materials to fit your jurisdiction's capabilities.
Whether you serve 500 voters or 500,000, resources on security, crisis response, and public communication can be useful to have on hand when scenarios may arise.

Making the Toolkit Work for You

	•	Adapt: Pre-written press releases and response templates are just starting points. A large municipality might need to hold a media briefing, while a small town may achieve the same goal by posting on social media. 
	•	Right-Size Your Response: Security measures and crisis scenarios can feel intimidating, but the framework of identifying the risks, communicating clearly to the public, and knowing what to do first applies universally. For example, a crisis team in a small town might simply be the clerk, a deputy, or a local sheriff, rather than a multi-agency crisis team. 
	•	Scale as need: While smaller municipalities have fewer resources, they often can build more trust by having direct lines of communication with their voters. Use that community connection to your advantage.


Remember: We are here to help! Reach out to the PIO office if you need assistance by emailing elections@wi.gov or calling 608-261-2028.
 






Table of Contents

	•	Proactive Communication Templates
	•	Dedicated volunteers, poll workers 
	•	Public observations 
	•	Crisis Scenarios and Recommended Response Templates
	•	Social media rumors about cybersecurity attacks, vulnerabilities 
	•	Attempts to disrupt election infrastructure outside Wisconsin
	•	Vulnerabilities in state or local election infrastructure 
	•	Unsuccessful attempt to disrupt state or local infrastructure
	•	Cyberattack
	•	Severe voting machine malfunctions
	•	Sample News Release Templates 
	•	Voter ID Laws, Voter ID Petition Process
	•	Closing Polling Location(s)
	•	Extending Polling Place Hours
	•	Public Test of Voting Equipment
	•	Post-Election Audits
	•	Clerk Resources 
	•	Voter Outreach (brochures, posters, voter guides, videos, social media calendars)
	•	Emergency Response Materials and Contingency Planning Webinar
	•	A-Z Election Topics
	•	Clerk Communications
	•	Election Manuals
	•	Media 101: How to Communicate with Reporters 









Part 1: Proactive Communication Templates 
Press templates designed to pitch positive news stories to members of the press to bolster confidence in our elections. 


Dedicated Volunteers
Pitch Summary
The goal is to find someone who’d be comfortable sharing their experience working in elections and if possible, make them available for interviews.
Press Release
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
MONTH, DATE, YEAR						CONTACT: [name, phone and email]
[Full name] is ready for his/her [XX] election
With volunteers like [name], the 2026 Election is in good hands
[Note: Include a photograph]
[Municipality], Wis.— All politics are local. And each year, election officials in every community throughout Wisconsin turn to volunteers like [name] to help them keep things running smoothly every election day. 
“[First name] is such a wonderful volunteer,” said [election clerk name/title]. “They always have a smile on their face and are ready to help in any way to make things easier for our community.”
For [insert name], it’s a great way to give back to the community that has meant so much to them and their family. 
“We moved here [XX] years ago,” [last name] remembers. “We raised our family here. So many people have helped us in many ways throughout the years, so we wanted to find ways to give back to the community. So when [insert name] asked me to help at the polls a few years ago, it was one small way I could give back to the community.”
“I look forward to each election,” [last name] continued. “In my own small way, I am making a difference for my community, and that feels great.”
The next time you run into [name], say hi. They will likely remind you to be sure to vote in the next election (with a smile).
Sound interesting? Our community is always looking for poll workers like [name]. If that sounds like you, please contact [clerk’s name].
\###
Social Media Posts
	•	Meet [name]. They’ve volunteered as a poll worker in our community for [XX] years. Want to find a way to give back to your community? See how [insert name] volunteers a few days during each election cycle.  
	•	Want to help your community and get paid? Serve as a poll worker! To learn more, visit: https://myvote.wi.gov/en-us/Become-PollWorker 
Public Observations
Pitch Summary
Wisconsin law allows public observations of events such as testing the voting equipment, observing the Election-Day process, and more. Encouraging members of the public to watch these processes can help boost confidence and transparency in elections.  
Press Release
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
MONTH, DATE, YEAR						CONTACT: [name, phone and email]

We’re Looking for Observers to Participate in the 2026 Election Process
[Municipality], Wis.— Many people in our community have asked questions about whether we’re ready for the 2026 election. In short, we are.  [Municipality] encourages members of the public to observe the 2026 election. 
If you’re interested in observing our community’s readiness, here are some dates to jot down:
	•	Public test of voting equipment [Insert date or say within 10 days of each election]
	•	Public observation of counting of votes after the polls close on Election Day [Insert date]
For more information on observing elections in our community, visit https://elections.wi.gov/wec-form/election-observers-rules-glance 
\###
Social Media Posts
Curious about how local elections stay secure and transparent? You can have a front-row seat in your neighborhood!
Two ways to observe the election process:
	•	Public test of voting equipment (within 10 days of each election)
	•	Public observation of counting of votes after the polls close on Election Day




Part 2: Crisis Scenarios and Recommended Response Templates

Step-by-step instructions to prepare for and handle emergencies while communicating clearly to the public. 


SCENARIO #1: Social media rumors about cybersecurity attacks or vulnerabilities
Communications Goal:
Responding quickly to keep the rumor(s) from spreading in your community.
How to Respond:
Step 1: Confirm the rumor, is just a rumor. If the rumors turn out to be true, activate the crisis recommendations for a successful cyberbreach (view Elections Emergency Planning Tool packet). 
Step 2: Once you’ve confirmed it’s not a credible threat, distribute a holding statement (see below) to the media. A holding statement is a prepared message you should send as soon as possible. It allows officials time to better understand the situation, collect facts and eventually issue something more detailed, when applicable, to the media. It helps stop the rumor before it spreads. Post the holding statement on your website and social media. You should also provide talking points to your frontline employees and/or poll workers.
Step 3: Monitor the situation. If the rumor continues to spread, you may need to take additional steps to resolve the issue, such as issuing a press release.
Step 4: Alert the WEC Public Information Office (PIO) of the inquiry. WEC staff can assess best next steps in dealing with the misinformation.
Customizable Response Tools:
Holding Statement
“We have received several calls that [give general description of rumor]. We can confirm the information is completely false. We appreciate you bringing it to our attention. To learn more visit, [insert website or link to press release, if applicable].”
Press Release
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
MONTH, DATE, YEAR						CONTACT: [name, phone and email]
Local Officials Report All Systems are a Go for Upcoming Election
Rumors about [rumor details] are false
[Municipality], Wis.—[Community] leaders today reassured the public that rumors about election interference in our community are not true and want to make sure voters have all the facts.
“Some of you have called our office with concerns about [rumor details],” said [clerk name/title]. “Our election processes are performing as expected and any rumors to the contrary are false.”
Rumors arise during every election season and it’s important for everyone to know that the Wisconsin Elections Commission and your local officials are here to help answer any questions you may have. 
Feel free to contact [name and phone/email] or go to [URL] to learn more. 
\###

Talking Points
	•	There is no cyberattack or vulnerability in our local election infrastructure.
	•	The rumors that are circulating are false.
	•	If you have questions, please contact us directly.
Media Questions and Spokesperson Answers
Q: Is it true that [rumor] impacted voter data in our community?
A: No. There is no truth to that rumor and our data is secure.
Q: How would you know if someone hacked into your server?
A: Wisconsin has many systems in place to alert us if there are any abnormalities in the data or access issues. And we have back-up systems to ensure we always have access to the correct information at all times.
Q: Is it possible for someone to manipulate the data without your knowledge?
A: No. We are constantly monitoring the systems we use to ensure they’re working as they should. 
Q: If the state election system is impacted, how does that affect us at the local level?
A: The Wisconsin Elections Commission has many security systems in place to secure the data. We would receive a timely notification if there are any concerns, as well as what we need to do to move forward. 
Q: Have other states been impacted by this problem?
A: We have not received any reports from any other communities about this issue.
Q: If Russia hacked us before, how do we know that it won’t happen again?
A: First let me put one rumor to rest. While there were attempts in Wisconsin in 2016, no one got into the system because of our strong security system. While we can’t predict the future, we know that we’re doing everything we possibly can to prepare for what’s next.
Q: On a scale of 1–10, how confident are you that our community won’t be hacked in 2026?
A: We are very confident that we have secure systems and processes in place to protect our data in 2026 and beyond.
Q: Do you think other states will have problems in 2026?
A: We are focusing on the elections in our community. 
Q: Are there more things you can do to protect our data for 2026?
A: We have put many systems and security features in place to protect our data for 2026 and beyond. As new technologies become available, we will look at them to assess the value for our community.
Social Media Post
“All systems in [community] are a go for the 2026 election. Rumors about [rumor details] are false. Please reach out to us if you have any additional questions. Thank you.”
SCENARIO #2: Vulnerabilities in state or local election infrastructure
Communications Goal:
Correcting misinformation before it can spread.
How to Respond:
Step 1: You should inform your key staff members and organizational leaders so everyone hears the same information. Also, please notify the WEC.
Step 2: Prepare a holding statement to be used only if someone in the media contacts you about the issue. A holding statement is a prepared message you should send as soon as possible. It allows officials time to better understand the situation, collect facts and eventually issue something more detailed, when applicable, to the media.
	•	If you issue a statement to the press, post the same information on your website and social media sites you have.
Step 3: Monitor media and social media reports and correct misinformation about the situation. If the situation escalates, you may need to take further action to reduce the possibility of rumors. 
	•	If there is an escalation, call the local editor/reporter and share what you know about the situation.
	•	Reassure everyone that no attempt to infiltrate your systems was made and that everything is secure.
	•	Post any updates on your website and social media sites.
	•	Contact the WEC Public Information Office (PIO) 
Step 4: Consider activating your proactive media relations plan. Sharing positive stories about Wisconsin’s election security can buy public trust and can help cushion the impact of unfounded rumors and election security situations before Election Day. 
Customizable Response Tools:
Holding Statement
“We are aware of reports questioning the security of our election system and want to be clear: these claims are false. Our election infrastructure is continuously monitored and protected by dedicated cybersecurity experts. Operations remain fully underway as state and local election officials prepare for the 2026 elections.”
Press Release
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
MONTH, DATE, YEAR						CONTACT: [name, phone and email]
[Municipality] Reassures Community of Election Security Measures 
[Municipality], Wis.— Community leaders and election officials in [municipality] are reassuring residents that recent rumors regarding election tampering in Wisconsin are false. Local officials remain fully dedicated to maintaining a safe, transparent, and secure voting process for all residents.
"We are aware of rumors circulating regarding election security in Wisconsin," said [Clerk Name, Title]. "When people reached out to inquire about our systems, our message was clear: there is zero truth to these claims. All voting systems are fully operational, tested, and secure for our upcoming election."
Unverified rumors and misinformation often surface during election cycles. Municipal clerks across the state work year-round with the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) to enforce security measures, conduct public equipment testing to ensure a smooth and secure election. 
“Wisconsin's election systems are decentralized, heavily audited, and built with robust checks and balances. We are fully prepared to deliver a secure election.” added [name, title].

\###
Talking Points
	•	Our election infrastructure is secure in our community.
	•	The rumors that are circulating through our community and state about vulnerabilities in our state election system are completely false.
	•	Wisconsin election officials have dedicated significant resources to make sure our election infrastructure is safe.
Media Questions and Spokesperson Answers
Q: Is it true that [rumor details] impacted data in Wisconsin?
A: No. There is no truth to that rumor. We’ve been in contact with the WEC and they assured us that their systems are secure.
Q: Are you telling us the truth?
A: Yes, you can depend on us to always tell you the truth about election security.
Q: How would you know if someone hacked the servers?
A: We have alert systems in place to notify us of any abnormalities. This is something we take very seriously and are diligent in ensuring we are doing everything we can to protect the data.
Q: Is it possible for someone to manipulate the data without their knowledge?
A: No. All security features provide us with ongoing reports about the system. If there are any abnormalities, we would receive a notification. 
Q: If the system was breached, what do we do?
A: First, let me assure you the system was not breached. If something abnormal occurs, we are ready to activate operational responses to ensure the core system remains protected at all times.
Q: Have other state systems been attacked?
A: Wisconsin was not attacked. We can’t speak on behalf of other states’ systems.
Q: Are there more things states can do to protect election data for 2026?
A: Like Wisconsin, many states have put systems and security features in place to protect election data for 2026 and beyond. As new technologies become available, we will all look at them to assess the value for all communities around the United States.
Social Media Post
“We are happy to report there are NO problems with our local election system or anywhere in Wisconsin. Our systems are secure. For more information about election security, visit:  https://elections.wi.gov/elections/election-security-integrity.“
SCENARIO #3: Unsuccessful attempt to disrupt state or local election infrastructure
Communications Goal:
Making sure the public understands their local elections remain safe. 
How to Respond:
Step 1: You should inform your internal team so everyone hears the same information.
	•	Provide talking points to frontline employees and/or poll workers in case they get questions from the community.
Step 2: Prepare a holding statement to use if the media hears about the unsuccessful attack. This should be used only if you get a call from the media. A holding statement is a prepared message you should send as soon as possible. It allows officials time to better understand the situation, collect facts and eventually issue something more detailed, when applicable, to the media. 
	•	If you get a media inquiry, post the statement on your website and social media sites.
	•	If you receive more information that will help your community better understand the situation, contact the local reporter or editor to share more details. 
	•	Reassure everyone that the attempt to infiltrate the system was not successful and everything is secure.
Step 3: Be sure to update your website and social media sites if you are continuing to share information with the media.
	•	Monitor local media and social media reports and correct misinformation about the situation.
Customizable Response Tools:
Holding Statement

SCENARIO #4: Attempts to disrupt election infrastructure outside Wisconsin
Communications Goal:
Taking control of the message immediately.
How to Respond:
Step 1: Do not feel pressure to answer reporters’ questions immediately, especially if the question is a technical one. 
	•	Reporters may tell you they’re on deadline, but don’t let expediency get in the way of providing the correct answer. If the reporter is on the phone, ask them to email you the questions (along with background on what you’re being asked about).
Step 2: If you’re not sure about what’s happening in other communities in Wisconsin, contact the WEC’s Public Information Office (PIO) team for assistance. 
	•	It may require a statewide response, especially if you start getting calls from multiple media outlets. Never speculate about what might be happening in another community or state.
Step 3: Once you’re sure you’ve got all the background and the correct information, formulate answers to the questions. 
	•	Depending on the type of media asking, you can return the phone call, reply by email or schedule an in-person interview.
Step 4: Share information with others in your organization to ensure everyone knows about the inquiry. In your absence, they will be ready to issue the holding statement if other reporters make similar inquiries.

SCENARIO #5: Cyberattack
Communications Goals:
Accurately communicating the attack’s impact and reducing the chance that rumors will make the situation worse.
How to Respond:
Step 1: Notify your staff or other officials about the incident. 
	•	Hold internal meetings to ensure that everyone hears the information directly from you, and emphasize that all communications must come from the organization’s spokesperson, who could be the clerk, an elected official or a public information officer.
	•	Provide talking points for your staff and poll workers if they receive questions from the public. 
Step 2: Prepare materials for the media.
	•	Do your best to provide the media with a holding statement within one hour of learning there is an incident. Social media in the community will likely begin to spread the news quickly, so the sooner you make a statement, the more likely you’ll be able to manage the narrative.
	•	Use the holding statement template in this toolkit to help you get one out quickly.
	•	Post the holding statement on your website and your social media sites.
Step 3: Prepare additional materials for the media, as needed.
	•	Modify the draft press release in this toolkit to address the specifics of the cyberattack that has occurred.
	•	It may be necessary to meet with the local media to make sure they get all the facts about the incident from you.
	•	Update the media with any additional information you receive from the state about the incident.
Step 4: Monitor local media and social media reports and correct misinformation about the incident.
Step 5: When the incident is resolved, assess how your team performed in a crisis situation.
	•	Each crisis is an opportunity to learn more about how to address future issues.
	•	Take some time to talk with your team about what they learned and what they might do differently if another crisis takes place in the future.
Additional Strategic Considerations:
	•	Be completely transparent with your community. Communication and immediacy are important to mitigating the damage. 
	•	Make sure communications are posted prominently, where people who live in the community will see them. 
	•	Restore trust by communicating security measures the state is pursuing to prevent a future data breach.
Customizable Response Tools:
Holding Statement:

We are working with law enforcement, cybersecurity IT professionals and the Wisconsin Elections Commission to assess the exact nature of the breach. We have built in many data redundancies and backup procedures to keep things running smoothly. We take this situation very seriously and will take whatever steps are necessary to protect our elections. We will provide you with more information as soon as it becomes available.”

Part 3: Sample News Release Templates

In addition to the crisis scenarios outlined above, the WEC offers news release templates on a variety of topics including voter ID laws, closing and extending polling location(s), public testing of voting equipment, and post-election audits. 

Voter ID Laws, ID Petition Process 

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
MONTH, DATE, YEAR						CONTACT: [name, phone and email]
Voters Still Have Time to Get a Free Photo ID for the Election 

[Municipality], Wis. – The Wisconsin Elections Commission reminds voters that if they don’t have an acceptable photo ID, they still have time to get one to vote. 
“If you don’t have an acceptable photo ID, you can get one for free after just one visit to a Wisconsin DMV office through the ID Petition Process,” said [clerk’s name, title]. 
Photo ID Required to Vote 
To vote in Wisconsin, whether at the polls or absentee in-person at their clerk’s office, voters must show an acceptable photo ID. [Insert clerk’s name] said most people already have the photo ID they need to vote like a Wisconsin driver license, state ID card or other DMV-issued photo ID document.  
Voters can also use a U.S. passport, military and veteran’s IDs, some student IDs, tribal IDs, or a certificate of naturalization. The full list is available at https://elections.wi.gov/voters/photo-id/photo-id-bring-it-ballot 
“Your photo ID does not need to have your current address, and your name on your ID does not have to exactly match the name on the poll list,” [insert clerk’s name] said.  “Your driver license or state ID card may even be expired, but it must have expired after the date of the most recent general election, which was the November 5, 2024.”
Make Plans Now to Get a Photo ID  
[Insert clerk’s name] urges voters who do not have an acceptable photo ID to make plans now to get one for free from the DMV. Voters who find they do not have an acceptable ID on Election Day can still cast a provisional ballot that will be counted if they bring an acceptable ID to their city, village or town clerk’s office by 4 p.m. the Friday after the election. 
To find your nearest DMV service center, please visit the DMV website: https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/online-srvcs/find-dmv/default.aspx 
How to Get a Free Photo ID to Vote with Wisconsin’s ID Petition Process
The Wisconsin DMV will provide a state ID card for free to any person who needs it for voting purposes.  If an applicant does not have all the required documentation to get a regular state ID card, DMV has an ID Petition Process available in order to obtain a free ID card for voting. 
For more information, visit https://elections.wi.gov/how-do-i-get-free-state-id-card

Extending Polling Place Hours

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
MONTH, DATE, YEAR						CONTACT: [name, phone and email]

[Municipality] Extends Polling Place Hours [State Reason, e.g., Power Outage/Emergency]

[Municipality], Wis. – Due to [specific reason for closure] that disrupted voting operations earlier today, [municipality] has successfully petitioned for a court order to extend polling hours. To ensure every eligible elector has a fair opportunity to cast their ballot, the polling location at [Insert Address/Location Name] will remain open until [Insert New Closing Time].

Pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 6.78, standard polling hours in Wisconsin are from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. However, state law allows for extensions in emergency situations where access to a polling place is obstructed or operations are significantly interrupted.

"Our priority is ensuring that every citizen has an adequate opportunity to vote," said [clerks name, title]"After consulting with the municipal attorney and the Wisconsin Elections Commission, we moved quickly to secure a court order to make up for the time lost during today's disruption."

Key Information for Voters:

	•	New Closing Time: The polls will now close at [Time] p.m.
	•	Eligibility: Any voter who was unable to access the polls during the closure or who arrives before the new designated closing time will be permitted to vote.
	•	Legal Authority: This extension was granted by a duty judge in coordination with the [County Name] Clerk and the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC).

For further updates, please visit [municipality website URL] or follow us on [social media handle].

Public Test of Voting Equipment

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
MONTH, DATE, YEAR						CONTACT: [name, phone and email]

[County/Municipality] Prepares for Pre-Election Testing of Voting Equipment

[Municipality], Wis. – Residents in [county/municipality] can have a front-row seat as local election officials conduct pre-election testing of voting equipment that will be used in the [date] Election.

On [date], election workers in [name municipalities] will conduct an open-to-the-public pre-election test of voting equipment. The testing will take place at [name location and time where testing will occur]. 

The testing provides an additional way to ensure that voting equipment is working properly, and that the election will be conducted accurately.

By state law, a pre-election test of voting equipment occurs before every election and in every municipality across Wisconsin. In the public tests, voting equipment programming is verified by feeding a set of pre-marked ballots into each machine and reviewing the results tape that is generated. An errorless count is required at the conclusion of the testing. According to Wis. Stat. 5.84(1), any errors detected must be corrected before the equipment can be used in an election. 

More information about the public testing of voting equipment can be viewed here: 
https://elections.wi.gov/voting-equipment-security. 


Post-Election Audits

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
MONTH, DATE, YEAR						CONTACT: [name, phone and email]

[County/Municipality] Completes Post-Election Audit

[Municipality or County], Wis. – Residents in [county/municipality] can be confident that votes were counted accurately in the November General Election following the completion of a post-election audit of voting equipment used in [county/municipality] for the [date] election.  

On [date], election workers completed an audit of voting equipment in [x] reporting units (typically a ward or wards that report out election results) in [name municipalities audited], which were randomly selected for audit by the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) during an event open to the public. The audit provides an additional way to ensure that voting equipment worked properly, and that the election was conducted accurately.

Wisconsin Statute § 7.08(6) requires a post-election audit of voting systems used in Wisconsin after each General Election. During the audit, election officials check to make sure the vote totals compiled by the voting equipment on Election Night are accurate by conducting an independent hand count of ballots and tallying the results of the selected contests. The final hand-count tally total is compared to the election night voting system results. 

[Optional: Provide a summary of your municipality’s audit results. If there is a discrepancy, you may wish to discuss the discrepancy once a full analysis has been conducted by the WEC.]

Audit materials are submitted to the WEC for review. The WEC analyzes the audit results and investigates any discrepancies and can request that a voting machine vendor investigate and provide explanation for any discrepancies. Once this work is complete, WEC staff will prepare a public report for review by the six Commissioners during an upcoming Commission meeting.

Post-election audits, covering approximately 10% of the reporting units in the state, serve as a final check on the election results. While not every reporting unit or municipality is selected for post-election audit, state election officials ensured that the 2026 sample included at least one reporting unit per county, and at least five reporting units for each type of equipment used.

Discrepancies in the vote totals are infrequently reported, and if they are, they are typically due to human error, which election officials then work to prevent by developing new training protocols. 

In a separate pre-election voting equipment test that occurs before every election for each tabulator, programming is verified by feeding a set of pre-marked ballots into each machine and reviewing the results tape that is generated. An errorless count is required at the conclusion of the testing. 

Additionally, election officials at the county and state level review state and federal election results for any discrepancies before they are certified by the chair of the WEC. 

Information about audits conducted in Wisconsin can be found here: 
https://elections.wi.gov/voting-equipment-security

UOCAVA Federal Forms Update
1. Summary
The Federal Voting Assistance Program announced minor changes to the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA) and Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot (FWAB). These federal forms are regularly used by military and overseas voters in Wisconsin. The changes do not affect voter eligibility. The changes do not alter clerk processing of the forms. Both old and new forms are acceptable until further notice. For more information about processing federal forms, please see Chapter 7.4 of the ELAW manual:
https://elections.wi.gov/elaw
2. Changes
The new versions of the FPCA and FWAB are available on FVAP.gov and at the U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) website:
Standard Form 76, “Federal Post Card Application (FPCA)”:
https://www.gsa.gov/reference/forms/voter-registration-and-absentee-ballot-request-federal-postcard-
application-fpca
Standard Form 186, “Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot (FWAB)”:
https://www.gsa.gov/reference/forms/federal-writein-absentee-ballot-fwab
The most noteworthy change is at the top of the new forms, where a voter selects an option under “1.
Who are you? Pick one.”
On the new forms, the final option under “1. Who are you? Pick one.” has been removed: “I am a
U.S. citizen living outside the country, I have never lived in the United States.” See example
below.
Permanent overseas voters who might have previously checked the “never resided” option in
Box 1 would now check the “return is uncertain” option, which is also intended for permanent
overseas voters.
The new form clarifies that the last-four of a Social Security Number (SSN) is acceptable in most
states and voters should only provide their full SSN if their state requires it. Wisconsin does not
require a full SSN.
OLD FPCA FORM
NEW FPCA FORM
3. Key Points
a) If a voter already submitted a previous version of the FPCA or FWAB on file with their clerk,
they do not need to submit a new form.
b) Clerks may process previous versions of the FPCA and FWAB forms submitted before their
statutory deadlines for receipt.
c) The changes are only to the forms themselves, and do not alter voter eligibility.
4. Questions?
If you have any questions please contact the WEC Help Deck at
elections@wi.gov
or by phone at (608) 261-2028. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

2026 General Election Ballot Access Challenge Info Memo
Summary.
On April 1, 2026, new permanent administrative rules from the Wisconsin Elections Commission (“the Commission”) went into effect. The new rules amend and create new standards for sufficiency of nomination papers, declarations of candidacy and create the challenge procedures used for both types of challenges. The new rules will first apply to the partisan candidate circulation period that begins on April 15, 2026.
Summary of Provisions (discussed in further detail below):
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05: Treatment and Validity of Nomination Papers.
The previous version of EL
§
2.05 was repealed and recreated, mainly to incorporate recent Commission guidance.
Wis.
Admin. Code § EL 2.06: Treatment and Sufficiency of Declarations of Candidacy
. This is a new rule that provides set standards for declaration of candidacy sufficiency.
Wis
.
Admin. Code § EL 2.07
: Challenges to Nomination Papers: The previous version of EL
§
2.07 was repealed and recreated to provide more detailed procedures for nomination paper challenges.
Wis
.
Admin. Code § EL 2.08: Challenges to Declarations of Candidacy
: This is a new rule that creates a separate challenge process for challenges against a declaration of candidacy. It largely mirrors the nomination paper challenge rule with a few differences.
Background.
These administrative rules were created for better consistency and clarity for candidates and challengers. The rules address several shortcomings in the former versions and mostly codify existing Commission guidance and practice. This will ensure that all candidates and challengers are on equal footing, and that everyone is able to rely on one detailed playbook whenever a ballot access challenge is filed.
§ EL 2.05: Treatment and Validity of Nomination Papers
Most of the content of § EL 2.05 remains the same, but it has been reorganized and expanded to include additional detail.
Changes to § EL 2.05 – Treatment and Sufficiency of Nomination Papers
New Definition Section
. The definitions in the new rule codify how the Commission has consistently interpreted terms such as “substantial compliance” and “facial sufficiency” in the context of nomination papers and challenges. The former rule did not define any of these terms.
Clarity for Facial Review
. The new rule clarifies the scope and purpose of an initial facial review for ballot access paperwork, which is something filing officers typically offer before the filing deadline as a courtesy to candidates when they turn in their paperwork. Facial review refers to the process by which a filing officer, or their staff, review ballot access paperwork for compliance and determine if any required elements are missing, illegible, or incorrect.
Candidates in the past have sometimes been upset when challenged over something the filing officer did not notice, so the rule clarifies and confirms that initial facial review is done only as a courtesy and is subject to any challenges.
Correcting Affidavits
. Some, but not all, insufficiencies in nomination papers can be corrected by an affidavit of the circulator, the candidate, or the person who signed the nomination papers. Under the new deadline, correcting affidavits must be filed within three days after the filing deadline for challenges to nomination papers. They can sometimes resolve the basis of a challenge before it is even filed. The new rule provides much more detail on correcting affidavits than the former rule.
Common Challenges
. The new rule also establishes the interpretations from common nomination paper challenges that the Commission has decided over the past several years. For example, the new rule provides standards for a signatory’s information to be legible, and what happens when information is missing from the header of the nomination paper.
Header Sufficiency
. The new rule addresses each aspect of the nomination paper header and provides guidance on standards for sufficiency. The former rule never addressed the header of the nomination paper. This has been the source of many recent challenges.
§ EL 2.06: Treatment and Sufficiency of Declarations of Candidacy
This provision creates standards for the review and sufficiency of declarations of candidacy.
How to Review a DOC
. The new rule makes it clear that initial facial review of a DOC when it is filed is done as a courtesy only and does not immunize a candidate from challenges for issues that are not noticed by the filing officer. Until this rule, there was no statute or administrative code provision that offered direction on how a filing officer should review a DOC for sufficiency.
No Correcting Affidavits
. The new rule confirms that correcting affidavits cannot be used to fix a DOC, and the DOC must be sufficient by the deadline. Instead, the candidate should file an amended DOC if information changes after it has been filed.
Missing Information
. The new rule directs a filing officer to notify the candidate if any information is missing on the DOC, or if the filing officer cannot accept it.
Information provided
. The new rule goes through each required element of the DOC and provides details about what needs to be included by the candidate.
§ EL 2.07: Challenges to Nomination Papers
Most of the underlying principles of § EL 2.07 are the same, but the proposed rule significantly expands the existing rule, mostly to be consistent with current Commission practice.
Challenge Type Clarity
. The new rule removes references to filing ballot access challenges under Wis. Stat. §§ 5.05 or 5.06, which are two statutes that create administrative complaints for the Commission to decide. The former rule directed challenges to file ballot access challenges under those statutes. The new rule also confirms that a ballot access challenge is its own, special type of administrative complaint brought under Chapter EL 2 of the Admin Code.
More Procedural Detail
. The new rule provides much more detail and clarity on what constitutes a challenge and what constitutes a response. The former rule lacked detail for how the challenge and response materials are filed, and what they should contain. Commission staff frequently receive questions about what form their filings are supposed to take.
Better Public Access to Nomination Papers
. The new rule requires filing officers to make nomination papers available to the public within one business day of when they are filed. The window to challenge nomination papers is very short, meaning it is critical for the public to have quick access to candidates’ nomination papers.
Deadline Clarity
.
The new rule is unambiguous in that filing deadlines for challenge materials are due by 5:00 p.m. The former rule did not provide a clear time by which challenge materials should be filed, and in the past, there has been confusion from both candidates and challengers of whether their materials should be filed by 4:30 p.m. or 5:00 p.m.
The new rule confirms that a “calendar day” does include weekends and holidays for any deadline set by the rule. The former rule used “calendar day” without clarifying whether that includes weekends or holidays. This change is necessary to ensure that the challenge process can be completed in the short time window between the nomination paper filing deadline and the deadline to certify candidates to the ballot. This rule does not, and cannot, affect the statutory deadline for when nomination papers are filed, but it does clarify the deadlines for challenges that are governed by the rule.
Rebuttal Filing
. A new feature of the rule is giving the challenger the option of filing a rebuttal. Under the former rule, the challenger filed the challenge, the candidate responded, and then the challenger did not get a meaningful opportunity to respond to the candidate’s response. Under the new rule, the rebuttal is optional, and multiple provisions ensure that it cannot delay the filing officer’s ultimate ballot access decision by the statutory deadline.
More Clarity for Hearings
. The new rule provides much more detail on whether to hold a hearing to decide ballot a ballot access challenge, including requiring that the hearing be noticed and open to the public. While the former rule did allow for the filing officer to hold a hearing on a ballot access challenge, it provided no detail or guidance for what that entails. The Commission has established hearing procedures in place, but the rule offers little to no guidance to local filing officers who may struggle to understand what is required during a hearing.
Guidance in Case of Extension
. The new rule offers guidance on how to offer the same amount of challenge time to both parties when an incumbent fails to file a notification of noncandidacy and also fails to file nomination papers. The former rule did not address this uncommon, but important, situation that arises. In these cases, the filing deadline for nomination papers gets extended by 72 hours, which ensures the filing officer can meet the statutory deadline to certify the candidates to the ballot.
Basis for Challenges
. Challengers can challenge any aspect of nomination papers including individual signature lines, information in the header, circulator information, or any aspect of how the paperwork was prepared or filed. The new rule addresses each possible ground and directs challengers to identify the grounds under which they are bringing their challenge. This is an important improvement because challengers, especially those representing themselves, sometimes fail to clearly articulate what they are challenging and why. The former rule did not clearly address on what basis a challenger could challenge nomination papers, except to generally refer to the standards in § EL 2.05.
Final Decision for Challenge
. The new rule specifies that a filing officer must issue a written decision on a challenge, along with a directive to immediately transmit it to the parties. This is especially important if a candidate or challenger wishes to appeal the decision. The former rule merely stated that a filing officer shall “decide” the challenge, without providing greater detail about what that means.
Appeal
. The new rule provides a process for when a candidate or challenger wishes to appeal the decision of a local filing officer to the Commission. The former rule did not address appeal at all. The new rule also confirms that any ballot access challenge decision can be appealed to a circuit court pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 5.06(8).
§ EL 2.08: Challenges to Declarations of Candidacy
Since 2020, the Commission has received and decided about half a dozen challenges to candidates’ declarations of candidacy (“DOC”). The former administrative code did not provide any guidance for how to address these types of challenges, but the Commission has historically used the nomination paper challenge process nonetheless as a matter of equity. The new rule creates an administrative code procedure for these types of challenges so that everyone may be on equal footing and not subject to the discretion of the filing officer.
Challenge Process Largely the Same
. The challenge process, mechanics, and deadlines mirror those in the proposed nomination paper challenge rule.
Basis for Challenges
. The proposed rule restricts this type of ballot access challenge to one or more of the enumerated grounds listed in the rule. It also requires a challenger to identify the specific grounds of the challenge. The proposed rule language makes it clear that general challenges to a candidate’s “character,” for example, would not be permitted under this rule.
Questions?
Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at
elections@wi.gov
or 608-261-2028.

the Commission to decide. The former rule directed challenges to file ballot access challenges 
under those statutes. The new rule also confirms that a ballot access challenge is its own, special 
type of administrative complaint brought under Chapter EL 2 of the Admin Code. More 
Procedural Detail. The new rule provides much more detail and clarity on what constitutes a 
challenge and what constitutes a response. The former rule lacked detail for how the challenge 
and response materials are filed, and what they should contain. Commission staff frequently 
receive questions about what form their filings are supposed to take. 
• Better Public Access to Nomination Papers. The new rule requires filing officers to make 
nomination papers available to the public within one business day of when they are filed. The 
window to challenge nomination papers is very short, meaning it is critical for the public to have 
quick access to candidates’ nomination papers. 
• Deadline Clarity. 
o The new rule is unambiguous in that filing deadlines for challenge materials are due by 
5:00 p.m. The former rule did not provide a clear time by which challenge materials 
should be filed, and in the past, there has been confusion from both candidates and 
challengers of whether their materials should be filed by 4:30 p.m. or 5:00 p.m. 
o The new rule confirms that a “calendar day” does include weekends and holidays for any 
deadline set by the rule. The former rule used “calendar day” without clarifying whether 
that includes weekends or holidays. This change is necessary to ensure that the challenge 
process can be completed in the short time window between the nomination paper filing 
deadline and the deadline to certify candidates to the ballot. This rule does not, and 
cannot, affect the statutory deadline for when nomination papers are filed, but it does 
clarify the deadlines for challenges that are governed by the rule.   
Law Change: New Ballot Access Administrative Rules 
4/15/2026 
Page 4 
 
 
• Rebuttal Filing. A new feature of the rule is giving the challenger the option of filing a rebuttal. 
Under the former rule, the challenger filed the challenge, the candidate responded, and then the 
challenger did not get a meaningful opportunity to respond to the candidate’s response. Under 
the new rule, the rebuttal is optional, and multiple provisions ensure that it cannot delay the filing 
officer’s ultimate ballot access decision by the statutory deadline. 
• More Clarity for Hearings. The new rule provides much more detail on whether to hold a 
hearing to decide ballot a ballot access challenge, including requiring that the hearing be noticed 
and open to the public. While the former rule did allow for the filing officer to hold a hearing on 
a ballot access challenge, it provided no detail or guidance for what that entails. The Commission 
has established hearing procedures in place, but the rule offers little to no guidance to local filing 
officers who may struggle to understand what is required during a hearing. 
• Guidance in Case of Extension. The new rule offers guidance on how to offer the same amount 
of challenge time to both parties when an incumbent fails to file a notification of noncandidacy 
and also fails to file nomination papers. The former rule did not address this uncommon, but 
important, situation that arises. In these cases, the filing deadline for nomination papers gets 
extended by 72 hours, which ensures the filing officer can meet the statutory deadline to certify 
the candidates to the ballot.  
• Basis for Challenges. Challengers can challenge any aspect of nomination papers including 
individual signature lines, information in the header, circulator information, or any aspect of how 
the paperwork was prepared or filed. The new rule addresses each possible ground and directs 
challengers to identify the grounds under which they are bringing their challenge. This is an 
important improvement because challengers, especially those representing themselves, 
sometimes fail to clearly articulate what they are challenging and why. The former rule did not 
clearly address on what basis a challenger could challenge nomination papers, except to 
generally refer to the standards in § EL 2.05. 
• Final Decision for Challenge. The new rule specifies that a filing officer must issue a written 
decision on a challenge, along with a directive to immediately transmit it to the parties. This is 
especially important if a candidate or challenger wishes to appeal the decision. The former rule 
merely stated that a filing officer shall “decide” the challenge, without providing greater detail 
about what that means. 
• Appeal. The new rule provides a process for when a candidate or challenger wishes to appeal the 
decision of a local filing officer to the Commission. The former rule did not address appeal at all. 
The new rule also confirms that any ballot access challenge decision can be appealed to a circuit 
court pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 5.06(8).  
6. § EL 2.08: Challenges to Declarations of Candidacy  
Since 2020, the Commission has received and decided about half a dozen challenges to candidates’ 
declarations of candidacy (“DOC”). The former administrative code did not provide any guidance for 
Law Change: New Ballot Access Administrative Rules 
4/15/2026 
Page 5 
 
 
how to address these types of challenges, but the Commission has historically used the nomination paper 
challenge process nonetheless as a matter of equity. The new rule creates an administrative code 
procedure for these types of challenges so that everyone may be on equal footing and not subject to the 
discretion of the filing officer. 
• Challenge Process Largely the Same. The challenge process, mechanics, and deadlines mirror 
those in the proposed nomination paper challenge rule.  
• Basis for Challenges. The proposed rule restricts this type of ballot access challenge to one or 
more of the enumerated grounds listed in the rule. It also requires a challenger to identify the 
specific grounds of the challenge. The proposed rule language makes it clear that general 
challenges to a candidate’s “character,” for example, would not be permitted under this rule.  
7. Questions? 
Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at elections@wi.gov or 608-261-2028.

___________________________________________________________________________________________________________

DATE:  April 14, 2026 
 
TO:  2026 Spring Election Candidates and Potential Challengers  
 
FROM: WEC Staff 
 
SUBJECT:  Ballot Access Challenge Period – April 15, 2026 – June 1, 2026  
 
 
1. Introduction 
 
The purpose of this memorandum is to explain the ballot access challenge process to candidates, challengers, 
and other interested parties. 
 
Starting April 15, 2026, candidates for the 2026 General Election may begin circulating nomination papers to 
run for office. Nomination papers must be filed by 5 p.m. on Monday, June 1, 2026. After that deadline, the 
ballot access challenge period will begin. Ballot access challenges are filed with the appropriate filing officer 
who received the challenged candidate’s nomination papers.  
 
Federal and State candidates, including district attorney candidates, file nomination papers with the Wisconsin 
Elections Commission. Local candidates file nomination papers with their municipal or county clerk. The 
deadlines and legal procedure described in this memo apply to all candidates, federal, state, or local, though this 
memo will focus on the Commission’s ballot access challenge process. Local candidates should connect with 
their municipal clerk to understand the specifics of how local challenges will be handled.  
 
Challenges to nomination papers filed with the Commission for the 2026 General Election will be considered 
and determined by the Wisconsin Elections Commission at its June 9, 2026, meeting, beginning at 10:00 a.m. 
 
New Administrative Rules in Place April 1, 2026 
 
The Commission has promulgated new permanent administrative rules regarding ballot access paperwork 
sufficiency and challenges. The 2026 General Election circulation period is the first filing period after the new 
rules go into effect. The new rules provide greater clarity for ballot access sufficiency, expand the procedure 
and process for ballot access challenges, and create a separate, dedicated process for challenges to declarations 
of candidacy.  
 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL  2.05, Treatment and Validity of Nomination Papers 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06, Treatment and Sufficiency of Declarations of Candidacy 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07, Challenges to Nomination Papers 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.08, Challenges to Declarations of Candidacy 
 
 
Ballot Access Challenge Period – June 4 – June 9, 2026 
April 13, 2026 
Page 2 
 
 
2. Deadlines for the 2026 General Election Nomination Paper Challenge Period
1 
 
Monday, June 1, 2026, at 5:00:00 p.m. – Nomination papers must be filed not later than 5:00 p.m. Wis. Stat. 
§§ 8.15(1); 8.20(8)(a).  
 
Thursday, June 4, 2026, at 5:00:00 p.m. – Challenges to nomination papers must be filed not later than 
5:00:00 p.m. Wis. Adm. Code EL §§ 2.07(3)(b), 2.08(2)(b). The verified challenge may be filed in person with 
the Commission at its offices at 201 W. Washington Avenue, 2nd Floor, Madison, Wisconsin, 53703, or 
preferably emailed to: elections@wi.gov.   
 
Sunday, June 7, 2026, at 5:00:00 p.m. – Last possible deadline to file a response to the challenge. 
Responses must be filed within three calendar days of when the challenge is filed, so this deadline could be 
earlier depending on when the challenge was filed. Wis. Admin. Code EL §§ 2.07(3)(f); 2.08(2)(f). Responses 
filed on Saturday (June 6) or Sunday (June 7) must be submitted by email to elections@wi.gov or by fax to 608-
267-0500. 
 
Sunday, June 7, 2026, at 5:00:00 p.m. – NEW: Last possible deadline to file correcting affidavits. Under 
the Commission’s new administrative rules, correcting affidavits may now be filed not later than 5 p.m. on the 
third calendar day after the challenge deadline. Correcting affidavits submitted on Saturday (June 6) or Sunday 
(June 7) must be submitted by email to elections@wi.gov or by fax to 608-267-0500.  
 
Sunday, June 7, 2026, at 5:00:00 p.m. – Deadline by which candidate and challenger should indicate to the 
Commission if they wish to appear at the June 9 Commission meeting to address the Commission.  
 
Monday, June 8, 2026, with 24 Hours of Response Transmittal – Deadline by which challenger shall file a 
rebuttal (if any). If choosing to submit a rebuttal, it must be filed within 24 hours of when the filing officer 
transmits the response to the challenger. Wis. Admin. Code EL §§ 2.07(3)(g); 2.08(2)(g).  
 
Tuesday, June 9, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. – The Commission will meet to consider the challenges, responses, and to 
hear any oral presentations by the Commission staff, challengers, and candidates. Both the challenger (or by 
representation) and the candidate (or by representation) may appear before the Commission. The virtual 
meeting will begin at 10:00 a.m. and be held on Zoom. Instructions for appearing via Zoom will be provided 
separately. The challenger and the candidate will each receive 5 minutes for their presentation to the 
Commission. 
 
3. Ballot Access Challenge Basics 
 
All challengers and challenged candidates should thoroughly review Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL  2.05, EL 2.06, 
EL 2.07, and EL 2.08, as well as the Commission’s Ballot Access Resource page before filing or responding to 
a ballot access challenge. This memo should not be used as the exclusive resource for understanding ballot 
access challenge procedure.  
There are two types of ballot access challenges:  
 
1 Under Wis. Stat. §§ 8.15(1) and 8.20(8)(a), for any office for which an incumbent has failed to file a Notification of Non-candidacy 
and has also failed to file nomination papers and a declaration of candidacy, a 72- hour extension of the time in which to file 
nomination papers and a declaration of candidacy for that office will be granted to any person other than the incumbent . Therefore, the 
deadlines set forth in this Memorandum do not apply in such circumstances, and any challenges to nomination papers filed purs uant to 
that extension will be resolved on a case-by-case basis unless all materials are received with sufficient time before the June 9, 2026 , 
Commission meeting. 
Ballot Access Challenge Period – June 4 – June 9, 2026 
April 13, 2026 
Page 3 
 
 
 
1. Nomination Paper Challenges – Challenging any aspect of how a candidate prepared and 
circulated their nomination paper challenges, including to individual signature lines, to the header or 
circulator sufficiency, or to the timeliness and method of preparing, circulating, and filing.  
2. Declaration of Candidacy Challenges – Challenging any aspect of how a candidate prepared and 
filed their declaration of candidacy, including to a candidate’s certifications that they meet, or will 
meet, the qualifications for the office they seek.  
 
Regardless of which type of challenge is filed, the same general procedures apply to both:  
• All challenges must include a short, plain statement of the basis for the challenge. Factual allegations 
must be verified by individuals with personal knowledge. A brief or summary of legal standards may be 
filed as a part of, or simultaneously with, the challenge. The brief need not be verified, but if it is 
prepared by an attorney, the attorney must sign the brief. Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL 2.07(3)(ar), EL 
2.08(2)(ar).  
• The challenge should be well-organized so the Commission can easily determine which individual 
signatures are being challenged (if any) and which aspects of the header, circulator certification, or 
method of circulating and filing are being challenged. All challenges must refer to the nomination 
paper page number as shown on the nomination papers filed with the WEC for each signature or 
page challenged. If a nomination paper page does not have a page number, contact the Commission’s 
staff to establish a number for that page. (For example: John Smith. Page 1 or Tom Jones Pages 3–12 
and 15–23, etc.) 
• All responses must also include a short, plain statement covering why the ballot access paperwork is 
sufficient. The same standards for factual matters and brief filing discussed above apply to the response. 
Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL 2.07(3)(e), EL 2.08(2)(e). 
• The challenger may, but is not required to, file a rebuttal to the candidate’s response ahead of the 
Commission’s ballot access meeting on June 9. Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL 2.07(3)(g); EL 2.08(2)(g). 
• The initial burden is on the challenger to establish any deficiency in the candidate’s ballot access 
paperwork. If the challenger makes an initial showing by clear, satisfactory, and convincing evidence 
that establishes the deficiency, the burden shifts to the challenged candidate to establish the validity of 
their ballot access paperwork by clear, satisfactory, and convincing evidence. Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL  
2.07(4), EL 2.08(3).  
• Commission staff will prepare a report on the challenges and responses to present to the Commission on 
June 9.  
 
5.  Recommended Structure and Organization for a Ballot Access Challenge  
 
Step One: Clearly indicate whether the challenge is to the candidate’s nomination papers or declaration of 
candidacy.  
 
Step Two: For nomination paper challenges, organize the discrete components in the following suggested 
order:  
 
• First: Challenges that would invalidate an entire page (or pages) of signatures. These would include 
challenges to the header, the circulator certification, the timeliness of filing, or any other grounds other 
than individual signature lines. Starting with full-page challenges could avoid unnecessary work of 
analyzing individual signatures if the entire page is invalid (though challengers still should include any 
insufficient signatures as part of their challenge in case the Commission’ rejects the full-page challenge).  
Ballot Access Challenge Period – June 4 – June 9, 2026 
April 13, 2026 
Page 4 
 
 
o Challenges to an entire page or to a group of pages, because of a deficiency (or deficiencies) in 
the heading or in the certificate of the circulator, should include a copy of at least one of the 
pages with the deficiency (or deficiencies) circled and, again, must refer, by page number, to the 
page or pages challenged. (For example: John Smith pages 1 through 27 fail to name the 
candidate or Tom Jones pages 2,3,6-11 &15-19 fail to identify the office sought, and pages 5-23 
fail to contain the signature of the circulator, etc.)   
• Second: Challenges that would invalidate individual signature lines. Any aspect of individual signature 
lines of signers may be challenged, including:  
o The form of the signature itself 
o The signer’s eligibility to sign the nomination paper 
o The fact that a signer signed one candidate’s nomination papers more than once 
o Any other ground of invalidity covered by Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h).  
o Challenges to individual signatures on various pages should include a copy of each and every 
page on which one or more signatures are challenged. Each page should be numbered as 
described above and the challenge should refer to the signature(s) challenged, by page and line 
number. (For example: John Smith Page 3, Line 6 - the address of the signatory is outside the 
XX Assembly District.)  
 
Step Three: Neatly organize any supporting documentation or affidavits with attachment, appendix, or exhibit 
numbers or letters, and use those references throughout your complaint so the Commission knows where to look 
in your supporting materials.  
 
*** 
 
If you have any questions, please contact the Commission by email elections@wi.gov with “Attn: Legal” in the 
subject line, or call Angela O’Brien Sharpe at 608-264-6764 or Brandon Hunzicker at 608-267-0714 and ask to 
speak with an attorney.
