No.  2024AP408 
 
2 
 
Kormanik summary and declaratory judgment  for multiple reasons. 1  Based upon our review of 
the briefs and record, we conclude at conference that this case is appropriate for summary 
disposition.  See WIS. STAT. RULE 809.21 (2023 -24).2  Because the circuit court lacked 
competency to proceed to the merits of Kormanik’s dec laratory judgment action , we summarily 
reverse. 
The parties do not dispute the facts pertinent to this appeal.   Shortly before the Fall 
primary elections in 2022, Kormanik filed the circuit court action underlying this appeal.  She 
sought a declaratory jud gment invalidating the WEC’s guidance3 interpreting the election 
statutes as allowing voters who returned their absentee ballots early to spoil them before election 
day and cast a new ballot.   Both the DNC and Rise, Inc. successfully intervened in the acti on.  
The parties fought procedural battles that took issues up to our supreme court, through this court, 
and back to the circuit court .  See State ex rel. Kormanik v. Brash , 2022 WI 67, 404 Wis.  2d 
568, 980 N.W.2d 948. 
Upon the action’s return to the circuit court, t he court granted a temporary injunction 
against the enforcement of the challenged guidance, and the parties filed cross motions for 
summary judgment.  The court held oral argument on the motions and issued a written decision 
                                                 
1  Although the individual appellants present slightly differing arguments, we treat the appellants 
collectively for purposes of this summary disposition order.  Further, we do not address in this summary 
disposition order all of the arguments advanced by t he parties because we decide this appeal on the 
narrowest ground possible.  See Village of Slinger v. Polk Properties LLC , 2021 WI 29, ¶26 n.12, 396 
Wis. 2d 342, 957 N.W.2d 229. 
2  All references to the Wisconsin Statutes are to the 2023-24 version. 
3  We use the term “guidance” generally to refer to the memorand a WEC issued instructing how 
clerks should handle absentee ballots.  We do not reach the merits of Kormanik’s argument as to whether 
these memoranda constituted unpromulgated “rules.” 
Case 2024AP000408 Opinion/Decision Filed 02-11-2026
Page 2 of 6
Case 2022CV001395 Document 212 Filed 02-11-2026
Page 2 of 6

No.  2024AP408 
 
3 
 
granting Korman ik’s motion.  It first rejected the appellants’ threshold arguments that (1) the 
court lacked competency to proceed to the merits because Kormanik had failed to timely serve 
the pleadings on the joint committee for review of administrative rules (JCRAR)  as required by 
WIS. STAT. § 227.40(1), and (2) Kormanik lacked standing because she was not directly harmed 
by the challenged administrative guidance.  The court then proceeded to the merits .  It granted 
summary judgment in Kormanik’s favor, declaring that t he challenged guidance violated 
Wisconsin law.  The WEC, the DNC, and Rise, Inc. appeal. 
The appellants argue that the circuit court lacked competency to reach  the merits of 
Kormanik’s declaratory judgment action.   Specifically, citing WIS. STAT. § 227.40(5) and 
Richards v. Young , 150 Wis.  2d 549, 557, 441 N.W.2d 742 (1989), the appellants assert that 
because Kormanik did not timely serve a copy of her pleadings on the JCRAR, the court did not 
have competency to proceed to the merits of the declaratory judgment action.  Because we are 
bound by the statute and our supreme court’s interpretation of it  in Richards, we conclude the 
circuit court’s decision must be reversed. 
The circuit court lacks competency to proceed when a party fails to properly compl ete 
timely service.  See Wisconsin Power and Light Co. v. PSC , 2006 WI App 221, ¶11, 296 
Wis. 2d 705, 725 N.W.2d 423; see also Weisensel v. Wisconsin DHSS , 179 Wis. 2d 637, 643, 
508 N.W.2d 33 (Ct. App. 1993).  Whether a circuit court has lost competency is a question of 
law that we review de novo.  Village of Trempealeau v. Mikrut , 2004 WI 79, ¶7, 273 Wis. 2d 
76, 681 N.W.2d 190. 
A plaintiff who files a WIS. STAT. § 227.40(1) action must timely serve a copy of he r 
pleadings upon JCRAR, which enables JCRAR to become a party to the case, if it so chooses.  
Case 2024AP000408 Opinion/Decision Filed 02-11-2026
Page 3 of 6
Case 2022CV001395 Document 212 Filed 02-11-2026
Page 3 of 6

No.  2024AP408 
 
4 
 
See § 227.40(5).  WISCONSIN STAT. § 13.56(2) requires timely service on “[t]he cochairpersons 
of [JCRAR] or their designated agents [.]”  Our supreme court has hel d that t o properly 
commence a declaratory judgment action under § 227.40, a plaintiff must serve the JCRAR 
within the same timeframe as required to serve a defendant.   Richards, 150 Wis. 2d  at 555 
(citing WIS. STAT. § 893.02).  The JCRAR service requiremen t is “not permissive,” but rather 
“mandatory.”  Richards, 150 Wis. 2d at 555.  Failure to serve the JCRAR within the requisite 
time period deprives the circuit court of competency over the action.  Id. at 551-54, 558. 
As to the circuit court’s competency, Kormanik argues that we should affirm the court.  
She claims that she  served a designated agent of the  JCRAR by timely serving a file-stamped 
copy of the summons and complaint on a private attorney who had been retaine d as counsel for 
the Wisconsin State Legislature in a separate case.  Kormanik asserts that service on that attorney 
was within the spirit of the statute, asking us to affirm  the court’s conclusion that , although it 
would have been “preferable” for Kormani k to have served the co -chairs of the JCRAR, service 
on the attorney of record from a different court case was nonetheless “sufficient” to meet the 
statutory requirements.   
After thorough review and consideration, we conclude that strict compliance with s ervice 
requirements is mandatory and that Kormanik’s failure to properly serve the JCRAR deprived 
the circuit court of competenc y to decide the merits .  A failure to comply with WIS. STAT. 
§ 227.40(5)’s service requirement is fatal to a plaintiff’s claim.  See Wisconsin Power and Light 
Co., 296 Wis. 2d 705, ¶11 (holding “[t]he failure to comply with the mandatory time limitation” 
for “filing and serving a petition for judicial review of an agency decision” “results in the loss of 
the circuit court’s competency to proceed and the petition must be dismissed.”)  
Case 2024AP000408 Opinion/Decision Filed 02-11-2026
Page 4 of 6
Case 2022CV001395 Document 212 Filed 02-11-2026
Page 4 of 6

No.  2024AP408 
 
5 
 
We cannot conclude on the record before us that Kormanik made timely service of the 
pleadings on the JCRAR  because, as we now briefly explain, t his record contains no such 
evidence.  We reject Kormanik’ s argument that service on a private  attorney representing the 
legislature in a separate case in lieu of service on the cochairs of the JCRAR or their designated 
agents in this case is “sufficient”  to confer on the circuit court competency to proceed to th e 
merits of the declaratory judgment action.  This argument  implies that strict compliance with 
WIS. STAT. § 227.40 is not required.  However, as explained, Wisconsin caselaw has consistently 
held that strict compliance with service requirements is mandatory for a court to have 
competency to proceed with judicial review of an agency decision.  “Strict compliance” within 
this context requires timely service on the cochairs of the JCRAR or their designated agent , and 
we see nothing in the record suffic ient to establish that the JCRAR had designated the private 
attorney for the legislature in a different case as their agent for service of pleadings challenging 
the ballot-spoliation guidance.4 
In summary, despite Kormanik’s belief that it would be “suffic ient” to serve an attorney 
who might have a connection to the JCRAR , it remains that strict compliance with service 
                                                 
4  Kormanik also argues that she intended to bring  this declaratory judgment action  under WIS. 
STAT. § 806.04(11) rather than WIS. STAT. § 227.40(1).  However, this distinction does not matter as 
Kormanik’s argument relies on § 806.04(11), which also says:  
In any proceeding under this section in which the constitutionality, 
construction or application of any provision of ch . 227, or of any statute 
allowing a le gislative committee to suspend, or to delay or prevent the 
adoption of, a rule as defined in s . 227.01 (13) is placed in issue by the 
parties, the joint committee for review of administrative rules shall be 
served with a copy of the petition and, with the approval of the joint 
committee on legislative organization, shall be made a party and be 
entitled to be heard.    
(Emphasis added.) 
Case 2024AP000408 Opinion/Decision Filed 02-11-2026
Page 5 of 6
Case 2022CV001395 Document 212 Filed 02-11-2026
Page 5 of 6

No.  2024AP408 
 
6 
 
requirements is mandatory for the circuit court to have competency to reach the merits of 
Kormanik’s petition, and Kormanik failed to meet t hose requirements.  The court did not have 
competency to proceed to the merits.  Accordingly, it should have dismissed Kormanik’s action.   
Upon the foregoing reasons, 
IT IS ORDERED that the judgment of the circuit court is summarily reversed.  See WIS. 
STAT. RULE 809.21. 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that this summary disposition order will not be published.

The Wisconsin Elections Commission has developed a social media calendar designed to help inform and educate voters on key election-related topics.
We will be sending out a more robust version closer to the Spring Election, but we wanted to send out a few examples for those that will be having municipal primaries. Tuesday, November 4, 2025
To
Milwaukee County Election Commission
Wisconsin County Clerks

Type A Notice of Spring Election MEMO 2026.pdf
The Type A Notice of the Spring Election, to be held on
April 7, 2026
, contains all state level and judicial offices to be elected throughout the state. Please select the judicial offices that are up for election in your county, and add any county offices, multi-jurisdictional municipal judges and/or referenda. Please contact us immediately if you have any questions or concerns about the offices listed as up for election in your county.
The Type A Notice of the 2025 Spring Election must be published by all county clerks on
November 25, 2025
. Whenever a weekly newspaper is used for publication, the notices appear in the newspaper's closest preceding issue.
Please send a copy of the Type A Notice to each municipal clerk.
Municipal clerks are required to publish a Type A notice of municipal offices on the same date, November 25, 2025
.
Note
:
If a Circuit Court Judge resigns on or before December 1, 2025, that office will be up for election at the 2026 Spring Election. If a judicial vacancy occurs during this period, we will contact the affected county clerks with an amended Type A Notice.
Offices to Be Elected at the 2026 Spring Election
Justice of the Supreme Court
- This office appears on the judicial ballot in all counties.
Court of Appeals, District I
- This office appears on the judicial ballot in Milwaukee County.
Court of Appeals, District II
- This office appears on the judicial ballot in Calumet, Fond du Lac, Green Lake, Kenosha, Manitowoc, Ozaukee, Racine, Sheboygan, Walworth, Washington, Waukesha, and Winnebago counties.
Court of Appeals, District IV
-
This office appears on the judicial ballot in
Adams, Clark, Columbia, Crawford, Dane, Dodge, Grant, Green, Iowa, Jackson, Jefferson, Juneau, La Crosse, Lafayette, Marquette, Monroe, Portage, Richland, Rock, Sauk, Vernon, Waupaca, Waushara, and Wood counties.
Circuit Court Judge
- This office appears on the judicial ballot in Barron, Brown, Chippewa, Dane, Dodge, Dunn, Florence, Forest, Fond du Lac, Iron, Juneau, Marathon, Milwaukee, Outagamie, St. Croix, Washburn, Washington, Waukesha, Waupaca, and Wood counties.
Judicial Office Candidate Checklist
The
Judicial Candidates ballot access checklist
(ELIS-1) is available on the WEC website on the State Candidates page under Non-Partisan:
https://elections.wi.gov/candidates/state-candidates
. The
Multi-Jurisdictional Municipal Judge Candidate checklist
(ELIS-18) is on the Local Candidates page under Non-Partisan:
https://elections.wi.gov/candidates/local-candidates
. The checklists assist candidates in qualifying for ballot placement. The checklists may be reproduced and given to your candidates along with the proper ballot access forms:
Campaign Finance Registration Statement
(CF-1)
https://ethics.wi.gov/Resources/CF-1%20Registration%20Statement%20Fillable.pdf
Declaration of Candidacy
(EL-162)
https://elections.wi.gov/wec-form/declaration-candidacy-el-162-162sd
We also recommend that, in your initial discussions with candidates, you direct their attention to the WEC’s
Getting on the Ballot
page which can be found here:
https://elections.wi.gov/candidates/getting-ballot
. It is a good resource for both candidates and filing officers to prevent errors on nomination papers and avoid challenges.
Additional Information
State Referendum Questions -
At this time, there are no state referenda for the April 7, 2026, Spring Election. However, the legislature has until January 27, 2026, to direct that a referendum question be placed on the ballot, so that possibility still exists. Wis. Stat. § 8.37. We will monitor the activity of the legislature and keep you informed.
Non-Candidacy Notification - For the Spring 2026 Election, any incumbent officeholder for state office who does not intend to seek re-election should file a Notification of Noncandidacy Form (EL-163) no later than 5:00 p.m. on Friday, December 26, 2025.
The EL-163 is available from the Wisconsin Elections Commission website:
https://elections.wi.gov/wec-form/notification-noncandidacy-el-163
. If an incumbent not seeking re-election does not file the notification by the deadline and does not file ballot access documents by the required statutory deadline to seek re-election (January 6, 2026), the filing deadline will be extended an additional 72 hours for any other person wishing to run for that office. The deadline is not extended for the incumbent. If an incumbent not seeking re-election files the notification timely, the nomination paper deadline of January 6, 2026, is unchanged. If the incumbent decides to run for office after filing the notification, he or she can run for re-election by filing the appropriate ballot access papers by the January 6 deadline.
WEC staff recommends that you send the non-candidacy form, along with a short explanation, to all your incumbents
in early December to prevent any extension of the filing deadline.
Questions
If you have any questions concerning this memorandum, please contact the Help Desk at 608- 261-2028 or
elections@wi.gov
.

MEMORANDUM 
  
TO:  Wisconsin County Clerks  
Milwaukee County Election Commission  
 
FROM: Wisconsin Elections Commission  
Election Administration Team 
 
DATE: November 3, 2025 
 
SUBJECT:  Type A Notice of April 7, 2026, Spring Election and Other Important Information  
 
This memo includes useful information for the upcoming Spring Election. 
 
Notice of Election 
The Type A Notice of the Spring Election, to be held on April 7, 2026, contains all state level and judicial 
offices to be elected throughout the state. Please select the judicial offices that are up for election in your 
county, and add any county offices, multi-jurisdictional municipal judges and/or referenda. Please contact us 
immediately if you have any questions or concerns about the offices listed as up for election in your county. 
 
The Type A Notice of the 2025 Spring Election must be published by all county clerks on November 25, 2025. 
Whenever a weekly newspaper is used for publication, the notices appear in the newspaper's closest preceding 
issue. 
 
Please send a copy of the Type A Notice to each municipal clerk. Municipal clerks are required to publish a 
Type A notice of municipal offices on the same date, November 25, 2025. 
 
Note:  If a Circuit Court Judge resigns on or before December 1, 2025, that office will be up for election at the 
2026 Spring Election. If a judicial vacancy occurs during this period, we will contact the affected county clerks 
with an amended Type A Notice.   
 
Explanation of County Executive/County Supervisor Term Expirations 
The Type A Notice displays the expiration date of the terms of office for County Executive and County 
Supervisor as April 20, 2026. This is the day before winning candidates take office on the third Tuesday in 
April (April 21, 2026). 
 
The statutes do not definitively provide when the terms for County Executive and County Supervisor officially 
end. They simply state when the terms begin. If, due to your county's procedures, you are more comfortable 
with the expiration date of the term being the same as the date the new term begins, you may use that date. 
 
 
 
 
Type A Notice of April 7, 2026, Spring Election and Other Important Information  
November 3, 2025 
 
Offices to Be Elected at the 2026 Spring Election 
Justice of the Supreme Court - This office appears on the judicial ballot in all counties. 
 
Court of Appeals, District I - This office appears on the judicial ballot in Milwaukee County. 
 
Court of Appeals, District II - This office appears on the judicial ballot in Calumet, Fond du Lac, Green Lake, 
Kenosha, Manitowoc, Ozaukee, Racine, Sheboygan, Walworth, Washington, Waukesha, and Winnebago 
counties. 
 
Court of Appeals, District IV - This office appears on the judicial ballot in Adams, Clark, Columbia, 
Crawford, Dane, Dodge, Grant, Green, Iowa, Jackson, Jefferson, Juneau, La Crosse, Lafayette, Marquette, 
Monroe, Portage, Richland, Rock, Sauk, Vernon, Waupaca, Waushara, and Wood counties. 
 
Circuit Court Judge - This office appears on the judicial ballot in Barron, Brown, Chippewa, Dane, Dodge, 
Dunn, Florence, Forest, Fond du Lac, Iron, Juneau, Marathon, Milwaukee, Outagamie, St. Croix, Washburn, 
Washington, Waukesha, Waupaca, and Wood counties. 
 
Judicial Office Candidate Checklist  
The Judicial Candidates ballot access checklist (ELIS-1) is available on the WEC website on the State 
Candidates page under Non-Partisan: https://elections.wi.gov/candidates/state-candidates. The Multi-
Jurisdictional Municipal Judge Candidate checklist (ELIS-18) is on the Local Candidates page under Non-
Partisan: https://elections.wi.gov/candidates/local-candidates. The checklists assist candidates in qualifying for 
ballot placement. The checklists may be reproduced and given to your candidates along with the proper ballot 
access forms:  
 
• Campaign Finance Registration Statement (CF-1) https://ethics.wi.gov/Resources/CF-
1%20Registration%20Statement%20Fillable.pdf  
• Declaration of Candidacy (EL-162) https://elections.wi.gov/wec-form/declaration-candidacy-el-162-
162sd   
 
We also recommend that, in your initial discussions with candidates, you direct their attention to the WEC’s 
Getting on the Ballot page which can be found here: https://elections.wi.gov/candidates/getting-ballot. It is a 
good resource for both candidates and filing officers to prevent errors on nomination papers and avoid 
challenges.  
 
Additional Information 
State Referendum Questions - At this time, there are no state referenda for the April 7, 2026, Spring Election. 
However, the legislature has until January 27, 2026, to direct that a referendum question be placed on the ballot, 
so that possibility still exists. Wis. Stat. § 8.37. We will monitor the activity of the legislature and keep you 
informed. 
 
Non-Candidacy Notification - For the Spring 2026 Election, any incumbent officeholder for state office 
who does not intend to seek re-election should file a Notification of Noncandidacy Form (EL-163) no later 
than 5:00 p.m. on Friday, December 26, 2025.  
 
The EL-163 is available from the Wisconsin Elections Commission website: https://elections.wi.gov/wec-
form/notification-noncandidacy-el-163. If an incumbent not seeking re-election does not file the notification by 
the deadline and does not file ballot access documents by the required statutory deadline to seek re-election 
(January 6, 2026), the filing deadline will be extended an additional 72 hours for any other person wishing to 
run for that office. The deadline is not extended for the incumbent. If an incumbent not seeking re-election files 
Type A Notice of April 7, 2026, Spring Election and Other Important Information  
November 3, 2025 
 
the notification timely, the nomination paper deadline of January 6, 2026, is unchanged. If the incumbent 
decides to run for office after filing the notification, he or she can run for re-election by filing the appropriate 
ballot access papers by the January 6 deadline. 
 
WEC staff recommends that you send the non-candidacy form, along with a short explanation, to all your 
incumbents in early December to prevent any extension of the filing deadline.

Notice of Election
The Type A Notice of Election contains all the state and federal offices for the partisan primary on August 11, 2026, and the general election on November 3, 2026. The Type A Notice must be published by all county clerks on
April 14, 2026.
When a weekly newspaper is used for publication and the paper is not published on Tuesdays, the notice shall appear in the newspaper’s closest preceding issue.
It is not necessary for each county to publish all the information contained in the enclosed Type A Notice. The notice published by each county clerk lists the information regarding the general election, all applicable congressional district offices for which an elector in the county may vote, all applicable legislative offices for which an elector in the county may vote, and all county partisan offices within your respective county. The notice must also include the statement about circulation and filing of nomination papers.
All county clerks are required to send the Type A Notice to each municipal clerk in their county no later than
April 7, 2026
. Municipal clerks are not required to publish the Type A Notice for the partisan primary and general election unless any separate municipal referenda are appearing on the ballot.
Beginning of Terms for Federal Offices vs. State and County Offices
In the past, we have received inquiries about the January 3
rd
date for the beginning of federal office terms. Article XX, Section 1 of the Amendments to the United States Constitution states: “The terms of Senators and Representatives end at noon on the 3rd day of January . . . and the terms of their successors shall then begin.”
State office terms are different from federal terms. Article XIII, Section 1 of the Wisconsin Constitution states: “The political year for this state shall commence on the first Monday of January in each year, and the general election shall be held on the Tuesday next succeeding the first Monday of November in even-numbered years.”
Therefore, the term for state and county offices elected on November 3, 2026, will begin on January 4, 2027.
County Candidate Checklists
The ballot access checklist for county partisan candidates (ELIS-16) is available on the WEC website:
https://elections.wi.gov/candidates/getting-ballot
The checklist assists county candidates in qualifying for ballot placement. The checklist may be reproduced and given to your candidates along with the proper ballot access forms:

https://elections.wi.gov/forms/EL-162
Nomination Paper for Partisan Office (EL-168 Rev. 03/2016)
https://elections.wi.gov/forms/EL-168
We also recommend that, in your initial discussions with candidates, you direct their attention to the WEC’s ballot access resources, including a video and manual on ballot access which can be found here:
https://elections.wi.gov/candidates/getting-ballot
.
Candidates may also benefit from reviewing the Common Nomination Paper Challenges Manual which can be found here:
https://elections.wi.gov/resources/manuals/common-nomination-paper-challenges-manual
. The Manual is a good resource for both candidates and filing officers to prevent errors on nomination papers and avoid challenges. The Manual outlines common challenges and how these challenges have been decided in the past.
Notification of Noncandidacy
For the Fall 2026 Election, any incumbent officeholder who does not intend to seek re-election should file a Notification of Noncandidacy Form (EL-163) no later than 5:00 p.m. on
Friday, May 22, 2026
.
If a filing officer receives a notification of non-candidacy from an incumbent, the filing officer is now required to promptly post public notice of that fact on their website, or, if they do not have a website, they can post that information in at least three different locations within the jurisdiction.
If an incumbent not seeking re-election to the same office in the same district does not file the notification by the deadline, and does not file ballot access documents by the required statutory deadline to seek re-election (June 1, 2026), the filing deadline will be extended an additional 72 hours for any other person wishing to run for that office.
The deadline is not extended for the incumbent. If an incumbent not seeking re-election files the notification timely, the nomination paper deadline of June 1, 2026, is unchanged. If the incumbent decides to run for office after filing the notification, he or she can run for re-election by filing the appropriate ballot access papers by the June 1
st
deadline.
WEC staff recommend that in early May you send this form, along with a short explanation, to all your incumbents.
The EL-163 is available from the Wisconsin Elections Commission website.
https://elections.wi.gov/forms/el-163-fillable

### UOCAVA Online Ballot Delivery Changes

*Source: https://elections.wi.gov/memo/uocava-online-ballot-delivery-changes. Fetched: 2026-09-10 (first seen 2026-09-10). Publisher's currency statement: Index page (Wayback snapshot 2026-08-07) lists items through 'Update on Ballot Spoiling Litigation — Wednesday, July 29, 2026'; each item carries its own publication date. Friday, May 29, 2026
To
City of Milwaukee Election Commission
Milwaukee County Election Commission
Wisconsin County Clerks
Wisconsin Municipal Clerks
Priority
High Priority
File Downloads
File
Ballot Access Deadlines and Ballot Proofing Resources.pdf
1. Summary.
Effective May 28, 2026, online ballot delivery directly through MyVote for Military and Permanent Overseas Voters is temporarily suspended. Electronic ballot delivery requests will instead be fulfilled by clerks via email or fax. Voters with existing online delivery requests on file will automatically have their delivery preference updated from “online” to “email.” Clerks will be required to email individual electronic ballots to these voters unless they request a different deliver method.
2. Background.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) is currently performing usability and accessibility reviews of all agency websites, including the MyVote website. The reviews assess compliance with federal accessibility requirements that will be effective next year and analyze agency websites for future compatibility with WisVote 2.0. The temporary suspension of online ballot delivery is necessary to standardize electronic ballot delivery and develop a process compatible with WisVote 2.0.
To support implementation of these changes, the WEC has updated the necessary training materials and will deploy related system updates on May 28, 2026.
3. Action Items.
The WEC will provide municipalities with a list of voters who have active online ballot delivery requests on file, along with a template letter for notifying affected voters. WisVote will automatically update these voters’ absentee ballot delivery method from “online” to “email.” Clerks who do not receive a voter list are not required to take any action.
Because voters will no longer have the option to request online ballot delivery through MyVote, clerks may see an increase in requests for ballot delivery by email or postal mail for voters who previously selected online delivery. No other procedures are impacted at this time.
Clerks who receive a voter list should:
Send the provided template letter only to voters with active online ballot delivery requests on file.
Update voter delivery preferences if a voter requests an alternative method, such as postal mail.
Manually send ballots by email to affected voters when ballots become available if no alternative preference is provided by the voter.
4. Voter Questions.
Clerks may receive questions from Military and Permanent Overseas Voters regarding why online ballot delivery through MyVote is no longer available. Clerks should inform voters that the online ballot delivery option has been temporarily suspended as part of ongoing usability and accessibility updates to the MyVote website.
Eligible military and overseas voters may still request to receive their absentee ballot electronically by email or fax. To do so, voters must submit a written request to their municipal clerk. This request may be submitted through MyVote or by directly emailing the clerk. Upon receiving a written request for email delivery, clerks may continue providing absentee ballots electronically via email in accordance with existing procedures.
5. Questions.
Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at
elections@wi.gov
or 608-261-2028.

 SUBJECT: August Ballot Access and Proofing Dates and Reminders 
1. Summary 
As counties prepare, proof and print ballots for the August 11, 2026 Partisan Primary, please take note of 
the following dates and resources to assist clerks.   
• June 8 the WEC will draw for unofficial, preliminary ballot order. 
• June 9 at10:00 a.m. the WEC will meet to consider challenges and ballots access for all 
candidates and contests that fall in the normal deadlines. 
• June 10 at 3:00 p.m. the WEC will meet for a second time to consider challenges and ballot 
access for all candidates and contests where the deadline was extended for failure to file a 
notice of non-candidacy.  The WEC will also issue the Type B Notice (earliest possible date 
given deadlines).  
• June 24 is the deadline for county clerks to distribute ballots to all municipal clerks. 
• Because of the number of contests and candidates, clerks may need to plan for longer than 
usual ballot paper.  
• Please send county ballot proofs to the WEC as soon as they are ready for review.   
• Note additional resources at the end of this memo related to ballot access and challenges and 
ballot proofing. 
2. Ballot Access Timeline 
• June 1 – Nomination Paper Filing deadline for Fall Candidates 
• June 2 – Filing deadline for Partisan Primary Referenda 
• June 4 – Statement of Economic Interest deadline for Fall Candidates

• June 4 -- (5:00 p.m.) Deadline to file a challenge against a candidate’s nomination papers in

contests with an extension (Offices of Lieutenant Governor, Representative in Congress, District 
7, Representative to Assembly District 56, and Representative to Assembly District 50) 
• June 7-10 -- Various deadlines related to challenge responses, replies, rebuttals, and correcting 
affidavits for all contests including extended contests.

counties. WEC is unable to draw for preliminary ballot order before this date given correcting 
affidavits can be filed (determining who may have enough signatures to qualify) until Sunday, 
June 7 at 5:00 p.m.  
• June 9 (10:00 a.m.) – WEC Ballot Access Meeting for contests that have not been extended.  At 
the end of the day, WEC will send counties a list of candidates who have been approved for 
ballot access.  However, the Type B notice cannot be issued until all candidates, including those 
in races with an extension, have been approved.  
• June 10 (3:00 p.m.) –WEC Ballot Access Meeting for contests that have been extended.

• June 11 – County clerks send ballot proofs to the WEC as soon as possible before printing 
The WEC understands the urgency counties feel when trying to stay on top of deadlines for ballot 
design, proofing, printing and distribution. Because of the deadlines set in state statute for ballot access, 
some counties may have ballot proofs mostly prepared before the final Candidates on Ballot by Election 
Report – which includes candidate names and order – can be produced.  
3. Expect Long Ballots 
With five parties, dozens of contests, and a significant number of candidates, the 2026 August Partisan 
Primary ballot will be long. In some cases, counties may not be able to include all contests on the 
standard 14-inch ballot and must move to longer ballot stock instead. County Clerks should determine 
if that will be necessary for their ballots and prepare with relevant parties (vendors, printers, etc.) on the 
logistics. This may affect paper ballot stock as well as accessible equipment and counties should confirm 
with vendors.  
Counties or municipalities planning to use hand count ballots for the 2026 Partisan Primary should note 
there is not a sample consolidated hand count ballot template due to ballot size limitations. Jurisdictions 
may need to either use separate party-specific ballots or work with their vendor/printer to determine if a 
consolidated ballot can reasonably fit on available paper stock. 
 
Counties with questions or concerns about accessing paper stock or preparing hand count ballots should 
reach out to WEC staff to discuss further.

4. WEC Ballot Proofing Process  
Counties must provide a proof of their ballot to the WEC for review.  The WEC reviews ballot proofs to 
verify that the ballot format substantially complies with the templates approved by the Commission. 
WEC staff will review county ballot proofs within one business day.  If you have not received a response 
within one business day from submitting your proof, please reach out to us.  
 
The WEC ballot review process covers:  
• Ballot Title 
• Ballot Template Language (Notice to Electors, instructions, etc.) 
• Office Title for federal and state-level contests 
• Candidate names and spelling for federal and state-level contests 
• Candidate ballot order for federal and state-level contests 
• Write-in lines for federal and state-level contests 
The WEC does not review:  
• Local contests and write-in lines (sheriff, mayor, school board, etc.) 
• Spelling of a local candidate’s name 
• Ballot order of local offices and candidates 
• Ballot district combination accuracy (also called ballot style) 
o County clerks are responsible for determining the correct ballot combination for 
municipalities and for ensuring each municipality receives the correct ballots. 
This is a representative list.  When WEC proofs ballots, a checklist is sent to the county following 
review.

Update on Ballot Spoiling Litigation Clerk Communication
File
Bins v. WEC Court Ruling
1. Introduction
The purpose of this memo is to update clerks on a recent circuit court decision from Dane County Judge David Conway in the ballot spoiling litigation, Bins et al v. WEC et al, 2026CV002400.
The court upheld the Commission’s July 9, 2026 guidance on ballot spoiling. You can find the guidance here:
https://elections.wi.gov/memo/updated-ballot-spoiling-guidance
The court agreed with the Commission and ultimately concluded that once an absentee voter returns their ballot to the municipal clerk, they cannot attempt to spoil it and get a new ballot.
2. What did the court decision say?
The court concluded the ballot spoiling statute does not allow a voter to spoil an absentee ballot after it is returned. An absentee voter who has not yet returned their ballot and accidentally or mistakenly fills in the ballot for the wrong candidate may take the ballot back to the clerk, who can issue the voter a replacement ballot. But this does not apply to absentee voters who change their minds about who they wish to vote for once their absentee ballot is returned. In this scenario, the voter cannot “spoil” their ballots after they returned them.
3. What is the Commission required to do next?
Nothing. The July 9 guidance remains the Commission’s current guidance on the topic of ballot spoiling, and municipal clerks should be familiar with the reasoning of the court’s decision to the extent that it supplements the July 9 memo.
4. Will there be any further action on this case before August 11?
Maybe. At least one party could still appeal the judge’s decision. Commission staff will keep clerks updated on any appeals requests and outcomes as in-person absentee voting continues.
5. Questions?
Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at
elections@wi.gov
or 608-261-2028.

SUBJECT: Litigation Update: Ballot Spoiling Guidance – Bins et al v. WEC 
1. Introduction  
The purpose of this memo is to update clerks on a recent circuit court decision from Dane County Judge 
David Conway in the ballot spoiling litigation, Bins et al v. WEC et al, 2026CV002400.  
• The court upheld the Commission’s July 9, 2026 guidance on ballot spoiling. You can find the 
guidance here: https://elections.wi.gov/memo/updated-ballot-spoiling-guidance. 
• The court agreed with the Commission and ultimately concluded that once an absentee voter 
returns their ballot to the municipal clerk, they cannot attempt to spoil it and get a new ballot.  
2. What did the court decision say?  
The court concluded the ballot spoiling statute does not allow a voter to spoil an absentee ballot after it 
is returned. An absentee voter who has not yet returned their ballot and accidentally or mistakenly fills in 
the ballot for the wrong candidate may take the ballot back to the clerk, who can issue the voter a 
replacement ballot. But this does not apply to absentee voters who change their minds about who they 
wish to vote for once their absentee ballot is returned. In this scenario, the voter cannot “spoil” their 
ballots after they returned them.  
3. What is the Commission required to do next?  
Nothing. The July 9 guidance remains the Commission’s current guidance on the topic of ballot spoiling, 
and municipal clerks should be familiar with the reasoning of the court’s decision to the extent that it 
supplements the July 9 memo.

STATE OF WISCONSIN    CIRCUIT COURT                                DANE COUNTY 
BRANCH 17 
              
 
JOSEPH ALAN BINS, et al., 
         
  Plaintiffs,     MEMORANDUM AND ORDER 
 
 v.       Case No. 2026CV002400 
           
WISCONSIN ELECTIONS COMMISSION, et al.,  
 
  Defendants. 
              
 
 Ballot spoiling is the process by which a voter who has incorrectly marked or damaged a 
ballot can replace the “spoiled ballot” with a new one.  Plaintiffs Joseph Alan Bins, Thomas J. 
Elert, and Susan Roberts have filed an emergency motion for temporary injunctive relief 
contending that the Wisconsin Election Commission (“WEC”) has violated their constitutional 
rights and acted outside of its statutory authority by changing the agency’s longstanding absentee 
ballot spoiling guidance midway through the absentee voting period, after many voters, including 
Plaintiffs Bins and Elert, had already returned their absentee ballots.  Dkts. 6–7.  According to 
Plaintiffs, the WEC’s new guidance now prohibits voters from spoiling their absentee ballot if 
(1) they change their mind about a candidate or voted for a candidate who drops out of the race, 
or (2) they have already returned their first ballot to the municipal clerk.  Dkt. 7 at 4, 24. 
 
BY THE COURT:
DATE SIGNED: July 29, 2026
Electronically signed by David Conway
Circuit Court Judge
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 1 of 20
FILED
07-29-2026
CIRCUIT COURT
DANE COUNTY, WI
2026CV002400

2 
 
Plaintiffs have asked the Court for emergency injunctive relief prior to the August 11, 
2026 partisan primary election so that they may avail themselves of the ballot spoiling process 
under the WEC’s former guidance.  The Court held an emergency hearing on July 28, 2026, at 
which Plaintiffs appeared by attorneys Eduardo E. Castro II and Diane M. Welsh; the WEC 
appeared by attorneys Daniel P. Back and Dixon R. Gahnz; Intervenors Ann S. Jacobs and Mark 
Thomsen appeared telephonically by attorney Mark Leitner; and Intervenor Nathan Pollnow 
appeared by attorney Kurt A. Goehre.  The Court’s findings of fact and conclusions of law are 
stated below.  Based on this analysis, the Court will deny Plaintiffs’ motion.   
FINDINGS OF FACT 
I. 
 Wisconsin is currently in the midst of a quadrennial election campaign for state governor.  
The State will hold its partisan primary on August 11, 2026, followed by a general election on 
November 3, 2026.  The August 11 partisan primary will include a highly competitive statewide 
race for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination.  Although seven Democratic candidates will 
appear on the primary ballot, two of those candidates have already withdrawn from the race (i.e., 
Missy Hughes and Sara Rodriguez) and more may do so before election day.   
 Absentee voting in the Wisconsin partisan primary commenced on June 25, 2026.  All 
Wisconsin municipalities were required to distribute absentee ballots to eligible voters who had 
requested them as of that date and to fulfill any new requests received after June 25 within one 
business day.  By July 10, 2026, the WEC reported that 42,657 absentee ballots had already been 
returned to municipal clerks around the state, Dkt. 5 ¶ 5, Ex. 2; by July 20, the number had 
increased to 71,310 absentee ballots, Dkt. 5 ¶ 13, Ex. 10; as of July 27, the number exceeded 
100,000 absentee ballots, Dkt. 41 ¶ 5. 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 2 of 20

3 
 
II. 
The WEC has exclusive authority to administer the state’s election laws, including by 
providing guidance to local election officials on the proper interpretation of those laws.  Wis. 
Stat. § 5.05; Jefferson v. Dane Cnty., 2020 WI 90, ¶ 24, 394 Wis. 2d 602, 951 N.W.2d 556.  In 
exercising this function, the WEC has long provided guidance and interpretation to municipal 
election clerks on how to administer the ballot spoiling statutes set forth at Wis. Stat. §§ 
6.80(2)(c) and 6.86(5).  Those statutes provide as follows: 
Wis. Stat. § 6.80(2)(c) . Any elector who, by accident or mistake, spoils or 
erroneously prepares a ballot may receive another, by returning the defective ballot, 
but not to exceed 3 ballots in all. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.86(5) . Whenever an elector returns a spoiled or damaged absentee 
ballot to the municipal clerk, or an elector’s agent under sub. (3)  returns a spoiled 
or damaged ballot to the clerk on behalf of an elector, and the clerk believes that 
the ballot was issued to or on behalf of the elector who is returning it, the clerk shall 
issue a new ballot to the elector or elector’s agent, and shall destroy the spoiled or 
damaged ballot. Any request for a replacement ballot under this subsection must be 
made within the applicable time limits under subs. (1) and (3)(c). 
 
Prior to 2026, the WEC’s most recent ballot spoiling guidance on the topic was from 
August 1, 2022 (“August 2022 Guidance”).1  Dkt. 5 ¶ 8, Ex. 5.  There, the WEC advised 
municipal clerks that “[a]fter a voter has been issued an absentee ballot at the clerk’s office or by 
mail, they can request to spoil that ballot and receive a new one in the event the voter makes a 
mistake or changes their mind.”  Dkt. 5 ¶ 8, Ex. 5 at 2.  The WEC also advised that an absentee 
voter could still spoil his or her ballot after returning it to the clerk as long as he or she did so 
before the absentee voting deadline.  Id.  The WEC reiterated these points in an August 2, 2022 
press release.  Dkt. 5 ¶ 9, Ex. 6 at 1.   
 
1 Before August 2022, the WEC had issued materially identical ballot spoiling guidance in October 2020.  
Dkt. 5 ¶ 11, Ex. 8. 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 3 of 20

4 
 
Two months after the WEC issued the August 2022 Guidance, on October 10, the 
Waukesha County Circuit Court issued an injunction prohibiting the WEC from continuing the 
guidance upon finding it contrary to law.  See Kormanik v. WEC, Waukesha Co. Case No. 2022-
CV-001395, Dkt. 106.  The WEC promptly withdrew the August 2022 Guidance on October 28, 
2022, Dkt. 37 ¶ 9, Ex. E, and has not reissued it, Dkt. 41 ¶¶ 14–22.  The circuit court’s injunction 
remained in place from October 10, 2022, until February 11, 2026, when the Wisconsin Court of 
Appeals vacated the injunction because the plaintiff had failed to properly serve process.  See 
Kormanik v. WEC, 2024AP408, 2026 WL 380350 (Wis. Ct. App. Feb. 11, 2026).  Over this 
nearly four-year period, at least ten elections occurred without the WEC’s August 2022 
Guidance in effect.  Dkt. 41 ¶¶ 15–16. 
 On May 27, 2026, the WEC issued a new guidance to address the effect of the Wisconsin 
Court of Appeals’ decision vacating the Kormanik injunction (“May 2026 Guidance”).  Dkt. 5 ¶ 
6, Ex. 3.  In that document, the WEC explained that it had “opted not to reissue” the August 
2022 Guidance but had instead unanimously voted to approve the following guidance: 
Wisconsin law allows a voter who, by accident or mistake, spoils or erroneously 
prepares a ballot to receive another ballot by returning the defective ballot to the 
municipal clerk or election inspector. The municipal clerk should verify the identity 
of a person requesting to receive a replacement absent ee ballot to ensure that it is 
the voter making the request. This voter verification process should include having 
the voter confirm the same information necessary to request an absentee ballot (e.g. 
name, full address, date of birth) and this verification  process may include the 
municipal clerk asking the absentee voter to produce voter identification. The 
deadlines for requesting a replacement for a spoiled or erroneously prepared ballot 
are: [dates omitted] . . . A voter may only receive three replacement ballots in each 
election. 
 
Dkt. 5 ¶ 6, Ex. 3 at 1–2.  Notably, the May 2026 Guidance did not address whether voters can 
spoil a ballot if they change their mind, if they vote for a withdrawn candidate, or when they 
have already returned their first absentee ballot to the municipal clerk.   
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 4 of 20

5 
 
 Finally, on July 9, 2026, the WEC issued its most recent ballot spoiling guidance in 
which it withdrew the May 2026 Guidance and departed significantly from its previous advice 
about ballot spoiling (“July 2026 Guidance”).  Dkt. 5 ¶ 2, Ex. 1.  In particular, the July 2026 
Guidance now provides that “once an absentee ballot has been returned to the municipal clerk it 
cannot be spoiled or reissued for any reason.”  Dkt. 5 ¶ 2, Ex. 1 at 1.  It further provides that “if a 
voter returns their voted ballot and later changes their mind about who they would like to vote 
for or because the candidate they originally voted for has dropped out of the race, this does not 
constitute an ‘accident or mistake’” that would allow the ballot to be spoiled.  Dkt. 5 ¶ 2, Ex. 1 at 
1–2.  The WEC has since publicized its guidance on social media.  Dkt. 5 ¶ 7, Ex. 4.  As a result 
of this new guidance, the City of Madison municipal clerk, Lydia McComas, no longer allows 
absentee voters to spoil their returned ballots, whereas before the July 2026 Guidance she 
believed that doing so was legally allowed.  Dkt. 35, ¶ 3; Dkt. 40 ¶¶ 2–3.  
III. 
 Plaintiffs are three Dane County voters who have already obtained and returned absentee 
ballots for the August 2026 partisan primary election and who now wish to spoil their ballot and 
vote for a different candidate because their chosen candidate has dropped out. 
A. 
 Plaintiff Joseph Alan Bins is a registered voter residing in the Village of Waunakee who 
wishes to participate in the August 2026 primary election and who routinely votes by absentee 
ballot.  Dkt. 8 ¶¶ 2–4.  At his request, the Waunakee clerk sent him an absentee ballot on June 
18, 2026.  Id. ¶ 5.  Bins promptly completed and returned the ballot to the clerk’s office on June 
29.  Id.  On his ballot, Bins indicated that he wished to vote for Sara Rodriguez in the 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 5 of 20

6 
 
Democratic gubernatorial primary.  Id. ¶ 6.  Rodriguez has since dropped out of the race, and 
Bins now considers his vote for her to have been a mistake.  Id. ¶¶ 6–7.   
On July 17, 2026, Bins contacted the village clerk asking to spoil his ballot because his 
chosen candidate had dropped out.  Id. ¶ 8, Ex. 1.  The village clerk responded on July 19, that 
Bins could not spoil his ballot for that reason.  Id. ¶ 9, Ex. 1.  When Bins originally requested his 
absentee ballot and returned it to the clerk, he was aware of the WEC’s previous guidance 
allowing absentee voters to spoil their ballot if they wished to vote for a different candidate.  Id. 
¶ 12.  At that time, the WEC had not yet issued the July 2026 Guidance and Bins believed that he 
would be able to spoil his ballot if his preferred candidate dropped out.  Id. ¶ 11.  If allowed to do 
so, Bins would spoil his ballot and vote for a primary candidate who is still in the race.  Id. ¶ 13. 
B. 
 Plaintiff Thomas J. Elert is a registered voter residing in the City of Madison who 
routinely votes by absentee ballot due to disability.  Dkt. 3 ¶¶ 2–4.  At his request, the Madison 
clerk sent him an absentee ballot on June 24, 2026.  Id. ¶ 5.  Elert completed and returned the 
ballot to the clerk’s office on July 8.  Id.  On his ballot, Elert indicated that he wished to vote for 
Sara Rodriguez.  Id. ¶ 6.  He now considers his vote to have been a mistake.  Id. ¶¶ 6–7. 
 When Elert returned his absentee ballot to the clerk on July 8, Elert believed that 
Wisconsin law would allow him to spoil his ballot if his preferred candidate dropped out of the 
race.  Id. ¶ 9.  The WEC has since issued the July 2026 Guidance.  Id. ¶ 8.  Had he known he 
could not spoil his ballot if his candidate withdrew, Elert would have delayed returning his 
absentee ballot.  Id. ¶ 10.  If allowed to do so, Elert would spoil his ballot and vote for a primary 
candidate who is still in the race.  Id. ¶ 11.

C. 
 Plaintiff Susan Roberts is a registered voter residing in the City of Madison who routinely 
votes by absentee ballot due to age and disability.  Dkt. 4 ¶¶ 2–4.  Roberts placed her absentee 
ballot in the mail on July 16, 2026, and the Madison clerk received it on July 20.  Id. ¶ 6.  On her 
ballot, Roberts indicated that she wished to vote for Sara Rodriguez.  Id. ¶ 7.  She now considers 
her vote for Rodriguez to have been a mistake.  Id. ¶¶ 7–8. 
 When Roberts returned her absentee ballot to the clerk on July 16, she was not yet aware 
of the July 2026 Guidance stating that absentee voters cannot spoil their ballot if they change 
their mind about a candidate or their candidate withdraws.  Id. ¶ 9.  Had she known of this 
guidance at the time, Roberts would have delayed returning her absentee ballot.  Id. ¶ 10.  If 
allowed, Roberts would spoil her ballot and vote for a candidate who is still in the race.  Id. ¶ 11. 
IV. 
 On July 23, 2026, Plaintiffs initiated this lawsuit by filing a complaint for declaratory 
judgment under three separate theories.  First, Plaintiffs ask the Court to declare the July 2026 
Guidance invalid because it conflicts with Wis. Stat. § 6.80(2)(c) and Wis. Stat. § 6.86(5).  Dkt. 
2 ¶¶ 68–70.  Second, Plaintiffs ask the Court to declare that the July 2026 Guidance violates their 
right to vote established by Article I, Section 1 and Article III, Section 2 of the Wisconsin 
Constitution.  Id. ¶¶ 71–75.  Third, Plaintiffs ask the Court to declare that the July 2026 
Guidance violates their right to equal protection guaranteed by Article I, Section 1 of the 
Wisconsin Constitution.  Id. ¶¶ 76–83.   
Plaintiffs have contemporaneously filed the emergency motion for temporary injunctive 
relief presently before the Court, in which they ask to enjoin the WEC from continuing the July 
2026 Guidance while this case proceeds.  Dkts. 6–7.  The Court entered a case management 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 7 of 20

8 
 
order on July 24, setting a temporary injunction hearing for July 28, 2026, and requiring that a 
copy of the order be served on the WEC at least 24 hours prior to the hearing.  Dkt. 10.  Plaintiffs 
served the WEC on July 24, more than 96 hours before the hearing.  Dkt. 12.  The WEC filed an 
opposition brief with declarations and exhibits on July 27.  Dkts. 33–34, 41. The Court has also 
accepted a non-party brief from the Wisconsin Institute of Law & Liberty. Dkt. 25. 
On July 28, 2026, the Court granted two motions to intervene in this action—one from 
WEC Commissioners Ann S. Jacobs and Mark Thomsen, Dkts. 21–23, 43; and another from 
Nathan Pollnow, a candidate for Secretary of State, Dkts. 30–31, 51.   
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW 
I. JURISDICTION 
 A. Subject Matter Jurisdiction and Venue 
In Wisconsin, “the exclusive means of judicial review of the validity of a rule or guidance 
document shall be an action for declaratory judgment as to the validity of the rule or guidance 
document brought in the circuit court for the county where the party asserting the invalidity of 
the rule or guidance document resides.”  Wis. Stat. § 227.40(1).  “A declaratory judgment may 
be rendered whether or not the plaintiff has first requested the agency pass upon the validity of 
the rule or guidance document in question.”  Wis. Stat. § 227.40(1).  Here, Plaintiffs are Dane 
County residents who have brought this declaratory judgment action in Dane County Circuit 
Court to seek judicial review of the validity of the WEC’s July 2026 Guidance.  This is sufficient 
to establish the Court’s subject matter jurisdiction and venue over this action. 
 B. Personal Jurisdiction 
 When a plaintiff files a declaratory judgment action seeking judicial review of an agency 
guidance document, he or she must serve process “by delivering a copy to that officer or, if the 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 8 of 20

9 
 
agency is composed of more than one person, to the secretary or clerk of the agency or to any 
member of the agency.”  Wis. Stat. § 227.40(1).  The plaintiff must also serve the Legislature’s 
joint committee for review of administrative rules (“JCRAR”) with a copy of the petition for 
declaratory judgment.  Wis. Stat. § 227.40(5).  Here, Plaintiffs have filed proof that on July 23, 
2026, they personally served the WEC’s administrator, Meagan Wolfe, as well as the legislative 
assistants to Senator Stephen Nass and Representative Adam Neylon—the two co-chairs of the 
JCRAR—with copies of their complaint and emergency motion.  Dkt. 9.  This is sufficient to 
give the Court personal jurisdiction over the WEC. 
II. JUSTICIABILITY 
The Wisconsin Declaratory Judgments Act sets forth the general rules governing 
declaratory relief.  Wis. Stat. § 806.04.  The purpose of the law is “to settle and to afford relief 
from uncertainty and insecurity with respect to rights, status, and other legal relations.”  Id. § 
806.04(12).  Under the statute, circuit courts may “declare rights, status, and other legal relations 
whether or not further relief is or could be claimed.  Id. § 806.04(1).  Any person “whose rights, 
status, or other legal relations are affected by a statute . . . may have determined any question of 
construction . . . arising under the [statute] . . . and obtain a declaration of rights, status, or other 
legal relations thereunder.”  Id. § 806.04(2).  The statute is to be liberally construed to affect its 
remedial purpose.  Id. § 806.04(12).   
 A justiciable controversy must exist before a court can exercise jurisdiction over a 
declaratory judgment claim.  Olson v. Town of Cottage Grove, 2008 WI 51, ¶ 28, 309 Wis. 2d 
365, 749 N.W.2d 211.  Justiciability requires four things: (1) a claim of right must be asserted 
against one who has an interest in contesting it; (2) the controversy must be between persons 
whose interests are adverse; (3) the party seeking relief must have a legally protectible interest in 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 9 of 20

10 
 
the controversy; and (4) the issue must be ripe for judicial determination.  Id. ¶ 29 (citing Loy v. 
Bunderson, 107 Wis. 2d 400, 320 N.W.2d 175 (1982)).  “If all four factors are satisfied, the 
controversy is ‘justiciable,’ and it is proper for a court to entertain an action for declaratory 
judgment.”  Olson, 2008 WI 51, ¶ 29 (quote omitted). 
 Here, Intervenor Nathan Pollnow argues that Plaintiffs have not satisfied the third 
justiciability factor—a legally protectible interest—which addresses the concept of standing.2  
See Dkt. 36 at 13–15; City of Madison v. Town of Fitchburg, 112 Wis. 2d 224, 228, 332 N.W.2d 
782 (1983).  Wisconsin courts apply a two-prong test for standing to challenge an agency action 
under Wis. Stat. § 227.40: “(1) Does the challenged action cause the petition injury in fact? and 
(2) is the interest allegedly injured arguably within the zone of interests to be protected or 
regulated by the statute or constitutional guarantee in question?”  Friends of Black River Forest 
v. Kohler Co., 2022 WI 52, ¶ 18, 402 Wis. 2d 587, 977 N.W.2d 342 (quote omitted). 
 Mr. Pollnow’s standing argument appears to be predicated upon the assumption that 
Plaintiffs have misinterpreted the ballot spoiling statutes and therefore have suffered no injury.  
See Dkt. 36 at 13–15.  This argument puts the cart before the horse: the Court must first 
determine whether Plaintiffs have asserted a legally protectible interest before it can determine, 
on the merits, whether the challenged guidance has injured that interest.  Framed this way, the 
Court concludes that Plaintiffs have satisfied both prongs of the standing analysis.  Under the 
first prong, the Court must ask “whether the petition alleges injuries that are a direct result of the 
agency action.”  Id. ¶ 21 (quote omitted).  Plaintiffs meet this requirement by alleging that the 
WEC has issued a legally invalid guidance that has prevented them from exercising the statutory 
 
2 No party disputes the first, second, and fourth factors.  Plaintiffs have sued the WEC claiming that its 
July 2026 Guidance has unlawfully deprived them of a statutory right.  The WEC has an adverse interest 
in defending its guidance.  And the facts of this case are sufficiently developed for the Court to resolve 
the ultimate question—namely, whether the July 2026 Guidance is in conflict with the law. 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 10 of 20

11 
 
right to spoil their absentee ballots.  Under the second prong, the Court must consider “whether 
the injury is to an interest which the law recognizes or seeks to regulate or protect.”  Id. ¶ 23 
(quote omitted).  An agency action that prohibits a citizen from exercising his or her ballot 
spoiling rights undoubtedly falls within the zone of interest protected by the absentee voting 
statutes.  The Court concludes that Plaintiffs’ claims are justiciable and that it is proper for the 
Court to entertain this action. 
III. TEMPORARY INJUNCTION ANALYSIS 
A temporary injunction’s function is “to maintain the status quo, not to change the 
position of the parties or compel the doing of acts which constitute all or part of the ultimate 
relief sought.”  Codept, Inc. v. More-Way North Corp., 23 Wis. 2d 165, 173, 127 N.W.2d 29 
(1964).  It remains in effect only “until the trial and determination of the action.”  Laundry 
Workers Int’l Union, 4 Wis. 2d at 557.   
The Court may grant a temporary injunction “at any time before judgment upon its 
appearing satisfactorily to the court . . . by the complaint or answer or by affidavit that sufficient 
grounds exist therefor.”  Wis. Stat. § 813.04.  When deciding whether to issue a temporary 
injunction, a circuit court must consider four criteria: (1) whether the movant has a “reasonable 
probability of success on the merits”; (2) whether the movant is “likely to suffer irreparable 
harm” absent an injunction; (3) whether the movant has “no other adequate remedy at law”; (4) 
whether an injunction is “necessary to preserve the status quo.”  Gahl ex rel. Zingsheim v. 
Aurora Health Care, Inc., 2023 WI 35, ¶ 17, 413 Wis. 2d 418, 989 N.W.2d 561 (citing Serv. 
Emps. Int’l Union, Loc. 1 v. Vos, 2020 WI 67, ¶ 93, 393 Wis. 2d 38, 946 N.W.2d 35).  If the 
Court grants or denies a temporary injunction, it must “set forth the findings of fact and 
conclusions of law which constitute grounds of its action.”  Wis. Stat. § 805.17(2). 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 11 of 20

12 
 
 A. Probability of Success on the Merits 
 In an action for judicial review of an agency guidance, “the court shall declare the . . . 
guidance document invalid if it finds that it violates constitutional provisions or exceeds the 
statutory authority of the agency.”  Wis. Stat. § 227.40(4)(a).  Here, Plaintiffs seek judicial 
review of the July 2026 Guidance arguing that it conflicts with the plain language of Wis. Stat. 
§§ 6.86(5) and 6.80(2)(c); that it violates their right to vote; and that it deprives them of equal 
protection.  The Court will examine their probability of succeeding on each theory. 
  1. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.80(2)(c), 6.86(5) 
An agency may not “implement or enforce any standard, requirement, or threshold” 
unless it is “explicitly permitted by statute.”  Wis. Stat. § 227.10(2m).  Where an agency issues a 
guidance document contrary to a statute, the agency acts outside of its authority and the guidance 
document is invalid.  Wis. Stat. § 227.40(4)(a).  Here, Plaintiffs ask the Court to declare the July 
2026 Guidance invalid because the following two statements within that document conflict with 
Wis. Stat. §§ 6.80(2)(c) and 6.86(5):  
(1) “[O]nce an absentee ballot has been returned to a municipal clerk, it cannot be 
spoiled for any reason,” Dkt. 5 ¶ 2, Ex. 1 at 1; and  
(2) “If a voter returns their ballot and later changes their mind about who they 
would like to vote for or because the candidate they originally voted for has 
dropped out of the race, this does not constitute and ‘accident or mistake.’  The 
ballot cannot be spoiled and reissued for any reason,” Dkt. 5 ¶ 2, Ex. 1 at 2. 
 
Dkt. 2 ¶¶ 68–70; Dkt. 7 at 23–30.  In response, the WEC and Nathan Pollnow argue that the July 
2026 Guidance is consistent with the statutes and that Plaintiffs have misinterpreted those laws.  
Dkt. 33 at 6–8; Dkt. 36 at 8–13. 
To resolve this dispute, the Court will need to perform its own statutory interpretation of 
Wis. Stat. §§ 6.80(2)(c) and 6.86(5).  Statutory interpretation “begins with the language of the 
statute” and it ends there if the meaning is unambiguous.  State ex rel. Kalal v. Circuit Ct. for 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 12 of 20

13 
 
Dane Cnty., 2004 WI 58, ¶ 45, 271 Wis. 2d 633, 681 N.W.2d 110.  The Court gives the language 
“its common ordinary and accepted meaning.”  Id.; see also Wis. Stat. § 990.01(1).  “A 
dictionary may be utilized to guide the common, ordinary meaning of words.”  Noffke ex rel. 
Swenson v. Bakke, 2009 WI 10, ¶ 10, 315 Wis. 2d 350, 760 N.W.2d 156.  The Court interprets 
the language “in the context in which it is used; not in isolation but as part of a whole; in relation 
to the language of surrounding or closely-related statutes; and reasonably, to avoid absurd or 
unreasonable results.” Kalal, 2004 WI 58, ¶ 46.  When interpreting election statutes, courts must 
construe them “to give effect to the will of the electors.”  Wis. Stat. § 5.01(1).   
First, Plaintiffs argue that the July 2026 Guidance violates Wis. Stat. § 6.86(5) by 
prohibiting voters from spoiling their absentee ballot after they have already returned it to the 
municipal clerk.  Dkt. 7 at 23–26.  Wis. Stat. § 6.86(5) provides as follows: 
Whenever an elector returns a spoiled or damaged absentee ballot to the municipal 
clerk, or an elector’s agent under sub. (3) returns a spoiled or damaged ballot to the 
clerk on behalf of an elector, and the clerk believes that the ballot was issued to or 
on behalf of the elector who is returning it, the clerk shall issue a new ballot to the 
elector or elector’s agent, and shall destroy the sp oiled or damaged ballot. Any 
request for a replacement ballot under this subsection must be made within the 
applicable time limits under subs. (1) and (3)(c).3 
 
According to Plaintiffs, this statute “does not prohibit spoiling a ballot after it is returned to the 
clerk.”  Dkt. 7 at 24.  The WEC and Pollnow disagree.  Dkt. 33 at 6–8; Dkt. 36 at 8–13. 
The Court concludes that the unambiguous language of the statute does not allow a voter 
to spoil an absentee ballot after it is returned.  The clerk’s duty to issue a new ballot is triggered 
whenever a properly identified voter “returns a spoiled or damaged ballot.”  “Returns” is a

5pm on the 5th day immediately preceding the election,” and an in-person application must be made “no 
earlier than 14 days preceding the election and no later than the Sunday preceding the election.”  Wis. 
Stat. § 6.86(1)(b).  Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(c) sets a separate deadline for hospitalized electors. 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 13 of 20

14 
 
present tense verb.  “Spoiled or damaged ballot” is a compound noun in which “ballot” is 
modified by past participial adjectives, “spoiled” and “damaged,” that indicate an already 
finished action.  On its face, the first sentence plainly requires an absentee ballot to already be 
“spoiled” or “damaged” at the time the voter returns it.  If the Legislature’s intent was to allow 
absentee voters to obtain new ballots after already returning their original ballot, it would have 
said so using the appropriate language in the proper grammatical tense (e.g., “Whenever an 
elector has returned an absentee ballot to the municipal clerk that is or becomes spoiled . . .”). 
Plaintiffs challenge this interpretation by pointing to two nearby statutory phrases that 
they believe support an opposite reading.  They first argue that the word “request” in the second 
sentence of Wis. Stat. § 6.86(5) would be surplusage if the first sentence contemplates an 
automatic exchange of an already-spoiled ballot for a new one.  Dkt. 7 at 25 (“The voter has 
nothing to ‘request’ in that circumstance”).  To the contrary, a “request” is simply “the act or an 
instance of asking for something.”4  An absentee voter who returns a spoiled or damaged ballot 
must ask the clerk to replace it or else the clerk will not know how to assist the voter.  And it 
makes sense that the Legislature would require an absentee voter to make this “request” by no 
later than the statutory deadline for requesting an absentee ballot in the first instance. 
Plaintiffs secondly assert that the very next subsection of the statute also undercuts the 
Court’s interpretation.  Wis. Stat. § 6.86(6) provides that a municipal clerk may not return an 
absentee ballot to a voter once the voter has submitted the ballot, “[e]xcept as authorized” by 
Wis. Stat. § 6.86(5).  It is not clear what situation this exception envisions.  No aspect of Wis. 
Stat. § 6.86(5) involves the municipal clerk returning a previously-submitted absentee ballot to a 
voter.  Plaintiffs do not interpret the statute this way.  Nor do they seek a return of their own

15 
 
ballots.  Instead, Plaintiffs’ interpretation would have the clerk locate and destroy their spoiled 
ballots and issue them new ones.  Although the Court can only speculate as to what Wis. Stat. § 
6.86(6) contemplates, the statute says nothing about (and sheds no useful light upon) whether 
absentee voters may or may not spoil their ballots after returning them.  It therefore does not 
change the Court’s interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 6.86(5). 
 Second, Plaintiffs contend that the July 2026 Guidance contradicts Wis. Stat. § 6.80(2)(c) 
by prohibiting voters from spoiling their absentee ballot if they change their mind about a 
candidate or vote for a candidate who drops out of the race.  Dkt. 7 at 26–30.  Wis. Stat. § 6.80 
governs the mechanics of in-person voting at a polling place on election day.  While voting in 
person, “[a]ny elector who, by accident or mistake, spoils or erroneously prepares a ballot may 
receive another, by returning the defective ballot, but not to exceed three ballots in all.”  Wis. 
Stat. § 6.80(2)(c).  An “accident” is “an unforeseen and unplanned event or circumstance,” and a 
“mistake” means “to blunder in the choice of” something.5  In other words, an in-person voter 
can “spoil” his ballot and obtain a new one if he fills in the ballot for the wrong candidate due to 
an unforeseen event or by simply blundering in his choice.  This language would plainly include 
a scenario where the voter changes their mind about a candidate or learns that their chosen 
candidate has dropped out of the race.  In practice, the voter would take his “spoiled” ballot back 
to the poll worker, exchange it for a new one, and proceed to correctly vote the new ballot.  The 
poll worker would then “immediately destroy[]” the spoiled ballot.  Wis. Stat. § 7.37(11). 
While Wis. Stat. § 6.80(2)(c) does not govern absentee voting, it does appear to provide a 
definition of “spoiling” that is absent elsewhere in the law.  “Typically, a term used in multiple 
 
5  “Accident” and “Mistake,” Merriam-Webster.com Dictionary, Merriam-Webster, 
https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/accident, https://www.merriam-
