16 
 
subsections within a statute is given the same meaning.”  Phelps v. Physicians Ins. Co. of Wis., 
2005 WI 85, ¶ 58, 282 Wis. 2d 69, 698 N.W.2d 643.  It therefore makes sense to interpret the 
term “spoiled” in Wis. Stat. § 6.86(5) to have the same meaning as it does in Wis. Stat. § 
6.80(2)(c).  In effect, this means an absentee voter who has not yet returned his ballot and who 
accidentally or mistakenly fills in the ballot for the wrong candidate may take the “spoiled” 
ballot back to the clerk and exchange it for a new one.  But it does not mean that persons in 
Plaintiffs’ position can still “spoil” their ballots after they have returned them. 
Furthermore, the July 2026 Guidance is still consistent with the law even under this 
interpretation.  The July 2026 Guidance does not say that a voter changing his mind or voting for 
a withdrawn candidate can never constitute an “accident or mistake” that would allow for 
spoiling.  Instead, the guidance says that these things do not constitute an “accident or mistake” 
once the voter has already returned his or her ballot: 
If a voter returns their voted ballot and later changes their mind about who they 
would like to vote for or because the candidate they originally voted for has dropped 
out of the race, this does not constitute an “accident or mistake.” The ballot cannot 
be spoiled and reissued for any reason. 
 
Dkt. 5 ¶ 2, Ex. 1 at 2.  This is really just another way of saying that an absentee voter cannot 
spoil his or her ballot for any reason, including “accident or mistake,” once it has been returned 
to the clerk, which the Court concludes above is a correct interpretation of the law. 
For all of these reasons, the Court concludes that Plaintiffs are unlikely to prevail on their 
claim that the July 2026 Guidance is contrary to statute. 
  2. Right to Vote 
 The Wisconsin Constitution guarantees the right to vote to all adult citizens of this State.  
Wis. Const. Art III, § 1; State ex rel. McGrael v. Phelps, 144 Wis. 1, 128 N.W. 1041, 1046 
(1910).  The Legislature is constitutionally authorized to regulate the election process, including 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 16 of 20

17 
 
by passing laws defining residency, controlling voter registration, and providing for absentee 
voting. Wis. Const. Art III, § 2. Pursuant to this authority, the Legislature has enacted numerous 
statutes governing the absentee voting process, including laws specifically allowing absentee 
voters to “spoil” their ballots under certain circumstances.  See Wis. Stat. Chapters 5–12 
(election laws generally); Wis. Stat. §§ 6.20, 6.84–89 (absentee voting requirements); Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.86(5) (ballot spoiling requirements). 
 Plaintiffs ask the Court to declare that the July 2026 Guidance violates their right to vote 
as established by Article I, Section 1 and Article III, Section 2 of the Wisconsin Constitution.  
Dkt. 2 ¶¶ 71–75; Dkt. 7 at 30–31.  But they do not dispute that the ballot spoiling requirements 
set forth at Wis. Stat. §§ 6.86(5) and 6.80(2)(c) are valid and reasonable exercises of the 
Legislature’s constitutional power to regulate absentee voting.  The Court has already decided 
above that the July 2026 Guidance is consistent with these statutes.  Therefore, the Court 
concludes that Plaintiffs are unlikely to prevail on their claim that the July 2026 Guidance 
unlawfully burdens their constitutional right to vote. 
  3. Equal Protection 
 Plaintiffs finally ask the Court to declare that the July 2026 Guidance violates their right 
to equal protection guaranteed by Article I, Section 1 of the Wisconsin Constitution.  Dkt. 2 ¶¶ 
76–83; Dkt. 7 at 31–34.  This constitutional provision “has been interpreted as providing the 
same equal protection and due process rights afforded by the Fourteenth Amendment to the 
United States Constitution.”  Mayo v. Wisconsin Injured Patients & Families Comp. Fund, 2018 
WI 78, ¶ 35, 383 Wis. 2d 1, 914 N.W.2d 678.   
 As an initial matter, the Court has already determined that the July 2026 Guidance is 
consistent with statutory law.  To prevail on their claim that the July 2026 Guidance violates 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 17 of 20

18 
 
equal protection, Plaintiffs would essentially need to prove that the statutes themselves are 
unconstitutional.  Plaintiffs have made no such claim in this lawsuit.  See Dkt. 2.  Nevertheless, 
the Court will analyze Plaintiffs’ equal protection claims as though they challenge only the 
constitutionality of the July 2026 Guidance and not the statutes it interprets. 
 When asserting an equal protection challenge, the Court must first determine whether the 
regulation “treats members of similarly situated classes differently.”  Id. ¶ 37 (quote omitted).  
Here, Plaintiffs allege that the July 2026 Guidance creates two class distinctions that impinge 
upon their fundamental right to vote: (1) absentee voters who spoiled their absentee ballots 
before July 9, and those who did not; and (2) voters who cast their ballots on election day and 
those who cast their ballots absentee.  Dkt. 7 at 32.  The Court will accept these classifications 
for purposes of the next stage of the analysis. 
 Next, the Court must determine the level of judicial scrutiny to apply to the classification 
at issue.  Generally, a court will sustain a rule “that creates a distinction between treatment of 
different groups, if there exists a rational basis to support that distinction, provided that the 
distinction does not implicate a suspect class or impinge upon a fundamental right.”  Mayo, 2018 
WI 78, ¶ 36 (quote omitted).  Under rational basis review, the Court must uphold a regulation 
“unless it is patently arbitrary and bears no rational relationship to a legitimate government 
interest.” State v. Smith, 2010 WI 16, ¶ 12, 323 Wis. 2d 377, 780 N.W.2d 90 (quote omitted).  In 
contrast, when a distinction implicates a suspect class or impinges a fundamental right, then strict 
scrutiny usually applies and the regulation “must serve a compelling state interest; the 
[regulation] must be necessary to serving that interest; and the [regulation] must be narrowly 
tailored toward furthering that compelling state interest.”  Mayo, 2018 WI 78, ¶ 28 (cite omitted).   
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 18 of 20

19 
 
Although voting is a fundamental right, Wisconsin courts deviate from the standard equal 
protection analysis and do not always apply strict scrutiny in voting cases.  See Milwaukee 
Branch of NAACP v. Walker, 2014 WI 98, ¶¶ 23, 26–39, 357 Wis. 2d 469, 851 N.W.2d 262.  
Instead, the courts have adopted a balancing test whereby they determine the level of judicial 
scrutiny to apply to a voting regulation based on the severity of the burden it imposes on the right 
to vote.  Id.  In applying this analysis, the court focuses first on the “character and magnitude” of 
the burden in order to decide the level of judicial scrutiny— rational basis for non-severe 
burdens, strict scrutiny for severe burdens.  Id. ¶¶ 39, 71 (“Strict scrutiny applies only when a 
statute imposes a severe burden on the exercise of the franchise”).  The Court then applies the 
appropriate level of scrutiny to the State’s identified interests to determine whether the voting 
regulation is constitutional.  Id. ¶ 39. 
Here, the Court concludes that the “character and magnitude” of Plaintiffs’ classifications 
impose minimal to no burden on their right to vote.  As to the first classification, the only 
difference between absentee voters who spoiled their ballot before and after July 9, 2026, is the 
level of detail contained in the WEC’s active guidance at the time of their vote.  Prior to July 9, 
the May 2026 Guidance did not address whether an absentee voter could spoil a ballot after 
returning it to the clerk.  Dkt. 5 ¶ 6, Ex. 3 at 1–2.  After July 9, the July 2026 Guidance 
accurately answered this question in the negative.  This difference did not burden Plaintiffs’ right 
to vote.  At no time before or after July 9, did the law allow absentee voters to spoil their 
returned ballots, even if some clerks may have mistakenly allowed this to happen out of 
confusion or misunderstanding about the law.  Plaintiffs cannot establish an equal protection 
violation based on being members of a class that was subject to lawful guidance. 
Case 2026CV002400 Document 52 Filed 07-29-2026
Page 19 of 20

20 
 
The second classification—voters who cast their ballots on election day vs. those who 
cast their ballots absentee—poses at most a minimal burden on Plaintiffs’ right to vote.  As 
explained, an absentee voter who has not yet returned his or her ballot and who mistakenly fills 
in the ballot for the wrong candidate may take the “spoiled” ballot back to the clerk, exchange it 
for a new absentee ballot, and then proceed to correctly vote the new ballot.  Analogously, an 
election day voter who has not yet dropped his ballot in the ballot box and who mistakenly fills 
in the ballot for the wrong candidate can take his “spoiled” ballot back to the poll worker, 
exchange it for a new one, and then correctly vote the new ballot.  Under either scenario, once 
the voter returns his ballot to the clerk or ballot box, the voter cannot then return later in the 
absentee voting period or on election day to “spoil” the ballot and cast a new one.  The law treats 
these classes of voters as similarly as possible accounting for the practical differences in how 
they choose to exercise their right to vote.  The Court therefore concludes that any minimal 
burden this arrangement imposes on the absentee voter easily satisfies rational basis review. 
As a result, the Court concludes that Plaintiffs are unlikely to prevail on their claim that 
the July 2026 Guidance violates their right to equal protection. 
* * * * * 
 The Court has concluded that Plaintiffs are unlikely to prevail on any of their three 
declaratory judgment claims.  “A temporary injunction is not to be issued unless the movant has 
shown a reasonable probability of ultimate success on the merits.”  Werner v. A.L. Grootemaat & 
Sons, Inc., 80 Wis. 2d 513, 520, 259 N.W.2d 310 (1977) (cite omitted).  The Court must 
therefore deny Plaintiffs’ motion regardless of the other three temporary injunction factors. 
ORDER 
 IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that Plaintiffs’ emergency motion for temporary 
restraining order and temporary injunction (Dkt. 6) is DENIED.

Background
On April 17, 2025, the Wisconsin Elections Commission authorized staff to undertake a project to modernize and consolidate existing election administration guidance. The primary goal of this initiative was to combine all relevant resources and information currently distributed across more than 15 separate manuals into a single, unified manual. At the same time, staff prioritized maintaining a structure that allows clerks to easily access and extract Election Day-specific sections for quick reference and poll worker use.
In addition to consolidation, this project included a thorough review of all substantive materials and existing guidance. This review was conducted to ensure that statutory requirements and best practices are clearly identified, guidance is consistent throughout, and content is expanded where appropriate. The updated manual now also includes enhanced information intended to better serve not only municipal and county clerks, but also political parties, candidates, and members of the public seeking to understand election processes.
Commissioners plan to approve the final remaining chapters of the manual at their April 22, May 7, and May 28 meetings.  Once the Commissioners have approved the manual, Commission staff will alert county and municipal clerks that the new manual is available and provide instructions on how to access the new manual.
Rollout of New Manual Materials
To support implementation of the new manual, Commission staff will host a series of live virtual meetings for clerks on June 11, June 18, and June 25. These sessions will include:
An overview of the new combined manual and the goals of the project
A walkthrough of how the manual is structured and organized
Guidance on how clerks can incorporate the manual into poll worker training and day-to-day operations
Dedicated time to ask questions to Commission staff regarding the manual
In addition, release notes will be provided alongside the manual. These notes will summarize key updates, including changes to existing guidance and areas where content has been expanded or clarified.
Staff will also provide information about the new manual and how it can be used in clerk and poll worker trainings throughout 2026. Additional details regarding registration for the live sessions and access to the new manual will be shared soon.
Structure of New Manual
The style of the new manual incorporates the existing WEC Style Guide design and features updated formatting to help local election officials quickly find information. The following features are incorporated in the manual:
Numbered headers that help users easily navigate between topics
Blue text boxes that clearly identify Best Practices so users can easily understand the difference between legal requirements and the Commission’s recommended practices
Red text boxes to immediately draw the eye to the most important information on the page in question
Please find Part 8 (Local Election Officials) in Appendix A as an example of a standalone manual section.
Please note that there may be small edits to the formatting and appearance of the manual as it is in the final stages of approval.

manuals into a single, unified manual. At the same time, staff prioritized maintaining a structure that 
allows clerks to easily access and extract Election Day-specific sections for quick reference and poll 
worker use. 
In addition to consolidation, this project included a thorough review of all substantive materials and 
existing guidance. This review was conducted to ensure that statutory requirements and best practices 
are clearly identified, guidance is consistent throughout, and content is expanded where appropriate. The 
updated manual now also includes enhanced information intended to better serve not only municipal and 
county clerks, but also political parties, candidates, and members of the public seeking to understand 
election processes. 
Commissioners plan to approve the final remaining chapters of the manual at their April 22, May 7, and 
May 28 meetings.  Once the Commissioners have approved the manual, Commission staff will alert 
county and municipal clerks that the new manual is available and provide instructions on how to access 
the new manual. 
2. Rollout of New Manual Materials  
To support implementation of the new manual, Commission staff will host a series of live virtual 
meetings for clerks on June 11, June 18, and June 25. These sessions will include: 
• An overview of the new combined manual and the goals of the project 
• A walkthrough of how the manual is structured and organized 
Rollout of New Combined Election Manual 
4/20/2026 
Page 2 
 
 
• Guidance on how clerks can incorporate the manual into poll worker training and day-to-day 
operations 
• Dedicated time to ask questions to Commission staff regarding the manual 
In addition, release notes will be provided alongside the manual. These notes will summarize key 
updates, including changes to existing guidance and areas where content has been expanded or clarified.  
Staff will also provide information about the new manual and how it can be used in clerk and poll 
worker trainings throughout 2026. Additional details regarding registration for the live sessions and 
access to the new manual will be shared soon. 
3.  Structure of New Manual 
The style of the new manual incorporates the existing WEC Style Guide design and features updated 
formatting to help local election officials quickly find information. The following features are 
incorporated in the manual: 
• Numbered headers that help users easily navigate between topics 
• Blue text boxes that clearly identify Best Practices so users can easily understand the difference 
between legal requirements and the Commission’s recommended practices 
• Red text boxes to immediately draw the eye to the most important information on the page in 
question 
 
Please find Part 8 (Local Election Officials) in Appendix A as an example of a standalone manual 
section.  Please note that there may be small edits to the formatting and appearance of the manual as it is 
in the final stages of approval. 
4. Questions? 
Please direct any questions to our Help Desk at elections@wi.gov or 608-261-2028.

Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 1
Part 8  
Local Election Officials
County Clerks; Municipal Clerks; Election 
Inspectors; Election Registration Officials
An election official is defined as “an individual who is charged with 
any duties relating to the conduct of an election.” Wis. Stat. § 5.02(4e). 
County, municipal and school district clerks are election officials, as are 
election inspectors, chief inspectors, election registration officials (EROs), 
tabulators, greeters, and canvass board members.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 2
Chapter 8.1: County Clerks
Sec. 8.1.1: Election & Qualifications
County clerks must be eligible electors of their county and are elected 
for a term of four years during the partisan General Election in the Fall. 
Wis. Stats. §§ 59.20(1), (2)(a).
Sec. 8.1.2: Duties
County clerks serve as the chief election official in each county. 
Wis. Stat. § 59.23(2)(i). A county clerk’s election duties include preparing and 
providing ballots for every election for all national, state, and county offices and 
referendums, publishing applicable public notices relating to a national, state, 
or county election, and assisting with training and general voter education. 
Wis. Stats. §§ 7.10, 59.23(2)(i). For more information on the county clerk’s role in 
the ballot printing and distribution process, see Part 5, Chapter X.
The county clerk also serves as the filing officer for county offices and multi-
jurisdictional judges. Wis. Stats. §§ 8.10(6)(b), 8.15(8)(b), 8.20(7).
On election night, the county clerk is required to keep the office open to receive 
reports from all wards and also to post the unofficial results of elections. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.60(1). The county clerk is required to post unofficial returns no later 
than two hours after receiving them. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(1).
Additionally, the county clerk is one member of the County Board of Canvassers 
(CBOC), and is responsible for the canvass and return of votes at general, 
judicial, and special elections. Wis. Stats. §§ 7.60(2), 59.23(2)(i). The county clerk 
chooses the other members of the CBOC from lists submitted by political party 
county committees, and at least one member of the CBOC must be from a 
political party other than the county clerk’s. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(2). The county 
clerk designates a deputy clerk who performs the county clerk’s duties on 
the CBOC in the event that the county clerk’s office is vacant or if the county 
clerk is unable to perform these duties. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(2). The county clerk 
cannot serve on the CBOC if the clerk is on the ballot unless the clerk is running 
unopposed. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(2).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 3
Chapter 8.2: Municipal Clerks
Sec. 8.2.1: Appointment 
& Qualifications
Municipal clerks are elected by the electors or appointed to their positions by 
the governing body of a given town, village, or city, and if elected, must be 
electors of the municipality. See Wis. Stats. §§ 60.30(1)(a)2., (1e)(a) (towns),  61.19 
and 61.195 (villages); and 62.09(1)(a), (2)(a), (3).
Sec. 8.2.2: Duties
The municipal clerk’s far ranging election duties include managing elections 
and voter registration in the municipality, equipping polling places, purchasing 
and maintaining election equipment, preparing ballots and notices, and 
conducting and tracking the training of other election officials. Wis. Stat. § 7.15.
Sec. 8.2.3: Training Requirements
Each municipal clerk must attend training sponsored by the Wisconsin Elections 
Commission every two years. Wis. Stats. §§ 7.15(1m), 7.315(2).. All municipal 
clerks must receive an initial certification by attending the Municipal Clerk 
Core Curriculum Training course, which counts as three hours of training. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.03(1) and (2). The initial certification must be completed 
before a clerk may administer an election. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.03(1).
Clerks must earn a minimum of six hours of training during the current 
election cycle, which begins January 1 of even-numbered years and ends 
on December 31 of odd-numbered years, to maintain certification for the 
next election cycle. Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL 12.01(2), 12.03(2). For new clerks 
who completed a three-hour initial certification, this means completing an 
additional three hours of training during an election cycle, and for clerks 
renewing a certification, the clerks must complete six hours of training within 
an election cycle. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.03(2). Training hours beyond the 
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 4
6 required do not count toward certification in subsequent election cycles. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.03(4). Please see elections.wi.gov for Training Tables 
listing the approved methods of accumulating training hours for clerks.
Municipal clerks may attend approved training from certified trainers, but 
the clerks must report any training not conducted by Commission staff or 
obtained from the Commission’s ElectEd website to the Commission for it 
to count toward the 6-hour requirement. Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL 12.02(5), 
12.03(5)(e). Clerks must register for trainings appearing on the ElectEd 
website, and Commission staff will compare registration with attendance to 
assign credit. See Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.03(4). Clerks must report trainings 
taken with certified trainers and the number of hours to the Commission 
using the Offline Training Hours Request Form which is found on ElectEd. 
See Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.03(5)(e). All in-person or live online training 
conducted by WEC staff or taken in ElectEd will be tracked in ElectEd, along 
with training taken from certified trainers and reported to the WEC on the 
Offline Training Hours Request Form. See Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.03(4). See the 
ElectEd catalogue or reach out to elections.training@wi.gov for more details 
about training opportunities.
Clerks must provide the municipal mailing address and an email address for a 
municipality’s top elected official to the Commission, and a clerk must provide 
any new address or email within 21 days of a change to that information. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.02(7). If a new clerk does not complete an initial 
certification prior to an election, the Commission must notify the top elected 
official of the municipality by mail and email of the deficiency before the 
election takes place. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.02(7). For a renewal certification, 
the Commission must notify the top elected official of a deficiency within 30 
days of an election cycle’s end. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.02(7).
In an emergency, a clerk, in an expeditious manner, may request that the 
Commission Administrator grant a waiver of a training requirement by 
describing the facts that establish the basis of the emergency and details 
the steps taken to obtain the required training. Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL 12.05(1), 
(2), and (3). The Administrator may grant the waiver for one election cycle, 
but for an initial certification, the waiver is only valid for one election. 
Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL 12.03(1), 12.05(4).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 5
Chapter 8.3: Election 
Inspectors (General)
Election inspectors, also known as “poll workers,” are charged with the statutory 
duties of running the election on Election Day. Thousands of election inspectors 
are needed across the state for each election, especially during high-turnout 
General Elections in presidential years. The law outlines a specific process for 
order of preference of those interested in serving, a process which is designed 
to ensure that both major political parties have fair participation of their 
affiliated election inspectors at polling places.
As this chapter explains in more detail, election 
inspectors are chosen in the following order:
1. Consideration of all appointed partisan inspectors
2. Consideration of all appointed unaffiliated inspectors
3. Temporary appointments to fill the remainder of inspectors needed
Sec. 8.3.1: Duties
Election inspectors staff the polling place on Election Day. Election inspectors’ 
duties include setting up the polling place, preserving order, registering electors, 
recording voter numbers, issuing ballots, monitoring voting equipment, counting 
votes, and properly completing required forms. Wis. Stat. § 7.37.
Best Practice: Election inspectors should not serve at elections in which 
they, their spouse, or an immediate family member is a candidate 
on the ballot or under other circumstances where a candidate’s 
success or failure would affect the election inspector financially.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 6
Sec. 8.3.2: Number of Election 
Inspectors Required
Each polling place should have at least seven inspectors. The governing body 
may increase the number where more than one voting device is used or polling 
places are combined in accordance with Wis. Stats. §§ 5.15(6)(b), 7.30(1)(a). This 
governing body action need not be done by ordinance.1
By ordinance, the governing body may provide for the selection of alternates 
or for the selection of two or more sets of inspectors to work at different times 
on Election Day. Alternate officials shall be appointed in a number sufficient to 
maintain adequate staffing of polling places. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(a).
The governing body of the municipality may reduce the number of election 
inspectors by resolution. However, no polling place may have fewer than three 
election inspectors. Wis. Stat. § 7.32.
There must always be an odd number of election inspectors at the polling place, 
regardless of increase or reduction by the governing body. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(a). 
See Sec. 8.4.2 for how to determine which political party receives the dominant 
number of election inspectors from within this odd number.
1  See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 7
Sec. 8.3.3: Qualifications
Election inspectors must meet specific, statutory criteria. The Commission 
has determined that municipal clerks, or governing bodies, must be able 
to take some reasonable steps to certify that election inspectors meet the 
requirements of Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2).2
Criteria 1 – Nomination
The two major political parties have the first right to submit lists of their 
preferred election inspectors for appointment by the municipal governing body. 
If there is a greater need than those who are nominated, the remaining election 
inspectors are politically unaffiliated. For detailed information on the nomination 
and appointment process for partisan election inspectors see Chapter 8.4.
Criteria 2 – English Comprehension
Inspectors must be able to read, write, and understand the English language. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a). The municipal clerk may administer an examination, if 
required by the governing body, to all persons nominated as election inspectors 
to prove their ability to read, write and understand the English language, and 
their general knowledge of the election laws. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(c).
Criteria 3 – Capable & of Good Understanding
Election inspectors must also “be capable, and be of good understanding.” 
Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a). The Commission has concluded that the requirements 
of “strong clerical skills” and “being an effective communicator” are consistent 
with this statutory requirement, and do not exceed it.3 The work of an election 
inspector is clerical by nature—inspectors review documents and complete 
and process paperwork. Capable election inspectors who are of good 
understanding must also by definition be effective communicators—they must 
be able to discuss and understand how to facilitate the voting procedure, and 
how to assist voters in the process.4
2  See EL 23-55, Kosloski v. Yenter (Decided April 8, 2024) and  
EL 24-39, Hanna v. Woodall et al (Decided July 18, 2025).
3  See EL 23-55, Kosloski v. Yenter (Decided April 8, 2024).
4  Id.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 8
Criteria 4 – Training
Inspectors are required to receive training from the municipal clerk within the 
two years preceding the election event at which the inspector intends to work. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.315(1)(b)1.
Criteria 5 – Election Presence/Service
An inspector may not be a candidate for any office to be voted on at an 
election at which they serve. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Criteria 6 – Qualified Elector Status
Election inspectors must be qualified electors of the county in which the 
municipality where the official serves is located. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
 Ɋ  The chief inspector(s) must be a qualified elector of the 
municipality in which they serve, except if a qualified 
candidate is not available. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
 Ɋ A high school student may be appointed to serve as an 
inspector, but not a chief inspector, only in the polling place 
that serves the student’s residence. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
Criteria 7 – Bipartisan Involvement
The municipal clerk should identify any election inspectors appointed by one of 
the two major political parties. The chief inspector must ensure that any Election 
Day tasks which require completion by two election inspectors are represented 
by each party, whenever possible. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 9
Sec. 8.3.4: Hiring & Background Checks
In order to pay election inspectors and manage them, municipalities often 
use the same or similar hiring policies and procedures as other municipal 
employees. This raises questions about what election inspectors can be 
required to provide, including consenting to background checks, as a condition 
of their service.
Applications
Application forms are generally permissible if their purpose is to gather only the 
information required for the municipal clerk, or governing body, to confirm that 
the election inspector meets the legal requirements of Wis. Stat. § 7.30. Name, 
address, date of birth, qualification to vote, and felony status are all relevant 
to that inquiry.5 Additional information (such as comfort level with technology, 
willingness to travel, and hours of availability) are likewise permissible as 
long as answering them is optional.6 When asking about felony convictions, 
the application should not require the election inspector to certify that they 
have never been convicted of a felony, it should instead ask “Have you been 
convicted of a felony, and if so, have you received a pardon or completed the 
terms of imprisonment, extended supervision, parole, or probation.”7
Background Checks
The Commission has determined that background checks are not per se 
unreasonable, but depending on the level of information they seek, they can 
cross the line and rise to an unreasonable condition for election inspectors.8 
For example, a background check form, which requires election inspectors to 
provide their date of birth, signature, Wisconsin driver’s license number, and 
social security number likely goes too far.9 Whenever municipalities determine 
that background checks or other hiring procedures are a required term or 
condition of employment for paid or unpaid municipal employees, the forms 
cannot go beyond what Wis. Stat. § 7.30 permits.10
5  See EL 24-39, Hanna v. Woodall et al (Decided July 18, 2025).
6  Id.
7  Id.
8  See EL 23-55, Kosloski v. Yenter (Decided April 8, 2024).
9  Id.
10  Id.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 10
Sec. 8.3.5: Term of Office
Election inspector terms run from January 1 of an even-numbered year through 
December 31 of the subsequent odd-numbered year. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4). If there 
is an election inspector vacancy, a new appointee will fill the remainder of the 
prior appointee’s two-year term. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(6)(a).
Sec. 8.3.6: Filling Vacancies
Permanent vacancies in Republican or Democratic positions are filled by 
the municipal clerk from the remaining names on the lists submitted by the 
parties or from names submitted by the parties to supplement the original lists. 
Wis. Stats. §§ 7.30(2)(b), (4)(d). Temporary vacancies created by a candidacy, 
illness, or other temporary causes can be filled by the municipal clerk to serve 
for one election only. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(b). Temporary vacancies are filled with 
temporary appointments and permanent vacancies are filled with permanent 
appointments, but the method of appointment from the appropriate party list 
does not change based on the type of vacancy.11
Note: Vacancies are filled from the lists submitted by the 
parties, not the list appointed by the governing body—thus, the 
number of partisan nominated election inspectors is not fixed 
at the amount initially appointed by the governing body.12
While the parties have the right to submit additional names for the purpose 
of filling vacancies under Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d), a clerk does not have a duty 
to solicit names from them and may proceed with filling a permanent or 
temporary vacancy immediately as the need arises, turning to remaining 
names or supplemental names on lists if any are available.13
11  See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
12  Id.
13  Id.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 11
 Ɋ A party that did not submit a list by November 30 may not submit 
a list of names after that deadline. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(b).
 Ɋ If there are no lists or the lists have been exhausted, 
the municipal clerk may fill the vacancy without regard 
to party affiliation. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
 Ɋ If an unaffiliated inspector vacates his or her position, and the party 
entitled to that position has submitted supplemental names, the 
vacancy is filled from the supplemental list. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
 Ɋ If no supplemental list has been submitted since the unaffiliated 
appointment was made, the clerk may fill the vacancy with 
another unaffiliated inspector. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
Sec. 8.3.7: Training Requirements
Election inspectors are required to attend training every two years and must 
have attended training within each appointment term prior to any election 
at which they will serve. Wis. Stat. § 7.315(1)(b)1. Please see elections.wi.gov for 
Training Tables listing the approved methods of accumulating training hours 
toward recertification of election inspectors.
 Ɋ It is the responsibility of the municipal clerk to see that all 
election inspectors are provided with adequate training for the 
performance of their duties. Wis. Stats. §§ 7.315(1)(b)1., 7.30(2)(c).
 Ɋ Clerks may remove an inspector for failure to attend 
required training sessions. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(6)(c).
Best Practice: The Wisconsin Elections Commission 
suggests, at a minimum, that the clerk go over the 
election day duties listed in this manual.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 12
Best Practice: Because all election inspectors must receive 
training before administering an election, the Commission strongly 
recommends holding training classes in January of each even 
numbered year. Because election inspectors are appointed at the 
end of odd numbered years and many municipalities will need to 
administer a February primary, there can be a very short amount 
of time during which required training must take place. Clerks have 
discretion concerning how to provide this training and may make 
use of the Commission’s resources in ElectEd for this purpose.
Sec. 8.3.8: Oaths of Office
All election officials are required to take and file an oath, including those who 
are filling vacancies Wis. Stat. § 7.30(5).Municipal clerks must notify, by mail, 
appointed official within five days of appointment of the requirement to file an 
official oath, and the official must file the oath with the clerk within 10 days after 
mailing the notice. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(5).
Best Practice: The Commission recommends also emailing 
each official who is appointed to ensure they receive the 
information concerning the oath as quickly as possible.
Election officials who have taken the oath may administer any oath required 
to conduct an election. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(5). The oath must be filed before the 
commencement of the official’s duties. Wis. Stats. §§ 7.30(5), 6.875(5). The oath is valid 
for the entire two-year term of the appointment. See Wis. Stats. §§ 7.30(5), (6)(a).
Note: The following oaths may be obtained from the WEC website:
Official Oath (EL-154): Filed by Election Inspectors, 
Chief Inspectors, Election Registration Officials, 
Greeters, and Tabulators. See Wis. Stat. § 19.01.
Oath of Special Voting Deputy (EL-155): Filed by 
Special Voting Deputies. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(5).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 13
Sec. 8.3.9: Scheduling of 
Election Inspectors
 Ɋ Once election inspectors (partisan and unaffiliated) have been 
nominated and appointed, municipal clerks have some discretion to 
make scheduling decisions based on the needs of their jurisdiction. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.15(1). Municipal clerks should communicate with the 
political parties prior to nomination so that election inspectors know 
what form of communication will be used for scheduling information 
and announcements (phone, email, mail, online portal). This will 
ensure that those who have been appointed to serve don’t miss 
out due to missed communication between them and the clerk.
 Ɋ Some election day tasks require the involvement of 2 or more 
inspectors, each of whom should be from one of the political 
parties (insofar as practicable) if lists were submitted, so those 
requirements must be considered when scheduling election inspectors. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2). Wherever an Election Day action requires 2 or more 
election inspectors, at least one inspector from each party should 
be assigned to the work if it is practicable to do so.14 Election day 
tasks are assigned by the Chief Inspector. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Sec. 8.3.10: Removing Election Officials
Municipal clerks can discharge an election official summarily if he or she is 
found to lack the qualifications for the position, fails to attend required training, 
neglects his or her duties during an election, electioneers, commits official 
misconduct, or otherwise carries out improper conduct or willfully neglects 
duties. Wis. Stats. §§ 7.15(1)(f),  7.30(6)(c). Further, an election official required to 
use voting equipment who does not understand the equipment cannot be 
allowed to serve. Wis. Stat. § 7.25(5)
14  See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 14
 Best Practice: Prior to dismissing an election official, the 
Commission recommends that a clerk contact any appointing 
political party and explain any issue with the official so that 
the party may address the issue with the election official. The 
Commission also recommends notifying the governing body of 
any issue with an election official that may lead to dismissal, and 
to notify the governing body if a clerk dismisses the official.
A municipal clerk who removes an election official without sufficient legal 
reason could become the subject of an administrative complaint brought 
under Wis. Stat. § 5.06.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 15
Chapter 8.4: Nomination 
& Appointment of Partisan 
Election Inspectors
State law openly permits and invites the participation of major political parties 
in the nomination and appointment of election inspectors in their communities. 
Each odd-numbered year, political parties submit their list of nominees to 
the municipal clerk or governing body. The clerk confirms the nominees are 
qualified to serve as election inspectors, and then prepares the information 
needed for the governing body to consider and decide appointments. The 
governing body of each municipality then appoints the election inspectors. This 
chapter describes that process.
Sec. 8.4.1: Nomination by Political Party
The two political parties whose candidates for governor or president received 
the largest number of votes in the previous general election may submit lists of 
election inspector nominees no later than November 30 of an odd-numbered 
year. The political parties determine on their own who to nominate as election 
inspectors, and a clerk does not have any power to alter the names that are 
included.15 See Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(b). The political parties that submit lists shall 
certify that they contacted every person included on the list and they have 
agreed to serve as election officials. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(b). When party lists 
are received, election inspector appointments must be made from them. 
Wis. Stats. §§ 7.30(4)(b), (2).
15  See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 16
Best Practice: Municipal clerks should contact the appropriate 
statutory committeeperson or voluntary county party 
chairperson before the first week in November and advise him 
or her of their responsibility to submit a list of nominees to the 
Mayor, Village President, Town Board Chairperson, or municipal 
clerk. A clerk may recommend election inspectors who have 
proven to be effective workers. Clerks should also explain to 
the parties exactly how they plan to contact nominated and/
or appointed election inspectors (email, phone, letter, online 
portal) so the election inspectors know what to look out for.
If the list of appointed election inspectors is emailed, a signed original of the 
document must also be received, either postmarked or delivered by, the filing 
deadline. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 6.04(3).
Nominated election inspectors still must meet all of the legal requirements 
in Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2), and municipal clerks, or governing bodies, retain the 
right to reasonably certify that nominated election inspectors meet statutory 
requirements, including by requiring nominated election inspectors to complete 
the appropriate paperwork.16
Sec. 8.4.2: Determining Party 
Imbalance at Each Polling Place
The party whose candidate for governor or president at the last general election 
received the most votes at that polling place (the “dominant” party) is entitled 
to one extra inspector. Wis. Stats. §§ 7.30(4)(b), (2).
Best Practice: Determine party imbalance for each 
polling place in anticipation of receiving lists of inspector 
nominees from the political parties to ensure proper 
assignment and adequate staffing for shift or election.
16  EL 24-39, Hanna v. Woodall et al (Decided July 18, 2025).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 17
Example: The Republican candidate for governor received the most votes at 
the polling place at the last general election, seven total inspectors are needed. 
Thus, the clerk should ensure the assignment of four Republican positions and 
three Democratic positions. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Positions identified as Republican and Democratic remain as such for the 
duration of the term. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(6)(a).
Sec. 8.4.3: Contact Nominees 
for Willingness to Serve
Best Practice: Clerks should contact each party’s nominees 
to confirm their willingness to serve before submitting 
the names to the governing body for appointment.
 Ɋ Clerks should make at least two attempts to contact each party’s 
nominees, though those attempts can be by any reasonable method 
(phone, email, mail, online portal).
 Ɋ Document any nominees not willing to serve and provide the party 
those names.
 Ɋ The clerk may also inquire as to willingness to serve as a chief 
inspector and arrange for training for those who are interested.
Just because a nominee has declined to work at a previous election, even more 
than one previous election, does not mean the clerk is excused from contacting 
them to confirm their willingness to serve.17
Note: Refusal to serve as a chief inspector is 
not grounds for non-appointment.
17  See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 18
Appointments must be made from the lists submitted by the parties for as long 
as election inspector positions are available. If party lists have been timely 
received, positions must be filled from the lists until the names on those lists 
have been depleted. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
Nominees must be qualified electors of the county in which they reside. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
The lists may also designate individuals as first choice nominees, who must be 
appointed first. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(b).
Best Practice: If “first choice” is not indicated in some manner, but the 
names are numbered, they should be appointed in numerical order.
If the governing body has good cause not to appoint an individual whose 
name is submitted as a “first-choice” nominee, it may request the commission 
authorize non-appointment, and may not decline to appoint such individual 
until receiving the Commission’s authorization. Wis. Stat. §§ 7.30(4)(e), (b).
Best Practice: Seeking non-appointment from the Commission 
is a public process which might expose the election inspectors 
in question to embarrassment or unnecessary scrutiny. Before 
seeking non-appointment, municipal clerks could share their 
concerns with the nominating political party in an attempt to inquire 
whether the political party wishes to withdraw the nominee.
When party lists are received, the clerk must adhere to “party imbalance” 
at each polling place. The dominant party is entitled to one more election 
inspector at that polling place than the other party. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Example: Five election inspectors are to be placed at a polling place. The Democratic 
candidate for governor or president received the most votes at the polling place at 
the last general election. This means that three positions are Democratic, and two 
positions are Republican, and they should be appointed as such.
Note: It is possible that the dominant party will differ 
between polling places in the same municipality.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 19
Sec. 8.4.4: If Lists are Received 
but are Insufficient to Fill Need
If the Democratic and Republican parties’ lists are insufficient or the 
nominees decline to serve in the positions available for that party’s 
nominees, the remaining positions are filled without regard to party affiliation. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(c).
Example: Seven inspectors are to be placed at a polling place. The Republican 
candidate for governor or president received the most votes at the polling place 
at the last general election. This party imbalance gives the Republican Party 
the extra inspector so the ratio is four Republican positions to three Democratic 
positions. If sufficient lists from both parties were submitted, four names would 
be appointed from the Republican list, and three names would be appointed 
from the Democratic list.
However, if there are only three names on the Republican list and no Democratic 
list was submitted, the governing body will appoint the three Republican names. 
The Mayor, Village President, or Town Board Chairperson of the municipality will 
then nominate other qualified individuals, regardless of party affiliation, and 
submits the names to the governing body for appointment to the remaining 
four positions.
Note: Regardless of an appointee’s separately conveyed 
political affiliation, they are an unaffiliated appointee 
if they were not submitted on a party list.
If the Democratic Party submitted a list with two names, the two Democratic 
nominees and two unaffiliated nominees would be appointed along with the 
three Republican nominees.
The parties may supplement their initial list of nominees at any time during the 
term. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 20
Sec. 8.4.5: If No Lists are 
Received from Parties
If no lists of inspector nominees are submitted, the Mayor, Village President 
or Town Board Chairperson of the municipality nominates other qualified 
individuals, regardless of party affiliation, and submits the names to the 
governing body for appointment. All appointments are made without regard to 
party affiliation. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(c).
Sec. 8.4.6: Appointment of 
Inspectors by Governing Body
Appointment of inspectors must occur no later than December 31st of an odd-
numbered year. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(a).
The clerk submits the party lists to the governing body. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(b)2. 
The clerk should clearly indicate which partisan election inspectors were 
appointed by which party as this information might be critical to a governing 
body appointing the right balance of election inspectors.18
 Ɋ Advise the governing body of the requirement to appoint 
any first-choice nominees first. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(b)2.c.
 Ɋ Advise the governing body if lists are insufficient so that unaffiliated 
inspectors may be nominated. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(c). However, the 
parties may supplement their initial list of nominees at any time during 
the term to fill vacancies, but an appointment need not be delayed 
because of lack of availability of party nominees. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
The governing body must appoint at least as many inspectors as there are 
positions to be filled. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(a). See Sec. 8.3.2: “Number of Election 
Inspectors Required” on page 6
Appointments are made from the party lists until each party’s positions have 
been filled or until the lists are depleted. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
18  See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 21
If positions remain open and the lists have been depleted, “unaffiliated” 
inspectors may be appointed to the remaining positions. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
Additional inspectors may be appointed as alternates. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(a).
If a municipality establishes a municipal board of absentee canvassers 
(“central count”) by ordinance, who will then separately count the absentee 
ballots in lieu of canvassing absentee ballots at the polling place, the governing 
body will appoint the clerk, or another qualified elector designated by the clerk, 
and two other qualified electors of the municipality appointed by the clerk, to 
serve on that board. Wis. Stats. §§ 7.53(2m)(b), 7.52(1)(b).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 22
Chapter 8.5: High School 
Student Election Inspectors
State law permits certain qualified high school students to work at the polls 
on Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am). Students may decide for themselves 
to serve as election inspectors or in response to a school sponsored initiative. 
Civics, government or political science teachers may see this as an opportunity 
for a real-life learning experience. Student organizations may find this to be an 
attractive form of community service and an interesting learning opportunity. 
Allowing students to work as election inspectors provides an opportunity for 
students to become involved in the election process and also offers clerks 
another resource for filling election inspector positions. Students with foreign 
language skills can help voters who may need assistance understanding 
the ballot, voting equipment, and other election-related materials. In many 
locations, Hmong and Spanish speaking voters need special assistance, or 
the municipality may have specific language assistant requirements in place 
under Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act that can be met with the placement 
of bilingual inspectors. Municipal clerks are encouraged to work with their local 
high schools to enable students to serve as election inspectors.
Sec. 8.5.1: Qualifications
A student qualifies to serve as an election inspector if the student:
 Ɋ Is 16 or 17 years of age. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
 Ɋ Is enrolled in grades 9 to 12 in a public, private, or tribal school, or 
private home-based educational program. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
 Ɋ Has at least a 3.0 grade point average or the 
equivalent. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
 Ɋ Has the written approval of the student’s parent 
or guardian. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
 Ɋ Has the written approval of the principal of the school in 
which the student is enrolled, if the student has less than 
a 3.0 grade point average. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
 Ɋ Is a resident of the municipality of the polling place at 
which he or she serves. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 23
Sec. 8.5.2: Written 
Authorization Required
Before a student may be appointed as an inspector, the municipal clerk 
shall obtain written authorization from the student’s parent or guardian. If 
the student has less than a 3.0 grade point average, the clerk will also need 
authorization from the principal of the school where the student is enrolled. 
Upon appointment, the municipal clerk shall notify the principal of the school 
where the student is enrolled regarding the date of the election at which the 
student will serve. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
Sec. 8.5.3: Restrictions
 Ɋ A student may only serve as an inspector at a polling place 
if at least one inspector, other than the chief inspector, is a 
qualified elector of the municipality. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
 Ɋ A student may not serve as chief inspector at a 
polling place. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
 Ɋ A student serving as an election inspector may not challenge 
any person offering to vote. Wis. Stat. § 6.92(2).
 Ɋ A student must serve at the polling place that corresponds 
to their residential address, even if there are other polling 
places within the municipality. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 24
Chapter 8.6: Chief Election 
Inspectors
The Chief Election Inspector (also referred to as the Chief Inspector) is a 
specialty election inspector with additional training who directs the conduct of 
activities assigned to the inspectors at the polling place.
Sec. 8.6.1: Designating a Chief Inspector
The municipal clerk designates one of the inspectors as chief inspector (CI) 
for the polling place. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(6)(b). The clerk is not required to honor a 
political party’s or governing body’s request or instruction that a specific election 
inspector be designated as a CI.19 This individual acts as liaison between the 
election inspectors and the municipal clerk and is in charge of the polling place 
on Election Day. The CI must be a qualified elector of the municipality, except 
when no qualified candidate is available or a vacancy is being filled pursuant 
to Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(b), in which case they need not be a qualified elector of the 
municipality. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a). The CI is counted in the overall odd number of 
inspectors at the polling place. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(a).
Although the municipal clerk ultimately designates the CI, care should be taken 
to maintain the party imbalance. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Best Practice:
 Ɋ If all positions at the polling place have been filled from party lists, 
clerks are encouraged to select one of the party appointees as the CI.
 Ɋ If none of the party appointees are qualified as chief inspectors, 
select a qualified unaffiliated inspector. (Keep party representation 
even.)
 Ɋ If there are a mixture of affiliated and unaffiliated inspectors, choose 
any qualified inspector.
 Ɋ If it is necessary to remove an inspector in order to insert a qualified 
CI, replace an unaffiliated inspector if possible.
19  See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 25
Sec. 8.6.2: Municipal Residents 
vs. County Residents
Wisconsin Statute § 7.30(2)(a) indicates a preference for the CI to be a municipal 
resident, but offers an exception: “…each chief inspector shall be a qualified 
elector of the municipality in which the chief inspector serves. If no qualified 
candidate for chief inspector is available…the person so appointed need not be 
a qualified elector of the municipality…” (emphasis added)
Again, the municipal clerk chooses the CI, but the statute confines the selection 
to municipal residents unless no qualified municipal resident is available. 
This requirement, when intertwined with the requirement to maintain party 
imbalance, can be a challenge to implement.
Best Practice:
It is recommended to choose a CI using the following priority order:
1. Affiliated municipal resident
If there is an affiliated inspector who is a resident of the municipality 
who is trained or willing to be trained as a CI, arrange for training and 
use for CI. Maintain party imbalance at the polling place.
2. Unaffiliated municipal resident
If no affiliated municipal resident is trained or willing to be trained as 
a CI, arrange for training of an unaffiliated municipal resident. If this 
means replacing an affiliated inspector, keep the party representation 
even.
3. Affiliated resident of the county
If there is no affiliated or unaffiliated municipal resident trained 
or willing to be trained as a CI, arrange for the training of a willing 
affiliated inspector who is a resident of the county.
4. Unaffiliated resident of the county
If there is no municipal resident or affiliated county resident trained or 
willing to be trained, arrange for training of a willing unaffiliated county 
resident. If this means replacing an affiliated inspector, keep the party 
representation even.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 26
Sec. 8.6.3: Training Requirements
Chief inspectors are required to attend “Baseline” training in order to be initially 
certified. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 11.02(2). Attending Baseline training certifies the 
attendee as a chief inspector for the current term. In order to re-certify for the 
following term, a chief inspector must attend at least six hours of Wisconsin 
Elections Commission approved continuing election education during the 
current term. (Attendance at Baseline training also counts toward recertification 
for the following term, if the course retaken.) Wis. Admin. Code § EL 11.03(1). 
Please see elections.wi.gov for Training Tables listing the approved methods 
of accumulating training hours toward recertification of chief inspectors. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.31(4).
The county or municipal clerk conducting recertification training for other 
clerks or election inspectors must submit an agenda or course outline to 
the Wisconsin Elections Commission for approval. Training hours of election 
inspectors are documented and tracked by the municipal clerk. Chief inspectors 
may be given a self-administered evaluation as part of training, the results of 
which will not affect the chief inspector’s appointment or qualifications to serve. 
The results do not have to be reported to the WEC.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 27
Chapter 8.7: Greeters & 
Tabulators
Sec. 8.7.1: Greeters
Each municipality may appoint one additional inspector per polling place 
regardless of party affiliation to act as a greeter and substitute for other officials 
as necessary on Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(b). Greeters may not participate 
in canvassing after the polls close. Wis. Stats. §§ 7.51(1), 7.53(1)(a). Greeters do not 
count towards the number of election inspectors, unless they are stepping in to 
complete official duties, such as if another election inspector goes on a break. 
See Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(b). Only greeters who are currently trained and certified as 
election inspectors may cover for other election inspectors. Wis. Stat. § 7.315(1)(b)1. 
Because greeters are classified as additional election inspectors, and because 
they are able to substitute for election inspectors making up the appointed 
number for the polling place, they should receive the same training as other 
inspectors. See Wis. Stats. §§ 7.30(1)(b), 7.315(1)(b)1. An individual appointed as a 
greeter cannot serve as a chief inspector. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(6)(b).
Best Practices for Greeters:
 Ɋ Direct voters to the correct ward, registration table, or poll book table.
 Ɋ Answer general questions about the voting process or direct 
questions to another election inspector or the Chief Inspector.
 Ɋ Review a voter’s proof of residence or photo ID and advise the voter 
if the document(s) is acceptable. The voter must still provide the 
document(s) to the election inspectors to register to vote or be issued 
a ballot.
 Ɋ Confirm if a voter is in the right polling place or direct the voter to the 
proper polling place by searching for the voter’s address in MyVote, 
on a district map, or on another copy of the poll list.
 Ɋ  Substitute for election inspectors taking a break
 Ɋ Help maintain clear pathways for voters to enter and move through 
the polling area in an orderly manner.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 28
Sec. 8.7.2: Tabulators
Not less than 30 days before an election, the governing body or board of 
election commissioners may, by resolution, authorize the municipal clerk to 
select and employ tabulators for the elections specified in the resolution or, if 
not specified, until the resolution is modified or revoked. Wis. Stats. §§ 7.30(3)(a), 
(b), 7.30(3)(a). Tabulators are to assist and be under the direction of the election 
inspectors after the polls close. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(3)(b).
Separately, a recount board of canvassers may select and employ tabulators 
under their direction to assist in recount duties, and such tabulators cannot 
make determinations on the validity of any vote tabulated. Wis. Stat. § 9.01(5)(b).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 29
Chapter 8.8: Election 
Registration Officials
Election Registration Officials (EROs) are specially designated election officials 
who are authorized to register voters. They should not be confused with Special 
Registration Deputies, which were eliminated from Wisconsin law in 2016. See 2015 
WI Act 261. They should also not be confused with Special Voting Deputies (SVDs).
Sec. 8.8.1: Appointment 
& Qualifications
An Election Registration Official (ERO) is an election official who is assigned 
under Wis. Stats. §§ 6.28(1)(a) or 7.30 to register electors. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(4g). 
Municipal Clerks may appoint Election Registration Officials to conduct voter 
registration at the polling place on Election Day, at residential care facilities 
during the open registration period, and in the clerk’s office during in-person 
absentee voting. Wis. Stat. § 6.28(1)(a). EROs do not count towards the number of 
inspectors at a polling place. See Wis. Stat. § 6.55.
Best Practice: An ERO should be a qualified elector of the county for 
the polling place, residential care facility or clerk’s office at which they 
serve, however, a non-resident clerk or deputy clerk could serve as an 
ERO in case of a vacancy. See Wis. Stats. §§ 5.02(4g) and 7.30(2)(a).
Party lists may also be used for selections of EROs if there are additional names, 
or inspectors can be trained as EROs in addition to inspectors so that they can 
assist in registration during IPAV or SVD voting. Sending an ERO to an SVD facility, 
or training the SVDs as EROs, can allow eligible electors residing in the homes or 
facilities to register during the open registration period.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 30
Sec. 8.8.2: Duties
 When appointed by a municipal clerk, EROs can process registrations and 
sign registration forms when an elector registers at a polling place, IPAV site, 
or SVD location. Wis. Stats. §§ 6.28(1)(a), 6.33(2)(b), 6.55. For a description of 
how EROs register voters, see Section 6 Chapter 2 and Chapter XX (Election 
Day Registrations) as the processes are the same as when carried out by 
municipal clerks or election inspectors.
Sec. 8.8.3: Training Requirements
EROs are required to receive training from the municipal clerk within two years 
of any election at which they serve and take an oath. Wis. Stat. § 7.315 (4). 
It is the responsibility of the municipal clerk to see that EROs are provided 
with the same training as election inspectors for the performance of 
their duties. Wis. Stat. § 7.315(1)(b)1. and (4). The training must be complete 
before the ERO can take part in registration during a specific election. See 
Wis. Stats. §§ 7.315(1)(b)1., (4).
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 31
Chapter 8.9: Frequently Asked 
Questions
Q What if a trained election inspector is not available to 
work at an election, and I have to use an inspector who 
has not been trained within the last two years?
A In the event that a trained election inspector has an emergency 
and cannot work on Election Day, an inspector who has not received 
training may be appointed to serve as an inspector, but not as a chief 
inspector, Election Registration Official, or Special Voting Deputy. The 
appointment of an untrained individual is for a specific election only, 
and the untrained individual may only be appointed once in the two-
year period beginning on January 1 of each even-numbered year. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.315(1)(b)2. If the clerk is aware of the vacancy prior to Election 
Day, the clerk must provide some type of election training to the election 
inspector. Otherwise, the same qualifications that applied to original 
appointees shall be required of persons who fill vacancies except that 
if a municipal clerk or deputy clerk fills the vacancy, the clerk or deputy, 
but not more than a total of 2 individuals in any municipality, may serve 
without regard to the clerk’s or deputy’s county of residence, if the 
clerk or deputy meets the other qualifications. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(b).
Q What should I do if there is an emergency and I 
do not have a certified chief inspector?
A You should contact an Elections Specialist at the Wisconsin Elections 
Commission who will direct you on the actions to be taken. Best Practice: 
The Wisconsin Elections Commission recommends that all municipalities 
make advance arrangements to have alternate trained chief inspectors 
available in case of emergency. This type of pre-planning can be critical, 
and it may be coupled with an emergency polling place relocation plan 
or contingent staffing plan for elections.
Part 8:  Local Election Officials – 32
Q What is “Baseline” training?
A Baseline training is a two or three-hour chief inspector training 
course on basic election-day administration conducted by 
Wisconsin Elections Commission staff or WEC certified clerk-
trainers. The Baseline class is also available online in the 
Commission’s ElectEd learning management system. Baseline 
training is required for initial certification as a chief inspector.
Q I have a person who is interested in becoming a certified 
chief inspector. What does the person have to do to qualify 
as a certified chief inspector for the current term?
A The individual may accomplish certification by attending the Baseline 
training. Attendance at Baseline training will certify the new chief 
inspector for the current term. The newly certified chief inspector is 
then eligible to serve at all subsequent elections during the current 
term. See Wis. Admin. Code Chapter EL 11 for further information.
Q My chief inspector is certified for the current term. What else 
must he or she do in order to re-certify for the next term?
A In order to re-certify for the next term, the inspector will need to 
accumulate a minimum of six hours of Wisconsin Elections Commission 
approved training during the current term. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 11.03(1).

### UPDATED Ballot Spoiling Guidance

*Source: https://elections.wi.gov/memo/updated-ballot-spoiling-guidance. Fetched: 2026-09-10 (first seen 2026-09-10). Publisher's currency statement: Index page (Wayback snapshot 2026-08-07) lists items through 'Update on Ballot Spoiling Litigation — Wednesday, July 29, 2026'; each item carries its own publication date. Source verified official on 2026-09-10. Capture note: Memo page captured through a headless browser session because the Commission's site blocks automated clients; the memo's attachment(s) were fetched from the Commission's static document path and are appended in full.*

Friday, July 10, 2026
To
City of Milwaukee Election Commission
Milwaukee County Election Commission
Wisconsin County Clerks
Wisconsin Municipal Clerks
Priority
High Priority
File Downloads
File
Clerk Communication - UPDATED Ballot Spoiling Guidance - 7.10.26.pdf
1. Purpose.
Following feedback and questions from clerks, the Wisconsin Elections Commission voted on July 9, 2026 to withdraw the ballot spoiling guidance that was previously issued on May 27, 2026, and to issue new guidance. This guidance document replaces the May 27 guidance, and constitutes the Commission’s current guidance on the topic.
The Commission made two substantive changes
to the May 27 guidance
:
Clarified that a voter may receive up to two replacement absentee ballots for a total of three (which includes the original).
Determined that if a voter returns their voted ballot and later changes their mind about who they would like to vote for or because the candidate they originally voted for has dropped out of the race, this does not constitute an “accident or mistake.” The ballot cannot be spoiled and reissued for any reason.
In summary, once an absentee ballot has been returned to the municipal clerk, it cannot be spoiled and reissued for any reason. WEC staff will hold a training, which will include an opportunity for clerks to ask questions, during the week of July 13.  More information to follow.
2. Background.
The Wisconsin Court of Appeals for District II recently reversed the Waukesha trial court’s decision in
Nancy Kormanik v. Wisconsin Elections Commission
. The circuit court order in Kormanik had enjoined the Wisconsin Election Commission (Commission) from publishing its previous guidance on ballot spoiling and from similarly interpreting certain statutes pertaining to spoiling. After the reversal of that order, the Commission met in a public meeting on May 7, 2026, and opted not to reissue its two guidance documents from August of 2022. Instead, the Commission approved and issued guidance on May 27, and then revisited that guidance at the July 9 meeting after reviewing feedback from municipal and county clerks ahead of the August Partisan Primary.
3. Guidance.
Wisconsin law allows a voter who, by accident or mistake, spoils or erroneously prepares a ballot to receive another ballot by returning the defective ballot to the municipal clerk or election inspector. If a voter returns their voted ballot and later changes their mind about who they would like to vote for or because the candidate they originally voted for has dropped out of the race, this does not constitute an “accident or mistake.” The ballot cannot be spoiled and reissued for any reason.
The municipal clerk should verify the identity of a person requesting to receive a replacement absentee ballot to ensure that it is the voter making the request. This voter verification process should include having the voter confirm the same information necessary to request an absentee ballot (e.g. name, full address, date of birth) and this verification process may include the municipal clerk asking the absentee voter to produce voter identification. The deadlines for requesting a replacement for a spoiled or erroneously prepared ballot are:
Regular by-mail absentee voters requesting a ballot for one election; and overseas voters
: not later than 5 p.m. on the 5th day immediately preceding the election.
Indefinitely confined absentee voters; absentee voters making a calendar year request; and military voters who are not away from home due to service or who have requested a ballot for an election not including a national office
: not later than 5 p.m. on the Friday immediately preceding the election.
Absentee voters making an in-person request at the clerk’s office or in-person absentee voting location
: depending on the local hours as provided in a Type E notice, not later than the Sunday preceding the election.
Absentee voters requesting a ballot during a Special Voting Deputy visit
: depending on the schedule of Special Voting Deputy visits scheduled by the municipal clerk, not later than 5 p.m. the Monday preceding an Election Day.
Hospitalized voters by authorized representative; Military voters who are away from home due to service and have requested a ballot for an election including a national office; and sequestered jurors
: not later than 5 p.m. on Election Day.
A voter may only receive two replacement ballots, for a total not to exceed three, in each election. Wis. Stat.
§
6.80(2)(c).
4. Questions.
Questions about this process can be directed to local counsel or the Wisconsin Elections Commission at 608-261-2028 or
elections@wi.gov
. In addition, Commission staff are working to develop an administrative rule relating to ballot spoiling.

2026 to withdraw the ballot spoiling guidance that was previously issued on May 27, 2026, and to issue 
new guidance. This guidance document replaces the May 27 guidance, and constitutes the Commission’s 
current guidance on the topic.   
The Commission made two substantive changes to the May 27 guidance:  
1. Clarified that a voter may receive up to two replacement absentee ballots for a total of three 
(which includes the original).  
2. Determined that if a voter returns their voted ballot and later changes their mind about who they 
would like to vote for or because the candidate they originally voted for has dropped out of the 
race, this does not constitute an “accident or mistake.” The ballot cannot be spoiled and reissued 
for any reason.  
In summary, once an absentee ballot has been returned to the municipal clerk, it cannot be spoiled and 
reissued for any reason.  
WEC staff will hold a training, which will include an opportunity for clerks to ask questions, during the 
week of July 13. More information to follow.  
2. Background.  
The Wisconsin Court of Appeals for District II recently reversed the Waukesha trial court’s decision in 
Nancy Kormanik v. Wisconsin Elections Commission. The circuit court order in Kormanik had enjoined 
the Wisconsin Election Commission (Commission) from publishing its previous guidance on ballot 
spoiling and from similarly interpreting certain statutes pertaining to spoiling. After the reversal of that 
order, the Commission met in a public meeting on May 7, 2026, and opted not to reissue its two 
guidance documents from August of 2022. Instead, the Commission approved and issued guidance on

7/10/2026 
Page 2 
 
 
 
May 27, and then revisited that guidance at the July 9 meeting after reviewing feedback from municipal 
and county clerks ahead of the August Partisan Primary.  
3. Guidance. 
Wisconsin law allows a voter who, by accident or mistake, spoils or erroneously prepares a ballot to 
receive another ballot by returning the defective ballot to the municipal clerk or election inspector. If a 
voter returns their voted ballot and later changes their mind about who they would like to vote for or 
because the candidate they originally voted for has dropped out of the race, this does not constitute an 
“accident or mistake.” The ballot cannot be spoiled and reissued for any reason. 
The municipal clerk should verify the identity of a person requesting to receive a replacement absentee 
ballot to ensure that it is the voter making the request. This voter verification process should include 
having the voter confirm the same information necessary to request an absentee ballot (e.g. name, full 
address, date of birth) and this verification process may include the municipal clerk asking the absentee 
voter to produce voter identification. The deadlines for requesting a replacement for a spoiled or 
erroneously prepared ballot are: 
• Regular by-mail absentee voters requesting a ballot for one election; and overseas voters: not 
later than 5 p.m. on the 5th day immediately preceding the election. 
• Indefinitely confined absentee voters; absentee voters making a calendar year request; and 
military voters who are not away from home due to service or who have requested a ballot for an 
election not including a national office: not later than 5 p.m. on the Friday immediately 
preceding the election. 
• Absentee voters making an in-person request at the clerk’ s office or in-person absentee voting 
location: depending on the local hours as provided in a Type E notice, not later than the Sunday 
preceding the election. 
• Absentee voters requesting a ballot during a Special Voting Deputy visit: depending on the 
schedule of Special V oting Deputy visits scheduled by the municipal clerk, not later than 5 p.m. 
the Monday preceding an Election Day. 
• Hospitalized voters by authorized representative; Military voters who are away from home due to 
service and have requested a ballot for an election including a national office; and sequestered 
jurors: not later than 5 p.m. on Election Day. 
A voter may only receive two replacement ballots, for a total not to exceed three, in each election. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.80(2)(c). 
4. Questions.  
Questions about this process can be directed to local counsel or the Wisconsin Elections Commission at 
608-261-2028 or elections@wi.gov. In addition, Commission staff are working to develop an 
administrative rule relating to ballot spoiling.
