Part 2 
Getting on the Ballot
Candidate Qualifications; Ballot Access Procedure; Ballot 
Access Challenges; Nomination by Caucus; Notifications 
of Noncandidacy; Write-In Candidate Registration
Every federal, state, and local office has qualifications that interested 
candidates must meet. To appear on the ballot, candidates seek ballot 
access, either by circulating and signing nomination papers or by being 
nominated at a caucus. Ballot access paperwork can be challenged if not 
completed correctly, or if the candidate is not qualified for the office they 
seek. Candidates can also receive votes, but not have their names printed on 
the ballot if they register as a write-in candidate by the deadline to do so.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 1
Chapter 2.1: Qualifications 
for Office
All candidates must meet the office-specific qualifications and complete and 
file proper ballot access documents to appear on the ballot. See Chapter 2.2 for 
Ballot Access Procedure.
This chapter outlines the specific requirements to appear on the ballot in Wisconsin.
Sec. 2.1.1: Federal Offices:
Federal candidates file with the Wisconsin Elections Commission.
Candidates who have been convicted of a felony are still eligible for federal 
office, even if they have not been pardoned. See Wis. Const. Art. XIII, § 3(2), (3), 
Wis. Stat. § 8.21(4)(a) (limiting the requirement to “state and local office”).
President & Vice President:
A natural born citizen, at least 35 years old, and a resident of the United States 
for at least 14 years. U. S. Const. Art II § 1.
United States Senator
At least 30 years old, a citizen of the United States for at least 9 years, and an 
inhabitant of the state on Election Day. U. S. Const. Art. I § 3 (“when elected, be 
an Inhabitant of that State for which he shall be chosen”). U.S. Senators need not 
be an inhabitant of the state when circulating nomination papers or submitting 
ballot access paperwork.
Representative in Congress
At least 25 years old, a citizen of the United States for at least 7 years, and an 
inhabitant of the state on Election Day. Must also reside in their districts when 
they take office. U. S. Const. Art I § 2 (“when elected, be an Inhabitant of that 
State in which he shall be chosen”). Representative need not be a resident of 
his or her district at the time of filing nomination papers and a declaration of 
candidacy. 61 Atty. Gen. 155.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 2
Sec. 2.1.2: State & Local Offices
The Wisconsin Constitution and state law specify the requirements needed for 
a candidate to qualify for state or local office. The text below compiles the legal 
requirements for each state and local office. It is always incumbent upon each 
candidate to certify that they meet the qualifications of the office they seek. See 
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.21(2)(b), (c).
Many state and local offices in Wisconsin require candidates to be “qualified 
electors” of their jurisdictions, either before they file ballot access paperwork, 
before election day, on election day, or at the time they take office. “Qualified 
elector” and “eligible elector” mean the same thing, and both refer to an 
individual who meets the proper voter eligibility requirements for a jurisdiction, 
including the residency requirement. Town of Washington v. City of Altoona, 
73 Wis. 2d 250, 243 N.W.2d 404 (1976). Eligible electors are U.S. citizens, age 18 
or older, who have resided in their jurisdiction for at least 28 consecutive days 
before an election. Accordingly, when the law requires a candidate to be a 
“qualified elector” on election day, the candidate must be a U.S. citizen, age 18 
or older, who has lived in that jurisdiction at least 28 days prior to election day to 
be eligible. Additionally, qualified electors cannot be ineligible to vote for any of 
the reasons listed in Wis. Stat. § 6.03.
Qualifications for All State & Local Candidates
No candidate for state or local office is eligible for that office if they have been 
convicted of any misdemeanor that violates public trust, or any felony for 
which they have not been pardoned. Wis. Const. Art. XIII, § 3(2), (3), Wis. Stat. § 
8.21(4)(a). Further, no one elected to Congress or “holding any office of profit or 
trust under the United States except postmaster, or under any foreign power” is 
eligible for a state or local office in Wisconsin. Wis. Const. Art. XIII § 3(1).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 3
Sec. 2.1.3: Specific State-
Level Office Qualifications
State-level candidates file with the Wisconsin Elections Commission.
In addition to the qualifications listed in Sec. 2.1.2, the following offices  
must meet additional qualifications:
Governor & Lt. Governor
A U.S. citizen, and a “qualified elector” of the state at the time of taking office. 
Wis. Const. Art. V § 2.
Attorney General
No additional qualifications required, other than those listed in Sec. 2.1.2.
Secretary of State
No additional qualifications required, other than those listed in Sec. 2.1.2.
Treasurer
No additional qualifications required, other than those listed in Sec. 2.1.2.
Superintendent
No additional qualifications required, other than those listed in Sec. 2.1.2.
State Senator or Representative to the Assembly
A resident of the state for one year before and a “qualified elector” of the district 
at the time of taking office. Article IV, Section 6, Wis. Constitution. See also 65 
Atty. Gen. 159 (Representative need not be a resident of his or her district at the 
time of filing nomination papers and a declaration of candidacy).
Justice of the Supreme Court
A “qualified elector” of the state “at the time of election” and “an attorney 
licensed to practice law in this state [who has] been so licensed for 5 years 
immediately prior to election.” Wis. Const. Art. VII §§ 10, 24.
Court of Appeals Judge
A “qualified elector” of the appeals court district “at the time of election” and 
“an attorney licensed to practice law in this state [who has] been so licensed for 
5 years immediately prior to election.” Wis. Const. Art. VII §§ 5(2), 10, 24.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 4
Circuit Court Judge
A “qualified elector” of the circuit court district “at the time of election” and “an 
attorney licensed to practice law in this state [who has] been so licensed for 5 
years immediately prior to election.” Wis. Const. Art. VII §§ 7, 10, 24.
District Attorney
Licensed to practice law in Wisconsin and a resident of the prosecutorial unit 
(county) at the time of taking office. Wis. Stat. § 978.02
Sec. 2.1.4: County-Level 
Office Qualifications
County-level offices file either with the county clerk or county election 
commission. Multijurisdictional judicial candidates, in places that have enacted 
agreements under Wis. Stat. § 755.01(4), file with the county clerk of the county 
having the largest portion of the population in the jurisdiction served by the 
judge. Wis. Stat. § 8.10(6)(bm).
County Supervisor (Including Milwaukee County)
Qualified elector of district at the time of filing nomination papers. Wis. Stat. § 
59.20(1)(“elector of the supervisory district”).
Other County-level Offices (Register of Deeds, Treasurer, etc.)
A qualified elector of the county at the time of filing nomination papers. Wis. 
Stat. § 59.20(1) (“elector of the county”).
Sec. 2.1.5: Municipal-Level 
Office Qualifications
Municipal-level offices file either with the municipal clerk or city election 
commission.
Alderperson (Including City of Milwaukee)
A qualified elector of the city on Election Day, and aldermanic district “and 
actually residing therein.” Wis. Stat. § 62.09(2)(a) (“elector of the city”).
Other City Office (Including City of Milwaukee)
A qualified elector of the city on Election Day. Wis. Stat. §§ 62.09(2)(a) (“elector of 
the city”), 64.04(1).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 5
Village Offices
A qualified elector of the village and residing in village on Election Day. Wis. Stat. 
§ 61.19 (“no person not a resident elector in such village shall be elected to any 
office therein”).
Town Offices
A qualified elector of the town at the time of taking office. Wis. Stat. § 60.30(2)(a) 
(“only an elector of the town may hold a town office”). Town Assessors must be 
certified under Wis. Stat. § 73.09 before taking office. Wis. Stat. § 60.30(2)(d).
Sec. 2.1.6: School District 
Office Qualifications
School district offices file with the school district clerk, not the municipal clerk.
School Board Member (At-Large)
A qualified elector of the school district at the time of filing a Declaration of 
Candidacy. Wis. Stat. § 120.05(1)(d) (“resident of the school district”), 120.06(2)(a) 
(“electors of the school district”), (6)(b)2. (“any qualified elector of the school 
district may file a sworn declaration of candidacy”), 120.06(7)(a).
School Board Member Representing an Apportioned Area
A qualified elector of the school district at the time of filing a Declaration of 
Candidacy and a “resident of the apportioned area” at the time of taking 
the oath of office. Wis. Stat. § 120.05(1)(d) (“resident of the school district”), 
120.06(2)(b), (6)(b)2. (“any qualified elector of the school district may file a sworn 
declaration of candidacy”), 120.06(7)(a).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 6
Chapter 2.2: Ballot Access 
Procedure
All candidates must go through an affirmative process to qualify to have their 
names placed on the ballot. This process is referred to as “ballot access.” 
Candidates seek ballot access either by circulating and filing nomination 
papers or by being nominated by their local caucus. Major-party presidential 
and vice-presidential candidates are nominated by their party’s national 
nominating conventions in presidential election years.
Sec. 2.2.1: Filing Officers
“Filing Officer” refers to the government official or entity responsible for 
accepting and reviewing ballot access paperwork, and making decisions about 
whether candidates are granted ballot access. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(4v).
Note: It is crucial for candidates to submit their ballot access 
documents to the correct filing officer. If documents are given to the 
incorrect filing officer, there is no guarantee that they will be forwarded 
to the intended recipient in time to meet filing deadlines. For example, 
if a school board candidate mails their declaration of candidacy to the 
municipal clerk, instead of the school district clerk, on the day of the 
filing deadline, that clerk may be unable or unwilling to forward the 
document to the school district.
Commission as the Filing Officer
The Commission is the filing officer for all federal and state offices. Wis. 
Stat. §§ 8.10(6)(a) (nonpartisan offices), 8.15(8)(a) (partisan offices), 8.20(7) 
(independent offices). State office includes District Attorneys and Circuit 
Court Judges. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(23). The Commission is also the filing officer 
for seats on the metropolitan sewerage commission (if those seats are 
elected). Wis. Stat. § 8.10(6 )(a).
County Clerk as the Filing Officer
The County Clerk or County Board of Elections Commissioners (Milwaukee) is 
the filing officer for county offices. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(6)(b) (nonpartisan offices), 
8.15(8)(b) (partisan offices), 8.20(7) (independent offices).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 7
Multijurisdictional judges file with the County Clerk or County Board of Elections 
Commissioners (Milwaukee) of the county composing of the largest portion of 
the population in the area served by the judge. Wis. Stat. § 8.10(6)(bm).
Municipal Clerk as the Filing Officer
The Municipal Clerk is the filing officer for most other local races, including 
citywide offices, alderpersons, and municipal judges entirely within the local 
jurisdiction. Wis. Stat. § 8.10(6)(c). Multijurisdictional judges file with the county 
clerk of the county composing of the largest portion of the population in the 
area served by the judge. Wis. Stat. § 8.10(6)(bm).
School District Clerk as the Filing Officer
The School District Clerk is the filing officer for school board races.  
Wis. Stat. § 8.10(6)(d).
Sec. 2.2.2: General Procedures
All candidates, regardless of office sought, must complete the ballot access 
paperwork required for the office. Ballot access must be granted by the 
filing officer, meaning the filing officer must take an affirmative step to place 
candidates on the ballot. For statutory support for this premise, see Wis. Stat. 
§§ 7.08(2), 7.10(2), 7.15(1)(h), 10.06, 120.06(7). In other words, if a filing officer 
determines that a candidate is not qualified for the office they seek, the action 
taken is to refuse to grant access, as opposed to removing a candidate from 
the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 8.30.
Most candidates are nominated for office through the filing of nomination 
papers. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10 (nonpartisan candidates), 8.15 (partisan candidates), 
8.20 (independent candidates), 8.50(3) (special elections). However, some towns 
and villages use the caucus procedure to nominate candidates for town or 
village office. Wis. Stat. § 8.05(1). For detailed information on caucus procedures, 
see Chapter 2.4 on page 59.
Best Practice: The Commission maintains a number of Ballot 
Access Checklist resources on its website. Clerks should 
familiarize themselves with these checklists and make them 
available to candidates seeking office in their jurisdictions.

Sec. 2.2.3: Ballot Access Documents 
Required for All Candidates
All candidates, regardless of the nomination 
procedure used, must file two documents:
 Ɋ Campaign Finance Registration Statement (CF-1, CF-1L). Wis. Stat. § 11.0102(1).
 Ɋ Declaration of Candidacy (EL-162). Wis. Stat. § 8.21.
Campaign Finance Registration Statement
A campaign registration statement is required to be filed with the  
Wisconsin Ethics Commission for state offices, and this form is filed online. 
Wis. Stat. § 11.0102(1) . For local offices, the statement must be filed with the 
appropriate filing officer until December 1, 2027. After December 1, 2027, local 
candidates will file it directly with the Ethics Commission. Id.
Candidates who file nomination papers are required to file their CF-1 either 
before or with their Declaration of Candidacy. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(5) (nonpartisan 
candidates), 8.15(4)(b) (partisan candidates), 8.20(6) (independent candidates), 
8.50(3) (special elections). Candidates nominated by caucus also file their CF-1 
with their Declaration of Candidacy. Wis. Stat. § 8.05(1)(j).
Any candidate who is required to file a CF-1 and fails to do so by the deadline1 
cannot be placed on the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 8.30(2).
For questions related to the CF-1 or campaign finance, please contact the 
Wisconsin Ethics Commission at ethics@wi.gov, 608-266-8123, or the local 
filing officer.
Note: On December 1, 2027, local candidates will begin filing their CF-
1s directly with the Wisconsin Ethics Commission instead of their local 
filing officer. Until then, local candidates should continue filing these 
forms with their local clerks.
1 Candidates are required to file their CF-1 as soon as practicable after they qualify as a candidate 
under Wis. Stat. § 11.0101(1). Wis. Stat. § 11.0202(1)(a).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 10
Declaration of Candidacy
Candidates who file nomination papers must file their Declaration of 
Candidacy no later than the deadline provided for filing their nomination 
papers. Wis. Stat. § 8.21(1).
 Ɋ Candidates nominated by caucus must file their Declaration of 
Candidacy no later than 5 p.m. on the fifth day after the notification is 
sent. Wis. Stat. § 8.05(1)(j).
 Ɋ Candidates for U.S. president and vice president from parties that have 
received ballot status pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 5.62(1)(b) (also known as 
“major” political parties) are required to file a Declaration of Candidacy. 
Wis. Stat. § 8.21(1).
Best Practice: Wisconsin statutes do not provide a specific deadline 
for ballot status presidential candidates to file a Declaration of 
Candidacy, but the Commission advises that these candidates 
should file this form no later than 5 p.m. on the first Tuesday of 
September preceding a presidential election. See Wis. Stat. § 8.16(7).
Any candidate who fails to file a Declaration of Candidacy by the deadline 
cannot be placed on the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 8.30(4).
Sec. 2.2.4: Additional Filing 
Requirements for Certain Offices
All state office candidates as well as Municipal judge candidates also need to 
submit a Statement of Economic Interests to the Wisconsin Ethics Commission 
in order to meet ballot access requirements. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.05(1)(j)3., 8.10(5), 
8.15(4)(b), 8.20(6). Ballot Access Checklists indicate this requirement and 
the appropriate filing deadline. Forms and instructions are available from 
ethics.wi.gov or by contacting the Wisconsin Ethics Commission at 608-266-8123.
Additionally, some municipalities may have an ethics ordinance under  
Wis. Stat. § 19.59(3)(b), requiring a Statement of Economic Interests to be filed 
with the local filing officer in order to achieve ballot status.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 11
Best Practice: Municipal clerks who are unsure whether 
their municipality has an ethics statement requirement, 
should check with their municipal attorney. If a required 
statement is not filed by the deadline, the candidate’s 
name cannot appear on the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 8.30(3).
Best Practice: Clerks should make “candidate packets” available 
for all prospective local candidates. All ballot access forms and 
checklists are available on the respective Wisconsin Elections 
Commission and Wisconsin Ethics Commission websites.
Candidate packets should include the following forms:
 Ɋ Campaign Finance Registration Statement (CF-1). This form 
is available from the Wisconsin Ethics Commission.
 Ɋ Declaration of Candidacy (EL-162)
 Ɋ Nomination Paper for Nonpartisan Office (EL-169), if required
 Ɋ Appropriate Ballot Access and Campaign Finance 
Checklists located on the Commission’s website.
Sec. 2.2.5: Declarations of Candidacy
The Declaration of Candidacy is available on elections.wi.gov as Form EL-162.
Note: School District Candidates use the EL-162sd. Where the 
requirements below require specific language, that language is 
already included on the Commission’s versions.
Review Procedure
Declarations of candidacy must be filled out correctly by the candidate, and 
may be filed by the candidate or by proxy. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06(2)(a). The 
filing officer cannot accept a declaration of candidacy that does not contain all 
of the information required by Wis. Stat. § 8.21. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06(3)(d).
Upon receipt of a completed declaration of candidacy, the filing officer should 
immediately review the filed papers to determine sufficiency. See Wis. Admin. 
Code § EL 2.06(3)(a).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 12
Best Practice: Some filing officers choose to offer an initial review of 
declarations of candidacy as a courtesy to candidates. This initial 
review can be used to notify candidates of potential issues so they 
have the opportunity to remedy defects before the filing deadline. 
Candidates should understand that facial review is a courtesy only. 
Facial review is not binding, and will not serve as a defense to a 
challenge to their declaration of candidacy. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 
2.06(3)(a). Candidates are solely responsible for the sufficiency of 
their declaration of candidacy. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06(2)(a).
Any facially sufficient information which appears on a declaration of candidacy is 
entitled to a presumption of validity. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06(3)(b). Information 
is facially sufficient when it is substantially compliant with proper format and 
does not have one or more elements of missing, illegible, or obviously incorrect 
information. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(1)(h). Unlike nomination papers, a 
declaration cannot be accepted if it is missing required information, even if there 
has been substantial compliance with the law. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06(3)(d).
Requirements
 Ɋ The candidate’s name.  Wis. Stat. § 8.21(2) . The name must match the 
name used in the header of the candidate’s nomination papers.  
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06(4 )(ar).
 Ɋ The proper title of the office the candidate is seeking. Wis. Stat. § 8.21(2)(a). 
The name of the office must include the district, branch, or seat number 
as follows: 
 ɉ legislative offices: title and district number
 ɉ district attorneys: title and county
 ɉ circuit court offices: title, county, and branch number
 ɉ municipal and school board offices: title and any district seat number. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06(4)(b).
 Ɋ A statement that the signer meets, or will at the time he or she assumes 
office meet, applicable age, citizenship, residency, or voting qualification 
requirements, if any, prescribed by the constitutions and laws of the United 
States and of this state. Wis. Stat. § 8.21(2)(b).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 13
 Ɋ A statement that the signer will otherwise qualify for the office if 
nominated and elected. Wis. Stat. § 8.21(2)(c).
 Ɋ The candidate’s name in the form that the candidate wishes the name to 
appear on the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 8.21(3). The preferred ballot name cannot 
contain the word “incumbent,” include a professional title, or include an 
attempt to manipulate the electoral process. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06(5)(b). 
An intended name containing a nickname or initial, middle name, or formal 
legal surname is permitted provided that it does not include quotation marks 
or parentheses. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06(5)(b).
 Ɋ The form must be notarized or signed by a person authorized to 
administer oaths. Wis. Stat. § 8.21(2). See Chapter 2.3 on page 35 for 
examples of common challenges resolved by the Commission involving 
issues or defects with notarizations of declarations of candidacy.
State & Local Candidates Only
 Ɋ A statement that the candidate has not been convicted of any 
misdemeanor designated under state or federal law as a violation of the 
public trust or any felony for which the candidate has not been pardoned. 
Wis. Stat. § 8.21(4)(a).
 Ɋ The candidate’s municipality of residence for voting purposes, and the 
street and number, if any, on which the candidate resides. Wis. Stat. § 
8.21(4)(b). The residential address must include the street and number, and 
cannot be a post office box or other address at which the candidate does 
not reside. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06(5)(a).
Note: Certain judicial candidates or judicial officers may have the 
line “Residence Certified with WEC” in lieu of their address if they 
have completed the certification of residence process with the WEC. 
Wis. Stat. § 8.10(8). Such candidates whose residence is certified are 
not required to list their residential address on their declaration of 
candidacy. Local filing officers should check with the Commission to 
confirm whether a candidate’s address has been certified in order to 
be properly exempt.

Amending Declarations of Candidacy
If any information in a Declaration of Candidacy changes at any time after  
the original is filed, a state or local candidate must file an amended 
Declaration of Candidacy before the candidate assumes office or is defeated. 
Wis. Stat. § 8.21(6). The amended Declaration of Candidacy is filed with the 
same filing officer as the original. Id. If the Declaration of Candidacy that was 
filed by the filing deadline is later determined to be insufficient, an amended 
Declaration of Candidacy cannot cure the error(s). Wis. Stat. § 8.21(1) and (2). 
A Declaration of Candidacy will remain timely if the original Declaration was 
filed by the statutory deadline, even if an amended Declaration is filed.  
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06(2 )(b).
Correcting affidavits cannot correct or amend declarations of candidacy. Wis. 
Admin. Code § EL 2.06(3)(c).2
Sec. 2.2.6: Nomination Paper Procedure
Nomination papers are the primary method by which candidates in 
Wisconsin seek ballot access. Candidates circulate nomination papers 
within the jurisdiction represented by the office sought to collect the 
required number of signatures. All cities and some villages and towns use 
the nomination paper process. School board candidates should confirm 
with their school board clerk or administrative office to determine whether 
nomination papers are required and how many signatures are required. See 
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(3)(km), (ks), (3s), 120.06(6)(a).
The Commission maintains nomination form templates on its website. 
Candidates are free to use the template forms, and they may modify the header 
of the templates to contain their personal campaign information or graphics.
Best Practice: Candidates who modify the header of a nomination 
paper should ensure that it still conforms to all of the nomination 
paper header requirements of the office they seek.
Candidates are responsible for the completeness, legibility, and accuracy of the 
information contained on their nomination papers. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(3)(a).

Partisan races in Wisconsin appear on the Partisan Primary ballot and fall 
General Election ballot in even-numbered years. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.02(5), 5.02(12s). 
Partisan candidates file nomination papers either with their County Clerk or 
with the Commission. The form for partisan nomination papers is available on 
elections.wi.gov as EL-168.
Nomination papers for partisan office candidates may be circulated no sooner 
than April 15 preceding the general election, and may be filed no later than 5 p.m. 
on June 1 preceding the partisan primary. Wis. Stat. § 8.15(1).
Note: Independent candidates for president and vice president circulate 
nomination papers on a different timeline, though the procedure is 
largely the same. These candidates circulate nomination papers no 
sooner than July 1 and not later than 5 p.m. on the first Tuesday in 
August preceding a presidential election. Wis. Stat. § 8.20(8)(am).

First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 16
Nonpartisan races in Wisconsin appear on the Spring Primary ballot and Spring 
Election ballot every year. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(21), 5.02(22). Nonpartisan candidates 
file nomination papers with municipal clerks, school district clerks, county clerks, 
and with the Commission. The form for nonpartisan nomination papers is on 
elections.wi.gov as EL-169.
Nomination papers for nonpartisan office candidates may be circulated no 
sooner than December 1 preceding the election and no later than 5 p.m. on 
the first Tuesday in January preceding the election. Wis. Stat. § 8.10(2)(a). If 
the first Tuesday of January is a holiday, the nomination paper deadline is the 
next day. Id.
Filing Nomination Papers
In order to be timely filed, the original nomination papers must be in the 
physical possession of the filing officer by the statutory deadline. Wis. Admin. 
Code § EL 2.05(3)(b). No other format is acceptable. Id. Candidates are required 
to number their nomination papers before turning them in, but neither the 
absence of a page number nor incorrect or non-consecutive numbering will 
invalidate the signatures on that page. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(3)(c).
After a nomination paper has been signed, but before it has been filed, a signature 
may be removed by the signer or the circulator. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(4)(d).  
After nomination papers have been filed, no signature may be added or 
removed. Id. After a nomination paper has been filed, it may be amended, or an 
error or omission corrected, only through a valid correcting affidavit. Id.
Best Practice: The filing officer should issue a receipt to the candidate 
or candidate’s agent when nomination papers are filed. A sample 
Nomination Paper Receipt (EL-151) is available on elections.wi.gov.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 17
Sec. 2.2.7: Nomination Paper 
Review: Procedure
Upon receipt of completed nomination papers, the filing officer should 
immediately review the filed papers to determine sufficiency. See Wis. Admin. 
Code § EL 2.05(4).
Best Practice: Some filing officers choose to offer an initial review of 
nomination papers as a courtesy to candidates. This initial review 
can be used to notify candidates of potential issues so they have the 
opportunity to remedy defects, including by submitting a correcting 
affidavit under Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(5), before the filing deadline. 
However, header defects cannot be amended by affidavit after the 
paper has been circulated. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(5)(ag). A facial 
review before the filing deadline or correcting affidavit deadline is 
not required by statute or rule, and is separate from a filing officer’s 
ultimate determination of sufficiency. Candidates should understand 
that facial review is a courtesy only. Facial review is not binding, and will 
not serve as a defense to a challenge to their nomination papers. Wis. 
Admin. Code § EL 2.05(4)(a)(2). Candidates are solely responsible for the 
sufficiency of their nomination papers. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(3)(a).
Any facially sufficient information which appears on a nomination paper 
is entitled to a presumption of validity. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(4)(b). 
Information is facially sufficient when it is substantially compliant with proper 
format and does not have one or more elements of missing, illegible, or 
obviously incorrect information. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(1)(h). The filing 
officer must accept the information as complete if there has been substantial 
compliance with applicable statutes and the administrative code, even  
if a required item of information on a nomination paper is incomplete.  
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(4)(c). Information is substantially compliant when 
it demonstrates intent to fully comply with the statute and that the purpose of 
the statute is shown to have been served. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(1)(r).
Nomination papers must be filled out correctly by the candidate. Wis. Admin. Code 
§ EL 2.05(3)(a). It is also the candidate’s responsibility to ensure that all text is legible.
The recommended first step of review for nomination papers is the candidate 
information in the header (top of form).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 18
Best Practice: Review the header information first because 
if there is a defect in the header that cannot be cured, 
all of the signatures on that page are invalid.
All information concerning the candidate must be completed in full before 
circulating this form to obtain signatures of electors. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(b) 
(nonpartisan candidates), 8.15(5)(a) (partisan candidates), and 8.20(2)(a) 
(independent candidates).
Reviewing the Header
Name of the Candidate
The candidate must provide their last name and first name. Wis. Admin. Code 
§ EL 2.05(7)(c). They may provide a nickname or initial for their first or middle 
name. Id. In addition to their name, they may also provide a former legal 
surname. No other abbreviations or titles are permitted. Id. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(b)  
(nonpartisan candidates), 8.15(5)(a) (partisan candidates), 8.20(2)(a) 
(independent candidates).
Best Practice: The candidate’s name should be 
included as it will appear on the ballot.
Note: Nomination papers must be accepted even if they contain 
biographical data or campaign advertising. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 
2.05(7)(e). The campaign finance disclaimers specified in Wis. Stat. 
§ 11.1303(2) are not required on nomination papers. Wis. Admin. Code 
§ EL 2.05(7)(e).
Candidate’s (Physical) Residential (Street & Number) Address
The residential address must be the street address where the candidate 
resides; no other address is acceptable. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(7)(d). The 
candidate must also provide their voting municipality. Id. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(b)  
(nonpartisan candidates), 8.15(5)(a) (partisan candidates), 8.20(2)(a) 
(independent candidates).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 19
Note: Certain judicial candidates or judicial officers may have the line 
“Residence Certified with WEC” in lieu of their address if they have 
completed the certification of residence process with the WEC. Wis. 
Stat. § 8.10(8). Such candidates whose residence is certified are not 
required to list their residential address on their nomination papers. 
Local filing officers should check with the Commission to confirm 
whether a candidate’s address has been certified in order to be 
properly exempt.
Candidate’s Municipality for Voting Purposes
Candidates must provide their voting municipality in the header. Wis. Admin. 
Code § EL 2.05(7)(d). “Voting municipality” means where the candidate is eligible 
to vote on the date of signing. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(1)(s).
Candidate’s Mailing Address
If the candidate’s mailing address is different from their residential address, 
the mailing address must also be provided. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(7)(d),  
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(c) (nonpartisan candidates), 8.15(5)(b) (partisan candidates), 
8.20(2)(b) (independent candidates). If the full residential (physical) address 
is identical to the mailing address, the mailing address can be left blank. See 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(7)(d).
Type & Date of Election
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(b) (nonpartisan candidates), 8.15(5)(a) (partisan candidates), 
and 8.20(2)(a) (independent candidates). Incomplete or incorrect election 
dates can be found substantially compliant if the filing officer finds that signers 
could have determined the correct election date based solely upon information 
provided in the header. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(7)(b).
Title of Office
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(b) (nonpartisan candidates), 8.15(5)(a) (partisan candidates), 
and 8.20(2)(a) (independent candidates). The title of office must be listed 
along with any branch, district, or seat number that clearly identifies the office 
the candidate is seeking i.e., Town Board Supervisor number, if applicable; 
aldermanic district number if not an at-large seat. This portion will be valid if 
the filing officer finds that the signers could determine the office and district the 
candidate was pursuing based solely upon information provided in the header. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(7)(a).

Political Party of Candidate
If the race is for a partisan office, the header must include the political party of 
the candidate, or their statement of interest (for independent candidates). Wis. 
Admin. Code § EL 2.05(7)(f). If the race is for a non-partisan office, the header 
must not include the political party of the candidate. Id.
Reviewing Elector Signatures
Only eligible electors may sign nomination papers. An elector is anyone who 
is qualified to vote in the jurisdiction in which the candidate is seeking ballot 
access. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(1)(g). Electors need not be registered to vote 
in order to sign nomination papers. 
State law requires each elector signing nomination 
papers to provide the following: 
 Ɋ Signature
 Ɋ Printed name
 Ɋ Address including street number 
and name
 Ɋ Municipality for voting
 Ɋ Date of signing
Each of these required components are discussed in greater detail below.
Each Row Should Contain the Following:
 Ɋ Signature of elector: Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(4)(b) (nonpartisan candidates), 
8.15(2) (partisan candidates), 8.20(5) (independent candidates). An elector 
must sign his or her own name unless unable to do so because of a 
physical disability. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(b). If an elector is unable 
to sign because of a disability, they must specifically authorize another 
person to sign on their behalf and be present when that person signs. Id.
 ɉ Signature and Printed Name Legibility: If the filing officer cannot 
discern the signer’s first and last name, after reviewing both the 
signature and printed name, it is illegible and should not be counted. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h)(6).

Note: A person may not sign nomination papers for his or her spouse, 
or on behalf of anyone else (except a signer with a disability who has 
requested assistance), even if they have been given power of attorney. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(c).
 ɉ Signers must live within the circuit, county, district, or jurisdiction that 
the candidate seeks to represent, otherwise their signature is invalid. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h)(5).
 ɉ A signature must be counted when identical residential information

This is true even if the person will be 18 years old and eligible to vote at 
the date of the election. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h)(8).

they signed. Id.

if the address of the signer is missing or incomplete, or the municipality 
is abbreviated, unless the address can be determined by the information 
provided on the nomination paper. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h)(3). 
Neither apartment number nor state and ZIP code is required. Id.

Reviewing the Circulator Certification
At the bottom of each nomination paper, there is a certification section that 
is completed by the person who collected the signatures. There are several 
required components of this section, and all should be reviewed when 
examining nomination paper sufficiency.
A nomination paper circulator must be eligible to vote in Wisconsin.3 Wis. Stat. 
§§ 8.10(3), 8.15(4)(a), 8.20(3), as amended by 2025 WI Act 126.
Review the Certification of Circulator for the following:
 Ɋ Name of Circulator, which must be legible. The circulator’s last name 
must be present. Wis. Stat. § 8.15(4)(a)
 ɉ Legibility: If the filing officer cannot discern the signer’s first and last name, 
after reviewing both the signature and printed name, it is illegible and 
should not be counted. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h)(6).
 Ɋ Address of Circulator (number and street). This must be a Wisconsin 
address. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(3), 8.15(4)(a), 8.20(3), as amended by 2025 WI 
Act 126. No signature on the page can be counted when the residency 
of the circulator cannot be determined by the information given on the 
nomination paper. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(g).
 Ɋ Signature of Circulator. Wis. Stat. § 8.15(4)(a). Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(g). 
Signature need not be legible if the circulator’s first and last name can be 
determined in the printed name line. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h)(6).
 Ɋ Date of certification. Date must be on or after the latest date of a signer. 
Wis. Stat. § 8.15(4)(a), Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(g), 2.05(8)(b).
 Ɋ Only one circulation per candidate per office permitted. If the circulator 
has circulated nomination papers for two or more candidates for the 
same office in the same election and different times, the earlier papers 
are valid and the later papers are invalid. Wis. Stat. § 8.04. Circulators are 
only allowed to circulate for one candidate, even for at-large seats where 
voters can vote for more than one candidate. The administrative code 
makes an exception for signatories to sign the papers of more than one 
candidate in an at-large race, but not circulators. See Wis. Admin. Code  
§ EL 2.05(6)(d).

circulators were not required to be Wisconsin residents, and could still circulate if they were a U.S. 
citizen, at least 18 years old, and would be eligible to vote in Wisconsin if they were a resident.

Sec. 2.2.8: Counting Valid Signatures
The number of signatures required depends on the office sought.
Best Practice: The number of signatures required for office 
should be included in the candidate packet for each office.
Candidates often submit more than the maximum number of signatures 
necessary, but it is not necessary for a filing officer to review every single one 
of them. See Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(4)(a)(1). However, filing officers must 
continue to review as many signatures as the candidate submits to achieve the 
sufficient minimum number. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(7), 8.15(9), 8.20(10).
For example, Candidate A wishes to run for mayor in Badger City, which is a 
second-class city. Candidate A must submit 200–400 signatures for that office, 
so Candidate A submits 420. Clerk Clark reviews up to 400 signatures, but finds 
that only 190 of them are sufficient. State law directs that Clerk Clark must 
continue to review the remaining 20 signatures until the minimum threshold of 
200 sufficient signatures is reached.
Only one signature per person for the same office is valid. Wis. Stat. § 8.04, 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(d). If there are duplicate signatures, the earlier 
signature is valid, and the later signature is invalid. Wis. Stat. § 8.04. Exception: 
Where an signer is entitled to vote for more than one candidate for the same 
office, they may sign the nomination papers of as many candidates for the 
same office as they are entitled to vote for at the election. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 
2.05(6)(d). For these offices, duplicate signatures for different candidates should 
not automatically be rejected.
