Sec. 2.2.9: Correcting Affidavits
Any insufficiencies, such as incorrectly dated signatures or inaccurate circulator 
information can be corrected with a correcting affidavit. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 
2.05(5)(ag). However, correcting affidavits may not provide new or additional 
signatures or signature pages in addition to what was originally submitted to 
the filing official. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(5)(d).
Affidavits may be submitted by the circulator, the candidate, or a person who 
signed the nomination paper. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(5)(ag). The person 
giving the correcting affidavit must have personal knowledge of the correct 
information. Id. The WEC has templates for correcting affidavits available upon 
request.
The affidavit must be filed with the filing officer not later than 5 p.m. central 
time on the 3rd calendar day after the applicable statutory due date for when a 
challenge to nomination papers may be filed. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(5)(ar).  
If a correcting affidavit is submitted on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, it 
must be submitted via facsimile transmission or electronic mail directly to the 
filing officer. Id.
The filing officer must determine whether any correcting affidavit resolves the 
identified insufficiency. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(5)(c). If a correcting affidavit 
is accepted, it amends the affected nomination papers on its own, and it is 
not necessary for the filing officer to edit or mark the nomination papers to be 
consistent with the changes in the affidavit. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(5)(b).
Note: Nomination papers with insufficient headers cannot be cured by 
a correcting affidavit after the paper has been circulated. Wis. Admin. 
Code § EL 2.05(5)(ag).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 29
Sec. 2.2.10: Public Access of 
Ballot Access Paperwork
The timeline for filing ballot access challenges is a short one — just three 
calendar days — so filing officers must prioritize making nomination papers and 
declarations of candidacy available to the public as soon as they are filed. See 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07, 2.08.
Filing officers are required to make nomination papers available for public 
inspection, either physically or electronically, within one business day of when 
they are filed. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(2).
Best Practice: The easiest and quickest way to make nomination 
papers available to the public is to scan and upload nomination 
papers and declarations of candidacy and post them to a website 
where the public can access them at any time. If web access is not 
feasible, filing officers should take steps to ensure that the public 
can access filed ballot access paperwork in a timely fashion. 
Filing officers should plan for how they plan to make paperwork 
available to the public well before each filing deadline.
Sec. 2.2.11: Frequently Asked Questions
Q Can a candidate who has properly filed nomination papers and qualified for the 
ballot withdraw their nomination papers to remove their name from the ballot?
A Yes, but only candidates who file nomination papers with the Commission 
(excluding district attorneys), and only those who follow the specific 
process to do so, including paying the fee. Wis. Stat. § 8.35(1m)(a). 
Candidates wishing to withdraw must submit their request and pay 
the required fee to the Commission no later than the 7th business day 
before the June 10 preceding the partisan primary or no later than the 
7th business day before the 4th Tuesday in August preceding the general 
election. Wis. Stat. § 8.35(1m)(a). The withdrawal of a candidate under 
this process will not affect the ballot order if the order has already been 
determined. Wis. Stat. § 8.35(1m)(c). The Commission will notify the county 
clerk if any candidates withdraw. Wis. Stat. § 8.35(1m)(d).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 30
Local candidates may not withdraw their candidacy under Wis. Stat.  
§ 8.35(1m).
State law states that any person who files nomination papers and 
qualifies to appear on the ballot may not decline nomination, unless they 
qualify to withdraw as described above. The name of that person shall 
appear upon the ballot except in the case of death of the person. Once 
an individual has filed nomination papers with a filing officer, and has 
qualified for ballot placement, nomination papers or other ballot access 
documents cannot be withdrawn to remove a person’s name from the 
ballot. Wis. Stat. § 8.35(1).
Q Are incumbents required to file ballot access documents?
A Yes. All candidates including incumbents are required to file the 
appropriate ballot access documents for each election for which he or 
she is seeking office. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(b), 8.15(5), 8.20(2)(a).
Q Where can I find residency requirements for candidates?
A Specific residency requirements and other minimum qualifications can be 
found within the governing statutes of the office sought. Information can 
also be found on the relevant candidate page on elections.wi.gov.
Q A prospective candidate wants to give me their Declaration of Candidacy 
for an election that is two years from now. Can I accept it?
A Yes. Make sure to follow protocol (give them a receipt of 
acknowledgement) and store it safely until that election.
Q It is not December 1st yet and a prospective candidate wants me to give him 
a Campaign Finance Registration Statement (CF-1). May I give it to him?
A Yes. As soon as a person takes a candidate action (files nomination papers, 
is nominated by a political party, receives a contribution), he or she is 
required to register as soon as practicable. Wis. Stat. § 11.0202(1)(a). Therefore, 
candidate packets, which include the Campaign Finance Registration 
Statement (CF-1), should be available for candidates at all times.
Q  It is not December 1st or April 1st yet and a prospective candidate wants 
me to give him nomination paper form (EL-169). May I give it to him?
A Yes. A nomination paper form may be given to a prospective candidate at any time.
Best Practice: The EL-169 should be included in the candidate packet.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 31
Q The filing officer is refusing to review my submitted nomination papers 
before the deadline. I am worried that I won’t have enough time to get 
more signatures if I fall below the minimum. Are they required to review 
my nomination papers immediately?
A No. It is up to the discretion of the filing officer whether to do an initial 
review and when that review would take place. It is not a requirement of 
the filing officer to ensure that the minimum number of signatures is met.
Best Practice: Filing officers should review nomination papers as 
they are filed and reach out to any candidate who falls close to the 
minimum threshold. Candidates should submit more signatures than 
the minimum required in case of insufficiencies and challenges.
Q What if a candidate is campaigning before the Campaign Finance 
Registration Statement (CF-1, CF-1L) is filed?
A Failure of the candidate to file a Campaign Finance Registration 
Statement (CF-1) if they are collecting or spending money toward the 
campaign is a violation of campaign finance law and should be reported 
to the Wisconsin Ethics Commission. Wis. Stat. §§ 11.1400, 11.1401(1)(a).
Q What is the deadline to challenge a Declaration of Candidacy?
A Challenges to declarations of candidacy must be filed by 5 p.m. on the third 
calendar day after the declaration of candidacy filing deadline. Wis. Admin. 
Code § EL 2.08(2)(b). The challenge must be in the physical or electronic 
possession of the filing officer by 5 p.m. on the challenge deadline. Id. If a 
challenge is submitted on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, it must be 
submitted via facsimile transmission or electronic mail. Id.
Q If a candidate brings in paperwork to the filing officer, but the filing officer is 
not present, it is okay for to leave the paperwork with another staff person?
A Yes. State law does not require candidates to hand their paperwork 
directly to the filing officer. Each filing officer, however, should establish 
procedures in their office so that their staff are trained on how to properly 
accept ballot access paperwork.
Best Practice: The system should be the same for every 
single candidate so questions do not arise.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 32
Q What happens if no candidates qualify for ballot placement?
A If no candidates properly complete and file ballot access documents in 
the time frame allotted, the ballot will contain only a space for a write-in 
candidate. See Sec. 2.4.3: “Selecting Candidates at a Caucus” on page 
62 for information on this topic with respect to the caucus nomination 
procedure.)
Q What should I do if I believe that an individual filing ballot access 
documents is a convicted felon?
A The restriction on convicted felon candidates only applies to candidates 
for state and local office, not federal candidates. Wis. Stat. § 8.21(4)(a). If it 
is brought to the filing officer’s attention that a convicted felon has filed 
ballot access documents, the matter needs to be resolved in consultation 
with the municipal attorney or local counsel.
Best Practice: It is the position of the Wisconsin Elections Commission 
that the municipality should only act on information presented in the 
form of a sworn ballot access challenge, alleging that a candidate 
has been convicted of a felony and evidence is provided in support 
of that allegation. The municipal attorney or local counsel can 
assist the filing officer in verifying the basis of the challenge.
Once it has been determined that a candidate or an elected official has 
been convicted of a felony, the municipal attorney can assist the filing 
officer in determining whether the person’s name should not be placed on 
the ballot
Best Practice: A formal notice should be sent to the candidate 
or elected official informing him or her of the filing officer’s 
decision not to place his or her name on the ballot.
Q Should the filing officer check to make sure that no candidate has been 
convicted of a felony?
A The filing officer is not required to verify that every candidate for elected 
public office has not been convicted of a felony for which they have not 
been pardoned. The filing officer should rely on the sworn statement of the 
candidate on the Declaration of Candidacy. Wis. Stat. § 8.21(4)(a).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 33
Q What if the filing officer’s office is closed the first Tuesday in January for a 
holiday?
A If it is a state-recognized holiday, the deadline for filing ballot access 
documents is extended to the next business day. Wis. Stat. § 990.001(4)(b).  
Note: This only applies to state holidays, not county holidays or federal 
holidays that are not state holidays (such as Columbus Day and Veterans 
Day). If it is not, the filing officer must be available for candidates filing 
ballot access documents.
Q A candidate went to turn in my paperwork and the office was closed. The 
deadline to turn in paperwork is today. What do they do?
A The candidate should start by contacting anyone they can think of in 
the municipal or county government who might be able to get ahold of 
the filing officer. The candidate can also contact the Wisconsin Elections 
Commission at 608-266-8005 if they don’t know who to call, and staff can 
assist the candidate by putting them in touch with local officials.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 34
Chapter 2.3: Ballot Access 
Challenges
A ballot access challenge is a verified complaint brought against a proposed 
candidate. It alleges that the candidate’s nomination papers or declaration of 
candidacy are insufficient or that the candidate is otherwise unqualified for the 
office sought. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(2), 2.08(2). Ballot access challenges are 
not specifically mentioned in statute, but statute does give the Commission the 
ability to establish administrative rules to determine the validity of nomination 
papers. Wis. Stat. § 8.07, and see generally Wis. Admin. Code Chapter 2. 
Accordingly, the rules and procedures authorizing and governing ballot access 
challenges are covered by administrative code.
Ballot access challenges are filed with the appropriate filing officer for the 
office the candidate seeks. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(2), 2.08(2). They are their 
own special type of complaint governed by the procedures in Wis. Admin. 
Code §§ EL 2.07, 2.08. They have different standards of review and deadlines 
than the other types of administrative complaints the Commission considers. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(2), 2.08(2).
Filing officers must make filed nomination papers and declarations of candidacy 
available for public inspection, either physically or electronically, within 1 business 
day of when they are filed. Id.
Sec. 2.3.1: Types of Ballot 
Access Challenges
There are two different types of ballot access challenges, each of which is 
discussed further below:
Nomination Paper Challenges: Brought by a challenger against a candidate’s 
nomination papers.
Declaration of Candidacy and Candidate Qualification Challenges: Brought 
by a challenger against a candidate’s declaration of candidacy, including the 
certifications on that document that the candidate is qualified for the office 
they seek.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 35
Nomination Paper Challenges
The majority of ballot access challenges allege that the challenged candidate’s 
nomination papers are insufficient in some way. Wis. Stat. § 8.07, Wis. Admin. 
Code § EL 2.07(5). 
Nomination paper challenges usually allege one 
of three general areas of insufficiency:
 Ɋ Issues with the nomination paper header
 Ɋ Issues with the circulator certification statement
 Ɋ Issues with individual signature line challenges
Declaration of Candidacy & Candidate 
Qualification Challenges
Since 2020, the Commission and local filing officers have received and 
decided ballot access challenges that allege that the candidate’s 
declaration of candidacy was insufficient or that the candidate was 
otherwise ineligible for the office they sought. As of Apr. 1, 2026, the 
administrative code expressly addresses when and how these challenges 
can be brought and decided. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.08 .
Declaration of candidacy challenges allege that the challenged 
candidate’s declaration of candidacy is insufficient in some way.  
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.08(4) . 
Declaration of candidacy challenges usually allege one of three general areas:
 Ɋ Issues with missing or incomplete candidate information
 Ɋ Issues with missing or incomplete certification information
 Ɋ Issues with the qualifications of a candidate
The new rule lists the specific grounds under which individuals can bring 
challenges to declarations of candidacy. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.08(4)(ag). The 
above three are just the most common.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 36
Sec. 2.3.2: Filing Requirements & Deadlines
A challenge is a short, plain statement of the basis upon which the challenger 
seeks to invalidate any signatures on one or more nomination papers, or 
invalidate a declaration of candidacy. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(ar), 2.08(2)(ar). 
All factual allegations upon which the challenge relies must be verified by on 
or more persons who certify that they possess personal knowledge of the facts 
alleged therein. Id. See Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(1)(b)(7). Individuals other than 
the challenger may support a challenge with sworn affidavits or declarations 
pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 887.015. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(ar), 2.08(2)(ar).
A brief or summary of the legal standards applicable to a challenge and their 
application to the alleged facts may be filed simultaneously with, or as a part 
of, the challenge pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 887.015. Id. The brief or summary need 
not be verified, but if it is prepared by an attorney, that attorney shall sign the 
brief and that signature shall meet the requirements of Wis. Stat. § 802.05. Id.
Best Practice: A challenger’s legal representative may prepare 
and sign a legal brief in support of the challenge, but the actual 
verified challenge itself must be signed by the challenger.
Deadline: Filing Challenge
Challenges must be filed by 5 p.m. on the third calendar day after the filing 
deadline for the challenged papers. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(b), 2.08(2)(b).  
The challenge must be in the physical or electronic possession of the filing 
officer by 5 p.m. on the challenge deadline. Id. If a challenge is submitted 
on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, it must be submitted via facsimile 
transmission or electronic mail. Id. Challenges received after 5 p.m. on the 
challenge deadline shall not be accepted. Id.
The filing officer must make instructions for filing challenges electronically 
publicly available no less than 24 hours before the challenge deadline. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3 )(c)(1), 2.08(2)(c)(1). Challenges that are filed 
electronically must conform to those instructions. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 37
Filing challenges electronically
If the challenge and all supporting materials are filed in electronic form, 
the filing officer shall electronically transmit a copy of the challenge to the 
challenged candidate no later than 4 hours after the deadline for filing of the 
challenge complaint. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(c)(1), 2.08(2)(c)(1).
Filing challenges in paper form
If the challenge and supporting materials are filed in paper form, the filing 
officer shall deliver a copy to the challenged candidate, either in paper or 
electronic form, no later than noon the day after the challenge is filed. Wis. 
Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(c)(2), 2.08(2)(c)(2).
Deadline: Notification of Challenge to Candidate
Regardless of how a challenge is filed, the filing officer must also provide the 
challenged candidate with a copy of the challenge, notice of the response deadline, 
notice of how and when the challenged candidate may file rebuttal, as well as 
notice that either Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07 or 2.08 govern the procedures for the 
type of ballot access challenge. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(c)(3), 2.08(2)(c)(2).
Best Practice: Send notice of the challenge to the affected candidate 
by email whenever possible. The Commission recommends 
that the filing officer get written or verbal confirmation from 
the candidate that they have received the challenge. This is 
especially important as challenge filing deadlines often fall on 
Friday afternoons. If a filing officer cannot contact the challenged 
candidate by email or phone to confirm receipt of the challenge, 
they should make arrangements to hire a process server to 
ensure that a copy of the challenge is delivered to the candidate’s 
residence as provided on their Declaration of Candidacy.
Deadline: Candidate’s Response to Challenge
A challenged candidate may submit a response to a challenge. Wis. Admin. 
Code § EL 2.07(3)(f), 2.08(2)(f). A response to a challenge is a short, plain 
statement of the basis upon which the challenged candidate asserts that 
any challenged nomination papers or declarations of candidacy are valid. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3 )(e), 2.08(2)(e). All factual allegations upon which 
the response relies must be verified by one or more persons who certify that 
they possess personal knowledge of the facts alleged therein. Id. Individuals 
other than the challenger may support a challenge with sworn affidavits. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 38
A brief or summary of the legal standards applicable to the challenged 
signatures or pages and the application of those legal standards to the alleged 
facts may be filed simultaneously with the response and any affidavits. Id. The 
brief or summary need not be verified, but if it is prepared by an attorney that 
attorney shall sign the brief and that signature shall meet the requirements of 
Wis. Stat. § 802.05(1).
Deadline
Responses must be filed by 5 p.m. on the third calendar day after the date the 
challenge was filed Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(f), 2.08(2)(f). The Response shall be 
in the physical or electronic possession of the filing officer by 5 p.m. on the response 
deadline. Id. If a challenge is submitted on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, 
it shall be submitted via facsimile transmission or electronic mail. Id. Responses 
received after 5 p.m. on the challenge deadline shall not be accepted. Id.
Deadline: Notification of Response to Challenger
If the candidate files a response, the filing officer must provide the response and 
any correcting affidavits to the challenger. If filed in electronic form, the filing 
officer must electronically transmit a copy of the materials to the challenger no 
later than 4 hours after the deadline for filing of the materials. If filed in paper 
form, the filing officer must deliver a copy of the materials to the challenger, 
either in paper or electronic form, no later than noon the day after the materials 
are filed. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(f), 2.08(2)(f).
Deadline: Challenger Rebuttal
If the candidate files a response and one or more correcting affidavits, the 
challenger may file a short rebuttal brief and one or more rebuttal affidavits. Any 
rebuttals and rebuttal affidavits must be filed electronically by the challenger, 
and the materials must be in the electronic possession of the filing officer within 
24 hours of the filing officer’s transmission of the response or correcting affidavits. 
Whenever the rebuttal deadline would occur after 10 a.m. on the deadline for 
the filing officer to certify the names of candidates to appear on the ballot, the 
deadline to file the rebuttal is changed to be 10 a.m. on that day. Paper copies and 
late submissions will not be accepted. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(g), 2.08(2)(g).
A rebuttal brief need not be verified, but if it is prepared by an attorney, that 
attorney shall sign the brief and that signature shall meet the requirements of 
Wis. Stat. § 802.05. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(g), 2.08(2)(g).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 39
Sec. 2.3.3: Burdens of Proof
The initial burden is on the challenger to establish any deficiency in the 
challenged candidate’s nomination papers. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(d), 
2.07(4), 2.08(2)(d), 2.08(3). If the challenger makes an initial showing by clear, 
satisfactory, and convincing evidence that establishes one or more of the 
challenged candidate’s nomination papers is deficient, the burden shifts to the 
challenged candidate to establish the validity of their nomination papers by 
clear, satisfactory, and convincing evidence. Id.
“Clear, satisfactory, and convincing evidence” means evidence which when 
weighed against that opposed to it clearly has more convincing power to a 
reasonable degree of certainty. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(1)(e). A “reasonable 
certainty” means persuasion based upon a rational consideration of the 
evidence. Id. Absolute certainty is not required, but a guess is not enough to 
meet this burden of proof. Id. Clear, satisfactory, and convincing evidence 
cannot be shown by bare assertions that are unsupported by a sworn affidavit 
or declaration. Id.
Sec. 2.3.4: Reviewing the Challenge
A ballot access challenge may challenge the validity of a candidate’s 
nomination papers or a candidate’s declaration of candidacy.
In a nomination paper challenge, filing officers must apply the standards 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05  to determine the validity of nomination  
papers. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(2) . In a declaration of candidacy 
challenge, filing officers must apply the standards in Wis. Admin. Code  
§ EL 2.06  and Wis. Stat. § 8.21.  Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.08(2 )(ag).
As a starting point in both kinds of challenges, recall that it is the candidate’s 
responsibility to ensure that his or her nomination papers and/or declaration 
of candidacy are prepared and ultimately filed in compliance with applicable 
statutory provision and requirements under the administrative code. Wis. 
Admin. Code § EL 2.05(3)(a), 2.06(2)(a). This means candidates are also 
responsible for the work — and potential mistakes — of individuals who are 
circulating nomination papers or filing a declaration of candidacy on their 
behalf. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 40
Challengers and candidates often submit evidence in support of the challenge 
or in opposition to any challenge. Filing officers must examine this evidence as 
part of the challenge if it is offered. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(d), 2.08(2)(d).
Hearings
A hearing is not required. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(h), 2.08(2)(h). Filing 
officers may elect to hold a hearing if they determine that a hearing would 
assist them in the adjudication of the challenge. Id.
If the filing officer elects to hold a hearing, the hearing shall be noticed in 
advance, per Wis. Stat. § 19.84, and open to the public, per Wis. Stat. §§ 19.83, 
19.88, 19.89, and 19.90. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(i), 2.08(2)(i). The filing officer 
must conduct the hearing in a manner that affords the same offered rights 
and opportunities to all parties. Id. This includes oral presentations by the 
parties or their assigned representative, if the filing officer elects to accept oral 
presentations. Id. Factual evidence being offered as oral testimony shall not 
be received at a hearing unless the filing officer elects to swear in witnesses, in 
which case all witnesses shall be sworn in. Id.
Sec. 2.3.5: Deciding the 
Challenge & Appeals
Issuing Decision
When there is no hearing, the filing officer shall promptly issue a written 
decision on the challenge and a signed order memorializing their disposition of 
the challenge not later than the date for certifying candidates to the ballot. Wis. 
Admin. Code § EL 2.07(6), 2.08(5).
When there is a hearing and the filing officer announces an oral ruling during 
that hearing, any party seeking to appeal from the filing officer’s adjudication 
of a challenge decided at the hearing may submit a proposed order, 
memorializing the filing officer’s ruling in writing, to the filing officer for adoption 
and signature. Id.
The filing officer shall promptly transmit all signed orders to the challenger and 
the challenged candidate electronically. Id. The filing officer may draft and sign 
their own order rather than using a version proposed by any party. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 41
Deadlines
The filing officer shall decide the challenge after the deadline for filing any 
rebuttal brief and rebuttal affidavits, but not later than the date for certifying 
candidates to the ballot. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(h), 2.08(2)(h).
Deadline: Filing Extension
In the event an extension is necessary for any office pursuant to Wis. Stat. §§ 
8.10(2) (a), 8.15(1), or 8.20(8)(a), the prior deadlines do not apply. Instead, the filing 
officer must calculate the deadlines for the challenge, response, and rebuttal 
under this paragraph. The filing officer must calculate the total number of hours 
between the extended filing deadline and 10 a.m. on the day of the deadline 
for the filing officer to certify the names of candidates to the ballot. The filing 
officer must then divide that number by 2 so that there is an equal number of 
hours allotted to file a challenge and file a response. From each of these totals, 
the filing officer shall subtract an equal number of hours to form a rebuttal 
deadline, which shall not exceed 24 hours. The filing officer must communicate 
the deadlines to the public by all reasonable methods as soon as they know an 
extension will be necessary. The communication must include the specific office 
that was extended, and must specify that the extension challenge deadlines 
are for that office only. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(j), 2.08(2)(j).
Example: For the office of Circuit Court Judge of Brewer County, the current 
incumbent did not file a notification of candidacy, and also did not file 
nomination papers by the statutory deadline of January 6, 2026 (second 
Tuesday in January).
Extended Deadline to File Nomination Papers: Jan. 9 (Fri) at 5 p.m.
 Ɋ Remaining Hours on Jan 9 – 7 (between 5 p.m. and midnight)
 Ɋ Two Full Days (Jan. 10 and Jan. 11) – 48 Hours total
 Ɋ Hours on Jan. 12 – 10 hours between midnight and 10 a.m.
 Ɋ Total Hours: 65
 ɉ 65 divided by two is 32.5. Take 10 hours off each of those halves and we 
are left with:
 Ɉ Challenge Deadline: 22.5 Hours after 5 p.m. on Jan. 9 – 3:30 p.m.
 Ɉ Response Deadline: 22.5 Hours after Challenge is Filed
 Ɉ Rebuttal Deadline: 20 Hours after Response is Received
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 42
Appeal
Any order of a local filing officer disposing of a challenge may be appealed 
to the commission pursuant to Wis. Stat. §§ 5.05 or 5.06. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 
2.07(7), 2.08(6). The party aggrieved by the filing officer’s decision shall notify 
the commission of its intent to appeal within 48 hours of receipt of the filing 
officer’s signed order. Id. The commission administrator, in consultation with 
the commission chair, must establish a briefing schedule that will allow for 
commission decision before the deadlines for ballot printing. Id. Any signed 
order of the commission disposing of a challenge or adjudicating an appeal 
from a local filing officer’s order disposing of a challenge may be appealed to a 
circuit court. Id.
Sec. 2.3.6: Common Ballot 
Access Challenges
The Commission and its predecessor agencies have analyzed numerous types 
of challenges and developed a consistent methodology for resolving the most 
common challenges that have been filed. This portion of the manual should 
help candidates and political parties concentrate their efforts on challenges 
with a supportable legal basis, and reduce the filing of frivolous challenges 
or those involving legal issues which have been well settled. This portion is 
also intended to serve as a resource for local filing officers to learn how the 
Commission has interpreted similar issues in ballot access challenges.
While challenges are not limited to those described in the administrative 
rules, there are three general categories of challenges:
 Ɋ Challenges to the header of the nomination papers that may result in 
declaring all signatures contained on nomination papers using that 
header to be invalid
 Ɋ Challenges to the circulator’s certification that also may result in 
declaring all signatures contained on the affected pages to be invalid
 Ɋ Challenges to individual signatures that do not affect the validity of other 
signatures on the nomination papers. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(5).
This portion of the manual summarizes previous decisions of the State Elections 
Board, the Government Accountability Board and the Wisconsin Elections 
Commission related to the most common challenges to nomination papers 
and declarations of candidacy. It is intended to itemize and consolidate 
previous decisions which state and local filing officers may rely on as guidance 
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 43
regarding the general legal questions and principles involved. However, the 
facts of individual circumstances and challenges vary, and the application of 
these principles must be determined on a case-by-case basis.
General Process Challenges
Nomination papers and declarations of candidacy must be filed by the 
statutory deadlines governing each election, and they must be filed properly. 
“Each candidate for public office has the responsibility to ensure that his or her 
nomination papers are prepared, circulated, signed, and filed in compliance 
with statutory provisions and requirements under the administrative code.”  
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(3)(a).
Blurry, Obscured, or Illegible Nomination Paper Language
Q Challenge: Portions of the header certification language, or circulator 
certification language, are blurry, obscured, or illegible as the result of bad 
photocopying, water damage, excessive wrinkling or creasing, or other 
obstructions.
A Analysis: Candidates have the responsibility to ensure their nomination 
papers are prepared correctly, including ensuring that the critical 
certification language is present and legible for their signatories and 
circulators. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(3)(a).
If a few non-critical words are obscured, the page may still be 
substantially compliant under Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(4)(c) depending 
on how much of the information was preserved and visible to the 
signatories. As long as each essential point within the certification 
language is preserved and legible, the nomination papers are 
substantially compliant even if there are words missing or obscured.
Example: In the nomination paper header on the following page, poor 
photocopying caused visual distortions that obscured several words in 
the header. However, the Commission determined that the header still 
substantially complied with the law because it was not so obscured or 
defective that any required piece of information was completely missing.4
4 The Commission’s interpretation in this case was affirmed in litigation. Hess v. Wis. Elections Comm’n, 
413 Ws. 2d 285, 11 N.W.3d 201 (Wis. Ct. App.), overruled on other grounds by Brown v. Wis. Elections 
Comm’n, 2025 WI 5, 414 Wis. 2d 601, 16 N.W.3d 619.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 44
Figure 1: Obscured Header
Nomination Papers or Challenge Materials were Not Timely Filed
Q Challenge: A candidate arrived at the filing officer’s building at 4:55 p.m., 
but by the time she got into the building, it was 5:02 p.m. before the filing 
officer took physical possession of the nomination papers.
A Analysis: 
Statute specifies that the nomination paper filing deadlines are as follows:
 Ɋ First Tuesday in January by 5 p.m. for Spring Election.
 Ɋ June 1 by 5 p.m. for the General Election.
 Ɋ First Tuesday in August by 5 p.m. for independent presidential candidates.
 Ɋ By 5 p.m. on the specified filing deadline for special elections.  
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(a), 8.15(1), 8.20(8)(am), and 8.50(3)(a).
Papers are timely filed so long as they are in the physical possession of 
the filing officer by 5:00:00 p.m. on the day of the deadline. See e.g. Wis. 
Admin. Code § EL 2.05(5)(ar).
5 p.m. means 5 p.m. on the dot, and any nomination papers received 
after 5:00:01 p.m. are untimely filed. This interpretation was confirmed by 
the Brown County Circuit Court upon litigation filed by an independent 
presidential candidate who filed his nomination papers with the 
Commission at 5:00:14 p.m. and was considered untimely. See Kanye West 
et al v. Wisconsin Elections Commission, Case No. 2020CV000812, (Brown 
County Circuit Court, Sept. 11, 2020) (decision denying plaintiffs’ relief).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 45
Best Practice: Plan ahead for nomination paper filing deadlines. 
Make sure that all doors are unlocked prior to 5 p.m., and consider 
posting a staff member in the lobby of the building. It is also a best 
practice to video record the window between 4:55 and 5:00 p.m. to 
create a time-stamped record of when candidates arrive to avoid 
factual disputes of when papers were submitted.
Important: Timely filed is not the same as sufficiently filed. 
Nomination papers may still be rejected due to other insufficiencies 
even if they are received in a timely manner. The filing officer 
determines the sufficiency of nomination papers, not the individual 
tasked with accepting the paperwork in the office.
Q Challenge: The complaint filing, or the response filing, for a ballot access 
challenge were untimely filed, and should not be accepted or considered.
A Analysis: Challenges to nomination papers must be filed “by 5 p.m. on the 
3rd calendar day” after the deadline to file the nomination papers. Wis. 
Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(b). The response to the challenge must be filed 
“by 5 p.m. of the 3rd calendar day” after the date the challenge was filed. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.07(3)(f).
Delays caused by technology or circumstances outside the candidate’s 
control do not exempt parties from these deadline requirements for 
challenge filings. See Wis. Admin. Code § EL 6.04(4) (“any document which 
is filed by facsimile process or by email process under this rule shall be 
considered received at the time of transmission as recorded and entered 
by the receiving equipment by the filing officer’s staff when the facsimile 
copy or email copy is delivered to the filing officer’s offices”). Candidates 
and challengers should take extreme care not to leave their filings until the 
last minute in case of any unexpected issues.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 46
Declaration of Candidacy Challenges
As of April 1, 2026, the Commission now has administrative rules specific 
to declaration of candidacy sufficiency standards and challenges to the 
declaration of candidacy itself. See Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.06, 2.08.
Challenges to Candidate Qualifications
Q Challenge: A challenger wants to challenge the candidate’s general 
qualifications for office.
A Analysis: This is a permissible ground for a declaration of candidacy 
challenge, but must be limited only to the certifications that candidates are 
required to make under Wis. Stat. § 8.21. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.08(4)(b). 
When completing and submitting a declaration of candidacy, a candidate 
is certifying that they meet, or will meet, the applicable age, citizenship, 
residency, or voting qualification requirements for the office sought, and 
that they will otherwise qualify for the office if nominated or elected. 
Wis. Stat. § 8.21(2)(c). State and local candidates are required to make 
additional certifications, including that they have not been convicted of 
disqualifying criminal offenses. Wis. Stat. § 8.21(4)(a).
Example: In 2024, an independent candidate for U.S. President filed nomination 
papers with the Commission. A challenger claimed he did not meet the 
constitutional requirements for that office because he had not been born 
in the United States. The candidate conceded that he was not a natural 
born citizen. The Commission voted to sustain the challenge to exclude the 
candidate and his running mate from the ballot under Wis. Stat. § 8.30(4) 
because he did not meet the qualifications for the office he sought, even 
though he had certified to them on the declaration of candidacy. The 
candidate’s name was not placed on the ballot. 5
5 See EL 24-81, Michael Hoffman v. Shiva Ayyadurai.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 47
Issues with Notarization on Declaration of Candidacy
Q Challenge: The candidate’s notarization was completed in another state, 
and did not confirm to that state’s notary requirements.
A Analysis: Wisconsin law provides that a notarial act performed in another 
state “has the same effect under the law of this state as if performed by a 
notarial officer” of Wisconsin. Wis. Stat. § 140.11(1). Wis. Stat. § 140.26 includes 
all authorized notaries within Chapter 140, including out of state notaries. 
Accordingly, the failure of an out of state notarial officer to perform a duty 
or meet a requirement does not invalidate a notarial act performed by the 
out of state notarial officer.6
Q Challenge: The candidate’s spouse completed the notarization of the 
declaration of candidacy.
A Analysis: A spouse may not notarize any documents for their partner 
in Wisconsin. Wis. Stat. § 140.04(2) provides, “a notarial officer may not 
perform a notarial act with respect to a record to which the officer or the 
officer’s spouse or domestic partner is a party or in which either of them 
has a direct beneficial interest. A notarial act performed in violation of this 
subsection is voidable.” (Emphasis added). If the candidate did not file an 
amended declaration of candidacy by the appropriate deadline, this is an 
incurable error and the candidate cannot be placed on the ballot. 7 The 
candidate was not placed on the ballot.
Candidate Information (Header Portion of Paper)
None of the information in the header of the nomination paper (i.e., candidate’s 
name, candidate’s residential address, candidate’s municipality for voting 
purposes, candidate’s mailing address, type of election, election date, 
office sought, and name of jurisdiction or district in which candidate seeks 
office), may be altered, amended, corrected or added after circulation of the 
nomination paper. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(5)(ag). See Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(b),  
8.15(5)(a), 8.20(2)(a) (requiring certain information to appear in the header of 
nomination papers). This is the nomination information that each signatory 
saw and relied upon in deciding to sign the paper in support of placing the 
candidate’s name on the ballot, and therefore cannot be changed.
6 See EL 24-80, David Strange v. Cornel West et al.
7 See Kyle Schroeder v. Christine Hansen (EL 26-01)
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 48
Office Title & District Designation
Q Challenge: Irregularities in the name of the office as required by  
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2 )(b), 8.15(5)(a), 8.20(2)(a).
A Analysis: The Commission has typically allowed for variances in listing 
the office name, such as “Assembly,” “State Representative,” “State 
Assembly,” plus the district number. Abbreviations are common such as 
“AD” for “Assembly District” or “SD” for “Senate District.” The Commission 
determined that the papers were substantially compliant as long as 
the electors could determine the office and district the candidate was 
pursuing by the information provided in the nomination paper heading. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(7)(a). Additionally, where the title or district 
designations are illegible or in the incorrect boxes, the Commission has 
found these pages to substantially comply when the required information 
could be determined elsewhere in the nomination paper heading.
However, the Commission has consistently interpreted “name of office” to 
require the district or jurisdiction number necessary to identify the office. 
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(b), 8.15(5)(a), 8.20(2)(a). “State Assembly” alone, for 
example, would not be substantially compliant, as it is missing the district 
number that identifies that office. Likewise, circuit court judges must 
identify the branch number of the office they are seeking.
Election Date
Q Challenge: Incomplete or missing date of election as required by Wis. Stat. 
§§ 8.10(2)(b), 8.15(5)(a), 8.20(2)(a).
A Analysis: When a date of election is completely missing from the header, 
the Commission has sustained the challenge and struck all the signatures 
on those pages. When a date is listed but incomplete or incorrect (e.g., 
using the date of the primary, not indicating the year, indicating the month 
and year but not the day, indicating an incorrect date, or incorrectly 
indicating “general” as the type of election on the petition heading), the 
date can be found substantially compliant if there was sufficient notice 
to signers to determine the correct election date based solely upon 
information provided in the header. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(7)(b).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 49
Candidate Address
Q Challenge: The candidate has not specified a municipality for  
voting purposes.
A Analysis: This is now required by Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(7)(d).
Q Challenge: The space in the header for candidate street number, fire 
number, rural route number, box number if a rural route and street 
name is blank.
A Analysis: When the candidate’s basic address information (number and 
name of street) is blank in the header, the Commission has approved the 
challenge and struck the signatures on those pages. Wis. Admin. Code 
§ EL 2.05(7)(d) and Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(b) and (c), 8.15(5)(a) and (b), and 
8.20(2)(a) and (b). A residential address means the street and number, if 
any, and municipality for voting purposes, all of which must be accurate. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(1)(a).
Best Practice: If a candidate’s residential address contains an 
apartment number or unit number, and that number is missing from 
the header, the filing officer should assess whether the nomination 
paper is still substantially compliant with the law. If the rest of the 
address is complete, leaving off an apartment number or unit 
number likely means there is still substantial compliance unless the 
challenger demonstrates that the residence cannot be determined. 
Leaving off an apartment number usually means the header is still 
substantially compliant because it still contains the street, number, 
and municipality of where the candidate lives. In rare cases, lack of an 
apartment number could raise questions over where the candidate 
actually resides, and accordingly, whether they meet the residency 
requirement for the office sought. In that circumstance, the challenger 
bears the burden of demonstrating how the missing apartment number 
affected whether signatories knew where the candidate resides.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 50
Q Challenge: A candidate has listed inconsistent mailing addresses on their 
nomination papers and declaration of candidacy.
A Analysis: These types of challenges are fact-intensive inquiries, and 
should always be handled on a case-by-case basis. The filing officer 
may, but is not required to, consult extrinsic sources of information, such 
as seeking information on how mail is handled in the municipalities listed. 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(3).
In some instances, USPS can confirm that overlaps exist in ZIP codes, and 
mail delivered to either municipality is interchangeable. In instances 
where two different addresses (usually differing municipalities) refer to the 
same physical location, the challenge should not be sustained.
Where the two addresses are totally different, and cannot be explained 
by overlapping ZIP codes, the filing officer should examine whether the 
candidate has met the legal requirements to provide correct address 
information. If they have not, the challenge should be sustained.
Candidate Certification
Q Challenge: The candidate has not completed the gender identification 
checkbox in the candidate certification statement.
A Analysis: Gender identification is not required in the header of nomination 
papers. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(8)(a).
Candidate Dates of Circulation
Q Challenge: The candidate circulated nomination papers prior to the 
date he or she filed a campaign registration statement or declaration of 
candidacy.
A Analysis: The Commission has dismissed these challenges. Candidates 
are not required to file campaign registration statements prior to 
circulating nomination papers.
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(5) , 8.15(4)(b), 8.20(6) provide that if a candidate has 
not filed a campaign registration statement prior to the time of filing 
nomination papers, “the candidate shall file the statement with the 
papers.” Wis. Stat. § 8.21(1)  provides that each candidate shall file a 
declaration of candidacy “no later than the latest time provided for 
filing nomination papers.”
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 51
Circulator Information
Circulator Address
Q Challenge: The circulator’s address, required by Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(3), 8.15(4)(a), 
or 8.20(3) is insufficient because it is missing the municipality of residence.
A Analysis: The circulator must include their residential address, including 
their voting municipality, for it to substantially comply with the statutory and 
administrative code requirements. See Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(g).  
Signatures cannot be counted when the nomination paper lacks the 
circulator’s address. The only exception is when the circulator’s residential 
address could be determined by the information on the nomination paper. 
For example, signatures may be counted when the circulator’s residence 
is not included, but the circulator is the candidate and the candidate has 
included their residential address in the header of the nomination paper.
Q Challenge: The circulator’s address, required by Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(3), 
8.15(4)(a), or 8.20(3) is insufficient because the circulator has not indicated 
type of municipality of residence (e.g., “Town of” or “City of”).
A Analysis: Staff has recommended dismissing these challenges. Wis. Stat.  
§ 8.15(4)(a) (which both 8.10(3) and 8.20(3) incorporate) states in the relevant 
portion that “the certification of a qualified circulator stating his or her 
residence with street and number, if any, shall appear at the bottom of each 
nomination paper, stating he or she personally circulated the nomination 
paper and personally obtained each of the signatures.” There is no separate 
requirement that the circulator indicate the type of municipality of residence.
Circulator Date and Signature
Q Challenge: The date of certification is incomplete or incorrect, as required 
by Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(3), 8.15(4)(a), or 8.20(3).
A Analysis: A circulator may correct date errors in their certificate via a correcting 
affidavit filed with the filing officer no later than 5 p.m. on the 3rd calendar day 
after the deadline to file a challenge. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(5)(ag).
Correctable date errors include the circulator failing to sign or otherwise 
complete the certificate, or entering inadvertently erroneous data (for 
instance: the circulator dated the certificate before circulation, not after). If 
the circulator has not corrected these errors by affidavit by the correction 
deadline, the challenge must be approved and the signatures on those 
pages struck.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 52
Elector Signatures
Only one signature per person for the same office is valid. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(4)(b),  
8.15(2), 8.20(5), Wis. Amin Code § EL 2.05(6)(d). In addition to his or her 
signature, in order for the signature to be valid, each signer of a nomination 
paper shall legibly print his or her name in a space provided next to his or her 
signature and shall list his or her municipality of residence for voting purposes, 
the street and number, if any, on which the signer resides, and the date of 
signing. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(4)(b), 8.15(2), 8.20(5). Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(e).
Multiple Signatures
Q Challenge: The elector has signed nomination papers for more than one 
candidate for the same office.
A Analysis: Only the elector’s first signature is valid. See Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(4)(b),  
8.15(2), 8.20(5), Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(d). Where the elector has 
signed another candidate’s papers prior to the signature on the challenged 
papers, the later signatures should be struck. Exception: Where an elector is 
entitled to vote for more than one candidate for the same office, they may 
sign the nomination papers of as many candidates for the same office as 
they are entitled to vote for at the election. Id. For these offices, duplicate 
signatures for different candidates should not automatically be rejected.
Signature
Q Challenge: The elector has “signed” with a printed name.
A Analysis: There is no requirement that a signature needs to be in cursive 
or script. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(b) requires that the elector “sign his 
or her own name.” Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(1)(p) defines “signature” as a 
“tangible symbol … that evidences the signing of a nomination paper.” The 
rule does not require that the signature be made in cursive.
Q Challenge: The elector’s signature is illegible.
A Analysis: There is no requirement that a signature must be legible, and 
individual signers may mark their signatures in a wide variety of ways 
(e.g., by marking an “X”). Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 53
Printed Name
Q Challenge: The elector’s printed name is illegible or in cursive.
A Analysis: The statutory requirement is that “…in order for the signature to be 
valid, each signer of a nomination paper shall legibly print8 his or her name 
in a space provided next to his or her signature…” Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(4)(b), 
8.15(2), 8.20(5).
If the filing officer cannot discern the signer’s first and last name, after 
reviewing both the signature and printed name, it is illegible and should 
be struck. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h)6. The filing officer may, but 
is not required to, consult extrinsic sources of information if it assists in 
discerning a possible name. Id. If the printed name is illegible, but the 
signer’s full first and last name are legible in their signature, the name 
should not be struck.
Best Practice: A filing officer can correctly discern a 
signer’s name even if it is not spelled correctly. For example, 
“Michale” is perfectly discernible as “Michael.”
Signatory Address
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(4)(b), 8.15(2), 8.20(5) require that an elector who signs a 
nomination paper “shall list his or her municipality of residence for voting 
purposes, the street and number, if any, on which the signer resides.” In order 
for the signature to be valid, the address must be complete or otherwise 
determinable by the information provided on the nomination paper.  
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h)(3). A signature should not be invalidated due 
to an abbreviated municipality or absence of an apartment number or ZIP 
Code. Id. Errors in which the elector used an address or listed a municipality 
which does not reflect his or her actual residence or wrote an incomplete 
address may be corrected by the elector or by the circulator in a correcting 
affidavit filed by the correction deadline. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(5).
8 The phrase “legibly print” was added to the existing statutes by 2013 Wisconsin Act 160. The legislative 
record emphasized that the purpose of Act 160 was to preserve the ability of opposing candidates to 
identify petition signers in order to consider filing challenges, and not to reject signatures that were 
legible.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 54
Q Challenge: The elector’s address is not a valid address or does not exist 
because the challenger couldn’t find it on MyVote or using commercial 
third-party websites.
A Analysis: Only registered voters’ addresses will be searchable on MyVote. 
MyVote is not a database of all existing residential addresses in the state. 
Signatories need not be registered voters in order to sign, they just need to 
be eligible electors. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(b), 8.15(5)(a), and 8.20(2)(a). Without 
more, the fact that a signatory’s address does not return a result in MyVote 
does not establish clear, convincing, and satisfactory evidence that the 
address does not exist.
Challenges that addresses are not valid and do not exist based on other 
evidence, including commercial third-party websites, should be examined 
on a case-by-case basis. In some circumstances, certain evidence may 
be sufficient to meet the challenger’s burden of insufficiency. In those 
cases, the burden would then shift to the candidate to demonstrate that 
the address is valid. These types of challenges are often fact-intensive.
Q Challenge: The elector’s address as written is not a valid residential 
address because the elector has written down the wrong municipality. 
For example, the elector’s house is located in Exampleville but they put 
down Mailville because that’s how USPS formulates their address when 
delivering mail.
A Analysis: The law requires signatories to list their “municipality for voting 
purposes,” in addition to other required fields. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(4)(b), 8.15(2), 
8.20(5). “Voting municipality” means the municipality in which the signer is 
eligible to vote at the date of signing. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(1)(s).  
The Commission’s nomination paper template labels this field as 
“Municipality of Residence,” and further instructs “check the type and write 
the name of your municipality for voting purposes.” Municipality for voting 
purposes and municipality of residence refer to the physical location of 
the residence and the municipal jurisdiction in which it resides. In the 
example above, the Mailville address formulation is a mailing address, 
and is insufficient to meet the legal requirements for elector address. 
Accordingly, signatures should be struck on this ground.
Q Challenge: The elector’s address is missing an apartment number.
A Analysis: A signature should not be invalidated because an apartment 
number is not included. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h)(3).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 55
Q Challenge: The elector’s address is missing the municipality designation 
or the elector has checked a box in error.
A Analysis: The Commission has advised candidates and challengers that 
a signatory’s failure to check the correct box to indicate “Town, Village or 
City” is not a basis for disqualifying a signature unless a challenger can 
show that the given address is outside the subject jurisdiction or district.
For instance, the challenger needs to show that a given address has to 
be in the Village of X, not in the Town of X and, therefore is outside District 
Y. The signatory’s error or omission in checking a box on a form, without 
more, is not sufficient evidence for a challenge.
Q Challenge: The elector’s address is incomplete because the elector has 
abbreviated the name of the municipality.
A Analysis: If the municipality can be determined by other information 
contained on the nomination paper, a challenge to a signature that 
includes an abbreviated municipality name should be rejected.  
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(15 )(c).
For instance, the municipality of “WFB” was determined by the mailing 
address to indicate “Whitefish Bay,” or “Gtown” was determined by the ZIP 
code to indicate “Germantown.”
Q Challenge: The elector has used a P.O. Box, or other commercial courier 
address, as his or her address.
A Analysis: The plain text of the statute requires signatories to provide the 
“street and number on which they reside.” Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(4)(b), 8.15(2), 
8.20(5). See also Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(1)(a). Accordingly, a challenge 
should be sustained and signatures struck in instances where the 
signatory has provided a P.O. Box address instead of a residential address. 
This guidance also applies if the challenger meets the burden to show 
that the address provided is a mailing address of a commercial courier, 
such as FedEx or UPS.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 56
Q Challenge: The signer lives outside the candidate’s district.
A Analysis: A challenger’s bare assertion, without more, of the signer’s non-
residency is not sufficient to sustain the challenger’s burden of proof, 
which is clear, convincing and satisfactory evidence. Wis. Admin. Code § 
EL 2.07(3)(d), 2.07(4). A complaint challenging the eligibility of a signatory 
to a nomination paper based on the signer’s non-residency can be 
accompanied by reference to MyVote Wisconsin or “Who is My Legislator?” 
web searches, by a map of the district demonstrating that the address 
is outside the district, or by a signed statement from the election official, 
(municipal clerk or deputy clerk), whose responsibility it is to determine 
the residency of electors of the district. Time permitting, Commission staff, 
or local filing officers, may attempt to verify the location of the address via 
MyVote Wisconsin and WisVote.
Signature Date
Q Challenge: The date of the elector’s signature, as required by Wis. Stat.  
§§ 8.10(4)(b), 8.15(2), 8. 20(5), is incomplete or missing.
A Analysis: An incomplete or missing date can survive an incomplete date 
challenge if “the date can be determined by reference to the dates of 
any of the other signatures on the paper, including those dates above or 
below the signature.” Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h)(1). For example, if a 
signature line is missing a date, but all the other signatures on that page 
are of the same date, which is also the same date as when the circulator 
signed, it can be assumed that the signature line in question should also 
be that date.
Q Challenge: The elector’s signature is dated after the date of the circulator’s 
certification.
A Analysis: A signature may not be counted if it is dated after the date of the 
certificate of the circulator. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 2.05(6)(h)(2).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 57
Pre-Filled Signatory Information
Q Challenge: It appears as if the municipality of residence and date of 
signature columns were pre-filled, or all filled out by the same person in 
the signatory information section.
A Analysis: The law states that, in order for a signature to be valid, “each 
signer of a nomination paper shall legibly print his or her name in a space 
provided next to his or her signature and shall list his or her municipality 
of residence for voting purposes, the street and number, if any, on which 
the signer resides, and the date of signing.” Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(4)(b), 8.15(2), 
and 8.20(5). The Commission has taken the position that the signatory is 
only required to print their name and sign. Nothing in the statutes cited 
above requires that the signatory be the one to write the other required 
information, such as their address, municipality, and date of signing.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 58
Chapter 2.4: Nomination by 
Caucus
Sec. 2.4.1: Introduction
The caucus is a method that may be used by towns and villages for nominating 
local candidates to be placed on the Spring Election ballot.
 Ɋ The caucus is open to the public, but only qualified voters of the 
municipality may nominate and vote for candidates.
 Ɋ A person is not required to be a registered voter in order to participate in 
the caucus.
 Ɋ Caucuses cannot be used for nominating candidates for the office of Town 
Sanitary District Commissioner or Multi-Jurisdictional Municipal Judge.
 Ɋ Candidates for these offices must use nomination papers.
There is no spring primary for town or village offices when candidates are 
nominated by caucus. However, there may still be a spring primary held within 
the municipality for state, county, or school district office.

Sec. 2.4.2: Preparing for a Caucus
Timing: When to Hold the Caucus
 Ɋ Between December 1 and January 1 preceding a spring election, the 
governing body of a town or village nominating candidates by caucus 
must decide the date on which the caucus will be held.
 Ɋ The caucus must be held between January 2 and January 21.
 Ɋ The deadline to hold a caucus is not extended if January 21 falls on a weekend.
 Ɋ When possible, preference should be given to having the caucus on 
January 21. The caucus is not required to be conducted on a Tuesday.9
9 Wis. Stat. § 8.05 (1)(a).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 60
Public Notice of the Caucus
The municipal clerk must give proper public notice of the caucus by posting 
a notice in the clerk’s office and publishing a notice in a newspaper at least 
five days before the date of the caucus. This notice must contain the location, 
date, and time of the caucus.10 If a newspaper is not published within the 
municipality, clerks can meet the publishing requirement by posting the notice 
of the caucus in at least three locations within the municipality.11 The clerk must 
post these no later than five days before the date of the caucus. The notices 
should be where they are most likely to be seen by voters, or in one location 
within the municipality and on the municipality’s website.
Caucus Personnel
Town Chairperson/Village President
The caucus is conducted by the town board chairperson or the village president 
as long as they are not a candidate at the Spring Election.
What If They are a Candidate?
If the chairperson or president is a candidate, they must call for an election 
of officials to conduct the caucus. This can be done either by ballot or 
acclamation (voice vote).
Municipal Clerk
The municipal clerk serves in an administrative capacity and usually takes 
the minutes. 12
Tellers
The voters must also select two tellers to canvass the vote for each office to be 
nominated at the caucus.13
10 Wis. Stat. § 8.05 (1)(b).
11 Wis. Stat. § 10.05.
12 The Commission recommends that clerks keep a sign-in sheet of all attendees so they can be 
contacted if the caucus is reconvened.
13 Wis. Stat. § 8.05 (1)(c).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 61
Sec. 2.4.3: Selecting 
Candidates at a Caucus
Who May Nominate Candidates at a Caucus?
Only qualified voters of the municipality may nominate and vote for candidates 
at a caucus.
Qualified voters are:
 Ɋ United States citizen
 Ɋ Eighteen years of age or older
 Ɋ Resided within the municipality for at least 28 days before the caucus
The voter list from a previous election or voter information from MyVote may be 
used as an aid in determining if a person qualified as a voter in the municipality 
at the last election. Any person whose name does not appear on the voter list 
or on MyVote may be asked to provide documentation that they are a qualified 
voter of the municipality.14 Any qualified voter of the municipality may nominate 
themselves as a candidate for office.
Candidate Eligibility
A candidate does not have to be a qualified voter or resident of the village or 
town at the time of the caucus. A candidate may be nominated for more than 
one municipal office. There is no requirement that a candidate be a registered 
voter in the municipality.
Villages
A candidate for a village office must be a qualified voter and a resident of the 
village by the time of the election.15
Towns
A candidate for a town office must be a qualified voter of the town at the time 
of taking office, except an assessor appointed under Wis. Stat. § 60.307.
14 For more information on valid proof of residence documents, consult the document “Proof of 
Residence (POR) vs. Proof of Identification (POI)” available at elections.wi.gov.
15 Wis. Stat. § 61.19.

Procedures for Nomination
Nomination Method
Nominations can be made separately for each office that will appear on the 
Spring Election ballot. This can be done in one of two ways, either by taking 
nominations from the floor (“acclamation” or voice vote) or by conducting a 
vote by secret ballot.
The chairperson should announce the method to be used before asking for 
nominations, in case there are objections to using that nomination method.
Note: Incumbents must be nominated at the caucus and follow the 
same ballot access procedures as any other municipal candidate. 
Incumbents are not automatically nominated or placed on the ballot.
Floor Nominations
When nominations are taken from the floor, each nomination must receive a 
second. After each nomination is made and seconded, the caucus chairperson 
must ask, “Are there any more nominations?” and if hearing none, must announce, 
“Nominations are closed.”16 The chairperson should ensure that all eligible 
attendees have the opportunity to nominate a candidate if they wish to do so.
16 Wis. Stat. § 8.05 (1)(d).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 63
Secret Ballot Nominations
If nominations are made by secret ballot, the tellers will distribute a piece of 
paper to each voter, which will serve as a ballot. The voters will be instructed to 
write in the name of his or her nominee for the office. The ballots will then be 
collected and tallied by the tellers.
Selecting Candidates
After nominations are made, the caucus chairperson should announce the 
names of the nominees. They may use a flip chart or chalkboard to record 
these names. If voting is necessary, only these nominees will be voted on at 
the caucus.
Offices with a Single Candidate
For offices where only one person is to be elected and no more than two 
candidates are nominated, there is no need to conduct a vote. If more than 
two persons have been nominated, the chairperson should conduct a vote at 
the caucus to reduce the number of candidates to two. If a vote is required, 
the caucus chairperson will announce the names of all candidates. Each voter 
at the caucus may vote for one candidate. The two candidates receiving the 
highest number of votes are nominated and certified to the municipal clerk by 
the caucus chairperson and tellers.17
Offices with Multiple Seats
Nominations for the offices of town supervisors elected to unnumbered seats 
should be considered together with nominations for the offices of village 
trustee. If there are nominations for more than twice the number of candidates 
to be elected, conduct a vote to reduce the number of candidates to twice the 
number of seats to be filled. Each voter at the caucus may vote for as many 
candidates as there are seats to be filled at the election.
Example: If three village trustees are to be elected, each person can vote 
for three candidates. The six candidates who receive the most votes at the 
caucus will be nominated and certified to the municipal clerk by the caucus 
chairperson and tellers.
17 Wis. Stat. §§ 8.05 (1)(f), (g), (h).
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 64
In Case of a Tie
If two or more candidates receive an equal number of votes, but not the 
greatest number of votes, so that only one of the candidates with equal votes 
may advance to the election, the tie between the candidates with equal votes 
may be broken either by drawing lots or by conducting another vote.18
Sec. 2.4.4: After the Nomination is Decided
Notify Candidates of Their Nomination
As soon as the nominated candidates are certified by the chairperson 
and tellers to the municipal clerk, the clerk is responsible for notifying the 
candidates, in writing, of their nomination. 
The clerk must also inform each candidate of the requirements to file:
 Ɋ Campaign Registration Statement (CF-1L).19
 Ɋ Declaration of Candidacy (EL-162).20
 Ɋ Candidates for municipal judge must also be informed of the requirement to 
file a Statement of Economic Interests with the Wisconsin Ethics Commission.21
A copy of the Campaign Registration Statement (CF-1L) and the Declaration of 
Candidacy (EL-162) should be provided by the clerk to each nominated candidate.22
If any of the nominated candidates are present at the caucus, the municipal clerk 
can provide them with a written notice, the Campaign Registration Statement (CF-1L), 
and the Declaration of Candidacy (EL-162). Because the candidates are to receive a 
notification of nomination in writing, it is suggested that the clerk prepare a notifica-
tion form that can be completed at the caucus with the name of the candidate and 
the office to which he or she was nominated. The clerk should also prepare a receipt 
that can be dated and signed by the candidate stating that he or she received a 
written notice of nomination at the caucus. A sample Notification of Nomination and 
Receipt of Notification of Nomination can be found at the end of this chapter.
18 The chairperson should decide upon the method by which a tie is broken at the beginning of the caucus.
19 Wis. Stat. §§ 11.0202, 11.0203.
20 Wis. Stat. §§ 8.05 (1)(j), 8.21.
21 Wis. Stat. §§ 8.05 (1)(j), 19.43(4).
22 Except for the CF-1L, the forms mentioned in this chapter are available on elections.wi.gov. For the 
CF-1L form, please contact the Wisconsin Ethics Commission.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 65
If a candidate is not present at the caucus, the written notification, the 
Campaign Registration Statement (CF-1L) and the Declaration of Candidacy 
(EL-162) should be delivered to the candidate as soon as possible. Delivery can 
be made in person or by mail. If the written notification is delivered in person, 
the clerk should use a prepared receipt that can be dated and signed by 
the candidate. If the notification is mailed, it should be sent by certified mail. 
Certified mail will provide the clerk with a receipt showing the date that the 
notification was received by the candidate.
Best Practice: Get a Receipt
Clerks can deliver required notifications and forms in person or by mail.
If the written notification is delivered in person, the clerk should use 
a prepared receipt that can be dated and signed by the candidate.
If the notification is mailed, it should be sent by certified mail. 
Certified mail will provide the clerk with a receipt showing the 
date that the notification was received by the candidate.
It is important to have a receipt. If the notification is personally 
delivered, the candidate has five days after the date personal 
delivery is made to file the necessary forms with the clerk. The five-
day period begins the day after the date indicated on the receipt.
Notification of Noncandidacy (EL-163)
An incumbent is required to file a notification of non-candidacy to put everyone, 
especially the clerk, on notice that they do not intend to be a candidate at the 
upcoming spring elections. For this reason, the clerk may want to send the 
Notification of Noncandidacy form to all incumbent officeholders whose term of 
office is up the next election.
If a filing officer receives a notification of noncandidacy from an incumbent, 
the filing officer is required to promptly post public notice of that fact on their 
website, or, if they do not have a website, they can post that information in at 
least three different locations within the jurisdiction.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 66
In addition, if an incumbent fails to file a declaration of candidacy by the filing 
deadline of five days after the notification of nomination after a caucus, the 
filing officer is required to post that information on their website or in three 
locations withing the jurisdiction. See Figure 2 below.
In jurisdictions where caucus is used, if an incumbent is nominated 
at caucus but does not file either a notification of noncandidacy or a 
declaration of candidacy by 5:00 p.m. on the fifth day after notification 
of their nomination from the caucus, the filing deadline for that office is 
extended by 72 hours after the original deadline for all candidates certified 
at caucus except the incumbent. 23

Qualifications for Ballot Placement of Candidates
In order to qualify for ballot placement, each candidate nominated at the 
caucus is required to complete and file the two forms listed below. The candidate 
must file these forms with the municipal clerk no later than 5:00 p.m. on the fifth 
day after receiving written notification that they have been nominated for office. 
The municipal clerk or someone appointed by the clerk must be available until 
5:00 p.m. on the fifth day following the candidate’s receipt of the written notice.
 Ɋ Campaign Registration Statement (CF-1L)
 Ɋ Declaration of Candidacy (EL-162)
A candidate for municipal judge must also file a Statement of Economic 
Interests with the Wisconsin Ethics Commission no later than 4:30 p.m. on the 
fifth day after receiving written notification that he or she has been nominated.
If a candidate fails to file any of the required forms within five days after receipt 
of written notification, the candidate does not qualify for ballot placement and 
the clerk cannot place the candidate’s name on the ballot.24 When a candidate 
fails to file the required forms on time, the clerk should treat that failure as 
declining nomination. If no candidates for an office qualify for ballot placement, 
the ballot will contain only a space for a write-in candidate. The number of 
write-in lines on the ballot must match the number of seats to be filled, so a 
“vote for two” contest would have two write-in lines.25
Selecting Order of Candidates on the Ballot
No later than the end of the third day following the qualification of candidates, 
the municipal clerk must conduct a drawing of lots for each office to 
determine the order in which the candidates’ names will be placed on the 
Spring Election ballot. 26 The drawing of candidate order does not require a 
public meeting notice. 27
24 Wis. Stat §§ 8.05 (1)(j), 8.21, 8.30(2), (3).
25 Clerks are encouraged to remind candidates of the filing requirement as the deadline approaches 
to avoid allegations that the requirements were not clear.
26 Wis. Stat. § 8.05 (1)(j).
27 Candidates may attend, but the clerk is not required to notify or invite them to the drawing. 
Municipal clerks should document the drawing of ballot order in writing and to not conduct the 
drawing alone.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 68
Reconvening the Caucus
The town board chairperson or the village president may reconvene the caucus 
to correct a procedural error. The caucus can also be reconvened to nominate 
a candidate for a position for which no candidate was nominated at the original 
caucus, or when no candidate nominated at the original caucus qualifies for a 
position. The reconvened caucus must be held within 10 days of the date of the 
original caucus, and public notice must be given in the same manner as notice 
of the original caucus. Wis. Stat. § 8.05 (1)(k).
The reconvened caucus may be held after January 21, as long as that day is 
within 10 days of the original caucus and proper notice has been given. The 
only office(s) addressed at a reconvened caucus are those where a procedural 
error occurred or where there were no nominations. The clerk must notify the 
attendees of the original caucus to inform them if the caucus is reconvened. 
For further information, contact an elections administration specialist at the 
Commission at (608) 261-2028 or elections@wi.gov.
Sec. 2.4.5: Frequently Asked Questions
Q Does Wisconsin’s photo ID law apply to caucus procedures?
A No. The attendee may need to provide some type of documentation 
that proves he or she is a qualified voter of the municipality in order to 
nominate candidates.
Q Can members of the governing body nominate candidates?
A Yes. Any qualified voter of the municipality may nominate candidates at 
the caucus.
Q Can a person who was nominated at the caucus but not selected run as a 
registered write-in candidate?
A Yes. Any qualified voter can run as a registered write-in candidate.
Q If a candidate fails to submit the required documents by the deadline, 
can a person who was nominated but not selected be chosen as a 
replacement?
A Not automatically. The caucus would have to be reconvened to take 
nominations for that office.
Q What is a teller?
A A teller is a person selected at the caucus to count the votes if necessary.
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 69
Q What if the clerk is not available on the deadline to receive the ballot 
documentation through 5:00 p.m. on the fifth day?
A The clerk should appoint someone to be available through the deadline. 
This person must be prepared to conduct the tasks the clerk would on 
ballot documentation.
Q What if the municipal clerk is on the ballot?
A The municipal clerk can be present at the caucus and nominate 
candidates. The clerk’s duties at the caucus are only administrative.
Q Is the clerk required to notify candidates that their name will not be 
on the ballot due to not submitting the required documentation by the 
filing deadline?
A No, but it’s recommended that the clerk inform candidates if they fail to 
qualify for ballot status.
Notification of nomination by caucus can be sent by certified mail or 
personally delivered. If personally delivered, the candidate should sign 
a receipt indicating that notification was received. Sample Notice of 
Nomination at Caucus and Receipt of Notice of Nomination are included 
on the following pages. Wis. Stat. § 8.05 (1)(j).
