Chapter 2.5: Notification of 
Noncandidacy
An incumbent officeholder who does not intend to run again for the position 
they currently holds can file a Notification of Noncandidacy (EL-163) with the 
appropriate filing officer. This alerts the public and potential candidates that 
the incumbent does not intend to run for re-election. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.05(1)(j)2. 
(caucus nominations), 8.10(2)(a) (spring election candidates), 8.15(1) (partisan 
election candidates), 8.20(8)(a) (independent candidates), 120.06(6)(b)3, 
120.06(6)(b) (school district candidates).
Best Practice: While incumbent officeholders are not legally required 
to file a Notification of Noncandidacy, incumbents who know they 
will not seek reelection should still file an EL-163 with their filing 
officer for smoother ballot access and nomination processes. 
Clerks are required to promptly provide public notice of all Notification of 
Noncandidacy information received from incumbents on the municipal, county, 
or school district internet site or by posting notice in three places if no internet 
site is maintained. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.05(1)(j)2m., 8.10(2)(am), 8.15(1m), 8.20(8)(ae), 
120.06(6)(b)3m. 
Best Practice: During November before the Spring Election and March 
before the Fall Election, the filing officer should remind each incumbent 
to file a Notification of Noncandidacy (EL-163) if they do not intend to 
seek re-election to the office they currently hold. The Notification of  
Noncandidacy (EL-163) is used in municipalities using nomination papers.
Incumbents in nomination paper jurisdictions who have filed a Notification  
of Noncandidacy by the deadline retain the option of filing nomination 
papers for ballot access or running as a write-in candidate for the office.  
Wis. Stat. §§ 8.05(1 )(j)2m., 8.10(2)(am), 8.15(1m), 8.20(8)(ae), 120.06(6)(b)3m.

In jurisdictions where caucus is used, if an incumbent is nominated at caucus 
but does not file a declaration of candidacy by 5:00 p.m. on the fifth day after 
notification of their nomination from the caucus, the filing deadline for that 
office is extended by 72 hours after the original deadline for all candidates 
certified at caucus except the incumbent. Wis. Stat. § 8.05(1)(j)2. 
Sec. 2.5.1: Filing Deadlines
 Ɋ For nomination paper jurisdictions, the deadline for filing a Notification 
of Noncandidacy (EL-163) is the second Friday before the deadline for 
filing nomination papers. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(2)(a) (spring election), 8.15(1) 
(partisan primary), and 8.20(8)(a) (independent candidates). 
 Ɋ For nomination paper jurisdictions, if an incumbent candidate fails to 
file a Notification of Noncandidacy (EL-163) on time and does not file the 
appropriate documents to qualify for the ballot on time:
 ɉ The deadline for filing ballot access documents is extended by 72 hours 
for that office. 
 ɉ This means that anyone, except the incumbent, can file the required 
ballot access documents and sufficient nomination papers within the 
extension period and qualify for placement on the ballot.
 Ɋ For jurisdictions who nominate candidates by caucus, if an incumbent 
whose name is certified as a nominee fails to file a declaration of 
candidacy by the applicable deadline, and also fails to file written 
notification that they do not intend to be a candidate, the deadline for 
each certified candidate, except the incumbent, to file a declaration of 
candidacy is extended 72 hours after the latest time allowed to file a 
declaration of candidacy. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.05(1)(j)2., 8.05(1)(j)(2m).

Sec. 2.5.2: Frequently Asked Questions
Q Can an incumbent file a Notification of Noncandidacy, change their mind, 
and still run for reelection? 
A Yes. The non-candidacy form is non-binding, so the incumbent could 
change their mind and decide to run.
Q Our district lines have changed. Some of the incumbent officeholders 
have been redistricted out of their current district and/or have had 
their district’s number change because of the update. What does the 
Notification of Noncandidacy look like for them? 
A The incumbents should file a Notification of Noncandidacy for their current 
district unless they plan to move into the new district and run again for the 
same office. 
Q Is an electronic copy sufficient for a Notification of Noncandidacy, or 
should the filing officer require the physical original? 
A The Wisconsin Elections Commission accepts electronic receipt as 
sufficient for Notification of Noncandidacy. 
Q An incumbent would like to run for a different office within the same 
municipality/county. Do they still file a Notification of Noncandidacy? 
A Yes. If the incumbent does not plan to seek another term for the office they 
currently hold, they should file a Notification of Noncandidacy. 
Q The incumbent officeholder was appointed to fill a vacancy for the remainder 
of a term but does not intend to run for the office. Do they still need to file a 
Notification of Noncandidacy to prevent an extension of the deadline? 
A Yes.

Chapter 2.6: Write-In 
Candidates
A write-in candidate is someone who does not circulate nomination papers, 
is not nominated at caucus, and whose name does not appear printed on 
the ballot. All offices that appear on all ballots are required to have a line for 
write-in candidates. See generally Wis. Stat. §§ 5.58, 5.60, 5.62, 5.64, 5.65, 5.82. 
Voters can write whatever candidate or name they choose as write-in vote, but 
most write-in votes can only be counted if the write-in candidate has filed the 
necessary paperwork by the applicable deadline, which is discussed below. 
In this chapter, a “registered write-in candidate,” means a candidate who 
has filled out the necessary paperwork by the correct deadline. Except in 
a few unique circumstances, only votes for registered write-in candidates 
may be counted. In other words, if someone wants to cast a write-in vote 
for Bucky Badger, they are free to write that on the ballot. But the vote will 
only count if Bucky Badger became a registered write-in candidate by the 
appropriate deadline. 
Figure 3: Example of how a write-in line appears on an optical scan ballot
A candidate who wishes to run as a registered write-in must file a Campaign 
Finance Registration Statement (CF-1 for state candidates, CF-1L for local 
candidates) with the appropriate filing officer before collecting or spending any 
money on the campaign and no later than 12:00 p.m. on the Friday preceding 
the election. Wis. Stat. §§  7.50(2)(em), 11.0202(1)(a). 
First Edition, June 2026 Getting on the Ballot 2 – 76
Important Law Change: As of December 1, 2027, the Wisconsin Ethics 
Commission will become the filing officer for local candidates filing a 
CF-1L. 2025 Wisconsin Act 7, amending 2023 Wisconsin Act 126. Until 
that date, write-in candidates for local office will continue to file their 
reports with the local filing officer. If the candidate has already filed a 
CF-1 with the filing officer and subsequently decides to run as a write-
in, the Commission recommends that the candidate submit a short 
written statement to the filing officer reflecting their intent to run as a 
write-in. 
In general, votes cast for write-in candidates who have not filed a campaign 
registration statement cannot be counted. Wis. Stat. § 7.50(2)(em). See 
Chapter 14.21 for detailed guidance on how to count write-in votes. 
Best Practice: The Commission, and other filing officers, post 
the names of registered write-in candidates online ahead of 
Election Day. The Commission recommends that clerks prepare 
a list of registered write-in candidates for use on Election Day 
if a voter asks to see it. The Commission does not recommend 
that clerks post this list at the polling place, or direct voters’ 
attention to it as doing so could be seen as inadvertently 
electioneering in support of one of the write-in candidates.

Part 3 
Voter List Maintenance
Voter List Maintenance Processes; Registration List 
Alerts; Individuals Ineligible to Vote; Deceased Voters; 
Voter Requests; Duplicate Registrations
This section of the manual attempts to provide a simplified overview of each 
of the processes conducted in Wisconsin. It is not a complete description 
of each process. To better understand list maintenance, clerks should 
also review relevant law, the WisVote manual, and the Commission’s clerk 
communications. As always, local election officials may also wish to consult 
with their own attorneys regarding these processes.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 1
Chapter 3.1: Voter List 
Maintenance
Sec. 3.1.1: Introduction
The statewide voter registration list, also known as the official voter registration 
list, is maintained electronically within a Commission-developed database 
called WisVote. Registration list maintenance refers to the processes performed 
by election officials to update the status of voter records in WisVote. As 
described below, some of the processes are simple and well-defined in statute. 
Other processes are complex and may have several pathways.
This section of the manual attempts to provide a simplified overview of each 
of the processes conducted in Wisconsin. It is not a complete description of 
each process. To better understand list maintenance, clerks should also review 
relevant law, the WisVote manual, and the Commission’s clerk communications. 
As always, local election officials may also wish to consult with their own 
attorneys regarding these processes.
A Note about Providers and Reliers
Sometimes, a municipal clerk (a relier) enters into agreement with another clerk 
(a provider) for the provider to complete WisVote work on the relier’s behalf. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.33(5)(b). The provider can be either a county clerk or another municipal 
clerk. Reliers and providers enter into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) 
that governs how the data entry and list maintenance work will be covered 
between them.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 2
This section of the manual covers:
 Ɋ Introduction
 Ɋ Four-Year Maintenance
 Ɋ Voters Who Move
 Ɋ ERIC Movers
 Ɋ Deceased Voters
 Ɋ Voters Residing in a Condemned 
Structure
 Ɋ Voter Requests for Deactivation
 Ɋ Voters Adjudicated Incompetent 
by a Court
 Ɋ Voters Convicted of a Felony/
Treason/Bribery
 Ɋ Duplicate Voter Records and 
Other Situations

 Ɋ Special Notes for Reliers
The requirements for the state’s Official Registration List (WisVote) are described 
in Wis. Stat. § 6.36(1)(a).
Many (but not all) registration list maintenance processes are described in  
Wis. Stat. § 6.50.
Chapter 2 of the WisVote manual provides instructions on how to perform 
specific list maintenance processes in WisVote.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 3
Chapter 3.2: Four-Year 
Maintenance (Inactive Voters)
By June 15 of every odd numbered year, the Commission is required to identify 
registered voters who have not participated in an election for four or more 
consecutive years. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(1). Thus, this process occurs every two 
years, in the summers of odd-numbered years. The identified voters receive a 
postcard from the Commission advising them that their voter registration will be 
suspended if they do not request continuation within 30 days. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(2).
Sec. 3.2.1: Commission Responsibilities
 When post cards are mailed by the Commission, the voter records are 
automatically changed in WisVote from “Active-Registered” to “Active-
Suspended.” Active-Suspended serves only as a label to indicate the 
voter record may be deactivated after 30 days. Voters who fail to request 
continuation within 30 days are automatically changed to “Inactive-4-Year 
Maintenance,” and thus changed to ineligible on the voter registration list. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.50(2) .
Sec. 3.2.2: Clerk Responsibilities
 Voter requests to continue their registration are sent to their municipal clerk.1 
The municipal clerk (or their designated Provider) may then change the voter’s 
status from “Active-Suspended” back to “Active-Registered.” No other notice to 
the Commission is required.
Sec. 3.2.3: Commission Reporting
No later than August 1 of each year when Four-Year Maintenance postcards 
go out, the Commission will publish data on the number of postcards that 
were mailed, the number that were returned as undeliverable, the number of 
voters who requested to continue their status, and the number of postcards not 
returned, among other fields. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(2r). Voter list maintenance data 
can be accessed under the Statistics and Data menu on elections.wi.gov.
1 This manual section exclusively uses the term “municipal clerk,” however the term also applies to a 
Board of Election Commissioners for large cities. Wis. Stat. § 7.20.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 4
Chapter 3.3: Voters Who Move
Voters who move to a different municipality must re-register to vote. Wis. Stat. § 6.27 
(requiring most voters to register before voting in any election). If the municipal clerk 
reasonably believes a voter has moved to a different municipality, they must mail 
the voter a “30-Day Notice” to the address listed on the voter’s registration advising 
the voter of a pending change in registration status. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(3). A municipal 
clerk may reasonably believe a voter has moved if a registration verification 
postcard is returned as undeliverable, in response to an ERIC movers notification, or 
by personal knowledge in their community. If the voter fails to respond, or confirms 
that they have moved to a different municipality, the municipal clerk may change 
the voter’s status from “Active-Registered” to “Inactive-Moved.” Wis. Stat. § 6.50(3). If 
a voter has moved within the municipality, the clerk may simply update the voter’s 
home address and send the voter a notice of the change. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(3).
Best Practice: The old voter record should be 
merged into the new record for continuity.
Sec. 3.3.1: Commission Responsibilities
When the Commission receives notice that a voter may have moved, the notice 
is provided to the municipal clerk. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.50(3), 7.15(1) (giving clerks 
charge and supervision of elections and registration in their municipalities). The 
Commission also performs a quarterly review of possible movers identified by 
ERIC (the Electronic Registration and Information Center).
Sec. 3.3.2: Clerk Responsibilities
The municipal clerk should review potential movers to identify voters they 
reasonably believe no longer reside in their municipality. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(3) 
(requiring action “upon receipt of reliable information”). Likewise, if a new voter 
moves into the municipality, clerks may receive a registration list alert for a 
duplicate record (from the voter’s previous residence).
Best Practice: In these cases, the old record should be merged into the 
new record. Do not alter or otherwise attempt to transfer the old record.
Registration list alerts are covered in Section 2.4 of the WisVote manual.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 5
Chapter 3.4: ERIC Movers
Wisconsin law requires the state to be a member of the Electronic Registration 
Information Center (ERIC). Wis. Stat. § 6.36(1)(ae)1. ERIC is a nonprofit, nonpartisan 
membership organization created by and composed of its member states 
and the District of Columbia. ERIC facilitates the exchange of information 
between states to identify voters who move, voters who die, and voters 
who attempt to vote in more than one state. More information about ERIC is 
available on ericstates.org.
To identify potential movers, ERIC obtains data from a variety of sources, such 
as the Wisconsin Department of Transportation (WI DOT), other member states’ 
data, and the National Change of Address (NCOA) database from the United 
States Postal Service. ERIC provides the State of Wisconsin with a list of voters 
who may have moved each quarter.
Sec. 3.4.1: Commission Responsibilities
The ERIC membership agreement, which is a legally-binding contract that 
Wisconsin is required to enter into by law, requires the commission to contact 
these voters. Wis. Stat. § 6.36(1)(ae)1. A notification postcard informs voters that 
a transaction they completed with one of the entities listed above (i.e., WI DOT 
Division of Motor Vehicles, NCOA, etc.) indicates their address may be different 
than their most recent voter registration address.
Voters who receive the postcard and have moved within the State of Wisconsin 
may choose to reregister online, by mail, at their clerk’s office, or at their polling 
place on the next Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 6.30.
The postcard also provides the following options for the 
voter to affirm the address on their record:
 Ɋ Return their signed postcard to their municipal clerk,
 Ɋ Visit the MyVote Wisconsin website and click the “Confirm Your Address” 
button, or
 Ɋ Vote in the next election where they can affirm with poll workers that they 
have not had a change of address.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 6
Sec. 3.4.2: Clerk Responsibilities
The voter records identified for this mailing remain eligible to vote and appear 
in “Active-Movers” status. A “Have you Moved?” watermark will also appear 
by these names in the poll book. Clerks have discretion to assess each case 
individually and may elect to deactivate records or restore records to “Active-
Registered” status. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(3). Clerks may want to contact their 
municipal counsel for assistance when they are not sure how to proceed with 
this process under this statute.
If a Movers postcard comes back to the clerk’s office as undeliverable, and the 
clerk would like to deactivate the record, they are required to send the voter the 
Undeliverable 30-Day Notice letter to the address the voter is registered to in 
WisVote. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(3). The letter template is available in the voter record 
within WisVote.
Should the Undeliverable 30-Day Notice letter come back as undeliverable, 
the clerk can inactivate the voter record, changing it from “Active-Movers” to 
“Inactive-Undeliverable.” Wis. Stat. § 6.50(3). If there is a forwarding address, the 
new voter record status may instead be “Inactive-Moved.” Wis. Stat. § 6.50(3). If 
the clerk does not receive a response to the letter, they can inactivate the voter 
record with a voter status of “Inactive-Moved.” Wis. Stat. § 6.50(3).
Should a voter receive the Undeliverable 30-Day Notice and respond that they 
still reside at that address, the clerk may return the voter record to “Active-
Registered” status. If a voter changes their residence within the municipality, the 
clerk must change the registration and mail the voter a notice of the change. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.50(3).
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 7
Chapter 3.5: Deceased Voters
When a municipality learns that a registered voter has died, the municipal 
clerk changes the voter record status from “Active-Registered” to “Inactive-
Deceased.” Wis. Stat. § 6.50(4). Municipal clerks discover voter deaths through 
the Commission’s registration list alerts (discussed further below), but may also 
learn this by personal knowledge in their community. See also  Wis. Stat. § 6.21 
regarding counting ballots of deceased voters.
Sec. 3.5.1: Commission Responsibilities
The Commission facilitates the exchange of information between public health 
officials and local election officials. When the Wisconsin Department of Health 
Services reports a deceased voter to the Commission, the information is relayed 
to municipal clerks through the registration list alert process. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(4).
Sec. 3.5.2: Clerk Responsibilities
Review registration list alerts regularly to identify deceased voters. Wis. Stat. § 
6.50(4). Clerks may also act independently if they receive reliable information 
from other sources that a voter has died. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(4). Registration list 
alerts are covered in Section 2.4 of the WisVote manual.
Sec. 3.5.3: Special Note: 
ERIC Death Reports
Wisconsin law requires the state to be a member of the Electronic Registration 
Information Center (ERIC). Wis. Stat. § 6.36(1)(ae)1. To identify potential deceased 
voters, ERIC obtains data from a variety of sources, such as member states and 
the Social Security Administration. ERIC provides the State of Wisconsin with a 
list of voters who may have died each month.
If a voter record identified by ERIC as deceased is not already marked as 
deceased, the Commission creates a registration list alert for the municipality. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.50(3).
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 8
Chapter 3.6: Voters Residing 
in a Condemned Structure
The law requires municipal clerks to investigate whether voters are registered 
at addresses of buildings their municipalities have condemned for human 
habitation. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(5).
Sec. 3.6.1: Commission Responsibilities
None.
Sec. 3.6.2: Clerk Responsibilities
When a municipality learns that a registered voter resides in a structure 
condemned for human habitation under Wis. Stat. § 66.0413(1)(j), the municipal 
clerk must investigate the situation to determine if the voter no longer resides at 
the address. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(5). If the voter has moved, the municipal clerk may 
change the voter record status from “Active-Registered” to “Inactive-Moved.” 
Wis. Stat. § 6.50(5). If the voter left a forwarding address with the U.S. Postal 
Service, the clerk must send a notice of change in status to the forwarding 
address provided. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(5).
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 9
Chapter 3.7: Voter Requests
Voters may voluntarily ask to be changed from active to inactive status and 
thus no longer be actively registered to vote. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(6). Such requests 
do not result in the deletion of voter information from WisVote — even inactive 
voter records must be preserved as public records. Wis. Stat. § 19.35(1)(a).
Sec. 3.7.1: Commission Responsibilities
None. When the Commission receives these requests from voters, the 
Commission directs the voters to contact their municipal clerk. Wis. Stat. § 7.15(1).
Sec. 3.7.2: Clerk Responsibilities
A clerk receiving a request for inactivation shall change the voter record from 
“Active-Registered” to “Inactive-Voter Request.” Wis. Stat. § 6.50(6). Note that, 
once inactivated, the only way for the voter to become active again is to re-
register. Wis. Stat. § 6.27.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 10
Chapter 3.8: Voters 
Adjudicated Incompetent by 
a Court
Wisconsin competency proceedings are governed by Wis. Stat. Chapter 
54 of state statutes. A person may be disqualified from voting if a court 
determines they are incapable of understanding the objective of the electoral 
process and are therefore ineligible to vote. Wis. Stat. § 6.03(1)(a). The grant 
of a guardianship order alone is not sufficient. A court must make a specific 
finding of incompetence to vote under Wis. Stat. § 54.25(2)(c)1.g. Once made, 
an incompetency determination “shall be communicated in writing by the clerk 
of court to the election official or agency charged … with the responsibility for 
determining challenges to registration and voting.” Wis. Stat. § 54.25(2)(c)1.g. 
Some county Registers in Probate choose to send a notice of such guardianship 
orders, or changes, to the Commission, while others send notice to municipal or 
county officials, and opt not to communicate with the Commission. The notice 
forms are called Notice of Voting Eligibility (NVE) forms, or GN-3180 (CCAP) forms. 
The NVE, or GN-3180, does not contain a copy of the court order itself, and only 
informs election officials that a court order exists.
Best Practice: The NVE forms contain substantively the same 
information as the court order itself, which is a confidential record 
under law. Wis. Stat. § 54.75 (“All court records pertinent to the 
finding of incompetency are closed” subject to few exceptions). 
The NVE form is exempt from disclosure under both public records 
law and Wis. Stat. § 54.75. Wisconsin Voter Alliance v. Reynolds, 
2023 WI App 66, 410 Wis. 2d 335, 1 N.W.3d 748. Once an individual 
is adjudicated incompetent to vote, their right to vote can only be 
restored by a court order. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.03(1)(a), 6.03(3), 54.25.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 11
Sec. 3.8.1: Commission Responsibilities
The Commission has no role in determining if, when, or why a court may find 
that an individual is incapable of voting. When the Commission receives 
notice from the Court System, the information provided is recorded in a small 
searchable database. A daily query compares court orders in the database 
with voter records, and possible matches result in a notice for the appropriate 
municipal clerk. Municipalities may also review the database on their own to 
identify voters in their municipality.
Sec. 3.8.2: Clerk Responsibilities
If the clerk identifies a match between a person named in a court notice and a 
voter registration record, they may change the voter record status from “Active-
Registered” to “Inactive-Incompetent.” Wis. Stat. §§ 6.03(1)(a), 7.15(1). If the clerk 
does not assess a match, then no action is taken. Adjudicated Incompetent 
recordkeeping is covered in Section 2.6 of the WisVote manual.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 12
Chapter 3.9: Voters Convicted 
of a Felony/Treason/Bribery
A person is not eligible to vote if they are convicted of a felony and still serving their 
term of imprisonment, probation, parole, or extended supervision for the crime. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.03(1)(b). The Wisconsin Department of Corrections provides felony conviction 
information to the Commission pursuant Wis. Stat. § 301.03(20m). The information is 
provided to municipalities through two processes: (1) the registration list alert process, 
and (2) the ineligible felon list. Registration list alerts are used by clerks to identify 
registered voters who have become ineligible to vote due to a felony conviction. The 
ineligible felon list is used by clerks to review new voter registration applications to 
ensure the applicant is not currently ineligible to vote. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.29(2)(am) (for 
use during late registration), 6.55(2)(cs) (for use on election day), 6.79(2)(dm) (for use 
on election day), 6.56(3m) (for use during reconciliation).
Sec. 3.9.1: Commission Responsibilities
The Commission facilitates the exchange of information between the Wisconsin 
Department of Corrections and local election officials. Information about 
felony convictions is provided to municipalities through the registration list alert 
process and the Ineligible Felon list.
Sec. 3.9.2: Clerk Responsibilities
Review registration list alerts regularly to identify ineligible voters. These voters will have 
their status changed from “Active-Registered” to “Inactive-Felon.” Wis. Stat. § 6.03(1)(b).
Best Practice: The clerk may then send notice to the voter 
using a letter template in WisVote titled “Felon Letter.” Clerks 
should review new voter registration applications against 
the Ineligible Felon List to identify applicants who may be 
ineligible due to a felony conviction. Wis. Stat. § 6.03(1)(b).
Best Practice: Clerks may call the Commission to obtain updated 
information from the Wisconsin Department of Corrections, 
particularly in situations where a person may recently have satisfied 
their sentence and regained their eligibility to vote. Registration 
list alerts are covered in Section 2.4 of the WisVote manual. The 
Ineligible list is covered in Section 4.6 of the WisVote manual.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 13
Chapter 3.10: Duplicates
Duplicate records are a common occurrence because voters who move often 
register in their new municipality without notifying their old municipality that 
they have moved. Duplicate records may also be created when a registered 
voter believes they are not registered and submits a new registration request. In 
addition to being good database management practice, reviewing the voter list 
for duplicates and resolving them is required by the federal Help America Vote 
Act (HAVA). 52 U.S.C. § 21083(2)(B)(iii). The registration list alert process identifies 
possible duplicate records. When identified, duplicate records are merged 
into the newest record. During a merge, the old record changes from “Active-
Registered” to “Inactive-Merged” status.
Sec. 3.10.1: Commission Responsibilities
The Commission provides the registration list alerts for possible duplicate records. 
Registration list alerts are covered in Section 2.4 of the WisVote manual.
Sec. 3.10.2: Clerk Responsibilities
Review registration list alerts regularly to identify duplicate records. Wis. Stat.  
§ 7.15(1). Note that possible duplicates must be reviewed by the clerk (or clerk 
staff) to confirm a duplicate exists. The automated registration list alert process 
may incorrectly identify possible duplicates because of similar names or birth 
dates. For example, junior/senior situations may sometimes trigger a false 
duplicate alert.
Sec. 3.10.3: Other Situations
The registration list maintenance processes described above represent the 
most common processes, but other situations may arise where a voter’s 
eligibility is called into question. In these other situations, the appropriate 
mechanism to review eligibility is the Wis. Stat. § 6.48  challenge process. This 
process requires both the challenger and the challenged voter to present 
evidence that establishes the voter’s eligibility or ineligibility. Municipal 
clerks are encouraged to familiarize themselves with Wis. Stat. § 6.48  before 
a challenge is presented. The standard for such challenges is beyond a 
reasonable doubt, the highest burden of proof under law. Wis. Stat. § 6.325.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 14
Chapter 3.11: OVR-DMV Check 
Process
OVR-DMV checks are required by state law to validate online voter registration 
requests. Wis. Stat. § 6.30(5). The OVR-DMV check occurs nearly instantly to 
verify that a voter’s name, date of birth, license number, and residency match 
DMV records. If the OVR-DMV check does not match, the voter is not permitted 
to register online. Therefore, all records with a source of “Online Registration” 
passed the OVR-DMV check with a 100% match.
Sec. 3.11.1: Commission Responsibilities
OVR-DMV checks occur automatically when the statewide voter registration 
system attempts to match data from voters with data from the Wisconsin 
Department of Transportation. Wisconsin law requires anyone who registers 
to vote online to correctly match four separate fields from their DMV record. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.30(5). OVR-DMV checks occur in real time, and there must be an 
exact match for the voter’s name, date of birth, DMV number and residence 
jurisdiction. This check is required for proof of residence in registration. Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.34(2m).
Sec. 3.11.2: Clerk Responsibilities
The OVR-DMV checks do not require clerk action. Online voter registration 
requests are only forwarded to clerks if the voter passed the check. Online 
Registration is covered in Section 2.7 of the WisVote manual.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 15
Chapter 3.12: HAVA-DMV 
Check Process
HAVA-DMV Checks are comparisons between a voter registration record and 
a DMV or Social Security record. The checks were created by the federal Help 
America Vote Act of 2002.2 They are designed to catch typos and data entry 
errors to improve the quality of the voter registration list. HAVA-DMV checks 
are not a list maintenance process, but they are an important tool to improve 
data quality.
Sec. 3.12.1: Commission Responsibilities
HAVA-DMV checks occur automatically for all voter registrations when the 
statewide voter registration system attempts to match data from voters with 
data from the Wisconsin Department of Transportation and the Social Security 
Administration. The checks are run in batches overnight on voters who register 
on a paper form, whether in person or by mail. This check attempts to match 
the voter’s name, date of birth and driver license (or state ID) number with WI 
DMV records once the registration information is entered into WisVote by the 
clerk. If the voter does not have a Wisconsin driver license or state ID card, the 
system tries to match the name, date of birth and the last four digits of their 
Social Security Number.
2 HAVA is the Help America Vote Act of 2002, which was passed in the wake of the problems in Florida 
following the 2000 election. Among other things, HAVA required Wisconsin to create a statewide voter 
registration database and provided funding for that system. Before 2006, when the system went online, 
Wisconsin law only required voter registration in larger cities. In smaller towns, there was no voter 
registration, just a book where poll workers would write the names of voters when they came to vote.
Section 303 of HAVA, titled “Computerized Statewide Voter Registration List Requirements and 
Requirements for Voters Who Register by Mail,” mandates the creation of a computerized list 
containing the name and registration information of every legally registered voter in the State, which 
shall serve as the official voter registration list for federal and state elections. HAVA § 303(a)(1)(A) 
codified at 52 U.S.C. § 21083(a)(1)(A). HAVA requires that individuals, upon registering to vote, provide 
a current driver license number, if they have one, or last four digits of their Social Security Number, for 
those who do not. Voters who have neither a driver license nor a Social Security Number are assigned 
a separate identification number for purposes of the official registration list. HAVA § 303(a)(5)(A) 
codified at 52 U.S.C. § 21083(a)(5)(A).
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 16
Sec. 3.12.2: Clerk Responsibilities
When the nightly DMV check identifies a mismatch, in most cases, it is the result 
of errors. The most common error (63%) is a mismatched name, often due to 
misspelling, name variation (Bob instead of Robert), nickname or a missing 
suffix missing (Jr. or Sr.). The next most common error (22%) is a driver license 
or state ID number mismatch. Wisconsin DMV numbers have one letter and 13 
digits, and non-matches often result from writing the number incorrectly on 
the voter registration form or entering it incorrectly in the voter database. Other 
innocent reasons for mismatches include typos in the data. For example, one 
voter registered at the polling place on Aug. 11, 2020. The clerk inadvertently 
recorded the voter’s birth date as July 5, 1990, instead of July 15, 1990, resulting in 
a non-match.
When there is a non-match, a registered voter is never “removed” from the 
statewide voter database. Neither Wisconsin nor federal law requires a match, 
and Wisconsin law does not permit clerks or the Commission to remove a voter 
from the list for not matching.3
Instead, the voter’s record is flagged in the statewide voter database for clerks 
to review, and the clerk receives a DMV Check alert. Clerks are asked to review 
non-matches to ensure a data entry error was not responsible for the non-
match result. Clerks often can identify data entry errors but should also attempt 
to contact voters whose non-matches they cannot resolve. WisVote provides 
a standardized letter for voters called a “DMV Check Non-Match Letter.” DMV 
Checks are covered in Section 2.5 of the WisVote manual.
3 The issue of what happens with a HAVA Check mismatch was extensively litigated in 2008 when 
the Wisconsin Attorney General sued the Government Accountability Board (The Commission’s 
predecessor agency). In J.B. Van Hollen et. al v. Government Accountability Board et. al, the court 
found that none of the provisions of HAVA affect the fundamental voter eligibility qualifications. HAVA 
establishes no additional voter qualifications, except in the limited case of a first-time voter who 
registered by mail and who must either provide a photo identification or current proof of residence, or 
else must vote by provisional ballot. A successful HAVA match eliminates this additional requirement.
The court further determined that HAVA does not mandate the imposition of a consequence or penalty 
for a voter whose voter registration data does not precisely match information contained in the DOT or 
SSA databases. The HAVA match process also does not alter the voter eligibility requirements established 
by state law. The court ultimately concluded that HAVA Checks are intended to assist in improving the 
quality of voter data in the State’s official voter registration list on an ongoing basis, not to convert an 
otherwise qualified voter into an ineligible voter. The GAB adopted the court’s findings on Jan. 15, 2009. 
J.B. Van Hollen et. al v. Government Accountability Board et. al, Dane County Court Case 08CV4085
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 17
Chapter 3.13: Special Notes 
for Reliers4
Best Practices: While WisVote reliers may not perform the processes 
described above in WisVote, they are responsible for ensuring 
compliance with the law and should be familiar with the nature of each 
process. Clerks who do not use WisVote should still ask their Provider to 
share relevant information about these processes (for example, their 
registration list alerts). Better still, relier clerks may ask their Providers 
to show them the various processes in WisVote so as to better 
appreciate the actual work that must be performed. Reliers seeking 
information about any of the processes described in this manual are 
encouraged to contact the WEC Help Desk at elections@wi.gov.
4 A note about providers and reliers: Sometimes, a municipal clerk (a relier) enters into agreement 
with another clerk (a provider) for the provider to complete WisVote work on the relier’s behalf. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.33(5)(b). The provider can be either a county clerk or another municipal clerk. Reliers and 
providers enter into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) that governs how the data entry and list 
maintenance work will be covered between them.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter List Maintenance 3 – 18


Part 4 
Election Notices
Type A; Type B; Type C; Type D; Type E; Publication 
Procedures; Frequently Asked Questions
An election notice is a statutorily required posting containing specific 
information relating to each election. The Type A notice gives the basic 
information of the upcoming election, including the date, offices to be 
elected, and filing deadlines to get on the ballot. The Type B notice provides 
voting instructions for the ballot format and equipment to be used at the 
election. The Type C notice is used when there are referendum questions on 
the ballot, and provides the question and a statement explaining the effects 
of a “yes” and “no” votes. The Type D notice provides polling place locations 
and hours. The Type E notice is specific to absentee voting and also contains 
the office hours and location(s) for in-person absentee voting.
First Edition, June 2026 Election Notices 4 – 1
Chapter 4.1: Summary
County, municipal, and school district clerks are responsible 
for publishing five basic election notices:
 Ɋ Type A: Notice of Election
 Ɋ Type B: Sample Ballot and Voting Instruction Notice
 Ɋ Type C: Notice of Referendum
 Ɋ Type D: Polling Place Location and Hours Notice
 Ɋ Type E: Absentee Voting Notice
Best Practice: Sample election notices can be found on elctions.
wi.gov. These samples require modification based on offices up 
for election and voting equipment used in the municipality.
Additionally, Wisconsin law requires that meetings of all state and local 
governmental bodies, including governmental sub-units, shall be publicly 
noticed, held in places reasonably accessible to members of the public, and 
shall be open to all citizens at all times unless otherwise expressly provided 
by law. Wis. Stat. § 19.84. Election-related meetings such as the Board of 
Canvassers, voting equipment testing, post-election audits, etc., fall under this 
requirement, and the municipal clerk must properly notice such meetings. 
Please consult with a municipal attorney with specific questions about 
requirements for open meetings notices.

Combining Type B Notices & Costs
If the ballots in the wards or election districts within a county or municipality 
are identical except for the names of different candidates, districts or seats, 
the sample ballot may show the ballot for one ward or election district, 
accompanied by a list of candidates, districts and seats to be voted upon in the 
other wards or election districts, Wis. Stat. § 10.02(2)(c).
Best Practice: Notices may be combined under Wis. Stat. § 10.07:

portion of a notice under this chapter on the same date in the same 
newspaper, the text of which is identical, the clerks may publish one 
notice only. The cost of publication of such notice or the portion of 
the notice required shall be apportioned equally between the county 
and each municipality or school district sharing in its publication.
(2) When a voting machine ballot or ballot to be used 
with an electronic voting system includes 2 or more 
levels of government, the cost for publishing the type B 
notice shall be prorated under Wis Stat. § 5.68(3).”

Note about IPAV on the Type E
In-person absentee voting may begin “no earlier than 14 days preceding the 
election and no later than the Sunday preceding the election.” Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)
(b). The hours when in-person absentee is available in the clerk’s office or 
alternate site must be listed on the Type E notice. Wis. Stat. § 10.01(2)(e). The hours 
may be the same each day or vary from day to day. The municipal clerk may 
not conduct absentee voting outside of the hours listed in the Type E Notice. If 
in-person voting will be “by appointment,” the Type E Notice must specify when 
the clerk will be available for appointments.

Chapter 4.3: Newspaper 
Publication Procedures
Election notices must be published in the newspapers designated for the 
municipality and qualifying under Ch. 985 unless an exception applies.  
Wis. Stat. §§ 10.04  and 10.05.
County clerks must publish notices in all newspapers unless the county 
board provides otherwise by resolution. Wis. Stat. § 10.04(2)(a). In counties with 
populations over 200,000, whenever there is a requirement to publish more than 
one insertion, a jurisdiction may accomplish it by “publication in one or more 
newspapers on the dates prescribed or in different newspapers at least equal 
in number to the number of insertions required. When different newspapers 
are used, the publications shall always be in each newspaper’s latest issue 
preceding the last given date for publishing that notice.” Wis. Stat. § 10.04(3)(b).
If a weekly newspaper is designated, the notice must be published in the 
closest preceding issue to the required publication date. Wis. Stat. § 10.04(3)(a). 
When the publication date is the day before an election, a county or municipal 
clerk can determine that, due to the method of delivering newspapers in the 
municipality, more effective notice will be provided by an earlier publication; the 
clerk may publish the notice no more than three days before the election. Id.
The board of election commissioners or governing body of a municipality can, by 
resolution, decide to publish in more than one newspaper. Wis. Stat. § 10.04(2)(b).
Posting in Lieu of Publication is governed by Wis. Stat. § 10.05, which explains 
that: “Towns, villages, and school districts may post election notices in lieu of 
publication whenever there is not a newspaper published within the respective 
jurisdiction.”
 Ɋ Only the governing body can change between posting and newspaper 
publication, and, if it changes manner of notices, a notice must be given in 
the current manner before it can take place.
 Ɋ The same manner of notification must be used for all notices pertaining 
to an election.
First Edition, June 2026 Election Notices 4 – 9
 Ɋ Posting must be done in at least three conspicuous locations within 
the municipality. It is also possible under Wis. Stat. §§ 985.02(2)(a) and 
985.05(1) to post in one location within the municipality and on the 
municipality’s website.
 Ɋ For notices required to be published within one week of the primary or 
election (Types B, C, and D), posting must be done at least one week 
before the election. For all other notices (Type A and E), posting must be 
done no later than the required publication dates.
 Ɋ Posting may also be done to supplement publication.
Best Practices: If clerks add notice information into MyVote, such as the 
Type D and Type E, they will need to make sure to keep that updated 
for voters to ensure they are supplied with accurate information. 
Please note that any notices that are posted physically should be in 
18-point font or larger. The Commission also strongly recommends 
always posting notices to the municipal or school district website 
regardless of whether posting or newspaper publishing is used.
First Edition, June 2026 Election Notices 4 – 10
Chapter 4.4: Frequently 
Asked Questions
Q When can jurisdictions combine their notices to save on printing costs?
A Jurisdictions may combine their notices if the information on the notice 
is identical and when the levels of government share the same official 
newspaper. For example, only one Type B notice with sample ballots for 
each type of equipment, along with a list of candidates, districts and seats 
to be voted on in each municipality, needs to be published.
Q Who writes the explanatory statements for referendum questions?
A For statewide referenda, the explanatory statement is prepared by the 
Attorney General. For county questions, the statement is prepared by 
the county’s corporation counsel, and for municipal or school district 
referenda, the statement is prepared by the attorney representing the 
jurisdiction. Wis. Stat. § 10.01(2)(c).
Q What should a municipal clerk do if they miss a publication date for a 
notice or their newspaper of record makes an error?
A Clerks should attempt to fix any errors as soon as possible through an 
amended notice. If a periodic newspaper makes an error, it may not be 
possible to submit a timely correction. In this situation, municipal clerks 
should post the notice on their website, in their office, and anywhere else 
that may provide voters with needed information.
Q If an officeholder was appointed to finish a term, should they still be listed 
as an incumbent on the notice?
A Yes.
Q We accidentally published the notice early. Do we have to publish again?
A Yes. The notice needs to be published on the date designated by statute 
or as close to that date as possible.
First Edition, June 2026 Election Notices 4 – 11

Part 5 
Ballots
Ballot Procedures; Ballot Format and Style; A/B Ballots; 
Referendum Ballots; Presidential-Only Ballots; Sample Ballots
There are a variety of different ballot styles used in Wisconsin. Designing, 
creating, printing, and distributing ballots is a multi-step process in which 
the WEC, county clerks, and municipal clerks all play a role. Ballots must be 
formatted in specific ways. The law permits specialty ballot types for certain 
types of voters. Ballots are designed and printed to be used with all certified 
electronic voting systems.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 1
Chapter 5.1: Ballot Creation 
Procedures
Ballot creation, review, and printing is a multi-step process in which the 
Commission, county clerks, and municipal clerks all play an important role. This 
chapter will discuss the different types of ballot formats used across the state, 
as well as will outline the seven-step process by which ballots are created.
Sec. 5.1.1: Types of Ballots
There are three different ballot types in use in Wisconsin, depending 
on the type of ballot marking and tabulation system that is in use: 
 Ɋ Optical scan ballots
 Ɋ Direct recording electronic (DRE) ballots
 Ɋ Paper (hand-counted) ballots.
Some jurisdictions use separate ballots for different races, but most use 
consolidated, single ballots that contain all races for all jurisdictions. Wis. Stat. 
§ 5.655(1).
Optical Scan Ballots
 Most Wisconsin jurisdictions use optical scan ballots, in which voters mark their 
choices on a paper ballot by filling in an oval or completing an arrow in specific 
locations. An optical scan, electronic tabulator then reads the marks on the 
paper ballot to record the vote. Over 80 percent of the ballots cast in Wisconsin 
are optical scan ballots.
Direct Recording-Electronic (DRE) Ballot
Jurisdictions that use direct recording equipment (DRE) allow voters to mark 
their choices on a screen or interface, and those choices are then printed on 
a specially-formatted paper ballot that is inserted into the tabulator. With 
DRE technology, like optical scan, the voter is able to verify how they voted by 
reviewing that the paper ballot is marked as they intended before the vote is 
tabulated. It’s estimated that about 10 percent of ballots cast in Wisconsin use 
DRE technology.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 2
Paper (Hand-Counted) Ballots
And finally, some jurisdictions hand-count ballots. In these municipalities, voters 
use a paper ballot where a voter completes a box with an “X” for their choices 
and the votes are tabulated by the poll workers. State law only allows small 
jurisdictions, under 7,500 in population, to opt to use hand count ballots. All 
other jurisdictions are required to use electronic tabulation equipment. Wis. Stat. 
§ 5.40. All jurisdictions are required to offer electronic, accessible ballot marking 
devices. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(a). 52 U.S.C. § 21081(a)(3)(A) (HAVA provision requiring 
accessibility). See Sec. 11.3.4: “Marking a Ballot”.
Sec. 5.1.2: Planning & Ordering Ballots: 
Turnout & Timelines
Before ballots are constructed, proofed, ordered, or printed, it is important that 
clerks understand how many ballots they will need, and when they need to be 
sent out.
Predicting Turnout & How Many Ballots to Order
County clerks are responsible for ordering enough ballots to be printed for each 
of their municipalities. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.66(1); 7.10(1)(a). Municipal clerks are required 
to certify to the county clerk the approximate number of electors in their 
municipality no later than the first day of the second month before a primary. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.66(1).1 This number is used by the county clerk to determine the 
number of ballots to print for the election.
Best Practice: Municipal clerks should also plan to give their 
county clerks updated estimates ahead of general elections, 
especially in high turnout years where there may be large voter 
registration drives between the primary and the general election.
1 The statute only references the primary election, and doesn’t clarify whether municipal clerks should 
provide updated data to their county clerks ahead of the general election. In practice, most county 
clerks reach out to their municipalities ahead of the general to ask them to confirm an estimate. See 
the “Best Practice” on the next page.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 3
In municipalities that use direct recording electronic (DRE) equipment, the clerk 
must ensure that sufficient paper ballots are provided in case of equipment 
malfunction and to accommodate absentee ballot requests, assisted voters, 
and any other person who may request a paper ballot. Municipalities using 
DREs should also ensure that all machines have a full roll of paper and that 
there are paper rolls in reserve should they be needed.
Best Practice: Anticipated turnout can be challenging to predict, 
but before each election, clerks should consider past turnout 
as well as special considerations depending on what races are 
on the ballot. Ideally, clerks should always plan for one hundred 
percent turnout to ensure they don’t run out of ballots, but this 
is not always realistic given the cost. Past turnout is usually 
a good measure of future turnout, with a few exceptions.
First, in recent years, statewide races have generated high 
interest with voters, leading to higher-than-usual turnout at 
the Spring Election. State supreme court races, particularly 
when the outcome of the race will change the ideological 
makeup of the court, will likely mean higher voter turnout.
Second, at times, local races can also generate intense voter interest 
at the Spring Election. This can also occur when the Presidential 
Preference vote occurs during the Spring Election, or if a particular 
Partisan Primary in August is driving a lot of voter engagement. 
Likewise, statewide referenda can appear on Election Days 
that are typically low turnout, so it is important to keep all 
of these possibilities in mind when ordering ballots. 
If a clerk is unsure of how many ballots to order, they can contact 
the Commission for help analyzing past turnout data.
Important: Clerks should always assume that they have 
underestimated voter turnout. It is better to have extra ballots that are 
not used than to scramble on Election Day because polling places are 
running low or running out of ballots.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 4
Ballot Deadlines
State and federal law have specific deadlines for when absentee ballots must 
be sent to military and overseas voters (UOCAVA), as well as all other voters with 
absentee requests on file. There are also deadlines for when county clerks must 
deliver ballot materials to municipal clerks ahead of each election. These deadlines 
often result in an extremely tight window (between 1-3 weeks) for clerks to arrange, 
proof, order, print, and finalize their ballots before they must go out to voters. The 
following chart illustrates these deadlines, along with example election dates to 
illustrate how these deadlines fit together.2
Important: County clerks must be aware of absentee ballot delivery 
deadlines to ensure that they order and print their ballots on time. 
Refer to the chart below for the applicable deadlines.

Sec. 5.1.3: Creation of a Ballot: Overview
The Commission, county clerks, and municipal clerks all have statutory 
responsibilities in creating the official ballots. The following sections explain that 
process, starting with the Commission’s approval of the ballot templates ahead 
of each election.
 Ɋ Step 1: Commission Approves Ballot Templates
 Ɋ Step 2: Ballot Order Determined & Candidates Added
 Ɋ Step 3: County Clerks Add Candidates for Local Races
 Ɋ Step 4: Ballots are Reviewed & Proofed
 Ɋ Step 5: County Clerks Print & Review Ballots
 Ɋ Step 6: County Clerk Distributes Ballots to Municipalities
 Ɋ Step 7: Municipal Clerks Review & Proof Ballots
Note: Wisconsin law does not permit third party vendors to design or 
arrange ballots. Wis. Stat. § 7.08(1)(a).
Sec. 5.1.4: Step 1: Commission 
Approves Ballot Templates
Ahead of each election, the Commission approves the templates of the ballots 
that will be used across the state during the election. Wis. Stat. § 7.08(1)(a). The 
templates approved by the Commission do not have candidate names or the 
specifics of contests, but they do provide the look, feel, and format of each 
type of ballot. For instance, the Commission establishes the columns, spacing, 
and the appearances of lines and stylistic elements that separate contests on 
the ballot. The ballot templates contain spaces for all offices that could have 
candidates for the upcoming election. The ballot templates are approved by 
the Commission during a public meeting, usually three months ahead of each 
election. Wis. Stat. §§ 7.08(1)(a), 5.05(1e).
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 7
The Commission’s purpose in designing and approving ballot templates is 
twofold: 1) to ensure that all ballots used statewide conform to the specific 
layout and design components that are required by law; and 2) to ensure that 
the offices are listed in the correct, or suggested, order for all jurisdictions. Wis. 
Stat. §§ 5.51; 5.58, 5.60, 5.62, 5.64, and 5.65.
The format of all ballots in use in Wisconsin must conform to the templates that 
are approved by the Commission. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.51(6) and (8), 7.08(1)(a). See Sec. 
11.3.4: “Marking a Ballot” for specific information on the style and formatting 
requirements for ballots.
When the Commission approves ballot templates, it also sets the order of 
offices (not candidate names) on the ballot. Generally speaking, federal 
contests appear first, then statewide, then county, and then local.
Office Order for Nonpartisan Spring Election Ballots
Nonpartisan Elections occur in the spring of each year. The ballots for a 
nonpartisan spring election or primary are different from the partisan elections 
in the fall as the contests and candidates are not differentiated by political 
parties. Spring nonpartisan election ballots typically contain more contests 
than partisan elections as most municipal, county, and judicial races are 
nonpartisan.
Best Practice: State law does not specify the order of the offices on 
nonpartisan ballots. The Commission’s consistent practice is to list 
the offices in the following order: state, judicial, county, municipal, 
school district, and referendum. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(3), 5.60. In a 
Presidential Preference Vote year, that “office” will always appear 
as the first contest on the Nonpartisan Spring Election ballot.6
6 In the Presidential Preference Vote, the party receiving the greatest number of votes for governor at the 
preceding election has its presidential candidates listed first, and the remaining parties proceed in the 
same manner. Wis. Stat. § 5.60(8)(am), (c). Within each party, the order of presidential candidates on the 
Spring Election ballot is determined by the drawing of lots by the Commission. Wis. Stat. § 5.60(8)(am).
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 8
Office Order for Partisan Primary Election Ballots
The partisan primary ballot is organized by political party. Wis. Stat. § 5.62(1)(a). 
The political party whose candidate received the most votes for president or 
governor at the last election is listed first, and the other parties are arranged 
in descending order based on their votes for president or governor. Wis. Stat. 
§ 5.62(1)(a). After those parties, the political parties with ballot status are 
listed next. Wis. Stat. § 5.62(1)(a) and (b). In the partisan primary, the offices 
for each political party are listed in the following order for each political party 
participating in the primary: governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, 
secretary of state, state treasurer, U.S. senator, U.S. representative in congress, 
state senator, representative to the assembly, district attorney, and county 
offices. Wis. Stat. § 5.62(3).
Office Order for Partisan General Election Ballots
The office order for the general election ballot is the same as the partisan 
primary except the ballot is no longer organized by political party.
Sec. 5.1.5: Step 2: Ballot Order 
Determined & Candidates Added
After the ballot templates have been approved by the Commission, the next 
step is adding and arranging the names of the candidates who qualified for 
ballot access.
While the ballot templates are approved a few months prior to each election, 
the candidate order cannot be determined until the candidates are certified, 
which occurs after the ballot access challenge period following the filing 
deadline.
Certifying Candidates to Appear on the Ballot
Before the filing officer can determine the order of candidate names on 
the ballot, candidates must first be certified, meaning the filing officer has 
determined they meet the requirements to be granted access to the ballot. See 
Chapter 2.1: “Qualifications for Office” for more information on ballot access.
Note: Municipal and school district clerks use form EL-405 Certificate of 
Nomination to certify candidates and referenda to their county clerks. 
The form is available on elections.wi.gov and in the appendix.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 9
Where a caucus is held, the names of candidates must be certified to the 
county clerk as soon as possible following the qualification of candidates, but 
no later than the 3rd day after qualification of candidates. Wis. Stat. § 8.05(1)(j)4.
After any primary, the names of candidates advancing must again be certified 
to the county clerk as soon as possible after the canvass, but no later than the 
third day after completion of the municipal or school district canvass. Wis. Stat. 
§ 5.60(1)(b), (5), (6).
The municipal and school district clerks must certify any names of candidates 
and any referenda to the county clerk as soon as possible following the 
deadline for filing nomination papers or declarations of candidacy, but no later 
than the deadline for drawing for ballot order. Wis. Stat §§ 5.58, 5.60.
The filing officer for each office is responsible for determining the order and 
arrangement of candidate names This means that the Commission determines 
the candidate order of some races on the ballot, and the county, municipal, 
and school district clerks determine the candidate name order of their races. 
Candidate order is completed after the filing officer certifies candidates to the 
ballot and before the Type B notice is issued. With a few exceptions (such as 
offices like U.S. president where candidate name order is based on votes share 
of the candidate’s party in the last general election), candidate name order on 
the ballot is completed by random draw.
Recommended Procedures for Random Draw
Best Practice: The statutes that refer to random draw use the phrases 
like “drawing lots.” Any purely random process satisfies these 
requirements, including drawing names out of a hat or container, or 
flipping a coin if there are only two candidates to be arranged. It is 
not necessary for candidates to be present at the drawing, but as a 
courtesy they may be invited to attend. If all candidates are present, 
they may draw for themselves. Drawing of lots is not required to be 
done at a board meeting and should not be delayed for this reason.
When conducting the drawing of lots for placement of names on the ballot, the 
Commission recommends that at least three people participate in the drawing, the 
policy used by the Commission. The three people are generally the clerk and two 
other people selected by the clerk. The drawing should be properly documented.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 10
This can be achieved by making a video recording of the ballot draw (the practice 
used by the Commission) or by recording minutes. Documentation is important 
in case a candidate later contests the order of their name on the ballot. The 
documentation should include the date of the drawing for ballot order, the ballot 
order drawn, the signature of the people who actually drew out the names, and 
the signature of the two people who witnessed the drawing.
Candidate Order for Nonpartisan Spring Election Ballots
The Commission determines the order of the arrangement of candidate 
names for state superintendent of public instruction, Wisconsin supreme court 
justice, court of appeals judge, and circuit court judges. Wis. Stat. § 5.58(2). The 
Commission also determines the order of metropolitan sewerage commissioners. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.60(1)(b). The Commission determines the order of these candidates 
by drawing lots no later than the second Tuesday in January, or the next day if 
the first Tuesday is a state holiday. Wis. Stat. § 5.60(1)(b). Once the Commission 
certifies its candidates and determines candidate order, it publishes the Type B 
notice and transmits the candidate list to county clerks. Wis. Stat. § 10.06(1)(c), (e).
The city clerk or executive director of the city election commission arranges city 
candidates, also by random draw. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.60(3)(ag) , 5.62(4). School district 
candidate arrangement is determined by the school district clerk or the executive 
director of the city board of election commissioners, also by random draw. Wis. 
Stat. § 5.60(4)(c). Candidates for village and town offices are likewise arranged by 
random draw by the municipal clerk. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.60(5)(ar); 5.60(6)(a); 5.60(1)(b).
For a spring election, drawing of lots is held not later than seven days after the 
deadline for filing nomination papers. Wis. Stat. § 5.58. The drawing is done at this 
time for those offices requiring a primary and also for the election ballot for those 
offices where a primary is not required. Following the primary for any office, the 
names are of those advancing are redrawn for that office to determine the order 
of names on the election ballot. Wis. Stat. § 5.60(1)(b), (5), (6).
Where the caucus procedure is used for nominating candidates for municipal 
office, the drawing is held no later than the end of the third day following 
qualification of all candidates. Wis. Stat. § 8.05(1)(j)4. See Chapter 2.4: 
“Nomination by Caucus” for more information on Caucus procedure.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 11
Candidate Order for Partisan Primary & General Election Ballots
The Commission determines the candidate order for statewide offices and district 
attorney races by random draw. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.62(3); 5.60(1)(b). The county clerk or 
county board of election commissioners determines the ballot arrangement for 
county offices by random draw. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.62(4)(ag); 5.60(1)(b).
In the general election, partisan races will appear on the official ballot in 
the following order: president and vice president, statewide offices, federal 
congressional offices, state legislative offices, district attorneys, county offices, 
and county referendum. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.64(1)(d), 5.62(3).
Presidential and vice-presidential candidates are listed in the order in which their 
respective parties received votes in the gubernatorial race preceding the election, 
with the party with the most votes having the first position. Wis. Stat. § 5.64(1)(es). 
Independent presidential candidates are determined by random draw by the 
commission and appear after the ballot status candidates. Wis. Stat. § 5.64(1)(es).
Best Practice: For a fall election, the county clerk (for county 
offices) and Commission (for federal and state offices) draw for 
ballot order for the primary ballot not later than seven days after 
the deadline for filing nomination papers. Wis. Stat. § 5.62(1)(a).
Sec. 5.1.6: Step 3: County Clerks 
Add Candidates for Local Races
In addition to inputting candidate names to program their ballots, County and 
local clerks also enter information about local contests into WisVote.
Clerks can use reports from WisVote to determine which contests and candidates 
should appear on each ballot style. These documents provide the basis for the 
county clerks to begin the process of preparing the ballots. Wis. Stat. § 7.10(1)(a).
Important: Remember to use new WisVote reports not reports from 
previous elections!
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 12
County clerks construct a ballot style for each of their municipalities for all 
local contests. Wis. Stat. § 7.10(1)(a). Depending on the districts and wards on 
the ballot for the election, a county could have hundreds of ballot styles to 
construct for their municipalities. The county clerks use resources available 
from the Commission, from their own office as filing officer for county races, 
and information from their municipal and school district clerks to ensure that 
each ballot style has the correct districts, wards, contests, and candidates. Wis. 
Stat. § 7.10(1)(a). County clerks also ensure that the instructions are correct (such 
as vote for no more than 2 candidates), that candidates’ names are spelled 
correctly, and that referenda are displayed correctly. Wis. Stat. § 7.10(1)(a).
Best Practice: County clerks should compare their constructed 
ballots to the reports generated from WisVote twice: once as the 
ballot is being prepared and again when the proofs and printed 
copies are received. County clerks should pay special attention 
to making sure that each of the contests, and the candidates 
in them, appear in the correct ballot style. See Sec. 5.1.7: “Step 
4: Ballots are Reviewed and Proofed” on page 1414.
Exceptions to County Clerk Preparation of Ballots
Municipalities with populations over 500,000 may prepare their own official and 
sample ballots. Wis. Stat. § 7.15(2)(b). All other municipalities may prepare their 
own ballots with the consent of their county clerk wherever voting machines or 
electronic voting equipment are used, and whenever the election contains local 
races in addition to national, state, and county offices. Wis. Stat. § 7.15(2)(c).
Important: If a municipality chooses this option and obtains consent, 
then they are taking on all of the statutory responsibilities of the 
county in proofing and preparing ballots as described above.
The Commission recommends generating and using the District Combo 
Compare report and the Contests reports. Previous reports may not contain 
critical updated information, such as changes in boundaries of legislative 
districts, that have occurred more recently.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 13
Sec. 5.1.7: Step 4: Ballots are 
Reviewed and Proofed
Once candidate order is determined for all federal, statewide, county, and 
local races, and once those names are arranged properly on the ballots, 
county clerks begin the process of reviewing and proofing. Wis. Stat. § 7.10(1)
(a). County clerks should review the ballot periodically as it is being prepared, 
and again, in detail, once they receive the prepared proof back before placing 
their print order.
Ballot Proofing Best Practices
Additionally, every step of ballot proofing should 
review at least the following aspects:
 Ɋ The ballot used is the current form
 Ɋ The ballot contains all and only the offices up for election
 Ɋ All office titles are correct, spelled correctly, and in the correct order
 Ɋ All candidates’ names are spelled correctly and are in the correct order
 Ɋ The form of each candidate’s name reflects the candidate’s desire as 
indicated on the Declaration of Candidacy. Wis. § Stat. 8.21(3).
 Ɋ On optical scan ballots, the candidate names are justified so that the 
names are closest to the oval or arrow.
 Ɋ The number of write-in lines is equal to the “Vote for…” number.
Commission Review of Ballot Proofs
County clerks are required to submit one proof of each of their ballot formats to 
the Commission for review. Wis. Stat. § 5.72(1). The proofs should be submitted 
to the Commission as soon as possible but no later than 3 weeks before the 
election. This means if a county has municipalities who use optical scan 
equipment and hand count, the county should submit to the Commission an 
example of an optical scan ballot and a hand count ballot. County clerks do not 
need to send individual ballot styles (each possible combination of contests 
and candidates) to the Commission to proof.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 14
The Commission reviews the proofs and notifies the clerks of any errors as 
soon as possible, but no later than 7 days after submission. Wis. Stat. § 5.72(2). 
The Commission will proof the format to ensure that the structure of the ballot 
complies with what was approved by the Commission. Wis. Stat. § 7.10(1)(a).
Note: The Commission does not proof ballot styles for correct local 
contests, candidates, or things like spelling of names or referenda. If 
Commission staff notice an error like this in review, they will alert the 
clerk, but clerks should not expect this to be part of the Commission’s 
facial review process.
Best Practice: The Commission encourages county clerks to 
work with each of their municipalities and school district clerks 
during the ballot proofing and review stage. Before ballots go 
to print, it’s a best practice to have municipalities proof each of 
their ballot styles to ensure all ballot styles are included, and 
that all contests and candidates are displayed correctly.
Note: It is recommended that the county clerk also proof the final 
product as soon as they receive it from the printer so that any errors 
can be identified and corrected immediately
Sec. 5.1.8: Step 5: County Clerk 
Distributes Ballots to Municipalities
For an election or primary that contains a contest for a federal office, such as 
President of the United States or Representative to Congress, state law requires 
county clerks to distribute ballots to their municipal clerks no later than the 
48th day before the election or primary. Wis. Stat. § 7.10(3). For elections or 
primaries with only state or local level contests, state law requires county clerks 
to distribute ballots to their municipal clerks no later than 22 days before the 
election or primary. Wis. Stat. § 7.10(3).
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 15
Best Practice: When county clerks distribute ballots to municipalities, 
it is a good idea to get the “sign off” of each municipal clerk. This could 
be requiring a signed or emailed acknowledgment that the ballots 
were received timely and that the municipal clerk has reviewed the 
ballots they received and acknowledges that they are accurate.
Sec. 5.1.9: Step 6: Municipal 
Clerks Review & Proof Ballots
There are some best practices that municipalities should consider so they 
can ensure that voters receive the correct ballots. Counties will likely ask 
municipalities to review an electronic proof of the ballots before they go to print, 
but a second review should be completed when the ballots are delivered as 
well. Municipal clerks are often most familiar with the nuances of their districts, 
wards, and candidates, so they play an important role in ensuring ballots are 
correct.
Upon taking custody of the ballots from the county clerk, check each ballot 
style to ensure all contests and candidates are correct. Municipal clerks can 
rely on deputy clerk staff or experienced poll workers to help proof their ballots. 
The Commission provides reports that the municipality can use to assist with 
this proofing. Municipal clerks should use these reports, along with their own 
information about local races, to make sure that all of the information is correct.
Best Practice: Clerks should use the mandatory public test of 
voting equipment as another opportunity to review the ballot 
styles to catch any errors or mistakes that may have been missed. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.84(1). While this is too late to catch errors that were 
made on absentee ballots, it is an important time for municipal 
clerks to ensure that their ballots and their voting equipment is 
accurately reflecting contests and candidates before Election Day. 
If there is an error identified during the public test, it should be 
escalated to the county clerk and the Commission immediately.
