Chapter 5.2: Ballot Format & 
Style
Before preparing any ballots, the clerk must ensure they are working from the 
Commission’s most recently approved ballot templates. Using outdated ballot 
templates may result in missing required changes to statutory language 
or failure to meet ballot uniformity standards. The Commission approves 
the ballot templates ahead of each election cycle, which are available on 
elections.wi.gov. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.51, 7.08. See Sec. 5.1.4: “Step 1: Commission 
Approves Ballot Templates” on page 7 for more information on ballot 
template approval.
The ballot templates provided on elections.wi.gov contain virtually all 
offices (but not candidates) that could appear on each ballot. As such, it is 
important for clerks to confirm that only the offices up for election appear on 
their ballots, so they will need to modify the existing templates to eliminate 
any office from the ballot that is not up for election or add any offices that 
may be up for election that may be missing from the template ballot. 
Wis. Stat. §§ 5.51(6); 7.15(1)(c).
Sec. 5.2.1: Ballot Formatting
There are several basic requirements that apply to the preparation of all ballots, 
regardless of the type of election. These requirements are set out below.
Size
Ballot size depends on the number of offices and candidates that must be 
included. There is no actual size requirement for a ballot, but all ballots must be 
of sufficient width and length to provide space for all required information to 
be clearly printed on them. Wis. Stat. § 5.51(3). For jurisdictions that use a hand-
count paper ballot for partisan primary elections, each separate party ballot 
must be the same size. Wis. Stat. § 5.51(3), (6).
Columns
All ballot columns must be separated by lines at least one-eighth inch (1/8”) 
wide, except for ballots used with an electronic voting system. Wis. Stat. § 5.51(3).
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 18
Type Face
Ballots must use a clear, easy-to-read type face. Wis. Stat. § 5.51(1). The 
Commission has interpreted “easy to read type face” as follows:
 Ɋ The font is sans-serif font (Arial).
 Ɋ Except for certain headings, all print should be in mixed case. In no case 
should the font size be smaller than 8 point.
 Ɋ A sample of 8-point font is given below. Larger print should be used 
whenever possible.
8 POINT – 3.2 characters per pica
ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz
1234567890
Justification
Paragraphs, office titles, districts, candidate names, and “vote for” instructions 
should be left-justified. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.51(3); 5.56, 7.08.
Date
The date of the election must appear on the face of the ballot beneath the title 
of the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 5.55.
Paper Weight
Wisconsin statutes set a standard weight for hand-counted paper ballots: 35 
pounds per ream of 24” by 36” sheets. Wis. Stat. § 5.51(2).
Ballots will never be that large, so the paper weight must be proportionately 
equivalent. Clerks should work with their printer to ensure this requirement is 
being met. Clerks should contact the Commission if their printer has questions 
about how to properly fulfill ballot printing orders.
Paper Color
Statute does not require ballots to be a specific color (though the color of each 
ballot type must be uniform), and different colors may be used for each ballot 
type in an election. Wis. Stat. § 5.51(5).
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 19
The only legal requirements concerning the color of ballots are:
 Ɋ Paper hand-count referendum ballots must be printed on paper of a color 
that is different from other ballots used at the election. Wis. Stat. § 5.51(5).
 Ɋ At a partisan primary, paper hand-count ballots for each separate party must 
be printed on the same color paper and be the same size. Wis. Stat. §5.51(7)
 Ɋ Sample ballots cannot be the same color as the official ballots and 
cannot be white. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.51(7), 5.66(2).
Best Practices: When to Use Ballot Color Coding
Using different colors to distinguish one type of paper (hand 
count) ballot from another (federal, state, county ballots, 
municipal ballots, school district ballots, and referendum 
ballots) helps to ensure that the inspectors give one of each 
type of ballot to the voter. Wis. Stat. § 5.51(5). A block of color is 
sufficient, the ballot need not be printed on a full page of color.
Color coding is particularly helpful when two reporting units share 
a single polling place and can prevent mix-ups in shared polling 
places. Color coding makes it easier for the voter to deposit his 
or her ballot in the proper ballot box and also makes separating 
and counting of ballots much easier for the election inspectors.
Color coding can also be used to distinguish between ballots 
if the municipality uses optical scan equipment.
For example, ballots containing School District A offices and/
or referenda could be a different color than the ballots 
containing School District B offices and/or referenda.
Using different color-coded ballots requires coordination 
among county, municipal, and school district clerks to ensure 
that the ballot prepared by each clerk is of a different color.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 20
Note: Within WisVote, each ballot style can be given its own specific 
name, which appears next to the voter’s name on the poll list. For 
example, a ballot style for a certain school district can be named 
“green” to match the color of the ballot for that school district. This 
helps election workers to quickly identify which type of ballot to give to 
the voter.
Sec. 5.2.2: Write-in Lines, 
Boxes, & Ovals
The ballot must contain a number of write-in lines equal to the number of 
candidates to be elected for each office. This is true for both primaries and 
elections.1 See Chapter 14.21: “Write-In Votes”
For Paper (Hand Counted) Ballots
Do not include a box or oval on the write-in line.
The voter is not required to place an X or any other mark on the ballot when 
voting for a write-in candidate. Wis. Stat. § 7.50(2)(d). The voter needs only to 
write the name of the write-in candidate.
For Optical Scan Ballots
An oval is required to appear next to each write-in line. The voter is not required 
to fill in the oval when writing in a name in order to have the vote counted. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.50(2)(d). A completed oval next to a write-in line signals to most 
tabulating equipment types to deflect the ballot into the write-in compartment.
1 Wis. Stat. §§ 5.58(1a) (spring primary), (1g) (school district primary), 5.60(1)(ar) (spring 
election), (4)(c) (school district spring election), (5)(ar) (village spring election), (6)(a) (town 
spring election); (8)(am) (presidential preference), 5.62(1)(b)2. and (2)(b) (partisan primary), 
5.64(1)(ar)(1m) (general election, president and vice president), (1)(ar)(2) (general election, 
governor and lieutenant governor), (1)(g) (general election, other offices).
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 21
Sec. 5.2.3: Ballot Endorsement
Every ballot must have an endorsement. A ballot endorsement section contains 
important information about the election, and records information to show that 
the ballot was properly issued to the voter. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.55, 7.08(1)(a). On optical 
scan ballots, the endorsement looks like this:
Figure 1:  Example endorsement on an optical scan ballot.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 22
The endorsement must contain the following, as required by Wis. Stat. §§ 5.55:
 Ɋ The title and date of the election.
 Ɋ The municipality and wards applicable to the ballot. If all reporting units 
use the same ballot style, all reporting units may be printed on the ballot 
rather than printing separate ballots for each reporting unit. A rubber 
stamp may also be used to apply ward numbers to the endorsement.
 Ɋ Two lines for the official(s) issuing the ballot to initial before giving a ballot 
to a voter.
 ɉ Two inspectors initial before issuing a ballot on Election Day. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.80(2)(d); Wis. Stat. § 5.54.
 ɉ The municipal or deputy clerk initials when issuing an absentee ballot. 
Wis. Stat. §6.87(1); Wis. Stat. § 5.54.
 Ɋ A certification to be signed by a person who may assist a voter in marking 
the ballot. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.82(2)(a), 7.08(1)(a). This assistance should also be 
recorded in the poll book, preferably in a separate section. Wis. Stat. §§ 
6.82(2)(a), (d). See Chapter 14.11: “Voter Assistance on Election Day” for 
more information on voter assistance at the polling place.
 Ɋ A “For Official Use Only” area where inspectors record remaking an optical 
scan ballot. Wis. Stat. § 7.08(1)(a).
Endorsement Location
For paper (hand counted) ballots, the endorsement appears on the reverse side 
of the ballot. The Commission prescribes the required endorsement language 
for the back of hand counted ballots on the Reverse Side of Official Ballots (EL-
229), which is available on elections.wi.gov. If a jurisdiction is using consolidated 
hand-count paper ballots under Wis. Stat. § 5.655, the endorsement section may 
appear at the bottom of a column or on the back of the ballot.
For optical scan ballots, an endorsement section containing the Reverse 
Side of Official Ballots (EL-229) language, including the “For Official Use Only” 
section, may appear on the back of the ballot or at the bottom of any column.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 23
Sec. 5.2.4: Appearance of 
Candidates’ Names
All candidates’ names must be printed in the same font size, style, and color. 
Wis. Stat. §§ 5.51(6). The font size, style, and color of printing are established by 
the Commission in the ballot templates. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.51(6), 7.08(1)(a). Please 
see “Sec. 5.2.1: Ballot Formatting” on page 18 for further details.
The candidate indicates on the Declaration of Candidacy (EL-162) how he or 
she wishes his or her name to appear on the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 8.21(3). See Part 
2: “Getting on The Ballot” for guidance on the proper formatting of candidate 
names on the ballot.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 24
Chapter 5.3: Issuing & 
Processing A/B Ballots
In rare circumstances, municipal clerks may need to issue a second absentee 
ballot to a voter due to errors on the printed ballot or timing constraints caused 
by the Presidential Preference vote every four years at the April General Election. 
When this happens, the ballots are called A/B Ballots. This chapter outlines what 
A/B Ballots are, when an A/B Ballot situation may be needed, and how to issue 
and process the A/B Ballots to preserve voter confidence and ensure ballot 
integrity. A/B Ballots are a way to address the complicated situation when a 
clerk must issue two ballots for the same election. Currently, Wisconsin law does 
not address this situation. The Commission therefore provides this guidance as 
a “best practice,” and strongly recommends that it be followed.
Sec. 5.3.1: When are A/B Ballots Used?
There are only two extremely limited circumstances where A/B Ballots are ever used:
In Presidential Preference Vote Years.  This is done to meet federal and state 
law absentee ballot delivery deadlines when the Presidential Preference 
vote appears on the April General Election Ballot. Clerks are required to send 
absentee ballots to UOCAVA voters 47 days before a federal election, and 
the Presidential Preference vote is a federal election. Wis. Stat § 7.15(1)(cm). 
This means that in Presidential Preference vote years, clerks are required to 
send April General Election absentee ballots to UOCAVA voters before they 
know the results from the February primary for the state and local contests 
that also appear on the April General Election ballot. To avoid a statutory 
impossibility, A/B Ballots are used. The A Ballot is only the presidential 
preference vote, and the B Ballot is both the presidential preference vote and 
the state and local elections.
To Correct Mistakes on Ballots that Have Gone Out. This is also done in rare and 
exceptional cases where mistakes on ballots were discovered after absentee 
ballots were sent out. Despite best efforts by multiple layers of government to 
proof ballots, sometimes mistakes do still happen. These ballot content errors 
can include missing contests or candidates; incorrect ballot instructions; or 
misspelled or incorrectly listed candidates.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 25
Note: Municipal and county clerks are strongly encouraged to contact 
the Commission if there are any mistakes on ballots that have gone 
out. The Commission can assist with setting up WisVote to record A/B 
Ballots, and can also assist with drafting the voter notification letter.
Sec. 5.3.2: What are A/B Ballots?
“A” Ballot
The “A” ballot is the original absentee ballot issued to a voter.
“B” Ballot
The “B” ballot is a corrected ballot issued after the “A” ballot.
 Ɋ It is sent to the voter in a return envelope clearly marked “B” Ballot.
 Ɋ It is accompanied by an explanation of the A/B ballot process.
 ɉ In Presidential Preference vote years, the Commission provides this 
explanation for clerks to provide to voters. The Presidential Preference 
vote instructions to voters are available on the Commission’s 
website, most recently as part of a January 23, 2024 clerk 
communication.
 ɉ The Commission has advised that clerks draft this letter in situations 
where A/B Ballots are used to correct ballot errors. See Sec. 5.3.3: 
“Procedures for Issuing “A” & “B” Ballots” on page 2626 for more 
detail on what to include in this letter.
Sec. 5.3.3: Procedures for 
Issuing “A” & “B” Ballots
A municipal clerk will sometimes know in advance when an A/B Ballot situation 
will arise. Other times, a clerk may need to respond quickly to resolve a ballot 
printing error.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 26
Procedures for Presidential Preference Vote Years
Notably, when a Spring Primary is needed for a state or local office during a 
year with a Presidential Preference primary, and there are absentee ballot 
requests pending for a UOCAVA voter who can vote for that office. In this case a 
“B” ballot will be needed because the results of the state or local office primary 
will not be finalized until after the ballot must be mailed. Wis. Stat §§ 5.02(21) and 
(22), 7.15(1)(cm).
Procedures for Ballot Printing Errors
In circumstances involving a ballot error, a clerk will not know that a “B” ballot is 
needed until the clerk discovers the error. After an error is discovered, whether 
to issue “B” ballots is a decision that must be made by the municipal clerk in 
consultation with the clerk’s local counsel, though clerks are encouraged to 
immediately contact the Commission if an error is discovered. If B Ballots are 
necessary due to ballot error, they should be prepared and mailed out with the 
utmost urgency.
The Commission recommends considering the 
following factors when making this decision:
The Severity of the Error
 Ɋ If a contest or a candidate was omitted from a voter’s ballot, the 
Commission strongly recommends issuing “B” ballots.
 Ɋ If the instructions for the ballot are likely to mislead voters, such as if the 
ballot instructs voters to vote for an incorrect number of candidates for a 
given office (ex. a “vote for two” instructs voters to vote for only one), the 
Commission strongly recommends issuing “B” ballots.
 Ɋ If a candidate’s name is misspelled, the Commission recommends only 
issuing a “B” ballot if the error is likely to cause confusion to voters.
Whether the Error Affects Multiple Voters
If a clerk can determine that an error affects multiple voters, such as an error 
present on all ballots or a group of voters being sent a ballot for the incorrect 
ward, the Commission strongly recommends issuing “B” ballots.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 27
The Time Remaining before the Election
If there is a reasonable chance that the “B” ballot can be received by voters 
and returned before 8 p.m. on an Election Day, the Commission recommends 
issuing the “B” ballots. If there is not enough time, the Commission would not 
recommend issuing “B” ballots.
Issuing “B” Ballots
When issuing “B” ballots, either during a Presidential Preference vote year or as 
the result of a ballot error, the municipal clerk, or the clerk’s provider, should:
1. Generate a report of all voters with active absentee ballot requests.
2. Identify voters who may have received the incorrect “A” ballot using the 
absentee ballot log.
3. Coordinate with the county clerk to obtain a sufficient number of 
corrected “B” ballots.
4. Notify the Commission of the decision to issue “B” ballots, so that the 
additional “B” ballot record can be created and tracked. The municipal 
clerk or the clerk’s provider will need to track both ballot records for one 
individual in these instances.
As soon as a clerk has identified who needs to be sent a “B” ballot, the 
clerk should prepare a new absentee ballot packages with the following:
 Ɋ The corrected “B” ballot.
 Ɋ A return certificate envelope clearly marked with a “B” to ensure poll 
workers can clearly identify “B” ballots prior to opening and processing 
a sufficient absentee ballot envelope. Clerks should add “B Ballot” to the 
margin or reverse site of the certificate envelope in a way that does not 
appear within any of the text or graphics of the certificate itself. The words 
“B Ballot” can be handwritten, as long as it is written neatly. See Figure 2 
on page 30.
 Ɋ An informational insert that:
 Ɋ Explains that the voter is receiving a second ballot.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 28
 Ɋ Avoids referencing the specific error (e.g., missing candidate name, issue 
with office listed, etc.). The Commission has advised that clerks instead 
notify voters that there was an error, such as a misspelled name or an 
incorrect ballot instruction, without specifying exactly what the error is. 
Specifically stating the exact error (“John Doe’s name was spelled wrong in 
the Mayor contest”) can draw negative, unwanted attention to a specific 
candidate or race. See Sec. 5.3.7: “Example Letter” on page 34 for what 
this voter notice should look like.
 Ɋ Provides clear instructions for returning the “B” ballot.
Once these steps have been accomplished, the clerk should mail the “B” ballots 
as soon as possible and the clerk or the clerk’s provider should complete the 
“Date Ballot Sent” entry in WisVote. If the ballot is returned, the Date Ballot 
Returned entry must be completed.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 29
Figure 2: Example: Placement of “B Ballot” Language 
on “B Ballot” Certificate envelope
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 30
Sec. 5.3.4: Organizing & 
Sorting Returned Ballots
In an election with A/B Ballots, it is vital that all returned absentee ballots are 
properly organized. The following steps should be used whenever A/B Ballots are 
necessary.
1. Separate the returned “A” ballots from the returned “B” ballots
2. Separate the returned “A” ballots into different stacks depending on if the 
certificate envelopes are sufficient or not. See Sec. 14.15.12: “Absentee 
Certificate Envelopes” for examining absentee certificate envelope 
sufficiency. Each stack should be alphabetized, banded, and labeled 
appropriately.
3. Separate the returned “B” ballots into two different stacks depending on if 
the certificate envelopes are sufficient or not. See Sec. 14.15.12: “Absentee 
Certificate Envelopes” for examining absentee certificate envelope 
sufficiency. Each stack should be alphabetized, banded, and labeled 
appropriately.
Sec. 5.3.5: Processing “A” & 
“B” Ballots on Election Day
On Election Day, the processing of “A” and “B” ballots must follow a structured 
approach to ensure accuracy and compliance. It is critical that only one ballot 
per voter is counted.
Note: The Commission issues detailed A/B Ballot guidance to clerks 
ahead of Spring Elections with a Presidential Preference Vote, which 
should be reviewed alongside the guidance in this section.
Keep these general principles in mind:
 Ɋ For voters who returned both an “A” and a “B” ballot, the “B” ballot will be 
counted (if it is sufficient), and the “A” ballot will be rejected.
 Ɋ For voters who returned only an “A” ballot, the ballot should not be counted 
until after polls close at 8 p.m. in case a “B” ballot arrives later.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 31
 Ɋ Returned “B” ballots with sufficient certificate envelopes can be processed 
throughout Election Day.
Process the Following Absentee Ballots During Election Day
Assuming they have sufficient certificate envelopes, the following types of 
absentee ballots can be processed at any time during the day on Election Day:
 Ɋ “A” ballots of permanent overseas voters when A/B Ballots are used during 
a Presidential Preference Vote year. These “A” ballots can be counted 
during the day because permanent overseas voters won’t have a “B” 
ballot since they can only vote for federal contests. If the A/B ballots are 
used due to a ballot error, this guidance may not apply.
 Ɋ “B” ballots of all voters no matter why A/B Ballots are used. This is because 
the “B” ballot will always be considered the accurate ballot.
 Ɋ If a “B” ballot is counted, the corresponding “A” ballot should be rejected.
Hold the Following Absentee Ballots until after 8:00 p.m.
 Ɋ ALL “A” ballots for voters who have not returned a “B” ballot. The “A” ballot 
should never be opened or counted until after 8:00 p.m., after which poll 
workers can confirm that no “B” ballot for that voter has arrived.
 Ɋ Exception: If A/B Ballots are used because of the Presidential Preference 
Vote, permanent overseas voters will only ever have an “A” ballot, and 
those can be processed throughout Election Day.
 Ɋ ALL “A” or “B” ballots that have insufficient certificate envelopes. These 
should be set aside until 8 p.m. because the voter can correct the 
insufficiency, if the municipal clerk permits. See Sec. 14.15.12: “Absentee 
Certificate Envelopes” to Certificate Envelope Sufficiency. If the voter 
corrects the insufficiency, the “A” ballot can still be counted if the “B” ballot 
is not returned, or if it is returned and the “B” ballot envelope is insufficient.
Take the Following Actions after 8:00 p.m.
The following types of “A” ballots should be rejected:
 Ɋ “A” ballots of permanent overseas voters in Presidential Preference Vote 
years with insufficient certificate envelopes that the voter did not correct 
by 8:00 p.m.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 32
 Ɋ “A” ballots that were not already rejected when the corresponding “B” 
ballot was opened and counted.
 Ɋ Any other “A” ballot with an uncorrected insufficient certificate envelope.
The following types of “A” ballots should be counted:
 Ɋ “A” ballots for all voters who did not return a “B” ballot
 Ɋ “A” ballots for all voters who did return a “B” ballot, but the “B” ballot 
certificate was insufficient and not corrected by the voter.
 Ɋ “A” ballots of permanent overseas voters in Presidential Preference Vote 
years with insufficient certificate envelopes that the voter did correct by 
8:00 p.m.
 Ɋ “A” ballots with corrected certificate envelopes with returned “B” ballots 
that did not have a sufficient certificate envelope.
After processing, a thorough reconciliation must be conducted to match the 
total number of voters with the number of ballots processed. Any discrepancies 
must be carefully documented in the Inspector’s Statement (EL-104) and 
reported to the municipal clerk.
Sec. 5.3.6: Does This Affect My Ballot?
If you have already voted your absentee ballot and do not wish to make any 
changes, no further action is required, and your vote will be counted [unless 
the error is that a race is missing]. If you do wish to make a change, a corrected 
ballot has been enclosed with this notice. If you vote and return the enclosed 
ballot, the first ballot you returned (containing the mistake) will be rejected 
without penalty to you, and this ballot will be counted instead.
Example Language: Wisconsin Statutes Sections 5.64(1)(e)1. and 5.64(1)(es) allow 
independent candidates to include a statement of principle, if any, in five words 
or less, along with their name on the ballot. Due to an administrative error by 
state level election officials, county clerks in United States Congressional District 
2 did not receive all required information to include on the applicable ballots 
before having those ballots printed.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 33
Sec. 5.3.7: Example Letter
Important: Contact the Comission for assistance with drafting this notice
Important Notice To Voters
The ballot you received has a mistake in the listing for the [NAME OF OFFICE, 
INCLUDING SEAT NUMBER].
The ballot should have read:
Vote for 1
Candidate Name
(Party - If Applicable)
Write in: 
All candidates for [NAME OF OFFICE, INCLUDING SEAT NUMBER] remain the same despite this 
mistake. Votes cast on your ballot will not be affected by this mistake.
Does this Affect My Ballot?
If you have already voted your absentee ballot and do not wish to make any changes, no further 
action is required, and your vote will be counted [unless the error is that a race is missing]. If you 
do wish to make a change, a corrected ballot has been enclosed with this notice. If you vote and 
return the enclosed ballot, the first ballot you returned (containing the mistake) will be rejected 
without penalty to you, and this ballot will be counted instead.
Questions About this Notice?
If you have any questions about this notice, please contact your municipal clerk’s office. You 
can find their information at MyVote.wi.gov/en-us/My-Municipal-Clerk. You may also contact the 
Wisconsin Elections Commission’s Helpdesk at (608) 266-8005 or toll free at (866) VOTE-WIS.
What was the Mistake?
This section should not be overly detailed, and should not point out the 
specific candidate involved. An example has been included below from a real 
voter notice letter from 2022.

candidates to include a statement of principle, if any, in five words or less, along with their name 
on the ballot. Due to an administrative error by state level election officials, county clerks in 
United States Congressional District 2 did not receive all required information to include on the 
applicable ballots before having those ballots printed.

Chapter 5.4: Referendum 
Ballots
The Commission approves templates of both types of referendum ballots ahead of 
each election, and those templates can be found on elections.wi.gov in the “Forms 
and Ballot Template” section.
Sec. 5.4.1: Hand Counted Paper Ballots
 Ɋ A separate ballot is required for referenda. Wis. Stat. §  5.60(7), Wis. Stat. § 
5.64(2). However, “more than one referendum question may appear on the 
same referendum ballot whenever the questions are numbered and all 
electors voting the ballot are entitled to vote upon all questions appearing 
thereon.” Wis. Stat. § 5.64(2)(c).
 Ɋ Statewide and county referenda can be placed on the same ballot, but 
a separate ballot must be prepared for municipal and special purpose 
district referenda, which includes school districts. Id.
Sec. 5.4.2: Optical Scan & 
Consolidated Ballots1
 Ɋ There must be a separate referendum column or row section on the ballot 
whenever a separate ballot would be required above.
 Ɋ The ballot should clearly differentiate between state, county, municipal, 
and school district referenda. Wis. Stat. § 5.64(2)(c).
 Ɋ The title and endorsement of the ballot must include the language “and 
Referendum.” Wis. Stat. § 5.64.
1 See Wis. Stat. § 5.655.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots 5 – 35
Chapter 5.5: Presidential-
Only Ballots
The Presidential-only ballot only allows voters to cast votes for president and 
vice-president, but no other offices. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.15(1), 6.18.
Sec. 5.5.1: Introduction & Who 
is (and is not) Eligible
There are two types of individuals who may receive a Presidential-only ballot: 
new residents who move to Wisconsin after the 28th day before a presidential 
election, and former residents who left Wisconsin no more than 24 months 
before a presidential election and who are ineligible to qualify as an elector in 
the new state.
Examples of Individuals Who Do Not Qualify for Presidential-only Ballots:
 Ɋ Residents of other states who are only here temporarily or are passing 
through (e.g. over the road truckers passing through Wisconsin, people 
in the state temporarily for work). These individuals likely have not 
established Wisconsin residence. Wis. Stat. § 6.15(2)(a).
 Ɋ Individuals who qualify as Military voters under Wis. Stat. § 6.22: Military 
voters should be issued the full ballot with all contests included.
 Ɋ Individuals who qualify as Permanent overseas voters under Wis. 
Stat. § 6.24: Permanent overseas voters receive the federal-only ballot 
with only contests for federal office included (President, Senate, and 
Representative to Congress for 2024 General Election).
 Ɋ Temporary overseas voters: Temporary overseas voters are issued the full 
ballot with all contests included.
 Ɋ New Residents Only: Voters who meet the residency qualifications but do 
not have proof of residence: These voters will have to find an acceptable 
proof of residence document in order register and receive a ballot.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 36
 Ɋ Voters who moved within Wisconsin and do not meet residency 
requirements at a new address: Voters who have moved within the state 
but have not achieved residency at their new address are allowed under 
state law to vote either in person or absentee from their former address. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.02(2).
 Ɋ Voters who have proof of residence, but not photo ID. If a voter does not 
have valid photo ID, they are eligible to vote a provisional ballot, but should 
not use the Presidential-only ballot process.
Ballot Style
The ballot templates for Presidential-only ballots are prescribed by the 
Commission. Most municipal clerks choose to use the optical scan style of 
these ballots because they more closely resemble the rest of the ballots at the 
polling place, and because they contain the endorsement information needed 
to remake the ballots. If electronic voting equipment is used, the ballots will 
need to be remade before being tabulated.
Some municipal clerks opt to use the hand count style of these ballots either 
because they are a hand count jurisdiction or because the ballots will need to 
be remade onto optical scan ballots to be tabulated anyways.
Sec. 5.5.2: Applying for 
Presidential-Only Ballots
Regardless of whether the voter gets their Presidential-only ballot from the 
municipal clerk or at their polling place, the set of documents they must 
produce and complete is the largely same.
The individual must:
 Ɋ Complete an Application for Presidential Ballot – New Wisconsin Resident 
(EL-141) or Application for Presidential Ballot – Former Wisconsin Resident 
(EL-140). Wis. Stat. §§ 6.15(1), 6.18(1). The El-141 and EL-140 will be entered into 
WisVote using the application type “Presidential-only.”
 Ɋ Complete an Authorization to Cancel Registration (EL-139). Wis. 
Stat. § 6.15(2)(b). New residents only.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 37
 Ɋ Provide proof of identification (both) and proof of residence (new residents 
only). The clerk or election inspector must enter on the application form 
the type of document submitted as proof of residence, the name of the 
entity that issued the document, and, if the document includes a number 
unique to the individual, the last 4 digits, or, in the number has 6 or fewer 
digits, the last two digits. Wis. Stat. § 6.15(2)(bm).
Sec. 5.5.3: Issuing Presidential-
Only Ballots to New Residents
Any resident who moves to Wisconsin fewer than 28 days before a presidential 
election would not be able to meet the residency requirement for electors 
provided in Wis. Stat. § 6.02(1) and, as such, would not be able to register and 
vote a full regular ballot. However, if the individual is otherwise qualified to 
vote in Wisconsin, the individual can be issued a Presidential-only ballot. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.15(1). The individual does not need to have been registered in the 
previous state to cast a Presidential-only ballot in Wisconsin. Id.
Best Practice: Individuals in this situation may wish to first 
check with their former state of residency to see what voting 
options may be available for them there. This might be 
preferable to the voter because they may be able to vote 
a full ballot in their previous state of residence, though of 
course, that ballot would not have Wisconsin contests.
To get a Presidential-only ballot, the individual must appear in person in the 
clerk’s office between 27 days before the election and 5 p.m. the day before the 
election, or at the polling place for their new residence. Wis. Stat. § 6.15(2)(a).
Voting the Presidential-Only Ballot at the Clerk’s Office
Note: This process is distinct from in-person absentee voting as 
authorized by Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(a)2.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 38
 Ɋ Immediately mail the EL-139 Authorization to Cancel Registration to the 
proper election official of the individual’s former state of residence. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.15(2)(c).
 Ɋ Issue the voter a Presidential-only ballot and the voter privately, but in the 
clerk’s presence, votes the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 6.15(2)(d)1r.
 Ɋ The ballot is then placed in an envelope provided by the clerk, and then 
then clerk encloses that envelope in a carrier envelope endorsed with 
the clerk’s name and containing this statement: “This envelope contains 
the vote for president and vice president of a new resident and shall 
be opened only at the polls during polling hours on Election Day.” Wis. 
Stat. § 6.15(2)(d)2.
 Ɋ The EL 141 form must be available to the election inspectors processing 
these ballots and thus must be transported to the polling place or board 
of absentee ballot canvassers. Wis. Stat. § 6.15(4)(a). The Commission 
recommends keeping this paperwork with the voted ballot, and 
transporting it to the polling place along with the other voted absentee 
ballots. See Sec. 14.15.3: “How Absentee Ballots Arrive at Polling Places or 
“Central Count”” for procedures on transporting absentee ballots to the 
polling place or “central count.”
 Ɋ For transporting them, it is recommended to either enclose the form within 
the carrier envelope but outside of the envelope containing the ballot, or 
keep them separate and transport the EL 141s to the polling place or board 
of absentee ballot canvassers, while ensuring that the chief inspector 
knows where to find them.
 Ɋ On Election Day, the clerk must then deliver all such envelopes to the 
proper polling place or to the board of absentee ballot canvassers for 
processing. Wis. Stat. § 6.15(4)(a).
The clerk must keep a list of all individuals who vote a Presidential-only ballot 
in the clerk’s office containing the voter’s name, address, and application date. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.15(2)(d)3.
Best Practice: Clerks should use the Presidential-only 
process in WisVote to record this information. Clerks should 
also add this information to the public absentee ballot log 
with “Presidential Only” notated on log line for notes.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 39
Voting the Presidential-Only Ballot at the Polling Place
The voter can also request a Presidential-only ballot at their polling place if 
they’re unable or unwilling to do so at the clerk’s office ahead of the election.
Clerks should prepare copies of the Authorization to Cancel Registration (EL-139) 
and Application for Presidential Ballot – New Wisconsin Resident (EL-141) with 
the rest of the materials for the registration tables at each polling place. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.15(3).
Once the voter has completed the necessary forms, the election inspector 
gives the voter a Presidential-only ballot to vote in the same manner as a 
regular elector. Wis. Stat. § 6.15(3). The election inspector working with the voter 
must return the EL-139 cancellation form to the clerk, and the clerk must then 
mail it to the proper election official of the individual’s former residence. Id. 
If the tabulator has been programmed to accept Presidential-only ballots, 
then the voter may place their ballot in the tabulator. If the tabulator has not 
been programmed to accept Presidential-only ballots, then the voter returns 
their ballot to the election inspector. The ballot is then remade to reflect the 
presidential vote and placed in the tabulator. If the municipality hand counts its 
ballots then the voter deposits their ballot into the ballot box.
Sec. 5.5.4: Issuing Presidential-
Only Ballots to Former Residents
Former residents of Wisconsin who are unable to meet the eligibility 
requirements to register in their new state may request and vote a 
Presidential-only absentee ballot in their former Wisconsin municipality. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.18. Former residents may apply for a ballot up to 24 months 
after leaving Wisconsin.  Id. Former residents may not receive and vote a 
Presidential-only ballot at a Wisconsin polling place, they must instead do so 
by mail. Wis. Stat. § 6.18.
To issue a Presidential-only absentee ballot to a 
former resident, the individual must:
 Ɋ Complete an Application for Presidential Ballot – Former Wisconsin 
Resident (EL-140) – and return it to the former municipal clerk. Id. The EL-
140 must be notarized or sworn, or contain an unsworn declaration, to be 
considered a valid request. Wis. Stat. § 6.18.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 40
 Ɋ Provide proof of identification (proof of residence is not required) unless 
the voter would have been exempt from providing it due to being 
indefinitely confined under Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)2., had already provided 
proof of ID for an absentee ballot for the old residence and has not 
changed names under Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)3, or was an overseas or 
military voter. Id. 
There is no fixed deadline by which a former resident must provide a complete 
EL-140 and, if required, proof of identification. The required documentation must 
be received with sufficient time for a ballot to be mailed and returned prior to 
the election. Id.
Note: As with new residents, these voters are not required to complete 
and provide an EL-131.
Sec. 5.5.5: Processing Presidential-
Only Ballots on Election Day
Whether absentee ballots are counted at polling places or at locations of the 
board of absentee ballot canvassers (“central count”), the steps for processing 
Presidential-only ballots are largely the same.
Presidential-only ballots will be prepared and sent to each polling place in a 
separate carrier envelope but with the other returned absentee ballots. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.15(4)(a).
Processing Presidential-Only Ballots 
Received before Election Day
Best Practice: State law provides detailed procedures for how 
election inspectors should process Presidential-only ballots for 
New Residents, but the same statutes do not exist for Former 
Residents. Compare Wis. Stat. §§ 6.15(4) with 6.18. Accordingly, 
election inspectors should follow the New Resident processes for 
Former Resident Presidential-only ballots as a best practice.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots 5 – 41
Step 1: Confirm the Affidavit (Application) is included with the Ballot
New Residents Only. The election officials must check the affidavit enclosed 
in the carrier envelope to ensure it has been completed properly and that 
the voter is otherwise qualified to vote in the ward. Wis. Stat. § 6.15(4)(b). If the 
affidavit (application) is not included, check the rest of the ballot materials to 
see if it was stored somewhere else, and if not, contact the municipal clerk.
Former Residents will not have an affidavit (application) included with their ballot, be-
cause they would have sent it in to the municipal clerk to get their ballot, and accord-
ingly wouldn’t have it to include with the ballot when they sent it back. Wis. Stat. § 6.18.
Step 2: Open the Envelope & Retrieve the Ballot
Then, the election officials shall open the inner envelope containing the ballot and 
ensure only that the clerk has initialed it without examining the voted ballot. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.15(4)(c). If the voter is not otherwise qualified in the ward, or if the envelope 
is open and has been resealed, the election officials must reject the ballot, which 
is treated the same as other rejected absentee ballots under Wis. Stat. § 6.88(3)(b). 
Wis. Stat. § 6.15(4)(e). See Sec. 14.15.14: “Rejecting Absentee Ballots”
Step 3: Enter Voter Information into Supplemental Poll List
If everything is sufficient, then the election officials enter the voter’s full name, 
address, and serial number on the supplemental poll list. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.15(4)
(d), 6.79(2)(c), (4). New Residents Only: Election inspectors will also enter POR 
document type and issuing entity on the supplemental poll list
An indication, such as “6.15” (New), “6.18” (Former) or “Presidential Only,” that a 
voter voted under Wis. Stat. § 6.15 or must also be added to the supplemental 
poll list. Wis. Stat. § 6.15(4)(d). These voter names will not be printed in the poll 
book like other voters.
Step 4: Remake & Tabulate the Ballot
Presidential-only ballots will need to be remade by election inspectors before 
they can be tabulated by electronic voting equipment. Even though the ballot 
format for Presidential-only ballots is prescribed by the Commission, most 
voting equipment is not programmed to be able to read this ballot type 
because it is so uncommon.
Hand-count jurisdictions will not need to remake the ballots, and the 
Presidential-only ballots can be tabulated and counted along with other 
ballots. See Chapter 14.22: “Overvoted & Crossover Voted Ballots” for detailed 
procedures on how to properly remake ballots.

INSTRUCTIONS FOR 
      APPLICATION FOR PRESIDENTIAL BALLOT - NEW WISCONSIN RESIDENT 
  
Any person who is a United States citizen, at least 18 years old on E lection Day, who has moved into the State 
of Wisconsin less than 28  days before the presidential election, and is ineligible to vote absentee in his or her 
state of previous residence, may vote for president and vice president by completing this application, providing 
acceptable proof of residence and providing acceptable voter ID. 
 
A new Wisconsin resident making application for a presidential ballot need not be registered. 
 
A new Wisconsin resident can complete this application and vote for president and vice president either by 
absentee ballot in the office of the municipal clerk, or by voting at the polling place on Election Day. 
 
In addition to com pleting this application form ( EL-141), providing a acceptable proof of residence  and voter 
ID, the elector also must complete a voter registration cancellation card (EL-139). 
 
Both of these items are provided by the municipal clerk.  They also can be obta ined from an election inspector 
at the polling place on Election Day. 
 
    PROCEDURE FOR MAKING APPLICATION IN THE MUNICIPAL CLERK'S OFFICE 
 
1. The new Wisconsin resident shows acceptable proof of residence  and acceptable voter ID, completes the 
application form (EL-141), and the voter registration cancellation card (EL-139). 
 
2. If the new Wisconsin resident chooses to vote an absentee presidential ballot in the clerk's office, the 
municipal clerk provides the person with an absentee ballot certificate envelope ( EL-122) and a presidential 
ballot.  The clerk must keep a list which includes the name, address, date of application, and the date on 
which the ballot was cast. 
 
3. If the new Wisconsin resident making this application chooses to go to the polling place on E lection Day to 
vote, the municipal clerk must provide the person with a copy of the completed application form ( EL-141) 
to take to the polling place. 
 
4. The municipal clerk must keep a separate list of all new Wisconsin residents who vote under the provision s 
of Wis. Stat. § 6.15.  The list must include the person's name, address, and date of application, and if voting 
by absentee ballot, the date of receipt of the voted ballot. 
 
5. The municipal clerk shall send the voter registration cancellation card ( EL-139) to the elector's municipality 
of previous residence. 
 
        PROCEDURE FOR VOTING FOR PRESIDENT AT THE POLLING PLACE 
 
1. The new Wisconsin resident must show acceptable proof of residence  and voter ID , complete this 
application (EL-141), and complete the voter registration cancellation card ( EL-139) at the polling place, or 
bring a copy of the application form that was completed in the municipal clerk's office. 
 
2. The election inspector will provide the person with a paper ballot to vote for the offices of pre sident and 
vice president only. 
 
3. The election inspectors shall indicate on the voter list next to the new Wisconsin resident's name that he or 
she received only a presidential ballot. 
 
4. The application form ( EL-141) and the voter registration cancellation c ard ( EL-139) are returned to the 
municipal clerk along with the voter lists and other election documents. 
 
Chapter 5.6: Sample Ballots
Two samples of each type of ballot must be posted at each polling place on 
Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(a)3.
Sec. 5.6.1: Providing Sample Ballots
Unless a municipality supplies its own ballots, the county or board of election 
commissioners must print a sufficient number of sample ballots for each 
municipality. Wis. Stat. § 5.66(2). Once printed, approximately 45% of the sample 
ballots should remain in the county office, 45% in the municipal clerk’s office or 
alternate sites, and 10% reserved by the municipal clerk to be sent to the polling 
places on Election Day. Id. The number of ballots printed for each municipality 
should be in proportion to the number of electors residing in the municipality as 
certified to the county by the municipal clerk under Wis. Stat. § 5.66(1).
Note: Sample ballots must be available to voters who request them. 
Sec. 5.6.2: Sample Ballot Format
Sample ballots cannot be printed on white paper. They must be printed 
on colored paper and the color must be different than the color used for 
the official ballots. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.51(5), 5.66(2). The word ‘SAMPLE’ must be 
overprinted on all sample ballots. Id. The endorsement does not have to be 
printed on sample ballots. Id.
Electronic Voting Systems
Sample ballots that are marked by an electronic voting systems (i.e. ES&S 
ExpressVote) must be the same size as the actual ballots used in electronic 
voting machines. Id.
Best Practice: The sample ballots in hand-count 
municipalities should also be an actual size copy. 
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots 5 – 47
Voting Machines
Voting machine sample ballots shall be a reduced size diagram of the face of 
the board or screen inside the voting machine with all candidates, issues and 
voting instructions as they will appear on the official ballot. Id. 
Best Practice: Neither “Reduced sized diagram” nor “face of the 
board or screen inside the voting machine” is further defined in 
statute, and the Commission recommends that municipalities use 
the sample ballots described under Electronic Voting Systems to 
meet this requirement because the screens used on accessible 
voting equipment display the same candidates in the same order.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 48
Chapter 5.7: Frequently 
Asked Questions
Q For each office, the ballot indicates how many votes can be cast in that 
office. What is the proper format of that instruction?
A The number of candidates an elector is allowed to vote for, whether at 
a primary or an election, is the same as the number of officers to be 
elected. If there is only one position to be filled, such as with the office of 
mayor, the instruction is “Vote for 1.” If there are three trustee positions up 
for election, the instruction is “Vote for not more than 3.” Wis. Stat. §§ 5.52, 
7.08(1)(a).
Q How many write-in lines are required?
A The number of write-in lines required is equal to the number of candidates 
for which the elector is allowed to vote. If there is only one position to 
be filled, such as with the office of mayor, the instruction is “Vote for 1.” 
Therefore, one write-in line is required. If there are three trustee positions 
up for election, the instruction is “Vote for not more than 3.” Three write-in 
lines are required. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.58(1a) and (1g)(c);  5.60(4)(c), (5)(ar), (6)(a), 
(8)(am); 5.62(1)(b)2. and (2)(b); 5.64(1)(e)2.; and  5.82. 
Q In a primary, how many candidates may go on to the general election?
A The number of candidates that proceed from a primary to an election is 
equal to twice the number of candidates for which the elector can vote. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.58(3).
Example 1: If the instruction is “Vote for 1,” the two candidates receiving the 
highest number of votes will appear on the election ballot.
Example 2: If the instruction is “Vote for not more than 2,” the four 
candidates receiving the highest number of votes will appear on the 
election ballot.
Example 3: If the instruction is “Vote for not more than 3,” the six 
candidates receiving the highest number of votes will appear on the 
election ballot.
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 49
Q Can a municipality prepare a partially-consolidated ballot for some races, 
and use a packet ballot for others1? 
A No. If a municipality chooses to provide consolidated ballots, all races 
must appear on the consolidated ballot. Wis. Stat. § 5.655. A municipality 
cannot use a consolidated ballot for statewide and county races, for 
example, and then also use a packet ballot for municipal and school 
district races. All active contests should be listed on the same ballot 
whenever consolidated ballots are used. 
Q Are stickers allowed to be placed on ballots? 
A Generally, no. State law prohibits election officials from attaching any 
type of sticker to a ballot. The only exception is under the circumstance 
where a vacancy occurs because a candidate has died after his or her 
name has been printed on the ballot. Wis. Stat.  §§ 5.51(4), 7.37(6). To the 
Commission’s knowledge, this has never occurred. 
The Commission is aware that some write-in candidates prepare stickers 
for their voters to attach to ballots. State law does not prohibit a voter from 
affixing a sticker to their ballot, but neither does it permit it. Stickers can 
cause automatic tabulators to jam or otherwise stop functioning, so the 
Commission strongly discourages their use.
1 Packet ballots are the opposite of consolidated ballots wherein a separate ballot is prepared for each 
race or contest. Partially-consolidated ballots are a hybrid between consolidated and packet ballots. 
First Edition, June 2026 Ballots  5 – 50


Part 6 
Voter Qualifications 
& Registration
Voter qualifications and eligibility; pre-Election Day registration; 
proof of residence; confidential and protected voters.
Most electors are required to register as a condition of voting. When a voter 
registers, they are certifying that they meet all of the legal requirements 
to vote, including age, citizenship, and residence, and that they are not 
disqualified due to a felony conviction or adjudication of incompetency. Most 
electors are required to present proof of their residence when registering. 
Some types of voters, such as confidential voters, have additional procedures 
and protections in place to protect their information.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter Qualifications & Registration 6 – 1
Chapter 6.1: Voter 
Qualifications
Sec. 6.1.1: Summary
The Wisconsin Constitution grants the right to vote to all qualified electors 
(voters)1 and sets out the base elector qualifications that are further  
codified in statute. Wis. Const., Part. III, § 1(2) . In the State of Wisconsin, a 
qualified elector must be registered to vote before being issued a ballot.  
Wis. Stat. § 6.27 . The municipal clerk is responsible for maintaining records 
in order to track voter registration in the WisVote system, ensure elector 
qualifications, and possibly consider challenges to those qualifications. 
See Wis. Stat. § 7.15(1) (“Each municipal clerk has charge and supervision of 
elections and registration in the municipality.”)
Sec. 6.1.2: Voter Certifies 
that They are Qualified
When electors register to vote, they acknowledge that falsification of any of 
the information provided, or certified to, on the registration form is punishable 
under Wisconsin law as a Class I felony. Wis. Stat. § 6.33(1). In this way, clerks 
may rely on the voter’s assertions that they meet the legal requirements to vote, 
including their age, citizenship, residency, and felony status. It is not necessary 
to test or examine the voter’s qualifications to vote unless the municipal clerk 
“knows or has reliable information that the proposed elector is not qualified.” 
Wis. Stat. § 6.32(2). No one may be disqualified as an elector unless the 
municipal clerk, or challenger, demonstrates “beyond a reasonable doubt” that 
the person is not qualified to vote. Wis. Stat. § 6.325. Clerks cannot set voting 
requirements not set by law.
1 For clarity, Part Six will use the word “voter” instead of “elector,” but “elector” is the correct statutory 
term.
First Edition, June 2026 Voter Qualifications & Registration 6 – 2
Sec. 6.1.3: Voter Eligibility 
Requirements
In order to register to vote, an individual must:
 Ɋ Be a U.S. citizen. Wis. Stat. § 6.02(1).
 Ɋ Be age 18 or older on or before Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 6.02(1).
 Ɋ Have resided in an election district or ward for 28 consecutive days, with 
no present intent to move, before any election where the citizen offers to 
vote. Wis. Stat. § 6.02(1).
The following persons shall not be allowed to vote in any election:
 Ɋ Any person convicted of treason, felony, or bribery that has not been 
pardoned or completed the terms of their sentence including any term of 
probation, parole, or extended supervision. Wis. Stat. § 6.03(1)(b).
Best Practice: Clerks can contact the Wisconsin Department of 
Corrections to determine if the term of sentence of a potential 
elector has been fully completed, including whether the voter 
has completed any term of probation, parole, or extended 
supervision. This is often referred to as being “off paper.”
 Ɋ A person whom a court has declared as not competent to exercise the 
right to vote due to being incapable of understanding the objective of the  
elective process. Wis. Stat. § 6.03(1)(a). A court order granting guardianship 
or otherwise declaring a person’s incompetency should specifically 
declare if the person is incompetent to exercise the right to vote. If the 
order does not include a specific finding of incompetency to vote,  
the person retains the right to vote. Wis. Stat. § 54.25(2)(c)1.g., (2)(c)4.
 Ɋ Anyone who has made or become interested, directly or indirectly, in any 
bet or wager depending upon the result of the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.03(2).
First Edition, June 2026 Voter Qualifications & Registration 6 – 3
Residency
An individual’s residency in a ward or municipality for voting purposes is 
determined by the individual’s fixed habitation and present intent not to 
move from that location. Wis. Stat. § 6.10(1). The burden is always on the voter 
to declare their voting residence. The clerk facilitates the registration, then 
assesses whether that residence qualifies them to vote in their jurisdiction. See 
Wis. Stat. §§ 6.02, 6.10(1).
Temporary Presence/Absence
Residency is not lost when a person leaves home and goes to another location 
temporarily, with an intent to return home. Persons who have temporarily left 
their homes are still residents of the home municipality despite their temporary 
absence. Wis. Stat. § 6.10(5).
Residency cannot be established in any ward, town, village, city, county, or 
in this state, while living in that location for temporary purposes only. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.10(8) .
Moving
A person loses their residency if they move to another state with an intent to 
make a permanent residence there, or, if while there, the person exercises the  
right to vote in that state. Such a person cannot continue to vote at their previous  
Wisconsin residence without re-establishing residency. Wis. Stat. § 6.10(10). If 
a person moves to a different municipality within Wisconsin without intent to 
return to their previous address, they should register to vote in the new address. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.02(2), unless they have not lived there for 28 consecutive days yet, 
in which case they should vote in the previous municipality. Wis. Stat. § 6.10(3).
Student Status
Student status cannot be considered in determining residence. A student may 
choose to establish residency in the municipality where they live to attend 
school, or the student may base residency on an intent to return to their former 
municipality, thus continuing their existing residency. Wis. Stat. § 6.10(4), (12).
If a student registers to vote in the municipality where they attend school, the  
student loses residency in their prior municipality and must re-establish residency 
in the prior municipality and register to vote there. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.36(1)(d), 6.10(3).
First Edition, June 2026 Voter Qualifications & Registration 6 – 4
“Part-Time” Residents
A person may only register as an elector and vote in one municipality each 
election. Wis. Stat. § 12.13(1)(c), (1)(e). To vote in a municipality, a person with 
part-time residency in a municipality must consider that location their fixed 
habitation with no intention to move and therefore is their residence for voting 
purposes. Wis. Stat. § 6.10(1).
Merely owning property in a municipality is not sufficient to claim residency. A 
person must have established a fixed habitation paired with the intent to make 
that address their permanent residence. Wis. Stat. § 6.10(1).
New Residents
If a voter has not resided in a Wisconsin municipality for at least 28 days, they 
may not vote in any federal, state, or local contest in Wisconsin except for the 
office of U.S. President during a presidential year. Wis. Stat. § 6.15(1).
Best Practice: A person who has not resided in any ward in 
Wisconsin for at least 28 days should be advised to check 
with their former state of residence about any voting options 
they may have as former residents of that state.
New Wisconsin residents who do not meet the 28 day residency requirement 
may be eligible to vote by Presidential-only ballot. Likewise, former Wisconsin 
residents who do not qualify to vote for president and vice president in their new 
state may also be able to vote a Presidential-only ballot.  See Chapter 5.5 for 
more information on these procedures.
