Chapter 7.2: Types of 
Absentee Voters
“Regular” absentee voters are those who request and return their absentee 
ballots without qualifying or using any of the specialized procedures covered 
in Chapters 7.2, 7.3, and 7.4.
There are additional procedures for various special categories of absentee 
voters. All absentee voting information specific to these topics are contained in 
these sections and chapters.
Table 11: Absentee Request Types
Absentee Voter Type Manual Section or Chapter
Indefinitely Confined Voters Sec. 7.2.1
Calendar Year Requests Sec. 7.2.2
Hospitalized Voters Sec. 7.2.3
Sequestered Jurors Sec. 7.2.4
Voters using Special Voting DeputiesChapter 7.3
Military and Overseas Voters Chapter 7.4
Sec. 7.2.1: Indefinitely Confined Voters
A voter who is indefinitely confined because of age, physical illness or infirmity, 
or is disabled for an indefinite period may sign a statement to that effect and 
request that absentee ballots be sent to the voter automatically for every 
election. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2)(a). A voter must determine on their own whether 
they are indefinitely confined, and that determination must be based only on 
the voter’s own age, physical illness, or infirmity. Jefferson v. Dane Cty., 2020 WI 
90, ¶2, 394 Wis. 2d 602, 951 N.W.2d 556.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 7
Indefinitely Confined Voters Cannot Also 
be Military or Overseas Voters
Section 6 of the Application for Absentee Ballot (EL-121) contains a space for the 
voter to indicate they qualify as indefinitely confined. If this request is made, a 
voter cannot also select the Military or Overseas voting options. See Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.86(1)(a)3. If a voter is away on active duty, or is outside of the United States, 
the voter should select the Military or Overseas voting options.
Photo ID Exempt
Indefinitely confined voters are exempt from the photo ID requirement to receive 
an absentee ballot as long as their witness completes the certification on their 
absentee certificate envelope. See Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)2.
Indefinitely Confined Absentee Ballots are Not Forwardable
The envelope containing the indefinitely confined voter’s ballot should be clearly 
marked as not forwardable with “return service requested.” Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2)(a).
Grounds for Loss of Indefinitely Confined Status
There are three different ways a voter can lose their indefinitely confined status: 
1) by not returning a ballot in an election, 2) if the municipal clerk reliably 
believes the voter does not qualify, and 3) the voter requests to disqualify 
themselves. Each is explained further below.
Not Returning a Ballot
If an indefinitely confined voter fails to cast and return a Spring, General or Special 
Election ballot, the clerk shall send a First-Class letter or postcard informing the 
voter that their name will be removed from the list unless the voter applies for 
renewal within the 30-day period. See Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2)(b).1 A ballot has been 
returned even if it is ultimately rejected at the polls. See Wis. Stat. § 6.88. The voter 
is required to submit a renewal of their absentee request in writing, but a full 
Application for Absentee Ballot (EL-121) is not required. See Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(a), (2)(b).
Note: This includes voters who vote in person at the polls or who cast 
an absentee ballot in person in the clerk’s office or alternate site 
because such voters will necessarily fail to return the absentee ballot 
that was mailed to them under this process. See Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2)(b).
1 The Commission unanimously approved this interpretation in the Open Session Minutes for the 
November 2, 2023 Commission meeting.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 8
If an indefinitely confined voter returns a blank ballot, that is sufficient indication 
that they wish to retain their indefinitely confined status even though they did 
not make any ballot choices. For maintenance of indefinitely confined status, 
it does not matter if the blank ballot is returned in a blank (not completed) 
absentee certificate envelope, a completed certificate envelope, or a separate 
envelope. The clerk must notify the voter of the action within 5 days, if possible. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2)(b).
Best Practice: The Commission has designed a Notification of 
Indefinitely Confined Absentee Request Cancellation (EL-145) form 
that clerks should use when a voter fails to return the by-mail 
absentee ballot for a Spring, General, or Special Election. It contains 
the notice and a request for renewal that a voter can return to the 
clerk. Notification letters can be generated from WisVote if using the 
absentee functionality. Voters should be aware that in the weeks 
following a General, Spring, or Special Election, this “30-day” letter will 
arrive in the mail, and voters may return this letter asking the clerk to 
keep them on the mailing list for future absentee ballots.
Upon Reliable Information that the Voter is No Longer Qualified
If the municipal clerk has reliable information that the voter is no longer 
qualified for indefinitely confined status, the clerk may revoke their eligibility. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2)(b). The clerk must notify the voter of the action within 5 
days, if possible. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2)(b).
Best Practice: The Commission strongly recommends that clerks work 
with their local counsel if they believe they have reliable information that 
a voter who has certified that they qualify to receive absentee ballots 
as an indefinitely confined voter is no longer indefinitely confined. A 
belief that someone is no longer indefinitely confined that is not based 
on “reliable information” is insufficient to remove an individual from 
the mailing list. Not all medical illnesses or disabilities are visible, or 
may only impact the voter intermittently, so clerks should use caution 
before determining that reliable information shows that an individual no 
longer qualifies. Even if a voter has voted in-person absentee or at the 
polls, that does not mean that they no longer qualify for this service and 
may return the Notification of Indefinitely Confined Absentee Request 
Cancellation letter and remain active on the mailing list.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 9
Voter Requests Removal
A voter can lose eligibility for indefinitely confined status if they request that 
their name be removed from the list. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2)(b).
Best Practice: Clerks can contact voters to confirm that the voter still 
qualifies to receive absentee ballots under the indefinitely confined 
procedures. The Commission has designed a template form and 
instructions that clerks can use to send to the voters who have made this 
selection to clarify that it is still correct or to allow the voter to cancel the 
request under this status. No action should be taken regarding voters 
who do not return this form to the clerk, as those voters still have a valid 
request to receive absentee ballots on file, and the clerk has gained no 
information from the voter indicating that the status is incorrect.
Review of Indefinitely Confined Voter Statuses
The Commission has published guidance relating to how clerks can “clean up” 
their lists of indefinitely confined voters by sending voters a letter to allow the 
voter to confirm that they qualify for indefinitely confined status. That guidance, 
as well as a template of the letter, can be found on elections.wi.gov.
Sec. 7.2.2: Calendar Year Requests
Certain voters are eligible to indicate that they’d like to receive an absentee 
ballot for every election in their jurisdiction for a given calendar year. Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.86(2m)(a). Calendar year requests under this statute are not available to 
indefinitely confined voters, military voters, or permanent overseas voters.2 Wis. 
Stat. § 6.86(2m)(a).
Making the Request
Calendar year requests under Id. can be made using the Commission’s regular 
Application for Absentee Ballot (EL-121), which the Commission has prescribed as 
the designated form for this type of request. If requested, a clerk should provide 
a voter with the paper form and also inform the voter about the MyVote process. 
See Id. .
2 Indefinitely confined voters receive absentee ballots for each election continuously until they fail to 
return one or otherwise fail to qualify. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2). Military and overseas voters also continue 
to receive absentee ballots for the calendar year, but under their own statutes, not under this specific 
statute for “calendar year requests” under Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2m)(a).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 10
Upon receipt of a sufficient absentee ballot request, and as long as the voter 
remains registered and qualified, the municipal clerk must mail an absentee 
ballot to the voter for each election in the voter’s jurisdiction. Id. As with all 
absentee ballots, the envelope must be marked as not forwardable. Id.
What if a Calendar Year Request Voter Moves?
It is the voter’s responsibility to notify the clerk if the voter no longer resides at 
the same address as indicated on the application, and if notified, the clerk must 
either change the voter’s registration status to ineligible if the voter has moved 
outside of the municipality or update the address if the voter has moved within 
the municipality. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.50(3),(6), 6.86(2m)(a). If the voter notifies the 
clerk that the voter has moved to another Wisconsin municipality, the clerk shall 
forward the calendar year request to the new municipal clerk and the municipal 
clerk must honor that request, provided that the voter properly registers. See 
Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2m)(b).
When Does a Voter No Longer Qualify 
for a Calendar Year Request?
There are three circumstances in which voters will no longer 
qualify to receive calendar year absentee requests:
 Ɋ When the municipal clerk receives reliable information that the voter is no 
longer qualified to vote
 Ɋ If the voter fails to return any absentee ballot mailed to them
 Ɋ At the voter’s request
Reliable Information that the Voter is Not Qualified to Vote
The municipal clerk must remove the voter from the calendar year absentee 
ballot mailing list if the clerk receives reliable information that the voter no 
longer qualifies as a voter of the municipality. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2m)(a). The 
clerk should also follow any other registration list procedure based on the 
information. For example, if the reliable information is that the voter has died, 
the clerk must remove the voter from the registration list. Wis. Stat. 6.50(4).
Failure to Return an Absentee Ballot
Further, the municipal clerk must remove the voter from the calendar year 
absentee ballot mailing list if the voter fails to return any ballot that was mailed 
to the voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2m)(a).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 11
Voter’s Request
A voter may request that the clerk no longer send them an absentee ballot for 
each election in a calendar year. See Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2m)(a).
Notifying the Voter & Voter Regaining Calendar Year Status
If a clerk removes a voter’s name from the mailing list for any reason other than 
at the voter’s request, the clerk must notify the voter of the action within five 
days, if possible. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2m)(a). If the voter remains qualified, the voter 
can send a written notification to the municipal clerk that the voter wishes to 
be added back to the calendar year mailing list for the remainder of the year. 
Id. If received, the clerk should resume mailing absentee ballots to the voter as 
described in this section.
Sec. 7.2.3: Hospitalized Voters
Special absentee voting procedures exist for voters who cannot appear at 
their polling places on Election Day because they have been hospitalized. 
Hospitalized voters appoint an agent to conduct the absentee ballot request 
and delivery process, as well as the voter registration process (if needed), on the 
voter’s behalf. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(a)1. and 2.
This section provides an overview of this process, but hospitalized voters, their 
agents, and municipal clerks serving these voters should also carefully review 
the Commission’s Hospitalized Voter Guide for full procedures.
Best Practice: Municipal clerks should share a copy of this section of 
the manual, along with the Hospitalized Voters Guide with any local 
hospitals ahead of an Election Day so that hospital staff know there is a 
resource to provide voters who ask how they might be able to vote. The 
clerk may also refer voters or agents with questions to this form, as well 
as this section of the manual.
Deadlines
The hospitalized voter may not request a ballot by agent more than 7 days 
before an election or after 5:00 p.m. on Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(c).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 12
Voter Registration (If Required)
If the voter is not registered, the voter must complete a Voter Registration 
Application and provide proof of residence. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(a)2. If the voter 
is hospitalized in a location that is not their residence, they should not register 
to vote in the jurisdiction where the hospital is located. Instead, they should 
register in the jurisdiction of where they actually reside.
The voter’s agent must bring the completed Voter Registration Application and 
proof of residence to the clerk with the application for the absentee ballot and 
the voter’s photo ID. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(a)2.
Procedures for Making the Absentee Ballot Request by Agent
The hospitalized voter must complete an Absentee Ballot Request Form, and the 
hospitalized voter must send their proof of identification with the agent to the 
municipal clerk unless the voter is a confidential voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(a)1. 
The agent must provide their name, signature and address in Section 7 of the 
absentee application.
The agent for the hospitalized voter then must deliver the voter’s completed 
absentee ballot application and proof of identity, along with any registration 
form and proof of residence, to the municipal clerk for the hospitalized voter’s 
municipality of residence. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(a) and (b). See the Commission’s 
Proof of Residence (POR) vs. Proof of Identification (POI) page for more 
information about acceptable forms that the agent can bring to the clerk.
An agent must provide the agent’s own proof of identification before the 
municipal clerk may issue an absentee ballot to the agent on behalf of 
the voter. The clerk should ensure that the identification matches the 
information on the application. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(b). The clerk must also 
initial the application form and indicate that the voter’s proof of identity was 
provided. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(a).
Best Practice: The clerk may initial in the space next to 
“Temporarily Hospitalized Voters Only” and write “POI provided.”
Issuing the Voter’s Absentee Ballot via Agent
If the forms have been properly completed, the voter’s proof of identification 
conforms to the information on the absentee application form, and the voter is 
qualified to vote, the municipal clerk must issue an absentee ballot, absentee 
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 13
certificate envelope–checking the box that ID was provided–and uniform 
instructions in an absentee carrier envelope to the agent for the hospitalized 
voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(b).
Best Practice: The clerk should inform the agent concerning how best 
to return the completed certificate envelope, including informing the 
agent of the voter’s polling place location or, if applicable, “central 
count” location.
Facilitating the Voting of the Ballot
The agent then must transport the absentee ballot to the hospitalized voter, 
who may then vote the ballot in the presence of a witness. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(c). 
The agent may also be the witness provided the agent is a voter and not a 
candidate. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(2).
The hospitalized voter then places the voted ballot in the absentee certificate 
envelope, seals and signs the envelope. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(c). The witness signs 
the envelope and provides their printed name and address. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(2).
Returning the Voter’s Absentee Ballot
The agent must deliver or mail the absentee certificate envelope to the 
municipal clerk. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(c).
For in person delivery on Election Day the certificate envelope must be returned 
by the agent directly to the voter’s polling place or a board of absentee ballot 
canvassers location by 8:00 p.m.
Important: Due to the limited timeframe by which hospitalized voters 
can request absentee ballots under this process (within 1 week of 
Election Day), agents should not attempt to return the voter’s absentee 
ballot by mail. Instead, the agent should deliver the voter’s ballot in 
person, either to the municipal clerk or directly to the voter’s polling 
place or “central count” location.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 14
What if the Hospitalized Voter Needs Assistance Due to a Disability?
If the hospitalized voter is unable to sign the registration or absentee ballot 
request due to physical disability, they may authorize an assistant — who must 
be an elector — to sign on their behalf. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(a). The assistant 
must also sign their name in the assistant section on the Voter Registration 
Application, if needed, and the absentee ballot request form and provide their 
address. Id. The agent may also act as the assistant as long as the agent is 
a voter, meaning that the agent is qualified to vote, or the voter may choose 
another qualified individual to assist them. Id.
If the hospitalized voter is unable to mark the ballot due to disability or has 
difficulty reading, writing, or understanding English, the agent or another 
designee of the voter may assist in filling out the ballot and should sign the 
ballot as the assistant. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(5). The agent, assistant, and witness 
may be the same person, but the assistant in marking the ballot may not be 
the voter’s employer, the employer’s agent, or an officer or agent of the voter’s 
union. Id.
Maintaining Records of Hospitalized Voters
The clerk must keep a list of the names of hospitalized voters to check that the 
voters vote only once. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(c).
Best Practice: Clerks should also include the name of the agent on this 
list. Hospitalized voters will get the same Absentee Issued/Absentee 
Returned watermarks on the poll book so that poll workers will know if 
the hospitalized voter later tries to show up to vote an in person ballot.
Sec. 7.2.4: Sequestered Jurors
Similar to hospitalized voters, special absentee voting provisions exist for voters 
who may find themselves sequestered as jurors before or on Election Day.
Sequestered juries are under the order of a judge to be kept together, without 
separating, and often cannot have any contact with the world outside the 
courtroom while the trial is ongoing. See Wis. Stat. § 972.12. Merely being 
summoned for jury duty on Election Day is not sufficient for this process — the 
juror must be under an order of sequestration from a judge, which is very rare.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 15
If a voter indicates in their written request for an absentee ballot that 
they are a sequestered juror, the following special procedures apply:
 Ɋ The municipal clerk must receive the sequestered juror’s absentee 
request and proof of identification no later than 5:00 p.m. on Election Day. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(b).
 ɉ If the application is received at or before 5:00 p.m. on the Friday before 
the election, the clerk may mail the absentee ballot to the sequestered 
juror. See Id.
 Ɉ Note: The Commission cautions against using this process as 
it likely does not leave enough time for the sequestered juror to 
receive the ballot by mail, let alone complete and return it before 
8 p.m. on Election Day.
 ɉ If the application is received after 5:00 p.m. on the Friday before the 
election the clerk or the clerk’s agent must immediately take the ballot 
to the court in which the voter is serving as a juror and deliver the ballot 
to the judge. The judge must recess court, as soon as convenient, and 
give the voter the ballot. The clerk or agent must wait to receive the 
ballot back from the voter. Id.
 Ɉ The judge then must serve as witness for the sequestered juror and 
return the voted ballot to the clerk or clerk’s agent. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 16
Chapter 7.3: Types of 
Absentee Voters: SVDs
Sec. 7.3.1: Introduction
The Wisconsin Legislature has established a separate absentee voting process 
for individuals residing in Residential Care Facilities such as nursing homes, 
community-based residential facilities (CBRFs), qualified retirement homes, 
residential care apartment complexes (RCACs), and adult family homes. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.875. If an individual residing in one of these facilities requests an 
absentee ballot, it will first be brought to the voter by Special Voting Deputies, 
who are specially trained election officials who will act as witnesses for the voter 
and may provide assistance if the voter requests assistance. Id.
Sec. 7.3.2: Key Definitions
Adult Family Home: A facility that is certified or licensed to operate as an adult 
family home under Wis. Stat. §§ 50.032 or 50.033. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(1)(ab).
Community-Based Residential Facility (CBRF): A facility licensed under Wis. 
Stat. § 50.01(1g), except that it must be occupied by at least 10 unrelated adults 
who are not related to the operator or administrator. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(1)(ae).
Nursing Home: A facility occupied by 10 or more unrelated individuals for 
the primary purpose of obtaining full-time personal or nursing care which is 
necessitated by their physical or mental conditions, but does not include a 
hospital. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(1)(am).
Note:  This definition of nursing home is different than that  
in Wis. Stat. § 50.01(3).
Proof of Residence: A document listed under Wis. Stat. § 6.34(3) that shows 
where the individual resides. Regarding SVD voting, a resident of a Residential 
Care Facility may use a contract or intake document specifying that the 
individual currently resides in the facility. Wis. Stat. § 6.34(3)(a)12.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 17
Qualified Retirement Home, Retirement Home: A Retirement Home is a facility 
occupied as a primary place of abode by 10 or more unrelated individuals. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(1)(c). The clerk is not required to send SVDs to a Retirement 
Home, however, the municipal clerk or board of election commissioners 
may determine that SVDs will be sent to the Retirement Home if a significant 
number of the occupants lack adequate transportation to the appropriate 
polling place, need assistance in voting, are aged 60 or over, or are declared 
as indefinitely confined voters. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(1)(at), (2)(c). The clerk’s 
decision to send SVDs to a “Retirement Home” makes it a “Qualified Retirement 
Home.” Id.
Relative: A spouse or individual related within the 1st, 2nd or 3rd degree of kinship 
under Wis. Stat. § 990.001(16), as illustrated in the table below. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(1)(b).
Table 12: Degrees of Kinship
Kinship Relative
1st degree The voter’s children or parents
2nd degree The voter’s grandparents, grandchildren, 
brothers and sisters
3rd degree The voter’s great-grandparents, great 
grandchildren, uncles, aunts, nephews, nieces
Residential Care Apartment Complex: A facility that is certified or registered to operate as a residential care apartment complex under Wis. Stat. § 50.034. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(1)(asm).
Residential Care Facility: An adult family home, community-based residential 
facility, nursing home or residential care apartment complex. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(1)(bm).
Retirement Home: A facility occupied as a primary place of abode by ten or 
more unrelated individuals. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(1)(c).
Same Grounds: To determine whether a retirement home that is not a qualified 
retirement home is located on the “same grounds” as one or more residential 
care facilities. A clerk may look at several factors, including (but not limited to) 
whether the facilities are under the same ownership, whether they were built at 
the same time, whether their services are coordinated, or whether they are in 
the same geographic vicinity. See Wis. Stat. § 6.875(3)(b).
Note: Facilities do not need to be on the same parcel of land or on 
the same side of the street to be considered on the same grounds.  
See Wis. Stat. § 6.875(3)(b).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 18
Special Voting Deputies (SVDs): Individuals appointed by a municipal clerk 
or board of elections to conduct absentee voting at certain care facilities. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4).
Working Day: Any day except Saturday, Sunday and the holidays listed below:
 Ɋ January 1 (New Years’ Day)
 Ɋ Third Monday in January (MLK Day)
 Ɋ Last Monday in May (Memorial Day)
 Ɋ July 4 (Fourth of July)
 Ɋ First Monday in September (Labor Day)
 Ɋ Fourth Thursday in November (Thanksgiving Day)
 Ɋ December 24 (Christmas Eve)
 Ɋ December 25 (Christmas Day)
 Ɋ December 31 (New Years’ Eve)
The day following if January 1, July 4 or December 25 falls on Sunday.
Wis. Stat. §§ 6.875(1)(d), 227.01(14), and 230.35(4)(a).
Sec. 7.3.3: Who are Special 
Voting Deputies?
Special Voting Deputies (SVDs) are appointed by the municipal clerk to bring 
absentee ballots to residential care facilities and qualified retirement homes. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(a). The two major political parties may submit a list of 
nominees to the municipal clerk. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(b). If lists are submitted, 
then SVDs who represent each of the political parties must be selected from 
the lists, and those appointed as SVDs serve the same two-year term as other 
election officials. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(a). A clerk may revoke an appointment at 
any time. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(b).
Best Practice: Notify the two political parties before November of 
each odd numbered year if there are any residential care facilities 
or qualified retirement homes in your municipality and provide an 
estimate of how many SVDs you are likely to need from each party.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 19
Requirements to be an SVD:
 Ɋ Must be a qualified voter of the county. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
 Ɋ Must attend training. Wis. Stat. § 7.315(1)(b)1.
 Ɋ May not currently be employed by the facility. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(b).
 Ɋ May not have been employed by the facility within two years of the 
appointment. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(b).
 Ɋ May not be an immediate family member of anyone employed by the 
facility within two years of the appointment. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(b).
 Ɋ Must take the Oath of Special Voting Deputy (EL-155). Wis. Stat. § 6.875(5).
Though there is not a specific deadline by which a clerk must appoint SVDs, the 
SVDs will serve all elections within the period of a two-year election official term, 
spanning January 1 of an even numbered year and ending on December 31 of 
the following odd numbered year. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.875(4)(b), 7.30(6)(a), 7.315(1)(b)1.
Sec. 7.3.4: What are the SVD 
Training Requirements?
Before serving at any election, Special Voting Deputies must attend at least one 
training program every two years and must have attended training within two 
years of any election at which they serve beginning on January 1 of each even-
numbered year and ending on December 31 of the following odd-numbered 
year. Wis. Stat. § 7.315(1)(b)1. A Special Voting Deputy may not deputize other 
individuals to administer the voting process. See Wis. Stat. §§ 6.875. A clerk, if 
necessary, may appoint an individual who has not received training if, due to 
sickness, injury, or other unforeseen occurrence, a trained SVD is unavailable to 
serve at an election. Wis. Stat. § 7.315(1)(b)2. Such an appointment may only be 
for a specific election, and no individual appointed may be appointed to serve 
again within an election period without receiving training. Id.
Sec. 7.3.5: When are SVDs Required?
Municipal clerks are required to use SVDs in residential care facilities (see above 
definitions) if there are at least five registered voters of the municipality who 
are occupants of the facility and if the clerk has at least one absentee ballot 
application from an occupant of the facility. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(a), (am).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 20
Retirement homes may be served by SVDs if the municipal clerk makes the 
retirement home into a qualified retirement home by determining that a 
significant number of the occupants lack adequate transportation to the 
appropriate polling place, need assistance in voting, are aged 60 or over, or 
are declared as indefinitely confined voters. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(2)(c).
However, once the clerk has made this determination, the qualified retirement 
home will require SVD service for all elections until the clerk makes a contrary 
formal determination as to the facility’s eligibility for future SVD service. See 
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(1)(at), (2)(c).
Best Practice: Clerks should not switch a retirement home’s SVD 
eligibility in the period between a partisan primary and a general 
election, between a spring primary and a spring election, or between 
a special primary and a special election. The decision to make a 
retirement home a qualified retirement home is significant for all 
individuals who are occupants of the facility, and the Commission 
recommends carefully looking into the issue before making the 
designation, including consulting with the administrator of the facility.
The Commission recommends that designations changing a 
retirement home into a qualified retirement home, and vice versa, 
be communicated to the administrator of the facility in writing so 
that the administrator can properly inform the facility’s occupants 
regarding any change in status. Clerks, or a clerk’s provider, should 
also immediately make this change in WisVote.
If a municipal clerk is uncertain if there are any licensed facilities in their 
municipality or whether a certain facility qualifies for service by SVDs, check 
facility directories on the Wisconsin Department of Health Services website, 
which are updated monthly. Then search the facility address in WisVote 
to identify voters registered at the facility and see if any of them have an 
absentee request on file.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 21
These links may be helpful in identifying facilities:
 Ɋ Adult Family Home Directory
 Ɋ Community Based Residential Facility Directory
 Ɋ Residential Care Apartment Complex Directory
 Ɋ Nursing Home Directory
Once a municipal clerk has identified all qualifying facilities in their jurisdiction, 
the clerk should also understand the size and scope of each facility. For 
example, a Residential Care Facility encompasses the area or location that 
is defined by the license which governs its operations. There may be several 
facilities along with a Retirement or Qualified Retirement Home within a single 
building or complex located, for instance, on separate floors or in separate 
wings. It is important for a clerk to be aware of the different types of facilities 
to ensure that SVDs are being sent to the correct places.
Sec. 7.3.6: Arranging for the SVD Visit
The municipal clerk should arrange one or more convenient times with 
the administrator of each residential care facility and qualified retirement 
home to conduct absentee voting for the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(a). 
Though the statute says that SVDs themselves shall arrange the visits, 
the Commission strongly recommends that municipal clerks take on all 
scheduling duties, contact all such administrators in advance of the sixth 
Monday before an election to schedule the dates and times of all visits, 
ideally within the first allowable week of SVD voting.
Deadlines
The administrator of the facility must be contacted no later than 5:00 p.m. 
on the sixth working day before an election.  Id. Absentee voting may be 
conducted no earlier than the fourth Monday before the election and no 
later than 5:00 p.m. on the Monday before the election.  Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 22
Best Practice: Neither municipal clerks nor SVDs should wait until the 
statutory deadline of six business days before Election Day to contact 
the administrators of the qualifying facilities to set up SVD visits. 
Doing so, while legally permitted, creates a very short timeline for SVD 
voting, which could risk disenfranchising voters if something does not 
go to plan, and may affect residents’ abilities to cast a vote due to 
absence or illness.
Understand Facility Types and Make Lists 
of Eligible & Ineligible SVD Voters
If there are any retirement homes that are not qualified retirement homes on 
the same grounds as a residential care facility the municipal clerk must obtain 
a list of names and addresses of the retirement home occupants, who cannot 
vote with the SVDs, from the retirement home administrator to provide to the 
SVDs so that the SVDs know who is not able to cast a ballot when they serve the 
qualified locations. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(3)(b). See Same Grounds under Definitions.
Compile a List of Voters with Absentee 
Requests on File for Administrators
Best Practice: The municipal clerk should compile a list of occupants 
at the facility who have absentee ballot requests on file before 
contacting the facility administrator. This list should be shared with 
the facility administrator. The social worker for the facility may be 
consulted if there is a question of voter competency. The administrator 
should survey the occupants on the list to inform them of the date 
and time of the SVDs’ visit. The administrator should also note on 
the list which individuals will be able to meet the SVDs for voting and 
which are unable or unwilling to meet the SVDs at the designated 
time. Early, detailed communication between municipal clerks and 
facility administrators will make the SVD voting process much easier to 
administer.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 23
Sec. 7.3.7: Public Notice of SVD Visits
As soon as possible after arrangements are made for the visit, but no less 
than five working days before the visit, the municipal clerk shall prepare, 
post, and distribute a notice detailing the date and time of the visit and that 
absentee voting by SVDs will take place at that facility (see Sample Notice). 
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(a). The notice must be posted at the facility and on the 
municipality’s internet site, provided to those news media who have filed a 
written request for such notice, to the municipality’s official newspaper or, if 
none exists, to a news medium likely to give notice in the area. Wis. Stat.  
§§ 6.875(6)(a) and 19.84(1) and (2). A municipality that does not have an 
internet site may instead post the notice in three public places likely to give 
notice to people affected, or by a paid publication in a newspaper likely to 
give notice. Wis. Stat. § § 6.875(6)(a) and 19.84(1)(b).
Best Practice: Notice of multiple visits to a facility may be made  
and posted at the same time.
Upon the request of a relative of an occupant of a qualified retirement home or 
residential care facility, the administrator may notify the relative of the time or 
times at which SVDs will conduct absentee voting and permit the relative to be 
present in the room where the voting is conducted. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)2.
Sec. 7.3.8: Qualifying to Vote by SVD
Any qualified voter who for any reason is unable or unwilling to appear at the 
polling place on Election Day may vote by absentee ballot. Wis. Stat. § 6.85. A 
qualified voter is a United States citizen, age 18 or older on Election Day, who 
has resided in an election district for 28 consecutive days before Election Day 
and is not currently serving a felony sentence (including any term of extended 
supervision) or has not been adjudicated incompetent to vote. Wis. Stat. 
§§ 6.02(1), 6.03.
Adjudications of incompetency to vote are only made by a judge after a 
court proceeding. Wis. Stat. § 6.03(3). It is not a medical or family decision or a 
determination of facility staff. If a person has a guardian appointed to them, the 
guardianship order must specifically indicate that the person’s right to vote has 
been removed, otherwise they retain their right to vote. See Wis. Stat. § 54.25. 
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 24
If an individual has been adjudicated incompetent to vote, that information is 
provided to their clerk or the Wisconsin Elections Commission, and the clerk 
may then inactivate the registration. See Wis. Stat. §§ 6.03(1)(a) and 6.325.
Sec. 7.3.9: Voter Registration Required
Occupants of care facilities must be registered to vote prior to being issued an 
absentee ballot. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(3)(a).
Deadlines & Registration Methods
If an individual is not registered to vote, or now resides at the residential 
care facility or qualified retirement home and is not registered at that 
address, the individual may register to vote a variety of ways:
 Ɋ A qualified voter may register to vote by mail no later than the third 
Wednesday before an election. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.28(1)(a) and 6.30(4).
 Ɋ A voter may also register in-person at the municipal clerk’s office until 5:00 
p.m. the Friday before the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.29(2).
 Ɋ Voters may also register to vote in-person at the polling place on Election 
Day. Wis. Stat. § 6.55(2).
 Ɋ Election Registration Officials (EROs) may be assigned by the municipal 
clerk to register individuals at qualified care facilities and retirement 
homes until the third Wednesday before an election. Wis. Stat. § 6.28(1)(a).
Note: The Election Registration Official registration window only 
overlaps with the Special Voting Deputy window for three days.
 Ɋ See Chapter 14.6: “Election Day Registration” for more information on 
these registration options.
Best Practice: Schedule at least one SVD visit during the first three 
allowable days of SVD voting and appoint SVDs as EROs, so that they can 
register residents of the facility if necessary. Alternatively, it can be helpful 
to appoint a staff member of the facility as an ERO so they can register 
occupants to vote as they move to the facility throughout the year.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 25
Proof of Residence Required
Occupants of care facilities are required to present proof of residence when 
registering to vote. Wis. Stat. § 6.34(2). For more information on the variety of 
proof of residence documents, please see the voter registration section. Notably, 
an intake document at a residential care facility can be used as proof of 
residence. Wis. Stat. § 6.34(3)(a)12.
Note: When registering an occupant of a residential care facility, be 
sure that the voter registers at the proper address, which is where the 
voter resides. See Wis. Stat. § 6.10(1). While this may be the address of 
the residential care facility, it may also be another address within the 
municipality if the individual intends to return to that address. See 
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(3)(a). Further, the individual’s residence might be 
outside of the municipality, in which case the individual will need to 
register with that municipal clerk.
Sec. 7.3.10: Making the Absentee 
Ballot Request with SVDs
Any voter wishing to vote absentee at an election must make a written request 
to the municipal clerk or board of election commissioners. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(3)(a).  
See Chapter 7.6: “Proof of Identification for Absentee Voting” on page 107 for 
information on submitting a written request for an absentee ballot to a municipal 
clerk. Unique to SVD voting, the SVDs are also able to accept an application for an 
absentee ballot by a voter who has not properly filed one with the municipal clerk 
and issue a ballot to that voter provided they complete a sufficient application 
and otherwise qualifies. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1. With a single application, a voter 
may request an absentee ballot for a single election, all elections in a calendar 
year or as an indefinitely confined voter, which leads to ballots being sent for 
all future elections until the request is deactivated. with a single application. 
Wis. Stat. §§ 6.86(1), (2), (2m) and 6.875(3)(a).
SVDs are the exclusive method by which absentee voting in person may be 
conducted within a qualified retirement home or residential care facility. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.875(2)(a). This means if a municipal clerk receives an application 
for an absentee ballot from an occupant of such a home or facility, the clerk 
must send the ballots with the SVDs and cannot send it, initially, by mail.  
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(a). 
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 26
Alternatively, occupants of such a home or facility may vote by absentee 
ballot at the clerk’s office or alternate absentee voting site, or at the polls on 
Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(a). If an occupant’s residence is somewhere 
other than the facility or home, the voter may also apply for an absentee ballot 
by mail at that residence. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(ar)2.
Occupants of retirement homes that are not qualified retirement homes, 
meaning that they are not served by SVDs, may not vote with SVDs, and may 
vote using the methods available to all other voters within the municipality. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(3)(b). If a retirement home is located on the same grounds as 
one or more residential care facilities served by the SVDs, the municipal clerk 
must obtain from the management of the retirement home a list of the names 
and addresses of occupants, and provide that list to the SVDs to ensure that 
only occupants of the correct facilities are voting with the SVDs.  Id.
Sec. 7.3.11: Application by an 
Indefinitely Confined Voter
Many occupants of the facilities visited by SVDs may qualify as “indefinitely 
confined voters,” which means they are confined indefinitely due to age, physical 
illness, infirmity, or because they are otherwise disabled for an indefinite period. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2)(a). To qualify, the voter must determine that he or she is 
indefinitely confined and complete an absentee ballot application certifying 
that fact to the municipal clerk. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(2)(a). See Chapter 7.3: “Types of 
Absentee Voters: SVDs” on page 17 regarding the processes for requesting 
an absentee ballot as an indefinitely confined voter and how the list of such 
voters is maintained. Once a proper application is received, the municipal clerk 
will automatically send the voter an absentee ballot for each election. Id.
Indefinitely confined voters residing in a home or facility served by SVDs 
must receive their absentee ballot from the SVDs rather than by mail.  
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(a).
Sec. 7.3.12: Proof of 
Identification Exemption
Voters who cast absentee ballots with SVDs are exempt from providing proof 
of photo identification when making their absentee ballot request because the 
SVDs verify the voter’s address. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 27
Absentee Voter Residing in a Care Facility or 
Qualified Retirement Home Served by SVDs
Voters living in residential care facilities or qualified retirement homes who 
vote with SVDs are not required to provide proof of identification, regardless of 
whether the resident has applied for ballots as indefinitely confined. Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.875(6)(c)1.
The signatures of both SVDs in the “Certification of Witness” section on the 
EL-122SVD Absentee Ballot Certification envelope verifies that the name and 
address of the voter is correct, which satisfies the photo ID requirement. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1. However, if the voter does submit an acceptable photo ID, 
the SVDs must make a copy of the ID and enclose it in the certificate envelope. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1. State law does not specify any required steps to verify 
the voter’s name or address, so the SVDs or witness can use any available 
information to verify the voter’s name and address are correct as shown on the 
absentee certificate envelope. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1.
Note: Often times, this can be as simple as verifying the voter’s name 
and checking to see that the voter’s address is the home or facility 
address.
Figure 1: SVD Certification of Witness 
 
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 28
Voters Living at Facilities Not Served by SVDs
A voter who has requested an absentee ballot as an indefinitely confined voter 
and who is living at home, at a residential care facility, or at a retirement home 
not visited by SVDs, only needs the signature and address of a witness to satisfy 
the photo ID requirement because the EL-122 Standard Absentee Certificate 
Envelope contains the name and address of the voter and the witness verifies 
that the information on the certificate is correct. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)2.
Similarly, a voter at a residential care facility or at a retirement home not visited 
by SVDs who has not changed his or her name or residence and has previously 
provided a proof of identification for an absentee ballot is not required to provide 
it again in order to receive another absentee ballot, and therefore should also 
receive the EL-122 Standard Absentee Certificate Envelope. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)3.
Special Circumstance Requiring EL-122SP Certificate Envelope
A voter who is an occupant of a residential care facility or qualified retirement 
home that is not served by SVDs who has not applied as indefinitely confined, 
has not previously provided photo ID for an absentee ballot received at that 
address, and has not provided a photo ID with the current request should 
be sent the EL-122SP Absentee Certificate Envelope with their ballot. Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.87(4)(b)5. The EL-122SP Absentee Certificate Envelope contains a certification 
of care facility authorized representative section in step 4, which satisfies the 
photo ID requirement. Id. The Representative may also serve as the witness. See 
Wis. Stat. § 6.87(2).
Figure 2: Care Facility Certification of Witness
Best Practice: Because this circumstance is rare, instead of keeping 
an inventory of EL-122SP envelopes, the text of the envelope may be 
downloaded from the Commission website, cut to fit, and taped or 
glued onto an EL-122 standard envelope as needed.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 29
Sec. 7.3.13: Establishing Residence
Like any other voter, a person living in a residential care facility or qualified 
retirement home for at least 28 consecutive days before any election, who 
considers the residential care facility or qualified retirement home their 
permanent residence, must register to vote using the facility or retirement home 
address if the individual desires to vote. See Wis. Stat. § 6.02(1), 6.10(1). If such a 
voter requests an absentee ballot by mail, the ballot will be sent as described in 
this chapter. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(3)(a).
Such a voter may also vote in person at the voter’s polling place, or in person at an 
In Person Absentee Voting site in the voter’s municipality. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(ar)1.
Voters Temporarily Residing in Qualifying 
Care Facilities & Retirement Homes
A voter who is temporarily residing in a residential care facility or qualified 
retirement home may continue to vote using the address of the voter’s 
permanent residence, so long as he or she continues to have an intent to return 
to that residence. Wis. Stat. § 6.10(5) and (8), and 6.875(3)(a). Voters temporarily 
residing in a residential care facility or qualified retirement home may vote in 
person at the voter’s polling place, or in person at an In Person Absentee Voting 
site in the voter’s municipality. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(ar)1. Such a voter may also 
apply for and receive an absentee ballot by mail at the voter’s permanent 
residence. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(4)(ar)2. Finally, if the voter wishes for an absentee 
ballot to be delivered to the residential care facility or qualified retirement home 
where they are temporarily residing, and that facility is served by SVDs, the SVDs 
must bring the ballot of that voter’s residence when they make their visits. See 
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(3)(a) and (4)(a).
Example: The voter lives in Partyville but is temporarily residing in Safe Haven 
Care Facility. If Safe Haven is served by SVDs, the SDVs serving Safe Haven must 
coordinate with the Partyville municipal clerk and bring a Partyville ballot to the 
voter at Safe Haven.
If a clerk receives an absentee ballot application from a resident of the clerk’s 
municipality who temporarily resides in a residential care facility or qualified 
retirement home served by SVDs located in another municipality and the 
request asks that the ballot be sent to that home or facility, the clerk must send 
the absentee ballot to the municipal clerk where the facility or home is located 
for delivery to the voter by the SVDs. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(3)(a). 
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 30
If a clerk receives an absentee ballot application from a voter living in a 
residential care facility or qualified retirement home located in the clerk’s 
municipality, but who is a registered voter of another municipality, the clerk 
must, as soon as possible, notify the clerk of the municipality in which the voter 
is registered, and request that an absentee ballot be issued to the voter living 
in the facility and sent to the municipal clerk for the facility for delivery by the 
SVDs. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(3)(a).
Best Practice: Put simply, a voter temporarily residing in a facility or 
home served by SVDs might send an absentee ballot request either 
to the clerk of the municipality of the facility or home, or to the voter’s 
own municipal clerk. State law requires either request to be honored, 
and if this happens, the clerk receiving the request should immediately 
contact the other clerk and arrange for the voter’s ballot to be sent 
from the voter’s municipal clerk to the clerk of the facility or home, who 
will then send the ballot to the voter via the SVDs.
Sec. 7.3.14: Relatives
Relatives of voters who are eligible to vote with SVDs might understandably 
have many questions about the voting process for their loved ones. If a relative 
of a voter who is an occupant of a residential care facility or qualified retirement 
home asks the administrator of the facility or home when SVD voting will occur, 
the administrator may notify the relative concerning the date and time of the 
SVD visits, and also permit the relative to be present in the room where voting 
is conducted. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)2. Upon the request of the voter, a relative 
who is present in the room may assist the voter in marking the ballot, however, 
the relative cannot witness the ballot, as all SVD delivered ballots must be 
witnessed by the SVDs. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 31
Best Practice: Some relatives of voters residing in residential care 
facilities or qualified retirement homes served by SVDs may express 
concerns that the relative must vote absentee in this manner. In such 
cases, clerks, facility administrators, and SVDs should explain to the 
relative that this method of voting is required by law if the resident has 
requested an absentee ballot. Relatives should be informed that they 
may be present when the SVDs conduct absentee voting at the facility, 
and that they may assist the voter if the voter so requests. The resident 
also has the option to vote at the polling place or in the municipal 
clerk’s office rather than with the SVDs. If the voter’s permanent 
residence is a different location than the home or facility, the voter 
may also request that an absentee ballot be sent to that address.
Sec. 7.3.15: Rules for Observers
The SVDs may exercise the authority granted to the chief inspector under Wis. 
Stat. § 7.41 to regulate the conduct of observers. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1, Wis. 
Admin. Code § EL 4.05(4). See Sec. 7.3.15: “Rules for Observers” on page 32 
concerning the general rules for election observers that apply to all observable 
locations. There are several specific rules for observation of homes and facilities 
served by SVDs, which will be detailed here. See Wis. Admin. Code Chapter EL 4.
Best Practice: Clerks should ensure that all SVDs are familiar with Wis. 
Admin. Code EL 4 and provide 2 copies of the chapter for each pair of 
SVDs to distribute to any observers that may accompany them.
One election observer from each of the two recognized political parties 
whose candidate for governor or president received the greatest number 
of votes in the municipality at the most recent general election may 
accompany the SVDs to each facility where and when absentee voting will 
take place. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(7), Wis. Admin. Code § EL 4.05(4 )(a) and (b). Each 
party wishing to have an observer present must submit the name of the 
observer to the municipal clerk no later than the close of business on the 
last business day prior to the visit. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(7), Wis. Admin. Code  
§ EL 4.05(4)(a). Except for family members, no other observers may be present 
during absentee voting conducted by SVDs. See Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)2. and 
(7), Wis. Admin. Code EL 4.05(4) .
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 32
All observers must comply with the requirements imposed on visitors by a facility 
served by SVDs. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 4.05(4)(c). Observers may observe the 
process of absentee ballot distribution in the common areas of the home or  
facility, but they cannot enter a voter’s private room. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 4.05(4)(d). 
Further, a voter may opt to close his or her door or otherwise secure his or her 
voting privacy. Id. The SVDs may not permit observers to hear any discussion 
concerning the electoral choices of the voter, and SVDs must in all cases 
enforce the voter’s constitutional right to cast a secret ballot. If there is an issue 
with an observer causing a disturbance, both SVDs must agree that an observer 
should be removed, and the steps laid out in Wis. Admin. Code Chapter EL 4 
must be followed.
Best Practice: The Commission found that the municipal clerk, under 
Wis. Stat. §§ 6.875(6)(b) and 7.41(3), possesses the authority to remove 
an observer from an SVD site if the observer disrupts the operation of 
the site or violates the prohibitions against electioneering or posting 
election related materials.
Note: Because a municipal clerk may need to appoint multiple SVDs to 
conduct all absentee voting within a municipality or send more than 
one team of SVDs to a given facility, there may be more than two total 
observers allowed to participate. Each pair of SVDs assigned to conduct 
absentee voting may be accompanied by an observer from each party.
Sec. 7.3.16: Challenges to Voters 
in Residential Care Facilities, 
Qualified Retirement Homes
Challenges to a voter’s eligibility may not be made at the facility but must be 
made at the municipal clerk’s office or at the polling place or board of absentee 
ballot canvassers meeting on Election Day when the voter’s ballot is processed 
by the election officials. See Wis. Stat. §§ 6.48 and 6.93, Wis. Admin. Code EL 9. See 
Sec. 7.7.3: “Absentee Ballot Applications, Verification Process” on page 111 for 
more information concerning challenges to voter registrations and ballots.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 33
Sec. 7.3.17: Delivery of 
Ballots and Voting
Absentee ballots are brought to the care facility by the SVDs. Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.875(4)(at), (6)(c)1. The municipal clerk (or deputy clerk or board of election 
commissioners) shall issue to the SVDs a specific number of absentee ballots 
sufficient to provide for the number of absentee ballot applications received 
from residents of the care facility and an additional number of ballots and EL-121 
absentee ballot applications to handle any requests the SVDs may receive from 
other qualified occupants of the facility. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(b) and (6)(c)1. The 
municipal clerk should initial all ballots given to the SVDs. See Wis. Stat. § 6.87(1). 
The clerk must keep a record of the number of ballots issued to the SVDs. Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.875(6)(b). If unused ballots are left over, they must be returned to the municipal 
clerk along with all voted ballots. Id.
Best Practices: The Commission has designed a form, the EL-104SVD Log 
of Voting Activity, to best facilitate required record keeping of SVD voting 
and to ensure there is a chain of custody for the absentee ballots. SVDs 
should complete the EL-104SVD at the home or facility. The municipal 
clerk or board of election commissioners should issue all ballots to be 
used by the SVDs in a ballot container or envelope that is secured with 
a tamper-evident serialized tag or seal. The municipal clerk or board 
of election commissioners should record the number of the serialized 
tag or seal on the EL-104SVD. The SVDs should also be issued another 
tamper-evident serialized tag or seal to secure the container after the 
facility visit is complete. See Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(d). The number of this 
second serialized tag or seal should also be recorded on the EL-104SVD 
by the SVDs after the facility visit is complete. Both SVDs should verify 
the seal or tag number and that the seal or tag is intact before opening 
the ballot container. The SVDs should indicate that this verification was 
completed by initialing the respective section of the EL-104SVD. Upon 
opening the ballot container, the SVDs should confirm the total number 
of issued ballots is the same as the number indicated on the EL-104SVD 
and that they have the correct ballot styles, including for any voters who 
are not residents of the municipality. During the facility visit, both SVDs 
are jointly responsible for the security of the ballots issued to them and 
shall keep the opened ballot container in their presence at all times.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 34
Voting Procedure
Two SVDs shall visit the facility at the time designated in the posted notice. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(a). The SVDs shall conduct absentee voting as a team. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1. Both SVDs, together, shall personally offer each 
absentee voter who has filed the proper application an opportunity to cast his 
or her ballot. Id.
Note: Clerks with large care facilities in their municipalities may 
benefit from sending multiple pairs of SVDs, working in teams of two, 
in order to reach all voters in the facility in a timely manner. Facility 
staff may be of assistance in announcing the arrival of the SVDs and in 
identifying voters who will need assistance voting in the voter’s private 
room, but staff many not handle ballots or assist in the voting process. 
See generally, Wis. Stat. §§ 6.875, and 6.875(6)(c)1.
Best Practice: Voting should be conducted in a common area of the facility.
Visiting Voter Rooms
The SVDs shall also visit the room of each occupant with an absentee ballot 
request on file who does not arrive at the common area where voting was 
conducted to offer the voter a ballot or to confirm that the voter does not wish 
to vote in the election. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.875(4)(at) (“shall personally deliver the 
ballot to the elector” and (6)(c)1. (“shall personally offer each elector who has 
filed a proper application for an absentee ballot the opportunity to cast his or 
her absentee ballot”).
Note: This includes visiting the rooms of occupants who already have 
informed the administrator (or staff member) of the facility of their 
intent not to vote because the requirement is for the SVDs to offer 
the voter a ballot. This does not mean that SVDs may enter a voter’s 
private room without being invited in, but that the SVDs must go to the 
room to inquire if the voter wishes to vote the ballot. If the voter does 
not answer, or does not indicate that the voter wishes to vote a ballot, 
the SVDs can conclude that the voter has declined to vote the ballot 
during that visit.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 35
The SVDs should also visit the rooms of any occupants who have informed 
facility staff of their intent to vote, but whose names do not appear on the 
absentee ballot log. See Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1.The SVDs may accept a 
written request for an absentee ballot from a registered, qualified voter and 
conduct in-person absentee voting for the voter while at the qualified care 
facility. Id. The SVDs should offer such a voter an EL-121  
form to complete and ensure that applications are returned to the clerk 
when received. See Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(d).
Arranging a Second Visit of SVDs
The clerk must arrange for a second visit if an occupant is unable to vote at 
the time scheduled for the first visit due to any reason, including a quarantine, 
or if the clerk receives a new absentee application after the first visit. Wis. Stat. 
§§ 6.875(4)(at) and (6)(e). The Commission strongly recommends scheduling 
and noticing two visits in advance as part of the initial communication with 
the facility administrator as described above. If a requesting occupant has not 
voted with the SVDs after the second SVD visit but has not formally declined to 
vote the ballot as described below, the municipal clerk may mail the absentee 
ballot to the occupant of the facility in the same manner as other absentee 
ballots are mailed. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(e). Such a voter needing to be mailed 
a ballot who has not applied as an indefinitely confined voter and has not 
previously submitted proof of identification to the clerk for an absentee ballot 
at that address will need to provide photo ID or reapply as an indefinitely 
confined voter if they qualify. See Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)5.
Best Practice: For this reason, the Commission recommends that 
anyone in a qualified retirement home or residential care facility either 
apply as an indefinitely confined voter if they qualify and wish to 
receive ballots for each election, or provide an acceptable photo ID.
Voter is Entitled to Privacy to Vote
Special Voting Deputies, election observers, family members and facility staff 
must afford the voter privacy to vote his or her ballot. See Wis. Const. Art. III § 3.  
After marking the ballot in the presence of the SVDs, the voter places the 
marked ballot in the certificate envelope (EL-122SVD) and seals the envelope. 
See Wis. Stat. §§ 6.87(4)(b)1, 6.875(6)(c)1. The voter completes and signs the 
certification on the envelope. See Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 36
Completing the Certificate Envelope
Both of the SVDs must sign as witnesses on the certificate envelope.  
Wis. Stat. § § 6.87(2), 6.875(6)(c)1. The Commission finds that the SVDs may 
provide the clerk’s office address as part of the certification of witnesses 
on the certificate envelope. See Wis. Stat. § § 6.87(2), (6d), Rise, Inc. v. 
Elections Comm’n, 2024 WI App 48 ¶ 3, 413 Wis. 2d 366, 372, 11 N.W.3d 241, 244  
(finding that a witness address means “a place where the witness may be 
communicated with”). Because SVDs are appointed by the municipal clerk 
and are election officials under Wisconsin law, the municipal clerk’s office 
address is also the official address of the SVDs acting in their role as election 
officials and is a place where the SVDs may be communicated with.
Sec. 7.3.18: Best Practice: 
Voter Declines a Ballot
An indefinitely confined or calendar year voter whose name appears on the 
absentee ballot log may not wish to vote an absentee ballot but may want to 
maintain his or her status as an indefinitely confined or calendar year voter. 
See Wis. Stat. §§ 6.86(2)(b), (2m)(a). In that case, the SVDs should print the 
voter’s name on the Elector Decline of Ballot in Residential Care Facilities and 
Retirement Homes form (EL-126) in the appropriate section. Both SVDs must 
sign the form.
Any communication by a voter to decline a ballot should be between the voter 
and clerk prior to the visit by SVDs or between the voter and Special Voting 
Deputies during the visit. The municipal clerk should direct the SVDs as to which 
methods a voter may employ to decline a ballot to ensure that the voter’s 
decision has been documented and to maintain the integrity of the voting 
process in residential care facilities.
The municipal clerk may determine whether the following methods are acceptable:
 Ɋ Voter declines a ballot via telephone
 Ɋ Voter declines a ballot by signing a printed memo distributed by facility staff
 Ɋ Voter places signed note declining a ballot on door to room
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 37
Sec. 7.3.19: Persons Assisting Voters
Absentee ballots must be voted only by the absentee voter, unless the voter 
requests assistance in reading or marking the ballot or completing the absentee 
certificate envelope. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1. See Wis. Stat. § 12.13(3)(s). Generally, 
a voter may select any person (except their employer or an officer or agent of a 
labor union who represents the voter) to assist with the voting process. Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.87(5). However, when voting by SVD, assistance with these two tasks is limited 
to an SVD or a relative of the voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1.
Can SVDs Provide Assistance?
The SVDs shall assist the voter if requested. An assistor must always act under the 
direction of the voter. See Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1, Wis. Stat. § 12.13(3)(j). The SVD or 
relative providing the assistance must certify in the space provided on the ballot 
that it was completed with his or her assistance. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.87(5), 6.875(6)(c)1.
Best Practice: If assistance is required to complete the Absentee 
Certificate Envelope, the SVD or relative providing the assistance must 
certify in the space provided on the envelope that it was completed 
with his or her assistance. See Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1.
Note: There are other types of assistance that any person (except his 
or her employer or officer/agent of a labor union who represents the 
voter) may provide to a voter with a disability upon request. This person 
may assist a voter in completing election forms, such as the Voter 
Registration Application (EL-131) (Wis. Stat. § 6.33(2)(a)), Application for 
Absentee Ballot (EL-121) or letter requesting an absentee ballot (Wis. 
Stat. § 6.86(1)(ag). If the voter is unable to sign a voter registration form 
or an absentee ballot request, the voter may direct the assistor to sign 
the voter’s name to the document, and if this assistance is provided, 
the assistant must record his or her own name on the document in the 
proper field. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.33(2)(a) and 6.86(1)(ag).

Sec. 7.3.21: Return of Ballots
Upon completion of absentee voting at the facility, the SVDs shall count the 
number of voted, unvoted, and spoiled ballots, record those numbers on the 
EL-104SVD, and confirm all ballots are accounted for. See Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(d).  
Voted ballots, unvoted ballots, spoiled ballots, and any other voting materials, 
except for the EL-104SVD, are placed in the ballot container. See  Id. The 
SVDs should then re-secure the ballot container with a new tamper-evident 
serialized tag or seal, recording the number of the tag or seal on the EL-
104SVD before signing the certification section. See  Id. 
As soon as possible, but no later than 18 hours (including weekends) after 
visiting each residential care facility or qualified retirement home, the deputies 
must deliver any absentee ballot applications and the sealed certificate 
envelopes containing each ballot to the municipal clerk of the municipality in 
which the voter casting the ballot resides. Id.
Sec. 7.3.22: Special Advisory for 
Facility Administrators and Staff
In order to ensure the integrity of the absentee voting process, the Wisconsin 
Elections Commission recommends that the personnel in care facilities 
familiarize themselves with the absentee voting process. Administrators of these 
facilities should communicate regularly with the municipal clerk concerning the 
status of absentee voters at their facility. The administrator should also make 
an effort to ensure that any occupant who desires to vote is properly registered. 
Persons who are found by a court to be incapable of understanding the 
electoral process are not permitted to vote. Wis. Stat. § 6.03(1)(a), (3). The facility 
should have a social worker available who may be consulted regarding any 
competency determinations made by a court for an occupant.
Facility administrators and personnel, election observers, and occupants of 
care facilities should be aware that failure to comply with these requirements 
may result in invalidation of the votes of occupants. Wis. Stat. § 6.84(2). It is also 
a misdemeanor to interrupt or disturb the voting process. Wis. Stat. § 12.13(3)(x). It 
is a felony to impede or prevent the free exercise of voting through an agent or 
by duress or any fraudulent device or contrivance. Wis. Stat. § 12.09(2). 
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 40
If facility staff impede or do not cooperate with the SVD process, the municipal 
clerk should share this Manual section with the staff and administrator. The clerk 
may also request the assistance of Commission staff or ask the facility staff to 
contact the Commission.
Candidates are not allowed as observers in the voting area. Wis. Stat.  
§§ 6.875(6)(b), 7.41. The same restrictions on electioneering that apply to 
polling places on Election Day apply to the facility while SVDs are present, 
which means there should be no campaign activity in the facility or within 
100 feet of any entrance to the facility while voting is taking place, except 
on private property. Wis. Stat. § 12.03(2)(b)3.

Chapter 7.4: Types of 
Absentee Voters: UOCAVA
Sec. 7.4.1: Introduction
Military and overseas voters may face additional challenges when voting. 
There are many state and national laws that protect military and overseas 
individuals’ right to vote. Chief among them is the Uniformed and Overseas 
Citizens Absentee Voting Act (UOCAVA) of 1986 and the Military and Overseas 
Empowerment (“MOVE Act”) of 2009. Much of the clerk activity surrounding 
ballot requests, mailing, and receipt/processing is tracked and reported to 
the federal government so they can be sure that all states are following the 
federally mandated guidelines.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 42
Sec. 7.4.2: Sec. 7.4.2 Who are 
Military & Overseas Voters?
In Wisconsin, the term “military and overseas voters,” sometimes also referred 
to as “UOCAVA voters,” refers generally to three different types of voters:
Table 14: Examples of UOCAVA Voter Types
Type of Voter Examples
Military Voter  Ɋ Active duty services members 
stationed within the U.S. and abroad
 Ɋ Spouses
 Ɋ Dependents residing with or 
accompanying
Permanent Overseas Voters  Ɋ U.S. citizens who have moved 
permanently outside the U.S.
 Ɋ U.S. citizens born abroad whose 
parents last lived in Wisconsin
Temporary Overseas Voters  Ɋ Wisconsin voters who are 
temporarily outside the U.S.
 Ɋ Study abroad students
 Ɋ Vacationers
 Ɋ Business travelers
Military and overseas voters enjoy additional protections under the law that enable them to vote. The most significant protection is a specialized form of absentee voting that is very different than how non-UOCAVA voters request and receive absentee ballots. Military and overseas voting can be complicated, and this section serves as a resource for clerks, providing clarity around the many deadlines, voting and registration requirements, and other important processes.
Sec. 7.4.3: The Federal Voting 
Assistance Program (FVAP)
The Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP) is a federal program tasked with 
administering UOCAVA and MOVE. FVAP assists military and overseas voters 
through partnerships with the Military Services, U.S. Department of State, U.S. 
Department of Justice, election officials from 50 states, U.S. territories, and the 
District of Columbia. FVAP has a wealth of military and overseas voter-related 
resources on F VAP.gov.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 43
Sec. 7.4.4: Get to Know 
the Federal Forms
Federal law prescribes two different forms for military and overseas voters to use 
to register to vote and vote by absentee ballot. Both forms will be further described 
in detail in these chapters, but it is important to understand at the outset how 
they are similar and how they differ. An additional form — the National Mail Voter 
Registration Form — is commonly distributed at military installations, embassies, 
and consulates. It can only be used for voter registration, and the Commission has 
only prescribed it for use in specific circumstances.
It is likely that many municipal clerks, regardless of the size of their jurisdiction, will 
encounter at least one of these federal forms at least once during their tenure. 
It is important that clerks be able to recognize each form, understand how it is 
being used, and then use this manual to correctly review and process the form.
