Sec. 7.4.5: Overview: Voting 
Process for UOCAVA Voters
The section is structured to follow the voting process as shown below, with 
information about the requirements and actions for each group of voters as 
well as for the clerks. The process for military and overseas voting is similar to 
the process used by all absentee voters but with several important differences. 
Military and overseas voters have their own deadlines, their own forms, 
their own Uniform Instructions, their own certificate envelopes and, in some 
instances, their own ballot styles.
Step 1: Voter Qualifications   
Military and overseas voters are specifically defined 
by law. Only individuals who meet those definitions 
may vote using this method.
Step 3: Absentee Ballot Requests   
Military and overseas voters may use additional 
methods to request their absentee ballots, including 
unique federal forms.
Step 2: Voter Registration   
Military voters are exempt from registration when 
voting absentee. Overseas voters are required  
to register.
Step 4: Absentee Ballot Requests   
Military and overseas voters may choose to receive 
their ballot materials electronically, by mail, or in 
person.
Step 5: Returning the Absentee Ballot   
Military and overseas voters must return their 
ballots by mail.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 45
Sec. 7.4.6: Military Voters
“Military voters,” also known as “military electors,” is the general designation 
used in state and federal law to refer to the group of voters who are entitled to 
certain voting exemptions and benefits due to their qualifying service or civilian 
employment. There are many different types of military voters, including certain 
civilians, and the definition of “military voter” is not limited to individuals serving 
in one of the branches of the U.S. military. Military voters also include spouses 
and dependents residing with or accompanying the qualified military voters.
Who are Military Voters?
Military voter means any of the following individuals:
 Ɋ Members of a uniformed service who are on active-duty orders in the U.S. 
Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps or Coast Guard, the Commissioned 
Corps of U.S. Health Service or National Atmospheric Administration 
Commissioned Officer Corps. Wis. Stat. § 6.22(1)(b)1., (1)(c).
 ɉ The U.S. Space Force is part of the U.S. Air Force. 10 U.S.C. § 9081(a).
 ɉ The National Guard is part of the U.S. Army or U.S. Air Force. See 
generally U.S. Code: Title 32.
 Ɋ Members of the Merchant Marine of the United States. Wis. Stat. § 6.22(1)(b)2.  
The United States Merchant Marine is a civilian fleet of U.S.-flagged 
commercial ships and American mariners who fulfill both commercial 
and military transport needs.
 Ɋ Civilian employees of the United States and civilians officially attached 
to a uniformed service who are serving outside the United States.  
Wis. Stat. § 6.22(1)(b)3.
Best Practice: Examples of civilian employees include but are not 
limited to foreign service members with the U.S. State Department, 
USAID, etc.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 46
 Ɋ Peace Corps volunteers. Wis. Stat. § 6.22(1)(b)4. 
 Ɋ Spouses and dependents of those listed in the above categories residing 
with or accompanying them. Wis. Stat. § 6.22(1)(b)5.
Only Current, Active Service or Employment Qualifies
As illustrated above, there are several categories of people that fit under 
the umbrella of “military voters,” even though some of those categories 
consist of civilians. The most important qualifying criteria for all categories 
of military voters is that they need to be currently, actively serving or 
employed in the qualifying role.  That contrasts with veterans or former 
civilian employees — those types of voters are no longer engaged in 
the qualifying service. The Commission has interpreted the definition of 
“member of uniformed service” in Wis. Stat. § 6.22(1)(b) to be consistent with 
the definition in Wis. Stat. § 6.34(1), as well as to be consistent with UOCAVA, 
both of which contain an active-duty requirement.
 Ɋ For members of a uniformed service, this means they must have active-
duty orders, which is discussed further below.
 Ɋ For members of the merchant marine, civilian employees of the U.S. 
who are outside the U.S., and for Peace Corps volunteers, there is no one 
set of documents or status they need to qualify. Instead, military voters 
qualifying under those categories must be able to certify that they are 
currently employed or engaged in the qualifying service.
Important: Municipal clerks should not base eligibility for these voters 
on whether they have active-duty orders — instead, the question 
should be whether they are currently engaged or employed in the 
qualifying service.
28-Day Extension of Service Exception: The only exception to this 
requirement is the 28-day extension of privilege afforded by Wisconsin 
law, which states that individuals can continue to qualify as military 
voters for 28 days after the date of discharge from uniformed service 
or a termination of qualifying civilian employment. Wis. Stat. § 6.22(7).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 47
Best Practice: If a voter is unsure of whether they qualify as a military 
voter due to a less common service type, the municipal clerk should 
attempt to gather as much information as possible about the nature 
of their service, their rank (if any), and as much as they know about 
how their service structure is organized. The municipal clerk should 
then confer with their local counsel about whether the voter meets the 
definition of a military voter pursuant to Wis. Stat. §§ 6.22(1) and 6.34(1), 
or 52 U.S.C. § 20310(1). Ultimately, it is up to the voter to determine 
whether they fulfill the requirements, and certify that they do, under 
state statute to be a military voter.
Members of Uniformed Service Must 
Have Active-Duty Orders
The vast majority of military voters in Wisconsin are members of a uniformed 
service and their spouses and dependents. This section does not apply to 
members of the merchant marine, civilian employees of the United States, 
and Peace Corps volunteers because those individuals do not have active-
duty orders in the same way. However, members of the merchant marine, 
civilian employees of the United States, and Peace Corps still must be actively 
serving or employed in those roles, as discussed above.
Members of uniformed service must be on active-duty orders to qualify for any 
of the exemptions and benefits afforded to them as military voters under state 
and federal law. The Commission has interpreted “member” of a uniformed 
service to mean someone who is in active-duty orders. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.22(1)(b), 
6.34(1). If a voter does not currently have active-duty orders in a uniformed 
service, they do not qualify as a military voter on that ground of eligibility.
Best Practice: Generally speaking, “active-duty orders” are the 
paperwork that military members receive that authorizes them to 
perform full-time military service. There are different types of military 
orders, but the vast majority of service members and their dependents 
will know whether they have active-duty orders or not.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 48
Who is Not a Military Voter?
Veterans after 28 days following discharge: Military voter eligibility is extended 
for 28 days after the discharge from service or termination of qualifying service 
employment, but after that, the voter will need to re-register to vote. Wis. Stat.  
§ 6.24(7). Prior military service is not a basis of eligibility to vote as a military voter.
Members of the Reserves or National Guard without active-duty 
orders: Anyone serving as a reservist without active-duty orders also does not 
meet the definition of a military voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.34(1), 52 U.S.C. § 20310(1).
Family members of military voters who do not reside with or accompany the 
military voter: To be a qualifying spouse or dependent, the individual must 
be residing with or accompanying the military voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.22(1)(b)5. If 
a military voter is deployed overseas and her spouse stays to reside at their 
Wisconsin residence, her spouse does not qualify as a military voter.
Best Practice: If a spouse moves outside of Wisconsin to accompany 
a qualified military member and that military member is deployed 
overseas, the spouse residing outside of Wisconsin would still qualify 
as a military voter.
Do Military Voters Need to Be at 
Home or Away to Qualify?
Military voters can either be at home, or they can be absent from their 
Wisconsin residence due to their service. The difference changes which 
exemptions and voting procedures they are eligible for, but it does not change 
whether they meet the definition of a military voter.
Remember, the important question for whether someone qualifies as a military 
voter is whether they are currently, actively serving in the qualifying role, which 
means on active-duty orders for members of uniformed service. Whether the 
military voter is at home or absent from their residence informs how they vote, 
not whether they can qualify as a military voter.
The away from home distinction comes from how UOCAVA classifies military 
voters. UOCAVA uses the term “absent uniformed services voter,” and each 
qualifying definition specifies that the voter must be absent from their residence 
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 49
“by reason of” their active duty or civilian service. 52 U.S.C. § 20310(1). After 
UOCAVA became law, Wisconsin updated several of its statutes to add a similar 
definition of military voter, which also requires the voter to be absent “by reason 
of” the duty or service. Wis. Stat. § 6.34(1). However, the Legislature did not 
replace its original definition of military voter (which does not have an away 
from home requirement). Wis. Stat. § 6.22(1)(b).5 The outcome of all of this is 
that military voters who are absent from their Wisconsin residence have some 
different voting procedures than those who are at home, but military voters who 
are at home still retain some of the benefits of military voters.
Military Voters at Home
Military voters who are not absent from their Wisconsin residence still 
must either be on active-duty orders or currently, actively employed in 
qualifying service in order to benefit from the military voter provision 
described in this section.
If they are at home and voting by absentee ballot, they are still exempt from 
the voter registration requirement, and the proof of residence requirement by 
extension, and they are also exempt from providing photo ID as a condition of 
requesting their absentee ballot. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.22(3) (registration exemption), 
6.34(2) (proof of residence exemption), 6.87(1) (photo ID exemption).
Military voters at home can request an absentee ballot by mail, by email, or 
in person. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(a). If the request is made by email, it must be 
made by 5 p.m. on the Thursday before Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(b). If 
the request is made by mail, it must be made by 5 p.m. on the Friday before 
Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(c). If the application is made in person, it must 
be made no later than the Sunday preceding the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(b).
5 Wisconsin law is not consistent in how it defines military voters. In the statute that predates UOCAVA, 
the definition of “military voters” in Wis. Stat. § 6.22(1)(b) does not contain any references to “active 
duty” or being away from the voter’s residence. The federal UOCAVA definition (which uses the term 
“absent uniformed services voter” instead of “military elector”) contains an “active duty” requirement, 
and also a requirement that the voter be absent from home by nature of that active duty. 52 U.S.C. 
§ 20310. A second definition of “military elector” in Wisconsin law mirrors this federal language. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.34(1). The primary difference between the definition of “military elector” in Wis. Stat. § 6.22(1)(b) 
and 6.34(1) is that the latter contains a further specification that the voter must be active duty who, by 
reason of that duty, is absent from their residence. That does not mean that the definitions of “military 
elector” Id. are in conflict — the latter is just more specific. Wisconsin statutes cross-cite to the two 
state law definitions of “military elector” inconsistently. For statutes citing Wis. Stat. § 6.22 see Wis. Stat 
§§ 6.10(13), 6.25, 6.86(1)(a)3., 6.86(1)(c), 6.86(2m)(a). For statutes citing Wis. Stat. § 6.34(1) see 6.22(2)(e), 
6.22(4)(a), 6.22(6), 6.276, 6.86(1)(b), 6.865(1), 6.87(3)(d), 6.87(4), 6.88(1), 6.97(1).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 50
Military voters at home cannot request an absentee ballot by email using 
MyVote — if they want to request an absentee ballot by email, they must email 
their municipal clerk directly. Voters can find their clerk’s contact information 
on MyVote. 
Military Voters Away from their Wisconsin Residences
In addition to being exempt from registration, from providing proof of 
residence, and from providing photo ID when voting absentee, military voters 
who are away from their Wisconsin residence are entitled to additional voting 
procedures designed to make it easier for them to vote. Remember, military 
voters who are absent from their residence must be absent by reason of their 
service or employment. Military voters may be stationed all around the state, 
the country, and the world, including on marine vessels at sea. Accordingly, 
both the U.S. Congress and Wisconsin Legislature have determined that these 
voters need to have access to their ballot materials as quickly as possible to 
ensure they have sufficient time to return their ballots by mail.
The biggest benefit for this group of voters is the ability to request and 
receive their ballot materials electronically. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.86(1)(ac), 6.87(3)(d). 
“Electronically” means that the voter receives the materials directly from their 
clerk by email or fax. These methods and processes are discussed further in 
Sec. 7.4.10: “Requesting Absentee Ballots for UOCAVA Voters” on page 65.
Another benefit for military voters who are away from their Wisconsin residence 
is additional time to make their absentee ballot requests when making their 
request by email or online for federal elections. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(b). When 
making this type of absentee ballot request, military voters who are absent from 
their Wisconsin residence have until 5 p.m. on Election Day to do so. Practically 
speaking, however, since all voters, including military voters, are required to 
return their ballots by mail or in person, it is extremely unlikely that an overseas 
military voter who makes an absentee ballot request on Election Day will have 
enough time to return that ballot by 8 p.m.
What if Military Voters Go to the Polls on Election Day?
Military voters can vote at the polls on Election Day, but they would not be 
eligible for any of the exemptions and procedures discussed in this chapter if 
they do. In other words, military voters who go to their polling places on Election 
Day need to register and vote just like any other voter, even if they are home for 
the day while still on active-duty orders.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 51
If a military voter who has not previously registered to vote goes to the polling 
place to vote on Election Day, their name will have the “MILITARY RGSTR” in 
the poll book, which will prompt the poll workers to register them to vote with 
appropriate proof of residence.
Multiple statutory provisions support the conclusion that military voters can 
only ever be absentee voters. Military voters have their own specific section in 
Chapter 6, which is titled “Absentee voting for military voters.” Wis. Stat. § 6.22. In 
the sub-section titled “Voting Procedure,” the statute confirms that the ballots of 
military voters “…shall be marked and returned, deposited and recorded in the 
same manner as other absentee ballots.” Wis. Stat. § 6.22(5) (Emphasis added). 
Similarly, military voters “…may file an application for an absentee ballot…” Wis. 
Stat. § 6.22(2)(e) (Emphasis added). Within the proof of residence provision, 
military voter is more specifically defined, in part, as “a member of a uniformed 
service on active duty who, by reason of that duty, is absent from the residence 
where the member is otherwise qualified to vote…” Wis. Stat. § 6.34(1) (Emphasis 
added). In summary, no provision of Wisconsin law appears to contemplate a 
scenario where a military voter is not an absentee voter.
If a voter is registering to vote in-person on election day at their polling place, 
they do not meet the definition of a military voter because they are not voting 
via absentee ballot. While they may meet the service definition of a military 
voter in Wis. Stat. § 6.22(1), Wisconsin law is clear that military voters must be 
voting absentee in order to be exempt from voter registration and proof of 
residence requirements.
This distinction is only important for in-person voting on election day at the 
polls. If military voters are voting via in-person absentee ballot (IPAV), the 
exemptions for registration and proof of residence do apply as IPAV is a form 
of absentee voting.
Sec. 7.4.7: Overseas Voters
There are two types of overseas voters and the definitions for each type 
both depend on a voter’s intent to return. The word “overseas” is not limited 
to those residing literally in countries separated from the United States by 
bodies of water. “Overseas” legally means a voter who is outside the United 
States. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(12n), 52 U.S.C. § 20310(5).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 52
 Ɋ A permanent overseas voter is a U.S. citizen who has either never lived 
in the United States or has left the United States and has no intent to 
return or whose intent to return is uncertain. Wis. Stat. § 6.24(1). Permanent 
overseas voters must meet all of the legal requirements to vote except the 
residency requirement. Id. Permanent overseas voters are only eligible to 
participate in federal contests such as President (including the Presidential 
Preference Vote), Representative to U.S. Congress, and U.S. Senate.
 Ɋ A temporary overseas voter is a U.S. citizen who has lived in the United 
States and is away from their residence for temporary purposes, such as 
a student studying abroad, someone on vacation, or someone whose 
employment requires them to live in another country for a period of time. 
They meet all of the requirements to vote in Wisconsin, including the 
residency requirement. Temporary overseas voters are absentee voters, 
though the fact that they are overseas guarantees them some of the 
same protections as permanent overseas voters. There is no specific 
timeframe or definition as to what constitutes “intent to return”, so it is up 
to the voter to certify that they intend to return to the United States. See 
Wis. Stat. § 6.10(1). Temporary overseas voters receive a full ballot with 
federal, state, and local contests.
Permanent Overseas Voters
A permanent overseas voter must meet all of the following criteria:
 Ɋ Be a U.S. citizen who is not disqualified from voting in Wisconsin under 
Wis. Stat. § 6.03, and who does not qualify as a resident of this state 
under Wis. Stat. § 6.10. Wis. Stat. § 6.24(1).
 Ɋ Is or will be at least 18 years old by the date of the election in which they 
are voting. Id.
 Ɋ Either they have resided in Wisconsin previously or at least one of their 
parents resided in Wisconsin immediately prior to the parent’s departure 
from the United States. Id.
 Ɋ Not registered to vote in any other state, territory, or possession.  Id.
A permanent overseas voter may vote in any contest or election for federal 
office, which typically includes the Partisan Primary, General Election, the 
Presidential Preference Primary, and potential special elections. Wis. Stat. 6.24(2).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 53
These voters may vote for President, Representative to U.S. Congress, and 
U.S. Senate and vote a special federal-only ballot. Federal-only ballots are 
prescribed by the Commission ahead of each federal election and only contain 
federal offices.
This is not the same as a presidential-only voter who can only vote for the 
Office of President. For more information on presidential-only ballots for 
new Wisconsin residents and former Wisconsin residents, see Chapter 5.5: 
“Presidential-Only Ballots.”
Permanent overseas voters sometimes want to know what they need to do 
in order to be permitted to vote in state and local contests. However, they 
may not vote in an election for state or local office unless they qualify as a 
resident of the state and are registered as a voter who can satisfy the legal 
residency requirement for voting. To re-register as a regular voter rather than 
a permanent overseas voter, they must first establish a physical residency 
in Wisconsin for at least 28 days prior to Election Day and must register by 
completing a voter registration application, providing a proof of residence 
document, and photo ID when receiving a ballot. Wis. Stat. § 6.24(2).
Note: Permanent overseas voters may not cast ballots in-person  
on Election Day
In the past, this has occurred infrequently when voters who 
otherwise permanently reside outside the United States are back in 
their Wisconsin jurisdiction during election day. The state law that 
authorizes their voting procedure, as well as the federal UOCAVA law 
on which state law is based, are clear that the voting process is limited 
to absentee voting. Specifically, the law states that an “overseas voter 
who is properly registered may request an absentee ballot in writing” 
under applicable state statutes. Wis. Stat. § 6. 24(4)(a). Nothing in 
state law governing overseas voters contemplates in person voting on 
Election Day. This legal analysis is also consistent with polling place 
logistics. Since permanent overseas voters can only vote in federal 
contests, most polling places will not have a federal-only ballot 
prepared and available if a permanent overseas voter shows up.
Questions on Registering Overseas Voters? See Sec. 7.4.9: “Methods for Voter 
Registration for UOCAVA Voters” on page 57.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 54
Temporary Overseas Voters
The main difference between a permanent overseas voter and a temporary 
overseas voter is whether the voter can meet the legal residency requirements 
for voting. Permanent voters cannot — they have no intent to return to the 
United States, or their intent to return is uncertain. Wis. Stat. § 6.24(1). Temporary 
overseas voters do meet the residency requirements to vote — they are regular 
voters who are temporarily away from home. Prior to 2018, this used to mean 
that temporary overseas voters had to vote just like any other absentee voter 
and could not take advantage of the special procedures that permanent voters 
rely on to receive and vote their absentee ballots. However, federal law does 
not make a distinction between temporary and permanent overseas voters. 
UOCAVA applies equally to all overseas voters. 52 U.S.C. § 20310(5)(B) and (C).
In 2018, the State of Wisconsin entered into a consent decree with the U.S. 
Department of Justice and agreed to afford some of the same benefits and 
protections to temporary overseas voters that permanent overseas voters enjoy.6
Under federal law, temporary overseas voters are permitted to receive their 
blank absentee ballots by mail or electronically and also may use the Federal 
Write-in Absentee Ballot (FWAB) to cast their votes. See 52 U.S.C. §§ 20302(a)(7), 
20302(a)(3). The consent decree means that the State of Wisconsin has agreed 
that these federal provisions apply to temporary overseas voters.
Temporary overseas voters:
 Ɋ Must register to vote
 Ɋ Can receive their ballot by mail, email or fax
 Ɋ Cannot request a ballot through MyVote
 Ɋ Do not need to re-register as a temporary overseas voter when they leave 
the county
Temporary absentee voters may request to receive their absentee ballots either 
by mail or by email/fax. This is discussed further in the procedures sections below.
Temporary overseas voters have all of the same legal requirements to vote as 
regular, non-military and non-permanent overseas voters. See Wis. Stat. § 6.03. 
These voters can include short-term travelers, including students studying abroad 
or people on vacation, and individuals who have moved abroad but intend to 
6 Available at: justice.gov/crt/case-document/file/1075226/dl?inline=
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 55
return to Wisconsin in the future. They do not need to re-register as a temporary 
oversea voter when they leave the country and are not required to update any 
aspect of their registration to take advantage of UOCAVA’s provisions. Temporary 
overseas voters are permitted to vote a full ballot, including state and local 
contests, because they meet the residency requirement to vote in Wisconsin.

Sec. 7.4.8: Voter Registration 
for UOCAVA Voters
All voters who are required to register can only register to vote online through 
MyVote, by mail, or in person. Wis. Stat. § 6.30. Military and overseas voters 
cannot fax or email voter registration applications even if they are outside the 
United States.

Sec. 7.4.9: Methods for Voter 
Registration for UOCAVA Voters
Military and overseas voters may utilize a variety of methods to register to vote. 
Each of these registration methods are discussed further below.
Important Reminder: Military voters who are on active-duty orders, or 
are otherwise in a current, active qualifying status, are not required to 
register to vote when voting by absentee ballot but some choose to do 
so anyway. Wis. Stat. 6.22(3).
Best Practice: An absentee ballot cannot be issued to a voter if the 
voter does not have a voter record in WisVote. If a military voter is not 
registered, the clerk still must input enough information to create 
a voter record for them in the system. The minimum information 
required to create a voter record is First Name, Last Name, Date of 
Birth, Home Address, Voter Type, and Wisconsin Driver’s License or Last 
Four of Social Security Number (if the voter has one). Legally, creating 
a voter record is not the same thing as registering someone to vote, 
though the same functions are used in WisVote to achieve both results. 
Often, a clerk won’t have all of the information necessary to complete 
a full registration if the military voter is not intending to register to vote, 
and such a voter likewise will not need to provide proof of residence. 
For more detailed instructions on how to review and create voter 
records for military voters in WisVote, clerks should refer to Section 2.2 
of the WisVote User Manual.
Online Voter Registration
The easiest and most common way voters can register to vote is online at 
MyVote.wi.gov.
What is it? An online registration through MyVote is an electronic application for 
voter registration where the Commission’s MyVote website prompts the voter to 
input all information necessary for registration. Wis. Stat. § 6.30(5).
Where can I find it? By visiting MyVote.wi.gov.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 57
How and when is it returned? Online registration through MyVote is returned 
to the municipal clerk as soon as it is completed. Online registration must 
be completed no later than 11:59p.m. CST on the third Wednesday before the 
election. Wis. Stat. § 6.28(1)(a).
The Federal Post Card Application (FPCA)
For an example of the FPCA and instructions for how to properly review this 
form, see “Appendix 7.4.A: Reviewing the Federal Post Card Application 
(FPCA)” on page 85.
What is the FPCA? The FPCA is a postage-free postcard, printed and distributed 
by the U.S. Department of Defense Federal Voting Assistance Program 
(FVAP) for use by military and overseas voters. The FPCA is a combination 
voter registration form and absentee ballot request, and can be used for 
both of those purposes. The FPCA is a federal form that can be used in all 
50 states. This means that it is not Wisconsin-specific, so municipal clerks 
must take care when receiving an FPCA to make sure it contains all required 
information for completing Wisconsin processes. The FPCA must be accepted 
in Wisconsin if the voter has provided all required information on the form. 52 
U.S.C. § 20302(a)(4) (UOCAVA requirement), Wis. Stat. §§ 6.24(4)(b) (permanent 
overseas voters), 6.22(2)(c) (military voters).
How is the FPCA used in Wisconsin? As mentioned above, the FPCA can be 
used for two purposes. However, the form does not contain a box for the voter 
to indicate the purpose of the form. Municipal clerks should not complete a 
full registration for military voters unless the FPCA contains all the required 
information necessary, and it is clear that the military voter intends to 
register to vote (though military voters are still exempt from providing proof 
of residence). Instead, clerks should use the FPCA to either create a new voter 
record, or update an existing voter record, before processing the absentee 
ballot request. Clerks should refer to Section 2.2 of the WisVote User Manual 
for more detailed instructions.
Where can I find the FPCA? The online version of the FPCA can be obtained from 
the FVAP website at fvap.gov.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 58
How and when is the FPCA returned?
 Ɋ For Voter Registration: If it is being used for voter registration, it must be 
postmarked by the third Wednesday prior to the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.28(1)(a). 
If used for registration, it must be returned by mail or returned in person to the 
clerk. Wis. Stat. § 6.30(1) and (4). It cannot be emailed or faxed.
 Ɋ To Request an Absentee Ballot: If it is being used only as an absentee 
request, a voter may be mail, email, fax or take it to their municipal clerk. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.28(1)(a) The request must be received by the municipal clerk 
no later than 5 p.m. on the 5th day immediately before the election unless 
the voter is a military voter for a federal election. Wis. Sta. 6.86(1)(b). In that 
case, military voters may request absentee ballots by email, fax, or online 
through MyVote for federal elections until 5 p.m. on Election Day. Id.
Wisconsin’s Voter Registration Application (EL-131)
What is the EL-131? The standard voter registration form is the form that most 
voters use in Wisconsin to register to vote.
Where can I find the EL-131? The EL-131 Voter Registration form is available on the 
Wisconsin Elections Commission website.
How and when is the EL-131 returned? This form must be mailed and postmarked 
by the third Wednesday before the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.28(1)(a).
In-Person Registration with the Municipal Clerk
What is it? Any voter, including military and overseas voters, can register to vote 
in person with their municipal clerk. Wis. Stat. § 6.30(1) However, practically, this 
is not a common registration option for most military and permanent overseas 
voters.
Where can I do it? At the clerk’s office. Any voter can look up the contact 
information for their municipal clerk on MyVote.wi.gov.
How and when is it completed? In person registration closes at 5 p.m. on the 
3rd Wednesday before Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 6.28(1)(a).After that date, in 
person registration is handled as a late registration, and must be completed by 
5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 6.29(2)(a).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 59
Election Day Registration (EDR)
Note: Military voters can vote in person at their polling place on 
Election Day but if they do, they are considered regular voters as the 
special exemptions for military voters only apply when they are voting 
absentee. If they wish to vote in person at their polling place on Election 
Day, they must register to vote as a regular voter and must provide 
Proof of Residence.
Registration Information for Each Voter Type
Military Voters
Military voters do not need to register but can do so if they choose. They do not 
need to provide proof of residence if they do register.
They can register using the following methods:
 Ɋ FPCA
 Ɋ EL-131
 Ɋ Online at MyVote.wi.gov
Registration deadlines:
 Ɋ Online or By Mail: The form must be postmarked/completed by the third 
Wednesday before the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.28(1).
 Ɋ In Person: Registration in person at the clerk’s office closes at 5 p.m. on the 
Friday preceding the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.29(2).
Note: Military voters may also register at their polling place on Election 
Day but may not vote unless they are registering as regular voters.
Clerks must still obtain sufficient information to enter a military voter into 
WisVote, such as their name, address, date of birth, and Wisconsin Driver’s 
License Number or last four digits of Social Security Number (if they have one). 
Wis. Stat. § 6.22(3).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 60
If a military voter retires or wishes to change their status to a regular voter, they 
must register as a regular voter and provide a proof of residence document.
Overseas Voters
Overseas voters must register and vote in the last Wisconsin municipality where 
they (or in the case of some permanent overseas voters, their parent(s)) last 
had residency. Wis. Stat. § 6.24(3).
Best Practice: Some permanent overseas voters may not recall or know the 
address where they are attempting to register if they personally never lived 
there. It is also possible that the address no longer exists. In these instances, 
clerks should obtain as much information from the voter as possible about 
nearby landmarks, cross streets, municipal buildings and businesses, etc. 
to help the voter identify an address. The voter must provide a sufficient 
address for the municipal clerk to determine the correct jurisdiction and 
ward. See Wis. Stat. § 6.24(1). If you need assistance with creating a record 
for an address for a permanent overseas voter, please contact the WEC 
Help Desk at (608) 261-2028 or at elections@wi.gov.
Permanent Overseas Voters
Permanent overseas voters must register to vote, but do not need to provide a 
proof of residence document. See Wis. Stat. §§ 6.27, 6.34(2).
They can register using the following methods:
 Ɋ FPCA
 Ɋ EL-131
Registration deadlines:
 Ɋ By Mail: The form must be postmarked by the third Wednesday before the 
election. Wis. Stat. §6.28(1).
 Ɋ In Person: Registration in person at the clerk’s office closes at 5 p.m. on the 
Friday preceding the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.29(2).
For most permanent overseas voters, the only realistic way for them to register 
to vote is by mail. They are not prohibited from registering in person but 
someone living permanently abroad is unlikely to travel back to their clerk’s 
office to do so. Wis. Stat. § 6.30(1).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 61
Permanent overseas voters are also not prohibited from registering online but 
they can only do so if they have a valid Wisconsin driver’s license or ID card 
(which is unlikely for someone living permanently overseas). Wis. Stat. § 6.30(5).
They must be sure to follow registration deadlines, and their registration form must 
be the original signed version. It cannot be scanned and emailed or faxed, and it 
cannot be delivered in person by a friend or family member. See Wis. Stat. § 6.30.
Note: If a regular voter changes their registration status to 
permanently overseas, they must re-register to vote as a permanent 
overseas voter. See Wis. Stat. § 6.24(3). If a permanently overseas voter 
wishes to vote in person at their polling place on Election Day, they 
must register to vote as a regular voter and provide Proof of Residence.
Temporary Overseas Voters
Temporarily overseas voters must register to vote, but many may already be 
registered at their Wisconsin address. Wis. Stat. § 6.27. Temporary overseas 
voters do not need to re-register to vote if they go overseas, as this is an 
absentee application type, not a voter type. They may register online, by mail, 
or in person and must provide a proof of residence document, just like any 
other regular voter. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.30, 6.34.
They can register using the following methods:
 Ɋ FPCA
 Ɋ EL-131
 Ɋ Online at MyVote.wi.gov with a valid Wisconsin Driver License or State ID
Registration deadlines:
 Ɋ By Mail: The form must be postmarked by the third Wednesday before the 
election. Wis. Stat. §6.28(1).
 Ɋ Online: Registration through MyVote closes at 11:59p.m. CST on the third 
Wednesday before the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.28(1).
 Ɋ In Person: Registration in person at the clerk’s office closes at 5 p.m. on the 
Friday preceding the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.29(2).
 Ɋ At their polling place on Election Day.7
7 The voter would not be considered a temporary overseas voter at this point.

Frequently Asked Questions for Military & 
Overseas Voter Registration
Q If a clerk suspects that a voter is no longer a military voter, should they 
change their status?
A Not without attempting to contact the voter. Clerks may confirm with the 
voter that they are still qualified military voters but are not required to. 
However, clerks should not delay mailing the voter a ballot while waiting 
for confirmation. Please keep in mind that the military voter could still be 
living at home or visiting on leave while serving in the military. If the voter 
does not respond to the inquiry, their record should remain unchanged.
Q The voter lived in Wisconsin, moved to another state where they registered 
to vote, and now lives abroad permanently. The voter has family in 
Wisconsin, so they want to register to vote here. Can they?
A No. If the voter has moved to another state before they lived abroad, they 
cannot use their parents’ residence to qualify as a permanent overseas 
voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.24 Since the voter registered elsewhere after leaving 
Wisconsin, they must reestablish a physical presence in Wisconsin 28 days 
prior to an election to achieve residency and identify that as their address.
Q Someone accidentally registered as a military or overseas voter. What 
should the clerk do?
A If this was a typo on behalf of the clerk, this can be updated by the clerk 
in WisVote. Please note that both the “voter type” in the voter registration 
record AND the “application type” in the absentee request must be 
updated in the system. If the voter mistakenly checked something, the 
clerk should confirm in writing that this is a mistake and then work with the 
voter to update their registration accordingly.
Q The voter missed the by-mail and online registration deadlines and is 
overseas. Is there anything they can do?
A No. The voter can return to their municipality and register to vote in person 
by the appropriate deadline, but that is their only option if they are still 
overseas. Unfortunately, it is not possible to fax or email a voter registration 
form. Wis. Stat. § 6.34.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 64
Sec. 7.4.10: Requesting Absentee 
Ballots for UOCAVA Voters
The purpose of UOCAVA and related federal and state laws is to ensure that 
military and overseas voters can vote given complications that can arise from 
being out of the country. Accordingly, there are several different methods by 
which military and overseas voters can request and receive absentee ballots, 
some of which are unique to them.
Deadlines to Request an Absentee Ballot
Military Voters
 Ɋ If the request for an absentee ballot is made by mail, it must be received 
by the municipal clerk no later than 5 p.m. on the Friday immediately 
preceding the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(b).
 Ɋ If the request for an absentee ballot is made by a military voter who 
is away from their residence due to their active duty service, and the 
request is made other than by mail, the request must be received by the 
municipal clerk no later than 5 p.m. on election day.  Id.
Note: Regardless of how a military voter requests and receives 
their absentee ballot, all absentee ballots can only be returned by 
mail, by drop box, in person to the municipal clerk, or by the voter to 
their polling place. A voter must return their own ballot unless they 
determine they need assistance due to a disability. See Sec. 7.4.14: 
“Returning Absentee Ballots” on page 81 for more information on 
returning absentee ballots, all of which apply to military voters.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 65
Permanent & Temporary Overseas Voters
 Ɋ The request must be received no later than 5 p.m. on the Thursday before 
the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(b).
Methods for Requesting Absentee Ballots
There are several methods that military and overseas voters can use to request 
their absentee ballots. Some methods are the same methods that all voters 
use to request absentee ballots. Additionally, military and overseas voters can 
use special federal forms to request their ballots. Each of these methods is 
discussed in detail below.
The Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot (FWAB)
Citizens living overseas on a permanent or temporary basis and military voters 
often have difficulty receiving and returning ballots quickly. Federal and state 
law permit these voters to request and vote a special a write-in absentee ballot, 
called the Federal Write-in Absentee Ballot (FWAB), which is available on FVAP’s 
website F VAP.gov as well as at military posts, U.S. embassies, and consulates 
throughout the world. Wis. Stat. § 6.25. The FWAB is also known as the “Backup 
Ballot” because military and overseas voters can use it if they won’t receive their 
regular ballot in time to send it back before the election. 52 U.S.C. § 20303(a)(1), 
Wis. Stat. § 6.25. When the FWAB is submitted, the clerk secures the Backup 
Ballot and mails the voter a regular absentee ballot. If the regular absentee 
ballot doesn’t make it back in time, the clerk counts the Backup Ballot. Only one 
of these ballots is ultimately counted. The FWAB can be used at any election in 
which the voter is eligible to vote. Id.
The FWAB can be used both as an absentee ballot request form and a  
write-in ballot.
Important: The FWAB was developed by the federal government, 
not the Commission, and is intended for use nationwide. FWABs are 
submitted and processed in the manner provided by law for absentee 
ballots in the state involved. 52 U.S.C. § 20303(b). Wisconsin law 
implements these federal law provisions for military and overseas 
voters, and the 2018 consent decree permits temporary overseas 
voters to use the FWAB as well. Wis. Stat. § 6.25.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 66
The absentee ballot request form part of the FWAB, which contains the voter’s 
information as well as the required Declaration/Affirmation, appears on page 2 
of the FWAB packet. The page contains the following header. For a full copy of 
this form, including instructions, see “Appendix 7.4.B: Reviewing the Federal 
Write-In Absentee Ballot (FWAB)” on page 95.
Figure 3: FWAB Ballot Form
The write-in ballot part of the FWAB, which is where the voter makes their 
Backup Ballot candidate or party selections, appears on page 3 of the FWAB 
packet. The page contains the following header.
Figure 4: FWAB Backup Ballot
Important: The Backup Ballot cannot be counted if the Voter 
Information page is missing or incomplete. 52 U.S.C. § 20303(a)(1), 
Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)1. The absentee request form section of the FWAB 
contains areas for voters to provide required information and has a 
Declaration/Affirmation section where the voter must sign.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 67
 Ɋ The FWAB must also include the signature of the voter and the signature 
and address of an adult witness to be counted. This information should 
appear in Box 6 on the Voter Information/absentee ballot request part 
of the FWAB. Unfortunately, the instructions written by FVAP may mislead 
voters into thinking only a witness signature is required. This is not correct.
 Ɋ In order to count the Backup Ballot, Box 6 must contain all of the following:
 ɉ Witness Full Name
 ɉ Witness Signature
 ɉ Witness Address
Note: The witness for military and overseas voters need not be a U.S. 
citizen but they do need to be 18 years of age or older. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(2).

Important: The FWAB Backup Ballot cannot be counted unless the

timely received. If they completed the entire FWAB, including the Voter

First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 68
The Federal Post Card Application (FPCA)
The Federal Post Card Application (FPCA) is also known as Standard Form 76. Regular 
voters who are temporarily overseas may also use this form. Wis. Stat. § 6.24(4)(b). 
The FPCA is a dual-purpose form that functions as both a voter registration form 
and/or absentee ballot application depending on the circumstance and needs 
of the voter. See “The Federal Post Card Application (FPCA)” on page 58 for 
more information.
Standard Application for Absentee Ballot Form (EL-121)
This form is the standard absentee ballot application published by the 
Wisconsin Elections Commission. Military and Permanent Overseas voters 
are not required to provide a copy of their photo ID when submitting this 
application. Temporary Overseas voters are required to include a copy of their 
photo ID unless they already have one on file with the clerk’s office.
Online through MyVote.wi.gov
All UOCAVA voters may request their absentee ballots through the MyVote 
website. There is a separate section of the website for Military and Permanent 
Overseas voters to use.
Temporary overseas voters may request their absentee ballots through MyVote 
if they would like to receive their ballot by mail. To do so, they use the same 
MyVote workflow as a regular absentee voter and just input a foreign address 
as the delivery address. If a temporary overseas voter wishes to receive their 
ballot by email, they cannot make that request through MyVote and must 
instead contact their municipal clerk directly.
Email and Other Written Requests
Any other written request is acceptable, provided it gives all required 
information. Fax or email requests are valid if received by the application 
deadline and do not require a copy of the applicant’s signature. Wis. Stat. 
§§ 6.24(4)(a) and 6.86(1)(ac). A scan of the FPCA or EL-121 could be emailed 
to the clerk for the same purpose.
Note: The difference between an absentee ballot request application 
and a voter registration application. Absentee ballot requests can 
be scanned, emailed, and faxed but voter registration applications 
cannot. Voter registration applications can only be sent by mail or 
delivered in person by the voter, unless the voter registers online.

Frequently Asked Questions
Q Since military voters who are on active duty can request a ballot for federal 
elections until 5 p.m. on Election Day, does this mean that they still have to 
return their ballot by 8 p.m. on Election Day?
A Yes. All ballots must be returned by 8 p.m. on Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(6). 
All ballots must be mailed back or dropped off. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)1. It is 
unlikely that a military voter would be able to return a ballot by 8 p.m. if 
they request it at 5 p.m. on the same day, but it is a statutory possibility. For 
example, if someone in the National Guard is called into duty on Election Day, 
they could request a ballot and return it as they may be nearby to drop it off.
Q Can a military or overseas voter also request an absentee ballot under the 
indefinitely confined voter process?
A No. While an individual may meet the qualifications as both an indefinitely 
confined voter and a military or overseas voter, these processes are 
distinct and cannot be combined. However, neither procedure requires 
a qualified individual to show an ID under Wis. Stat. § 6.87(1) to make a 
sufficient request, and each procedure leads to a continuing request for 
the remainder of the calendar year unless otherwise specified. If a voter 
qualifies to receive ballots by email due to being military or overseas 
status, the Commission recommends that a voter select this status to 
receive the benefits they are entitled to under federal law.
Sec. 7.4.12: Reviewing UOCAVA Absentee 
Ballot Requests & Sending Ballots
Whenever a clerk receives an absentee ballot request from a military or 
overseas requestor, the request must be reviewed for sufficiency before the 
ballot is sent or made available to the voter. See Wis. Stat. § 6.87(1) (requiring 
a “proper” request made). As discussed in the previous chapter, there are a 
variety of methods by which military and overseas voters can request absentee 
ballots, and clerks should be familiar with each of them to ensure that any 
request that is received is sufficient.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 71
All absentee ballot requests, regardless of how they are received, need to be in 
writing. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(a). Military and permanent overseas voters do not need 
to provide a photo ID with their request. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(1). Temporarily overseas 
voters must provide a photo ID with their absentee ballot request or have a copy 
of their ID already on file with their clerk. See Wis. Stat. §§ 6.24(1) and (2), 6.87(1).
Reviewing Absentee Ballot Requests for Sufficiency
Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot (FWAB)
For detailed information, and sample forms, of how to review a FWAB for 
sufficiency as an absentee ballot request, see “Appendix 7.4.B: Reviewing the 
Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot (FWAB)” on page 95.
Federal Post Card Application (FPCA)
For detailed information, and sample forms, of how to review an FPCA for 
sufficiency as an absentee request, see “Appendix 7.4.A: Reviewing the Federal 
Post Card Application (FPCA)” on page 85.
Standard Application for Absentee Ballot Form (EL-121)
For detailed information, and sample forms, of how to review an EL-121 for 
sufficiency as an absentee request, see Sec. 7.1.2: “General Application 
Requirements” on page 2.
Email Requests through MyVote
If a military or overseas voter makes an email request for an electronic ballot 
through MyVote, they will receive their ballot materials electronically from their 
clerk by email. The voter will still have to follow the Uniform Instructions to print 
off their ballot, make their choices, and mail it back to their municipal clerk. 
Electronic ballot return is not authorized for any type of voter in Wisconsin.
Requests by Email or Other Written Requests
Absentee requests can be submitted by email or fax and are not required to be 
sent on any particular form. See Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(a)6. Requests received by 
email or fax do not need to include the voter’s signature. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(ac).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 72
Deadlines to Send Military & Overseas Ballots to Voters
Clerks must send out ballots to any military and overseas voters with active 
requests on file no later than 47 days prior to any election with a federal office 
on the ballot (typically spring election in Presidential Preference vote year, 
partisan primaries, general elections, and certain special elections) or 21 days 
before all other primaries and elections. Wis. Stat. §7.15(1)(cm). Ballot requests 
received after those deadlines must be processed and sent out within one 
business day (meaning any day from Monday to Friday, not including a legal 
holiday). Wis. Stat. §7.15(1)(cm).
A business day would be any day not including weekends or Wisconsin legal 
holidays. See Wis. Stat. §7.15(1)(cm) and 995.20). So, even if a clerk only has office 
hours once a week, they still must send a military or overseas voter’s ballot 
within one business day of receiving the request. For example, if a clerk has 
office hours every other Monday, and a voter puts in a request on a Friday, the 
clerk must get that ballot out either Friday or the next statutory Business Day 
(e.g. Monday). However, if the clerk’s office is open on Saturdays, or the clerk has 
a reason to be in office on that day, the ballot request should be processed on 
Saturday. Wis. Stat. § 990.001(4)(c).
Important: If the clerk has limited hours/days of operation, they must put 
procedures in place to watch for military and overseas ballot requests so 
that they can be processed within the deadlines laid out by statute.
Ballot Delivery Options
Military and overseas voters may request to have their ballots sent to them by 
mail or electronically. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(3)(d). The preferred method of delivery 
should be marked on or stated in the absentee ballot request.
Background: Electronic Ballot Delivery
Military and overseas voters are the only voters that may lawfully receive their 
absentee ballots electronically. This is a right specifically given to them by 
UOCAVA, and is also enshrined in Wisconsin law. 52 U.S.C. § 20302(a)(7), Wis. 
Stat. § 6.87(3)(d). Military and permanent overseas voters can receive their 
absentee ballots electronically by email from their municipal clerk, and they 
can make the request through MyVote. They can also make the request by 
email or fax. Both email and fax constitute electronic delivery of military and 
overseas ballots.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 73
As of 2018, temporary overseas voters can receive their ballots electronically by 
email, or by fax, though they need to request this directly from their municipal 
clerk. As of May 2026, military and overseas voters are no longer able to receive 
absentee ballots electronically directly through MyVote. Instead, they can 
receive their absentee ballots electronically by email or fax.10
Note: Electronic ballot return is not authorized for any voter type 
including military and overseas voters. Ballots cannot be printed, 
scanned, and returned by email, fax, or online. Military and overseas 
voters must return their absentee ballots by mail, using special 
instructions described below, or in person to their municipal clerk.
Review & Record the Voter’s Ballot Delivery Preference
If you receive a paper form or emailed request, the ballot delivery method requested 
by the voter will need to be recorded in the ballot request record when entered into 
WisVote. If the request came through MyVote, the voter should have chosen the 
preferred delivery method and in that case, it will already appear in WisVote.
Please note the Application Source field in WisVote shown below only lists how 
the voter made their request. The Ballot Delivery Method field must be reviewed 
to determine how the voter would like to receive their ballot.
10 The 2018 consent decree between the State of Wisconsin and the U.S. Department of Justice 
stipulated that all military and overseas voters, including temporary overseas voters, have the right 
to receive their ballots “electronically.” It did not specify whether “electronically” means by email/
fax, online, or both. The Commission originally began offering online ballot delivery to military and 
permanent overseas voters following another consent decree, in 2012. In May 2026, the Commission 
removed the functionality from MyVote that allowed military and overseas voters to access and 
download their electronic ballot directly from MyVote. That process relied on PDF-based ballots that do 
not meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1, which are newly required by federal law. 
The Commission removed the online ballot function while it works to make it fully compliant. Instead, 
military and overseas voters can receive ballots electronically by fax or email. Receiving an absentee 
ballot by email or by fax satisfies the electronic delivery requirements of UOCAVA.
The 2018 consent decree and 2012 consent decree are available on justice.gov.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 74
Figure 6: WisVote Application Source Field
Military and permanent overseas absentee ballot requests should always be 
entered as calendar-year requests unless specified by the voter to be specific 
to one election. Wis. Stat. § 6.22(4)(a), 6.24(4)(c) (permanent overseas). Calendar 
year ballot requests expire on December 31 of each year. All regular military and 
overseas voters must submit a new absentee request each year and can only 
request ballots for one calendar year in duration.
Sec. 7.4.13: Procedures for 
Sending Ballots
Step 1: Prepare the Correct Ballot
Clerks should always check first to ensure that they are preparing to send the 
correct ballot style to the correct type of voter. Military voters and temporary 
overseas voters get full ballots, including federal, state, and local contests. See 
Wis. Stat. § 6.22(2)(a) (permitting military voters to vote in their ward or district 
of residence prior to becoming a military voter). Permanent overseas voters get 
federal-only ballots. Wis. Stat. § 6.24(2).
Step 2: Prepare the Correct Ballot Paperwork 
for Mail, Email & Fax Ballots
For ballots going out by mail or by email/fax, clerks should ensure that they 
have all the correct paperwork in order that needs to go out with each ballot.
Note: This is especially important since there are different certificate 
envelopes and different uniform instructions utilized for each ballot 
return method.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 75
Delivery by Mail
Mailer should include:
 Ɋ Correct Ballot
 Ɋ Correct Certificate Envelope
 Ɋ Correct Uniform Instructions
 Ɋ Carrier Envelope with Correct Postage Markings
Step 1: The clerk should check again to ensure that the mailer includes the 
correct ballot style for the voter.
Step 2: The clerk initials the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(1).
Step 3: The clerk should confirm that the mailer includes the correct certificate 
envelope. Military and overseas voters should receive the EL-122M envelope 
(brown print). This certificate is specific to military and overseas voters because 
it removes the U.S. citizen requirement for the voter’s witness and also includes 
a space for military and permanent overseas voters to input their date of birth. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)1.
Step 4: The clerk initials the top of the certificate envelope to confirm that the 
voter is exempt from, or has me the proof of identification requirement.
Figure 7: Military and Overseas Ballot
Step 5: The clerk should confirm that the mailer includes the correct version of 
the Commission’s prescribed Uniform Instructions for absentee voting. Military 
and overseas voters who chose to receive their absentee ballots by mail should 
get the EL-128UP. A version of this form is also available in Spanish for voters who 
request it (EL-128-UPS).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 76
Step 6: The clerk will ensure the return carrier envelope (which will contain the 
voter’s completed ballot in its certificate envelope) has sufficient postage. If 
the ballot qualifies for free postage, the clerk will affix the appropriate legend 
required by U.S. postal regulations to the carrier envelope. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(3)(a). 
If the ballot will be mailed back to the clerk from within the United States, the 
clerk will pay for the return postage. Id. If the ballot is mailed back to the clerk 
from outside the United States, the voter must bay for return postage. Id.
Note about Free Federal Postage for Military and Overseas Ballot 
Materials: Per the United States Postal Service (USPS): Balloting 
materials may be sent through the mail without prepayment of 
postage for military and overseas voters. Federal law specifies that 
ballots can be returned to election officials using a free postage-paid 
symbol when mailed from a U.S. Post Office, Military Postal Service 
Agency (APO/FPO), or U.S. Diplomatic Pouch Mail. See also Wis. Stat. 
§ 6. 22(4)(e), 6.24(6), 6.87(3)(a). If a military or overseas voter elects to 
utilize a private carrier mail return service, they must cover the cost of 
that shipping themselves. For more information, see 8.0 Balloting Mail 
within the USPS 700 Special Standards.
Step 7: The clerk will also ensure that the voter’s address is properly formatted, 
particularly when sending ballot mailers overseas. Visit the Military & Diplomatic 
Mail page at USPS.com for more information.

Delivery by Email or Fax
Transmission should include:
 Ɋ Correct Ballot Style
 Ɋ Correct Certificate Envelope Print Template
 Ɋ Correct Uniform Instructions
Step 1: The clerk should check again to ensure that the transmission file includes 
the correct ballot style for the voter.
Step 2: The municipal clerk must initial the ballot in the endorsement section. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.87(1). Clerks can do this either by applying wet-ink initials to a 
paper ballot or by affixing digital initials to the electronic version of the ballot 
that is sent to the military or overseas voter.
Step 3: The clerk will then convert the ballot into a format that can be 
transmitted to the voter electronically. Clerks can scan the printed ballot to 
convert it to a PDF. Tip: Most county clerks provide their municipalities with a PDF 
of their ballot styles to use for military and overseas voters, so scanning may not 
be necessary.
Step 4: The clerk will confirm that the voter will receive the correct certificate 
envelope face. Military and overseas voters should receive the EL-122M envelope 
(brown print). This certificate is specific to military and overseas voters because 
it removes the U.S. citizen requirement for the voter’s witness, and also includes 
a space for military and permanent overseas voters to input their date of 
birth. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)1. Clerks can scan clear images of the EL-122M for 
voters to print themselves, or they can access electronic versions on elections.
wi.gov. Clerks can also generate the EL-122M in WisVote. The WisVote version 
is formatted differently than the brown version clerks may be accustomed to, 
but it contains all of the required information. See Section 3.7 of the WisVote 
manual for instructions on how to generate the EL-122M as part of the label 
generation process.
Step 5: The clerk initials the top of the certificate envelope to confirm that the 
voter is exempt from, or has me the proof of identification requirement. The 
clerk still must initial the top of the WisVote generated one, though the clerk can 
apply digital initials.

Figure 9: Clerk Initials
Step 6: The clerk should confirm that the mailer includes the correct version of 
the Commission’s prescribed Uniform Instructions for absentee voting. Military 
and overseas voters who chose to receive their absentee ballots by email or

voters who request it (EL-128-US).
Note: This is the most important part of the transmission package. 
The Uniform Instructions explain how to properly print and affix the 
certificate to the envelope containing the voter’s ballot.
Step 7: Transmit the entire package to the voter at the email address or fax 
number that the voter provided. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(3)(d).
Frequently Asked Questions
Q On the FPCA or FWAB, the voter said they want their ballot delivered 
“online/email”? How should I send the ballot?
A By email. As of May 2026, the Commission removed the functionality to 
deliver ballots to voters directly through MyVote. If the voter did not provide 
an email address, mail the voter a ballot. If the voter asks to get their ballot 
online, inform them that that option is no longer available, but that they 
will receive their absentee ballot electronically by email. Absentee ballot 
delivery by fax is also an option. 
Q Can UOCAVA voters send their ballot back by email?
A No. A Wisconsin voter can never return their ballot by email. They must 
deliver it by mail or in person. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)1.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 79
Expediting Late Ballots
There are three ways for a ballot to be considered sent out late:
 Ɋ Not sent out by the 47th day before a federal election.
 Ɋ Not sent out by the 21st day before any other election.
 Ɋ Not sent out within one business day after requesting.
State and federal law do not address specific steps that clerks should take if 
military and overseas ballots are sent out late. The following section should be 
considered Best Practices for resolving this situation for the voter if it does occur. 
Clerks should be aware that missing absentee ballot deadlines places them at 
risk of being subject to an administrative complaint or a lawsuit by the affected 
voter for failing to complete their statutory responsibilities.
Best Practices for Sending out Late Absentee Ballots
If the ballot is sent out late to a military or overseas voter, then the clerk must 
expedite the late ballot and include a prepaid expedited return mailing label. If 
the ballot is sent by email or fax, then the clerk can simply offer expedited return 
by including a message that says something like “this ballot was sent to you 
late. Would you like me to send you an expedited prepaid return label?” Then, 
the clerk can go to the post office, FedEx, UPS, or other mail service provider and 
get a prepaid expedited return label and scan it to the voter. Expedited delivery 
and return service can be expensive, but it is a cost the municipal clerk should 
incur to ensure that the voter is still able to cast their ballot. It is not the voter’s 
fault that the ballot was sent to them late, and clerks should never cite cost as a 
reason not to expedite the delivery or return of a voter’s otherwise lawful ballot.
Frequently Asked Questions: Reviewing and Sending Absentee Ballots
Q I only have office hours one day a week, do I have to come in special to 
send out ballots to military and overseas voters?
A Yes, all military and overseas ballots must be sent within one business day 
of receiving the request.
Q I am sending this ballot out one day late, do I really have to expedite it and 
offer a prepaid expedited return label?
A Yes, even if the ballot is just one day late.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 80
Sec. 7.4.14: Returning Absentee Ballots
No matter how a voter requests or receives an absentee ballot, the returned 
ballot must always be a hard copy enclosed within a physical envelope that 
contains a printed version of the completed certificate. Electronic ballot return is 
not authorized for any voter in Wisconsin.
Military and overseas voters must carefully follow the Uniform Instructions 
accompanying their ballot. Any questions or uncertainties about how to follow these 
instructions should be immediately communicated to the voter’s municipal clerk.
Important: It is never sufficient to just enclose the completed ballot in 
a plain envelope to be mailed back to the clerk.
Checklist for the Military & Overseas Voter 
before Returning an Absentee Ballot
 Ɋ Have you thoroughly reviewed the Uniform Instructions that accompanied 
your ballot to ensure you understand how to complete and return your 
absentee ballot?
 Ɋ Have you thoroughly reviewed your ballot to ensure you’ve made a 
selection for every contest?
 Ɋ Have you printed the EL-122M certificate label (brown style)  and filled 
it in completely?
 Ɋ Have you glued or taped the completed EL-122M certificate label (brown 
style) to a regular-letter size envelope?
Note: If you got your ballot by fax or email, you will have to provide 
this envelope.
 Ɋ Have you made a delivery plan and ensured you have covered sufficient 
postage for the ballot return, unless you are exempt from doing so? See 
Step 6 of “Delivery by Mail” on page 76.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 81
Ballot Delivery Guidance & Best Practices
The ballot must be returned so that it is delivered to the polling place no later 
than 8 p.m. on election day. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(6). Military and overseas voters are 
not exempt from this requirement. This means that military and overseas voters, 
especially those who need to rely on international mailing, should return their ballot 
with plenty of time for delivery to ensure it is received by the time polls close.
Best Practice: The voter should choose the delivery method that ensures 
the greatest likelihood that their ballot will be delivered on time to their 
municipal clerk. Many military and overseas voters choose overnight 
delivery, or some other form of expedited delivery, to ensure that the 
ballot returns on time. The municipal clerk is not responsible for return 
postage of a faxed or emailed absentee ballot. Overseas voters without 
access to public mail services may use a private mail carrier (such as 
UPS, FedEx, DHL, etc.) to return their ballot. The USPS recommends that 
ballots be mailed one week prior to the date of the Election to arrive on 
time. This timeline may be longer for voters who are overseas, so it is 
important they mail their ballot back as soon as possible.
Frequently Asked Questions
Q If a clerk is late in mailing absentee ballots to military or overseas voter, 
what can/will the U.S. Department of Justice do?
A Under Section 105 of UOCAVA, the Attorney General is authorized to bring 
civil actions to enforce UOCAVA requirements. When states have failed 
to make sure that ballots are sent to qualified UOCAVA protected voters 
in a timely manner, the Department of Justice has successfully obtained 
court orders and consent decrees to enforce UOCAVA protections. Many 
of these have required states to extend their deadlines for receiving 
these ballots and to count such ballots, even when they arrived after 
Election Day. In some cases, the states were required to make permanent 
changes to their laws or procedures to make sure the problems are not 
repeated in future elections. Through these cases brought to enforce the 
federal law, the Department has ensured that qualified servicemembers 
and overseas voters were able to cast their ballots with confidence that 
they were counted.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 82
Ahead of each federal election, Commission staff initiate and lead a call 
campaign to contact municipalities who have military and overseas 
absentee requests on file to remind them to send those ballots out as 
soon as they have received their ballots from the counties. Commission 
staff continue to follow up with all municipalities by phone or email until 
staff have confirmed that clerks are working on it or until the ballots are 
marked as sent in WisVote.
Q I received something back in the mail. I think it may be a ballot but I’m not 
sure. Should I open it?
A Yes. This is a tricky situation where the risk of opening a ballot prior to 
election day must be weighed against the benefit of helping a voter cast 
their ballot lawfully. Normally, absentee ballots cannot be opened until 
election day at the polling place. Wis. Stat. § 6.88(3)(a). This often is not an 
issue as voters contain their absentee ballots inside of sealed certificate 
envelopes, so clerks usually know when they’ve received a ballot back. 
However, sometimes voters misunderstand or misread absentee voting 
instructions and send their ballots back to the clerk in different ways. 
Sometimes, military and overseas voters will include their completed 
certificate inside the envelope with their ballot instead of taping or gluing 
the certificate to the outside.
If a clerk receives a mailer and suspects it might contain a ballot, the 
best practice would be to open it and figure out what it is. If the mailer 
contains a ballot and a completed certificate envelope, the ballot can still 
be counted. See Wis. Stat. § 6.87(3)(d). However, if the mailer just contains 
the ballot without a certificate envelope, the ballot cannot be counted. 
Id. Once the mailer has been opened, the clerk should draft a memo 
explaining the sequence of events and should reseal everything in a new 
envelope so that poll workers can understand what took place.
Q A military or overseas voter’s family member is trying to return their ballot 
on their behalf. Can I accept it?
A No — not unless the voter has requested their family member’s assistance 
in returning their ballot due to a disability. For more information on the 
proper return of absentee ballots, see Sec. 7.4.14: “Returning Absentee 
Ballots” on page 81.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 83
Sec. 7.4.15: Checking Compliance
Within 30 days after each general election, each municipal clerk shall transmit 
to the Commission a report of the number of absentee ballots transmitted by 
the clerk to absent military voters and overseas voters for that election and 
the combined number of those ballots that were cast by those voters in that 
election. Wis. Stat. §6.276(2).For WisVote users, entering the data into WisVote 
satisfies this requirement. When clerks maintain their UOCAVA-related data in 
WisVote, Commission staff are able to view an up-to-date report at any given 
time, requiring no further action by the clerk.
Within 90 days after each general election, the Commission the information 
contained in the reports received from municipal clerks under sub. (2) and transmit 
the information to the federal Election Assistance Commission. Wis. Stat. §6.276(3). 
Again, this information is pulled by Commission staff as a report from WisVote, 
and so as long as the information has been maintained at the municipal levels, 
no additional action is required by clerk.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 84
Appendix 7.4.A: Reviewing the Federal 
Post Card Application (FPCA)
The Federal Post Card Application (FPCA) can be used both as a voter 
registration form and an absentee ballot request. As described earlier in this 
chapter, the FPCA is a federal form designed to be used in all 50 states. This 
means that it both contains information that is not required in Wisconsin and 
also does not specifically contain information that is required in Wisconsin.
To aid municipal clerks in reviewing this form, the Commission has provided 
detailed instructions and guidance for reviewing each section of the FPCA.
Additional Documentation Required to Accompany the FPCA
Only temporary overseas voters are required to include 
additional documentation with their FPCA:
 Ɋ If the voter has indicated they are a temporary overseas voter, and they 
are using the FPCA to request an absentee ballot, they must also enclose 
a copy of their photo ID unless the clerk already has one on file.
 Ɋ Temporary overseas voters must also enclose proof of residence if they 
are attempting to use the FPCA to register to vote.
Military and permanent overseas voters can use the FPCA to register to vote 
and request an absentee ballot without needing to provide any additional 
documentation.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 85
Reviewing the FPCA for Sufficiency
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 86
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 87
Box 1: Voter Eligibility & Information
Box 1 of the FPCA determines the voter type (see above) and will determine how 
the voter is able to use the form. One of these boxes must be checked.
Table 19: FPCA Box 1 Options & Wisconsin Equivalent

This form also provides a place for the voter’s name (and previous name, if 
applicable) and date of birth. This information is always required.
Box 1 also asks for a driver’s license number and social security number. This 
information is required if the voter is using the FPCA to register to vote. Please note 
that some voters — especially permanent overseas voters who have never lived 
in the United States — may not have a Wisconsin driver’s license number or Social 
Security Number. In that case, the voter may write “I do not have this” or “N/A” in 
either box. The registration may still be completed even if this is the case.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 88
Box 2: U.S. Voting Residence Address
The voter will list the last address where they lived for at least 28 days in 
Wisconsin. This must be completed by all voters. Permanent overseas voters 
will list their last Wisconsin address (or their parent’s last address) prior to 
moving out of the country.
The clerk should be able to determine the voter’s address from the information 
provided. If the voter has written something like “Unknown” in Street Address but 
provides a town name, that is likely not sufficient.
Box 3: Voter’s Current Address
If the voter has a mailing address other than the address in Box 2, they will 
list it here. The clerk will send the voter’s ballot to this address if the voter has 
indicated they wish to receive their ballot by mail. In some cases, this box may 
not contain any information, and that is sufficient.
Box 4: Voter Contact Information
This information is not required but it is helpful for the municipal clerk in case 
the voter needs to be contacted. This is also where the voter will provide their 
email address or fax number if they choose to receive their ballot that way.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 89
Box 5: Voter Preferences
Question 5A is required if the FPCA is being used to request an absentee ballot. 
The voter must indicate how they wish to receive their absentee ballot, and they 
must provide the corresponding contact information in Box 4. The voter cannot 
select more than one option. If they do, the clerk should contact the voter and 
ask for their preference.
Note: If a voter selects “email or online” the clerk will have to send the 
voter their absentee ballot by email. As of May 2026, the Commission 
removed the ability to deliver absentee ballots online through MyVote. 
Question 5B is not required information in Wisconsin. Clerks should disregard 
anything the voter inputs in this box.
Box 6: Additional Required Information
Nothing is required in this box in Wisconsin. The voter may have provided 
additional information or instructions here, so please review those carefully.
Box 7: Additional Required Information
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 90
The voter must always sign and date the FPCA. By signing, they are swearing 
that they qualify to register to vote or receive an absentee ballot as a military or 
oveseas voter, which the municipal clerk is required to verify in order to accept 
the FPCA. Wis. Stat. § 6.22(2)(c), 6.24(4)(b).

The FPCA is a federal form that is provided to Military and Overseas voters 
(permanent and temporary) by the Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP).

U.S. military, through U.S. embassies, or online at FVAP.gov/election-materials. 
The FPCA form can serve as both a voter registration application as well as an 
absentee ballot request for most Wisconsin voters. The form was designed for 
use by all 50 states, so some of the information does not perfectly match the 
Wisconsin-specific forms.
