First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 92
What does the FPCA Look Like?
You can find the FPCA online at F VAP.gov.
What Should I Look for on the FPCA?
The FPCA may arrive in a military mailing envelope, or it may come to you in a 
regular envelope. Please open the envelope as soon as you receive it, you have 
1 business day to process the request if it is an absentee ballot application.
When looking at the FPCA, please note the information in the following boxes:
Box 1: This section of the form determines the voter type (see above) and will 
determine how the voter is able to use the form. This form also provides a 
place for the voter’s name (and previous name, if applicable). It also asks for a 
Wisconsin driver’s license number, social security number, and date of birth. A 
Wisconsin driver’s license number and social security number are not required.
Box 2: The voter will list the last Wisconsin address where they lived for at least 
28 days in Wisconsin. This must be completed by all voters. Permanent overseas 
voters will list their last Wisconsin address prior to moving out of the country.
Box 3: If the voter has a mailing address  other than the address in Box 2, 
they will list it here. Send the ballot to this address, if ballot delivery by mail 
is requested.
Box 4: These fields provide contact information in case you need to contact the 
voter or if they have specified fax or email delivery of their ballot.
Box 5: The first field allows a voter to specify their preferred method of ballot 
delivery — mail, email, online, or fax — if they are using the FPCA as an absentee 
ballot request. If a voter selects the email/online option, you must send the 
ballot by email. As of May 2026, online ballot delivery through MyVote is no 
longer available. The adjacent field, regarding political party, is not required or 
collected in Wisconsin. Please disregard anything listed in this box.
Box 6: Nothing is required in this box. Please look for any special instructions the 
voter may have listed.
Box 7: All voters must sign and date their request. A witness signature is never 
required on the FPCA.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 93
What are Some Tips for Processing a FPCA Request?
 Ɋ If a voter asks to receive their ballot by “Email/Online,” you must send it 
by email. As of May 2026, there is no longer an option to send a ballot 
electronically online through MyVote. Electronic delivery by fax is also an 
option. If the voter did not provide an email address, mail the voter a ballot. 
 Ɋ Photo ID is needed only if a Temporarily Overseas or Regular voter is using 
the FPCA as an absentee request. If the voter has already provided their 
Photo ID with a previous absentee ballot request, then they do not need to 
include a copy with their FPCA absentee ballot request.
 Ɋ Proof of Residence is needed only if a Temporarily Overseas or Regular 
voter is using the FPCA as a voter registration application.
If the voter is using the FPCA as an absentee ballot request, it should be 
considered a calendar year request. Voters need to submit a new request for 
each calendar year to continue receiving ballots.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 94
Appendix 7.4.B: Reviewing the Federal 
Write-In Absentee Ballot (FWAB)
Reviewing the FWAB for Sufficiency
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 95
Box 1: Voter Eligibility & Information
Box 1 determines the voter type so the clerk can confirm the voter is eligible to 
use the form the way they intend to. The voter should only check one of these 
boxes. If the voter checks more than one, the municipal clerk should contact 
the voter to confirm which ground of eligibility the voter intends to use. The form 
asks the voter to provide their SSN, date of birth, and driver’s license or state ID 
number, but those fields are not mandatory for an absentee ballot request.
Box 2: U.S. Voting Residence Address
The voter will provide the residential address that makes them eligible to vote 
in Wisconsin. Since military and overseas voters do not need to meet the same 
residency requirements as regular voters, this address may not be where they 
currently reside. The voter must provide sufficient information for the municipal 
clerk to identify their address. It is not sufficient for the voter to include only the 
name of a municipality.
Box 3: Voter’s Current Address
This is where the voter will enter their current mailing address. It is formatted as 
a free-form box due to the likelihood that this address will be outside the U.S.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 96
Box 4: Voter Contact Information
The voter is not required to provide this information unless they wish to receive 
their absentee ballot by email or fax.
Box 5: Voter Preferences
If the voter checks “yes” to Question 5.A., the municipal clerk will process 
the absentee ballot request as a calendar-year request, and the voter will 
automatically receive absentee ballots for each election in which they are 
eligible to vote in the current calendar year.
An answer to Question 5.B. is required, and the voter can only choose one 
option. If the voter checks more than one box, the municipal clerk will need to 
contact the voter to clarify their preference.
Note: If the voter checks “email or online,” the clerk will need to email 
the voter their ballot. Electronic delivery by fax is also an option. As of 
May 2026, online ballot delivery directly through MyVote is no longer an 
option.
Question 5.C. is not a required field in Wisconsin and should not be recorded in 
any way by the clerk.
Box 6: Additional Required Information
Box 6 is the most important box to review on the entire FWAB. If the voter is 
using the FWAB to request an absentee ballot, this box may contain additional 
information about how the voter wishes to receive their absentee ballot.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 97
If the voter is using the FWAB as a backup ballot, in order to count 
the ballot, all of the following must be present in Box 6:
 Ɋ Witness Printed Name
 Ɋ Witness Signature
 Ɋ Witness Address
Note: This differs from the instructions on Box 6 itself because those 
instructions are not accurate with respect to what is required by 
Wisconsin law.
If any of the fields above are missing, the FWAB cannot be counted as a 
backup ballot.
Box 7: Voter Affirmations & Signature
Regardless of whether the voter is using the FWAB as an absentee ballot request 
or a FWAB they must sign at the bottom.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 98
Page 2: Backup Ballot
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 99
The backup ballot will have handwritten or printed candidate names for each 
federal office on the ballot. Voters can still only vote for one candidate per 
federal office. Municipal clerks should use the following principles when reviewing 
the FWAB for sufficiency, and should see Sec. 14.15.12: “Absentee Certificate 
Envelopes” for detailed instructions on how to count the FWAB on election day.
The nature of the FWAB means that voters may not provide candidate names in 
the same way that they would normally appear on a Wisconsin ballot.
Poll workers should bear in mind the law governing voter intent, 
Wis. Stat. § 7.50, as well as the following best practices:
 Ɋ If the voter writes down only the name of a presidential candidate 
(omitting the vice presidential candidate), the vote for president still can 
be counted.
 Ɋ The voter omits the political party designation for any office, the vote can 
still be counted if the candidate’s name is present.
 Ɋ The candidate’s last name is sufficient to count the vote unless there are 
two candidates for the same office with the same last name.
 Ɋ A simple “Yes” or “No” for a ballot initiative answer is sufficient if there is 
only one question on the ballot, but not if there are multiple. “Yes to all” or 
“No to all” are sufficient for multiple ballot initiative questions.

What does the FWAB Look Like?

The FWAB may arrive in a military mailing envelope, or it may come to you 
in a regular envelope. When using the FWAB as a write-in ballot, voters are

but the ballot and affirmation are otherwise complete, the ballot can still be

When looking at the FWAB, please note the information in the following boxes:

place for the voter’s name (and previous name, if applicable). It also asks for a 
Wisconsin driver’s license number, social security number, and date of birth. A 
Wisconsin driver’s licence and Social Security number are not required.
Box 2: The voter will list the Wisconsin address they are registered at (or the 
address that ties them to Wisconsin). This must be completed by all voters.
Box 3: If the voter has a mailing address other than the address in Box 2, they will 
list it here. Send the ballot to this address if ballot delivery by mail is requested.
Box 4: These fields provide contact information in case you need to contact the 
voter or if they have specified fax or email delivery of their ballot.

collected in Wisconsin. Please disregard anything listed in this box.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 102
Box 6: If the voter is using the FWAB as an absentee ballot request only, then 
a witness signature is not required. If the voter is using the FWAB as a write-in 
ballot, then a witness signature, witness printed name, and witness address 
are required and should be placed in this box. Additionally, please look for any 
special instructions the voter may have listed.
Box 7: The voter’s signature is required.
What are Some Tips for Processing a FWAB Request?
 Ɋ If a FWAB is received from a voter who is eligible to use the form as a write-in 
ballot, the clerk must follow up by sending the voter an official absentee ballot.
 Ɋ If a Military or Permanently Overseas voter asks to receive their ballot by 
“Email/Online,” send you must send the absentee ballot by either email or 
fax. As of May 2026, the option to send an absentee ballot electronically 
directly through MyVote is no longer available. If the voter did not provide 
an email address, mail the voter a ballot. 
 Ɋ The clerk will hold onto the write-in FWAB until Election Day. If the voter’s 
official ballot is not received by Election Day, then the clerk will send the 
FWAB to the polls to be counted. If the voter’s official ballot is received by 
Election Day, then the official ballot is sent to the polls to be counted and 
the FWAB ballot is rejected.
If using the FWAB as a ballot, please remake the FWAB onto a standard ballot 
and issue a voter number as described in Sec. 14.15.12: “Absentee Certificate 
Envelopes”. If an eligible voter is using the FWAB as a write-in ballot, the clerk

participate. For example, if a Permanently Overseas voter writes in a local or 
state contest, the votes for those contests cannot be counted.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 103
Chapter 7.5: Processing 
Absentee Ballot Requests
The clerk must send the official absentee ballot to all approved absentee ballot 
applicants by the correct deadlines. As this section explains, having part time 
office hours or limited staff available to assist with processing applications is 
not an excuse for sending out absentee ballots late to voters.
Sec. 7.5.1: Procedure
Clerks must send an absentee ballot to a voter with a request on file by the 
official deadline or within one business day of receiving any subsequent 
requests. Wis. Stat. § 7.15(1)(cm). One business day means Monday to Friday, 
regardless of a clerk’s scheduled office hours but excluding holidays. Id. For the 
partisan primary and general election, the official deadline is 47 days before the 
election, and for all other elections the deadline is 21 days before the election. Id. 
For the presidential preference primary, the deadline for military and overseas 
ballots is also 47 days before the election. Id.
An absentee application is received when it is delivered to the clerk’s mailbox, 
email, or fax machine. Therefore, clerks must ensure that their office is staffed so 
that absentee ballots requests may be processed and sent within one business 
day of being received during the entire 47- or 21-day period before an election, 
which may require additional hours. For example, having staff able to process 
absentee ballot requests Monday, Wednesday, and Friday would meet this 
requirement provided that all valid pending absentee requests are processed 
on those days.
Absentee Ballot Requests from Ineligible Felons
Before issuing an absentee ballot, the clerk should review the Ineligible Felon 
List, which comes from information provided to the Commission by the 
department of Corrections, to confirm that the voter is eligible to vote on the 
day of the election. If the name of the voter appears on the list, the clerk should 
make a reasonable effort to verify the voter’s felony status. Clerks may call or 
email Commission staff to contact the Department of Corrections (DOC) to 
obtain any updated information, or they may contact the DOC on their own. If 
the Commission or clerk confirms the voter is eligible to vote, the clerk should 
document this on the Absentee Ballot Log (EL-124).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 104
If the Commission confirms the voter is not eligible or the Commission cannot 
be contacted the clerk should treat the absentee ballot request as insufficient 
due to the information concerning the voter’s ineligibility to vote due to felony 
status. The clerk should then send the voter written notice that the voter is 
ineligible to vote per Department of Corrections (clerks can generate this 
from WisVote; it is the “Felon Notice” form letter). The notice should state that 
if the voter believes this action was taken in error, they must contact the clerk 
immediately. With the written notice, the clerk should include a copy of the 
Commission’s Ineligible Voter Information Sheet explaining what the voter needs 
to do to resolve the issue with the Department of Corrections. The Clerk should 
also mark the registration as “ineligible to vote per Department of Corrections.”
If the voter confirms that they are ineligible to vote, the clerk should change the 
voter’s registration to inactive. Wis. Stat. § 6.50(6).
If the voter maintains that they are eligible to vote in the election, the clerk should 
issue an absentee ballot to the voter but ensure that the election inspectors or 
board of absentee ballot canvassers know to challenge the ballot if it is returned 
and the voter is still listed as a felon on the Ineligible Voter List. Wis. Stat. § 6.88(3)(c). 
The election inspectors or board of absentee ballot canvassers can also contact 
the Commission on Election Day with any DOC list questions. If the voter no longer 
appears on the list, the ballot does not need to be challenged.
Absentee Ballot Requests from Military and Overseas Voters
If requested, the clerk must transmit an absentee ballot by email or fax to military 
voters away from home or permanent and temporary overseas voters. Wis. 
Stat. § 6.87(3)(d). Clerks may not transmit an absentee ballot by fax or email to a 
regular voter. Id. Please see Chapter 7.4: “Types of Absentee Voters: UOCAVA” on 
page 42 for a full description of the military and overseas voting process.
Clerk Initials Ballot and Prepares Absentee Ballot Package for Voter
The clerk must initial all issued ballots in the endorsement section of each ballot 
under “Absentee ballot issued by.” Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(ar).
The clerk must complete the correct Official Absentee Ballot Application/
Certification (EL-122) depending on the voter type by filling out the “Clerk Use 
Only” section with the date of the election, county, municipality, and district or 
ward information. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(2). Municipal clerks or providers may also 
print labels containing this information from WisVote for both in-person and by-
mail absentee ballots.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 105
The clerk must also initial the certificate envelope indicating that proof of 
identification has been provided or that the voter is exempt from the photo ID 
requirement before sending the absentee ballot. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.86(1)(ar), 6.87(4)(b)2.
The clerk must provide First-Class postage on the certificate envelope if the ballot 
will be returned from within the United States. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(3)(a).The clerk is 
not required to provide postage on certificate envelopes that will be returned 
from outside of the United States, and the absentee voter must pay for this 
postage unless the voter unless the envelope qualifies for free postage when it is 
mailed. Id. For military and overseas voters, the clerk must use the postage paid 
envelopes; EL-120M mailer envelope and the EL-122M certificate envelope. Id.
The clerk will also need to ensure that the correct Uniform Absentee Ballot 
Instructions prescribed by the Commission given they type of absentee ballot 
request is included in the certificate envelope. Wis. Stat. § 6.869.
Once all materials are ready to mail, the clerk must place the following materials 
in the correct Absentee Ballot Mailer Envelope (EL-120) given the voter type:
 Ɋ Cover letter (optional)
 Ɋ Uniform Instructions (standard, 
military and overseas)
 Ɋ Ballot(s)
 Ɋ Certificate Envelope (standard, 
military and overseas, special)
The clerk must provide First-Class class postage on the envelope addressed to 
the voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(3)(a). The clerk must mail the Absentee Carrier Envelope 
to the mailing address provided by the absentee voter. Wis. Stat. § 7.15(1)(cm).
Sec. 7.5.2: Absentee Ballot Log
The clerk also maintains the Absentee Ballot Log (EL-124). See Wis. Stat. § 6.89. 
The Absentee Ballot Log (EL-124) is used to track the events that occur during the 
absentee ballot process (application received, ballot issued, ballot canceled, 
second ballot issued, ballot received, ballot counted, etc.). The Absentee 
Ballot Log (EL-124) enables the clerk to track any problems with the absentee 
certificate envelope (for instance, missing certificate, voter signature, witness 
signature and address, or SVD signature) and communicate this information to 
the election inspectors so they can reject the ballot if the error is not corrected 
by 8:00 p.m. on Election Day. See “Issuing a New Certificate Envelope” on page 
139 for information on correcting certificate envelope errors. The Absentee 
Ballot Log (EL-124) is sent to the polling place with the absentee ballots on 
Election Day.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 106
Chapter 7.6: Proof 
of Identification for 
Absentee Voting
Sec. 7.6.1: Proof of Identification 
Generally Required
Subject to limited exceptions (see below), absentee voters are required to provide 
Proof of Identification with their absentee application. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(ac).
Note: The limited exceptions to the identification requirement listed below 
do NOT apply to voters voting in the clerk’s office or the polling place. 
All voters who vote in the clerk’s office or the polling place must present 
acceptable proof of identification at that time. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.79(2)(a) and 
6.86(1)(ar). The only exceptions for in-person absentee voting or polling 
place voting are confidential voters and voters who have surrendered 
their license. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.79(6) and (7), and 6.86(1)(ar).
Proof of identification means identification that contains the name of the 
individual to whom the document was issued, which name conforms to the 
individual’s voter registration form, if the individual is required to register to vote, 
and that contains a photograph of the individual. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(16c).
Only the following documents issued to an individual 
satisfies the proof of identification requirement:
 Ɋ A Wisconsin Driver License, even if driving privileges are revoked or 
suspended; can be expired but only since the last General Election. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.02(6m)(a)1.
 Ɋ A Wisconsin DOT-issued Identification Card; can be expired but only since 
the last General Election. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(6m)(a)2.
 Ɋ A Military ID card issued by a U.S. uniformed service; can be expired but 
only since the last General Election. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(6m)(a)3.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 107
 Ɋ A U.S. passport; can be expired but only since the last General Election. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.02(6m)(a)4.
 Ɋ A certificate of naturalization that was issued not earlier than two years 
before the date of an election at which it is presented. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(6m)(b).
 Ɋ An unexpired WI Driver License receipt. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(6m)(c).
 Ɋ An unexpired Wisconsin DOT-Issued Identification Card receipt. Wis. Stat. 
§ 5.02(6m)(d).
 Ɋ An identification card issued by a federally recognized Indian tribe in 
Wisconsin. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(6m)(e).
 Ɋ An identification card issued by a Wisconsin-accredited university, college 
or technical college, which must contain the following:
 ɉ Student’s name
 ɉ Student’s photograph
 ɉ Date of issuance
 ɉ Signature of student
 ɉ Expiration date no later than two 
years after date of issuance. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.02(6m)(f).
Note: A school ID card does not have to include a proof of enrollment 
document if unexpired. Luft v. Evers, 963 F.3d 665, 677 (7th Cir. 2020). 
However, if the school ID card is expired, it must be presented with a proof of 
enrollment document. Common Cause v. Thomsen, 574 F. Supp. 3d 634, 641 
(W.D. Wis. 2021) (quoting a clarification by the court after the release of the 
decision in Luft v. Evers). Proof of enrollment documents include, but are not 
limited to, a fee receipt, class schedule or an enrollment verification form.
 Ɋ An unexpired Veterans Affairs ID Card issued by the Veterans Health Adminis-
tration of the federal Department of Veterans Affairs. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(6m)(g).
 Ɋ A temporary identification card receipt issued by Wisconsin DOT through the 
Identification Petition Process (IDPP) (valid for 60 days). Wis. Stat. § 343.165(8). For 
more information on obtaining a temporary voting ID, see the Commission’s 
Bring It To The Ballot page or the Wisconsin DMV ID card petition process page.
 Ɋ For Confidential Voters only, an identification card issued under Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.47(3). Wis. Stat. §§ 6.79(6) and 6.86(1)(ar).
 Ɋ For voters who have surrendered their license within 60 days of an election only, 
an original copy of the citation or notice. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.79(7), and 6.86(1)(ar).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 108
Note: If a clerk receives an absentee ballot request with this form of 
ID, the clerk must keep track of this ballot and if a certificate envelope 
containing a ballot is returned, the clerk must write “Ballot under 
s. 6.965, stats.” on the envelope to notify poll workers of special 
processing requirements on Election Day.
Sec. 7.6.2: Exceptions to 
Photo ID Requirements
The following groups may meet the proof of identification requirement by having 
another person certify the voter’s identity and residence on the absentee ballot 
certificate envelope instead of providing proof of identification with their application 
(Please refer to the “Special Categories of Absentee Voters” section below):
 Ɋ Indefinitely confined voters. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)2.
 Ɋ Voters residing in a facility served by Special Voting Deputies. Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.875(6)(c)1. In this instance, the two voting deputies are the witnesses 
and provide this certification. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(c)1.
 Ɋ Voters residing in a facility eligible for service by Special Voting Deputies 
(SVDs) but that were not served by SVDs. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)5. In this 
instance, the certification must be from an authorized representative of 
the facility. Id. The Commission has designed an EL-122 Special form for 
this purpose, along with Special EL-122 Instructions.
The following individuals are exempt from the proof of 
identification requirement when voting via absentee ballot:
 Ɋ Military voters. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(ac).
 Ɋ Permanent overseas voters. Id.
 Ɋ Confidential voters. Id.
 Ɋ Voters who have previously provided proof of identification for a by-mail 
absentee ballot received from the clerk are not required to provide proof 
of identification with subsequent requests as long as the voter has not 
moved or changed names. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)3.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 109
Chapter 7.7: In-Person 
Absentee Voting (IPAV)
Sec. 7.7.1: Introduction
In-Person Absentee Voting (IPAV) may occur in the clerk’s office or another 
designated absentee voting location no earlier than 14 days before an election 
and no later than the Sunday before an election, but never on a legal holiday. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(b). This is the only situation in which a clerk may accept an 
absentee ballot request from the voter in person, and all voters participating 
must complete an application in person.  Id.
Sec. 7.7.2: IPAV Hours: Best Practices
While there is no specific amount of time a clerk must allow IPAV, Wisconsin law 
permits all registered voters to request an absentee ballot in person at their 
clerk’s office or alternate site, and the Commission believes that clerks must offer 
at least some hours for IPAV before each election. See Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(a)2.
Clerks must specify the office hours during which voters may cast a ballot 
during the IPAV period in the clerk’s office or any alternate sites in the Type E 
Notice. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.86(1)(b), 10.01(2)(e).
Best Practice: The Commission recommends that clerks should 
also post the hours on the municipal website and any social media 
accounts used by the municipality. The legal requirements of where 
and how the Type E notice must be posted are a floor, not a ceiling. 
Clerks should take whatever steps are necessary to ensure that IPAV 
hours are fully communicated with their constituents. 
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 110
Sec. 7.7.3: Absentee Ballot 
Applications, Verification Process
All applicants must complete a written request before receiving a ballot, and 
the clerk must maintain that request along with other materials for the election. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(ar). While the absentee certificate envelope doubles as an 
absentee request and certification when completed in person in the clerk’s 
office, the Commission recommends that clerks have voters fill out an EL-121 
Absentee Ballot Request so that the EL-121 form may be retained for this purpose.
All in-person absentee voters, except for confidential voters who may show 
their identification card issued under Wis. Stat. § 6.47 or voters who have had 
their license revoked, must present proof of identification before receiving a 
ballot, and the clerk must verify that the name presented on the ID conforms to 
the name on the application and that any photograph reasonably resembles 
the voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(ar). see Chapter 7.6: “Proof of Identification for 
Absentee Voting” on page 107 for a list of acceptable proof of identification 
documents. After verifying the ID, the clerk must initial the absentee certificate 
envelope indicating that the clerk has viewed acceptable proof of identification 
for the in-person absentee voter. Id.
Best Practice: During IPAV, many clerks will also be managing late 
registration in person from the clerk’s office or alternate site. See 
Chapter 7.2: “Types of Absentee Voters” on page 7 for a description 
of this kind of registration. As part of that process, clerks must review the 
Ineligible Voter List to confirm that the voter is eligible to vote on the day 
of the election. Wis. Stat. § 6.29(2)(am). The Commission recommends 
following this process as well for in-person absentee voters who are 
already registered because it is possible that their names have been 
added to the Ineligible Voter List. If the name of the voter appears on the 
list, the clerk should inform the voter that the voter is ineligible to vote 
per the Department of Corrections.
If the voter agrees that they are ineligible, the absentee application should be 
rejected and the voter registration inactivated. If the voter maintains that they are 
eligible to vote in the election, the clerk should make a reasonable effort to contact 
the Commission to verify the voter’s felony status. If the voter is eligible to vote, the 
clerk should document on the Absentee Ballot Log (EL-124) that they confirmed the 
voter’s status with the Commission and then allow the voter to proceed to vote.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 111
If the clerk confirms that the voter is not eligible to vote or if the 
clerk is unable to contact the Commission, the clerk should:
 Ɋ Give the voter the Ineligible Voter Information Sheet that explains to the voter 
what they need to do to resolve the issue with the Department of Corrections.
 Ɋ Permit the voter to vote but mark the Absentee Certificate Envelope (EL-122) 
as “ineligible to vote per Department of Corrections.” On Election Day, the 
poll workers shall review the Ineligible Voter List and challenge the ballot if 
the name of the voter appears on the list and the clerk provides no contrary 
information (see Election Day Issues, Challenging Voters). Wis. Stat. § 6.92(1).
Sec. 7.7.4: Issuing the Voter a Ballot
Once the above steps are complete, the clerk gives the voter an absentee 
ballot, and the voter marks the ballot in private such that the selections 
cannot be observed except if the voter has asked for assistance in making the 
selections, seals in an Absentee Ballot Certificate Envelope (EL-122) that the voter 
completes and signs. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)1.
The ballot may not be taken from the clerk’s office. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(3)(a).
Sec. 7.7.5: Witness Requirement
All IPAV voting must be witnessed by the municipal clerk or an election official 
under the clerk, who must sign and print their name and provide their office 
(recommended) or home address. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(1)(b). The prohibitions 
against a candidate witnessing the voting of an absentee ballot do not apply to 
municipal clerks carrying out their IPAV responsibilities. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(8).
Sec. 7.7.6: Alternate 
Absentee Ballot Sites
The governing body of a municipality may elect to designate a site to replace 
the office of the municipal clerk as the location from which voters of the 
municipality may request, vote, and return absentee ballots. Wis. Stat. § 6.855(1).
The designated site shall be located as near as practicable to the office of the 
municipal clerk and cannot afford any advantage to any political party. The 
governing body shall not later than 14 days prior to the time absentee ballots 
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 112
are available (47 days before each primary or election for national office,  
21 days before each other primary or election) designate an alternate absentee 
ballot site. Wis. Stat. § 6.855(1). Once a designation is made, it remains in effect 
until at least the day after the election. Id.
If a designation is made, no function related to voting and return of absentee 
ballots that will take place in the alternate site may take place in the office of 
the municipal clerk. Id.
The municipal clerk shall display a notice of the alternate site in the office of the 
municipal clerk beginning on the date the site is designated until the absentee 
voting period has ended. Wis. Stat. § 6.855(2). If the municipal clerk maintains a 
website, the notice must also be posted on the website during the same period. Id.
Best Practice: The Commission recommends using the Type E notice 
for this purpose. See Wis. Stat. § 10.01(2)(e).
An alternate absentee ballot site shall be staffed by the municipal clerk or 
employees of the clerk. Wis. Stat. § 6.855(3). Each absentee ballot site must be 
accessible to all individuals with disabilities. Wis. Stat. § 6.855(4).
A governing body may designate more than one alternate site. Wis. Stat. § 6.855(5).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 113
Chapter 7.8: Cancelling 
& Issuing Replacement 
Absentee Ballots
Sec. 7.8.1: Introduction
Some Wisconsin voters choose to cast an absentee ballot by mail. Once the 
absentee ballot is mailed by the municipal clerk and received by the voter, 
the voter must complete and return it by 8 p.m. on Election Day to be counted. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.87(6). Because the process involves the postal system, there may 
be delays in both receiving and returning ballots.
If a voter contacts their municipal clerk and believes that their absentee ballot 
either got lost in the mail or is not going to make it back to the clerk in time to 
be counted, the Commission recommends that the clerk first confirm that the 
ballot has not been received and was not properly recorded as returned. If a 
clerk has not received the ballot, and the ballot is lost in transit, the clerk may 
cancel that ballot and issue a new absentee ballot to the voter as the ballot has 
not been returned.
However, once the voter has placed the absentee ballot in the mail (or returned 
it by drop box or to the clerk’s office), the option of voting in person at the polls is 
closed to them for that specific ballot, even if the ballot has not yet been received 
by the clerk. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(6). If a ballot that has not yet been received by the 
clerk is cancelled by the clerk due to being lost in the mail, the clerk must issue a 
replacement ballot either by mail or during IPAV. A by mail absentee voter who is 
issued a new absentee ballot who does not return it directly to the clerk or place 
it in the mail may still vote in person at the polls instead of returning the absentee 
ballot. See Wis. Stat. § 6.86(6).
Sec. 7.8.2: Spoiling Absentee Ballots
For guidance on how and when voters can spoil absentee ballots, see Chapter 
7.14: “Spoiling & Replacement of Absentee Ballots” on page 142.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 114
Sec. 7.8.3: Frequently Asked Questions
Q A voter contacts the clerk’s office and states that they have mailed their 
absentee ballot back but is concerned that it will not be delivered to the 
clerk’s office by 8:00 p.m. on Election Day, and they want to cancel their 
ballot and vote at the polls on Election Day. Can they get a new ballot at 
their polling place on Election Day?
A No. Once a voter has placed their ballot in the mail, it is considered 
mailed. They cannot be issued a new ballot at the polling place on 
Election Day, even if their absentee ballot will not be returned to the clerk’s 
office in time to be counted. See Chapter 7.14: “Spoiling & Replacement of 
Absentee Ballots” on page 142 for additional guidance.
Q A voter has mailed their absentee ballot many days ahead of Election Day, 
but it has not been delivered to the clerk’s office. The voter has called the 
clerk and is concerned that it may not arrive by 8:00 p.m. on Election Day. 
The voter asks if they can cancel their first ballot and have the clerk send 
them a new ballot?
A If the municipal clerk has not received a sufficient returned absentee 
ballot from the voter, they are able to be sent a new absentee ballot.
Q A voter has returned their absentee ballot and the clerk has determined 
that it is sufficient. The voter contacts the clerk’s office because they voted 
for a candidate they no longer wish to vote for. Can the clerk cancel their 
returned absentee ballot and issue them a new ballot?
A For detailed guidance on spoiling ballots, see Chapter 7.14: “Spoiling & 
Replacement of Absentee Ballots” on page 142.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 115
Chapter 7.9: Absentee 
Ballot Return
Sec. 7.9.1: Introduction
Only the voter may lawfully return his or her completed absentee ballot, either by 
mail or in person, to the office of the municipal clerk, subject to two exceptions. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)(1), Teigen v. Wis. Elections Comm’n, 2022 WI 64, 59, 403 Wis. 
2d 607, 976 N.W.2d 519, overruled in part by Priorities USA v. WEC, 2024 WI 32.
There are only two exceptions to the requirement that a voter must return his 
or her own ballot: 1) the voter requires assistance due to a disability, and 2) the 
voter is hospitalized and voting according to those special procedures. 
Exception 1: Voters Requiring Assistance
First, pursuant to the Voting Rights Act, any Wisconsin voter who requires 
assistance with mailing or delivering their absentee ballot to the municipal 
clerk because of a disability must be permitted to receive such assistance by 
a person of the voter’s choice, other than the voter’s employer or agent of that 
employer or officer or agent of the voter’s union. Carey v. Wis. Elections Comm’n, 
624 F. Supp. 3d 1020 (W.D. WI 2022).
When an election official is presented with an absentee ballot 
delivered in-person, the official may ask the following questions:
 Ɋ “Are you the voter?” If not, then:
 Ɋ “Are you delivering the voter’s ballot because the voter has determined 
that they require assistance returning their ballot due to their disability?”  
If yes, then:
 Ɋ “Are you someone other than the voter’s employer, an agent of that 
employer, or an officer or agent of the voter’s union?” If yes, then the ballot 
can be accepted.13
13 This guidance was approved by the Commission on September 6, 2022, and is available here: 
elections.wi.gov/news/guidance-absentee-ballot-return-options.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 116
Exception 2: Hospitalized Voters Voting by Authorized Agent
Second, an agent may return a completed absentee ballot on behalf of a 
hospitalized voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(3)(c). see “Procedures for Making the 
Absentee Ballot Request by Agent” on page 13 for a description of this 
process. For ballots being returned under this section, an election official should 
check the list of voters and agents who have been issued ballots and record 
that the ballot has been returned. See Id.
Sec. 7.9.2: Methods of 
Absentee Ballot Return
There are several lawful methods of absentee ballot return:
 Ɋ By mail
 Ɋ In person to the municipal clerk’s office or alternate absentee voting site
 Ɋ In person directly to the voter’s polling place or “central count”
 Ɋ Via drop box
All of these methods are authorized by the provision of state law that allows 
voters to mail, or “[deliver] in person,” their ballot “to the municipal clerk.” Wis. 
Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)1. Each is discussed further below. Voters can choose any 
method to return their absentee ballot.
Sec. 7.9.3: Returning Ballots by Mail
Absentee voters can return their ballots by mail by placing it in a USPS mailbox 
or taking it to a post office. The postage is pre-paid by the municipal clerk, 
unless the voter is mailing it back from outside the U.S. If mailing it back from 
outside the United States the voter must affix sufficient postage unless the ballot 
qualifies for free delivery. Id.
Note: The Commission recommends that voters mail their absentee 
ballots back as soon as possible but no later than 10 business days 
before Election Day. This ensures the greatest likelihood that the ballot 
will be returned to the municipal clerk by 8 p.m. on Election Day.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 117
Sec. 7.9.4: Returning Ballots in 
Person to the Clerk’s Office or 
Alternate Absentee Ballot Site
An absentee voter can also choose to take their ballot directly to their municipal 
clerk’s office or to an alternate absentee ballot site. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)1. Voters 
should contact their municipal clerk ahead of time to confirm the hours and 
availability of absentee ballot return. If municipalities are using alternate absentee 
ballot sites during in-person absentee voting, voters can’t take their ballots to the 
clerk’s office, but they can take it to an alternate site. Wis. Stat. § 6.855(1).
Some municipal clerks may set a cut off on Election Day after which they will 
no longer accept absentee ballots to ensure they have enough time to deliver 
them all to their polling places by 8 p.m. However, it is contrary to law to set an 
absentee delivery cutoff at the clerk’s office and also refuse to allow a voter to 
take their own ballot to their polling place.14 
Note: Municipal clerks cannot lead voters to believe that they must 
return their voted absentee ballots to their office by a certain time 
before 8 p.m. on Election Day or it will not be counted. Voters may 
lawfully cast ballots until 8 p.m. on Election Day. If the municipal clerk 
is unable to accept the return of voted absentee ballots in their office 
past a certain point, they must inform voters how they can still lawfully 
cast their ballots before 8 p.m.15
Sec. 7.9.5: Returning Ballots in Person 
Directly to Polling Place or “Central Count”
The Commission has consistently reiterated that direct return of an absentee 
ballot by a voter (or their lawful assistant) to their polling place (or “central 
count”) is a lawful method of absentee ballot return. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)1., 
6.87(6). A voter may lawfully return his or her voted absentee ballot in person 
14 See EL 23-47, Peters v. Goergen (Dec. May 27, 2025).
15 Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 118
to their polling place before 8 p.m. on Election Day and a voter who determines 
that he or she needs assistance returning her ballot due to a disability may also 
permit their assistant to return their ballot directly to their polling place.16
Sec. 7.9.6: Drop Boxes
On July 5, 2024, the Wisconsin Supreme Court overruled its prior decision, in 
part, in Teigen v. WEC, and held that secure drop boxes were permitted under 
state law as a valid method of absentee ballot return. The decision is binding on 
all lower Wisconsin courts. The use of drop boxes is not mandatory and is at the 
discretion of the municipal clerk.
On July 11, 2024, the Commission held a public meeting 
to review and issued the following guidance:
Q Does the decision affect all municipal clerks?
A Yes. The decision permits all municipal clerks to choose to use secure 
absentee ballot drop boxes in their jurisdiction if they wish.
Q What does the decision say?
A The Wisconsin Supreme Court determined that the statute that permits 
voters to return their absentee ballots “to the municipal clerk issuing the 
ballot or ballots” refers to a person, not a location. The court asserted 
that this interpretation of state law is consistent with Wisconsin’s highly 
decentralized system whereby municipal clerks have broad statutory 
discretion to administer elections in their jurisdiction. Accordingly, since 
voters may return their absentee ballots to the municipal clerk, or his or 
her authorized representatives, they may do so via drop box, if that’s a 
method the municipal clerk chooses to utilize.
Q Did the decision change any established practice?
A Yes. The decision reversed a prior Wisconsin Supreme Court decision, in 
part, and held that secure drop boxes are a legal method of absentee 
ballot return under Wisconsin law.
16 See also EL 24-23, Yunker v. Luedtke (Dec. May 27, 2025) (Determining that an opposite conclusion by 
a municipal clerk was contrary to law). 
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 119
Q Do clerks have to use drop boxes?
A No. The decision explicitly states that it does not require clerks to use 
drop boxes, it just says that the law permits clerks to utilize them if 
they choose. So, if a municipal clerk decides not to use drop boxes in 
an exercise of clerk election administration discretion, they will not be 
violating the Priorities USA  decision. Clerks should note, however, that 
choosing not to use drop boxes because of a belief that they are not 
legal is likely inconsistent with the reasoning of the decision and raises 
the risk of a legal challenge.
Q Can a clerk be successfully sued if he or she chooses not to utilize drop boxes?
A Likely not. If a clerk chooses not to use drop boxes in upcoming elections, 
it is very unlikely that a challenger would be successful in arguing that 
Priorities USA requires them to be used.
Q Are the Commission’s previous memos related to drop boxes prior to the 
Teigen decision back in effect?
A No. The Commission withdrew memoranda dated March 31 and 
August 19, 2020, relating to drop boxes as part of the Teigen litigation 
on February 16, 2022. The Priorities USA  decision does not mean 
either of those memoranda are back in effect. The information in this 
chapter, which was approved by the Commission on July 11, 2024, is 
the Commission’s sole issued guidance related to drop boxes.
Q Did the decision discuss where drop boxes may be located and who can 
set them up?
A Yes. The decision stated that drop boxes are set up, maintained, secured, 
and emptied by the municipal clerk, which includes their authorized 
representatives. A single person need not set up, maintain, secure, and empty 
all drop boxes in a municipality. The drop boxes may be placed in a location 
other than the municipal clerk’s office and may be placed in any location 
that the municipal clerk, within his or her statutory discretion, designates.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 120
Q Do drop boxes need to be secure? What should clerks consider when 
examining drop box security?
A Yes. The decision held that state law permits clerks to lawfully utilize 
secure drop boxes in an exercise of their statutorily conferred discretion. 
The decision did not provide guidance on what it means for a drop 
box to be “secure.” The Commission recommends that clerks keep the 
following non-exhaustive security considerations in mind when planning 
to utilize drop boxes, which are consistent with guidance from the U.S. 
Election Assistance Commission (EAC) and the U.S. Cybersecurity and 
Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). These considerations are merely 
a starting point — the Commission recommends that clerks thoroughly 
complete a security assessment for each intended drop box location prior 
to deployment.
The Commission recommends the following best practices:
Best Practices: Physical Security of the Drop Box Itself
 Ɋ The drop box be securely affixed to the ground or the side of the 
building, or secured such that the drop box cannot be removed or 
tampered with.
 Ɋ If located outside, the drop box be sturdy enough to withstand the 
elements so the ballots inside will remain unspoiled.
 Ɋ The drop box be secured against unlawful access or emptying.
 Ɋ The slot of the drop box be appropriately sized so that only an 
absentee ballot can be deposited and not other objects or liquids.
 Ɋ Any damage to or tampering with the drop box be documented and 
the drop box be inspected to ensure that it remains secure for the 
purpose of depositing absentee ballot envelopes.
 Ɋ The drop box be clearly marked or labeled that the drop box is for the 
purpose of collecting absentee ballots in return envelopes.
 Ɋ The time of final retrieval of ballot return envelopes be clearly marked 
on or near the drop box. After the time of final retrieval, the drop 
box be secured to prevent the submission of absentee ballot return 
envelopes.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 121
Best Practices: Security of the Drop Box Surroundings
 Ɋ The drop box be located in a safe location with adequate parking 
and safe access for pedestrians.
 Ɋ The drop box be located in a well-lit area.
 Ɋ The drop box be clearly visible, and the path to the drop box be 
accessible with clear and level ground space in front.
Best Practices: Security of Ballot Retrieval/Emptying
 Ɋ The drop box be emptied often enough to avoid the box from being 
filled with ballots, and a record of the times and dates of retrieval, 
number of ballots retrieved and the person or persons participating 
in the retrieval be maintained.
 Ɋ Ballots retrieved from a drop box be securely transported to the office 
of the clerk.
 Ɋ The drop box be equipped with unique locks or seals to secure 
ballots.
 Ɋ Absentee ballots that are returned via drop box be secured 
and transported in the same manner as all other absentee 
ballots received by clerks. Please refer to page 113 of the Election 
Administration Manual for guidance on how to secure and transport 
voted absentee ballots.
The Commission recommends that clerks review the following 
resources from the EAC and CISA as a starting point for procedures on 
the secure administration of drop boxes:
 Ɋ EAC Quick Start Guide on Drop Boxes (PDF)
 Ɋ EAC Election Management Guidelines, Pages 53, 80, 100 (PDF)
 Ɋ EAC Sample FAQ Language for How Drop Boxes Work that Can be 
Adapted for Wisconsin (PDF)
 Ɋ CISA Drop Box Considerations (PDF)
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 122
Q Does the governing body of the municipality need to be the one to 
designate drop box locations?
A No. The governing body of the municipality designates the location of alternate 
absentee voting sites under Wis. Stat. § 6.855. The Priorities USA decision clearly 
states that state law “requires only that the ballot be delivered to a location the 
municipal clerk, within his or her discretion, designates.”17 The municipal clerk 
has the authority to designate drop box locations.
Q Who can return a ballot to a drop box?
A A voter may return his or her own ballot. An individual may also return 
the ballot of anyone he or she is lawfully assisting, such as a voter with 
a disability or a hospitalized voter. An individual is permitted to provide 
assistance to more than one disabled or hospitalized absentee voter. 
These principles were issued in Commission guidance following the 
litigation in Carey v. WEC, and are unchanged by the Priorities USA 
decision.18 The decision does not say that drop boxes need to be staffed, 
nor does the decision require a clerk to ask any questions of a voter who is 
attempting to return a ballot to a drop box.
Q What steps should clerks take if they want to display their drop box 
locations on MyVote?
A Clerks and WisVote providers can add drop box locations and information 
to WisVote under Election Specific Absentee Options, which will make the 
drop box locations viewable to voters in their municipality on MyVote. 
Registered voters in these municipalities will be able to see the information 
under “Find My Local Absentee Options” button from the Vote Absentee 
section. Clerks are encouraged to communicate to voters as to the dates, 
times, and locations of drop boxes, as well as final retrieval dates and times. 
Please ensure that this information is up to date for your municipality before 
absentee ballots are available to voters for any election.
Q Does the decision require clerks to track which ballots are received by 
drop box?
A No. Nothing in the decision requires or permits clerks to track, mark, or 
otherwise separate or indicate which returned absentee ballots were 
received via secure drop box.
17 Priorities USA v. WEC, 2024 WI 32, P26. The Priorities USA decision also states that Wis. Stat. § 6.855 
“ … simply does not apply to drop boxes.” Id. at P29.
18 Available at: elections.wi.gov/memo/guidance-absentee-ballot-return-options-under-federal-
voting-rights-act
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 123
Q May a clerk place an insert informing voters of the availability of drop boxes?
A Yes. Clerks may place an insert informing voters of the availability of drop  
boxes for the return of absentee ballot envelopes. Those inserts are 
recommended to include the locations of the drop boxes, dates and times of 
availability, and date and time of final retrieval of absentee ballot envelopes.
Q Are private citizens permitted to watch drop boxes if they are located in public?
A Yes, but not if the watching interferes with voting. Whoever “interrupt[s] or 
disturb[s] the voting … proceedings” may be fined not more than $1,000, or 
imprisoned not more than 6 months or both.19 Additionally, anyone who 
“by abduction, duress, or any fraudulent device or contrivance, impede[s] 
or prevent[s] the free exercise of the franchise at an election” is guilty of 
a Class I felony.20 Clerks must immediately contact law enforcement if 
anyone tampers with, defaces, destroys, unlawfully empties, or interrupts, 
impedes, or prevents the use of a drop box.
19 See Wis. Stat. §§ 12.13(3)(x), 12.60(1)(b).
20 See Wis. Stat. §§ 12.09(2), 12.60(1)(a).

Chapter 7.10: Certificate 
Envelope Examples
Sec. 7.10.1: Introduction
There are four variations of the Absentee Ballot Certificate Envelope:
 Ɋ EL-122 Standard Absentee Certificate Envelope: Used in most situations.
 Ɋ EL-122M Absentee Certificate Envelope: Used for military and permanent 
and temporary overseas voters.
 Ɋ EL-122SVD: Used for absentee voting conducted by Special Voting Deputies 
in residential care facilities and retirement homes.
 Ɋ EL-122SP: Used for voters in SVD-eligible facilities that are not served by SVDs.
The Commission reviewed and approved these certificate envelopes after a 
thorough redesign and testing campaign in 2023.21 The envelopes were tested 
and reviewed by six populations who interact with the absentee envelope: the 
clerk who prepares the envelope, the voter who completes the certification, 
that voter’s chosen witness, that voter’s chosen assistant (if applicable), the poll 
worker who reviews the envelope for sufficiency and processes it at a polling 
place, and the United States Postal Service (USPS), which is responsible for its 
delivery. The colors selected to differentiate the EL-122 certificate envelopes 
were selected from the standardized options used nationally. These colors were 
selected for absentee envelopes because they meet accessibility contrast 
requirements and are easy for the USPS to identify in the mails stream.
21 For a description of the envelope redesign project, see the Open Session Materials from the 
Commission’s August 4, 2023 meeting. Available at: elections.wi.gov/event/special-meeting-842023

Chapter 7.11: Review Certificate 
Envelopes for Sufficiency
Sec. 7.11.1: Open or Damaged Envelopes
Before looking at the details of the certificate, poll workers should first 
examine each certificate envelope to see if any are opened or damaged. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.88(3)(b). If a ballot is open, or has been opened and resealed, 
the poll workers shall not count the ballot.  Id.
Best Practice: Wis. Stat. § 6.88(3)(b) is intended to prohibit absentee 
ballots from being counted that have been obviously re-opened and 
resealed (torn flap, slit seams, clumsy repair of paper). Sometimes, 
voters tape their absentee ballots closed. Tape on a certificate 
envelope flap alone is not necessarily an indication that the ballot 
has been opened and resealed. Ideally, the municipal clerk will have 
noticed taped or open absentee ballots as they are returned. Poll 
workers should contact the municipal clerk if they encounter any 
certificate envelopes that are either opened or resealed. Ultimately, it 
is the decision of the municipal clerk and the boards of canvassers to 
decide whether these ballots should be accepted or rejected.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 132
Sec. 7.11.2: Certificate Envelope Sufficiency
Extensive detail on how to review absentee certificate envelopes for sufficiency 
is covered by Sec. 14.15.12: “Absentee Certificate Envelopes.” Poll workers 
should review that section in its entirety for step-by-step guidance on how to 
review certificate envelopes, and to understand the Commission’s guidance for 
resolving common omissions or errors.
Important: It is always up to the municipal clerk to decide whether 
a certificate envelope is insufficient, so it’s also important to 
understand any jurisdiction-specific guidance or training from the 
clerk in addition to the Commission’s guidance.
Information on correcting incomplete certificate envelopes is covered by 
Chapter 14.18: “Correcting Defective Certificate Envelopes.”
Information on setting aside incomplete certificate envelopes for rejection is 
covered by Sec. 14.15.14: “Rejecting Absentee Ballots.”
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 133
Chapter 7.12: Witness Address 
Requirements
All certificate envelopes for returning absentee ballots require the witness, 
or for SVD voting, witnesses, to provide an address, and the ballot may not 
be counted if the address is missing entirely. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.87(2) and (6d) 
(requiring but not defining a witness address).
Following litigation, a 2024 Wisconsin Court of Appeals decision, Rise, Inc. v. 
Elections Comm’n, provided a statewide definition of a witness address. Below, 
the Commission’s guidance applies this definition and addresses several 
common questions.
If a municipal clerk, or poll worker, believes a witness address on a certificate 
envelope is not sufficient, see Chapter 7.13: “Correcting Defective Certificate 
Envelopes” on page 137 for more information on correcting insufficient 
certificate envelopes or Sec. 14.15.14: “Rejecting Absentee Ballots” for more 
information on rejecting absentee ballots.
Sec. 7.12.1: Frequently Asked Questions
Q Can an election official modify or add information to absentee ballot 
witness certifications?
A No. Election officials cannot modify or add information to absentee ballot 
witness certifications.22
Q What does “address” mean as used in Wis. Stat. §§ 6.87(2) and (6d)?
A It means “a place where the witness may be communicated with.”23
22 Rise, Inc. v. Elections Comm’n, 2024 WI App 48, ¶ 11, 413 Wis. 2d 366, 377, 11 N.W.3d 241, 246 quoting 
White v. WEC, Waukesha Cnty. No. 2022CV1008 (order issued Oct. 3, 2022).
23 Rise, Inc. v. Elections Comm’n, 2024 WI App 48, ¶ 3, 413 Wis. 2d 366, 372, 11 N.W.3d 241, 244.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 134
Q What information is required for a sufficient witness address?
A No particular components or information are required, but an absentee 
ballot cannot be rejected under Wis. Stat. § 6.88(3)(b) or Wis. Stat. § 7.52(3)(b), 
or returned to a voter for correction under Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9), as long as 
“the face of the certificate contains sufficient information to enable a 
municipal clerk to reasonably identify a place where the witness may be 
communicated with.”24 This does not prevent returning an absentee ballot 
to a voter or rejecting an absentee ballot after 8 p.m. on Election Day if this 
standard cannot be met or if there is a separate issue, such as a missing 
witness signature or missing voter signature.
The Commission has determined that it is an abuse of discretion for 
a municipal clerk to apply this standard to reject absentee ballots if a 
witness address is missing the state and ZIP code and there is more than 
one municipality of the name given in the United States.25
Q What information is enough for the municipal clerk to reasonably identify 
a location where the witness can be communicated with?
A “As long as the address information provided by the witness is sufficient 
to enable communication with the witness, the purposes of the address 
requirement are fulfilled” and “specific address components are not 
necessary”26 A municipal clerk may reasonably rely upon the clerk’s “own 
knowledge of community places, building names, and local addresses” 
to determine if the envelope contains enough information to identify a 
location where the witness may be communicated with.27
Q Where on a certificate envelope can a clerk look for a witness address?
A A clerk may look for witness address information “on the face of the 
certificate,” rather than just the information on the “address” line.28 If a 
witness writes “same as the voter” or “ditto” on the witness address line, 
“that is sufficient information to enable the municipal clerk to identify a 
place where the witness can be communicated with, so long as sufficient 
address information is provided in the voter’s certificate.”29
24 Rise, Inc. v. Elections Comm’n, 2024 WI App 48, ¶ 59, 413 Wis. 2d 366, 408, 11 N.W.3d 241, 261.
25 See 2026-0002, In re City of Mequon (Decided April 30, 2026).
26 Id. ¶ 56–57 (finding that the purposes of a witness address are 1. “to prevent abuses like fraud and 
undo influence” and 2. “to streamline and simplify the absentee voting process”).
27 Id. ¶ 64–65.
28 Id. ¶ 65.
29 Id. ¶ 65 note 23 and ¶ 66.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 135
Sec. 7.12.2: Best Practices for 
Acceptable Witness Addresses
The Commission believes that the four scenarios below would provide a 
municipal clerk with a place where the witness can be communicated 
with and that a clerk need not examine an address further if:
 Ɋ The witness’s street number, street name, and municipality are present, 
regardless of whether a state name or a ZIP code are provided.
 Ɋ The witness’s street number, street name, and ZIP code are present, but 
there is neither a municipality nor a state name provided.
 Ɋ The witness’s street number and street name are present and match 
the street number and street name of the voter, but no other address 
information is provided.
 Ɋ The witness certification indicates that the witness address is the same 
as the voter’s address with any or any combination of the following words: 
“same,” “same address,” “same as voter,” “same as above,” “see above,” 
“ditto,” or by using quotation marks and/or an arrow or line pointing to or 
from the voter address.
Q If one of these four scenarios is not present, should the absentee ballot 
be rejected?
A Not on that basis. If an election official determines that one of the four 
scenarios above is present, the Commission believes that the witness has 
provided a sufficient address, and no further determination is needed. 
If one of these scenarios is not present, an election official must apply 
the standard in Answer 3, which is to look to the face of the certificate for 
information that would allow the municipal clerk to reasonably identify a 
place where the witness may be communicated with. If the information 
can be found on the face of the certificate, it is sufficient.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 136
Chapter 7.13: Correcting 
Defective Certificate Envelopes
Note: This section of the manual covers a clerk’s ability to return 
absentee ballots to voters under Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9), or to set the 
absentee ballot aside for rejection under Wis. Stat. § 6.88(3)(b) when 
there are defects on the certificate envelope. For information on a 
municipal clerk’s ability to issue a new absentee ballot to a voter under 
Wis. Stat. § 6.86(5) when the ballot is spoiled or damaged, See Chapter 
7.14: “Spoiling & Replacement of Absentee Ballots” on page 142. Be 
advised that these two sections of the manual are not interchangeable.
Sec. 7.13.1: Reviewing the 
Certificate Envelope
Municipal clerks should make every effort to review absentee certificate 
envelopes as they receive voted absentee ballots from voters so that they can 
choose to exercise their authority under Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9) or role under Wis. 
Stat. § 6.88(3)(b) ahead of Election Day if the certificate has any defects. Defect, 
as used in this chapter, means anything that would lead the certificate to be 
rejected. Doing this review as the ballots arrive leaves the largest amount of 
time for a voter or witness to correct the defect as described below. The clerk 
should document any certificate defects on the Absentee Ballot Log (EL-124).
If the information on the absentee certificate envelope is incomplete, or if 
the certificate is missing, the clerk has two options for how to proceed:
 Ɋ Return the Ballot to the Voter: Time permitting, the clerk may attempt to 
return the ballot and incomplete certificate envelope to the voter for the 
voter to correct the defect.
 Ɋ Set the Ballot Aside for Rejection: When the certificate cannot be 
corrected, the clerk should set is aside and inform poll workers that it is 
insufficient under Wis. Stat. § 6.88(3)(b).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 137
Sec. 7.13.2: Returning the 
Ballot to the Voter
If the information on the absentee certificate envelope is missing, incomplete, 
otherwise defective, or if the certificate is missing entirely, the clerk “may return 
the ballot to the voter … whenever time permits the voter to correct the defect 
and return the ballot” so that the municipal clerk can cause the completed 
ballot to be delivered to the proper polling place by 8 p.m. on Election Day. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9).
There is not a specific method by which a municipal clerk may “return the 
ballot” to the voter. See Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9). The Commission recommends 
that if the defect is correctable — meaning that the issue has to do with how 
the certificate was filled out rather than the qualifications of the voter or 
witness — the clerk contact the voter directly if possible, such as by phone, 
email, or another convenient method, to notify the voter and advise the voter of 
how they may correct the defect. Whenever time permits, a clerk may choose to 
return the ballot to the voter by returning it by mail, or by returning it to the voter 
in person in the clerk’s office or at the polling place on Election Day. How much 
time is enough is a matter of local discretion, but for mailing the absentee back 
to the voter less than one week is likely not enough time.
For correcting the certificate envelopes in person in the clerk’s office or alternate 
site, the Commission recommends that the clerk allow this possibility until 
the clerks must prepare ballots for delivery to the polling places or board of 
absentee ballot canvassers. See Wis. Stat. § 6.88(2). After the ballots have been 
sent to the proper polling place or board of absentee ballot canvassers, the 
Commission recommends that clerks have a notice, or a staff member on duty, 
to explain to voters where they must go to make a correction.
It is incumbent upon the voter to correct the defect and municipal clerks and 
election officials cannot correct voter or witness errors on the certificate.30 If 
necessary, a clerk may include a new certificate envelope to the voter when 
returning a ballot for a voter to correct Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9).
30 See Rise, Inc. v. Elections Comm’n, 2024 WI App 48, ¶ 11, 413 Wis. 2d 366, 377, 11 N.W.3d 241, 246 (quoting 
White v. WEC, Waukesha Cnty. No. 2022CV1008 (order issued Oct. 3, 2022)).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 138
If the certificate envelope containing the ballot has been returned to the voter, 
the voter must ensure that the corrected certificate envelope is returned so it 
is delivered to the polling place no later than 8 p.m. on Election Day. Wis. Stat. 
§ 6.87(9). A voter may accomplish this by mailing the ballot back to the clerk 
or delivering the ballot to the clerk or at the voter’s polling place or board of 
absentee ballot canvassers meeting. If a municipal clerk returns a ballot to a 
voter, the clerk or the clerk’s provider should choose the “not returned, sent to 
voter for resolution” status for the ballot in WisVote. If a voter does not return it or 
place it in the mail with the defect corrected, the voter may still vote in person at 
the polls on Election Day, or vote in person absentee. See Wis. Stat. § 6.86(6).
Defect in Voter Information Section
If the voter is correcting the original certificate envelope (to fill in a missing 
required field, for example), the original witness does not need to be present to 
witness the voter correcting the defect under Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9).
Defect in Witness Information Section
Regarding the Witness’s Printed Name: If an absentee certificate is missing the 
witness’s printed name, it is within the clerk’s discretion how to proceed. Statute 
directs that the absentee ballot certificate language appear in “substantially” 
the form listed in Wis. Stat. § 6.87(2), which includes a field for a witness’s printed 
name, in addition to the signature. A clerk should determine whether a missing 
witness printed address renders the certification “insufficient” when determining 
if they should take action under Wis. Stat. § 6.88(3)(b).
If the witness address or witness signature is missing, the certificate is defective 
but can be corrected. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(2) and (6d), and (9). See Chapter 14.17: 
“Witness Address Requirements” for a description of what constitutes a 
sufficient witness address. To correct the certificate, the Commission believes 
that the voter and their original witness may go together to the clerk’s office 
or polling place for the witness to correct the defect and, if the voter consents 
and communicates that consent to the clerk, the witness alone may go to the 
clerk’s office or polling place for the witness to correct the defect in the witness 
information section. The clerk may not issue a new certificate envelope to the 
witness only — if a new certificate envelope is issued to allow a witness to correct 
a defect, the voter must also be present.
Issuing a New Certificate Envelope
A new certificate envelope may be necessary if the voter or witness are unable 
to correct the defect on the existing envelope. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9). The certificate 
may only be replaced “if necessary” and the Commission cautions against 
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 139
issuing a new certificate unless the original has been damaged and can no 
longer be used due to the potential difficulty of both the voter and the original 
witness being able to complete a new certificate envelope.
The clerk may not issue a new certificate envelope to the witness only — if a new 
certificate envelope is issued to allow a witness to correct a defect, the voter must 
also be present because the voter must complete the voter signature section. An 
election inspector at the polls may issue a new envelope, if necessary, pursuant 
to the clerk’s authority under Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9). If a new certificate envelope 
is issued and completed, the Commission recommends labeling the original 
defective certificate envelope with “void – new certificate envelope issued” but 
still maintaining the record so that it is accounted for in the event of a recount.
If the municipal clerk has provided the voter with a new envelope, the voter 
must request that their original witness re-complete the witness portion of 
the absentee envelope. See Wis. Stat. § 6.87(2). The original witness must be 
used in this case because they were the one who witnessed the voter marking, 
folding, and depositing the ballot into the envelope. A new witness cannot be 
used because there is no way for a new witness to witness the voter marking 
their ballot if a voter is attempting to correct a defect of the certificate envelope 
under Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9).
If the voter is correcting a defect and the clerk has issued a new 
certificate envelope, the voter should take the following steps:
 Ɋ Open the original certificate envelope (if present)
 Ɋ Verify their ballot
Best Practice: The voter should not remove the ballot from the polling 
place or the clerk’s office.
 Ɋ Seal the ballot in the new certificate envelope and complete the 
certifications with their original witness. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(2).
If the voter corrects a defect of the certificate envelope, they may only correct the 
defect — they may not vote a new ballot. See Wis. Stat. §§ 6.86(5) and 6.87(9).
The clerk or election inspector should document that a correction was made (and 
if the ballot was accepted on Election Day) on the Absentee Ballot Log (EL-124).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 140
Sec. 7.13.3: Setting the Ballot 
Aside for Rejection
Best Practice: If the clerk determines that there is not enough time 
for a voter to correct the defect, if the clerk has notified the voter of 
the defect but the voter has not come in to correct it and has not 
responded to the inquiry, or if the defect cannot be corrected, the 
clerk should gather all such ballots, label them as “to be rejected” and 
separate them when preparing ballots for delivery to the polling places 
or board of absentee ballot canvassers under Wis. Stat. § 6.88(2).
If there are ballots that cannot be corrected, such as for voters who died before 
an Election Day, a clerk should also make clear to the election inspectors or 
board of absentee ballot canvassers which ballots can still be corrected by the 
voters, and which cannot. Keeping the different kinds of ballots separate — those 
that appear sufficient, those that appear insufficient but are correctable, and 
those that are insufficient and uncorrectable — will help the polling places and 
absentee ballot board of canvassers stay organized.
The clerk should package these ballots together and make clear to the inspectors 
who will be responsible for processing the ballots at the polling places under Wis. 
Stat. § 6.88(3) or the board of absentee ballot canvassers under Wis. Stat. § 7.52(3) 
which ballots the clerk believes could still be corrected and which ballots the clerk 
believes could not be corrected due to the voter or witness being unqualified. 
Though the inspectors or canvassers will need to make their own determinations 
regarding the sufficiency of the absentee ballot and are responsible for officially 
rejecting defective envelopes, knowing which ballots have certificate envelope 
defects right away will greatly simplify their Election Day processes, and better 
allow them to facilitate correction by voters or witnesses during before 8 p.m.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 141
Chapter 7.14: Spoiling 
& Replacement of 
Absentee Ballots
Sec. 7.14.1: Introduction
Wisconsin law allows a voter who, by accident or mistake, spoils or erroneously 
prepares a ballot may receive another ballot by returning the defective ballot to 
the municipal clerk or poll worker. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(5).
The Wisconsin Court of Appeals for District II reversed the trial court’s decision 
in Nancy Kormanik v. Wisconsin Elections Commission, which is the court case 
that prohibited ballot spoliation by the voter when there was nothing otherwise 
wrong with the ballot. Any guidance from the Commission on the topic of ballot 
spoiling that was issued prior to May 2026 is accordingly out of date.
This section covers a municipal clerk’s ability to return absentee ballots to voters 
when the ballot is spoiled or damaged. For information on a municipal clerk’s 
ability to return absentee ballots to voters when the certificate is incomplete 
or missing, see Chapter 7.8: “Cancelling & Issuing Replacement Absentee 
Ballots” on page 114. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9).
Note: Be advised that these two sections of the manual are not 
interchangeable.
Sec. 7.14.2: When is a Ballot 
Spoiled or Damaged?
The Commission has not issued specific guidance on what it means for a ballot 
to be “spoiled or damaged” within the meaning of Wis. Stat. § 6.87(9). That 
determination should be made in the clerk’s discretion.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 142
Sec. 7.14.3: What to Do with a Spoiled 
or Damaged Absentee Ballot
The municipal clerk should verify the identity of a person requesting to receive 
a replacement ballot to ensure that it is the voter making the request. This 
voter verification process should include having the voter confirm the same 
information necessary to request an absentee ballot (e.g. name, full address, 
date of birth) and this verification process may include the municipal clerk 
asking the absentee voter to produce voter identification.
If the clerk does not believe the person requesting the replacement ballot is 
the one to whom the original ballot was provided, the clerk should not issue 
the replacement ballot, document the incident for a subsequent challenge on 
Election Day under Wis. Stat. § 6.92, and contact law enforcement immediately. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.15(1)(g).
If the clerk issues a new ballot, the clerk should destroy the spoiled or damaged 
ballot. Wis. Stat. § 6.86(5). However, the spoiled or damaged ballot should be 
destroyed only to the extent that it cannot be tabulated, and should still be 
preserved as a defective ballot and retained for the applicable retention period 
for election materials for that election. Wis. Stat. § 7.51(2)(b).
Sec. 7.14.4: When the 
Request Must be Made
The deadlines for requesting a replacement for a spoiled or  
erroneously prepared ballot are:
 Ɋ Regular by-mail absentee voters requesting a ballot for one election; 
and overseas voters: Not later than 5 p.m. on the 5th day immediately 
preceding the election.
 Ɋ Indefinitely confined absentee voters; absentee voters making a 
calendar year request; and military voters who are not away from 
home due to service or who have requested a ballot for an election 
not including a national office: Not later than 5 p.m. on the Friday 
immediately preceding the election.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 143
 Ɋ Absentee voters making an in-person request at the clerk’s office or in-
person absentee voting location: Depending on the local hours as provided 
in a Type E notice, not later than the Sunday preceding the election.
 Ɋ Absentee voters requesting a ballot during a Special Voting Deputy 
visit: Depending on the schedule of the Special Voting Deputy visits 
scheduled by the municipal clerk, not later than 5 p.m. the Monday 
preceding an Election Day.
 Ɋ Hospitalized voters by authorized representative; military voters who 
are away from home due to service and have requested a ballot for an 
election including a national office; and sequestered jurors: Not later 
than 5 p.m. on an Election Day.
Sec. 7.14.5: Can a Voter Who Spoils 
a Ballot Still Vote in Person?
A voter who did not receive the replacement ballot, or chose not to return it, is 
able to vote in-person on Election Day.
Sec. 7.14.6: How Many Replacement 
Ballots Can be Issued?
A voter may only receive up to three ballots in each election, including the 
initial ballot.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 144
Chapter 7.15: Absentee 
Ballot Handling, Transfer to 
Polling Place, & Post-Election 
Procedures
Sec. 7.15.1: Introduction
This section provides municipal clerks, poll workers, and boards of canvassers 
with standardized best practices for physically managing absentee ballots. 
These best practices are designed to ensure that all properly returned absentee 
ballots are accurately handled by the clerk’s office, transferred to the polling 
place or board of absentee ballot canvasser location for processing and 
counting, and properly reconciled in compliance with Wisconsin Statutes and 
the Commission’s guidance.
Clerks must establish clear systems to track and secure absentee ballots prior 
to Election Day. This ensures that ballots are reviewed as they arrive in the clerk’s 
office so that any possible certificate issues are identified and materials can be 
organized ahead of the election.
Important: It is the legal responsibility of the municipal clerk to ensure that 
all absentee ballots are properly delivered to their polling places by 8 p.m. 
on Election Day, or to the “central count” facility. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.87(6), 7.52.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 145
Sec. 7.15.2: Required Processes
The following procedures are required by statute for 
each absentee ballot received by the clerk:
 Ɋ Once reviewed, the ballot in the certificate envelope must be enclosed in 
a carrier envelope that is securely sealed and endorsed with the name 
and title of the clerk, and the words:31
 ɉ This envelope contains the ballot of an absent voter and must be 
opened in the same room where votes are being cast at the polls 
during polling hours on Election Day or, in municipalities where
