Sec. 7.15.3: Best Practices for 
Managing Absentee Ballots
This section covers the Commission’s best practices for managing and 
transporting absentee ballots.
Pre-Election Procedures
Enter Absentee Ballots as “Returned” in Wisvote as They Arrive
Marking absentee ballots as “returned” in WisVote immediately upon receipt 
is the best way to ensure that the clerk’s office has a complete record of the 
number of absentee ballots received before the polls open. All clerks must 
record the status of a returned absentee ballot within 48 hours of receiving the 
ballot, or if the clerk has a provider, notify the provider within 48 hours and then 
the provider must enter the information within 24 hours of the notice, though 
if any of these deadlines end on a Saturday or Sunday, the deadline moves to 
the next business day. Wis. Stat. § 6.33(5)(a)2. If a clerk has a provider, the clerk 
is required to “immediately” forward all registration changes and voting record 
changes, which includes absentee ballot requests and returns, to the clerk’s 
provider for entry on the registration list. Wis. Stat. § 6.33(5)(b). In particular, 
clerks and providers should ensure that every returned ballot has been entered 
into WisVote prior to printing the poll book or preparing an electronic poll book 
for use on Election Day.
Organize Ballot Carrier Seal Log Electronically or by Ward
Municipal clerks are responsible for securely organizing all returned absentee 
ballots for delivery to polling places or boards of absentee ballot canvassers. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.88(1) and (2). The Commission recommends that tamper 
evident seals be applied to courier bags or packages. When seal numbers 
are generated and recorded for absentee carrier envelopes, courier bags, 
or packages, the best practice is to keep that log electronically so that seal 
numbers are easily searchable. Another best practice is to organize the seal 
numbers by ward so that a record exists of the number of absentee ballot 
vessels that exist for each ward or polling place.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 147
Provide Each Polling Place with a Log of Absentee Ballot Carrier Bags or Envelopes
Each polling and board of absentee ballot canvassers location place should be 
equipped with the total number of carrier bags, envelopes, packages, or other 
transport vessels that are expected at that site. This is especially important for 
absentee ballots that are received by the clerk’s office ahead of Election Day. 
Couriers delivering absentee ballots on Election Day should have a chain of 
custody document that details the number of absentee ballot bags that are 
delivered to each polling place, and the number of ballots in each bag. This can 
be done by providing a polling place or absentee ballot board of canvassers 
with the list of seal numbers for each vessel that will be transporting absentee 
ballots, or by labelling absentee ballot bunches as “1 of 10” or similar.
Generate the Number of Total Absentee Ballots 
Returned & Share with Polling Places
If ballots are marked as returned in WisVote as they are received, clerks can 
access real-time data of the number of returned absentee ballots at any time.
The best practice is for clerks to generate this number at least twice:
 Ɋ Once at the close of business the day before the election.
 Ɋ Again an hour before polls close on Election Day.
Once this number has been generated, it should be shared with each polling 
place in the way that makes the most sense for each jurisdiction. It can be 
emailed, relayed by telephone, or printed and distributed to the polling places. 
The important thing is that Chief Inspectors and poll workers should be trained 
on where to find this number and how to use it to ensure that the total number 
of recorded absentee voters in the poll book matches the total number of 
absentee ballots received.
Print Poll Books as Close to Election Day as Possible
Printing the poll book as close as possible to Election Day will ensure that 
the poll book accurately reflects which voters were issued and returned an 
absentee ballot. An accurate poll book will help poll workers better determine if 
there are returned absentee ballots that have not been processed.
Provide Absentee Ballot Processing Training with Poll Workers
Providing poll workers with absentee-specific training ahead of Election Day will 
help ensure that inspectors are up to date with the statutory requirements to 
process an absentee ballot. Training will also allow inspectors to confirm their 
understanding of the process and can prevent processing slow-downs or errors.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 148
Delivering Absentee Ballots to the Polling Place
All absentee ballots are required to be at the polling place by 8 p.m. on Election 
Day to be eligible to be counted. Wis. Stat. § 6.87(6). These best practices will 
help ensure all absentee ballots are sent to the correct polling place or “central 
count” location for review and processing.
Develop a Record for the Number of Carrier Envelopes & Courier Bags that are 
Prepared & Delivered to Each Polling Place or Board of Absentee Ballot Canvassers Site
This record should be provided to each polling place or board of absentee 
ballot canvassers site on Election Day. This allows inspectors to account for all 
the bags that are delivered by the clerk’s office and ensures that there are no 
unprocessed absentee ballots that were properly delivered.
Communicate the Location of Carrier Envelopes & Courier 
Bags to Poll Workers when Delivering Supplies
Many materials are being delivered to the polling place or board of absentee 
ballot canvassers site for an election, and there can be new inspectors serving 
at a location for the first time. It is vital that the inspectors know where ballot 
bags are being securely stored after their delivery so that they can process 
ballots throughout the day.
Require Poll Workers on Election Day to Confirm the Correct 
Number of Carrier Envelopes & Courier Bags Received
Poll workers should be asked to confirm that they have received the correct number 
of courier bags and carrier envelopes to ensure that no materials are unaccounted. 
These materials should also be clearly labeled with the materials that are contained 
in the envelopes and bags for easy identification and confirmation.
Counting Votes Procedures
These best practices focus on specific steps poll workers should take to ensure 
that all absentee ballots have been accounted for, including end-of-night 
procedures to check the number of absentee ballots counted against the total 
number of absentee ballots received by the clerk.
Review the Log of Absentee Ballot Carrier Bags or Envelopes
A municipal clerk should provide the total number of absentee ballot carrier bags 
or envelopes that will be delivered to the polling place or board of absentee ballot 
canvassers on Election Day. Poll workers should ensure that all the absentee 
ballot carrier bags or envelopes have been received by 8 p.m. on Election Day.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 149
Review the Number of Voters & the Number of 
Ballots Cast Throughout the Day
The Commission recommends comparing the first and last number on each 
page of the two copies of the poll book, as well as every third or fifth number 
to make sure they match. Reviewing the number of voters and the number of 
ballots cast throughout the day can prevent differences in the number issued 
to voters and ensure that there are not unexplained differences in the total 
number of voters and the total number of ballots cast at the end of the night.
Thoroughly Document Any Incidents that Occur on 
Election Day in the Inspectors’ Statement
The Inspectors’ Statement is the official record of the events that occurred in 
the polling place on Election Day. This document is also referenced during the 
canvass. It is vital that the various boards of canvass be able to easily identify 
and understand any anomalies that may have occurred during the day.
Post-Election Procedures
These best practices are focused on prioritizing the organization of election 
materials before the convening of the municipal canvass to ensure no 
uncounted absentee ballots were missed.
Ensure All Materials have been Returned from the Polling Place & Reviewed
To canvass the election, the municipal clerk will need to ensure all materials 
have been returned to the clerk’s possession.
Those materials include:
 Ɋ All voted ballots in their sealed ballot bags
 Ɋ Any provisional ballots in their sealed bag
 Ɋ Original tally sheets and voting equipment results tapes
 Ɋ Original Inspectors’ Statement and any attachments
 Ɋ One original poll book
 Ɋ An absentee ballot log
 Ɋ The provisional ballot reporting form
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 150
Review All Voting Equipment Ballot Bins for Any Possible Ballots
Each piece of voting equipment should be thoroughly inspected to ensure that 
no ballots remain in either the ballot bin or any auxiliary bin.
Route Materials to the County Clerk & School District Clerk, If Necessary
Any non-municipal contests that are on the ballot will require a separate board 
of canvass to review the election returns and certify their contests.
If the clerk receives an absentee ballot from a voter who is recorded as having 
voted on Election Day, the clerk should mark the ballot “To Be Rejected” and 
set the ballot aside for processing by the Municipal Board of Canvassers.  
Wis. Stat. § 6.86(6). The clerk should also contact law enforcement 
immediately. Wis. Stat. § 7.15(1)(g).

Chapter 7.16: Boards of 
Absentee Ballot Canvassers 
(“Central Count”)
Instead of canvassing absentee ballots at individual polling places, the governing 
body of a municipality may provide by ordinance that absentee ballots may be 
canvassed (counted) at a meeting of the board of absentee ballot canvassers. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.52(1)(a). The use of this procedure is often referred to as “central 
count” by election officials, though it should not be confused with the “central 
counting locations” authorized by Wis. Stat. § 7.51(1). When this manual uses the 
term “central count,” it is referring to a meeting of the board of absentee ballot 
canvassers under Wis. Stat. § 7.52(1)(a).
In “central count” jurisdictions, all absentee ballots for the municipality are 
delivered to and counted at the same location, which is usually not a polling place. 
The Commission maintains a list of all jurisdictions that have authorized “central 
count” operations at elections.wi.gov.
This chapter will cover establishing “central count” jurisdiction and pre-
Election Day procedures. Chapter 14.16: “Processing Absentee Ballots: 
“Central Count”” is dedicated to absentee processing and other Election Day 
procedures at “central count” locations. 
Sec. 7.16.1: Establishing a 
“Central Count” Jurisdiction
The decision to use “central count” proceedings must be made by the 
municipality’s governing body, not by the municipal or county clerk. Wis. Stat. 
§ 7.52(1)(a). The governing body can pass a similar ordinance to rescind their 
previous decision to authorize “central count” proceedings. Wis. Stat. § 7.52(9). 
The municipal clerk must also consult with the Commission whenever they have 
questions about the proper “central count” procedures. Wis. Stat. § 7.52(1)(a).
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 152
Considerations for Becoming a “Central Count” Jurisdiction
Counting absentee ballots at a “central count” location using a board of 
absentee ballot canvassers offers certain advantages for efficient election 
administration, namely that all absentee ballots go to one location to be counted, 
instead of to polling places all across the municipality. Municipalities with high 
levels of absentee voting may also appreciate the ability to purchase high-speed 
tabulators which can count many absentee ballots in a short period of time. 
Some municipalities value the time flexibility of using “central count” procedures, 
though this can cut both ways. The board of absentee ballot canvassers can 
begin any time after polls open at 7 a.m., if they start before 10 p.m. Wis. Stat. § 
7.52(1)(a). If the counting of absentee ballots begins too late in the day, however, 
voters may be surprised that results are not yet available by the time they turn on 
the local news at 10 p.m. on Election Day. This can lead to questions and concerns 
about late night “ballot dumps” if voters do not understand that the processing 
of absentee ballots can continue after the polls close. Likewise, if absentee ballots 
are still being counted past 10 p.m., observers are less likely to stay late into the 
night, which decreases overall transparency into the election process. 
Step 1: Clerk Notifies Commission of Proposed Enactment
Prior to the ordinance passing, the municipal clerk must notify the Commission 
in writing of the proposed enactment. Wis. Stat. § 7.52(1)(a). This notification 
should include the proposed ordinance language as well as their intended 
procedures for the operation of the “central count” location. If the jurisdiction 
also uses e-poll books (Badger Books), the “central count” procedures should 
include this detail. Commission staff review both the proposed ordinance and 
procedures, and will notify the clerk if anything is cause for concern or further 
explanation. 
Sample notification materials are included as a reference in “Appendix 7.16.A: 
Sample Central Count Absentee Ballot Processing Procedures” on page 156.
Step 2: Governing Body Authorizes Process by Ordinance
After the Commission has been notified about the intended enactment, the 
governing body must pass an ordinance for the enactment to take effect. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.52(1)(a). After the ordinance is enacted, all elections in the 
municipality need to follow the “central count” procedure.  Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 153
Sec. 7.16.2: Composition of the Municipal 
Board of Absentee Ballot Canvassers
The work of processing absentee ballots at “central count” locations is completed 
by the municipal board of absentee ballot canvassers. 
This board is made up of:
1. The municipal clerk (or their designee), and
2. Two other qualified voters who are appointed by the municipal clerk. 
The members of the board of canvassers serve for two-year terms starting on 
January 1 of even-numbered years, and members who are appointed to fill 
vacancies complete the remainder of that term. Wis. Stat. § 7.53(2m)(b). 
If the office of municipal clerk is vacant, the clerk cannot perform their duties, or 
if the clerk is up for election with an opponent on the ballot; the mayor, president, 
or board chairperson appoints another qualified voter to the board of absentee 
canvassers in the clerk’s spot. Id. If any member is a candidate at that election, 
the clerk shall appoint a different qualified voter to temporarily fill the vacancy. Id.
The municipality may appoint additional poll workers under Wis. Stat. § 7.52(1)(b) 
to assist the board of absentee ballot canvassers with processing absentee 
ballots. See Chapter 8.4: “Nomination & Appointment of Partisan Election 
Inspectors” for more information.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 154
Sec. 7.16.3: Public Notice
Although processing all absentee ballots at one central location is more 
efficient for a municipality, the law still protects public access and observation 
of this process by the public. 
Public Notice
The municipal clerk must give at least 48 hours of notice to the public of when 
the board of absentee ballot canvassers intends to convene to start processing 
absentee ballots at the “central count” location. Wis. Stat. § 7.52(1)(a). The board 
can convene any time after the opening of the polls and before 10 p.m. on 
Election Day. Id.
Best Practice: The law does not address what type of notice needs to 
be given in this context, but to ensure the greatest reach, municipal 
clerks should notice the meeting of the board of absentee ballot 
canvassers the same way they would notice any public meeting.

 Approve Ordinance Establishing A Board Of Absentee Ballot Canvassers thus Creating A 
Central Count Location For The City Of Municipality 
 
1. Background 
The City of Municipality has a proud tradition of citizens voting in large numbers. Historically, 
voter turnout in the City exceeds the statewide average turnout for elections. More and more 
citizens are choosing to vote absentee instead of voting at the polls in person. 
Wisconsin law allows for citizens to vote absentee. Wisconsin has “no excuse” absentee voting 
which means a voter may cast an absentee ballot without providing a reason. The City has 
experienced an increase in absentee voters.  
Currently all absentee ballots are sorted by district/ward, then delivered to the appropriate polling 
locations on Election Day, at which time, poll workers begin to process the absentee ballot.  Two 
poll workers are required to process every absentee ballot received at the polling place. The poll 
workers must check the ballot envelope for defects, open the envelope, sort and organize the 
ballots, and announce that they are placing absentee ballots into the tabulator. Poll workers often 
have to disrupt voters who vote in person at the polls by creating lines at the check-in table and 
the tabulator.  
The November General Election is expected to be very busy. In the last two presidential 
Elections, the City has had XXXX (2024) and XXXX (2020 / Covid) absentee voters.   
Wisconsin Statutes 7.52 and 7.53(2)(m) allows for the creation of a Board of Absentee Ballot 
Canvassers. These individuals are appointed by the City Clerk to serve two-year terms. The 
Board of Absentee Ballot Canvassers process all absentee ballots in the City regardless of ward. 
In order to create a Board of Absentee Ballot Canvassers, the City Council must adopt an 
ordinance under State Statutes 7.52 and 7.53(2)(m). The ordinance is required to be created at 
least 30 days prior to the election for which it will be implemented.  
2. Analysis 
By removing absentee ballot processing from polling places to a centralized facility will make 
voting at the polling places more efficient for citizens and poll workers. Chief Election 
Inspectors will no longer need to dedicate two or more poll workers to the processing of absentee 
ballots. This will allow those poll workers to be put into other positions to serve the citizens 
voting in person at the polling place on Election Day. 
Key benefits of establishing a central processing location include: 
• Resource Optimization: Establishing a CCL will provide relief to individual polling locations 
and their respective poll workers. Poll workers will be able to focus on managing in-person 
voting, assisting voters, and ensuring a smooth Election Day experience without the added 
complexity of handling and processing absentee ballots.  
• Improved Efficiency: Centralizing the processing of absentee ballots will help expedite the 
verification and count process, and reduce delays at polling locations. 
• Enhanced Security: A designated central location will ensure enhanced security measures are 
in place to safeguard the integrity of absentee ballots. 
It is important to create a Board of Absentee Ballot Canvassers prior to the [Upcoming Election] 
so the board can be appointed, trained, and have one election to work before the [Next Major 
Election]. 
Adoption of this Ordinance will allow for the Absentee Board of Canvassers to work the 
[Upcoming Election] and be better prepared for the [Next Major Election] and all future 
elections in the City of Municipality. 
 
3. Recommendation 
The City recommends that the City Council adopt ORD 24-xxx creating a Board of Absentee 
Ballot Canvassers.

Chapter 7.17: Tips & Tools: 
Absentee Ballot Data 
Management
This section describes best practices for documenting absentee ballots in 
WisVote. Prompt, accurate, and consistent data entry in WisVote can help poll 
workers ensure that all absentee ballots are accounted for.
Sec. 7.17.1: Data Entry Prior to Election Day
When an absentee ballot is returned, it must be recorded in WisVote. All 
clerks must record the status of a returned absentee ballot within 48 hours 
of receiving the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 6.33(5)(a)2. Marking absentee ballots as 
“Returned” in WisVote immediately upon receipt is the best way to ensure that 
the clerk’s office has a complete record of the number of absentee ballots 
received before the polls open.
Clerks should enter absentee ballots as “Returned” in WisVote as they arrive. 
Knowing which status to select when recording a returned absentee ballot will 
ensure accurate recording of ballots upon receipt.
Absentee ballot status options (aka “status reasons”):
 Ɋ Returned
 Ɋ Not Returned
 Ɋ Undeliverable
 Ɋ Ballot Returned After Deadline
 Ɋ Returned, to be Rejected
 Ɋ Voter Refused
 Ɋ Not Returned, sent to voter for resolution
More in-depth information on how to record “Returned” absentee ballot in 
WisVote can be found in section 3.8 of the WisVote manual.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 165
Sec. 7.17.2: Share Absentee Ballot 
Data with Polling Places
Note: Municipal clerks should share the Number of Absentee Ballots 
Returned with all polling places (or “central count”).
There are several reports in WisVote that clerks can maximize absentee ballot 
management. If ballots are marked as returned in WisVote as they are received, 
clerks can access the number of returned absentee ballots at any time.
The total number of absentee ballots returned is helpful to understand:
 Ɋ Whether additional poll workers are needed to process them at wards with 
unusually high absentee return rates.
 Ɋ Whether the clerk’s office can expect an increase in returns in the days 
before Election Day (if only 50% of absentee ballots issued are returned on 
the Friday before the election, it may be a sign to expect many more over 
the next few days).
 Ɋ Whether poll workers can confirm that they received and processed the 
same number of absentee ballots that were returned.
Clerks should access and share the total number of 
absentee ballots returned at least twice:
 Ɋ The night before Election Day
 Ɋ An hour before polls close on Election Day.
Chief Inspectors and poll workers should be trained on where to find this 
number and how to use it to ensure that the total number of recorded absentee 
voters in the poll book matches the total number of absentee ballots received.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 166

Sec. 7.17.4: How Election Inspectors 
Can Use Absentee Returned Data
Poll workers at polling places (or “central count”) are responsible for processing all 
absentee ballots on Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 6.88(3)(a). The easiest way to ensure 
that they can confirm they have received all ballots that were returned is to ensure 
that they can access the data showing how many ballots they should expect.
If poll workers have the number of returned absentee ballots on hand (updated 
by the clerk as necessary), reconciliation of the poll book and counting becomes 
much easier.
Throughout Election Day, poll workers can and should review and compare 
poll book absentee ballot participation with the number of absentee ballots 
reported returned. Reviewing and comparing the numbers throughout the 
day can prevent differences in the number of absentee ballot participation vs. 
absentee ballot returned and ensures that there are no unexplained differences 
in the total number at the end of the night.
First Edition, June 2026 Absentee Voting 7 – 169

Part 8 
Local Election Officials
County Clerks; Municipal Clerks; Election 
Inspectors; Election Registration Officials
An election official is defined as “an individual who is charged with any 
duties relating to the conduct of an election.” Wis. Stat. § 5.02(4e). County, 
municipal and school district clerks are election officials, as are election 
inspectors, chief inspectors, election registration officials (EROs), tabulators, 
greeters, and canvass board members.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 1
Chapter 8.1: County Clerks
Sec. 8.1.1: Election & Qualifications
County clerks must be eligible electors of their county and are elected for a 
term of four years during the partisan General Election in the Fall. Wis. Stat. §§ 
59.20(1), (2)(a).
Sec. 8.1.2: Duties
County clerks serve as the chief election official in each county. Wis. Stat. § 
59.23(2)(i). A county clerk’s election duties include preparing and providing 
ballots for every election for all national, state, and county offices and 
referendums, publishing applicable public notices relating to a national, state, 
or county election, and assisting with training and general voter education. 
Wis. Stat. §§ 7.10, 59.23(2)(i). For more information on the county clerk’s role in 
the ballot printing and distribution process, See Chapter 5.1: “Ballot Creation 
Procedures.”
The county clerk also serves as the filing officer for county offices and multi-
jurisdictional judges. Wis. Stat. §§ 8.10(6)(b), 8.15(8)(b), 8.20(7).
On election night, the county clerk is required to keep the office open to receive 
reports from all wards and also to post the unofficial results of elections. Wis. 
Stat. § 7.60(1). The county clerk is required to post unofficial returns no later than 
two hours after receiving them. Id.
Additionally, the county clerk is one member of the County Board of Canvassers 
(CBOC), and is responsible for the canvass and return of votes at general, 
judicial, and special elections. Wis. Stat. §§ 7.60(2), 59.23(2)(i). The county clerk 
chooses the other members of the CBOC from lists submitted by political party 
county committees, and at least one member of the CBOC must be from a 
political party other than the county clerk’s. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(2). The county 
clerk designates a deputy clerk who performs the county clerk’s duties on the 
CBOC in the event that the county clerk’s office is vacant or if the county clerk is 
unable to perform these duties. Id. The county clerk cannot serve on the CBOC if 
the clerk is on the ballot unless the clerk is running unopposed. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 2
Chapter 8.2: Municipal Clerks
Sec. 8.2.1: Appointment & Qualifications
Municipal clerks are elected by the electors or appointed to their positions by 
the governing body of a given town, village, or city, and if elected, must be 
electors of the municipality. See Wis. Stat. §§ 60.30(1)(a)2., (1e)(a) (towns), 61.19 
and 61.195 (villages); and 62.09(1)(a), (2)(a), (3).
Sec. 8.2.2: Duties
The municipal clerk’s far ranging election duties include managing elections 
and voter registration in the municipality, equipping polling places, purchasing 
and maintaining election equipment, preparing ballots and notices, and 
conducting and tracking the training of other election officials. Wis. Stat. § 7.15.
Sec. 8.2.3: Training Requirements
Each municipal clerk must attend training sponsored by the Wisconsin Elections 
Commission every two years. Wis. Stat. §§ 7.15(1m), 7.315(2). All municipal clerks 
must receive an initial certification by attending the Municipal Clerk Core 
Curriculum Training course, which counts as three hours of training. Wis. Admin. 
Code § EL 12.03(1), (2). The initial certification must be completed before a clerk 
may administer an election. Id.
Clerks must earn a minimum of six hours of training during the current election 
cycle, which begins January 1 of even-numbered years and ends on December 
31 of odd-numbered years, to maintain certification for the next election cycle. 
Id., Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL 12.01(2). For new clerks who completed a three-
hour initial certification, this means completing an additional three hours of 
training during an election cycle, and for clerks renewing a certification, the 
clerks must complete six hours of training within an election cycle. Wis. Admin. 
Code § EL 12.03(2). Training hours beyond the 6 required do not count toward 
certification in subsequent election cycles. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.03(4). 
See elections.wi.gov for Training Tables listing the approved methods of 
accumulating training hours for clerks.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 3
Municipal clerks may attend approved training from certified trainers, but the 
clerks must report any training not conducted by Commission staff or obtained 
from the Commission’s ElectEd website to the Commission for it to count toward 
the 6-hour requirement. Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL 12.02(5), 12.03(5)(e). Clerks must 
register for trainings appearing on the ElectEd website, and Commission staff 
will compare registration with attendance to assign credit. See Wis. Admin. 
Code § EL 12.03(4). Clerks must report trainings taken with certified trainers and 
the number of hours to the Commission using the Offline Training Hours Request 
Form which is found on ElectEd. See Wis. Admin. Code § EL 12.03(5)(e). All in-
person or live online training conducted by WEC staff or taken in ElectEd will be 
tracked in ElectEd, along with training taken from certified trainers and reported 
to the WEC on the Offline Training Hours Request Form. See Wis. Admin. Code § 
EL 12.03(4). See the ElectEd catalogue or reach out to elections.training@wi.gov 
for more details about training opportunities.
Clerks must provide the municipal mailing address and an email address for a 
municipality’s top elected official to the Commission, and a clerk must provide 
any new address or email within 21 days of a change to that information. Wis. 
Admin. Code § EL 12.02(7). If a new clerk does not complete an initial certification 
prior to an election, the Commission must notify the top elected official of the 
municipality by mail and email of the deficiency before the election takes place. 
Id. For a renewal certification, the Commission must notify the top elected 
official of a deficiency within 30 days of an election cycle’s end. Id.
In an emergency, a clerk, in an expeditious manner, may request that the 
Commission Administrator grant a waiver of a training requirement by 
describing the facts that establish the basis of the emergency and details the 
steps taken to obtain the required training. Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL 12.05(1), (2), 
and (3). The Administrator may grant the waiver for one election cycle, but for 
an initial certification, the waiver is only valid for one election. Wis. Admin. Code 
§§ EL 12.03(1), 12.05(4).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 4
Chapter 8.3: Election 
Inspectors (General)
Election inspectors, also known as “poll workers,” are charged with the statutory 
duties of running the election on Election Day. Thousands of election inspectors 
are needed across the state for each election, especially during high-turnout 
General Elections in presidential years. The law outlines a specific process for 
order of preference of those interested in serving, a process which is designed 
to ensure that both major political parties have fair participation of their 
affiliated election inspectors at polling places.
As this chapter explains in more detail, election 
inspectors are chosen in the following order:
1. Consideration of all appointed partisan inspectors
2. Consideration of all appointed unaffiliated inspectors
3. Temporary appointments to fill the remainder of inspectors needed
Sec. 8.3.1: Duties
Election inspectors staff the polling place on Election Day. Election inspectors’ 
duties include setting up the polling place, preserving order, registering electors, 
recording voter numbers, issuing ballots, monitoring voting equipment, counting 
votes, and properly completing required forms. Wis. Stat. § 7.37.
Best Practice: Election inspectors should not serve at elections in which 
they, their spouse, or an immediate family member is a candidate 
on the ballot or under other circumstances where a candidate’s 
success or failure would affect the election inspector financially.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 5
Sec. 8.3.2: Number of Election 
Inspectors Required
Each polling place should have at least seven inspectors. The governing body 
may increase the number where more than one voting device is used or polling 
places are combined in accordance with Wis. Stat. §§ 5.15(6)(b), 7.30(1)(a). This 
governing body action need not be done by ordinance.1
By ordinance, the governing body may provide for the selection of alternates 
or for the selection of two or more sets of inspectors to work at different times 
on Election Day. Alternate officials shall be appointed in a number sufficient to 
maintain adequate staffing of polling places. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(a).
The governing body of the municipality may reduce the number of election 
inspectors by resolution. However, no polling place may have fewer than three 
election inspectors. Wis. Stat. § 7.32.
There must always be an odd number of election inspectors at the polling place, 
regardless of increase or reduction by the governing body. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(a). 
See Sec. 8.4.2 on page 14 for how to determine which political party receives 
the dominant number of election inspectors from within this odd number.
Sec. 8.3.3: Qualifications
Election inspectors must meet specific, statutory criteria. The Commission 
has determined that municipal clerks, or governing bodies, must be able 
to take some reasonable steps to certify that election inspectors meet the 
requirements of Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2).2
Criteria 1: Nomination
The two major political parties have the first right to submit lists of their 
preferred election inspectors for appointment by the municipal governing 
body. If there is a greater need than those who are nominated, the remaining 
election inspectors are politically unaffiliated. For detailed information on the 
nomination and appointment process for partisan election inspectors see 
Chapter 8.4 on page 13.
1 See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
2 See EL 23-55, Kosloski v. Yenter (Decided April 8, 2024) and  
EL 24-39, Hanna v. Woodall et al (Decided July 18, 2025).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 6
Criteria 2: English Comprehension
Inspectors must be able to read, write, and understand the English language. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a). The municipal clerk may administer an examination, if 
required by the governing body, to all persons nominated as election inspectors 
to prove their ability to read, write and understand the English language, and 
their general knowledge of the election laws. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(c).
Criteria 3: Capable & of Good Understanding
Election inspectors must also “be capable, and be of good understanding.” 
Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a). The Commission has concluded that the requirements 
of “strong clerical skills” and “being an effective communicator” are consistent 
with this statutory requirement, and do not exceed it.3 The work of an election 
inspector is clerical by nature — inspectors review documents and complete 
and process paperwork. Capable election inspectors who are of good 
understanding must also by definition be effective communicators — they must 
be able to discuss and understand how to facilitate the voting procedure, and 
how to assist voters in the process.4
Criteria 4: Training
Inspectors are required to receive training from the municipal clerk within the 
two years preceding the election event at which the inspector intends to work. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.315(1)(b)1.
Criteria 5: Election Presence/Service
An inspector may not be a candidate for any office to be voted on at an 
election at which they serve. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Criteria 6: Qualified Elector Status
Election inspectors must be qualified electors of the county in which the 
municipality where the official serves is located. Id.
 Ɋ The chief inspector(s) must be a qualified elector of the municipality in 
which they serve, except if a qualified candidate is not available. Id.
 Ɋ A high school student may be appointed to serve as an inspector, but 
not a chief inspector, only in the polling place that serves the student’s 
residence. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
3 See EL 23-55, Kosloski v. Yenter (Decided April 8, 2024).
4 Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 7
Criteria 7: Bipartisan Involvement
The municipal clerk should identify any election inspectors appointed by one of 
the two major political parties. The chief inspector must ensure that any Election 
Day tasks which require completion by two election inspectors are represented 
by each party, whenever possible. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Sec. 8.3.4: Hiring & Background Checks
In order to pay election inspectors and manage them, municipalities often use 
the same or similar hiring policies and procedures as other municipal employees. 
This raises questions about what election inspectors can be required to provide, 
including consenting to background checks, as a condition of their service.
Applications
Application forms are generally permissible if their purpose is to gather only the 
information required for the municipal clerk, or governing body, to confirm that 
the election inspector meets the legal requirements of Wis. Stat. § 7.30. Name, 
address, date of birth, qualification to vote, and felony status are all relevant 
to that inquiry.5 Additional information (such as comfort level with technology, 
willingness to travel, and hours of availability) are likewise permissible as 
long as answering them is optional.6 When asking about felony convictions, 
the application should not require the election inspector to certify that they 
have never been convicted of a felony, it should instead ask “Have you been 
convicted of a felony, and if so, have you received a pardon or completed the 
terms of imprisonment, extended supervision, parole, or probation.”7
Background Checks
The Commission has determined that background checks are not per se 
unreasonable, but depending on the level of information they seek, they can cross 
the line and rise to an unreasonable condition for election inspectors.8 For example, 
a background check form, which requires election inspectors to provide their date of 
birth, signature, Wisconsin driver’s license number, and social security number likely 
goes too far.9 Whenever municipalities determine that background checks or other 
hiring procedures are a required term or condition of employment for paid or unpaid 
municipal employees, the forms cannot go beyond what Wis. Stat. § 7.30 permits.10
5 See EL 24-39, Hanna v. Woodall et al (Decided July 18, 2025).
6 Id.
7 Id.
8 See EL 23-55, Kosloski v. Yenter (Decided April 8, 2024).
9 Id.
10 Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 8
Sec. 8.3.5: Term of Office
Election inspector terms run from January 1 of an even-numbered year through 
December 31 of the subsequent odd-numbered year. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4). If there 
is an election inspector vacancy, a new appointee will fill the remainder of the 
prior appointee’s two-year term. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(6)(a).
Sec. 8.3.6: Filling Vacancies
Permanent vacancies in Republican or Democratic positions are filled by the 
municipal clerk from the remaining names on the lists submitted by the parties 
or from names submitted by the parties to supplement the original lists. Wis. 
Stat. §§ 7.30(2)(b), (4)(d). Temporary vacancies created by a candidacy, illness, 
or other temporary causes can be filled by the municipal clerk to serve for 
one election only. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(b). Temporary vacancies are filled with 
temporary appointments and permanent vacancies are filled with permanent 
appointments, but the method of appointment from the appropriate party list 
does not change based on the type of vacancy.11
Note: Vacancies are filled from the lists submitted by the parties, 
not the list appointed by the governing body — thus, the number of 
partisan nominated election inspectors is not fixed at the amount 
initially appointed by the governing body.12
While the parties have the right to submit additional names for the purpose 
of filling vacancies under Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d), a clerk does not have a duty 
to solicit names from them and may proceed with filling a permanent or 
temporary vacancy immediately as the need arises, turning to remaining 
names or supplemental names on lists if any are available.13
 Ɋ A party that did not submit a list by November 30 may not submit a list of 
names after that deadline. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(b).
 Ɋ If there are no lists or the lists have been exhausted, the municipal clerk 
may fill the vacancy without regard to party affiliation. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
11 See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
12 Id.
13 Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 9
 Ɋ If an unaffiliated inspector vacates his or her position, and the party 
entitled to that position has submitted supplemental names, the vacancy 
is filled from the supplemental list. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
 Ɋ If no supplemental list has been submitted since the unaffiliated 
appointment was made, the clerk may fill the vacancy with another 
unaffiliated inspector. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
Sec. 8.3.7: Training Requirements
Election inspectors are required to attend training every two years and must 
have attended training within each appointment term prior to any election at 
which they will serve. Wis. Stat. § 7.315(1)(b)1. See elections.wi.gov for Training 
Tables listing the approved methods of accumulating training hours toward 
recertification of election inspectors.
 Ɋ It is the responsibility of the municipal clerk to see that all election 
inspectors are provided with adequate training for the performance of 
their duties. Wis. Stat. §§ 7.315(1)(b)1., 7.30(2)(c).
 Ɋ Clerks may remove an inspector for failure to attend required training 
sessions. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(6)(c).
Best Practice: The Wisconsin Elections Commission suggests, at a 
minimum, that the clerk go over the election day duties listed in  
this manual.
Because all election inspectors must receive training before 
administering an election, the Commission strongly recommends 
holding training classes in January of each even numbered year. 
Because election inspectors are appointed at the end of odd 
numbered years and many municipalities will need to administer a 
February primary, there can be a very short amount of time during 
which required training must take place. Clerks have discretion 
concerning how to provide this training and may make use of the 
Commission’s resources in ElectEd for this purpose.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 10
Sec. 8.3.8: Oaths of Office
All election officials are required to take and file an oath, including those who 
are filling vacancies Wis. Stat. § 7.30(5).Municipal clerks must notify, by mail, 
appointed official within five days of appointment of the requirement to file an 
official oath, and the official must file the oath with the clerk within 10 days after 
mailing the notice. Id.
Best Practice: The Commission recommends also emailing 
each official who is appointed to ensure they receive the 
information concerning the oath as quickly as possible.
Election officials who have taken the oath may administer any oath required 
to conduct an election. Id. The oath must be filed before the commencement 
of the official’s duties. Id., 6.875(5). The oath is valid for the entire two-year 
term of the appointment. See Wis. Stat. §§ 7.30(5), (6)(a).
Note: The following oaths may be obtained from the WEC website:
Official Oath  (EL-154): Filed by Election Inspectors, Chief Inspectors, 
Election Registration Officials, Greeters, and Tabulators. See Wis. 
Stat. § 19.01 .
Oath of Special Voting Deputy (EL-155): Filed by Special Voting 
Deputies. Wis. Stat. § 6.875(5).
Sec. 8.3.9: Scheduling of 
Election Inspectors
Once election inspectors (partisan and unaffiliated) have been nominated 
and appointed, municipal clerks have some discretion to make scheduling 
decisions based on the needs of their jurisdiction. Wis. Stat. § 7.15(1). Municipal 
clerks should communicate with the political parties prior to nomination so 
that election inspectors know what form of communication will be used for 
scheduling information and announcements (phone, email, mail, online portal). 
This will ensure that those who have been appointed to serve don’t miss out 
due to missed communication between them and the clerk.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 11
Some election day tasks require the involvement of 2 or more inspectors, each 
of whom should be from one of the political parties (insofar as practicable) 
if lists were submitted, so those requirements must be considered when 
scheduling election inspectors. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2). Wherever an Election Day 
action requires 2 or more election inspectors, at least one inspector from each 
party should be assigned to the work if it is practicable to do so.14 Election day 
tasks are assigned by the Chief Inspector. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Sec. 8.3.10: Removing Election Officials
Municipal clerks can discharge an election official summarily if he or she is 
found to lack the qualifications for the position, fails to attend required training, 
neglects his or her duties during an election, electioneers, commits official 
misconduct, or otherwise carries out improper conduct or willfully neglects 
duties. Wis. Stat. §§ 7.15(1)(f),  7.30(6)(c). Further, an election official required to use 
voting equipment who does not understand the equipment cannot be allowed 
to serve. Wis. Stat. § 7.25(5)
Best Practice: Prior to dismissing an election official, the 
Commission recommends that a clerk contact any appointing 
political party and explain any issue with the official so that 
the party may address the issue with the election official. The 
Commission also recommends notifying the governing body of 
any issue with an election official that may lead to dismissal, and 
to notify the governing body if a clerk dismisses the official.
A municipal clerk who removes an election official without sufficient legal 
reason could become the subject of an administrative complaint brought 
under Wis. Stat. § 5.06.
14 See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 12
Chapter 8.4: Nomination 
& Appointment of Partisan 
Election Inspectors
State law openly permits and invites the participation of major political parties 
in the nomination and appointment of election inspectors in their communities. 
Each odd-numbered year, political parties submit their list of nominees to 
the municipal clerk or governing body. The clerk confirms the nominees are 
qualified to serve as election inspectors, and then prepares the information 
needed for the governing body to consider and decide appointments. The 
governing body of each municipality then appoints the election inspectors. This 
chapter describes that process.
Sec. 8.4.1: Nomination by Political Party
The two political parties whose candidates for governor or president received 
the largest number of votes in the previous general election may submit lists of 
election inspector nominees no later than November 30 of an odd-numbered 
year. The political parties determine on their own who to nominate as election 
inspectors, and a clerk does not have any power to alter the names that are 
included.15 See Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(b). The political parties that submit lists shall 
certify that they contacted every person included on the list and they have 
agreed to serve as election officials. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(b). When party lists are 
received, election inspector appointments must be made from them. Wis. Stat. 
§§ 7.30(4)(b), (2).
15 See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 13
Best Practice: Municipal clerks should contact the appropriate 
statutory committeeperson or voluntary county party 
chairperson before the first week in November and advise him 
or her of their responsibility to submit a list of nominees to the 
Mayor, Village President, Town Board Chairperson, or municipal 
clerk. A clerk may recommend election inspectors who have 
proven to be effective workers. Clerks should also explain to 
the parties exactly how they plan to contact nominated and/
or appointed election inspectors (email, phone, letter, online 
portal) so the election inspectors know what to look out for.
If the list of appointed election inspectors is emailed, a signed original of the 
document must also be received, either postmarked or delivered by, the filing 
deadline. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 6.04(3).
Nominated election inspectors still must meet all of the legal requirements 
in Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2), and municipal clerks, or governing bodies, retain the 
right to reasonably certify that nominated election inspectors meet statutory 
requirements, including by requiring nominated election inspectors to complete 
the appropriate paperwork.16
Sec. 8.4.2: Determining Party 
Imbalance at Each Polling Place
The party whose candidate for governor or president at the last general election 
received the most votes at that polling place (the “dominant” party) is entitled 
to one extra inspector. Wis. Stat. §§ 7.30(4)(b), (2).
Best Practice: Determine party imbalance for each 
polling place in anticipation of receiving lists of inspector 
nominees from the political parties to ensure proper 
assignment and adequate staffing for shift or election.
16 EL 24-39, Hanna v. Woodall et al (Decided July 18, 2025).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 14
Example: The Republican candidate for governor received the most votes at 
the polling place at the last general election, seven total inspectors are needed. 
Thus, the clerk should ensure the assignment of four Republican positions and 
three Democratic positions. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Positions identified as Republican and Democratic remain as such for the 
duration of the term. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(6)(a).
Sec. 8.4.3: Contact Nominees 
for Willingness to Serve
Best Practice: Clerks should contact each party’s nominees 
to confirm their willingness to serve before submitting 
the names to the governing body for appointment.
1. Clerks should make at least two attempts to contact each party’s 
nominees, though those attempts can be by any reasonable method 
(phone, email, mail, online portal).
2. Document any nominees not willing to serve and provide the party 
those names.
3. The clerk may also inquire as to willingness to serve as a chief 
inspector and arrange for training for those who are interested.
Just because a nominee has declined to work at a previous election, even more 
than one previous election, does not mean the clerk is excused from contacting 
them to confirm their willingness to serve.17
Note: Refusal to serve as a chief inspector is not grounds for nonappointment.
Appointments must be made from the lists submitted by the parties for as long 
as election inspector positions are available. If party lists have been timely 
received, positions must be filled from the lists until the names on those lists 
have been depleted. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
17 See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 15
Nominees must be qualified electors of the county in which they reside. Wis. 
Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
The lists may also designate individuals as first choice nominees, who must be 
appointed first. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(b).
Best Practice: If “first choice” is not indicated in some manner, but the 
names are numbered, they should be appointed in numerical order.
If the governing body has good cause not to appoint an individual whose name 
is submitted as a “first-choice” nominee, it may request the WEC authorize non-
appointment, and may not decline to appoint such individual until receiving the 
WEC’s authorization. Wis. Stat. §§ 7.30(4)(e), (b).
Best Practice: Seeking nonappointment from the Commission 
is a public process which might expose the election inspectors 
in question to embarrassment or unnecessary scrutiny. Before 
seeking nonappointment, municipal clerks could share their 
concerns with the nominating political party in an attempt to inquire 
whether the political party wishes to withdraw the nominee.
When party lists are received, the clerk must adhere to “party imbalance” 
at each polling place. The dominant party is entitled to one more election 
inspector at that polling place than the other party. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Example: Five election inspectors are to be placed at a polling place. The 
Democratic candidate for governor or president received the most votes at 
the polling place at the last general election. This means that three positions 
are Democratic, and two positions are Republican, and they should be 
appointed as such.
Note: It is possible that the dominant party will differ between polling 
places in the same municipality.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 16
Sec. 8.4.4: If Lists are Received 
but are Insufficient to Fill Need
If the Democratic and Republican parties’ lists are insufficient or the 
nominees decline to serve in the positions available for that party’s 
nominees, the remaining positions are filled without regard to party 
affiliation. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(c).
Example: Seven inspectors are to be placed at a polling place. The Republican 
candidate for governor or president received the most votes at the polling place 
at the last general election. This party imbalance gives the Republican Party 
the extra inspector so the ratio is four Republican positions to three Democratic 
positions. If sufficient lists from both parties were submitted, four names would 
be appointed from the Republican list, and three names would be appointed 
from the Democratic list.
However, if there are only three names on the Republican list and no Democratic 
list was submitted, the governing body will appoint the three Republican names. 
The Mayor, Village President, or Town Board Chairperson of the municipality will 
then nominate other qualified individuals, regardless of party affiliation, and 
submits the names to the governing body for appointment to the remaining 
four positions.
Note: Regardless of an appointee’s separately conveyed political 
affiliation, they are an unaffiliated appointee if they were not 
submitted on a party list.
If the Democratic Party submitted a list with two names, the two Democratic 
nominees and two unaffiliated nominees would be appointed along with the 
three Republican nominees.
The parties may supplement their initial list of nominees at any time during the 
term. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 17
Sec. 8.4.5: If No Lists are 
Received from Parties
If no lists of inspector nominees are submitted, the Mayor, Village President 
or Town Board Chairperson of the municipality nominates other qualified 
individuals, regardless of party affiliation, and submits the names to the 
governing body for appointment. All appointments are made without regard to 
party affiliation. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(c).
Sec. 8.4.6: Appointment of 
Inspectors by Governing Body
Appointment of inspectors must occur no later than December 31st of an odd-
numbered year. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(a).
The clerk submits the party lists to the governing body. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)
(b)2. The clerk should clearly indicate which partisan election inspectors were 
appointed by which party as this information might be critical to a governing 
body appointing the right balance of election inspectors.18
 Ɋ Advise the governing body of the requirement to appoint any first-choice 
nominees first. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(b)2.c.
 Ɋ Advise the governing body if lists are insufficient so that unaffiliated 
inspectors may be nominated. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(c). However, the parties 
may supplement their initial list of nominees at any time during the term 
to fill vacancies, but an appointment need not be delayed because of lack 
of availability of party nominees. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
The governing body must appoint at least as many inspectors as there are 
positions to be filled. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(a). Please see “Sec. 8.3.2: Number of 
Election Inspectors Required” on page 6.
Appointments are made from the party lists until each party’s positions have 
been filled or until the lists are depleted. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
If positions remain open and the lists have been depleted, “unaffiliated” 
inspectors may be appointed to the remaining positions. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(4)(d).
18 See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 18
Additional inspectors may be appointed as alternates. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(a).
If a municipality establishes a municipal board of absentee canvassers 
(“central count”) by ordinance, who will then separately count the absentee 
ballots in lieu of canvassing absentee ballots at the polling place, the governing 
body will appoint the clerk, or another qualified elector designated by the clerk, 
and two other qualified electors of the municipality appointed by the clerk, to 
serve on that board. Wis. Stat. §§ 7.53(2m)(b), 7.52(1)(b).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 19
Chapter 8.5: High School 
Student Election Inspectors
State law permits certain qualified high school students to work at the polls 
on Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am). Students may decide for themselves 
to serve as election inspectors or in response to a school sponsored initiative. 
Civics, government or political science teachers may see this as an opportunity 
for a real-life learning experience. Student organizations may find this to be an 
attractive form of community service and an interesting learning opportunity. 
Allowing students to work as election inspectors provides an opportunity for 
students to become involved in the election process and also offers clerks 
another resource for filling election inspector positions.
Students with foreign language skills can help voters who may need assistance 
understanding the ballot, voting equipment, and other election-related 
materials. In many locations, Hmong and Spanish speaking voters need 
special assistance, or the municipality may have specific language assistant 
requirements in place under Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act that can be 
met with the placement of bilingual inspectors.
Municipal clerks are encouraged to work with their local high schools to enable 
students to serve as election inspectors.
Sec. 8.5.1: Qualifications
A student qualifies to serve as an election inspector if the student:
 Ɋ Is 16 or 17 years of age. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
 Ɋ Is enrolled in grades 9 to 12 in a public, private, or tribal school, or private 
home-based educational program. Id.
 Ɋ Has at least a 3.0 grade point average or the equivalent. Id.
 Ɋ Has the written approval of the student’s parent or guardian. Id.
 Ɋ Has the written approval of the principal of the school in which the student 
is enrolled, if the student has less than a 3.0 grade point average. Id.
 Ɋ Is a resident of the municipality of the polling place at which he or she 
serves. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 20
Sec. 8.5.2: Written 
Authorization Required
Before a student may be appointed as an inspector, the municipal clerk 
shall obtain written authorization from the student’s parent or guardian. If 
the student has less than a 3.0 grade point average, the clerk will also need 
authorization from the principal of the school where the student is enrolled. 
Upon appointment, the municipal clerk shall notify the principal of the school 
where the student is enrolled regarding the date of the election at which the 
student will serve. Id.
Sec. 8.5.3: Restrictions
 Ɋ A student may only serve as an inspector at a polling place if at least 
one inspector, other than the chief inspector, is a qualified elector of the 
municipality. Id.
 Ɋ A student may not serve as chief inspector at a polling place. Id.
 Ɋ A student serving as an election inspector may not challenge any person 
offering to vote. Wis. Stat. § 6.92(2).
 Ɋ A student must serve at the polling place that corresponds to their 
residential address, even if there are other polling places within the 
municipality. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(am).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 21
Chapter 8.6: Chief Election 
Inspectors
The Chief Election Inspector (also referred to as the Chief Inspector) is a 
specialty election inspector with additional training who directs the conduct of 
activities assigned to the inspectors at the polling place.
Sec. 8.6.1: Designating 
a Chief Inspector
The municipal clerk designates one of the inspectors as chief inspector (CI) 
for the polling place. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(6)(b). The clerk is not required to honor a 
political party’s or governing body’s request or instruction that a specific election 
inspector be designated as a CI.19 This individual acts as liaison between the 
election inspectors and the municipal clerk and is in charge of the polling place 
on Election Day. The CI must be a qualified elector of the municipality, except 
when no qualified candidate is available or a vacancy is being filled pursuant 
to Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(b), in which case they need not be a qualified elector of the 
municipality. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a). The CI is counted in the overall odd number of 
inspectors at the polling place. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(a).
Although the municipal clerk ultimately designates the CI, care should be taken 
to maintain the party imbalance. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(a).
Best Practice:
 Ɋ If all positions at the polling place have been filled from party lists, 
clerks are encouraged to select one of the party appointees as the CI.
 Ɋ If none of the party appointees are qualified as chief inspectors, select 
a qualified unaffiliated inspector. (Keep party representation even.)
 Ɋ If there are a mixture of affiliated and unaffiliated inspectors, choose 
any qualified inspector.
 Ɋ If it is necessary to remove an inspector in order to insert a qualified 
CI, replace an unaffiliated inspector if possible.
19 See EL 24-26, Charneski v. Birk-LaBarge (Decided Dec. 1, 2025).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 22
Sec. 8.6.2: Municipal Residents 
vs. County Residents
Wisconsin Statute § 7.30(2)(a) indicates a preference for the CI to be a municipal 
resident, but offers an exception: “…each chief inspector shall be a qualified 
elector of the municipality in which the chief inspector serves. If no qualified 
candidate for chief inspector is available … the person so appointed need not be 
a qualified elector of the municipality…” (emphasis added)
Again, the municipal clerk chooses the CI, but the statute confines the selection 
to municipal residents unless no qualified municipal resident is available. 
This requirement, when intertwined with the requirement to maintain party 
imbalance, can be a challenge to implement.
Best Practice:
It is recommended to choose a CI using the following priority order:
1. Affiliated municipal resident
If there is an affiliated inspector who is a resident of the municipality 
who is trained or willing to be trained as a CI, arrange for training and 
use for CI. Maintain party imbalance at the polling place.
2. Unaffiliated municipal resident
If no affiliated municipal resident is trained or willing to be trained as 
a CI, arrange for training of an unaffiliated municipal resident. If this 
means replacing an affiliated inspector, keep the party representation 
even.
3. Affiliated resident of the county
If there is no affiliated or unaffiliated municipal resident trained 
or willing to be trained as a CI, arrange for the training of a willing 
affiliated inspector who is a resident of the county.
4. Unaffiliated resident of the county
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 23
If there is no municipal resident or affiliated county resident trained or 
willing to be trained, arrange for training of a willing unaffiliated county 
resident. If this means replacing an affiliated inspector, keep the party 
representation even.
Sec. 8.6.3: Training Requirements
Chief inspectors are required to attend “Baseline” training in order to be 
initially certified. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 11.02(2). Attending Baseline training 
certifies the attendee as a chief inspector for the current term. In order to 
recertify for the following term, a chief inspector must attend at least six hours 
of Wisconsin Elections Commission approved continuing election education 
during the current term. (Attendance at Baseline training also counts toward 
recertification for the following term, if the course retaken.) Wis. Admin. Code § 
EL 11.03(1). See elections.wi.gov for Training Tables listing the approved methods 
of accumulating training hours toward recertification of chief inspectors. Wis. 
Stat. § 7.31(4).
The county or municipal clerk conducting recertification training for other 
clerks or election inspectors must submit an agenda or course outline to 
the Wisconsin Elections Commission for approval. Training hours of election 
inspectors are documented and tracked by the municipal clerk. Chief inspectors 
may be given a self-administered evaluation as part of training, the results of 
which will not affect the chief inspector’s appointment or qualifications to serve. 
The results do not have to be reported to the WEC.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 24
Chapter 8.7: Greeters & 
Tabulators
Sec. 8.7.1: Greeters
Each municipality may appoint one additional inspector per polling place 
regardless of party affiliation to act as a greeter and substitute for other officials 
as necessary on Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(b). Greeters may not participate 
in canvassing after the polls close. Wis. Stat. §§ 7.51(1), 7.53(1)(a). Greeters do not 
count towards the number of election inspectors, unless they are stepping in to 
complete official duties, such as if another election inspector goes on a break. 
See Wis. Stat. § 7.30(1)(b). Only greeters who are currently trained and certified 
as election inspectors may cover for other election inspectors. Wis. Stat. § 
7.315(1)(b)1. Because greeters are classified as additional election inspectors, 
and because they are able to substitute for election inspectors making up 
the appointed number for the polling place, they should receive the same 
training as other inspectors. See Wis. Stat. §§ 7.30(1)(b), 7.315(1)(b)1. An individual 
appointed as a greeter cannot serve as a chief inspector. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(6)(b).
Best Practices for Greeters:
 Ɋ Direct voters to the correct ward, registration table, or poll book table.
 Ɋ Answer general questions about the voting process or direct 
questions to another election inspector or the Chief Inspector.
 Ɋ Review a voter’s proof of residence or photo ID and advise the voter 
if the document(s) is acceptable. The voter must still provide the 
document(s) to the election inspectors to register to vote or be issued 
a ballot.
 Ɋ Confirm if a voter is in the right polling place or direct the voter to the 
proper polling place by searching for the voter’s address in MyVote, 
on a district map, or on another copy of the poll list.
 Ɋ Substitute for election inspectors taking a break
 Ɋ Help maintain clear pathways for voters to enter and move through 
the polling area in an orderly manner.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 25
Sec. 8.7.2: Tabulators
Not less than 30 days before an election, the governing body or board of 
election commissioners may, by resolution, authorize the municipal clerk to 
select and employ tabulators for the elections specified in the resolution or, if 
not specified, until the resolution is modified or revoked. Wis. Stat. §§ 7.30(3)(a), 
(b). Tabulators are to assist and be under the direction of the election inspectors 
after the polls close. Id.
Separately, a recount board of canvassers may select and employ tabulators 
under their direction to assist in recount duties, and such tabulators cannot 
make determinations on the validity of any vote tabulated. Wis. Stat. § 9.01(5)(b).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 26
Chapter 8.8: Election 
Registration Officials
Election Registration Officials (EROs) are specially designated election officials 
who are authorized to register voters. They should not be confused with Special 
Registration Deputies, which were eliminated from Wisconsin law in 2016. See 2015 
WI Act 261. They should also not be confused with Special Voting Deputies (SVDs).
Sec. 8.8.1: Appointment & Qualifications
An Election Registration Official (ERO) is an election official who is assigned 
under Wis. Stat. §§ 6.28(1)(a) or 7.30 to register electors. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(4g). 
Municipal Clerks may appoint Election Registration Officials to conduct voter 
registration at the polling place on Election Day, at residential care facilities 
during the open registration period, and in the clerk’s office during in-person 
absentee voting. Wis. Stat. § 6.28(1)(a). EROs do not count towards the number of 
inspectors at a polling place. See Wis. Stat. § 6.55.
Best Practice: An ERO should be a qualified elector of the county for 
the polling place, residential care facility or clerk’s office at which they 
serve, however, a non-resident clerk or deputy clerk could serve as 
an ERO in case of a vacancy. See Wis. Stat. §§ 5.02(4g) and 7.30(2)(a).
Party lists may also be used for selections of EROs if there are additional names, 
or inspectors can be trained as EROs in addition to inspectors so that they can 
assist in registration during IPAV or SVD voting. Sending an ERO to an SVD facility, 
or training the SVDs as EROs, can allow eligible electors residing in the homes or 
facilities to register during the open registration period.
Sec. 8.8.2: Duties
When appointed by a municipal clerk, EROs can process registrations and sign 
registration forms when an elector registers at a polling place, IPAV site, or SVD 
location. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.28(1)(a), 6.33(2)(b), 6.55. For a description of how EROs 
register voters, see Chapter 6.2: “Voter Registration Prior to Election Day” and 
Chapter 14.6: “Election Day Registration” as the processes are the same as 
when carried out by municipal clerks or election inspectors.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 27
Sec. 8.8.3: Training Requirements
EROs are required to receive training from the municipal clerk within two years 
of any election at which they serve and take an oath. Wis. Stat. § 7.315 (4). It is the 
responsibility of the municipal clerk to see that EROs are provided with the same 
training as election inspectors for the performance of their duties. Wis. Stat. § 
7.315(1)(b)1. (4). The training must be complete before the ERO can take part in 
registration during a specific election. See Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 28
Chapter 8.9: Frequently 
Asked Questions
Q What if a trained election inspector is not available to work at an election, 
and I have to use an inspector who has not been trained within the last 
two years?
A In the event that a trained election inspector has an emergency and 
cannot work on Election Day, an inspector who has not received training 
may be appointed to serve as an inspector, but not as a chief inspector, 
Election Registration Official, or Special Voting Deputy. The appointment 
of an untrained individual is for a specific election only, and the untrained 
individual may only be appointed once in the two-year period beginning 
on January 1 of each even-numbered year. Wis. Stat. § 7.315(1)(b)2. If the 
clerk is aware of the vacancy prior to Election Day, the clerk must provide 
some type of election training to the election inspector. Otherwise, the 
same qualifications that applied to original appointees shall be required 
of persons who fill vacancies except that if a municipal clerk or deputy 
clerk fills the vacancy, the clerk or deputy, but not more than a total of 2 
individuals in any municipality, may serve without regard to the clerk’s 
or deputy’s county of residence, if the clerk or deputy meets the other 
qualifications. Wis. Stat. § 7.30(2)(b).
Q What should I do if there is an emergency and I do not have a certified 
chief inspector?
A You should contact an Elections Specialist at the Wisconsin Elections 
Commission who will direct you on the actions to be taken. Best Practice: 
The Wisconsin Elections Commission recommends that all municipalities 
make advance arrangements to have alternate trained chief inspectors 
available in case of emergency. This type of pre-planning can be critical, 
and it may be coupled with an emergency polling place relocation plan or 
contingent staffing plan for elections.
Q What is “Baseline” training?
A Baseline training is a two or three-hour chief inspector training course 
on basic election-day administration conducted by Wisconsin Elections 
Commission staff or WEC certified clerk-trainers. The Baseline class is 
also available online in the WEC’s ElectEd learning management system. 
Baseline training is required for initial certification as a chief inspector.
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 29
Q I have a person who is interested in becoming a certified chief inspector. 
What does the person have to do to qualify as a certified chief inspector for 
the current term?
A The individual may accomplish certification by attending the Baseline 
training. Attendance at Baseline training will certify the new chief inspector 
for the current term. The newly certified chief inspector is then eligible to 
serve at all subsequent elections during the current term. See Wis. Admin. 
Code Chapter EL 11 for further information.
Q My chief inspector is certified for the current term. What else must he or 
she do in order to recertify for the next term?
A In order to recertify for the next term, the inspector will need to 
accumulate a minimum of six hours of Wisconsin Elections Commission 
approved training during the current term. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 11.03(1).
First Edition, June 2026 Local Election Officials 8 – 30


Part 9 
Voting Equipment
Types of Voting Equipment; Hand Counting; Testing and 
Certification; Security; Pre-Election Testing; Post-Election Audit
Electronic voting equipment is tested and certified by the Commission for 
use in Wisconsin. Most municipalities rely on electronic voting systems to 
tabulate election results. State law requires pre-election testing of voting 
equipment before every election. Following each general election, selected 
municipalities conduct a post-election audit to ensure that the voting 
equipment accurately counted the votes it reported. Both the Commission 
and clerks follow detailed security procedures to ensure that electronic 
voting systems safely, securely, efficiently, and accurately count votes in 
all elections.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 1
Chapter 9.1: Types of Voting 
Equipment Authorized in 
Wisconsin
Sec. 9.1.1: Introduction
All votes cast in Wisconsin produce a paper record, regardless of whether the 
ballots are counted by hand or with the aid of an electronic tabulator. This 
means that there is a hard copy record of each voter’s choices that can always 
be examined after any election.
“Voting equipment” is another term for “voting system,” which means 
the total combination of mechanical, electromechanical, or electronic 
equipment — including the software, hardware, and documentation required to 
program, control, and support the equipment — that is used to define ballots, to 
cast and count votes, to report or display election results, and to maintain and 
produce any audit trail information. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(24w)(a).
“Electronic voting system” means a system in which votes are recorded on 
ballots and the votes are subsequently counted and tabulated by automatic 
tabulating equipment. Wis. Stat. § 5.02(4m). It also includes a voting machine on 
which votes are recorded and tabulated by electronic means.
In the past 25 years, electronic voting systems have become more common, and 
mechanical systems (such as those that punch out holes in paper ballots) have 
mostly gone by the wayside, especially in the wake of the 2000 presidential election.
The widespread use of electronic voting equipment has led to understandable 
questions and curiosity about the security and integrity of these systems. The 
proper use and security of voting equipment is integral to ensuring accuracy and 
maintaining voter confidence in the electoral process. Voting equipment accuracy 
and security has long been an issue of extreme importance for both election officials 
and voters. Voter confidence in the equipment used to count votes is an aspect of 
elections administration which continues to grow in significance. Careful execution 
and documentation of the procedures detailed in this section will address concerns, 
confirming the voting equipment used in each municipality is reliable and accurate.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 2
Sec. 9.1.2: Use of Voting 
Equipment in Wisconsin
Voting equipment is designed and manufactured by specialized vendors who 
are familiar with the federal and state legal requirements for voting systems in 
each state. The two major vendors of voting equipment in Wisconsin are Election 
Systems & Software (ES&S) and Liberty Vote (formerly Dominion Voting Systems).
No voting equipment may be used in Wisconsin unless it has been certified by 
the Commission. Wis. Stat. §§ 5.40(2), 5.91. When a vendor wishes to offer a new 
electronic voting system for sale, it must seek Commission certification and 
approval before any sale takes place. The Commission certifies the entire voting 
system, including all software and hardware components that make up the system. 
Please see “Chapter 9.3: Voting Equipment Testing & Certification” on page 10.
Municipalities with a population of 7,500 or more are required to use electronic 
voting equipment in every ward in every election. Wis. Stat. § 5.40(1).
Additionally, all municipalities, regardless of size, are required to purchase and 
offer accessible voting equipment. All polling places must be equipped with 
at least one accessible voting equipment component to permit all voters to 
vote privately and independently. HAVA § 301(a)(3)(A). For more information on 
accessible voting equipment, see Sec. 11.7.6: “Voting Area.”
Individual municipalities decide which state-certified and approved electronic 
voting system they will use, meaning different municipalities can use different 
equipment. State law grants a certain amount of leeway when mandating 
voting equipment usage. This means that some municipalities use hand-
count paper ballots, some use optical scan equipment, and some use direct 
recording electronic (DRE) equipment. Municipalities also choose which 
unofficial results transmission method they’d like to use when selecting a voting 
system. Each of these features are explained below. Some municipalities use a 
combination of these equipment types.
The Commission maintains a list of voting equipment by municipality on its 
website. The document is titled “Municipal Voting Equipment Lists” and can be
