accessed on elections.wi.gov.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 3
Sec. 9.1.3: Types of Voting Equipment
Optical Scan
This is the most common type of voting equipment used in Wisconsin. Voters 
make their choices on paper ballots by filling in ovals next to the names of 
their preferred candidates. Optical scan tabulators then scan the ballots and 
tabulate the voter’s choices based on which ovals they completed. The paper 
ballots are always retained to show a hard copy record of the total votes cast.
Direct-Recording Electronic (DRE) Equipment
The ImageCast X (ICX) is the only DRE system in use in Wisconsin. In that system, 
voters insert a “voter activation card,” which is configured with the voter’s ballot 
style. The DRE then automatically displays the electronic version of that ballot 
on the screen. Voters then make their choices on the touchscreen display. The 
DRE then presents the voter with a “review page” that allows voters to double-
check their choices. The DRE then records the voter’s choices directly into the 
voting system’s memory and creates a voter-verifiable paper audit trail (VVPAT) 
to preserve a hard copy of the voter’s choices.
Accessible Ballot Marking Devices
All municipalities are required to have accessible voting equipment, which is 
specially designed to assist voters with disabilities who may have trouble voting 
by other methods. Accessible voting equipment is discussed further in Sec. 
11.7.6: “Voting Area.”
Hand Count Paper Ballots
This method is obviously not an electronic voting system, but rather a method 
by which smaller jurisdictions review paper ballots and tabulate the results by 
hand.
Sec. 9.1.4: Types of Results 
Transmission Methods
In addition to the different types of voting configurations (like optical scan or 
DRE), electronic voting systems also have different methods of unofficial results 
transmission after polls close. When municipalities choose and purchase an 
electronic voting system, they also choose how their polling places transmit 
results at the end of the night.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 4
Telecommunications Transmission by Wireless or Analog Modem
One fast and secure option for unofficial results transmission is 
telecommunications transmission by wireless or analog modem. This 
option is offered by voting equipment vendors as a modification to the base 
electronic voting system. For this option, unofficial results are transmitted via 
secure, encrypted modem from each polling place directly to a receiver in 
the clerk’s office.
Transmission by USB or Memory Stick
Voting equipment can also be configured to download results from the 
tabulator to a USB or other detachable memory stick, which is then physically 
transported to the clerk’s office.
Printed or Oral Relay Transmission
Some municipalities opt out of choosing a specific transmission method with 
their voting systems and instead transport either paper copies of the results 
tapes back to the clerk’s office or have their polling places call the clerk’s office 
to orally transmit the results.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 5
Chapter 9.2: Hand Count 
Paper Ballots vs. Electronic 
Voting Systems
Sec. 9.2.1: Introduction
All ballots in Wisconsin are paper ballots. See Wis. Stat. § 5.91(18) (requiring all 
electronic voting machines to generate a complete, permanent paper record).
The main distinction between hand-count paper ballots and ballots 
processed by an electronic voting system is how those ballots are counted:
 Ɋ Hand-count paper ballots:  Voters deposit their ballots in ballot boxes 
and poll workers sort and tally paper ballots by hand at the polling 
place. Wis. Stat. § 6.80(2)(e).
 Ɋ Electronic tabulation: Voters deposit their ballots in an electronic 
tabulator, which reads and counts the votes. See Wis. Stat. § 5.87(1).
In either case, the paper ballot remains the official record of the votes made 
by voters.
Important: This chapter makes an important distinction between 
electronic tabulating equipment (machines that count votes on 
paper ballots) and electronic accessible voting equipment (machines 
available to all voters that can assist voters with disabilities to 
independently mark their ballots). In some municipalities, using 
electronic tabulating equipment is optional, as this chapter explains. 
All municipalities of all sizes must utilize electronic accessible voting 
equipment, no exceptions. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(a).
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 6
Sec. 9.2.2: Which Municipalities 
May Choose to Hand Count?
Municipalities with fewer than 7,500 people may choose to hand count the 
ballots cast at their elections instead of using electronic tabulating equipment.1 
Wis. Stat. § 5.40(1). The decision to hand count ballots is made by the 
municipality’s governing body. Id. Municipalities with fewer than 7,500 people 
need not seek the Commission’s approval to switch to hand counting, even if 
they have used or are currently using electronic tabulation equipment.2
Important: Municipalities that hand count paper ballots must 
still have accessible electronic voting equipment, which permits 
individuals with disabilities to vote without the need for assistance 
and with the same degree of privacy that is accorded to any other 
voter, that is tested and made available at every polling place for every 
election. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(a). Additionally, the Help America Vote Act 
of 2002 (HAVA) requires every polling place used in a federal election to 
offer accessible voting equipment to all voters to ensure they are able 
to vote privately and independently. 52 U.S.C. § 21081(a)(3)(B).
For types of electronic accessible voting equipment, see Sec. 11.7.6: “Voting 
Area.”
1 Additionally, any municipality which had a population of 10,000 or more before July 1, 1995, cannot 
hand count.
2 See Webster v. Pinnow (EL 24-91), Decided May 27, 2025. Available at: elections.wi.gov/resources/
complaints/el-24-91-webster-v-pinnow.
As of December 2025, this decision is currently on appeal before the Dane County Circuit Court 
(2025CV002087).
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 7
Sec. 9.2.3: When Electronic 
Voting Equipment is Required
Any municipality with a population of 7,500 or more must use voting machines 
or electronic voting systems in every ward at every election. Wis. Stat. § 5.40(1). 
A municipality with a population of 7,500 or more that wants to switch to hand 
counting can petition the Commission for permission, and the Commission 
may, but is not required to, grant the request. Wis. Stat. § 5.40(5m).
Best Practice: A governing body seeking the Commission’s permission 
to switch to hand counting should prepare a detailed petition that 
covers all bases and justifications for why hand counting is necessary. 
The petition should specifically account for the additional tabulation 
time that will result and should detail how the municipality plans to 
report its election results in a timely manner. If electronic tabulators 
are available to the municipality, the petition should also explain 
why the voters of the jurisdiction would be better served by hand 
counting ballots instead of relying on electronic tabulators.
State law provides for only a few limited exceptions for municipalities over 7,500 
people to use paper ballots and voting booths instead of electronic voting equipment 
without needing the Commission’s permission to switch. Wis. Stat. § 5.40(3).
The exceptions are:
 Ɋ In situations where a small portion of a municipality (100 voters or fewer) is 
within the boundaries of a representative district, such as a congressional 
district, legislative district, etc.
 Ɋ If the voting equipment is needed again but a recount is still pending, 
preventing the municipality from clearing the memory of a sufficient 
number of voting machines for the upcoming election.
 Ɋ Whenever substitute ballots are used under Wis. Stat. § 7.15(6)(a).
 Ɋ Whenever a clerk assigns a voter to a different polling place as an 
accommodation under Wis. Stat. § 5.25(5)(b).
Note: These situations are uncommon.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 8
Sec. 9.2.4: What are the 
Important Considerations when 
Considering Hand Counting?
Municipalities who wish to switch to hand counting ballots and are eligible to do 
so should consult with their municipal attorneys before making the decision.
Hand counting can be slower, more expensive, 
and more prone to human error:
 Ɋ An electronic tabulator can count hundreds of ballots in a matter of 
minutes, and can do so more accurately than humans, who are often 
prone to making mistakes with repetitive work.
 Ɋ Although electronic tabulators can be expensive, this cost could quickly be 
eclipsed by needing to pay poll workers and additional human tabulators 
hourly to complete the work. See Wis. Stat. § 7.30(3).
 Ɋ Votes are counted after polls close as part of the local board of 
canvassers public meeting. The canvassers are required to continue 
“without adjournment until the canvass of all ballots cast and received 
on or before election day is complete and the return statement is made.” 
Wis. Stat. § 7.51(1). This means that poll workers and tabulators (people, not 
machines) hand counting ballots must finish doing so on Election Night. 
They cannot stop at midnight and start again in the morning.
Hand counting can get very complex, very quickly, 
especially with multiple races on the ballot:
 Ɋ Hand counting may seem more feasible when there are only one or two 
races on the ballot, but this is rarely the case during Spring and General 
Elections. The more races there are on the ballot, the longer the tally sheet 
needs to be, and the more likely it is that someone will make a mistake.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 9
Chapter 9.3: Voting 
Equipment Testing & 
Certification
Before any electronic voting system can be sold or used in the State of 
Wisconsin, it must first be certified by the Wisconsin Elections Commission. 
Wis. Stat. §§ 5.40(2), 5.91.
Sec. 9.3.1: Introduction: 
A Six-Step Process
There are generally six steps vendors take to receive certification of their 
systems from the Commission. This chapter of the manual will provide an 
overview of each step. More detailed information about the process can be 
found in the certification materials prepared by Commission Staff ahead of 
approval of each voting system.
Certification Process:
1. Vendor submits their systems for testing at a federally accredited 
Voting Systems Test Laboratory (VSTL) to ensure compliance with the 
U.S. Election Assistance Commission’s (EAC) Voluntary Voting Systems 
Guidelines (VVSG).
2. Vendor submits, seeks, and receives federal certification from the U.S. EAC. 
This is not a required step for certification in Wisconsin, but most vendors 
seek it because it is required by other states.
3. Vendor submits an application to the Commission for Wisconsin testing 
and certification.
4. Commission Staff review system configuration documentation and 
perform functional testing of the equipment. An advisory panel of local 
election officials also weighs in. Commission Staff then prepare a report 
for the Commission with recommendations of whether or not the system 
should be certified.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 10
5. The Commission reviews the voting system in an open session meeting. 
The vendor attends this meeting to answer any questions. The Commission 
then votes on whether to certify the system for use in Wisconsin.
6. If the Commission votes to certify the system, the vendor receives an 
approval letter, which lists the terms of the approval. Vendors pay the 
costs the Commission incurred in testing the system and place copies of 
their programs, documentation, and source code in escrow.
Sec. 9.3.2: Step One: Voting 
Systems Test Laboratory (VSTL)
Voting Systems Test Laboratories (VSTL) are federally certified laboratories that 
review and test all firmware, software, and hardware of the voting system. The 
purpose of the VSTL is to confirm that the equipment has been qualified to meet 
current voting equipment standards and guidelines. Vendors are required to 
submit their VSTL testing reports of their systems to the Commission as part of 
their certification application.
VSTLs are private companies that receive federal certification from the 
EAC, meaning not just anyone with a testing lab can test voting equipment. 
Currently, there are only two companies in the country that have EAC 
certification as federally tested VSTLs — Pro V&V and SLI Compliance. Certified 
VSTLs complete thorough testing to ensure that the voting systems meet the 
relevant standards that are set by the EAC. These standards are known as the 
Voluntary Voting Systems Guidelines (VVSG) and span over 200 pages. They 
include performance guidelines such as testing requirements for functionality, 
usability, accessibility, hardware, software, telecommunications, security, quality 
assurance, and configuration management.
VSTLs test voting systems to ensure that they meet the EAC’s standards, 
including the standards for telecommunications components and security. The 
VSTL will complete a source code review, a physical configuration audit, some 
telecommunications testing, and an extensive review and test of the entire 
voting system. After testing, the VSTL prepares a detailed report supporting its 
findings and summarizing all the testing and results.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 11
Sec. 9.3.3: Step Two: Federal 
Certification with the U.S. EAC
Most vendors choose to seek federal certification from the U.S. Election 
Assistance Commission (EAC) because some states require it as a condition of 
approval. In Wisconsin, the Commission may certify voting systems regardless 
of whether it has also received EAC approval.3 Wis. Stat. § 5.91. All base systems 
currently in use in Wisconsin currently do have EAC approval. The Help America 
Vote Act (HAVA) sets specific requirements for voting systems but does not 
require federal certification by the EAC.
In order to achieve federal certification, a voting 
equipment manufacturer must:
1. Apply to the EAC for testing and certification of the voting system.
2. Submit the equipment to a Voting System Test Laboratory (VSTL), which 
reviews and tests all firmware, software, and hardware. Following the 
rigorous test campaign, the VSTL issues a report to the EAC.
3. Receive an EAC-accredited certification number. The EAC issues 
certification numbers after reviewing the VSTL reports and confirming that 
the voting equipment conforms to the Voluntary Voting System Guidelines 
established by the EAC.
3 The law was amended in 2016 in direct response to how the EAC struggled to keep up with certifying 
new election equipment. New voting systems were becoming available, but the Commission’s 
predecessor agency (the Government Accountability Board) was unable to certify them because it 
had to wait for EAC approval. The Legislature specifically amended the law so that the Commission 
is not beholden to the EAC for certifying new voting equipment systems. See LC Hearing Materials for 
SB295 on 10/13/2015.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 12
Sec. 9.3.4: Step Three: State 
Certification Application
In order to be granted Wisconsin state certification, 
a voting equipment manufacturer must:
1. Submit an application to the State of Wisconsin. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 7.01(1). 
A voting equipment manufacturer may apply to the State of Wisconsin if it 
has received federal certification. However, any voting system submitted for 
approval must be federally tested and meet all standards put forth by the 
EAC. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 7.01(1)(e).
2. Prepare the voting system for testing by Commission Staff in three mock 
elections.
3. The voting system must pass testing using election definitions from a 
General Election, Partisan Primary, and Presidential Preference Election. 
Each of the three elections contains a special contest. Wis. Stat. § 5.91, 
Wis. Admin. Code § EL 7.02(1).
4. Hold a public demonstration. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 7.02(1). A public 
demonstration isn’t specifically required, but the Commission chooses 
to make parts of its public test open to the public in an exercise of its 
discretion.
5. Submit equipment to the Voting Equipment Review Panel (VERP) for review. 
The VERP is a group of municipal clerks, county clerks, and representatives 
from advocacy groups who gather to review and offer feedback on voting 
systems being tested by the Commission. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 7.02(2).
6. Receive approval in a regularly scheduled meeting of the Wisconsin 
Elections Commission. This approval will permit the use of the voting 
system for any election in the State of Wisconsin. Wis. Stat. § 5.91.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 13
Sec. 9.3.5: Step Four: Commission 
Staff Review & Testing
Once a vendor submits an application for certification, Commission Staff 
review the system configuration documentation and perform functional 
testing of the equipment.
Review of Configuration Documentation
Staff examine all documentation and components submitted by the vendor 
in its application. Often, vendors seek certification due to modifications they 
have made to existing systems. Staff examine the components in detail to 
ensure that the proposed system complies with state and federal law. Staff also 
examine the VSTL testing report in detail to ensure that the system meets the 
EAC’s standards for acceptable voting equipment.
Voting Equipment Test Protocol
The voting system undergoes functional testing which requires all components 
of the system to correctly process three mock elections: the partisan primary, 
general election with both a presidential and gubernatorial vote, and presidential 
preference and spring election. These mock elections use offices, referenda 
questions, candidates, and a special contest provided by the Commission.
Staff create a test deck of 400 ballots for each election in accordance with 
a predetermined marking script. The test deck includes ballots that are 
intentionally over-voted, crossover-voted, left blank, torn, folded, and marked 
with ink of different colors as well as pencil. If the voting system includes a ballot 
marking device, ballots marked using the device are included in the test deck. 
Test decks were also marked to determine exactly what constitutes a readable 
mark by each piece of tabulation equipment in this voting system. A subset of 
ballots for each mock election includes atypical marks, such as partially filled 
ovals, X’s, and check marks.
Testing occurs in the Commission office. The marked ballots are processed, 
and the results must match the expected results from the test script. If errors 
are found, they are investigated, and it is determined whether they indicate 
a deficiency in the voting system. All testing discrepancies or aberrations 
are reported to the Commission and factor into their certification decision. If 
a discrepancy cannot be resolved and is indicative of a failure in the voting 
system’s ability to correctly tabulate votes, staff will make a recommendation to 
the Commission to not certify the equipment for use.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 14
The system components are also assessed to ensure compliance with 
Wis. Stat. § 5.91 and HAVA § 301(a).
To solicit valuable feedback from local election officials and community 
advocates, the Commission formed the Voting Equipment Review Panel (VERP). 
In accordance with Wis. Admin. Code § EL 7.02(2), this panel includes municipal 
and county clerks, representatives of the disability community, and other 
advocates for the interest of the voting public. Following the VERP a public 
demonstration is held with representatives of the vendor available to answer 
questions and guide attendees through the functionality of the equipment.
Telecommunications Test Protocol
Certain voting systems are capable of transmitting unofficial results from the 
polling place after polls close on Election Day via a secure modem. Vendors 
who offer this option typically submit two electronic voting systems for 
certification: the underlying, or base, system without the modem components 
and the system that includes the modem components, sometimes called the 
modem-capable system. The Commission reviews and certifies the entire 
voting system, including all of its hardware and software, and does not approve 
specific, individual components.
To test the ability of these systems to accurately and reliably transmit these 
unofficial results, the Commission approved a Telecommunications Testing 
Protocol. These protocols were first developed by the Government Accountability 
Board in 2013, and they were recently revised by the Commission in 2021.
The purpose of the Telecommunications Protocols is to ensure that the 
modem-capable system is tested by Commission Staff and reviewed for 
access to election data, security, accuracy, data integrity, and reliability. The 
Telecommunications Protocols permit the Commission to request and rely 
upon testing of the modem-capable system that is performed by the federally 
certified VSTL to confirm that the modem components have been tested to the 
standards set by the EAC. The telecommunications testing conducted pursuant 
to the Telecommunications Protocols is in addition to the testing of the modem-
capable systems performed by the VSTL.
The Telecommunications Protocol testing is a two-step process. First, staff 
thoroughly review all submitted documentation including, but not limited to, 
EAC and/or VSTL report(s), technical system schematics, telecommunications 
specifications (including network diagrams), system security protocols, and any 
other documents submitted with the vendor’s application. Second, staff conduct 
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 15
testing to ensure that the voting system can successfully and securely transmit 
unofficial test results packages according to system specifications. In determining 
whether the objectives of the system testing have been achieved, staff rely both on 
the review of system documentation as well as the test results themselves.
Sec. 9.3.6: Step Five: Commission 
Review & Certification
After staff have completed review of the voting system, including testing, the 
Commission considers the certification request in a meeting that is open to 
the public. Commissioners have the option of receiving a demonstration of the 
voting system and also review the detailed certification report prepared by staff. 
The vendor usually attends the certification meeting to answer any questions 
directly from Commissioners. The Commission then votes on whether to certify 
the system for use in Wisconsin.
Sec. 9.3.7: Step Six: Certification 
& Approval Letter
If the Commission votes to certify the system for use in Wisconsin, the 
vendor receives an approval letter which lists the terms of the approval. As 
part of the approval, the vendor agrees to pay the costs the Commission 
incurred in testing the system and agrees to place copies of their programs, 
documentation, and source code in escrow.
Sec. 9.3.8: Approved Voting 
Equipment Vendors
The following is a list of all manufacturers of voting equipment 
currently approved for use in the State of Wisconsin:
 Ɋ Clear Ballot Group
 Ɋ Liberty Vote (formerly Dominion 
Voting Systems)
 Ɋ Election Systems & Software 
(ES&S)
 Ɋ Hart InterCivic
Detailed information on each voting system certified for use in Wisconsin can 
be found at elections.wi.gov.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 16
Chapter 9.4: Pre-Election 
Electronic Voting Equipment 
Testing
Sec. 9.4.1: Introduction
Wisconsin statutes require that all municipalities test voting equipment for 
accuracy prior to every election. The purpose of testing electronic voting 
equipment is to ensure that the equipment will correctly tabulate votes for all 
offices and referenda. Wis. Stat. § 5.84(1).
Sec. 9.4.2: What Equipment is Tested?
Each individual tabulator must be tested as part of the pre-election electronic 
voting equipment testing. Id. In other words, if a municipality has seven DS-
200 tabulators it plans to use at an upcoming election, it must test all seven 
of them. It is not sufficient to just test one DS-200 and assume the others will 
work. State law requires that municipalities test “the equipment,” which refers to 
the equipment that will be used during an election. If more than one tabulator 
is used, then “equipment” comprises more than one tabulator. A test of only 
one tabulator when more than one tabulator will be used is not a test of “the 
equipment” used during an election.4
Sec. 9.4.3: Public Notice
The testing of electronic voting equipment, either DRE or optical scan 
equipment, shall be open to the public. Id.
The test may not be conducted more than ten days before Election Day.
Public notice of the time and location of the testing shall be given by the clerk at 
least 48 hours before the test is to take place.
4 This interpretation of law was addressed and decided by the Commission in the matter of Nedvidek 
v. Nelson et al. (EL 24-120).
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 17
Best Practice: If there are issues in the timing or posting 
of the public notice, the Commission recommends 
that the municipal clerk re-notice a new public test 
correctly and then re-test the voting equipment.
Sec. 9.4.4: Procedure
To conduct a pre-election test for accuracy, the municipal clerk must create 
a group of test ballots, often called a test deck.5 Wis. Stat. § 5.84(1). A test deck 
contains a predetermined number of valid votes for each candidate and 
referendum. While there is no requirement for the number of ballots to be 
included in the test deck, the Commission recommends testing as many vote 
combinations as possible, as detailed below. The test deck must reflect all 
of the required testing components described in this section for optical scan 
equipment, direct recording electronic equipment, and ballot marking devices.
Optical Scan Equipment
Ballots should be marked to reflect a pre-determined number of valid votes for 
each candidate and referendum. The totals for candidates should be different, 
so clerks can verify the equipment’s tabulation accuracy.
Pre-marked ballots shall be run through the optical scan voting unit.
The tabulation totals from the results tape for the pre-marked ballots are then 
compared to the pre-determined number to verify the voting equipment is 
tabulating properly.
Best Practice: If clerks normally transmit results on Election Day, 
they should contact the county before the public test to verify 
whether performing a test transmission is feasible as well.
5 The statute uses the term “preaudited group of ballots,” but all of these terms are exchangeable. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 18
Direct Recording Electronic (DRE) Equipment
Votes should be cast on the DRE unit in a manner reflecting a pre-determined 
number of valid votes for each candidate and referendum. The totals for candidates 
should be different, so clerks can verify the equipment’s tabulation accuracy.
The printout after the tabulation of the votes cast will then be compared to the 
pre-determined number to verify the voting equipment is tabulating properly.
Best Practice: At least two individuals should participate 
in the DRE test to ensure votes selected on the test 
deck are entered correctly in the voting system.
Ballot Marking Devices (BMDs)
Any test deck created for the purposes of testing optical scan voting equipment 
must also contain ballots printed from the municipality’s ballot marking device, 
where applicable. BMD ballots should be run through the tabulation equipment 
along with ballots marked by hand.
Best Practice: The public test is an excellent opportunity 
for clerks and poll workers to familiarize themselves with 
the BMDs, including accessible features like audio, that 
will be present at their polling places on Election Day.
Ballot marking devices approved for use in Wisconsin:
 Ɋ AutoMark
 Ɋ Clear Access
 Ɋ ExpressVote
 Ɋ ImageCast Evolution
Errorless Count Requirement
If an error is detected during the testing, the municipal clerk shall determine the 
cause and correct the error. Id.
The clerk must make an errorless count before the electronic tabulating 
equipment is approved by the clerk for use in the election. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 19
Note: The Commission recommends that municipal clerks formulate a 
test deck that is unique to the municipality and refrain from using test 
decks provided by the manufacturer/programmer. This is to ensure 
any errors not discovered by the programmer will be uncovered by the 
clerk during the test.
Sec. 9.4.5: Testing Protocol
When testing voting equipment prior to every election, each candidate for 
every office, for every party, as well as every referendum needs to be tested. 
Id.. Please refer to the following information for a breakdown of specific testing 
requirements. For questions related to programming, clerks should contact 
their vendor or the county if the county programs equipment at their office. 
Questions on testing protocol and requirements can be addressed to the 
Commission Staff.
State law requires clerks to generally test that the equipment will correctly count 
the votes cast for all offices and on all measures and specifically requires that 
clerks test for overvotes and crossover votes. Id.
Overvotes
Overvotes are votes in excess of the number allowed by law, such as a candidate 
voting for two candidates on a “vote for one” contest. Test decks must include 
overvotes for every office and referendum on the ballot. Id.
Voting equipment must be programmed to automatically reject ballots with 
overvotes. Wis. Stat. § 5.91(7).
Crossover Votes
Crossover votes are votes that cross party lines in an election where doing so is 
strictly prohibited, e.g. the Presidential Preference and Partisan Primary.
When creating a test deck for these specific elections, clerks must include 
crossover votes on the ballots to be tested. Wis. Stat. § 5.84(1).
Crossover votes for every party and every candidate should be included in the 
pre-election test.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 20
At the Partisan Primary especially, clerks should take care to test all possible 
tabulating logic of votes for each particular ballot type. For detailed scenarios 
on crossovers and tabulating logic during the Partisan Primary, see Chapter 
14.20: “Counting Votes.”
Blank Ballots
Blank ballots are ballots that have no votes recorded.
A blank ballot should be included in every test deck to ensure that they are 
rejected by the voting equipment. A message to notify the voter that no votes 
have been recorded promptly follows ballot rejection.
Write-in votes
On DRE equipment, the write-in function for each office is to be tested to ensure 
that it is functioning properly and recording choices written in by voters.
On optical scan voting equipment, it should be tested with ballots containing 
write-in votes in the test deck. The tabulated results must confirm a correct 
write-in vote count. For optical scan equipment with a write-in diversion bin, the 
write-in report also serves to determine that ballots containing write-in votes for 
each office are properly separated into the write-in bin.
Partisan Primary
The clerk shall test for one or more ballots that have votes cast for a candidate 
of more than one recognized party, and verify these are rejected. See the 
information above related to crossover votes.
Sec. 9.4.6: Securing the Tabulators 
Following the Public Test
After the clerk has confirmed an errorless count for each piece of equipment, 
the clerk should take steps to secure the equipment prior to Election Day. See 
Wis. Stat. § 7.25(4).
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 21
Best Practices: The memory device should remain in the equipment 
with a tamper-evident seal used to secure memory device 
compartments. A chain-of-custody log should to be maintained 
that documents any access to each memory device or tabulator. 
Verification of the serial numbers must take place before the polls 
open in the morning and after the close of polls. Wis. Stat. § 7.25(6).
Sec. 9.4.7: Election Day Zero-
Count Requirement
On Election Day, before any ballots have been cast on the electronic voting 
equipment, and prior to the opening of polls, election officials shall witness a 
test of the tabulator by securing a printed results “zero tape” showing a zero 
count for every candidate and referendum. Wis. Stat. § 5.84(2), 7.25(6).
The zeroing of the tabulator is a public event that is open to observers. The 
designated election official should be ready to receive members of the public 
wishing to check in as observers at least 10 minutes before any voting activity 
starts so that observers intending to see the zeroing of any tabulators may 
see this event. Wis. Stat. § EL 4.05(1)(a). For more information on observers and 
observer management, see Chapter 14.5: “Election Observers.”
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 22
Chapter 9.5: Security 
Procedures for Electronic 
Voting Systems (EVS)
Sec. 9.5.1: Introduction
The Commission has developed a series of security procedures for electronic 
voting systems that comply with state law and ensure that voting is safe, 
secure, efficient, and accurate. See Wis. Stat. § 5.91(10). These procedures should 
be followed for each election, recount, or referenda. These procedures apply to 
all memory devices, including programmable memory packs, memory cards, 
USB memory sticks, and any other removable memory devices that can be 
programmed or that function to store and transfer ballot images or tabulation 
data. These procedures are intended to protect against malicious breaches to 
electronic voting equipment components as well as provide transparency of 
proper access.
A video tutorial on voting equipment testing and security is posted on the 
ElectEd website.
Following the procedures in this chapter ensures that the legal requirements for 
security are met, as well as ensuring that the security procedures of the voting 
equipment itself are correctly followed.
Sec. 9.5.2: Overview of Legal 
Requirements for Secure 
Electronic Voting Systems
State law provides a general framework for electronic voting system security. 
When preparing electronic voting systems for elections, clerks are required 
to “arrange the machine and ballot so both will meet all the requirements 
for voting and counting the election in the manner provided for in machine 
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 23
construction.” Wis. Stat. § 7.25(3). This means that all voting equipment must be 
configured according to how it was certified by the Commission, including all 
security features and procedures.
Once voting equipment arrives at the polling place, state law requires it to be 
“locked and sealed against any movement,” and each municipality must “provide 
proper protection to prevent tampering with the machines.” Wis. Stat. § 7.25(4). 
The custodians who deliver the equipment must return the keys to the clerk with a 
written report of each machine’s condition. Id.
Before opening the polls on Election Day, poll workers are required to “examine 
the seal on each machine to see that the seal has not been broken.” 
Wis. Stat. § 7.25(6)(b)1.b. These seals are placed on the machines after the 
conclusion of the public test of the voting equipment. Wis. Stat. § 5.84.
After the polls close, “as soon as the count is complete and fully recorded, the 
[election] inspectors shall seal, close and lock the machine, or remove the 
record so it cannot be voted on or tampered with.” Wis. Stat. § 7.51(3)(c).
Sec. 9.5.3: General Electronic Voting 
System Security Procedures
Throughout the life of the electronic voting system, the municipal or county clerk 
maintains control of all memory devices and keys to the voting systems. Access 
to voting equipment should be strictly controlled and granted in a secure 
manner at all times. Document authorized access to secured components by 
election officials. This documentation serves as a chain of custody showing who 
has accessed the voting equipment outside of Election Day, when, and why. 
The EL-104 can be used for this purpose, or clerks can draft their own forms to 
document this information.
For each election, there should be a separate, written chain-of-custody record 
for every programmed memory device. All memory devices used with an 
electronic voting system have a unique and permanent serial number. Each 
transfer of the memory device should be logged in the written chain-of-custody 
record. Information collected should include name(s), date of access, reason, 
time access keys were taken, and time access keys were returned.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 24
For each election, the municipal clerk should record on the Inspectors’ 
Statement (EL-104), which memory devices and which serialized tamper-evident 
seals are assigned to particular voting stations or units.
Sec. 9.5.4: Election Day Procedures
Before any ballots are cast on any voting system, the integrity of the tamper-
evident seals shall be verified by the Chief Inspector. Wis. Stat. § 7.25(6)(b). This is 
done to confirm that the tamper-evident seal serial number on the Inspectors’ 
Statement (EL-104) matches the tamper-evident seal serial number placed 
on the electronic voting equipment. Once the polls have opened, the Chief 
Inspector should perform the same verifications at regular intervals and record 
the time and outcome of the additional seal checks on the EL-104.
Best Practice: If a polling place operates in shifts for workers, 
change of shifts is a good time for this. After the close of polls, the 
chief inspector should conduct a final inspection of the voting 
equipment seals, noting the results in the inspectors’ statement.
After the polls have officially closed at 8:00 p.m., election officials follow the 
proper end-of-night procedures for the voting equipment. Wis. Stat. § 7.25(3). 
Election officials should then print a results report prior to breaking the seal 
specific to the compartment housing the memory device on the tabulator and 
before the removal of the memory device from any piece of voting equipment.
Following the printing of the results report, the memory device shall be secured in 
a separate, tamper-evident sealed container or envelope by the Chief Inspector. 
Alternatively, the device may remain sealed in the voting system. Wis. Stat. § 7.51(3)(c).
Sec. 9.5.5: Overview of Legal 
Requirements for Securing Ballots
Official ballots are ordered by each county clerk, who is then required to 
enclose them in a sealed package to be delivered to the municipal clerk. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.10(1)(b). The county clerk separately wraps an adequate supply 
of ballots to be used as absentee ballots and then sends separately sealed 
packages clearly designating the ward for which each is intended and the 
approximate number of ballots of each kind enclosed. Wis. Stat. § 7.10(3)(b).
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 25
After voting concludes on Election Day, and after the local board of canvassers 
canvass the results, voted ballots are secured together so that they cannot 
be untied or tampered with without breaking the seal. Wis. Stat. § 7.51(3)(a). 
The Chief Inspector and one other inspector of the opposite party affiliation 
then secure the ballots in the ballot container in such a manner that the 
container cannot be opened without breaking the seals or locks or destroying 
the container. Id. Provisional ballots are secured in a separate, securely sealed 
carrier envelope. Id. All ballots are then delivered back to the municipal clerk. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.51(3)(d). For more detailed end-of-night procedures, see Chapter 
14.24: “Closing the Polls, LBOC, & End of Night Process.”
Ballots counted by the board of absentee ballot canvassers (sometimes referred 
to as “central count”) follow similar ballot security statutes at the conclusion of 
counting all absentee ballots on Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 7.52(4)(g).
Best Practice: A ballot container shall be considered 
“sealed” or “locked” only if no voted ballot may be removed 
from or deposited into the container, and no other form of 
access to the ballots inside may be gained without leaving 
evidence of that entry or access into the container.
Ballot bags should be sealed with a tamper-evident seal on which a serial 
number should be printed. The serial number should be recorded on the signed 
Ballot Container Certification (EL-101) attached to the bag. Serial numbers of the 
seals should also be recorded on the Inspectors’ Statement (EL-104).
Sec. 9.5.6: Best Practices for Secure 
Storage of Voting Equipment
The need for proper voting equipment security does not stop at the end of 
election day. Once the polls have closed, municipal and county election officials 
must ensure that the voting equipment used in their jurisdiction is stored securely 
until the next election. This means more must be done than simply putting the 
equipment out of the way somewhere in the clerk’s office. The Commission 
recommends placing voting equipment in a locked and secured area within the 
clerk’s office that is only accessible by the clerk or another authorized individual. 
Voting equipment can be stored in the municipal clerk’s office, the office of the 
county clerk, or at an agreed-upon and secure third location.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 26
Chapter 9.6: Post-Election 
Audit
Sec. 9.6.1: Introduction
Wisconsin statutes require a post-election audit of the performance of each 
voting system used in the state of Wisconsin. Wis. Stat. § 7.08(6).6 The audit is 
designed to assess how electronic voting systems performed on Election Day 
through a hand-count of electronically tallied ballots. The audit is required 
following each General Election. However, nothing in these procedures prevents 
a municipality or county from conducting an audit after other elections or from 
auditing a larger number of voting machines or reporting units than those 
selected by the Commission or required under these procedures.
The purpose of the post-election audit is to determine the error rate (if any) of 
voting systems in counting ballots.
Note: Wisconsin law directs the Commission to prescribe how the 
audit will be conducted. For example, the Commission can choose the 
number of jurisdictions and other perimeters of the audit. Therefore, 
the exact mechanics of the audit will vary for each General Election. 
If a municipality has been selected for a post-election audit, the 
procedures most recently adopted by the Commission supersede the 
guidance in this chapter if there is a conflict or ambiguity.
Those instructions additionally contain much more detail than this chapter 
and should be relied upon as the primary resource for conducting the post-
election audit.
6 This provision of state law was enacted pursuant to § 301(a)(5) of the Help America Vote Act (“HAVA”). 
52 U.S.C. § 21081(a)(5).
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 27
Sec. 9.6.2: What if There’s a Recount?
Clerks should not begin the post-election audit until it is known whether there 
will be a recount for any of the contests selected. In the event of a recount 
following a general election, the Commission will provide guidance on how to 
proceed with the post-election audit.
Sec. 9.6.3: Which Reporting 
Units Will be Audited?
State law requires municipalities and counties to comply with the post-election 
audit if selected. Wis. Stat. § 7.08(6). The specific procedures for how the 
Commission runs the post-election audit are not specifically set by statute, but 
the Commission has established a consistent practice for which municipalities 
are selected to participate and how the audit should be performed.7
That being said, the Commission reviews its post-election audit procedures and 
practices for each General Election; for each audit, the Commission will determine 
how many pieces of voting equipment of each type should be selected for the 
audit. Likewise, the Commission has also, historically, selected the minimum 
number of reporting units from each of the 72 counties that should be selected.
For example, following the 2024 General Election, the Commission directed that 
the post-election audit be conducted according to the following procedures:
1. A certain percentage of statewide reporting units were randomly selected 
by the Commission, the Wednesday following the November general 
election. This was done as part of a publicly noticed meeting.
 ɉ At least five reporting units for each type or version of voting system 
used throughout the state were selected.
 Ɉ If five reporting units were not represented in the original selection, 
additional reporting units were selected until all types or versions 
are represented.
7 The State Elections Board (SEB) first discussed and passed standards relating to the post-election 
audit at the August 30, 2006, open session meeting after the law authorizing it went into effect on 
January 1, 2006. Extensive public comment on the topic was accepted and reviewed at this meeting. 
Current standards largely reflect those originally implemented by the SEB and have been periodically 
updated.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 28
 ɉ A minimum of one reporting unit from each of Wisconsin’s 72 counties 
was chosen. Additional reporting units were randomly chosen until one 
from each county was selected, if the original selection did not produce 
a sufficient representation of counties.
2. Four contests on the ballot were selected. The highest office on the 
ballot, president or governor, was selected automatically. The remaining 
three contests were drawn by lot from all other contests on every ballot 
statewide. An exception was been made for the office of State Senate. 
While no more than half of the ballots statewide will ever contain the office 
of State Senator, the Commission determined that this office should be 
subject to audit.
Sec. 9.6.4: How are Selected 
Clerks Notified?
1. Municipalities with reporting units selected for audit will be notified the 
day following the election.
 ɉ County clerks will also be notified.
 ɉ It is the responsibility of the municipal clerk to make arrangements with 
the county to access election materials for the purpose of the audit 
following the county canvass. Materials needed for conducting the 
audit include voter lists, inspectors’ statement(s), tally sheets, reports 
printed or generated by the voting systems, ballots, and any other 
required materials.
2. The municipal clerk and county clerk may choose to have the county 
conduct the audit, and the county may choose to conduct the audit 
following the county canvass.
3. The deadline for when the audit must be completed is set by the 
Commission. Municipalities may request an extension for cause. 
Commission Staff will review all extension requests for possible approval 
on a case-by-case basis.
4. The audit is considered a public meeting and proper notice shall be 
posted or published at least 48 hours in advance. A sample notice can be 
found on elections.wi.gov, and is also shared by the Commission ahead of 
each audit.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 29
Sec. 9.6.5: Procedure for 
Conducting the Audit
A list of procedures, instructions, and documentation forms are provided to 
municipalities selected for audit at the time of notification.
Generally, the procedure for conducting a post-election audit is as follows:
1. Two individuals shall conduct independent counts of the ballots from the 
voting system. The individuals need not be poll workers and can include 
the municipal clerk and anyone they choose to assist. Note that for direct 
recording electronic systems, the official ballots are the voter-verified 
paper audit trail.
2. Auditors should only count votes as the equipment would have counted 
them.8 Voter intent is not a factor. Auditors should document in the 
minutes any ballots where it is unclear how the voting system would count 
the ballot. The auditors should include in the minutes how they counted 
the ballot as well as all reasonable alternatives on how the machine may 
have counted the ballot.
 ɉ Example 1: A voter circled candidate named Jane Doe on the optical 
scan ballot where they should have filled in the oval next to the 
candidate’s name. No vote for this office should be counted as the 
voting equipment would not have counted a vote cast for a candidate 
in this manner.
 ɉ Example 2: A voter wrote in a candidate name on an optical scan ballot 
and did not fill in the oval next to the write-in line. The voting equipment 
would not have identified this as a write-in vote on the results tape. So, 
it should not be included in the write-in totals for purposes of the audit.
8 See 52 U.S.C. § 21081(a)(5) (HAVA provision stating that the error rate that is calculated by the post-
election audit is “determined by taking into account only those errors which are attributable to the 
voting system and not attributable to an act of the voter”).
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 30
 ɉ Example 3: A voter marked both Jane Doe and John Smith and 
attempted to erase the mark for John Smith. This can be counted as 
a vote for Jane Doe, but the machine may have read it as an overvote 
in the contest. Pay close attention and count such ballots as auditors 
feel the machine would have counted them. Counting this as a vote for 
Jane Doe may result in the tally having one more vote for Jane Doe and 
one less undervote in this contest.
 ɉ Example 4: While considering their choices, a voter rested their pen on 
the edge of the oval for John Wayne. This left a small mark inside the 
oval. The voter then fully filled in the oval next to Jesse James’ name in 
the same contest. Auditors may not know if the mark at the edge of the 
oval next to John Wayne was big enough to be counted as an overvote 
by the voting equipment. As a result, the manner in which this vote is 
tallied in the audit should be noted in the minutes.
3. The individual tallies shall be compared to each other, and any 
discrepancies shall be resolved to an agreed upon final hand-count tally 
total. If the hand counts differ from each other, the paper records/ballots 
must be recounted. Make sure all compartments of the voting equipment 
are checked for tabulated ballots.
4. The final hand-count tally total shall then be compared to the Election 
Night results tally tape and discrepancies noted (i.e. +2, −1), if any. It may 
be possible that the auditors’ totals do not match the voting equipment 
results report, but the auditors should be able to reasonably explain any 
difference in totals by reference to specific ballots. Should there be a 
discrepancy that is not reasonably explained, the auditors may need to 
reconvene to confirm their count.
5. Note any errors encountered and separate them into those caused by 
tabulator error and those caused by election administration, auditor, or 
other human error.
6. Each municipality conducting an audit must submit the designated 
reporting form(s) and supporting documents from the audit, including 
tally sheets, to the Commission to indicate that the audit was completed 
and whether any discrepancies were found.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 31
7. Commission Staff will request that the vendor investigate and explain the 
reasons for any unexplained differences between the voting equipment 
tally and the paper record tally.
 ɉ Should the vendor fail to provide a sufficient written explanation, 
including recommendations for preventing future occurrences, within 
30 days of notification, the Commission will revoke certification of all 
voting systems manufactured or serviced by the vendor in Wisconsin. 
See Wis. Stat. § 5.91 (failure to respond to post-election audit could 
constitute cause for the revocation of certification).
 ɉ This revocation will be implemented immediately, pending an 
appeal by the manufacturer to the Commission, which must be filed 
within 30 days.
 ɉ Investigations of discrepancies shall be open and transparent, with 
active involvement of interested parties.
Sec. 9.6.6: Additional Resources
Sample audit notices, audit instructions and procedures, tally sheets, audit 
reporting forms, audit reimbursement forms, and the full audit selection list for 
the most recent audit are maintained on elections.wi.gov.
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 32
Chapter 9.7: Frequently Asked 
Questions
Q What is a voter-verified paper audit trail?
A Wisconsin Stat. § 5.91(18) requires that all direct recording electronic (DRE) 
voting systems produce a complete, permanent paper record showing 
all votes cast by the voter. This is the ballot receipt that is generated when 
each voter uses the machine. The voter-verified paper audit trail (VVPAT) 
is considered the official ballot and is to be used in a recount of each vote 
cast by the voter.
Q Who pays for the purchase of voting equipment?
A Municipal clerks are responsible for the purchase and maintenance of 
voting equipment. Wis. Stat. § 7.15(1)(b). In some situations, an arrangement 
is reached between the county and the municipality to share the cost of 
the equipment. Municipal and county clerks should discuss purchasing/
maintenance options.
Q Who is responsible for storing equipment after an election?
A Either the municipal or county clerk must store the voting equipment in a 
locked and secured location. Wis. Stat. § 7.21(5).
Voting equipment can be stored in the municipal clerk’s office, the 
office of the county clerk, or at an agreed upon, and secure, third 
location. Id.
Q What should be done with the zero tape while voting occurs on Election Day?
A The zero tape should be left attached to the results tape, then folded and 
attached to the tabulator in the most secure manner possible.
Q Can clerks reuse removable memory media?
A Nothing prohibits reuse of removable memory media, though 
municipalities must comply with Wis. Stat. § 7.23(g), 7.23(2).
First Edition, June 2026 Voting Equipment 9 – 33
Wis. Stat. § 7.23(g)
“Detachable recording units and compartments for use with tabulating 
equipment for an electronic voting system may be cleared or erased 
14 days after any primary and 21 days after any other election. Before 
clearing or erasing the units or compartments, a municipal clerk shall 
transfer the data contained in the units or compartments to a disk or 
other recording medium which may be erased or destroyed 22 months 
after the election to which the data relates. The requirement to transfer 
data does not apply to units or compartments for use with tabulating 
equipment for an electronic voting system that was approved for use 
prior to January 1, 2009, and that is not used in a federal election.
Wis. Stat. § 7.23(2) 
If a recount is pending or if the time allowed for filing a recount 
petition at any election or an appeal or petition for review of any

the applicable time period has expired. In addition, if there is litigation 
pending with respect to a recount at an election, materials may be 
destroyed and recording units or compartments may be cleared or

petition of the attorney general or a district attorney or U.S. attorney 
for the affected jurisdiction, a circuit judge for the affected jurisdiction 
may order that specified materials not be destroyed or that specified 
recorders, units or compartments not be cleared or erased as 
otherwise authorized under this subsection until the court so permits.”

Part 10 
Introduction to Badger Books
Electronic poll books; history; how they work; 
Badger Books are the Commission’s certified electronic poll books. They are the 
only electronic poll books currently certified for use in Wisconsin.
First Edition, June 2026 Introduction to Badger Books 10 – 1
Chapter 10.1: Introduction
The “Badger Book” is an electronic poll book (e-poll book) tailor-made 
for Wisconsin election practices and statutes. The Badger Book is the only 
electronic poll book software created with direct WisVote integration and is the 
only electronic poll book currently authorized for use in Wisconsin.
Chapter 10.2: History of 
Badger Books
Electronic poll books are expressly authorized by state law. Wis. Stat. § 6.79(1m). Any 
electronic poll book must be approved by the Commission. Id. In 2017, Wisconsin 
Elections Commission staff started developing an electronic poll book to be used in 
polling places on Election Day.
Electronic poll books were initially considered by the Government Accountability 
Board (GAB) in 2013 after some municipal clerks first inquired about their use. 
In 2014 and 2015, GAB staff prepared detailed research on electronic poll books, 
including two surveys of clerks and their interest. The GAB explored standards 
for approval of electronic poll books and authorized a cost-benefit analysis for 
both vendor electronic poll books and in-house development. Commission staff 
revitalized the topic in 2017, and on June 20, 2017, the Commission unanimously 
authorized staff to begin building and implementing an electronic poll book 
solution that is compatible with WisVote. Badger Books were used for the first 
time in the August 2018 Partisan Primary in eight municipalities.
First Edition, June 2026 Introduction to Badger Books 10 – 2
Chapter 10.3: How Do Badger 
Books Work?
Badger Books replace the paper poll books in a polling place. Just as paper poll 
books are generated by WisVote, the data used by Badger Books comes from a 
file exported from WisVote. Instead of using paper, the municipality downloads a 
file ahead of Election Day. On Election Day, the Badger Books are used to record 
in-person participation, absentee participation, and information from Election 
Day Registrations (EDR). After Election Day, participation data and EDR data are 
taken from the Badger Book and uploaded into WisVote.
The Badger Book is primarily used to check in voters, register voters on Election 
Day, and process absentee ballots. The Badger Book maintains the voter 
number and counts independent of poll worker input. Each process was chosen 
and designed based on feedback provided by clerks and poll workers from 
across the state. After Election Day, a data file generated from the Badger 
Book is used to upload election participation and Election Day Registration 
information into WisVote. Badger Books do not use an internet connection.
One Badger Book station includes the main terminal computer with a touch 
screen for electronic signature capture, a wireless mouse, a wireless keyboard, 
a barcode scanner, a case of printer paper, and a printer that can either 
be integrated into the terminal base column or as a stand-alone printer. 
Additionally, a separate router and USB device must be purchased for each 
polling place. The router facilitates communication locally between the Badger 
Book machines. The USB device is used to transfer data between an internet-
connected computer to the Badger Book server machine.
First Edition, June 2026 Introduction to Badger Books 10 – 3
Badger Books CAN
 Ɋ Check in a registered voter
 Ɋ Record assistor information
 Ɋ Record curbside voters
 Ɋ Record voters who are unable to sign
 Ɋ Document typos in a name or 
address
 Ɋ Check in a confidential voter
 Ɋ Provide redirection information 
for a registered Wisconsin voter 
who appears at the incorrect 
polling place 
 Ɋ Register a new voter
 Ɋ Update an existing voter’s name 
or address
 Ɋ Register a voter at an address 
that does not yet exist in WisVote
 Ɋ Process absentee ballots
Badger Books CANNOT

ineligible voter list

(EL-104)
