 Ɋ Create or track challenged ballots
 Ɋ Automatically determine a 
voter’s districts when a new 
address is added
This section is intended to familiarize clerks and poll workers with Badger Books. 
It is not a substitute for the Badger Book user manual or hands-on Badger Book 
training. Municipalities interested in Badger Books should contact the Wisconsin 
Elections Commission.
For more information on how the Badger Book is used on Election Day, see 
Chapter 14.9 “Voting Procedure.”
First Edition, June 2026 Introduction to Badger Books 10 – 4
Chapter 10.4: Pros & Cons of 
Badger Books
Pros
 Ɋ Faster voter check-ins and registrations.
 Ɋ Process absentees easily.
 Ɋ Improve polling place flow.
 Ɋ No more splitting poll books, each Badger Book has the entire poll book.
 Ɋ Reduce poll worker mistakes; Badger Book helps with reminders and 
process checks.
 Ɋ Require fewer poll workers.
 Ɋ Streamline post-election data entry and reconciliation.
 Ɋ Voters will be able to view their participation sooner in MyVote.
Cons
 Ɋ Cost: Badger Books are expensive to purchase, must be maintained, can 
break, and eventually require replacement.
 Ɋ Training: The commission’s staff developed the Badger Book application 
to be user friendly; however, staff recommend that poll workers 
possess basic computer skills. Consider assigning poll workers that 
have enhanced skills, especially typing skills, to focus on Election Day 
Registrations. Moreover, each polling place using Badger Books should 
have at least one person with more advanced computer skills, including 
a basic understanding of networks and Windows operating systems. If a 
municipality has dedicated IT staff, they should be involved in the entire 
procurement, training, and implementation process.
 Ɋ Storage: Each stand-alone Badger Book device will be delivered in a 
box that is 26 in x 20 in x 12 in. Each integrated Badger Book device will be 
delivered in a box that is 17.5 in x 20 in x 12 in. In addition, there will be some 
smaller boxes delivered with accessories. The secure, year-round storage 
of the equipment must be considered.
First Edition, June 2026 Introduction to Badger Books 10 – 5
Chapter 10.5: Frequently 
Asked Questions
Q Does a polling place need internet to use Badger Books?
A No. Badger books are never connected to the internet. Badger Books 
communicate via a wireless router, but only within the polling place and 
never outside the polling place. They can also be connected with wires 
(called hardwiring) if necessary. This may be a good option if you have a 
polling place in a multi-use space, such as a fire station, or if you are in 
the basement of an old building. Reach out to the Commission’s Badger 
Book team if you are considering hardwiring your Badger Books.
Q How is voter information protected?
A Like a paper poll book, only the data necessary to run an election is 
included, so no Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is accessible. Voter 
and participation data are encrypted on the device. Each Badger Book is 
password protected, and each poll worker has their own user credentials 
to log in to the application
Q Are the Badger Books connected to the voting equipment?
A No. The Badger Books have no ability to connect to the electronic voting 
equipment. They do not, and cannot, record how a person votes.
Q Do municipalities have to use Badger Books?
A No. Badger Books are an optional resource that can aid in more efficient 
election administration, but nothing compels their use. Each municipality 
decides for itself whether to purchase and use Badger Books.
Q What about other E-Poll Book options?
A There are several commercial E-Poll Book brands sold in the United States. 
None are approved for use in Wisconsin as of late 2025.
Q How can I learn more about Badger Books?
A Contact the Wisconsin Elections Commission at elections@wi.gov.
First Edition, June 2026 Introduction to Badger Books 10 – 6


Part 11 
Accessibility
Voter Assistance; Accommodations; Polling Place Self-
Assessments; Polling Place Set Up; Accessibility Reviewers
Accessibility is a required component of the voting process. Accessible polling 
places ensure privacy and independence for all voters casting ballots. Voters 
with disabilities may need assistance with all aspects of voting, and the law 
guarantees that they receive that assistance. Polling places should be assessed 
carefully to ensure that they meet accessibility guidelines.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 1
Chapter 11.1: Introduction
Accessible polling places that ensure privacy and independence for all voters 
casting a ballot not only benefit voters with disabilities and older adults 
but are key to developing and maintaining public trust in the accessibility 
and transparency of the election process for all participants. Municipalities 
are responsible for ensuring that their polling places are accessible. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(a). The Commission understands “accessible” to mean in 
compliance with state elections statutes and federal laws like the Americans 
with Disabilities Act (ADA), Help America Vote Act (HAVA), and Voting Rights Act 
(VRA).
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 2
Chapter 11.2: Training Poll 
Workers: Accessibility
Poll workers should be instructed on how to ensure the greatest level of 
accessibility on Election Day. See Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(a). Municipal clerks should 
review polling place set-up requirements with poll workers. To ensure polling 
places are accessible, poll workers must be aware of all types of assistance and 
accommodation available to voters. Municipal clerks are encouraged to reach 
out to local disability rights organizations, such as the Disability Vote Coalition, 
to assist in training poll workers.
Poll workers should also know how to use the accessible voting equipment 
in their polling place and be able to instruct a voter on how to use it. See Id., 
Wis. Stat. § 7.37(8). Clerks may suggest that poll workers use the accessible 
equipment to cast their own ballots to learn firsthand how the equipment works.
Best Practice: The public test preceding Election Day is a good 
opportunity for poll workers to refresh their knowledge of the accessible 
voting equipment used in their polling place. See Wis. Stat. § 5.84(1).
Many poll workers have had little interaction with people with 
disabilities; here are a few courtesies and guidelines:
 Ɋ Remember that all voters deserve courteous attention in exercising their 
right as citizens to vote
 Ɋ Remember that not all disabilities are visible. Each individual knows their 
own abilities best. If an individual requests assistance, trust that it is 
necessary
 Ɋ There is no requirement for a voter to explain the nature of their 
disability or to provide proof of it before receiving assistance. See 
Wis. Stat. § 6.82(2)(a). Thus, poll workers should not inquire about the 
nature of a disability or ask for any sort of proof
 Ɋ Be considerate of the extra time it might take for a person with a disability 
or an elderly person to get things done
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 3
 Ɋ Animals that assist people with disabilities must be admitted into all 
buildings. Such animals are highly trained and need no special care other 
than that provided by the owner.
 Ɋ Greet a person who is visually impaired to let the person know who and 
where you are.
 Ɋ When offering walking assistance, allow the person to take your arm 
and tell them if you are approaching steps or inclines or are turning 
right or left.
 Ɋ If someone uses a mobility aid like a wheelchair, ask if they would like 
assistance. If they would like assistance, ask how you can assist them. Do 
not push their chair without their consent.
 Ɋ Speak directly to the person who has a disability rather than just to a 
companion who may be accompanying them.
 Ɋ Speak calmly, slowly, and directly to a person who is hard of hearing. Your 
facial expressions, gestures, and body movements help in understanding. 
Don’t shout or speak in the person’s ear. If full understanding is doubtful, 
try writing a note to the person.
 Ɋ Pre-printed signs or a notepad should be available to assist 
communication with deaf or hard-of-hearing voters.
 Ɋ Give unhurried attention to a person who has difficulty speaking.
 Ɋ Provide a guiding device such as a ruler or a signature guide for signing 
forms.
 Ɋ Anyone can help a voter fill out the information on a registration form, 
but if the voter needs assistance signing the form, the signature must 
be made by another voter and the “Assistant” section in box 10 must be 
completed. Wis. Stat. § 6.33(2)(a).
 Ɋ Voters with disabilities may be accompanied by a person of their choosing 
(except the voter’s employer or labor organization representative) and 
receive assistance in the voting booth. Wis. Stat. § 6.82(2)(a).
Best Practice: Poll workers should go through the Election Day 
Accessibility Checklist. See “Figure 19: Appendix 3” on page 40. 
developed by the Disability Vote Coalition before polls open.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 4
Chapter 11.3: Voter Assistance
Voters with disabilities have the right to receive assistance in completing the 
following tasks.
Sec. 11.3.1: Signing a Voter 
Registration Application
Q Who has the right to this assistance?
A Voters who are unable to sign a form due to a disability. Wis. Stat. § 6.33(2)(a).
Q Who can provide assistance?
A Any other voter authorized by the voter. Id.
Q How is assistance provided by another voter?
1. The assistant fills in the fields on the form at the direction of the voter.
2. The assistant signs the voter’s name in Section 9.
3. The assistant signs their own name in Section 10 and provides their address.
4. When an assistant signs the voter’s Registration Application by reason 
of the voter’s disability, the voter is exempt from signing the poll book 
when voting in person, and the poll workers should write “exempt” on the 
signature line. Wis. Stat. § 6.36(2)(a).
Sec. 11.3.2: Stating Name And 
Address at the Poll Book
Q Who has the right to this assistance?
A Voters who are unable to state their name and address. Wis. Stat. § 6.79(8).
Q Who can provide assistance?
A The poll worker at the poll book or another person the voter chooses. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 5
Q How is assistance provided?
1. The voter communicates to the poll worker that they are unable to state 
their name and address.
2. The poll worker verifies the voter’s photo ID. Wis. Stat. § 6.79(8).
3. The poll worker or an assistant states the voter’s name and address. Id.
4. The voter signs the poll book if able. Wis. Stat. § 6.79(2)(a).
Best Practice: The Commission has the optional form State Your Name 
and Address Card (EL-503) that a voter can use to facilitate receiving 
assistance. This card is not required to access this type of assistance. 
It is best practice to have copies of this card available to voters at the 
poll book table. Note that there is also a wallet-sized version of the 
State Your Name and Address Card (EL-503) that voters might bring 
to the polls with them. See “Figure 17: Appendix 1” on page 38.
Sec. 11.3.3: Signing the Poll Book
Voters who completed an election day registration, or who previously completed 
a registration, and had an assistant sign their name on the registration form are 
exempt from signing the poll book, and the poll workers must write “exempt” on 
the voter’s signature line. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.36(2)(a), 6.79(2)(a).
If the voter previously signed their registration form, or was exempt from 
registration, and is unable, due to physical disability, to sign the poll book, 
the poll workers must waive the signature requirement and enter “exempt by 
order of inspectors” on the voter’s signature line if the poll workers determine 
that the voter is unable to enter their signature due to physical disability. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.79(2)(am). If both officials do not waive the signature requirement, 
the official or officials must challenge the voter’s ballot for cause under Wis. 
Stat. §§ 6.92(1). Id. In the challenge, the voter may provide evidence of their 
physical disability to the board of canvassers. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 6
Note: Unless a poll worker has specific evidence available at the 
polling place that a voter is incorrectly asking for a waiver of the 
signature requirement, the poll workers should waive the requirement. 
Unless a poll worker would swear under oath that they know a voter 
is able to sign the poll book, and can articulate the specific reasons 
why the poll worker knows that to be the case, a voter should not be 
challenged. No evidence of any kind is required in order to ask for a 
waiver, and the challenge process can only be used if a poll worker 
has cause to believe that a voter is fraudulently attempting to attain a 
waiver of the signature requirement.
Best Practice: If a voter explains that they cannot sign the poll 
book due to a disability, the poll workers can ask if the voter had 
an assistant sign their voter registration form. If the voter says 
yes, write “exempt” on the voter’s signature line in the poll book, 
and if the voter says “no” or “I don’t know,” write “exempt by 
order of inspectors” on the voter’s signature line. No additional 
information of any kind needs to be provided by the voter.
Sec. 11.3.4: Marking a Ballot
Q Who has the right to this assistance?
A Voters who are unable to or have difficulty reading, writing, or 
understanding English and voters who are unable to mark a ballot 
or depress a button or lever on a voting machine due to disability. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.82(2)(a).
Q Who can provide assistance?
A Anyone of the voter’s choosing who is not the voter’s employer or an agent 
of that employer, or an officer or agent of a labor organization which 
represents the voter. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 7
Q How is assistance provided?
1. The voter explains to the poll workers that they need assistance to mark 
their ballot. Wis. Stat. § 6.82(2)(a).
2. The poll workers, if necessary, explain who can provide assistance and 
how it may be given. Id.
3. The poll workers enter the word “assisted” in the poll book after the name 
of the voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.82(2)(d).
4. Poll workers record the full name and address of the assistant in the poll 
book. Id.
Best practice: Enter the assistant’s name and address in 
the back of the poll book so that a person requesting ballot 
images and poll book images cannot use this information to 
identify a voter’s ballot. Please be aware that redaction may 
be necessary for public records releases in some cases, such 
as when there is only one voter who receives assistance.
1. The assistant goes into the voting booth with the voter. Wis. Stat. § 6.82(2)(b).
2. The assistant reads the names of all candidates on the ballot for each 
office and asks, “for which one do you vote?” Id.
3. The assistant marks the ballot or depresses the lever or button according 
to the voter’s expressed preference. Id.
4. The assistant cannot request, suggest, or seek to persuade a voter to vote 
for or against any candidate, party, or question. Wis. Stat. § 6.82(4).
5. The assistant cannot intentionally misinform the voter about what is 
printed on the ballot, intentionally fail to cast the ballot in accordance with 
the voter’s instructions, or disclose to any third person how the voter voted. 
Wis. Stat. § 12.13(3)(j). To do any of these things may be punishable as a 
Class I felony. Wis. Stat. § 12.60(1)(a).
6. The assistant signs the Certification of Voter Assistance on the ballot. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.82(2)(a).
7. If voting equipment is used, the assistant certifies on the registration list. 
Id.
Best Practice: At least one poll worker should be 
trained and ready to provide assistance marking a 
ballot to a voter who requests an assistant.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 8
Sec. 11.3.5: Returning an 
Absentee Ballot
Some voters with disabilities may select an assistant of their choice, who is 
not the voter’s employer or an agent of that employer or an officer or agent 
of a labor organization which represents the voter, to return their ballot to their 
polling place on election day. See Carey v. Wis. Elections Comm’n, 624 F. Supp. 
3d 1020 (W.D. WI 2022). See Part 7: “Absentee Voting” for a full description of the 
absentee voting process.
If a voter’s assistant returns the ballot to the polling place 
on election day, the poll workers should ask:
 Ɋ “Are you the voter?” If not, then:
 ɉ “Are you delivering the voter’s ballot because the voter has determined 
that they require assistance returning their ballot due to their 
disability?” If yes, then:
 Ɉ “Are you someone other than the voter’s employer, an agent of that 
employer, or an officer or agent of the voter’s union?” If yes, then the 
ballot can be accepted.
 Ɋ A poll worker does not need to confirm that a voter utilizing ballot 
return assistance is a voter who requires ballot return assistance due 
to a disability.
 Ɋ A poll worker does not need to confirm the disabled voter or assistant’s 
identity or otherwise request additional information.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 9
Chapter 11.4: Accommodations
Municipal clerks are required to make reasonable efforts to comply with 
requests for voting accommodations made by individuals with disabilities. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.36. The Commission cannot help a clerk determine whether 
a request for accommodation is reasonable. For more information see the 
Assistance and Accommodations webinar on ElectEd.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 10
Chapter 11.5: Polling Place 
Self-Assessments
Sec. 11.5.1: For New Polling Places
Polling places are established by a governing body at least 30 days before 
the election. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(2), (3)(a). For Commission staff to add new polling 
place to WisVote, clerks must submit a New Polling Place Self-Assessment 
(EL-501). The self-assessment is an abbreviated version of the survey used to 
evaluate polling places for accessibility on Election Day. It covers accessibility of 
permanent elements of the polling place with the understanding that when the 
self-assessment is conducted, the space is not set up the way it would be for 
Election Day. The self-assessment includes the Accessibility Supplies Order Form 
(EL-502) that clerks may use to receive free supplies to increase the accessibility 
of their polling places.
Sec. 11.5.2: For Changes to 
Existing Polling Places
If an existing polling place is renovated or the route voters take from the parking 
lot into the voting area is otherwise changed, the clerk should complete a New 
Polling Place Self-Assessment (EL-501) for the sections of the route that are 
different. For example, if the lobby of a building was renovated but the voting 
room and outdoor elements were not, only the Interior Route section of the self-
assessment would need to be completed.
Likewise, if the voting room in a polling place changes, the clerk should 
complete the Voting Area section of the self-assessment. If a change in voting 
room causes voters to use a different hallway, the Interior Route section needs 
to be completed too. When changing or adding a voting room, a new polling 
place record will be created in WisVote with the same name and address as the 
existing polling place but with a different voting room name. Clerks should take 
care to check the voting room field on a polling place record when creating an 
Election Plan in WisVote.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 11
Chapter 11.6: Accessibility 
Supply Program
The Accessibility Supply Program provides municipalities with free supplies 
to increase the accessibility of their polling places. View the Accessibility 
Supplies Order Form (EL-502) for a list of the products available. Instructions for 
submitting an order are on the order form.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 12
Chapter 11.7: Polling Place 
Set-Up
All eligible voters in the State of Wisconsin have the right to cast their ballot 
privately and independently on Election Day. Polling place accessibility begins 
in the parking area and continues along any route a voter with a disability 
would have to travel to gain access to the voting area. Polling places must 
comply with the ADA to ensure voters with disabilities are able to participate in 
the election process with minimal assistance. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(a), and see 42 
U.S.C. Ch. 126. The standards found in this chapter, except where noted, come 
from federal law and regulations under the ADA. Information specific to voting 
and polling places and more information about the polling place accessibility 
standards found below are available at ada.gov/topics/voting.
Figure 1: Accessible Polling Place Route
Image Courtesy of ADA.gov
Sec. 11.7.1: Curbside Voting
“Curbside voting” is voting that occurs outside of the polling place entrance. Each 
polling place must provide curbside voting for voters who are unable to enter 
the polling place due to disability. Wis. Stat. § 6.82(1)(a). There are many ways to 
set up curbside voting. If off-street parking is available, a parking space can be 
designated with a curbside voting sign that lists a phone number to text or call to 
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 13
let a poll worker know when a voter is there. When designating a parking space 
for curbside voting, it is important to leave the required number of accessible 
parking spaces closest to the accessible entrance available for voters going 
inside. Other methods to set up curbside voting include posting a sign in the 
parking area with a phone number or using a wireless doorbell on a sign in the 
parking area or at the entrance. Some polling places will station a greeter at the 
door to watch for curbside voters. See “Chapter 14.12: Curbside Voting.” 
Best Practice: If a phone number is provided for voters to call, 
and it can also receive texts, note that on the sign so D/deaf 
and hard of hearing voters can access curbside voting.
Signs and wireless doorbells are available through the Accessibility Supply Program.
Sec. 11.7.2: Parking Area
The required number of van-accessible and standard accessible parking 
spaces at a polling place is determined by the total number of parking spaces 
in the parking area, see the chart below. For more information on accessible 
parking areas see ada.gov/topics/parking.
Table 23: Accessible Parking Requirements
Total Number of 
Parking Spaces 
Provided
Minimum Van-
Accessible Parking 
Spaces
Minimum Standard 
Accessible Parking 
Spaces
1 – 25 1 0
26 – 50 1 1
51 – 75 1 2
76 – 100 1 3
101 – 150 1 4
151 – 200 1 5
201 – 300 2 5
Van-Accessible Parking
The ADA requires all off-street parking areas to have at least one van-
accessible parking space available.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 14
A van-accessible parking space must meet all the following criteria:
 Ɋ At least 96 in. wide.
 Ɋ Marked access aisle that is at least 96 in. wide.
 ɉ (Alternatively, the space can be 132 in. wide with a 60 in. access aisle. The 
total width of the parking space and access aisle must be at least 192 in.)
 Ɋ Sign with the international symbol of accessibility (ISA) and the words 
“van-accessible” posted at least 60 in. above the ground.
 Ɋ Vertical clearance of at least 98 in.
Figure 2: Van-Accessible Parking Sign
Image Courtesy of ADAChecklist.org
Standard Accessible Parking
In addition to van-accessible parking spaces, polling places may be required to 
have standard accessible parking spaces.
A standard accessible parking space must meet all the following criteria:
 Ɋ At least 96 in. wide.
 Ɋ Marked access aisle that is at least 60 in. wide.
 Ɋ Sign with the ISA posted at least 60 in. above the ground.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 15
Van-accessible and standard accessible parking spaces can share access aisles. 
All accessible parking spaces must be on level, firm, stable, and slip-resistant 
ground. Dirt, grass, sand, and gravel are not firm, stable, and slip-resistant. They 
must also be located on the shortest route to the accessible entrance.
Figure 3: Parking Spaces and Access Aisles
Best Practice: If a polling place does not have off-street parking, 
designate a street parking space for use by voters with disabilities.
Quick Fixes: Parking
Problem:  No accessible parking, not enough accessible parking, or the 
accessible parking does not meet all accessibility criteria.
Quick fix:
 Ɋ Create a temporary van-accessible parking space that meets all 
requirements.
 ɉ Signage: Post a sign with the with the words “van-accessible” and the 
ISA at least 60 in. above the ground.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 16
 ɉ Traffic cones: Block an adjacent parking space with traffic cones to 
create an access aisle.
 ɉ Ensure the space has 98 in. of vertical clearance.
 Ɋ Create a temporary standard accessible parking space that meets all 
requirements.
 ɉ Block an adjacent parking space with traffic cones to create an 
access aisle.
 ɉ Post a sign with the ISA at least 60 in. above the ground.
Figure 4: Temporary Accessible Parking Space
Van-accessible parking signs, standard accessible parking signs, and traffic 
cones are available through the Accessibility Supply Program individually and in 
the Temporary Accessible Parking Kits. Temporary signposts can be made using 
a 4x4 post, bucket, and bag of concrete mix.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 17
Sec. 11.7.3: Exterior Route
The exterior route is the route a voter would use to travel from the accessible 
parking area to the accessible entrance. In many cases, the accessible 
entrance is the main entrance to the facility, and all voters will follow the same 
path to reach that entrance. However, if the accessible entrance is not the 
same as the main entrance, large print signs must be used to direct voters with 
disabilities to the accessible entrance.
Figure 5: Accessible Entrance Sign
Accessible entrance signs with arrows pointing left or right are available 
through the Accessibility Supply Program.
An exterior route must meet all of the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ At least 36 in. wide, narrowing to no less than 32 in. for a maximum 
distance of 24 in.
 Ɋ Slope no greater than 5%.
 Ɋ Free of breaks or edges with a height difference greater than ½ in.
 Ɋ Firm, stable, and slip-resistant. Dirt, grass, sand, and gravel are not firm, 
stable, and slip-resistant.
 Ɋ Free of protrusions between 27 in. and 80 in. above the ground that extend more 
than 4 in. into the route. See “Figure 15: Signaling Obstacles” on page 30.
 Ɋ Kept clear of hazards like snow, ice, branches, leaves, or other debris.
Best Practice: Designate someone to keep the exterior route clear if 
snow or other hazards are expected to accumulate on Election Day.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 18
Changes in level with a height difference greater than ½ in., like curbs, must 
be ramped.
A curb ramp must meet all the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ At least 36 in. wide excluding flared edges.
 Ɋ Slope no greater than 8%.
 Ɋ Firm, stable, and slip-resistant.
 Ɋ Flared edges or edge protection.
Quick Fixes: Exterior Route
Problem:  The surface of the pathway has breaks or edges with a height 
difference greater than ½ in.
Quick Fix: Fill in areas with concrete or tar to provide a break-free pathway.
Problem:  The exterior route has a curb but no curb ramp.
Quick Fix: Install a temporary ramp. See “Figure 10: Portable Ramp” on 
page 23.
Sec. 11.7.4: Entrance
In many cases the main entrance used by voters is the accessible entrance. 
However, if there are barriers, like stairs, that cannot be mitigated, it may be 
necessary to designate a separate accessible entrance. The accessible entrance 
must be marked with the ISA, even when it is the only entrance to a building.
Accessible entrance decals are available through the Accessibility Supply Program.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 19
Ramps
Changes in level, like steps, must be ramped or a separate entrance with no 
change in level must be provided.
A ramp must meet all the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ At least 36 in. wide
 Ɋ Slope no greater than 8%
 Ɋ Firm, stable, and slip-resistant
 Ɋ Edge protection
 Ɋ Handrails that are between 34 and 38 in. above the surface of the ramp if 
the top of the ramp is more than 6 in. above the ground
Figure 6: Accessible Ramp Requirements
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 20
Doorways
An entrance must meet all of the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ The doorway is at least 32 in. wide
 Ɋ Hardware is useable with one hand without tight grasping, pinching, or 
twisting of the wrist
Figure 7: Accessible Door Hardware
 Ɋ Hardware is no higher than 48 in. above the ground
 Ɋ Force required to open door is no greater than 8.5 lbs.
Figure 8: Beveled and Ramped Thresholds
 Ɋ Threshold is beveled or ramped if greater than ½ in.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 21
Accessible entrances are not required to have features like automatic openers, 
power assist, or doorbells. However, if a door has an automatic opener, power 
assist, or a doorbell, the door does not have to meet the criteria for accessible 
hardware or maximum force to open.
Automatic openers and power assist must meet 
the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ Functioning properly on both sides
 Ɋ Remain open for at least 5 seconds
If there is a second set of doors creating a vestibule at the entrance, there must 
be clear space between them that measures at least 30 in. by 48 in.
Figure 9: Spacing Requirements Between Two Sets of Doors
Quick Fixes: Entrance
Problem:  There are stairs at the entrance but no ramp.
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Install a temporary ramp over the stairs.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 22
Figure 10: Portable Ramp
Problem:  The doorway is 1 or 2 in. too narrow.
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Install swing clear hinges.
Figure 11: Swing-Clear Door Hinges
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 23
Problem:  The door hardware requires tight grasping, pinching, or twisting of 
the wrist.
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Replace the hardware with an accessible type.
 Ɋ Install a doorknob adapter.
 Ɋ Install a wireless doorbell for voters to call for assistance.
Figure 12: Doorknob Adapter
 Ɋ Station a greeter to open the door.
Problem:  The door hardware is more than 48 in. above the ground.
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Install a wireless doorbell for voters to call for assistance.
 Ɋ Station a greeter to open the door.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 24
Problem:  The door requires more than 8.5 lbs. of force to open.
Figure 13: Door Closer Speed
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Adjust the swing speed of the door closer.
 Ɋ Install a wireless doorbell for voters to call for assistance.
 Ɋ Station a greeter to open the door.
Problem:  The threshold is greater than ½ in. and does not have a ramp.
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Install a threshold ramp.
Wireless doorbells and adjustable threshold ramps that can accommodate a 
threshold of 1 ¾ in. to 2 ¼ in. are available through the Accessibility Supply Program.
Sec. 11.7.5: Interior Route
In some polling places the entrance opens immediately into the voting area, so 
there is no interior route. In others, voters must navigate hallways and doorways 
to get to the voting room.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 25
Hallways
Similar to exterior routes, interior routes must meet 
the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ At least 36 in. wide, narrowing to no less than 32 in. for a maximum 
distance of 24 in.
 Ɋ Slope no greater than 5%
 Ɋ Slip-resistant
 Ɋ Rugs have a pile no greater than ½ in. and are secured
 Ɋ Free of protrusions between 27 in. and 80 in. above the ground that extend 
more than 4 in. into the route
 Ɋ Kept clear of obstacles
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 26
Figure 14: Common Obstacles
Doorways
Interior doors must meet the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ Doorway is at least 32 in. wide
 Ɋ Hardware is useable with one hand without tight grasping, pinching, or 
twisting of the wrist
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 27
 Ɋ Hardware is no higher than 48 in. above the ground
 Ɋ Force required to open door is no greater than 5 lbs.
 Ɋ Threshold is beveled or ramped if greater than ½ in.
Interior doors are not required to have features like automatic openers, power 
assist, or doorbells. However, if a door has an automatic opener, power assist, or 
a doorbell, the door does not have to meet the criteria for accessible hardware 
or maximum force to open.
Automatic openers and power assist must meet 
the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ Functioning properly on both sides
 Ɋ Remain open for at least 5 seconds
 Ɋ If there are two sets of doors creating a vestibule, there must be clear 
space between them that measures at least 30 in. by 48 in. See “Figure 9: 
Spacing Requirements Between Two Sets of Doors” on page 22.
Changes in Level
If there are changes in level between the entrance and the voting area, there 
must be a ramp, elevator, or wheelchair lift to allow independent access for 
voters with disabilities.
Ramps
See “Figure 6: Accessible Ramp Requirements” on page 20. 
A ramp must meet all the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ At least 36 in. wide
 Ɋ Slope no greater than 8%
 Ɋ Slip-resistant
 Ɋ Edge protection
 Ɋ Handrails that are between 34 and 38 in. above the surface of the ramp if 
the top of the ramp is more than 6 in. above the ground
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 28
Elevators
Elevators must meet all the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ Functioning properly
 Ɋ Doors open to a minimum of 36 in. wide
 Ɋ Cab is at least 16 sq. ft.
 Ɋ Controls outside and inside are no more than 48 in. above the ground
 Ɋ Controls are marked with raised lettering and/or braille
 Ɋ Audible tones, bells, or verbal enunciators announce each floor as it passes
Wheelchair Lifts
Wheelchair lifts must meet all the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ Functioning properly
 Ɋ Threshold is beveled or ramped if greater than ½ in.
 Ɋ At least 30 in. by 40 in. clear floor space.
 Ɋ Allows unassisted entry/exit.
 Ɋ Allows independent operation.
 Ɋ Controls are useable with one hand without tight grasping, pinching, or 
twisting of the wrist
 Ɋ Controls require no more than 5 lbs. of force to operate
 Ɋ Controls are no more than 48 in. above the ground
Quick Fixes: Interior Route
Problem:  There is a protrusion that is not cane detectable.
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Place a cone beneath the protrusion so it will be cane detectable.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 29
Figure 15: Signaling Obstacles
Cones are available through the Accessibility Supply Program.
Problem:  There is a change in level along the interior route.
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Install a temporary ramp that meets all accessibility criteria. See “Figure 
4: Temporary Accessible Parking Space” on page 17.
Problem:  A door on the interior route has hardware that requires tight 
grasping, pinching, or twisting of the wrist.
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Keep the door propped open while polls are open.
 Ɋ Install a doorknob adapter. See “Figure 12: Doorknob Adapter” on page 24.
 Ɋ Install a wireless doorbell for voters to call for assistance.
 Ɋ Station a greeter to open the door.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 30
Problem:  A door on the interior route requires more than 5 lbs. of force to open.
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Keep the door propped open while polls are open.
 Ɋ Install a wireless doorbell for voters to call for assistance.
 Ɋ Station a greeter to open the door.
Sec. 11.7.6: Voting Area
The voting area should be organized with accessibility concerns in mind and 
any barriers to voting should be eliminated or minimized.
A voting area must meet all the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ Circulation paths are at least 36 in. wide, narrowing to no less than 32 in. 
for a maximum distance of 24 in.
 Ɋ At least 60 in. by 60 in. of clear space
 Ɋ Free of protrusions between 27 in. and 80 in. above the ground that extend 
more than 4 in. into the route. See “Figure 16: Voting Area” on page 32.
Best Practice: Make seating available for voters to wait out of line.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 31
Figure 16: Voting Area
Notices
All required notices should be posted in at least 18 point font.
 Ɋ Type B Notice of Instructions to Voters and Sample Ballot
 ɉ The sample ballot does not have to be in 18 point font
 Ɋ Type C Notice of Referendum (if applicable)
 Ɋ Type D Notice of Polling Place Location and Hours
 Ɋ Election Fraud Notice (EL-111)
 Ɋ Notice of Crossover Voting (EL-112) (if applicable)
 Ɋ Voter Qualification Poster (EL-115)

 Ɋ Contact Information (EL-118)
Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6).
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 32
Voting Booth
Every polling place must have a voting booth where a voter can mark a paper 
ballot from a seated position.
The voting booth must meet all the following criteria to be accessible:
 Ɋ Entrance to the booth is at least 30 in. wide
 Ɋ Work top is between 28 in. and 34 in. above the ground
 Ɋ Knee clearance at least 9 in. deep at 27 in. above the ground
 Ɋ Toe clearance at least 17 in. deep from 0 in. to 9 in. above the ground
 Ɋ Clear space of at least 30 in. by 48 in. in front of the booth
 Ɋ Positioned to ensure no one can see how the voter is marking their ballot. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.35(2)
Best Practice: Have signature guides available at the poll book 
and task lighting as well as magnifying glasses available in 
voting booths. Signature guides and lighted magnifying glasses 
are available through the Accessibility Supply Program.
Accessible Voting Equipment
Every polling place must have accessible voting equipment set up, turned on, 
and properly functioning the entire time polls are open. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(a). 
All voters may use the accessible voting equipment; it is not only for voters with 
disabilities.
Accessible voting equipment must meet the 
following criteria while polls are open:
 Ɋ Set up, turned on, functioning properly
 Ɋ Headphones and tactile keypad are plugged in and ready for a voter to use
 Ɋ Booth or table that the equipment rests on meets the criteria for an 
accessible voting booth
 Ɋ Clearly available to voters. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(a)
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 33
 Ɋ Positioned to ensure no one can see how the voter is marking their ballot. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.35(2)
Best Practice: Poll workers should offer accessible voting equipment 
to each voter. Fact sheets are available at elections.wi.gov: Accessible 
Voting Equipment Fact Sheets as a resource for poll workers.
Best Practice: Position the accessible voting equipment so 
the screen is facing a wall and the criteria for clear space in 
front of the equipment and circulation path width are met.
Quick Fixes: Voting Area
Problem:   The accessible voting equipment is not set up, turned on, and 
functioning properly.
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Locate, set up, and turn on equipment. Poll workers should contact 
municipal clerk immediately. Clerks should contact the Commission 
and equipment vendor immediately if the equipment is broken or 
malfunctioning.
Problem:  The accessible booth for a voter to mark a paper ballot or the 
accessible voting equipment is not set up to ensure voter privacy.
Quick Fix:
 Ɋ Rearrange the voting area to ensure no one is able to see how the voter is 
marking their ballot.
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 34
Chapter 11.8: Polling Place 
Reviews
The Commission conducts reviews of polling places for accessibility on Election 
Days. The municipal clerk is not given notice that a review will be conducted. 
The goal of the review is to experience the polling place as a voter with a 
disability would on any normal Election Day. It starts in the parking area and 
moves through the exterior route, entrance, interior route, and voting area.
When a reviewer arrives at a polling place, they will introduce themselves to 
the Chief Inspector and provide a letter that explains the program to be kept 
with other election day materials. This letter has contact information for the 
Commission staff administering the program. The visit should be noted on the 
Inspector’s Statement (EL-104). The reviewer takes and records measurements 
and photos on a tablet to complete a survey. They are trained to avoid 
capturing voters’ faces in the photos. If the Chief Inspector is available, the 
reviewer will let them know they have completed their review before they leave. 
The Commission takes the data collected in the survey to create a report for the 
municipal clerk detailing any non-compliant findings.
Best Practice: The municipal clerk is informed when the report 
is ready to view online and has 60 days to complete a Plan of 
Action. To complete a Plan of Action, a clerk logs in to the online 
portal and chooses from a list of recommended solutions provided 
by the Commission to resolve each non-compliant finding in 
the report. The clerk also has the opportunity to write their own 
solutions. Though the Plan of Action itself is a best practice, all 
polling places must be accessible and therefore clerks must take 
action to address the non-compliant findings in the report.
Data collected from polling place reviews is included in the Report of Barriers 
Faced by Elderly Voters and Voters with Disabilities that the Commission is 
required to submit to the legislature by June 30 of every odd-numbered year. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(d).
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 35

Resources

While the scope of the Commission is limited to elections, public buildings 
and services must always be accessible. There are many resources available 
for municipalities and counties to learn more about and implement 
accessible practices.

Sec. 11.9.3: Local Resources
Aging and Disability Resource Centers (ADRC)
ADRCs are located in all 72 counties of Wisconsin and provide services to 
residents with disabilities and older adults. ADRCs may be aware of local 
services like transportation that are available to people with disabilities.
Independent Living Centers
There are eight independent living centers around the state that provide 
services to people with disabilities. Some independent living centers loan 
accessibility aids to individuals and may offer education on how to use 
accessibility aids. An independent living center may be able to assess a public 
building for accessibility outside of the context of elections.

Figure 18: Appendix 2
First Edition, June 2026 Accessibility 11 – 39
Election Day 
Accessibility Checklist ✔
The purpose of this checklist is to allow you, the poll worker, to quickly assess whether your 
polling place has barriers for people with disabilities on Election Day. If you identify barriers, 
you should inform the municipal clerk and/or your supervisor so the barrier can be ad-
dressed as soon as possible. Many barriers can be easily addressed on Election Day.*
PARKING 
For polling locations that have parking lots: 
The accessible space(s) are clearly marked with the standard accessible parking sign. 
The accessible space(s) are located nearest to the accessible entrance. 
There is at least one van-accessible space. 
There is an accessible way to get from the parking lot to the sidewalk. 
The parking lot is paved. 
For polling locations that do NOT have parking lots: 
There is an accessible passenger drop-off area, or temporary on- or off-street accessible 
parking that could be designated on Election Day. 
Accessible parking must be kept clear of snow, piles of leaves or other obstacles to persons 
with disabilities in order to be accessible. 
PATHWAYS TO THE BUILDING 
The path to the accessible entrance is clearly marked with large print signs if it is 
different from the primary route to the building. 
The path of travel is free of breaks and edges and is clear of debris such as snow, ice 
and leaves, and low-hanging objects such as tree branches. 
The path of travel has the necessary curb cuts and ramps so that a person using a 
mobility device could access the building with ease. 
All ramps have handrails (and edge protection), if necessary. 
The path of travel is well-lit when necessary. 
1 
*This checklist does not identify all barriers that a person may face at the polls. Answering
positively to the checklist does not mean a polling site is in compliance with such laws as
the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).
Figure 19: Appendix 3
ENTRANCE TO THE BUILDING 
The entrance to the building is free of steps or has a ramp or elevator. 
The accessible entrance to the building is unlocked. 
The accessible entrance to the building has an automatic door opener or a call button, 
or there is someone stationed at the door to open it. 
There is signage or a greeter stationed at the entrance with information on requesting 
curbside voting.  
TRAVEL WITHIN THE BUILDING 
The accessible route to the voting area is clearly marked with large print signs if it 
is different from the main route and/or if it is not immediately inside the accessible 
entrance. 
Interior doors along the accessible route are unlocked and either have automatic doors 
or are propped open. 
If there are stairs to get to the voting area, there is an accessible elevator available. 
Hallways are well-lit and free of low-hanging objects and items protruding from the wall 
or sitting on the floor. 
All rugs and mats along the accessible route have low pile and are securely fastened 
(or removed). 
VOTING AREA 
Instructions for voting are printed in Large Print (18-point font or larger) and displayed in 
a convenient and obvious location. 
The path of travel in the voting area is wide enough for an individual using a mobility 
device to navigate and turn around with ease (minimum of 5x5 feet). 
There is a table, counter or voting booth that is extra wide at the bottom (at least 36 
inches), and at good height (between 28 and 34 inches) to allow someone who uses a 
mobility device to use it comfortably and reach all parts of the equipment. 
Polling booths that hold the accessible equipment are: 
Housed in the same area of the room as all the other polling booths. 
Strategically placed to ensure the privacy of the voter using the machine AND contain 
a privacy screen. 
Electronic Accessible voting equipment is turned on, tested, and in proper working order 
for electors to use when the polls open on Election Day. 
2 
All accessible features are set up and working, including tactile devices and 
headphones. 
The polling site has the following: 
Signature guide or ruler to assist someone to sign their name in a straight line. 
Communication cards or pen/paper to communicate with someone who is deaf or 
hard of hearing. 
Magnifying glass to be used by someone with a sight impairment. 
Extra seating and a policy to allow voters who have trouble standing or walking to 
wait to vote and maintain their place in line. 
Task lighting at every space in the voting area. 
Poll workers are aware of the special needs of voters with disabilities and are willing to 
provide reasonable accommodations when requested. 
Poll workers are aware of the assistant process: 
Any elector may have an assistant. The assistant can be anyone, except the elector’s 
union representative or employer, and the assistant does not have to be a qualified 
elector. 
Electors may have an assistant state their name and address for them if they are 
unable. 
An elector can direct an assistant to mark their ballot and insert the ballot into the 
ballot box or tabulator. The assistant must sign the ballot in the designated location 
and must also sign and provide their address in the poll book. 
Election inspectors have reviewed the Poll Worker Common Courtesy Checklist. 
There is a feasible plan in place to identify when a voter wants to vote curbside, such as 
having signage, a phone number, or a greeter stationed outside, and poll workers are 
aware of the curbside voting policy. 
Your municipal or county clerk will have more detailed information about accessibility rules 
and laws. Additional information that may be helpful includes: 
3

If you have questions about this checklist or about accessibility, contact the Wisconsin Elections 
Commission at (608)261-2028 or DRW’s Voter Hotline at 844-DIS-VOTE / 844-347-8683.

Part 12 
Emergency Preparedness & 
Contingency Planning
Emergency response plans; establish response partners; 
alternate locations for voting activity; extensions of voting due 
to emergencies or unforeseen circumstances; sample plan.
Elections are not cancelled or postponed due to emergencies. Planning 
for emergencies is as important for election administration as any other 
election preparations. Although there is a wide range of possible scenarios, 
it is possible to account for most of them with just a handful of preparations. 
Election officials should prepare and/or update their contingency plan ahead 
of each election. In some circumstances, voting can be extended past 8 p.m. 
if an emergency or other situation prevented voters from casting ballots.
First Edition, June 2026 Emergency Preparedness 12 – 1
Chapter 12.1: Introduction
Elections are not cancelled or postponed due to emergencies. For example, 
at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic in April 2020, the Wisconsin Supreme 
Court ruled that the Governor could not delay by Executive Order the in-person 
voting on Election Day at Spring Election.1 Wisconsin municipal clerks have 
run successful elections despite severe weather, unexpected polling place 
infrastructure failure, power outages, unplanned staffing shortages, and other 
impactful circumstances.
Planning for emergencies is as important for election administration as any 
other election preparations. In an emergency, it is important to have already 
made important decisions and prepared necessary resources so the focus 
can be on a prompt, proper response. Although there is a wide range of 
possible scenarios, it is possible to account for most of them with just a 
handful of preparations.
Chapter 12.2 is designed for municipal clerks to develop a basic emergency 
response plan that accounts for the needs of their jurisdictions. The basic 
plan may be sufficient for small jurisdictions with a single polling place. Larger 
jurisdictions will want to go beyond basic plans to account for their more 
complex operating environment. In Chapter 12.3, there are additional topics 
and instructions for jurisdictions wishing to improve upon the basic plan.
The Commission maintains Election Day Emergency Planning resources 
available to clerks on ElectEd.
1 See Wisconsin Legislature v. Tony Evers (2020AP608-OA), Order Issued April 6, 2020.
First Edition, June 2026 Emergency Preparedness 12 – 2
Chapter 12.2: Creating a Basic 
Emergency Response Plan
An “emergency response plan” is a resource to prepare for and address 
potential future events. All poll workers — not just Chief Inspectors — should be 
familiar with the plan before it is needed. An effective plan need not be lengthy. 
A concise plan that people understand is more useful than a thick binder 
that sits on a shelf. The process of developing and maintaining the plan is 
particularly beneficial, because participants are forced to become familiar with 
plan elements. A sample plan is provided as Appendix 2 to this Part.
Contingency plans should contain detailed information on the following topics:
 Ɋ Contact information for emergency response partners
 Ɋ Polling places and alternate locations
 Ɋ Summary of normal operating procedures
 Ɋ A plan for securing and handling election materials
 Ɋ Common emergency scenarios
Sec. 12.2.1: Contact Information for 
Emergency Response Partners
Every emergency response plan should always contain a detailed contact 
information section for local, state, and federal emergency response 
partners. This can include staff at the clerks’ offices, law enforcement, fire 
department, public works, and anyone else who may need to assist with 
voting during an emergency.
First Edition, June 2026 Emergency Preparedness 12 – 3
Sec. 12.2.2: Polling Places & Alternate 
Locations
Some emergencies can be addressed by planning for, and relocating to, an 
alternate location that is unaffected by the emergency. Moving voting activity 
to an alternate location is not a simple matter that should be done on the fly. 
Alternate locations should always be designated prior to when the voting 
activity is scheduled to begin.
Planning for alternate locations need not be limited to polling places. Instead, 
municipal clerks should plan for disruptions at any location necessary to the 
voting process, including their own office, central count facilities, or locations 
served by Special Voting Deputies (SVDs).
Best Practice: If it is necessary to utilize an alternate location for 
voting activity, municipal clerks should also contact Commission 
staff to notify them of the change. Commission Staff can assist with 
ensuring the change is reflected in MyVote and WisVote if necessary.
Sec. 12.2.3: Summary of Normal 
Operating Procedures
Sometimes, emergency responses are hindered because the people with 
subject matter knowledge of what needs to happen are the ones directly 
affected by the emergency. This is why it is important for the emergency 
response plan to start with a summary of the normal functions and 
responsibilities. The level of detail can vary depending on need, but it should 
be detailed enough that anyone can pick up the emergency response plan 
and understand what responsibilities still need to be carried out despite the 
emergency. It could be as simple as listing the major functions of the polling 
place and the normal voting process.
First Edition, June 2026 Emergency Preparedness 12 – 4
Sec. 12.2.4: A Plan for Securing & 
Handling Election Materials
In an emergency, the priority should always be the safety of people over the 
safety of objects. If the polling place is burning down, no election official or voter 
should put themselves at risk by trying to rescue ballots or election equipment.
However, an emergency response plan should contain plans for how to properly 
secure and handle election materials, when it is safe to do so, for each of the 
common emergency scenarios identified at the end of this chapter.
The most critical election materials are:
 Ɋ Unmarked ballots
 Ɋ Voting equipment and ballot boxes
 Ɋ Unprocessed absentee ballots
 Ɋ Absentee ballot envelopes
 Ɋ Poll books
The emergency response plan should identify which election officials or poll 
workers are responsible for securing or transporting election materials during 
an emergency.
Sec. 12.2.5: Common 
Emergency Scenarios
It’s impossible to plan for everything, but identifying the most common 
scenarios can go a long way to ensuring election officials feel comfortable 
responding to the most likely emergencies.
Common Emergency Scenarios
 Ɋ Inclement or Severe Weather: Heavy snow, ice, freezing temperatures, 
heavy rain or flooding, severe thunderstorms, tornados, dangerous smog 
or smoke, excessive heat indexes, landslides, wildfire, or hail.
 Ɋ Structure Issues: Fire or fire alarm, power outages, burst pipes or backed 
up sewer lines, broken windows, collapsed roofs, pest infestations, or 
impact damage to walls or doors.
First Edition, June 2026 Emergency Preparedness 12 – 5
 Ɋ Infrastructure Issues:  Closed roads or highways, flooded parking lots, 
bridge collapses, public transit shutdowns, or loss of cell service or 
Internet connectivity.
 Ɋ IT Issues: Ransomware attacks, phishing attempts, distributed denial-of-
service (DDOS) attacks, file or system corruption, server failure, or viruses.
 Ɋ Safety Threats: Bomb threats, active shooters, theft of election materials 
or property, attacks on election officials or voters, or destruction of 
property.
 Ɋ Materials or Equipment Shortages:  Poll worker shortages, low 
ballots, tabulator or electronic poll book failure, or inability to procure 
necessary supplies.
 Ɋ Misinformation: Online rumors, deepfakes of election officials, or incorrect 
“viral” social media posts.
Considerations for Common Emergency Scenarios
 Ɋ Effects on people: What will happen if a key leader becomes unavailable? 
How can operations be adapted to account for unavailable staff? 
Are individual responsibilities and the chain of command clear to all 
personnel?
 Ɋ Effects on locations: What would its effect be on alternate absentee voting 
sites? Facilities served by Special Voting Deputies? Central count facilities? 
Other government buildings or meeting locations for the municipal or 
county canvass?
 Ɋ Effects on time: What would its effect be on the clerk’s office six months 
prior to Election Day? One month? One week? One day? How will the event 
affect post-election activities?
The emergency response plan should address what happens next for each 
identified common emergency. Because emergencies are unpredictable, it is 
more effective if the plan addresses general principles than specific actions. For 
example, in an emergency, certain streets or exits could become inaccessible, 
so a plan should be flexible enough for the poll workers to adapt.
First Edition, June 2026 Emergency Preparedness 12 – 6
Chapter 12.3: Contingency 
Planning Additional Topics
The following sections expand on the concepts introduced above and provide additional 
information for jurisdictions to consider when improving upon a basic contingency plan.
Sec. 12.3.1: The Clerk’s Office
Municipal clerks can relocate their office to a designated alternate location in 
the event of emergency as an exercise of their discretion. Wis. Stat. § 7.15(1). The 
emergency response plan should consider how this will occur, including how 
staff will be notified of the change and how work will be completed.
Sec. 12.3.2: Alternate 
Absentee Voting Sites
Alternate absentee voting sites are designated well in advance of an election, and no 
law specifically addresses what to do if an emergency or other circumstance affects 
their use. Generally speaking, a municipal clerk cannot designate an additional 
alternate absentee voting location once the deadline to do so has passed.2
If the governing body has designated more than one alternate absentee 
site, voters should be directed to those other locations, assuming they are 
unaffected by the emergency. If the governing body has only designated 
a single alternate site that becomes unusable due to an emergency, the 
Commission recommends that the emergency response plan include 
instructions for how the governing body may immediately convene to 
address the situation as consistently as possible with Wis. Stat. § 6.855 .
Sec. 12.3.3: Facilities Served by 
Special Voting Deputies
If an emergency or other situation impacts a facility served by Special Voting 
Deputies (SVDs), the municipal clerk should first take steps to arrange another 
time to visit, assuming that is feasible. See Wis. Stat. § 6.875(6)(a).
2 See October 5, 2020, Clerk Communication: Alternate Sites for In-Person Absentee Voting.
First Edition, June 2026 Emergency Preparedness 12 – 7
At times, public health outbreaks (influenza, MRSA, COVID-19) have prompted 
facilities served by SVDs to close to visitors, including to SVDs. The emergency 
response plan should contain steps for ensuring that voters in these facilities 
are still able to cast their ballots even if the facilities close to visitors due to 
some type of emergency.
Sec. 12.3.4: Emergencies at Polling 
Places Prior to Polls Opening
Whenever it becomes impossible or inconvenient to hold an election at the 
designated location, state law permits poll workers to adjourn to the nearest 
convenient place for holding the election. Wis. Stat. § 7.37(1).
Best Practice: The nearest convenient location should be identified 
in advance when the polling place location decisions are made.
When this is necessary, the poll workers shall make a proclamation of the move 
and shall station either a law enforcement officer or other person designated by 
the municipal clerk to be stationed at or near the original polling place to inform 
voters of the move. Id.
The prohibitions and restrictions on closing polling places under Wis. Stat.  
§ 5.25(3)(a) do not affect the ability of poll workers to adjourn to an alternate 
location on Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(3)(d). For more detailed information 
on the establishment, closing, and discontinuance of polling place locations, 
see Part 13: “Polling Places & Supplies.”
Sec. 12.3.5: Emergencies at Polling Places 
after Polls Opening or During Canvass
State law gives poll workers the full authority to maintain order and enforce 
obedience to their lawful commands during the election or canvass of the 
votes. Wis. Stat. § 7.37(2). While the procedures for relocating to alternate 
locations are limited to before the poll workers receive any votes, the 
Commission believes that state law, as well as common sense, grants poll 
workers with the authority to relocate during Election Day if an emergency 
arises after polls open. Accordingly, whenever it becomes impossible or 
First Edition, June 2026 Emergency Preparedness 12 – 8
convenient for an election to continue at a polling place after the polls have 
opened, poll workers should utilize the same procedures to relocate outlined 
by Wis. Stat. § 7.37(1) as an exercise of their authority under Wis. Stat. § 7.37(2).
Sec. 12.3.6: Emergencies at Absentee 
Canvassing Facilities (“Central Count”)
Note: When this manual uses the term “central count,” it is referring to a 
meeting of the board of absentee ballot canvassers under Wis. Stat. § 7.52(1)(a).
Municipalities may, by ordinance, choose to canvass all of their absentee 
ballots at one location (often referred to as a central count facility). Wis. Stat.  
§ 7.52(1)(a). If a central count facility has been authorized, the board of 
absentee ballot canvassers can convene any time after the opening of the 
polls and before 10 p.m. on Election Day. Id. Municipal clerks are required to 
give at least 48 hours’ notice ahead of the convening, and the counting is 
observable election activity under Id., Wis. Stat. § 7.41 .
If an emergency impacts the canvassing of absentee ballots at the designated 
location, the best practice would be for the board of absentee ballot canvassers 
to pause their work, notice the change in plan to the public, and then move to 
an alternate location. Statute does not specifically address whether a board of 
absentee ballot canvassers can do this, but in case of emergency, the safest 
path forward is to take measures to ensure that absentee ballots can still be 
canvassed. The municipal clerk should give as much notice of the move as 
possible but if giving 24 hours’ notice is impossible or impractical, they can 
provide shorter notice as long as it is still at least 2 hours ahead before the 
meeting will resume. Wis. Stat. § 19.84(3).
First Edition, June 2026 Emergency Preparedness 12 – 9
Appendix 12.A: Polling Place 
Extensions by Court Order
Under Wisconsin law, the polls must remain open on Election Day from 7 a.m. 
to 8 p.m. Wis. Stat. § 6.78. Municipal clerks cannot decide on their own authority 
to close their polling places early, or open late, to avoid an emergency that has 
not yet occurred, such as severe weather forecasts. Ongoing emergencies may 
disrupt voting on Election Day, and the safety of voters and staff is always the 
top priority.
The Commission has no role to play in considering or granting polling place 
extensions, except to provide guidance to municipal clerks who are seeking 
the extension or who have been named in an extension request filed by an 
interested party. Municipal clerks should contact the Commission with any 
questions relating to these types of petitions if not answered in this guidance.
When an emergency, or another unforeseen circumstance, disrupts voting on 
Election Day, interested parties may seek an extension of voting past 8 p.m. at the 
affected polling places by seeking a court order pursuant to Wis. Stat. § 6.96. This 
is sometimes done affirmatively by the municipal clerk, especially if the clerk is 
aware of and responding to an ongoing situation. In recent years, political parties, 
candidates, and voting rights groups have also made polling place extension 
requests with various courts.1
Seeking this kind of court order is especially important when a polling place 
is closed for a significant period of time, especially during the afternoon or 
evening hours, when voters may not have an adequate opportunity to return to 
the polls and vote. Id. provides for an extension of voting hours by federal court 
order. However, Wisconsin courts have regularly determined that they also have 
inherent jurisdiction and authority to issue orders to extend voting hours.2
1 See Democracy Docket for an example of a successful petition filed by someone other than the 
municipal clerk. 
2 In a recent example, Walworth County Circuit Court Judge David M. Reddy granted an extension for 
voting at polling locations in the City of Whitewater during the November 5, 2024, General Election. 
The extension came at the request of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), and alleged 
that the extension was needed due to inadequate staffing and insufficient number of electronic 
pollbooks due to unexpectedly high turnout. Judge Reddy cited Wis. Stat. § 6.96  as the basis for his 
authority, and extended voting at all polling places in the City of Whitewater until 10:30 p.m.
First Edition, June 2026 Emergency Preparedness 12 – 10
Time is of the essence when a court order is necessary so that election 
inspectors, voters, and the media can be advised whether voting hours will 
be extended. In such situations, it is important for the municipal clerk to 
immediately notify and consult with their municipal attorney to discuss the 
decision whether to extend voting hours and for how long. The extension should 
take into consideration the amount of time the polling location was closed and 
the time of day it was closed.
The Commission has prepared a number of templates and samples 
of paperwork needed to submit a petition to extend voting:
 Ɋ Petition: The petition for an extension of polling hours is straightforward. It 
should state which polling places should be extended, and until when.
 Ɋ Affidavit: The petition should be accompanied by an affidavit, or sworn 
statement, from someone with knowledge of why the extension is 
necessary. It should provide more detailed information regarding the 
reason the polling location was closed and the length of the closure. An 
affidavit allows the Court to rely on a sworn statement from either an 
election official or other interested party and creates a record supporting 
the extension request.
 Ɋ Stipulation: When the extension is sought by a municipal clerk in a partisan 
election, it may be helpful (though is not required) for the clerk to seek 
agreement from the major political parties regarding the extension request, 
if time permits. If time does not allow for a written stipulation, it is helpful to 
at least attempt to notify the major political parties in advance so that they 
have an opportunity to provide input or raise any concerns or objections 
with the court. When time permits, a written or oral stipulation demonstrates 
to the court that parties with potential interest in the extension requests 
have been provided notice and an opportunity to be heard.
 Ɋ Proposed Order: The requestor can include a proposed order for the court 
to execute if it agrees to grant the petition for the extension of polling hours. 
If the request is considered at an in-person court hearing, it is helpful to 
have multiple copies of the proposed order available for the court.
Note: Court document templates are available on elections.wi.gov.
First Edition, June 2026 Emergency Preparedness 12 – 11
If the court grants the extension, the municipal 
clerk should take the following steps:
1. Immediately notify the election inspectors at the affected polling places, and 
make plans to provide extra staff if necessary.
2. Communicate with the public by all possible means, including contacting 
local media, posting on social media and the municipality’s website, and 
posting signs at the affected polling places. The communication should 
detail:
•	 Which polling places are affected
•	 The deadline for voting as reflected in the court order
•	 A reminder that anyone in line by the new close of polls deadline will be 
permitted to vote
3. Prepare copies of the Commission’s Notice to Voters to be handed to voters 
at the polling places who are voting after 8 p.m. pursuant to the court order. 
4. Instruct election inspectors at the affected polling places to follow the 
procedures of Wis. Stat. § 6.96 with respect to marking the ballots of the voters 
who cast ballots during the polling place extension hours.

Introduction:
This document will serve as the emergency and contingency plan in case of an unexpected event 
that requires a change of polling place location or operating procedures on or around an election 
day. The purpose of this plan is to provide guidance for election officials and other relevant parties 
regarding the general safety of polling locations, all while maintaining the security of an election.
This document shall be reviewed with election inspectors as part of the clerk’s pre-election 
training. All relevant officials should be familiar with this plan and be ready to implement its 
provisions as may become necessary. The document and its contents shall be considered sensitive 
in nature. The county clerk, polling place property owners and facility managers, and other 
applicable parties should be apprised of relevant aspects of this plan.

City Clerk or any emergency personnel need to talk to you, these telephones may be our only 
means of communication. Those numbers are shared with all relevant municipal officials and 
emergency officials, and the contact information for each emergency service provide or official 
will also be in that pre-provided cell phone’s contact list. This list should include:

Election Official Responsibilities:
All election officials should be knowledgeable of what to do in the event of an emergency event, 
as described below or more generally. This plan addresses security issues relating to clerks and 
local officials, poll workers, voters, election records, and equipment.
General Responsibilities:
 Ɋ Know where the primary and secondary exits are for your facility.
 Ɋ Locate the fire extinguishers.
 Ɋ Learn where to go in your facility in case of an emergency, severe weather or tornado.
 Ɋ Have a specific point or location for all employees to assemble, both inside and outside your facility.
 Ɋ Report any unusual activity or persons at your location. Notify the Generic City Clerk’s Office 
at (608) 555-1234, or dial 911 for emergency services.
 Ɋ Document any evacuation or emergency activities on your Inspectors’ Statement.
Polling Place Details:
Voters may cast their ballots at the appropriate polling place from 7:00 AM until 8:00 PM on election day.
In the event of an emergency, a court order may be requested to extend polling place hours.
In the event of an emergency which renders any Primary Location impossible or inconvenient for 
use, the Emergency Location designated herein shall be used as a replacement location. The list of 
potential emergencies listed herein constitutes the minimum emergency types that may warrant 
movement to the Emergency Location for polling place activities. Similar emergencies not listed 
in this policy, but otherwise requiring movement, are hereby authorized.
Steps will be taken to ensure the primary and backup sites comply with the accessibility 
requirements of Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4), notice requirements of Wis. Stat. § 10.01(2)(d), and the 
designation requirements of Wis. Stat. § 5.25(3).
If for any reason the polling place needs to be permanently evacuated during an election, all election 
materials shall be brought to the alternate location. Depending on the reason for the evacuation, 
a police escort and/or their designee will be provided. A trained individual must be stationed at or 
as near as possible to the closed location to notify all voters of the closure and of their new polling 
location. In addition, a notice should be posted on the entrance to the polling place notifying voters 
of the evacuation and that they should report to the alternate location to vote.
Ballot materials, voting equipment, and all materials must remain locked or properly secured, 
and at no time may these items be out of the sight of the election inspectors or local officials 
unless the emergency puts those parties in danger warranting evacuation without the materials. 
In that case, time and safety permitting, the election inspectors or local officials may take other 
measures to secure the election materials.
Other forms of communication to voters will include… (e.g.	City	social	media	pages,	email	and	
text	blasts,	emergency	notification	systems,	city	website,	local	media	outlets,	etc.).

Threatening Phone Calls, Bomb Threats, and Suspicious Objects:
 Ɋ Keep anyone from handling the object or going near it. The object may be dangerous. In 
addition, preservation of evidence is important for law enforcement.
 Ɋ If a suspicious object is located, immediately evacuate the area, leaving the object undisturbed 
until the police arrive.
 Ɋ In the event of a threatening phone call or bomb threat, promptly write down everything 
you can remember about receiving the verbal or written threat, parcel, or suspicious object. 
Listen for background noise, the caller’s voice, and what was said. If the situation allows, ask 
questions about where the bomb is located, when it will explode, the person’s name and 
address. Police interviewers will need this information.

Threats of Violence:
Be aware of the possibility of an incident occurring at your polling location. Local officials 
should pre-plan for threats of violence, disruptions, and elections or other crimes in advance of 
election day. This includes de-escalation training, reminders of the chief inspector’s authority, 
threat landscape briefings between local officials and law enforcement, and planning for law 
enforcement presence or responses on election day. Please note the following:
 Ɋ Take all threats of violence seriously.
 Ɋ Report any threats to the chief inspector to make a determination as to the next course of action.
 Ɋ For any situation that involves an immediate threat of violence, an election official should 
notify law enforcement or the duty officer is one is predetermined. Dial 911.
 Ɋ In the event of a confrontation, do not panic. Do exactly what you are told—no more and no 
less. Do not do anything to surprise the threatening individual.
 Ɋ Document incident on the Inspectors’ Statement.

Active Shooter:
Active shooter situations are unpredictable and evolve quickly. Because active shooter 
situations are often over within three to five minutes, before law enforcement arrives on the 
scene, poll workers should be prepared both mentally and physically to deal directly with an 
active shooter situation. Keep safety first. If an active shooter event occurs at the polling place, 
use the Run | Hide | Fight model. Once shooting starts, it is too late for negotiation to help.
	Ɋ RUN: If it is safe to do so, exit the facility immediately to avoid the shooter. Run if the path is 
clear and you can easily reach an exit. Do not worry about the ballots or election supplies.
	Ɋ HIDE: If you are unable to safely exit the facility, lock yourself in any room and barricade the 
door to deny the shooter access. Because each polling location has different types of doors, 
each polling place is encouraged to develop plans in advance for where and how to barricade the 
door shut. Depending on the type of door and how it opens, you might barricade the door using 
a door stop, binder, table, or belt. T urn off the lights, silence cell phones, and remain quiet. If you 
barricade, prepare for your next response if the attacker finds you or gets into the room.
	Ɋ FIGHT: If you are unable to utilize the avoid and deny strategies successfully, defend yourself 
using whatever means are available. When the shooter is in close range and you cannot flee, 
your chance of survival is much greater if you try to incapacitate the shooter.
 Ɋ The weapon in the shooter’s hand is the biggest threat. If possible, attack the shooter 
immediately as the attacker enters the room, before they orient themselves. Grabbing the 
gun tightly with a c-shaped grip around its top or slide can hinder a handgun’s operation. 
After grabbing the gun by the slide, use your other hand with a hammer fist to strike at the 
shooter’s vision and wind, or just keep hitting their nose. If the shooter has a rifle, grab outside 
of the shooter’s hands from the side, and drive the rifle down toward the shooter’s legs and 
away from you. Do not stop fighting until the shooter is incapacitated or disarmed.
 Ɋ If you are within 20 feet of the shooter in an open area, you may be better off running toward 
the shooter than away from them; otherwise, you are giving them time to aim at you. Call 911 
as soon as possible.
