Part 13 
Polling Places & Supplies
Establishing, closing, relocating, and consolidating polling 
places; polling place supplies; supplies checklist
Polling places are where in person voters go on Election Day to cast their 
votes. They are established by the governing body of the municipality well 
in advance, and strict rules govern when they can be closed, relocated, or 
consolidated. Municipal clerks should use this chapter ahead of each election 
to ensure that each polling place in their jurisdiction has sufficient supplies.
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 1
Chapter 13.1: Introduction
A polling place is the actual location where the elector’s vote is cast. Wis. Stat. 
§ 5.02(15). Polling places are established by the governing body of a municipality 
ahead of Election Day, and municipal clerks perform all work necessary to 
adequately stock and staff each polling place for all voters in their jurisdictions.
Note: Clerks should rely on the Polling Place Checklist produced in 
Appendix 1 of this chapter to plan for each election.
Polling places can be the center of activity on Election Day, particularly in 
municipalities with only one polling place.
Best Practice: if the municipal clerk is on the ballot, they should 
not be stationed in the polling place. While their presence may be 
momentarily needed to assist with issues on Election Day, steps should 
be taken ahead of time to minimize voter interaction. If the polling 
place and the clerk’s office share the same building, clerks should 
attempt to use different walking routes or restrooms as to not put 
themselves in view of voters. If clerks on the ballot are needed at the 
polling place, they should make visits as short as possible or deputize 
someone to help in their place.
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 2
Chapter 13.2: Polling Place 
Establishment & Guidance
Polling places are established by the governing body of a municipality at least 
30 days before any election. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(3)(a). Polling places are usually 
public buildings, unless the governing body determines that the public building 
choices are impractical or that the use of a nonpublic building better serves the 
needs of their voters. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(1).
Polling places must be accessible to all individuals with disabilities. Wis. Stat. 
§ 5.25(4)(a).
Polling place locations can only be entered into WisVote by Commission staff. 
If there are new polling places, or changes to existing polling places, municipal 
clerks must contact Commission staff directly at elections@wi.gov.
Sec. 13.2.1: Guidance for Choosing 
Polling Place Locations
There are approximately 2,000 to 3,000 polling places in use throughout the 
state on Election Day, each of which are unique to the needs of the municipality. 
In addition to public buildings, most polling places are usually located in 
churches and schools. However, polling places have also been in bowling alleys, 
supper clubs, private businesses, retirement facilities, recreation clubs, zoos, and 
even empty storefronts. There are many considerations that go into choosing 
polling place locations, including sufficient space for voting, availability, cost, 
and accessibility.
Governing bodies choosing polling place locations should carefully consider 
whether a particular location, especially some private locations, may give 
the perception of electioneering or otherwise make voters uncomfortable. 
For example, some voters may perceive that certain houses of worship have 
political correlations that may make them hesitant to want to enter the space. 
Likewise, some voters may feel similarly about police stations or other public 
buildings where law enforcement are routinely present. Obviously, a polling 
place should never be in the headquarters of a political party or candidate’s 
campaign office, but proximity to those types of offices within the same multi-
use building can also pose an issue.
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 3
Sec. 13.2.2: Polling Place Accessibility
All polling places must be accessible to all individuals with disabilities. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4) .
Note: If a potential polling place location is not accessible, it cannot be 
chosen, no matter how good of a fit it is for the municipality.
The Commission is required to ensure that all polling places are accessible. Id. 
The Commission accomplishes this by requiring municipal clerks to certify to 
the Commission that all polling places used within the municipality satisfy the 
accessibility requirements established by the Commission. The Commission 
also hires accessibility reviewers to assess accessibility set up at polling places 
on Election Day.
For more detailed information on polling place accessibility, see Part 11: 
“Accessibility.”
Sec. 13.2.3: Who Votes Where? Single 
& Multi-Ward Polling Places
All electors within a ward must vote at the same polling place Wis. Stat. § 5.25(5)
(a). A single polling place can serve more than one ward in a municipality. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.25(5)(c).
Important Exception: if an elderly or disabled elector is unable 
to vote at the polling place that serves their residence due to age 
or an accessibility issue, the municipal clerk or board of election 
commissioners of a municipality may reassign the elector to another 
polling place within the municipality that is accessible to their needs. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.25(5)(b). If this is necessary, the municipal clerk should 
ensure that the polling place to which the elector is reassigned has the 
correct ballot style available for the voter’s ward.
When two or more wards are combined for voting purposes at a single polling 
place the governing body must do so by resolution at least 30 days before 
any election. Wis. Stat. § 5.15(6)(b). In municipalities where the population is 
less than 35,000, the governing body may provide in the resolution to combine 
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 4
the election results for each set of combined wards. The governing body of a 
municipality of 35,000 or more may by resolution combine election returns of a 
ward with an adjacent ward if the ward has a population of 20 or less and the 
total population of the combined wards would not exceed that municipality’s 
population range for wards. Election results can be combined only if electors in 
the combined wards vote for the same offices. Wis. Stat. § 5.15(6)(b).
If a municipality only has one ward or combines all of their wards into a single 
polling place, the municipal board of canvass can occur at that polling place 
after polls close. Wis. Stat. § 7.53(1)(a). See Chapter 14.27: “Municipal Boards of 
Canvassers.”
Sec. 13.2.4: Combining Polling 
Places for Multiple Municipalities
Municipalities may use the same polling place location (meaning the 
same room in the same building) so long as the location can be set 
up to accommodate voters from both areas in a way that minimizes 
confusion. For example, two neighboring villages may wish to utilize the 
same multipurpose room in one of the town halls because it is a large, free 
space that is also properly accessible to voters. If municipalities wish to do 
this, each municipality still must take all of the required steps to establish 
the location as the designated polling place for their jurisdiction. Each 
municipality must still have its own poll books, ballots, election materials, 
voting equipment, and poll workers even if sharing the same polling place 
location with another municipality.
Co-locating polling places for more than one municipality is not prohibited 
by state law, but municipalities contemplating this option should take care to 
ensure that all steps of establishing the co-location as a polling place for their 
voters are followed.
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 5
Chapter 13.3: Closing Polling 
Places
In 2023, a new law went into effect governing when polling places can be 
closed ahead of Election Day. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(3). The law has always required 
governing bodies to establish polling places at least 30 days ahead of Election 
Day. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(3)(a). However, the law was previously silent on whether 
anyone had the authority to close, consolidate, or otherwise make changes 
to polling places within 30 days of an election. This came to a head during 
the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic when virus mitigation efforts and 
poll worker shortages posed logistical problems for the 2020 Spring Election. 
Ahead of the 2020 Spring Election, the Commission had issued limited, election-
specific guidance stating that municipal clerks had authority to close and 
consolidate polling places for the upcoming election without the approval of 
their governing bodies in situations where the COVID-19 pandemic required 
changes to or consolidation of polling places, such as shortage of available 
poll workers. After the height of the pandemic, the Commission attempted to 
promulgate an administrative rule to effectuate that guidance, but that rule 
attempt was abandoned in the wake of the enactment of Wis. Stat. § 5.25(3).
The new law aims to address situations where municipalities closed or 
consolidated polling places within days or weeks of Election Day, causing 
confusion and lack of easy voting access for voters.
No established polling place may be closed to voters on Election Day unless a 
majority of the governing body of a municipality makes a finding of emergency. 
The majority of the governing body and the municipal clerk must both approve 
the closure. If this occurs, the municipal clerk must do the following, according 
to Wis. Stat. § 5.25(3)(a).
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 6
Closing a polling place during an emergency:
 Ɋ Post public notice of the closure on the municipality’s website or, if the 
municipality does not maintain a website, post notices in at least 3 
different locations within the municipality reasonably calculated to notify 
the most residents. Wis. Stat. § 10.05.
 Ɋ Publish a class 3 notice under ch. 985 notifying the public of the closure.
 Ɋ Publish a class 2 or class 1 notice under ch. 985 notifying the public of the 
closure if time does not permit publication of a class 3 notice.
 Ɋ Designate a person to be stationed at or as near as possible to the 
closed location to notify all electors of the closure and of their new polling 
location.
 Ɋ In a municipality establishing one polling place only, the municipal clerk 
must establish a new polling location approved by the majority of the 
governing body and the municipal clerk.
A municipality may never close more than one-half of its polling places within 
30 days of an election, except in cases where a municipality only has one 
polling place. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(3)(b).
After an election and more than 30 days before the next election, the location of 
a polling place in a municipality may not be discontinued without the approval 
of the municipality’s governing body after a public hearing. At the hearing, the 
public must be given an opportunity to present testimony on the proposed 
discontinuation. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(3)(c).
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 7
Chapter 13.4: Relocating 
Polling Places Due to 
Emergencies
When it becomes impossible or inconvenient to hold an election at the 
designated location, state law permits election inspectors to adjourn to another 
location under specific procedures. Wis. Stat. § 7.37(1).
For more information on planning for relocation, see Chapter 12.3: 
“Contingency Planning Additional Topics.”  It is crucial to have an updated 
Election Day Emergency Response Plan that is reviewed before each election. 
Election inspectors should be aware of any emergency preparedness or 
contingency plans, and plans should be shared with your county clerk and 
local emergency response crews, such as the police, fire, and emergency 
government departments.
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 8
Chapter 13.5: Consolidating 
Polling Places for School 
District Special Elections
Please note that there are specific statutes that allow a school board to 
consolidate the number of polling places during a special election. Under 
Wis. Stat. § 120.06(9)(a), a school board has the authority to consolidate 
polling places for its school district elections when no other elections are 
being conducted in the municipality on that same date. In such cases, 
instead of maintaining multiple polling locations, the school board may 
designate a single polling place within the district for voters to cast their 
ballots. The school board must officially designate the consolidated polling 
place and provide proper public notice so that electors are informed of 
where to vote. Wis. Stat. § 120.06(9)(c).
Important Exception: The school board may not close or consolidate 
a polling place if ten percent or more of the voters voting in the last 
school board election voted at that polling place or if the polling place 
is located in a municipality which is located entirely within the school 
district. Wis. Stat. § 120.06(9)(b).
For more information on school district clerk responsibilities for school district 
special elections, see the Election Administration Manual for Wisconsin School 
District Clerks.
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 9
Chapter 13.6: Polling Place 
Supplies
A checklist outlining what materials and set-up the municipal clerk must 
provide for each polling place follows this section.
This chapter should be used when preparing for each election. See Chapter 
11.7: “Polling Place Set-Up” and Chapter 14.5: “Election Observers” for more 
information on polling place set-up.
Each polling place must be provided with the following:
 Ɋ Voting Booths
 Ɋ Electronic Voting Systems
 Ɋ Paper Ballots
 Ɋ Ballot Boxes
 Ɋ National Flag
 Ɋ Election Laws and Manuals
 Ɋ Tables and Chairs
 Ɋ Signs
 Ɋ Observer Area
 Ɋ Voter Information and Notices
 Ɋ Election Day Forms and Supplies
Sec. 13.6.1: Voting Booths
Every polling location is required to have at least one voting booth for every 200 
electors who voted in the last general election. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(2). Tip: Municipal 
clerks should review their participation from the previous election in preparation 
for each upcoming election to confirm that each polling place will have 
sufficient voting booths.
At least one voting booth must meet specific accessibility criteria. See Wis. Stat. 
§ 5.25(4)(a). One booth must be at least 30 inches wide with a writing surface 
between 28 and 34 inches high in order to meet accessibility standards, 
in addition to the accessible voting equipment. Knee clearance from the 
floor to the underside of the booth should be at least 27 inches. Toe/knee 
clearance from the front to the back of the booth should be at least 17 inches. 
These specific standards are set by federal regulations that implement the 
Americans with Disabilities Act. Specifically, these standards come from the ADA 
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 10
Accessibility Guidelines, which Title II and Title III ADA facilities (which includes 
polling places) must follow. For more detailed information on polling place 
accessibility, see Sec. 11.7.6: “Voting Area.”
Booths must have a surface on which to write and be sufficiently enclosed to 
ensure privacy for the elector. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(2). It is important to remember 
that the accessible booth must also be sufficiently enclosed to ensure privacy 
for the elector. This can be achieved by using a privacy shield or by positioning 
the table so that the face of the equipment is directed away from the view of 
the room.
Pencils or appropriate marking pens must be provided. For municipalities 
using electronic voting systems with optical scan ballots, the vendor of the 
voting equipment will advise which writing implements may be used. For hand 
count jurisdictions, most writing implements are sufficient, provided they make 
legible marks.
Sec. 13.6.2: Electronic Voting Systems
All municipalities with a population of 7,500 or more are required to use 
electronic voting systems. Wis. Stat. § 5.40(1).
Every polling location must have at least one piece of voting equipment that 
meets accessibility standards set forth by the WEC to allow individuals with 
disabilities to vote privately and independently. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(a).
For more information see Part 9: “Voting Equipment.”
Sec. 13.6.3: Paper Ballots
Even where voter-verified paper audit trail (VVPAT) systems are used, there must 
be a supply of paper ballots available at the polling place. See Wis. Stat. § 7.50(1)
(a) (“Only ballots provided by the person authorized to have them printed shall 
be cast and counted in any election.”). This paper ballot supply is for cases in 
which the electronic voting equipment breaks down/malfunctions, an elector 
votes provisionally, curbside, is assisted or challenged after the normal closing 
time due to court order.
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 11
Sec. 13.6.4: Ballot Boxes
For municipalities using hand-count paper ballots, one ballot box is required for 
each type of ballot used in the election. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(3). For descriptions of 
ballot styles, see Chapter 5.2: “Ballot Format & Style.”
Where direct recording electronic equipment primarily is used at the polling 
place, a single ballot box for hand-counted paper ballots (such as absentee, 
assisted, and challenged ballots) is required. Id.
For municipalities using electronic tabulators, the ballot box is contained within 
the tabulator, and is where the paper ballots are securely stored after they are 
inserted into the tabulator by the voter.
If electors from more than one reporting unit use the same polling place, there 
should be separate ballot boxes provided for each reporting unit, unless the 
wards have been combined for reporting purposes. Id.
The boxes should be clearly labeled to indicate which ballots are to be deposited.
There should be a suitable lock and key for each ballot box, and the ballot box 
must have an opening no larger than is sufficient to receive a single ballot 
or single folded ballot. Id. In municipalities that use hand count paper ballot 
packets, a separate discard box should be provided for the paper ballots not 
marked by the elector, and the discard box should also be locked.
Sec. 13.6.5: National Flag
The American flag must be displayed during all hours the polling place is open. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.35(1).
Best Practice: The flag can either be displayed on an outside pole or in 
the voting area.
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 12
Sec. 13.6.6: Election Laws And Manuals
Best Practice: The Commission recommends having paper copies of 
Chapters 5 through 12 of the Wisconsin State Statutes, as well as a copy 
of this manual, at all polling locations. Copies of these statutes and the 
manual can be downloaded from the agency website or ordered for a 
processing charge.
Sec. 13.6.7: Tables and Chairs
Clerks should ensure that there are enough tables and chairs for election 
inspectors to conduct their work. This need will vary depending on polling place 
size. Some electors may not be physically able to stand for extended periods of 
time. Chairs should also be available for these electors if they must stand in line. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(a).
Best Practice: Observers are entitled to use whatever chairs are 
available in the polling place, but municipal clerks are not required to 
purchase new chairs just for their use. Wis. Admin. Code § EL 4.03(3). 
Municipal clerks may include extra chairs, or tables, for observers in 
their discretion.
Sec. 13.6.8: Signs
Best Practice: Traffic in the polling place can be improved by 
posting “Enter,” “Exit,” and “Voter Registration” signs. Municipal 
clerks may prepare as many signs, and types of signs, as necessary 
to facilitate voting.
Signs indicating the location of an accessible entrance and marking the 
accessible path must be prominently posted and easy to read from the parking 
lot. See Wis. Stat. § 5.25(4)(a). For more detailed information on accessible signs 
at polling places, see Chapter 11.7: “Polling Place Set-Up.”
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 13
Best Practice: Signs containing written directions for poll workers 
can make the check-in process more efficient. This can be, but is not 
limited to, directions that instruct voters that they must give their 
name and address to the inspectors, provide proof of identification 
and sign the poll list can make the check-in process more efficient.
Sec. 13.6.9: Observer Area
A designated observation area at the polling place should permit observers 
to readily observe all public aspects of the voting process. When physically 
feasible, the observation area shall be not less than 3 feet, nor more than 
8 feet from the table at which electors are announcing their name and 
address and being issued a voter number and the Election Day Registration 
table. For more detailed information on election observers, see Chapter 14.5: 
“Election Observers.”
If necessary, additional observer areas may be established in other areas of 
the polling place to allow for observation of other public aspects of the voting 
process (challenges, ballot box security, etc.)
Best Practice: Municipal clerks may choose to include masking tape 
with their polling place supplies to clearly mark the observer areas in 
their polling places.
Please provide copies of the Commission’s Wisconsin Election Observers Rules-
at-a-Glance brochure and Elector Challenges brochures. Copies of each have 
been included in Appendix 1 for reference. These brochures should be provided 
to all observers upon check-in.
More information about how to handle election observers on Election Day see 
Chapter 14.5: “Election Observers.”
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 14
Sec. 13.6.10: Voter Information 
And Notices
All of the following notices, statements, and postings must be supplied to the 
polling place so that they can be posted and easily read by electors entering 
the polling place or waiting in line to vote. All Election Day notices, statements, 
and postings should be printed in size 18 font or larger to ensure readability. 
Copies of sample voter information notices can be found on elections.wi.gov.
Notices: The Type B and D notices must be posted. The Type C notice must also 
be posted, if applicable. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(a)1.
Sample Ballots: Two copies of each type of ballot. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(a)3.
Statement of Election Fraud (EL-111): This statement sets out the laws and 
applicable penalties for election fraud. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(a)2m.
Copy of the Election Fraud Laws: This requirement is met if the polling place 
contains a complete copy of Chapters 5 through 10 and 12 of the Wisconsin 
State Statutes. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(a)2.
Notice of Crossover Voting at a Partisan Primary (EL-112): This is a statement 
explaining the effect of crossover voting at a partisan primary and is posted at 
a partisan primary only. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(b).
Notice of Overvote (EL-113): This is a statement explaining the effect of overvoting 
the ballot and how to obtain a replacement ballot. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(b).
Notice of Crossover Voting at a Presidential Preference Vote (EL-114): This is a 
statement explaining the effect of crossover voting at a Presidential Preference 
Vote and is posted at that election only. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(b).
Voter Qualification Poster (EL-115): This notice explains the requirements for an 
individual to be a qualified elector. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(a)4b.
Voting Rights (EL-117): This notice provides general information on voting rights 
protected by federal law. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(a)4b.
First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 15
Contact Information (EL-118): This posting provides electors with contact 
information if they have concerns with the voting process. The blank sections 
should be filled in before Election Day by the municipal clerk. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(a)5.
Photo ID / Proof of Residence Information (EL-130): This posting provides 
electors with information regarding the state’s photo ID and proof of residence 
requirements. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(a)4a.
Ward Maps: A ward map clearly indicating all the wards in the municipality 
served by that polling place must be prominently displayed. Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(c).
Best Practice: Street Directory: A street directory that indicates which 
streets are in each ward along with the location of the polling place in 
each ward is recommended. This information can be found in WisVote 
under “Maps.”
Sec. 13.6.11: Election Day 
Forms And Supplies
Election Day forms and supplies are provided by the county, municipal, or 
school district clerk depending on the offices on the ballot.
Ballots and Sample Ballots: Two sample ballots for each ballot style should be 
posted at the polling place. See Wis. Stat. § 5.35(6)(a)3. For more information on 
preparing ballots, see Part 5: “Ballots.”
Ballot Bags (EL-101): A ballot bag/container should be provided for each ballot 
style. See Wis. Stat. § 7.51(3)(a).
Best Practice: For example, for municipalities that hand-count paper 
ballots, there should be (per reporting unit) one ballot bag for county, 
state, and federal ballots; one ballot bag for municipal ballots; one 
ballot bag for school district ballots; and one ballot bag for each 
referenda and special district ballot.
Where optical scan or direct recording electronic ballots are used, only 
one ballot bag

First Edition, June 2026 Polling Places & Supplies 13 – 17
Sec. 13.6.13: Frequently 
Asked Questions
Q Are polling places required to be in public buildings?
A No. Polling places should be in public buildings unless the governing body 
determines that the use of a nonpublic building better serves the needs of 
the voters. Wis. Stat. § 5.25(1).
Q Can the names of write-in candidates be posted at the polling place or in 
voting booths?
A No, names of known write-in candidates are not to be posted at the 
polling place. This is to avoid the perception of electioneering (which is 
prohibited) as even a list of candidates could be seen as activity which 
is intended to influence voting at an election. Wis. Stat. § 12.03(4). The 
Commission’s guidance has been that election inspectors may only give 
the names of write-in candidates when specifically asked by a voter. In 
those cases, answers must be given carefully to avoid the appearance of 
endorsing or announcing a write-in candidate to other voters.
The Commission recommends that the municipal clerk provide the election 
inspectors with a list of registered write-in candidates to give to any voters that 
request this information. This list should be kept in a folder or another way that 
guarantees it is out of sight of the voters. Further, election inspectors may not 
advise voters if any ballot candidates no longer wish to run for office, even if 
asked by a voter.

ELECTOR 
CHALLENGES
What a challenge 
looks like
When a voter is challenged, the 
election inspector will:
 ● Ask both the person 
challenging and the 
person being challenged, if 
present, to take an oath.
 ● The person being challenged 
will be asked questions 
to determine if they are 
allowed to vote.
 ● The inspectors will use the 
procedures spelled out in 
statute and administrative 
code to determine if the 
challenged elector will 
be issued a ballot.
WIS. STAT. § 6.92; WIS. ADMIN. CODE EL §§ 9.02 – 9.06.
What are Elector 
Challenges?
Any elector may challenge for 
cause any person offering to 
vote whom the elector knows 
or suspects is not a qualified 
elector. WIS. STAT . § 6.925.
A voting challenge is when 
someone claims a person is not 
qualified to vote, whether they are 
voting in person or absentee.
Who Can Make a Challenge?
Only eligible voters (called electors) 
can challenge someone for cause.
Challengers must be:
 ● Over the age of 18
 ● U.S. citizens
 ● Residents of Wisconsin
 ● Eligible to vote in Wisconsin 
(they do not need to be 
registered to vote)
WIS. STAT. § 6.925; WIS. ADMIN. CODE EL §§ 9.02 – 9.06.

Commission

Cover photo by Michael Newman via Creative 
Commons.
Scan the code to view this 
document online: 
elections.wi.gov/elector-
challenges
What is a proper 
challenge?
All challenges must be “for cause.” 
The term “for cause” has a specific 
legal meaning, and it relates to the 
qualifications of the challenged voter.
Specifically, a voter may only be 
challenged for the following reasons:
 ● The elector is not a U.S. citizen.
 ● They are not 18 or older.
 ● They do not reside in 
the district where they 
are trying to vote.
 ● They have a felony 
conviction and are still 
serving their sentence.
 ● They have been adjudicated 
incompetent by a judge 
with a loss of voting rights.
 ● They already voted in 
the same election.
WIS. STAT. § 6.925; WIS. ADMIN. CODE EL §§ 9.02, 9.04.
What cannot be challenged?
Challenges based on race, ethnicity, 
not speaking English, or other 
unsubstantiated claims are not 
allowed.
An elector cannot challenge:
 ● absentee certificate 
and application
 ● adherence to other 
voting requirements
Absentee Challenges
If someone is voting by absentee 
ballot, their qualifications can still be 
challenged by another elector, using 
the same process as if they were 
voting in person.
WIS. STAT. § 6.93.
Administering Challenges
If a person is challenged as unqualified by an elector, election inspectors 
must follow the procedures in Wis. Admin. Code EL §§ 9.02 – 9.06.
Inspectors should use form EL-104c to administer the challenge.
One of the inspectors may administer the oath or affirmation to the 
challenged and challenging electors and ask the electors appropriate 
questions to test the elector’s qualifications.
WIS. STAT. § 6.92.
Penalties for Misuse
Any elector who abuses the right 
to challenge under Wis. Stat. § 
6.925 may be subject to sanctions 
available to inspectors under Wis. 
Stat. § 7.41(3). The chief inspector 
of a polling place or the municipal 
clerk may order the removal of any 
such person if the person disrupts 
operations or violates Wis. Stats. §§ 
12.03(2) or 12.035. Wis. Stat. § 7.41(3).
WIS. STAT. §§ 7.41(3), WIS. ADMIN. CODE EL § 9.02.
Wis. Election Observers 
Rules-at-a-Glance
This guide presents the main rules 
for election observers. Situations 
may require consulting Wis. Stat. § 
7.41 and Wis. Admin. Code Chapter EL 
4., but this guide provides what most 
observers need to follow to observe 
an election. 
Members of the public (except 
candidates) may observe election 
activity at polling places, municipal 
clerk offices (that are in public 
buildings) or alternate sites, 
absentee ballot board of canvassers 
sites, central count sites, recount 
sites, and facilities being served by 
Special Voting Deputies.
Absentee Ballot Canvasser Sites:  
Observation is allowed during the 
hours an absentee ballot board of 
canvassers is meeting to process 
absentee ballots, starting no later 
than the zeroing of the tabulators. 
Observers may create and transmit 
photos, videos, or audio recordings.
SVD Facilities:  Only one observer 
appointed by each of the two major 
political parties may accompany 
each pair of Special Voting Deputies 
when they are administering 
absentee voting. Observers must 
comply with any visitor requirements 
of the facility. Observers cannot 
enter a voter’s private room, and 
the voter may opt to close the door 
when voting.
Central Count:  Observation is allowed 
during the hours ballots are tabulated 
at a central counting location. 
Observers may create and transmit 
photos, videos, or audio recordings.
Recounts:  Observation is allowed 
during the hours when recount 
activities are happening. The 
petitioner, opposing candidates, 
interested persons, and associated 
counsel are not observers and not 
subject to these rules. Observers may 
create and transmit photos, videos, 
or audio recordings.
After Voting Activity Ends:
Candidates may be present, 
and individuals remaining at 
the location may create and 
transmit photos, videos, and audio 
recordings if such activity does not 
disrupt any election administration 
activity, including the canvass 
meeting at a polling place.
Specific Locations:
Polling Place:  Observation begins 
at the earlier of 7: 00 a.m. or when 
election equipment is zeroed out, 
and ends at the later of 8:  00 p.m. 
or when the last voter in line has 
voted. When voting concludes, 
observers may remain to view the 
canvass meeting. Photos, videos, 
and audio recordings cannot be 
created or transmitted until the 
public canvass begins.
Clerk’s Office or Alternate Sites:  
Observation is allowed during 
the hours of in-person absentee 
voting (IPAV) in the clerk’s office (if 
in a public building) or at alternate 
sites. Observers may view the initial 
securing of ballots returned at the 
location during IPAV hours.

Observers must:
 ● Notify the designated election 
official that they wish to observe 
 ● Show photo ID with the observer’s 
name, sign the observer log, and 
print their name, address, and any 
organization being represented
 ● Follow the directives established by 
the designated election official
 ● Keep conversation to a minimum
 ● Wear an observer badge or sticker
 ● Depart the location if instructed to 
do so when the number of observers 
representing the same organization 
is limited due to space concerns 
 ● Following a warning, cease conduct 
violating the observer rules, and if 
then asked to leave due to violating 
the rules, depart the location. The 
observer will receive a written order 
stating the reason for removal 
before departing.
Observers may:
 ● Observe all public aspects of the 
voting process
 ● Observe from any observer area, 
which must be accessible and 3 to 8 
feet from each table for registration, 
check-in, absentee certificate 
processing, and ballot remaking. 
 ● Bring a chair, mobility equipment, 
or disability aids, and use available 
chairs and restrooms at the location
 ● Move between observer areas
 ● Observe absentee ballot certificate 
envelopes set aside to be rejected 
 ● Ask an election official to repeat, 
once, a name or address
 ● Direct questions to the designated 
election official
 ● If the observer is an elector, challenge 
a voter for cause under Wis. Admin. 
Code Ch. EL 9.
 ● Take notes, text, and email
 ● Assist a voter who requests the 
observer’s assistance to vote
 ● When not disruptive, view the poll 
list or observer log
Observers may not:
 ● Engage in electioneering, which 
means any activity intended to 
influence voting at an election, 
including displaying or discussing 
anything related to a candidate, 
referenda question, or political party
 ● Post or distribute any election-
related material, or imply that the 
observer is an election official
 ● Engage in loud, boisterous, or 
disruptive behavior, or initiate a 
conversation with a voter
 ● Make audio or visual calls
 ● Record any voted ballots or anyone 
returning or correcting an absentee 
certificate envelope 
 ● Create or transmit any photos, 
videos, or audio recordings unless 
expressly permitted (see “Specific 
Locations” section)
 ● See or hear how an elector’s votes
 ● Handle original election documents or 
view confidential information, including 
personally identifiable numbers (birth 
date, social security, bank account, 
etc.), confidential voter information, 
voted ballots, registration forms, proof 
of residence documents, and IDs
Communications media: individuals 
who communicate to the designated 
election official that they intend to 
record or report information outside 
of the voting area, and must identify 
themselves and any organization 
represented to the designated election 
official. Video and still camera use is 
allowed outside the voting area only 
at the discretion of the designated 
election official and within the limits 
set by that official, and they may not 
record confidential information or 
disrupt the election. Communications 
media members are not observers 
unless they sign in as an observer.
Polling Place Accessibility 
Assessments: Certain individuals 
are authorized by the Commission 
to monitor compliance with 
accessibility standards. Accessibility 
Reviewers are not observers.

Election Day
Election Day Roles; Setting Up and Opening the Polls; Observers; 
Registration; Challenges; Poll Books; Voting Procedure; Voting 
with Assistance; Curbside Voting; Provisional Ballots; Common

Overvotes & Crossvotes; Closing the Polls; End of Night; Local Board of 
Canvassers; Transmitting Results; Municipal Board of Canvassers
Part 14 contains the entirety of what used to be the Election Day manual. It 
contains all election administration topics election inspectors will need for 
Election Day, from start to finish. It can be printed or saved as a separate 
resource specific to everything clerks and election inspectors need on 
Election Day.
