EL-106 (Rev. 2016-10) Board of Canvassers Report – Tabular Statement
Completing the Tabular Statement of Votes Cast
Instructions for Municipal Canvass:
• Write the name of your municipality, the kind of election: primary, spring, or special election, etc., and the date of the
election in the heading.
• Enter the complete name of the office with the seat or district number in the shaded area.
• List the names of the candidates for the office in ballot order below the shaded area.
• Make sure that all wards or ward combinations are listed in proper numericalorder in the left hand column. The
smallest number in a combination determines the order. (Example: Wards 1&4; Wards 2,6 & 7; and Wards 3&5.)
• For each reporting unit, list the number of votes cast for each candidate.
• Don’t forget the write-in votes - they must be listed individually by name.
• Enter the total number of votes cast for each candidate in the Total Votes Casts – Candidates column.
• Enter the total number of votes cast (not voters!) for each office in the Total Votes Cast-Office column. This total
is the sum of the votetotals for each candidate plus the write-ins.
Instructions for County Canvass:
• Write the name of your county, the kind of election: primary, partisan primary, spring/general election, or special,
etc., and the date of the election in the heading.
• A separate report must be completed for each political party in a partisan primary only. Write in the name of the
political party on the line provided.
• Enter the complete name of the office with the branch or district number in the shaded area.
• List the names of the candidates for the office in ballot order below the shaded area.
• Please list all municipalities and wards in the correct order in the left hand column. The smallest number in a
combination determines the order. (Example: Wards 1&4; Wards 2,6 & 7; and Wards 3&5.)
1. Towns, alphabetically, wards numerically.
2. Villages, alphabetically, wards numerically.
3. Cities, alphabetically, wards numerically.
• Make sure that all wards or ward combinations are listed along with the municipality name. If a municipalityis
divided by wards, but combinesthem for voting purposes and reports onetotal, you must still identify the numbers
of the wards being reported. (Example: Town of Anywhere, Wards 1&2. If a municipality is not divided by wards
do not list “Ward 1.”)
• For each reporting unit, list the number of votes cast for each candidate.
• Don’t forget the scattering column - if there are no write-in votes for a reporting unit, list 0.
• Enter the total number of votes cast for each candidate in the Total Votes Casts – Candidates column.
• Enter the total number of votes cast (not voters!) for each office in the Total Votes Cast-Office column. This total
is the sum of the vote totals for each candidate plus the scattering.
EL-106 (Rev. 2016-10) Instructions: Board of Canvassers Report
Notes for Municipal and County Clerks:
Combining Reporting Units. A municipality may provide for combined wards by resolution up to 30 days before the
spring primary or election, if your population is under 35,000. It’s important to remember that for the spring primary
and the spring election, wards in a municipality may be combined for judicial offices even though separate results may
be required for county, municipal, or school districtoffices. The wards being combined must use the same polling 
place.
Reporting for annexations requires special attention. As long as the area being annexed belongs to the same
representative districts, i.e., congressional, legislative, and county supervisory districts, as the adjacent area to which
it’s being annexed, then the annexed area is reported together with the adjacent area using the same ward number. But
if the annexed area has different representative districts from its adjacent area or crosses county lines, the municipality
is required by law to create a separate ward giving it the next consecutive number. All election results from this new
ward must be reported under the new ward number.

Election Inspectors
• Provisional ballots of voters unable to provide the Wisconsin driver license or state identification card number
required by Wis. Stat. §6.55(2)(a)1., and/or unable to provide an acceptable form of photo identification pursuant
to Wis. Stat. § 6.79 (2)(a), shall be kept in their certificate envelopes.
• These ballots may not be counted, unless the voter returns with the required Wisconsin driver license or state
identification card number and/or an acceptable form of photo identification before the polls close.
• The names of provisional voters are assigned a serial number (PV#__) that is recorded on the registration list,
the back of the ballot, the Provisional Ballot Certificate Envelope (EL-123), the Provisional Ballot Reporting
Form (EL-123r), the EL-123is “Provisional Voting Information Sheet” for the elector and listed on the
Inspectors’ Statement (EL-104).
• The back of the ballot should be marked “Section 6.97,” voted by the elector, placed in the completed
provisional ballot certificate envelope and returned to the election inspectors.
• The inspectors make a notation (including the PV#) that the voter was issued a provisional ballot on the
Inspectors’ Statement (EL-104).
• The completed provisional ballot certificate envelopes containing the voted ballots are placed in this carrier
envelope. This carrier envelope and any other provisional ballot carrier envelopes must also be placed in a
separate ballot bag, secured with a tamper-evident seal and labeled with “Provisional Ballots.”
Municipal Clerks
• The municipal clerk shall promptly notify the appropriate boards of canvassers that the clerk has provisional
ballots that may be counted if the voter provides the required Wisconsin driver license or state identification
card number and/or an acceptable form of photo identification by 4:00 p.m. on the Friday following the election.

Wisconsin Election Observers 
Rules-at-a-Glance
This guide presents the main rules 
for election observers. Situations 
may require consulting Wis. Stat. § 
7.41 and Wis. Admin. Code Chapter 
EL 4., but this guide provides what 
most observers need to follow to 
observe an election. 
Members of the public (except 
candidates) may observe 
election activity at polling places, 
municipal clerk offices (that are 
in public buildings) or alternate 
sites, absentee ballot board of 
canvassers sites, central count sites, 
recount sites, and facilities being 
served by Special Voting Deputies.
 
Absentee Ballot Canvasser Sites:  
Observation is allowed during the 
hours an absentee ballot board of 
canvassers is meeting to process 
absentee ballots, starting no later 
than the zeroing of the tabulators. 
Observers may create and transmit 
photos, videos, or audio recordings.
SVD Facilities:  Only one observer 
appointed by each of the two major 
political parties may accompany 
each pair of Special Voting Deputies 
when they are administering absentee 
voting. Observers must comply with 
any visitor requirements of the facility. 
Observers cannot enter a voter’s 
private room, and the voter may opt to 
close the door when voting.
Central Count:  Observation is allowed 
during the hours ballots are tabulated 
at a central counting location. 
Observers may create and transmit 
photos, videos, or audio recordings.
Recounts:  Observation is allowed 
during the hours when recount 
activities are happening. The 
petitioner, opposing candidates, 
interested persons, and associated 
counsel are not observers and not 
subject to these rules. Observers may 
create and transmit photos, videos, or 
audio recordings.
After Voting Activity Ends: 
Candidates may be present, and 
individuals remaining at the location 
may create and transmit photos, 
videos, and audio recordings if such 
activity does not disrupt any election 
administration activity, including the 
canvass meeting at a polling place.
Specific Locations:
Polling Place:  Observation begins 
at the earlier of 7:00 a.m. or when 
election equipment is zeroed out, and 
ends at the later of 8:00 p.m. or when 
the last voter in line has voted. When 
voting concludes, observers may 
remain to view the canvass meeting. 
Photos, videos, and audio recordings 
cannot be created or transmitted until 
the public canvass begins.
Clerk’s Office or Alternate Sites:  
Observation is allowed during 
the hours of in-person absentee 
voting (IPAV) in the clerk’s office (if 
in a public building) or at alternate 
sites. Observers may view the initial 
securing of ballots returned at the 
location during IPAV hours.Wisconsin Elections 
Commission
WEC Helpdesk: 
608-266-8005
WEC Helpdesk e-mail: 
elections@wi.gov
EL-109R December 2025

Observers must:
 ● Notify the designated election 
official that they wish to observe 
 ● Show photo ID with the observer’s 
name, sign the observer log, and 
print their name, address, and any 
organization being represented
 ● Follow the directives established by 
the designated election official
 ● Keep conversation to a minimum
 ● Wear an observer badge or sticker
 ● Depart the location if instructed 
to do so when the number of 
observers representing the same 
organization is limited due to 
space concerns 
 ● Following a warning, cease conduct 
violating the observer rules, and if 
then asked to leave due to violating 
the rules, depart the location. The 
observer will receive a written order 
stating the reason for removal 
before departing.
Observers may:
 ● Observe the public aspects of the 
voting process
 ● Observe from any observer area, 
which must be accessible and 3 to 8 
feet from each table for registration, 
check-in, absentee certificate 
processing, and ballot remaking
 ● Bring a chair, mobility equipment, 
or disability aids, and use available 
chairs and restrooms at the location
 ● Move between observer areas
 ● Observe absentee ballot certificate 
envelopes set aside to be rejected
 ● Ask an election official to repeat, 
once, a name or address
 ● Direct questions to the designated 
election official 
 ● If the observer is an elector, 
challenge a voter for cause under 
Wis. Admin. Code Ch. EL 9.
 ● Take notes, text, and email
 ● Assist a voter who requests the 
observer’s assistance to vote
 ● When not disruptive, view the poll 
list or observer log
Observers may not:
 ● Engage in electioneering, which 
means any activity intended to 
influence voting at an election, 
including displaying or discussing 
anything related to a candidate, 
referenda question, or political party
 ● Post or distribute any election-
related material, or imply that the 
observer is an election official
 ● Engage in loud, boisterous, or 
disruptive behavior, or initiate a 
conversation with a voter
 ● Make audio or visual calls
 ● Record any voted ballots or anyone 
returning or correcting an absentee 
certificate envelope
 ● Create or transmit any photos, 
videos, or audio recordings unless 
expressly permitted (see “Specific 
Locations” section)
 ● See or hear how an elector votes
 ● Handle original election documents 
or view confidential information, 
including personally identifiable 
numbers (birth date, social security, 
bank account etc.) confidential 
voter information, voted ballots, 
registration forms, proof of residence 
documents, and IDs
Communications Media:  Individuals 
who communicate to the designated 
election official that they intend to 
record or report information outside 
of the voting area, and must identify 
themselves and any organization 
represented to the designated election 
official. Video and still camera use is 
allowed outside the voting area only 
at the discretion of the designated 
election official and within the limits 
set by that official, and they may not 
record confidential information or 
disrupt the election. Communications 
media members are not observers 
unless they sign in as an observer.
Polling Place Accessibility 
Assessments:  Certain individuals 
are authorized by the Commission 
to monitor compliance with 
accessibility standards. Accessibility 
Reviewers are not observers.

INELIGIBLE VOTER INFORMATION SHEET
You are being given this informational sheet today because your name and date of birth match a name 
and date of birth on a list of offenders who are currently serving a sentence for a felony conviction.  If 
this information is correct, you are ineligible to vote in Wisconsin and must wait until you have 
completed the terms of your felony sentence including any terms of extended supervision, probation, or 
parole.
• If the information was correct, but you have completed your sentence, have been discharged, or 
your sentence has been vacated, your registration or absentee ballot will be accepted if you can 
provide the poll workers or clerk with a copy of the Discharge Certificate which you received 
from your agent when you were discharged.  Page 2 of the certificate will contain a statement 
that restores your right to vote.  
If you do not have a copy of your discharge certificate, you may obtain one by contacting the 
Department of Corrections (DOC) Master Records Line at (608) 240-3750.  It will take DOC at 
least 24 hours to make a copy of the discharge certificate.  The DOC records office will need the 
address, email, or fax number where a copy of the discharge certificate can be sent.
• If the information on the list is incorrect or you maintain that you are not a felon, you will be 
permitted to register and to vote.  Your registration and any ballot that you cast will be marked as 
“ineligible to vote per Department of Corrections,” until you take steps to resolve the issue with
the Department of Corrections. Your ballot will also be challenged by the election inspectors at 
your polling place.
If you believe that your name and date of birth have been falsely matched or that you may be the 
victim of identity theft, contact the Wisconsin Department of Justice Crime Information Bureau 
(CIB).  CIB provides a process for clarifying a false match.  For assistance with this process 
please call: 
CIB Front Desk (608) 266-7314
Record Check Unit Supervisor (608) 266-9398
After you have resolved the issue contact your municipal clerk and provide them any documentation you 
have confirming that you are not currently serving a sentence for a felony conviction.

PROVISIONAL VOTING INFORMATION SHEET
You are being given a provisional ballot today because one of the following situations applies:
❑ You are unable or unwilling to list your Wisconsin driver license or identification card number
on your voter registration application.
❑ You are unable or unwilling to present an acceptable proof of identification.
Your provisional ballot number is PV#____________________________.
Your provisional ballot will not count unless you provide the poll workers with the required information 
before the polling place closes at 8:00 p.m. tonight, or you provide the required information to the 
municipal clerk by 4:00 p.m. the Friday after the election.
If you need to provide your Wisconsin driver license or identification card number, you may contact the 
municipal clerk using the information below no later than 4:00 p.m. Friday.
If you need to present an acceptable proof of identification, you must present your proof of identification 
to the municipal clerk no later than 4:00 p.m. Friday.  Acceptable forms of proof of identification may 
be found on the back side of this handout.

Acceptable Forms of Proof of Identification
The following photo IDs are acceptable f or voting purposes, and 
can be unexpired or expired after the date of the most recent 
general election:
▪ A Wisconsin DOT-issued driver license, even if driving
privileges are revoked or suspended
▪ A Wisconsin DOT-issued identification card
▪ Military ID card issued by a U.S. uniformed service (includes
Military ID cards issued to a retired service member)
▪ A U.S. passport book or card
The following photo IDs are also acceptable for voting purposes, 
but must be unexpired:
▪ A certificate of naturalization that was issued not earlier than 
two years before the date of an election at which it is presented
▪ A driver license receipt issued by Wisconsin DOT (valid for 45 
days)
▪ An identification card receipt issued by Wisconsin DOT (valid 
for 45 days)
▪ A temporary identification card receipt issued by Wisconsin 
DOT through the Identification Petition Process (IDPP) (valid 
for 180 days).
▪ A photo identification card issued by a Wisconsin accredited 
university or college that contains the following:
o Date of Issuance
o Signature of Student
o Expiration date no later than two years after date of 
issuance (can still be used if expired).
o If the university or college ID is expired, the ID must
be accompanied by a separate document that proves 
enrollment.
▪ A veteran’s photo identification card issued by the Department 
of Veterans Affairs
The following photo ID is acceptable for voting purposes,
regardless of the expiration date:
▪ An identification card issued by a federally recognized Indian
tribe in Wisconsin.
NOTE:  A photo ID without an expiration date is considered
unexpired.
Falsification of information on this form is punishable under Wisconsin law as a Class I felony

1 • If you did not check every box in this section, you are not eligible to vote in Wisconsin.  Do not complete this form.
• Provide your current and complete name.  Please provide your name as it appears on your WI driver license or state-issued 
ID card (Box 7), if applicable, and the proof of residence document you provided in Box 8. 
• Provide your month, day, and year of birth.  
• Providing your phone number and/or email address is optional and is subject to open records requests.  This information 
may be used by your municipal clerk to contact you about your voter record or absentee ballot request. 
• Provide your home address (legal voting residence) in Wisconsin.
• Provide your full street name, including the type (St, Ave, etc.) and any pre- and/or post-directional (N, S, etc.).
• You may not enter a PO Box as a residential address.  A rural route box without a number should not be used.
• A “military elector” is a person, or the spouse or dependent of a person who is a member of a uniformed service or merchant 
marine, a civilian officially attached to a uniformed service and serving outside the United States, or a Peace Corp volunteer.  
Military electors are not required to register as a prerequisite to voting at any election. 
• A “permanent overseas elector” is a US citizen, at least 18 years old, who does not qualify as a resident of this state, but 
who either last lived in this state, or whose parent last lived in this state immediately prior to the parent’s departure from the 
United States, and who is not registered to vote in any other state.
• If your mailing address is different from your home address, provide it here.  A PO Box is acceptable as a mailing address.  
Overseas electors should provide their complete overseas address here.
• Provide full previous name if changed and/or previous address if you have been registered to vote anywhere in the U.S.
• If you have a valid and unexpired WI driver license or WI DOT ID: provide that number.  If you do not know your number, 
please call (608) 266-2353 to get it.
• If you have an expired, canceled, suspended, or revoked WI driver license or WI DOT ID: you must provide the last four 
digits of your Social Security number.  In addition, you may also provide the number on your license or ID (optional). 
• If you have never been issued a WI driver license or WI DOT ID: provide the last four digits of your Social Security number.
• If you do not have a WI driver license or WI DOT ID nor a Social Security Number: please check the appropriate box.
If you are registering to vote on Election Day and have been issued a WI driver license or ID, but are unable or unwilling to 
provide the number, your vote will not be counted unless you provide the number to the election inspectors by 8:00 p.m. on 
Election Day or to your municipal clerk by 4:00 p.m. the Friday following Election Day.  
Assistant:  If you are unable to sign this form due to a physical disability, you may have an assistant do so on your behalf.  That 
assistant must provide his or her signature and address in the space provided.  By signing, the assistant certifies that he or she 
signed the form at your request.

Certificate of Registration Instructions 
 
General Instructions: 
Please Review Fully 
 
This form is used during the late registration period (between 20 days before the election 
and the day of the election) to certify that the voter is registered, since the voter’s  
registration information will not appear on the Poll List.  This form is completed after the 
voter completes a valid Voter Registration Application (EL-131) and the clerk approves the 
application. 
The municipal clerk completes this form and gives the top portion to the voter.  The voter gives 
the form to the Election Inspectors at the polling location on Election Day. 
Since the municipal clerk should keep a copy of the form, the bottom portion has been designed to 
duplicate the top portion.  The municipal clerk may also copy the completed form or use pressure-
sensitive or carbon paper to allow for a duplicate to be completed.  
1 Polling location: Complete the proper polling location. 
2 Ward #:  Complete the proper ward number. 
3 Voting #: Official Use Only.  Voter # is completed by the Election Inspectors at the polling location when voter 
presents the form to them. 
4 Voter Registration #:  Office Use only. The unique number given to a voter in WisVote. This is used when information 
is entered into WisVote at time of late registration. 
5 Certificate #:  The serial number issued by the municipal clerk when filing a late registration, i.e. starting with #1, #2, 
#3 and so forth.  The clerk’s agent (provider) issues a serial number followed by “c,”  i.e. #1c,  #2c, #3c and so
forth. 
6 Municipality:  Complete name of municipality. 
7 County:  Complete name of county in which municipality is located. 
8 Name, Address, City:  Complete name and voting address of voter. 
9 Election Date:  Complete the date of the primary or election event. 
10 Municipality Name:  Fill in the complete name of the municipality. 
11 Date:  Fill in the date the form was completed. 
Signature:  
By signing this form, the municipal clerk certifies that the elector has completed the voter registration application  
and directs the Election Inspectors to permit the elector to vote for the election to held on the date indicated on the  
form.

EL-141 (Rev.2020-07) 
The information on this form is required by Wis. Stat. § 6.15. 
 
 
 
INSTRUCTIONS FOR 
      APPLICATION FOR PRESIDENTIAL BALLOT - NEW WISCONSIN RESIDENT 
  
Any person who is a United States citizen, at least 18 years old on E lection Day, who has moved into the State 
of Wisconsin less than 28  days before the presidential election, and is ineligible to vote absentee in his or her 
state of previous residence, may vote for president and vice president by completing this application, providing 
acceptable proof of residence and providing acceptable voter ID. 
 
A new Wisconsin resident making application for a presidential ballot need not be registered. 
 
A new Wisconsin resident can complete this application and vote for president and vice president either by 
absentee ballot in the office of the municipal clerk, or by voting at the polling place on Election Day. 
 
In addition to com pleting this application form ( EL-141), providing a acceptable proof of residence  and voter 
ID, the elector also must complete a voter registration cancellation card (EL-139). 
 
Both of these items are provided by the municipal clerk.  They also can be obta ined from an election inspector 
at the polling place on Election Day. 
 
    PROCEDURE FOR MAKING APPLICATION IN THE MUNICIPAL CLERK'S OFFICE 
 
1. The new Wisconsin resident shows acceptable proof of residence  and acceptable voter ID, completes the 
application form (EL-141), and the voter registration cancellation card (EL-139). 
 
2. If the new Wisconsin resident chooses to vote an absentee presidential ballot in the clerk's office, the 
municipal clerk provides the person with an absentee ballot certificate envelope ( EL-122) and a presidential 
ballot.  The clerk must keep a list which includes the name, address, date of application, and the date on 
which the ballot was cast. 
 
3. If the new Wisconsin resident making this application chooses to go to the polling place on E lection Day to 
vote, the municipal clerk must provide the person with a copy of the completed application form ( EL-141) 
to take to the polling place. 
 
4. The municipal clerk must keep a separate list of all new Wisconsin residents who vote under the provision s 
of Wis. Stat. § 6.15.  The list must include the person's name, address, and date of application, and if voting 
by absentee ballot, the date of receipt of the voted ballot. 
 
5. The municipal clerk shall send the voter registration cancellation card ( EL-139) to the elector's municipality 
of previous residence. 
 
        PROCEDURE FOR VOTING FOR PRESIDENT AT THE POLLING PLACE 
 
1. The new Wisconsin resident must show acceptable proof of residence  and voter ID , complete this 
application (EL-141), and complete the voter registration cancellation card ( EL-139) at the polling place, or 
bring a copy of the application form that was completed in the municipal clerk's office. 
 
2. The election inspector will provide the person with a paper ballot to vote for the offices of pre sident and 
vice president only. 
 
3. The election inspectors shall indicate on the voter list next to the new Wisconsin resident's name that he or 
she received only a presidential ballot. 
 
4. The application form ( EL-141) and the voter registration cancellation c ard ( EL-139) are returned to the 
municipal clerk along with the voter lists and other election documents.

Part 15 
Post-Election Activities
Routing of Election Materials; Rehabilitating Provisional Ballots; County 
Board of Canvassers; Canvass Reporting System (CRS); Reconciliation; 
Commission Certification; Certificates of Election; EDR Postcards.
Election Day does not end when the polls close. Clerks immediately begin 
preparing materials for the various boards of canvassers, who meet after 
each election to publicly canvass the returns of the election. Clerks also 
complete important post-election data work like reconciliation and handling 
of Election Day Registration postcards. 
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 1
Chapter 15.1: Organization & 
Routing of Election Materials
Most election materials are routed back to the municipal clerk’s office after polls 
close on Election Night, but the municipal clerk must take additional steps after 
the election to prepare and further route some materials.
Sec. 15.1.1: Search for Uncounted 
Absentee Ballots
Before the Municipal Board of Canvassers (MBOC) convenes, the municipal 
clerk and their staff should examine every drop box, courier bag, carrier 
envelope, supply tote, ballot bin, tabulator, laptop bag, and any other vessel 
coming back from a polling place or “central count” to ensure that no 
absentee ballots were overlooked. This search should be performed before the 
MBOC convenes because if ballots were accidentally not counted, the issue 
can likely be resolved by the MBOC.
Sec. 15.1.2: Materials Routed 
to School District Clerk
The municipal clerk must route the following materials to the school district clerk 
(when there are school district races on the ballot) no later than 4:00 p.m. the 
day after the election. Wis. Stat. § 7.51(5)(b).
 Ɋ School district ballots (if nonconsolidated ballots are used)
 Ɋ Original Tally Sheet (EL-105) listing school district results
 Ɋ A copy of the voting equipment results tape (if any)
 Ɋ One copy of the Inspectors’ Statement (EL-104) plus accompanying 
documentation
 Ɋ A certified copy of the signed poll list (EL-107 and EL-107S)
 Ɋ A copy of the Provisional Ballot Reporting Form (EL-123r)
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 2
Sec. 15.1.3: Materials Routed 
to the County Clerk
The municipal clerk must route the following materials to the county clerk 
no later than 4:00 p.m. the day after the election. Wis. Stat. § 7.51(5)(b):
 Ɋ Ballot bags or containers with all federal, state, county, and technical 
college ballots
 Ɋ The brown carrier envelope (EL-102) containing rejected absentee ballots
 Ɋ The white carrier envelope (EL-103) containing used certificate envelopes 
from absentee voters
 Ɋ One copy of the Inspectors’ Statement (EL-104) and accompanying 
documentation
 Ɋ One original Tally Sheet (EL-105) for presidential, congressional, state, 
legislative, judicial, and county offices, as well as state, county, and 
technical college referenda
 Ɋ A copy of the voting equipment results tape (if any)
 Ɋ One original poll list including the supplemental poll list (EL-107S) that 
includes the voters’ signatures
 Ɋ A copy of the Provisional Ballot Reporting Form (EL-123R)
If the municipality is a “central count” jurisdiction, the municipality can 
deliver materials to the county clerk by 4 p.m. on the second day following 
the election. Wis. Stat. § 7.51(5)(b).
Sec. 15.1.4: Organize And 
Prepare for Municipal Board of 
Canvassers (MBOC) Meeting
In addition to routing required materials to other clerks, municipal clerks 
should also prepare their own materials and information for their meeting of 
the Municipal Board of Canvassers.
For detailed guidance on how to organize and prepare for the MBOC, see 
Chapter 14.27: “Municipal Boards of Canvassers.”
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 3
Sec. 15.1.5: Retention of 
Election Materials
State law directs that “each clerk shall retain ballots, statements, tally sheets, 
or envelopes” they receive after the election until destruction is authorized. 
Wis. Stat. §§ 7.51(5)(b), 7.23(1). However, this statute was written before the 
common use of consolidated ballots. Prior to consolidated ballots, it made 
sense for each clerk to keep their respective ballots, but in jurisdictions where 
all races appear on a single ballot, the question of who should retain election 
materials is more complicated.
Many county clerks retain election materials like ballots and used certificate 
envelopes because they are at the end of the materials routing road, and 
because they often have more space and capacity for document storage.
Municipal clerks, county clerks, and school district clerks should have a clear 
understanding of where ballots will be stored and under what conditions clerks 
can access those ballots in the future if needed.
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 4
Chapter 15.2: Rehabilitating 
Provisional Ballots
Municipal clerks must be available and plan for voters who were issued 
provisional ballots to come to their office in the days following the election to 
rehabilitate those ballots to have them counted.
This chapter is specific to the post-Election Day work of confirming that voters 
present photo ID so that the municipal board of canvassers knows if they should 
count or reject the ballots. For more detailed information on provisional voting in 
general, see Chapter 14.13: “Provisional Voting.”
Sec. 15.2.1: Deadlines to 
Rehabilitate Provisionals
In all elections except presidential elections, voters who were issued 
provisional ballots have until 4 p.m. on the Friday after Election Day to provide 
the required proof of identification to the municipal clerk. Wis. Stat. § 6.97(3)(b). 
For presidential elections, that deadline is not later than noon on the Friday 
after Election Day. Id., as amended by 2025 Wis. Act 214.
Sec. 15.2.2: Confirming 
Photo Identification
The municipal clerk should confirm the voter’s photo identification the same 
way a poll worker would do to check the voter into the poll book on Election Day. 
Wis. Stat. § 6.97(3)(b). If the voter appears to provide the required photo ID by the 
applicable deadline, the municipal clerk should update the Provisional Ballot 
Reporting Form (EL-123) accordingly.
Sec. 15.2.3: Notifying the MBOC
The municipal clerk should not open or count the provisional ballot.  That will 
be done by the MBOC at their public canvass meeting. Once the municipal 
clerk has confirmed photo ID and updated the EL-123, they must also notify the 
appropriate boards of canvassers responsible for canvassing the appropriate 
races. Id.
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 5
Chapter 15.3: Preparation for the 
Municipal Board of Canvassers 
(MBOC)
The Municipal Board of Canvassers meets after every election to canvass all 
ballots, regardless of whether there are municipal offices or referenda on the 
ballot. Wis. Stat. § 7.53.
The MBOC can meet on Election Night, if certain conditions are met. The 
information and procedures for it can be found in Sec. 14.27.2: “When Does the 
MBOC Meet?.”
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 6
Chapter 15.4: Reconciliation & 
Voter Participation Entry
This section of the manual addresses two of the many important tasks clerks 
must perform after an election: recording voter participation and completing 
election reconciliation.
Voter Participation Data consists of the records of who voted and registered 
to vote on Election Day, and state law requires municipal clerks to enter this 
information into the statewide voter registration list by certain deadlines.
Reconciliation is the statutorily required process where clerks validate that their 
election data is accurate before reporting that data to the Commission and to 
the public. See Sec. 15.4.5: “Election Reconciliation” on page 9.
Together, these two tasks provide the public with essential information about 
who participated in an election and how they chose to participate.
Sec. 15.4.1: Use the WisVote Manual for 
Instructions on Completing both Tasks
Municipal clerks enter voter participation data and complete reconciliation in in 
WisVote, and instructions on how to complete these tasks are found in Chapter 
5 of the WisVote manual.
Chapter 15.4 of this manual is only intended to generally describe each process 
and explain why it is important. Clerks should refer to the WisVote manual for 
detailed steps on how to complete this work.
Sec. 15.4.2: Considerations for 
Jurisdictions with Provider/Relier 
Relationships
Sometimes, a municipal clerk (a Relier) enters into an agreement with another 
clerk (a Provider) for the Provider to complete WisVote work on the Relier’s 
behalf. See Wis. Stat. § 6.33(5)(b). The Provider can be either a county clerk or 
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 7
another municipal clerk. Id. Reliers and Providers enter into a Memorandum of 
Understanding (MOU) that governs how the data entry and list maintenance 
work will be covered between them. The MOU should cover the specifics of voter 
participation data entry and reconciliation work.
Sec. 15.4.3: Legal Requirements 
for Post-Election Reporting
Both state and federal law require certain post-election reporting, and entering 
voter participation data and performing reconciliation confirms that the 
required data is reported accurately. Wis. Stat. §§ 6.275, 6.276, and 6.33(5)(a)3. 
See also Help America Vote Act of 2002 (HAVA) 52 U.S.C. 20922 and the 
Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act (UOCAVA) 52 U.S.C. 20301.
Numerous state and federal laws require documentation 
and reporting of election statistics:
 Ɋ Wis. Stat. § 6.275: Registration and voting statistics
 Ɋ Wis. Stat. § 6.276: Federal absentee voting statistics
 Ɋ Wis. Stat. § 6.36(1)(a): Official registration list
 Ɋ Wis. Stat. § 6.88: Voting and recording the absentee ballot
 Ɋ Wis. Stat. § 6.89: Absent electors list public
 Ɋ 52 U.S.C. § 20901-21145: Help America Vote Act
 Ɋ 52 U.S.C. § 20301-20311: Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act
Sec. 15.4.4: Recording 
Voter Participation
Wisconsin law requires that the name of each person who voted in an election 
is recorded within 30 days after the election. Wis. Stat. § 7.15(4). Recording 
participation lets voters know their vote was counted (via the MyVote Wisconsin 
website) and enhances election integrity by ensuring there is a person 
documented for each vote.
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 8
Prior to recording participation, municipalities must first ensure several 
preliminary tasks are complete and fully documented. These include:
1. Provisional ballots documented
2. Inspector statements completed
3. Recording all absentee ballots
4. Late registrations recorded
5. Election Day Registrations (EDRs) recorded
Once the necessary preliminary steps are complete, municipalities may record 
participation.
There are three ways clerks can record participation:
 Ɋ Manually selecting individual voter records in the poll book detail in WisVote
 Ɋ Scanning individual barcodes beside each voter’s name on the poll book
 Ɋ Uploading participation from a Badger Book e-poll book
The specific steps required to perform each process are found in the WisVote 
manual and the Badger Book manual.
Sec. 15.4.5: Election Reconciliation
The final process to validate election data and report municipal statistics is 
called Election Reconciliation. This process helps clerks ensure their election 
records are accurate before the information is made available to the public and 
reported to the federal government.
The Reconciliation process compares data found in canvass reporting, 
inspector statements, and WisVote. The data presented for review is:
1 Direct-Recording Electronic voting machine.
 Ɋ Votes cast by method  
(paper, optical scan, DRE1)
 Ɋ Total voters
 Ɋ Absentee voters and ballots 
(including military and  
overseas voters)
 Ɋ Provisional ballots
 Ɋ Total ballots
 Ɋ Total EDRs
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 9
The information recorded is presented in WisVote on a special Reconciliation 
page. This allows clerks to easily identify errors or omissions in reporting. If the 
canvass report, inspector statements, and WisVote records all match, then 
clerks can be assured that records were accurately recorded and complete the 
Reconciliation process. If the records do not match, clerks should investigate to 
determine the cause.
Figure 1: Example of Non-Matching Data
Mismatched figures do not necessarily indicate an error, but all mismatches 
should be investigated so the cause is determined and documented. For 
example, the number of total voters usually matches the number of total ballots. 
However, these numbers will not match if a voter signed the poll book and then 
elected not to complete a ballot. In this case, there should be a notation on the 
inspectors’ statement reflecting the situation. Clerks can make a notation in 
WisVote to explain the situation and complete Reconciliation.
Other common errors clerks experience include:
 Ɋ Absentee data mismatch caused by not entering absentee ballots 
received on Election Day into WisVote.
 Ɋ Not recording participation for a provisional ballot cured by the voter 
before the deadline.
 Ɋ A voter number was skipped, which will cause data mismatches.
 Ɋ Someone completed an Election Day Registration (EDR) but didn’t end up 
voting and participation was accidentally assigned to them.
Sometimes, determining the cause of a mismatch can prove challenging. In 
these cases, clerks should contact the Commission for assistance. Commission 
staff have experience with many unusual reconciliation scenarios and can often 
help to identify the root cause. The technical steps for the reconciliation process 
are described in Section 5.4 of the WisVote manual.
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 10
Chapter 15.5: Canvass 
Reporting System
The Canvass Reporting System (CRS) is the statewide database used by county  
clerks to report their official canvass results to the Commission. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(5)(a) 
requires county clerks to submit certified election results for all federal and state 
contests in an election to the Commission within specific statutory timelines. The 
CRS ensures that results are submitted consistently, accurately, and in a format 
that supports statewide aggregation, certification, and public reporting.
Chapter 15.5 is introductory. County clerks can find detailed steps on using the 
CRS in the CRS Manual, which is available on ElectEd.
Sec. 15.5.1: Purpose of the System
The Canvass Reporting System serves as the centralized location 
for all official county-level canvass results. It is designed to:
 Ɋ Provide a uniform method for reporting canvass results after each election 
through manual entry or file upload.
 Ɋ Support clerks in submitting results electronically.
 Ɋ Enable verification processes that reduce the risk of errors in reported results.
 Ɋ Produce the required Certification of Board of Canvassers document that 
must be signed and delivered to the Commission.
This system streamlines the canvass process and ensures compliance with 
statutory requirements for timely delivery of certified election results.
Sec. 15.5.2: Statutory Requirements
Under Wis. Stat. § 7.60(5)(a), county clerks must deliver a signed Certification 
Report to the Commission within the deadlines established in law:
 Ɋ Within 9 days after each primary (except the Partisan Primary)
 Ɋ Within 10 days after the Partisan Primary and all other elections except the 
general election
 Ɋ Within 14 days after the general election
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 11
These deadlines ensure the Commission can complete the statewide canvass 
and begin the certification process in accordance with state law. Wis. Stat. 
§ 7.70(1)(a). The CRS supports clerks by generating the required Certification 
Report directly from the system.
Sec. 15.5.3: How Clerks Use the System
The CRS guides county clerks through a standard workflow to ensure accurate 
and complete reporting.
Core System Functions Include:
Pre-Election Review
Before Election Day, clerks can run pre-election reports within the system 
to identify and correct potential issues in their election setup in WisVote. 
Addressing these issues ahead of time helps ensure the post-election canvass 
process proceeds smoothly.
Post-Election Entry or Upload of Results
After the official county canvass is completed, clerks may enter results 
manually or upload results using files generated by their voting equipment. The 
system includes built-in validation tools that help clerks confirm the accuracy of 
their reported results.
Certification Report Generation
Once results have been verified, clerks can generate and print the Federal/State 
Office Certification Report directly from the system. This report must be signed 
and delivered to the Commission by the applicable statutory deadline.
Sec. 15.5.4: Additional Resources
A comprehensive, step-by-step guide is available in the CRS Manual, which 
can be found on ElectEd. Clerks are encouraged to reference the manual 
before each election cycle to ensure continued compliance and familiarity 
with system updates.
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 12
Chapter 15.6: County Boards 
of Canvassers (CBOC)
The County Board of Canvassers (CBOC) meets after every election to 
canvass all ballots, regardless of if there are county offices or referenda on 
the ballot. Wis. Stat. § 7.60.
Sec. 15.6.1: What does “Canvass 
the Returns” Mean?
The purpose of the canvass is to determine and certify that the person who 
received the greatest number of votes is declared elected. Wis. Stat. § 5.01(3)(a). 
Though statute does not specifically define the term, many courts have 
confirmed that the “canvass” is “purely ministerial” or “purely administrative.”2 
In other words, the purpose of the CBOC is not to examine the legitimacy of the 
election, it’s to ensure that the unofficial results accurately reflect the ballots 
that were cast by voters (the “returns”). Canvassers cannot delay or wait for a 
recount to perform their duties.3 A majority of the board of canvassers may act 
to complete their duties, even if one member is absent.4
Sec. 15.6.2: When does the CBOC Meet?
The CBOC either meets no later than 9 a.m. on the Tuesday after the election. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.60(3), except when a presidential contest is on the ballot. For 
presidential elections, the CBOC meets no later than noon the Saturday after 
the election. Id., as amended by 2025 Wis. Act 214.
The CBOC is a public meeting and must be noticed in accordance with 
Wisconsin’s open meetings laws. Wis. Stat. § 19.83(1).
2 State ex rel. Husting v. State Canvassers, 159 Wis. 216 (WI 1914); Hammond v. Bd. Of Canvassers, 2003 
WI APP 22 (Ct. Appeals D3).
3 State ex rel. Husting v. State Canvassers, 159 Wis. 216 (WI 1914).
4 Karker v. Board of Unified School District, 51 Wis. 2d 542 (W 1971).
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 13
Sec. 15.6.3: Who Serves on the CBOC?
The CBOC consists of the county clerk and two other qualified voters of the 
county. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(2). Political party county committees submit lists of 
candidates for the CBOC to the county clerk, and the clerk chooses the other 
two board members from those lists. Id. One member of the CBOC must 
belong to a political party other than the clerk’s. Id. If the county clerk position is 
vacant, or the county clerk is unavailable, the county clerk appoints a deputy to 
perform their canvassing duties instead. Id. If both the county clerk and deputy 
are unavailable, the county executive, or if there isn’t one, the chairperson 
of the county board of supervisors appoints another member to serve. Id. In 
Milwaukee, the county board of election commissioners serves as the CBOC.
No one may serve on the CBOC if they are a candidate at that election, 
except the county clerk, who may serve if they are running unopposed. Id.
The county canvass board members serve two-year terms, which commence 
on January 1 of each even-numbered year. Id. Those appointed to fill a vacancy 
fill the remainder of that original term. Id.
Sec. 15.6.4: Obtaining the Election 
Materials for the Canvass
The municipal clerks of each jurisdiction in the county arrange for all election 
materials to be delivered to the county clerk no later than 4:00 p.m. on the day 
following the election, and no later than 4:00 p.m. on the second day following 
the election for jurisdictions that use “central count” for absentee ballots (except 
presidential contests). Wis. Stat. § 7.51(5)(b). In presidential elections, municipal 
clerks must transmit election materials to the county clerk no later than 9 a.m. 
the Saturday following the election. Id., as amended by 2025 Wis. Act 214.
Best Practice: The county clerk should develop and utilize a chain 
of custody document to check off materials delivered from each 
municipality in the county. The chain of custody document should 
be signed by the person delivering the materials and by the person 
checking the materials in. See accompanying “Appendix 15.6.A: 
Municipal Returns Checklist” for materials obtained from each 
municipality.
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 14
Sec. 15.6.5: Preparing for 
the CBOC Meeting
Before the canvassing meeting, county staff should sort all materials, 
examine them for completeness, and document obvious errors, omissions, or 
missing materials.
Best Practice: Whenever possible, problems should be remedied 
before the meeting. For example, if a municipality has not delivered 
their materials by the statutory deadline, county staff should 
contact that municipality to remind them to transmit their materials 
so that the CBOC does not need to wait until the meeting convenes 
to take that step.
Before the meeting, at least two county staffers should proof the Canvass 
Report generated from the Canvass Reporting System (CRS) against the returns 
from each municipality. The proofing process should be documented, and any 
issues or errors preserved for the CBOC.
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 15
Sec. 15.6.6: Procedures for 
Conducting the CBOC Meeting
By the time the CBOC convenes, all election materials and returns should have 
been received from every municipality in the county, and the results from each 
reporting unit should have been recorded in CRS.
Step 1: Assign Someone to Take Accurate and Detailed Minutes
The meeting of the CBOC is subject to Wisconsin’s open meetings laws, so 
minutes must be taken of all proceedings. Nothing is too trivial to include in the 
minutes, and the minutes should document every decision made by the CBOC.
Step 2: Ensure All Materials are Present and Assign Tasks
 Ɋ Check materials against the “Appendix 15.6.A: Municipal Returns 
Checklist” to ensure all materials are present for all municipalities.
 Ɋ When assigning tasks, build in redundancy or assign tasks to pairs of 
individuals to ensure that returns and materials from all reporting units are 
inspected, reconciled, and the official results are properly documented for 
certification.
 Ɋ Process one reporting unit at a time.
Step 3: Review the Poll Lists (Comparing 
Number of Voters to Number of Votes)
The purpose of Step Three is to ensure that the total number of people who cast 
ballots equals the total number of ballots that were counted.
For each poll list (poll book) for each reporting unit, ensure the following:
 Ɋ Verify that the poll list certification has been completed. This will usually 
be printed on the cover page of the poll book.
 ɉ Is the last voter number listed?
 ɉ Is the page on which the last voter number appears indicated?
 ɉ Is the number of absentee voters indicated?
 Ɋ Has the number of voters whose provisional ballots were counted  
been added?
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 16
 Ɋ Verify that there weren’t more ballots cast than there are registered voters 
in each municipality (accounting for Election Day Registrations).
 Ɋ Verify there aren’t any major discrepancies between the number of voters 
who cast ballots and the results of specific races. Each of these specific 
anomalies below should be further investigated, as should any other 
aspect of the returns that seems unusual.
 ɉ Example: 25,000 people voted in the county, but the U.S. Senate race 
only garnered 13,000 votes for the whole county.
 ɉ Example: 25,000 people voted in the county, but the top race on the 
ballot (President or Governor) received comparatively fewer votes for 
the contest than expected for the turnout.
 ɉ Example: The undervote rate for top-of-the-ballot contests is 1% or higher.
 ɉ Example: The comparative vote totals between municipalities for a 
down ballot race (like county supervisor) has one race where the vote 
totals are out of the norm.
 Ɋ If the number of voters is more than the number of ballots cast:
 ɉ Every effort should be made to discover the reason for the discrepancy. 
For example, one possible reason would be a voter leaving the polling 
place after checking in but before casting their ballot.
 ɉ Consult the Inspectors’ Statement (EL-104) for an explanation.
 ɉ Regardless of the explanation (or lack thereof), record discrepancy  
in minutes.
 Ɋ If the number of ballots cast is more than the number of voters:
 ɉ This is a problem that must be further investigated.
 ɉ Check the Inspectors’ Statement for an explanation.
 ɉ If the discrepancy cannot be determined, contact the municipal clerk.
 ɉ If the municipal clerk has no explanation or explanation is not sufficient, 
the poll workers must be called in to either find the error or explain 
the discrepancy. This may require hand counting the ballots, whether 
Optical Scan or Paper Hand Count ballots, to verify the error is not in the 
number of ballots.
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 17
 ɉ If poll workers cannot find an error and the discrepancy cannot be 
explained, the draw down procedure is conducted by the poll workers. 
Conducting a draw down is always a last resort and should not be 
done if the discrepancy can be logically explained.
 ɉ Note: If the polling place had more than one reporting unit, and the 
overall total of ballots cast at the polling place is not more than the 
overall number of voters at the polling place, note this in minutes but do 
not draw down. (This likely indicates a number of voters were given the 
wrong ballot.)
Note: The number of votes cast should never exceed the number of voters.
Step 4: Proof Data Against the Original Results
If municipalities have prepared some kind of compilation of results, those 
results must be checked against the original results received from the LBOCs 
on Election Night.
Step 5: Review Write-In Votes
The votes for federal, state, and county write-in candidates need not be listed 
on the canvass report by individual candidate, unless the write-in candidate 
has registered as such. Votes for unregistered write-in candidates should be 
recorded into one scattering column for each office. State- and federal-level 
write-in candidates will appear in a separate column on the applicable county 
canvass report from CRS. If the county has registered write-in candidates, the 
votes for those candidates should be recorded separately (unless they were 
entered into WisVote in which case they will appear on the CRS canvass report).
Votes attributed to eligible write-in candidates must be listed under the 
candidate’s name. The total number of votes that cannot be attributed to an 
eligible write-in candidate should be recorded in the scattering column.
Step 6: Review Inspectors’ Statements, 
Electronic Vote Records and Tally Sheets
Review the Tally Sheet (EL-105) or tabulator results tapes from each municipality 
for accuracy. Review results tapes for any adjustments made on the tapes and 
review the write-in tally sheets. If poll workers have added electronic votes and 
hand-count votes together, check their addition.
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 18
Ensure that the tamper-evident serial numbers from the voting equipment 
have been recorded and initialed by the Chief Election Inspectors on at least 10 
different Inspectors’ Statements (EL-104).
Step 7: Review Provisional Ballots
The municipal clerk will have notified the county clerk if there were provisional 
ballots issued in the municipality, and the provisional ballots themselves will 
have been counted or rejected by the MBOC.
The CBOC should take the following steps to 
check the work of provisional ballots:
1. Does the number of provisional ballots reported by the municipality 
match the total number of ballots that were counted and rejected?
2. For the ballots that were counted:
 ɉ Were the votes added to the affected candidates’ totals?
 ɉ Was the voter properly assigned a voter number and added to the 
poll book?
 ɉ Was all documentation preserved, including the carrier envelopes 
containing the provisional ballots?
3. For the ballots that were rejected:
 ɉ Does documentation show how many were rejected because they were 
not rehabilitated by the voter by the correct deadline?
 ɉ If provisional ballots were rejected for any other reason, is that decision 
documented in the MBOC minutes?
 ɉ Can the CBOC confirm that the affected candidates’ totals do not 
accidentally include rejected provisional ballots?
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 19
Sec. 15.6.7: What If There are 
Issues with the MBOC Returns 
or Documentation?
Sometimes, when the CBOC convenes, they may realize they are missing 
documents or information from one or more municipality that prevents them 
from canvassing the returns.
If Returns or Documentation are Missing
If returns have not been received from any jurisdiction in the county by the 
time the CBOC convenes, state law directs the District Attorney of the county to 
immediately initiate an enforcement action under Wis. Stat. § 5.07 to obtain the 
returns. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(3), as amended by 2025 Wis. Act 214.
Best Practice: Prior to the convening of the CBOC, the county clerk 
should put the District Attorney on notice if any returns are missing 
so that the Wis. Stat. § 5.07 action can be immediately initiated if the 
CBOC still doesn’t have the returns by the time they begin.
If Returns are Informal or Defective
If the returns are “so informal or defective that the [CBOC] cannot intelligently 
canvass them,” the CBOC shall dispatch a messenger back to the MBOC. Id. 
The CBOC will have to make its own determination, recorded in the minutes, of 
whether any municipal returns are “so informal or defective” that they cannot 
be “intelligently” canvassed.
Best Practice: In today’s modern world, the CBOC is not required 
to literally send a person to the municipality, though they should 
do so as a last resort if all other methods of communication fail. 
Contact by phone should be the first resort, along with email, fax, or 
any other method likely to reach the municipality. If the CBOC still 
cannot get ahold of the municipal clerk, they should also contact 
the municipality’s governing body as well as any other source likely 
to get them in contact with the municipal clerk.
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 20
If the CBOC sends returns back to the MBOC under this standard, they must 
provide “written specifications” of the informalities or defects, and must also 
“command” the MBOC to immediately complete the returns or remedy the 
defects in the manner required. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(3).
If sending back the returns is necessary, the CBOC may adjourn not longer 
than one day at a time nor more than two days total, except in a presidential 
election, where the CBOC may only adjourn to the extent permitted by the 
Commission. Id., as amended by 2025 Wis. Act 214.
Sec. 15.6.8: Completing the 
Canvass Statement
When all canvass steps are complete, and corrections are made (if any), the 
CBOC prepares the canvass statement in duplicate. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(4)(a). The 
canvass statement is completed on the Board of Canvassers Report (EL-106), 
which contains three sections.
Tabular Statement of Votes Cast
This section contains a detailed listing of the number of votes cast for each 
candidate in each ward, or combination of wards, for each federal, state 
and county office or referendum. Write-in votes are summed together in one 
scattering column for each office. Referenda results are reported by “yes” votes 
and “no” votes. There is no scattering column for referenda.
If any votes are rejected, the CBOC must specify the reasons in the minutes. 
Wis. Stat. § 7.60(4)(c).
Summary Statement
This section is a summary of the Tabular Statement of Votes Cast. Each 
summary statement states the total number of votes cast for each office, the 
names of all ballot candidates for each office, the number of votes cast for 
each candidate in each office, the number of scattering votes cast in each 
office, and the number of votes cast for and against any question submitted as 
a referendum. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(4)(a).
Certification of the Board of Canvassers
This is the portion of the canvass that is signed. It must be signed by all three 
members of the CBOC. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(4)(d).
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 21
Sec. 15.6.9: Breaking a Tie 
in a County Contest
If there are any tie votes in county offices, the canvassers break the tie.  
Wis. Stat. § 5.01(4)(a). Statute directs that this be done “by lot,” which can 
include flipping a coin, drawing names out of a hat, or by anything that will 
determine a random result. Id. If the tie occurs during a primary and only one 
candidate may advance, the tie is likewise broken by lots. Wis. Stat. § 5.01(4)(b). 
If all candidates in a tied contest are present, the candidates can draw the lots 
themselves. Wis. Stat. § 5.01(4)(c). If not all candidates are present, the CBOC 
shall break the tie. Id. There cannot be a tie for a referendum question — if both 
“yes” and “no” receive the equal number of votes, the question fails adoption. 
Wis. Stat. § 5.01(4)(d).
Sec. 15.6.10: Reporting Canvass Results
Immediately following the completion of the canvass, the CBOC must deliver 
or transmit to the Commission a certified copy of each Board of Canvassers 
Report for all state and federal races. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(5)(a). This shall be done by 
email immediately, and the original hard copies should be mailed.
Table 28: Deadlines to Report Canvass Results5
Election Type Deadline
Primary Election No later than 9 days after election
Partisan Primary Election No later than 10 days after election
General Election (Non-Presidential) No later than 14 days after election
Presidential General Election No later than 7 days after election
In addition, the CBOC must also transmit copies of the Board of Canvassers 
Report to the clerk of the technical college for technical college district offices, 
and to the county clerk having the largest portion of the population in the 
jurisdiction served by the judge for multijurisdictional judge contests.
5 Wis. Stat. § 7.60(5)(a)
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 22
Penalties for Untimely Transmission of Canvass Statements
If any county clerk fails or neglects to transmit the Board of Canvassers Report 
to the Commission, the Chair of the Commission may require them to do so 
immediately. Wis. Stat. § 7.70(1)(b). If the statement is still not received by the 
eighth day after a primary, the 8th day after a presidential election, or by the 
eleventh day after any other election, the Chair will notify the county clerk 
that the failure to transmit the canvass is a violation of law that will result in 
an immediate Commission enforcement action under Wis. Stat. §§ 5.05(1)(d), 
7.70(1)(b). If the statement is still not received within one day of that notice, the 
Commission will initiate that enforcement action. Wis. Stat. § 7.70(1)(b).
Sec. 15.6.11: Canvass Retention
One copy of the official canvass for county offices must be retained by the 
county clerk. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(5)(b). The canvass statement must be kept for 
10 years after the election for which it was prepared. Wis. Stat. § 7.23(1)(i).
Sec. 15.6.12: What if the CBOC Discovers 
a Mistake before the Deadline for the 
Chair to Certify the Election?
Though uncommon, it is possible that the CBOC could discover a “material 
mistake” in their canvass after adjourning. Wis. Stat. § 7.60(5)(b).
In such circumstances, the CBOC can petition the Commission to reopen the 
canvass, as long as they do so prior to the close of business on the day the 
Commission receives returns from the last county board of canvassers. Id. 
The Commission shall direct the canvass to be reopened and corrected if it 
determines “the public interest so requires.” Id. If the CBOC reconvenes, they 
must then transmit a certified corrected copy of the canvass statement to 
the Commission.

Chapter 15.7: Preparation for 
Commission Certification of 
Election Results
Following each statewide or federal election, the Wisconsin Elections 
Commission (“the Commission”) is responsible for certifying the official results 
for statewide, federal, and state legislative contests. Wis. Stat. § 7.70(3).
Sec. 15.7.1: What is “certification”?
Broadly speaking, “certification” is the process by which the Chairperson of 
the Commission completes the state-level canvass for the offices for which 
the Commission is the filing officer.6 See generally, Wis. Stat. § 7.70. After state 
certification, the unofficial results for these races become official.
Each of Wisconsin’s 72 counties conducts a county canvass of election results 
through its county board of canvassers. For more information about the CBOC, 
see Chapter 15.6: “County Boards of Canvassers (CBOC)” on page 13 After 
completing the canvass, counties submit their official results for state and 
federal offices to the Commission using the Canvass Reporting System (CRS). 
For more information about the CRS, see Chapter 15.5: “Canvass Reporting 
System” on page 11. This is the statewide reporting system used by all 
counties to enter and transmit certified vote totals to the Commission.
Sec. 15.7.2: When does the Commission 
Certify the Election?
The Chair of the Commission always completes the certification of election 
results in a publicly noticed meeting. The deadlines for Commission certification 
are set by state law. Wis. Stat. § 7.70(3)(a).
6 President and vice-president, governor, lieutenant governor, secretary of state, state treasurer, 
attorney general, state superintendent, U.S. senator, representative in Congress, state legislature, 
supreme court justice, court of appeals judge, circuit court judge, metropolitan sewerage commission, 
and statewide referenda. Wis. Stat. § 7.70(3)(d).
First Edition, June 2026 Post-Election Activities 15 – 25
